title: Wasted Wind and Solar Power Could Run Factories and Data Centers | OilPrice.com
description:
As the scale and reach of variable renewable energies expand around the world, more and more clean energy is being produced.
However, more and more of that clean energy is also going to waste.
But a new MIT study asks: what if that excess clean energy could be used to power some of the United States’ dirtiest sectors?
It would therefore be most efficient to divert that excess energy production to where it actually is needed – manufacturing and data centers.
It’s also an issue of being able to reliably model when and where that excess energy will be available in order to design systems around it.
text:
As the scale and reach of variable renewable energies expand around the world, more and more clean energy is being produced. However, more and more of that clean energy is also going to waste. In order to balance energy supply and demand, electric utilities rely on a process called curtailment, where they deliberately reduce the amount of energy produced by solar and wind farms in order to not overwhelm the energy grid. But a new MIT study asks: what if that excess clean energy could be used to power some of the United States’ dirtiest sectors?

While solar and wind energies are essential to achieving decarbonization goals and avoiding the worst impacts of climate change, their intermittency introduces new challenges and complexity to energy markets and infrastructure. The production patterns of these renewable energy sources are often at odds with demand patterns. The sun is setting on solar farms just as families are returning home and firing up their appliances. And during the day, when production is at its highest, demand slumps.

One of the most key approaches to this problem is energy storage, which can hold onto excess energy produced at peak hours and release it back onto the grid when demand outstrips supply. However, the energy storage sector is still in its infancy and battery storage can only hold onto energy for about four hours at a time. Long-term energy solutions, while very promising, are still in research and development stages and are not commercially viable or scalable.

It would therefore be most efficient to divert that excess energy production to where it actually is needed – manufacturing and data centers. The idea of diverting clean energy to where it’s needed isn’t new, but it has lacked the infrastructure and data to reliably be carried out. “The key challenge is how to harness that extra energy, sending it to places where demand is high, or storing it for still and sunless days,” reads a Zenobe report.

“At present, we don’t have sufficient network infrastructure to achieve this. This means that high levels of renewable generation put pressure on the grid, and sometimes even risk overloading it. At such times, the ESO safeguards the grid by paying generators to stop producing electricity,” Zenobe goes on to say. “This drives up bills for consumers, and wastes precious renewable energy.”

But it’s not just an issue of infrastructure. It’s also an issue of being able to reliably model when and where that excess energy will be available in order to design systems around it. A new study from MIT and Georgia Tech, published this week in the energy-focused scientific journal Joule, seeks to answer that need. The study models the future of wind and solar growth the the United States. Specifically, the study looks at the amount of excess energy to be produced as the domestic renewable sector continues to develop, and the patterns of when that excess energy will be produced.

“The researchers’ model reveals when excess electricity will likely be available,” explains a recent article from MIT News. “It shows that periods of excess will generally occur in the spring and fall and usually persist for several hours at a time.”

These models are based on a point in the future clean energy development wherein 80 percent of the electricity supplied to United States consumers is coming from solar and wind power. At that time, their model projects that the renewable energy sector will produce 10 percent more energy than the grid can use or store. This means that energy will go to waste if we don’t plan accordingly.

“In this era where there is a need for additional electricity, where demands are growing to support data centers and other end users, we wanted to understand what this excess electricity will potentially look like so we can design processes to benefit from these excesses,” says Jessika Trancik, a professor in the MIT Institute of Data Systems and Society (IDSS) and a senior author of this study. “Our work can help technology developers and other stakeholders plan for future infrastructure needs and start innovating toward these technologies now.”

text:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s pause on environmental permits for data center projects ended less than two weeks after he lost reelection to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who had predicted he would lift it after the election.

The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) had resumed issuing permits by November 16, after Abbott’s office told the agency that the state’s grid operator had finished gathering information on potential impacts on nearby communities.

Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa had said for months that this would happen.

Read More on News

"Greg Abbott invited data centers into Texas when he signed into law House Bill 2712 in 2015 to give hyperscale data centers 20-year tax breaks," her campaign website reads. "A temporary moratorium is a scam because Abbott will likely lift it on November 4th, right after the election. The only way Texans are protected is when real laws are passed."

Abbott's office sent its notice to the TCEQ on November 13, 10 days after the election and nine days after the date Hinojosa had predicted.

Newsweek reached out to Abbott's office and Hinojosa's transition team for comment via email on Friday.

What Abbott Did

Abbott signed House Bill 2712 in 2015, creating a 20-year sales and use tax exemption on eligible purchases for qualifying large data center projects. Last November, at an event with Google executives announcing a $40 billion investment in the state, he called Texas the "epicenter of AI development."

His tone shifted this summer, as rural communities pushed back against projects that critics said could strain the power grid and local water supplies.

At a June 30 campaign stop in Bullard, Abbott called for prohibiting AI data centers in rural Texas neighborhoods and said, "We must eliminate the tax break they are getting."

In August, Abbott asked the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) and state electricity regulators to audit every data center seeking a grid connection, looking at tax incentives, power and water use and neighborhood impacts. He paused approvals to power up new large data centers.

On September 21, he went further and wrote to the TCEQ, which handles air pollution permits for facilities and stormwater permits for construction sites. "Until they do, TCEQ will issue no permits sought by data center projects," Abbott said in announcing the directive, referring to the reviews by ERCOT and the Texas Water Development Board.

The pause leaked. In October, the advocacy groups Public Citizen and FracTracker Alliance found that some data center construction permits had cleared through the agency's automated filing system despite the order. The TCEQ then suspended 17 construction approvals, shut the electronic system down and required paper applications for staff review.

On November 5, two days after the election, ERCOT told the Public Utility Commission it had received responses from 433 of 465 loads, or 93 percent. ERCOT is aiming to publish its full findings on December 10, and regulators plan to discuss them at a December 17 meeting.

The permits started moving anyway. TCEQ spokesperson Laura Lopez said the agency "has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations."

One of the first approvals after the freeze was an air permit for a gas-fired power plant serving SpaceX’s proposed $24 billion data center project at Starbase in the Rio Grande Valley, according to Politico. The project includes a dedicated gas-fired power plant with 35 turbines producing about 750 megawatts.

Kathryn Guerra of Public Citizen said TCEQ leadership had "begun unilaterally issuing data center permits" without sharing ERCOT's results, and the group called on the agency's commissioners to resign. Sam Law of FracTracker Alliance called for "a true moratorium on data center development."

Wall Street noticed too. Analysts at the investment firm TD Cowen wrote that "Abbott's lame-duck-permitting push" would likely harden demands from Democrats that Hinojosa take a firm stand, lowering the odds of a near-term deal between her and developers.

What Hinojosa Says She Will Do

Hinojosa's campaign called for an immediate moratorium on new data center approvals, lasting "until the legislature can meet to put in place real protections," and a special session to repeal what her website calls "giant tax giveaways." In one campaign video, she burned a copy of the tax break law.

At a July press conference, she said data centers were "guzzling up all our water, guzzling up all our electricity" while residents had no say. "That is the Wild West of data centers that Greg Abbott has created in Texas," she said.

Speaking to KTAB News before the election, she said her moratorium would apply to "any new permits."

"I would have a moratorium or ban in place until we pass those laws that protect Texans and give them a seat at the table again to decide if and how data centers come into their communities," she said.

The legislation she wants would require licensed union labor on projects, bar nondisclosure agreements, make developers show households won't pay more for power or water, end subsidies and give communities a voice on where facilities go.

Since winning, she has worked to reassure business. "It is not that I hate data centers. I hate the way they are taking advantage of Texas, and that stops when I'm governor," she told CNN.

She told Houston's ABC13 that Texas has "always been a pro-business state," but that "what changes now with me as governor is it has to be a partnership that benefits Texans." On Fox News, she told Bret Baier she looked forward to working with Elon Musk as long as it benefited Texans. Musk spent about $224 million on Texas political efforts this cycle, including about $212 million backing Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, according to The New York Times.

The calendar works against her in the short term. The Legislature convenes January 12, and Hinojosa takes office January 19. Bills passed this spring generally would not take effect until September 1, 2027.

She will have some tools on day one. As governor, she can rescind or replace Abbott's directives and designate the chairs of the utility commission and the TCEQ and nominate commissioners as seats become available, subject to Senate confirmation. And repealing the data center sales tax exemption already has support in both parties: Republican Senator Joan Huffman, who chairs the Senate Finance Committee, is one of 23 senators backing the repeal bill.

A National Backlash

Texas was one front in a fight that spread across the country this year. Critics have pointed to rising power bills, noise, water use and pollution from new gas generators, often for facilities that employ relatively few people once built.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, issued the nation's first statewide moratorium on new hyperscale data centers in July, and lawmakers in more than a dozen other states weighed similar limits.

On November 3, voters in 10 states decided 41 local ballot measures on data centers. In 40 of those votes, the outcome favored restrictions or opposed development, according to Ballotpedia. Harwood, North Dakota, was the sole pro-development result in that tally.

An NBC exit poll found 56 percent of voters said AI and data centers were a "crucial or major factor" in their vote for Congress. In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor's race after campaigning for a statewide pause.

The polling had pointed that way for months. A Gallup survey in March found 7 in 10 Americans opposed building an AI data center in their area.

Republicans Split, Trump Mocked Critics

The opposition cut into the Republican base. An Economist/YouGov poll from August found 47 percent of 2024 Trump voters opposed a new data center in their community, compared with 35 percent who supported one.

Several Republicans broke with the White House. Michigan Senate nominee Mike Rogers called for a one-year statewide moratorium on new construction.

President Donald Trump went the other direction. "Communities that don't take a data center, they're making a mistake," he said in an August 21 interview with his former lawyer Michael Cohen. Trump also told reporters that, "If a Republican's against the data center, that's OK with me."

On August 31, he posted on Truth Social: "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor." He warned against killing the "Golden Goose" and added: "China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement."

Tennessee Republican Representative Tim Burchett answered with a line of his own. "I guess I'm backwards and poor," he told MeidasTouch.

Vice President JD Vance tried to clarify the post, telling reporters that most of the backlash had come in places where a data center meant higher utility bills.

Weeks later he changed his pitch, suggesting companies pay communities a "dividend" to make their projects popular. Political scientist Cal Jillson told Newsweek the shift was unlikely to move voters before November.

In Texas, the window between the resumption of environmental permitting and Hinojosa’s inauguration is about two months. ERCOT is aiming to publish its full report December 10. Hinojosa takes the oath on January 19.

text:
Controlled environment agriculture greenhouse to lead ‘CEA’ research across southern U.S.

The Texas A&M University SystemBoard of Regents has approved construction to begin on anadvanced greenhouse facility at theTexas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension Center at Dallas.

The 7,700-square-foot facility will boast technologies that can lead the rapidly emerging field of controlled environment agriculture, or CEA — the production of food in enclosed spaces using technologies that can precisely adjust the conditions within.

“The new greenhouse facility will serve as a critical research tool that will support impactful controlled environment agriculture programs to benefit producers throughout the southern U.S., especially for hot climates,” saidG. Cliff Lamb, director ofTexas A&M AgriLife Research. “It is a powerful resource in our agency’s mission to advance leading-edge discoveries and innovation, sustainable production systems, economic strength and healthy living.”

Advancing urban technologies and next steps

Controlled environment agriculture systems include greenhouses, hoop houses, hydroponics, aquaponics and other systems that employ tools for controlling light, temperature and a host of other production conditions.

The Texas A&M AgriLife center at Dallas is the sole urban center among the13 Texas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension Centers administered by AgriLife Research. Researchers at Dallas plan for the new greenhouse facility to enable solutions for sustainable production of nutritious foods within suburban and urban areas, including food deserts. They said the facility can also become a working example of food production, reconnecting urban populations to the food they consume.

text:
404 U.S. facilities turn food waste into biogas for renewable energy. Recycling more food waste could provide energy for 1.5 million additional households.

WASHINGTON, DC, UNITED STATES, November 27, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — As Americans prepare Thanksgiving meals, stock their refrigerators and eventually clear their plates, much of the food that goes uneaten will end up discarded. But food that can’t be eaten doesn’t have to go to waste entirely. Across the country, biogas capture facilities are recycling discarded food into renewable energy ─ and new research from the American Biogas Council (ABC) finds that the opportunity to do more is enormous.

Food waste naturally produces biogas when the microorganisms in it break down the organic material. Biogas systems capture all the biogas to keep it from going into the air and use it to generate renewable electricity and heat, or be processed into renewable natural gas (RNG).

ABC’s research team reports 404 operating facilities across 48 states that produce biogas from food waste. About 200 of these facilities operate at farms and wastewater treatment plants and combine food waste with manure or wastewater to capture biogas. Another 204 facilities make use of food waste alone, capturing approximately 36 billion cubic feet of biogas annually, and representing nearly $3 billion in capital investment.

ABC’s expanded research this year uncovered projects not previously included in its inventory. The increase of 73% over last year’s count reflects a more complete picture of the industry.

“America is literally throwing away enough renewable energy to power millions of homes,” said Patrick Serfass, Executive Director of the American Biogas Council. “The technology to make energy from food waste is already operating, but the potential to turn more of what we routinely discard into a valuable domestic energy resource is enormous.”

The facilities identified by ABC handle food waste from food manufacturers, grocery stores, restaurants and other sources. Some capture energy from food and beverage manufacturing. Others process consumer and retail food waste, including food that spoils, is rejected or remains unsold.

Of the 204 food-waste-only facilities, 161 process pre-consumer food waste, primarily wastewater from food processing and beverage manufacturing. Another 43 facilities handle retail and consumer food waste, capturing approximately 8.2 billion cubic feet of biogas annually.

Most facilities use their biogas to generate electricity and heat. In fact, 164 food-waste-only facilities produce power, heat or both. Another 38 upgrade biogas into RNG.

Food-waste biogas projects are getting larger and attracting more investment. The 42 facilities that have come online since 2020 account for 32% of the sector’s annual biogas production and 45% of its total investment. On average, these newer projects capture nearly twice as much biogas as earlier projects and cost about three times as much to build.

The momentum continued in 2025, when seven new food-waste projects came online, all of which produce RNG. Together, they added more than twice the biogas capture capacity of any other year since 2020.

The potential to expand food-waste energy recovery is substantial. ABC estimates that if all 70 million tons of discarded food generated in the United States in 2024 were processed through anaerobic digestion, it could produce approximately 181 billion cubic feet of additional biogas annually—roughly five times the amount currently captured by the country’s dedicated food-waste biogas facilities. That additional biogas represents approximately 113 million MMBtu of energy, enough to meet the annual energy needs of approximately 1.5 million U.S. households.

This holiday season, as Americans think about what happens to the food left behind, there’s another part of the story worth knowing: some of it can help produce the energy we use every day.

Explore the ABC’s Food Waste Fast Facts, additional graphs, biogas project profiles, and more in the American Biogas Council Newsroom.

About the American Biogas Council

The American Biogas Council is the voice of the U.S. biogas industry, representing all companies working to recycle organic waste into clean, locally made energy and fertilizer. Biogas capture systems recycle waste, food scraps, manure, and wastewater, keeping communities safe and clean, and supporting local economies. The ABC’s mission is to maximize the economic and environmental benefits of biogas while advancing sustainable solutions for energy, agriculture, and waste management. Learn more at AmericanBiogasCouncil.org, on X @ambiogascouncil, Facebook, and LinkedIn.

Alabama Power has filed with state regulators to cut customer rates by about $160 million in 2027, a reduction the utility says will show up automatically on bills starting in January.
Alabama Power filed the request with the Alabama Public Service Commission, as The Cullman Tribune reported, and the lower rate is set to kick in automatically with January 2027 bills without customers needing to enroll in any program or download an app.
al.com confirmed the $160 million filing with the commission, and the reduction itself runs through a formula called Rate Stabilization and Equalization, or Rate RSE, which the Alabama Public Service Commission established.

text:
Alabama Power has filed with state regulators to cut customer rates by about $160 million in 2027, a reduction the utility says will show up automatically on bills starting in January. The company says the savings trace mainly to new revenue expected from large data centers signing onto its grid — not a one-time credit, but a lower per-unit price for electricity that customers won't need to sign up for.

How the Numbers Break Down for Alabama Homes

According to Alabama Power, a home using 1,000 kilowatt-hours a month would save more than $50 a year compared with current rates at the same usage level, which works out to roughly $4 a month. Households using less power would see smaller savings — about $40 a year for a home at 750 kilowatt-hours monthly — while a heavier-use home at 2,000 kilowatt-hours would save about $106 a year, the utility says. Those examples apply to homes, not businesses, and a household that uses more electricity could still end up with a higher bill overall despite the lower rate, since usage still drives the total. Alabama Power filed the request with the Alabama Public Service Commission, as The Cullman Tribune reported, and the lower rate is set to kick in automatically with January 2027 bills without customers needing to enroll in any program or download an app.

The company frames increased 2027 revenue from agreements with large-load data centers as the primary reason for the reduction, saying those customers must pay the full cost of serving their own energy needs and also contribute toward the cost of the power system already in place. al.com confirmed the $160 million filing with the commission, and the reduction itself runs through a formula called Rate Stabilization and Equalization, or Rate RSE, which the Alabama Public Service Commission established. Alabama Power says the portion of the rate cut through Rate RSE is set to stay at or below its new lower level through 2028.

A Tax Credit Dispute Clouds the Data-Center Story

Not everyone agrees the data-center contracts are doing the heavy lifting. An Energy Alabama director argued there would be no cut at all without a roughly $180 million drop in the company's tax bill, which Alabama Power ties to nuclear tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act, according to the Alabama Reflector. That outlet also reported a slightly different framing of the typical savings, estimating about $50 a year, or about $4 a month, for a household using roughly 1,000 kilowatt-hours — in the same range as Alabama Power's own estimate but phrased without the “more than” qualifier.

State lawmakers have been quick to take credit for the cut. Sen. Garlan Gudger said Senate Bill 270, sponsored by Sen. Lance Bell, made the reduction possible, though he also acknowledged the bill strengthened customer protections and made them state law without itself creating revenue from past contracts. The bill passed the Alabama Senate 30-0 in March 2026 and cleared a House amendment 33-0 in April on Gudger's motion before taking effect October 1. It applies to qualifying data centers expected to need at least 150 megawatts at peak demand, and it requires the state commission to review those contracts for terms expected to cover added service costs over the life of a deal and benefit other customers — though the law itself sets neither a rate-cut order nor a specific date for one.

Regulators Tighten Review Timelines on Data-Center Deals

The Alabama Public Service Commission issued an order in October reviewing large data-center contracts under a rate policy first approved in 1996, extending the original 10-day review window to as much as 90 days. A contract can still be deemed approved if the commission does not vote within that 90-day span, and certain contract details, including pricing analyses, remain confidential. The commission's earlier reviews considered added costs and potential benefits for other customers, and lower costs for the broader customer base remain one possible upside of the data-center agreements.

Alabama Power has also asked regulators, in filings under docket U-5504, for authority to treat some large customers' charges as an accounting reserve meant to protect other ratepayers if a data-center project fails to meet its financial obligations. The company says this changes how charges are recorded rather than whether cash moves into a separate account, and that reserve amounts would not immediately help lower rates while the reserve builds. Alabama Power says it would begin releasing the reserve over time once most of the associated infrastructure is in service and protections exceed the remaining estimated risk. Energy Alabama has said it supports the proposal's underlying goal but wants more information about how defaults would be handled.

Open Questions the Filings Don't Yet Answer

Gudger has said the January rate calculation assumes the commission will authorize that accounting request, but The Cullman Tribune reported it has not obtained the supporting calculations needed to verify that assumption or its financial effect. The available records establish a link between data-center revenue and the proposed savings, but they do not establish exactly how much of the $160 million reduction is specifically attributable to Senate Bill 270 itself.

Alabama Power has also proposed extending its pause on annual-rate-formula increases through 2028, separate from a newer measure, House Bill 475, that bars increases before January 1, 2029 to retail base rates in effect as of October 1, 2026 — though that law does not freeze every individual charge on a customer's bill. As of November 24, the commission's public docket listed the November 20 filings as still pending. The commission has scheduled an informal review for December 8 at 9 a.m. in Room 900 of the RSA Union Building in Montgomery.

text:
VinFast says it is holding to electric vehicles in North America while other carmakers pull back. The company points to an October agreement with NexMove to bring its electric buses to US transit operators, three new US dealerships and a net-zero target for 2040.

The release, as issued by VinFast

An electric bus partnership in the U.S. and expanded sales and service options for drivers show how VinFast is putting its electric mobility strategy into practice. The company’s published climate roadmap outlines how it plans to reduce emissions as the business grows.

IRVINE, Calif., Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — While some automakers have scaled back their North American EV ambitions, VinFast continues to view electric vehicles as essential to addressing climate change. In the U.S. and Canada, the company is focused on making EVs easier to purchase, charge and service while helping customers understand operating costs. Its broader strategy centers on building a network of vehicles, charging infrastructure and services that can support more drivers and fleets over time.

One of the latest steps came on October 6, 2026, when VinFast announced an initial agreement with NexMove at the APTA TRANSform & EXPO in Chicago to bring its electric buses to U.S. customers. NexMove, a joint venture between Transportation Management Services and Zeem Solutions, plans to bundle buses, charging, maintenance and operations in a single agreement. It intends to offer a 97% uptime service-level commitment, with certified bus deliveries expected to begin in the first quarter of 2028. The announcement followed VinFast’s September 2026 franchise agreements for three U.S. dealerships in California and Pennsylvania.

Making electric mobility practical for fleets and drivers

For a transit agency, introducing electric buses requires decisions about depot charging, maintenance schedules and daily vehicle availability. NexMove’s proposed service brings these elements together into one agreement. Ahead of certified deliveries, NexMove plans to place demonstration buses at Zeem’s charging depots, where transit agencies and fleet operators can evaluate the vehicles firsthand. The demonstration units are intended for evaluation, with certified vehicles to follow on the planned delivery schedule.

VinFast’s buses combine camera- and radar-based driver assistance, fast charging capabilities, lithium iron phosphate batteries and corrosion protection. The company reported that approximately 2,000 of its electric buses were operating in Vietnam at the time of the announcement. VinFast’s experience in the market spans manufacturing, operations and maintenance, giving it firsthand knowledge of the demands fleet operators face when vehicles are in daily service.

“Bringing VinFast electric buses to the United States marks an important next step in our long-term commitment to this market,” said Brian Finnerty, CEO of VinFast North America.

For households, the questions are more personal: How much will it cost to charge a vehicle each month? Where can it be serviced? What options are available at a price the buyer can afford? The franchise agreements in Redondo Beach and Tustin, California, and Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, expand access to sales and after-sales service. The company’s U.S. certified pre-owned program gives buyers another option when weighing the upfront cost of an EV.

In Canada, VinFast offers a 10-year or 200,000-kilometre limited new-vehicle warranty on the VF 8, whichever comes first. Its online energy-cost calculator allows shoppers to compare estimated EV charging costs with the fueling costs of a gasoline vehicle over their expected mileage and ownership period. The comparison gives buyers a clearer picture of how an EV could fit their driving habits and household budget.

Annual EV charging costs can be 50% or more below gasoline fueling costs, depending on electricity rates, whether drivers charge at home or use public stations, driving habits, and vehicle efficiency. Coltura’s Q3 2024 analysis estimated that U.S. EV drivers saved an average of 7.4 cents per mile on fuel. At 1,200 miles a month, that works out to about $90 a month, or nearly $1,100 a year if the same per-mile savings hold.

Why a long-term climate commitment matters as markets change

VinFast announced its transition to all-electric vehicle production at CES in Las Vegas in 2022. Just over two years later, it became Vietnam’s best-selling vehicle brand in 2024, according to Vingroup’s annual report. Its expansion into North America brings a different set of considerations, including where to build out sales and service operations, how to support charging infrastructure and how to help commercial customers integrate electric vehicles into their existing operations.

Incentives, regulations and customer demand can change while a factory upgrade or charging project is still in development. VinFast’s 2040 net-zero goal provides a long-term framework for investments that take years to plan and implement. For example, the timing of an equipment replacement affects when a plant can shift more of its operations to electricity. The source of that electricity then affects the emissions associated with running the equipment. Decisions about materials and suppliers have a similar bearing on emissions across the value chain.

VinFast’s emissions inventory illustrates why those decisions matter as production grows. The company calculated that its emissions exceeded 1.12 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) in its 2022 base year. In a separate scenario, VinFast estimated that emissions could exceed 20 million metric tons of CO₂e if its existing production operations in Vietnam reached their maximum registered capacity, excluding future factories. The estimate illustrates the importance of factoring energy efficiency, electricity sourcing and supplier emissions into plans for higher production.

How the 3E Mission puts the 2040 pledge into practice

VinFast signed The Climate Pledge on August 17, 2022, and announced its participation in September 2022. It was the first Vietnamese enterprise to sign the pledge, an initiative co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism. The company’s stated goal is to reach net-zero emissions by 2040 across Scopes 1, 2 and 3, covering direct emissions from its operations, indirect emissions from purchased energy, and emissions across its wider value chain. Signatories commit to measuring and reporting greenhouse gas emissions regularly, reducing emissions and neutralizing the remainder.

In January 2025, VinFast’s chairwoman approved the company’s net-zero strategy through 2030, with a view to 2040. The strategy centers on the 3E Mission, which sets out how VinFast plans to change the equipment it uses, reduce the energy it needs and source cleaner power.

Electrification. VinFast plans to electrify equipment at company-owned production and business sites by 2030. The roadmap also includes expanding access to charging and developing battery energy storage.

Energy Saving. VinFast plans to introduce smart energy monitoring at manufacturing facilities by 2028. Monitoring production lines and major electricity-consuming equipment gives factory teams more detailed information on where energy is used and where operations can be made more efficient.

Energy Greening. VinFast aims to use 100% renewable electricity at all its plants by 2040. Its roadmap includes rooftop solar, battery storage to support renewable power use, and work with suppliers on lower-emission materials.

VinFast’s manufacturing complex in Hai Phong offers a practical example of what these priorities translate to on the factory floor. The company reported that upgrades to lighting and compressed-air systems, changes to how production robots operate, and other efficiency measures saved approximately 2.7 million kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2024, equivalent to an estimated 1,782 metric tons of CO₂e.

The company also said it initiated a 30-megawatt-peak rooftop solar project at the site. While the efficiency measures address how much electricity the plant needs, the solar project addresses the source of the electricity.

Against its 2022 baseline, VinFast aims to reduce Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 42% and Scope 3 emissions by 29% by 2030. By 2040, the strategy calls for cutting total emissions by at least 85% and neutralizing residual emissions of up to 15% through carbon offsetting mechanisms, which could include carbon credits. As VinFast serves more drivers and fleets, its reported emissions will show how far the company has progressed toward those targets across its operations, purchased energy and value chain.

The release, as issued by Wissen Research

SHERIDAN, Wyo., Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — The global lithium-ion battery market is valued at USD 209 billion in 2026 and is projected to reach USD 368.3 billion by 2031, an increase of roughly 76% over the forecast period (2026–2031), according to a new study by Wissen Research.

Three shifts explain the demand. The first is cheaper chemistry. The second is heavier vehicles: global electric truck sales exceeded 400,000 units in 2025, doubling year on year, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). The third is the grid: the IEA reports that 108 GW of battery storage capacity was added globally in 2025, roughly 40% more than in 2024. Together with passenger cars, where about one in four cars sold worldwide in 2025 was electric, they pushed global electric vehicle battery demand to around 1.2 TWh in 2025, up nearly 30% from the year before.

The constraint is cost and concentration, not demand. China accounted for more than 80% of global battery cell production in 2025, and battery pack prices there were 30% lower than in North America and 35% lower than in Europe. That gap is driving a wave of localization, and it is shaping the strategies of the industry’s leading manufacturers.

LFP Moves from Alternative to Default

The most important change inside the battery is chemistry. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries accounted for more than 55% of global electric vehicle battery deployment in 2025, up from nearly half in 2024, and for more than 90% of stationary storage installations, according to the IEA. The reason is cost. LFP battery packs were on average more than 40% cheaper per kilowatt-hour than nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) packs in 2025, and LFP prices fell by more than 15% in 2025 while NMC prices fell by less than 5%. LFP also avoids nickel and cobalt in the cathode, which removes exposure to those price swings and adds thermal stability.

NMC is not going away; it remains relevant where higher energy density matters. Newer chemistries are advancing alongside. Sodium-ion batteries are moving closer to production as a lower-cost option that performs better in cold climates, and solid-state batteries and silicon anodes are in development to address charging performance, material availability, and safety. The report notes that competitive differentiation increasingly depends on cost per kilowatt-hour, cycle life, safety, charging speed, and manufacturing yield.

Trucks and the Grid: Demand Moves Beyond Passenger Cars

Electric trucks are now the fastest-growing major vehicle category for battery demand. Global sales of electric heavy freight trucks rose from approximately 84,000 in 2024 to 230,000 in 2025, electric truck sales in Europe increased 40% to nearly 17,000 units, and one in four trucks sold in China in 2025 was electric. Battery-swap-capable trucks represented around 15% of China’s electric truck sales. Trucks accounted for approximately 8% of global EV battery deployment in 2025, up from less than 5% in 2024. The product response is visible: in September 2026, CATL launched its TECTRANS II commercial-vehicle battery at IAA Transportation 2026, supporting a driving range of up to 1,000 km and megawatt-level fast charging.

Battery energy storage systems (BESS) are the other growth engine. Utility-scale systems accounted for approximately 87 GW of the 108 GW added globally in 2025, and the price of battery storage has fallen by more than 90% between 2010 and 2025. About 90% of new battery storage projects in 2025 were for energy shifting, up from roughly 40% in 2015, meaning batteries are increasingly used to store electricity when it is cheap and release it when it is needed. In the United States, the Energy Information Administration estimates 18.2 GW of new utility battery installations in 2025. CATL reported a 30.4% share of global energy-storage battery shipments in 2025, showing how leading EV battery makers are diversifying beyond cars.

Localization Becomes the Strategy

With China’s cost advantage in place, manufacturers elsewhere are building closer to customers. Panasonic Energy started mass production at its Kansas factory in July 2025, targeting around 32 GWh of capacity in North America. India announced an incentive program of ₹18,100 crore aimed at 50 GWh of advanced lithium-ion cell production. And the latest agreements, covered below, tie European and North American battery capacity to Chinese and Korean cell makers, automakers, and energy-storage integrators.

What’s Fueling Growth in the Lithium-Ion Battery Market

Electric vehicle batteries: Global demand for EV batteries reached around 1.2 TWh in 2025, growing nearly 30% from the previous year.

Large-scale energy storage: U.S. utilities added 10.3 GW of new battery storage capacity in 2024, and utility-scale batteries are supporting grid stability as renewable generation grows.

Commercial transport electrification: Electric truck demand surged in 2024 and sales doubled in 2025, increasing battery consumption in freight transport.

Government support for local manufacturing: India’s ₹18,100 crore incentive program targets 50 GWh of advanced lithium-ion cell production and wider manufacturing investment.

Investment in large-scale production: Capacity is being added across Asia, Europe, and North America, including Panasonic Energy’s Kansas factory.

Renewable energy storage: Growing need to store renewable electricity is supporting demand for lithium-ion systems in utilities, commercial buildings, and data centers.

Challenges Facing the Lithium-Ion Battery Market

Cost and profitability are the central pressures. Regional pack-price gaps hurt manufacturers in North America and Europe, and many leading battery material producers have operated at a loss since 2023. Cathode active materials account for approximately 40–50% of NMC cell production costs and 25–30% for LFP, which makes materials pricing critical. Higher lithium prices in early 2026 are expected to affect production costs, investment decisions, and competitiveness, and the IEA’s Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2025 projected that announced mining projects could meet only around 60% of lithium requirements in 2035 under its stated-policies scenario.

Building new factories is hard. Battery manufacturers generally need production yields above 90% to compete, which makes defect reduction, automation, and process optimization essential, and a new plant requires large investment, qualified labor, stable raw material supply, and time to reach production efficiency. The collapse of a Swedish cell manufacturer shows how difficult it is to control defects while expanding several supply-chain stages at once. Supply-chain concentration, raw material price swings, recyclability requirements, and the localization of manufacturing remain the industry’s defining issues.

Recent Strategic Developments in the Lithium-Ion Battery Market

In September 2026, Gotion High-tech Co., Ltd. of China agreed to invest €1.1 billion for a 49% stake in Volkswagen’s Valencia battery plant in Spain. Volkswagen’s PowerCo also planned to invest €470 million in Gotion’s facilities in Slovakia and Morocco, strengthening European LFP battery manufacturing and supply-chain capabilities.

In September 2026, LG Energy Solution, Ltd. of South Korea signed a master supply agreement with Canadian energy storage integrator Eneon to supply North America-manufactured, LFP-based energy storage systems. The agreement supports regional battery supply chains, as the company plans to expand its global energy storage production capacity to more than 60 GWh.

In September 2026, Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL) of China launched its TECTRANS II commercial-vehicle battery at IAA Transportation 2026. The battery supports a maximum driving range of up to 1,000 km and megawatt-level fast charging, strengthening CATL’s portfolio for electric heavy-duty trucks and long-distance commercial transportation.

In August 2026, Samsung SDI Co., Ltd. of South Korea signed an agreement with General Motors to jointly develop next-generation prismatic battery cells for future electric vehicles. The company also acquired GM’s stake in their Indiana joint venture, making the facility its first wholly owned plant in North America and preparing it for energy storage battery production.

Three of the four announcements are about making batteries closer to customers, and the fourth is about the heaviest vehicles on the road.

Key Insights from Lithium-Ion Battery Market Analysis

LFP batteries held the largest share by battery type in 2025, supported by cost advantages, growing EV adoption, and extensive use in stationary storage. China continued to dominate LFP cathode material production and technical expertise.

Electric vehicles represented the largest application in 2025, accounting for more than 70% of global lithium-ion battery deployment according to the IEA, while battery storage accounted for more than 15%. Passenger cars and other light-duty vehicles represented more than 85% of EV battery deployment.

Asia-Pacific held the largest regional share in 2025. China produced nearly 75% of the world’s electric cars, accounted for approximately 85% of cathode active material production, and supplied more than 90% of anode active material for electric car batteries. Manufacturers headquartered in China, South Korea, and Japan supplied nearly all battery cells used worldwide.

The market is highly consolidated in cell manufacturing and key materials. CATL and BYD together accounted for more than 55% of global EV battery installations in 2025, while global manufacturing capacity exceeded 4 TWh at the end of 2025, increasing the importance of factory utilization, efficiency, and cost control. CATL reported RMB 72.2 billion in net profit for 2025, up 42% year on year.

Recycling is an emerging opportunity. The IEA reports that the market value of recycled battery metals grew nearly elevenfold between 2015 and 2023, and that recycling recovered more than 40% of available nickel and cobalt feedstock and around 20% of lithium feedstock in 2023. It expects end-of-life EV and stationary storage batteries to account for more than 90% of available recycling feedstock by 2050.

Regional Analysis and Growth Opportunities

Asia-Pacific leads the lithium-ion battery market, supported by developed supply chains, large-scale battery manufacturing, and substantial EV production and deployment. China remains the dominant global production hub. Stationary storage is also growing quickly in the region: the IEA reported that the volume of Australian electricity storage facilities increased almost ninefold in 2025 compared with 2024.

In the Middle East, installed battery capacity topped 3 GW, more than tripling from the previous year, with almost all installations in Saudi Arabia. In North America, U.S. utilities added 10.3 GW of battery storage in 2024, and Panasonic Energy’s Kansas factory, Samsung SDI’s Indiana plant, and LG Energy Solution’s North America-manufactured storage supply illustrate growing local production. In Europe, electric truck sales rose 40% in 2025, supported partly by stricter heavy-duty vehicle emissions standards, and Gotion and PowerCo’s investments are strengthening European LFP capacity. text:
404 U.S. facilities turn food waste into biogas for renewable energy. Recycling more food waste could provide energy for 1.5 million additional households.

WASHINGTON, DC, UNITED STATES, November 27, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — As Americans prepare Thanksgiving meals, stock their refrigerators and eventually clear their plates, much of the food that goes uneaten will end up discarded. But food that can’t be eaten doesn’t have to go to waste entirely. Across the country, biogas capture facilities are recycling discarded food into renewable energy ─ and new research from the American Biogas Council (ABC) finds that the opportunity to do more is enormous.

Food waste naturally produces biogas when the microorganisms in it break down the organic material. Biogas systems capture all the biogas to keep it from going into the air and use it to generate renewable electricity and heat, or be processed into renewable natural gas (RNG).

ABC’s research team reports 404 operating facilities across 48 states that produce biogas from food waste. About 200 of these facilities operate at farms and wastewater treatment plants and combine food waste with manure or wastewater to capture biogas. Another 204 facilities make use of food waste alone, capturing approximately 36 billion cubic feet of biogas annually, and representing nearly $3 billion in capital investment.

ABC’s expanded research this year uncovered projects not previously included in its inventory. The increase of 73% over last year’s count reflects a more complete picture of the industry.

“America is literally throwing away enough renewable energy to power millions of homes,” said Patrick Serfass, Executive Director of the American Biogas Council. “The technology to make energy from food waste is already operating, but the potential to turn more of what we routinely discard into a valuable domestic energy resource is enormous.”

The facilities identified by ABC handle food waste from food manufacturers, grocery stores, restaurants and other sources. Some capture energy from food and beverage manufacturing. Others process consumer and retail food waste, including food that spoils, is rejected or remains unsold.

Of the 204 food-waste-only facilities, 161 process pre-consumer food waste, primarily wastewater from food processing and beverage manufacturing. Another 43 facilities handle retail and consumer food waste, capturing approximately 8.2 billion cubic feet of biogas annually.

Most facilities use their biogas to generate electricity and heat. In fact, 164 food-waste-only facilities produce power, heat or both. Another 38 upgrade biogas into RNG.

Food-waste biogas projects are getting larger and attracting more investment. The 42 facilities that have come online since 2020 account for 32% of the sector’s annual biogas production and 45% of its total investment. On average, these newer projects capture nearly twice as much biogas as earlier projects and cost about three times as much to build.

The momentum continued in 2025, when seven new food-waste projects came online, all of which produce RNG. Together, they added more than twice the biogas capture capacity of any other year since 2020.

The potential to expand food-waste energy recovery is substantial. ABC estimates that if all 70 million tons of discarded food generated in the United States in 2024 were processed through anaerobic digestion, it could produce approximately 181 billion cubic feet of additional biogas annually—roughly five times the amount currently captured by the country’s dedicated food-waste biogas facilities. That additional biogas represents approximately 113 million MMBtu of energy, enough to meet the annual energy needs of approximately 1.5 million U.S. households.

This holiday season, as Americans think about what happens to the food left behind, there’s another part of the story worth knowing: some of it can help produce the energy we use every day.

Explore the ABC’s Food Waste Fast Facts, additional graphs, biogas project profiles, and more in the American Biogas Council Newsroom.

About the American Biogas Council

The American Biogas Council is the voice of the U.S. biogas industry, representing all companies working to recycle organic waste into clean, locally made energy and fertilizer. Biogas capture systems recycle waste, food scraps, manure, and wastewater, keeping communities safe and clean, and supporting local economies. The ABC’s mission is to maximize the economic and environmental benefits of biogas while advancing sustainable solutions for energy, agriculture, and waste management. Learn more at AmericanBiogasCouncil.org, on X @ambiogascouncil, Facebook, and LinkedIn.

title: LETTER: Environmental Organizations Send Letter to House of Representatives on BAAJA
description:
Today, environmental organizations sent a letter to the House of Representatives urging them to fix the damaging provisions of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 and to oppose any effort to rush it through the House without an open amendment process.
These policy improvements are desperately needed to remove key barriers to clean energy deployment – a foundational solution to the climate crisis.
More than two-thirds of Senate Democrats opposed final passage, including every single down-dais Democratic member of the Environment and Public Works Committee.
It is imperative that the House allow an open amendment process to fix provisions that lock in irreversible harms.

text:
Today, environmental organizations sent a letter to the House of Representatives urging them to fix the damaging provisions of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 and to oppose any effort to rush it through the House without an open amendment process.

The organizations that signed on include: League of Conservation Voters * National Wildlife Federation * Center for Earth, Energy & Democracy * Defenders of Wildlife * Earthjustice * Friends of the Earth * GreenLatinos * Natural Resources Defense Council * Ocean Defense Initiative * Oceana * Sierra Club * The Wilderness Society

Read the full letter below.

***

November 27, 2026

Dear Representative,

We write to urge you to insist on fixing the damaging provisions of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 and to oppose any effort to rush it through the House without an open amendment process. Specifically, we urge you to oppose bringing the bill to the floor under a closed rule, under suspension of the rules, or attached as-is to any must-pass legislation. As Leader Jeffries has made clear, House Democrats “will not rubber-stamp legislation without more constructive involvement with our Caucus.”

We appreciate the helpful reforms in the bill – positive policies related to transmission planning, permitting and cost allocation, interconnection, and grid improvements such as advanced transmission technologies and virtual power plants. These policy improvements are desperately needed to remove key barriers to clean energy deployment – a foundational solution to the climate crisis. Our organizations strongly support modernizing America’s electric grid, lowering energy costs for working families, and accelerating the clean energy buildout, which is why Congress must get permitting reform right, rather than rushing a sweeping, 500-plus-page rewrite of the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act through a closed rule.

This is generational legislation that was negotiated behind closed doors, without meaningful House input, and not a single hearing to examine or fully analyze the bill’s complex legal text and far-reaching consequences. More than two-thirds of Senate Democrats opposed final passage, including every single down-dais Democratic member of the Environment and Public Works Committee. It is imperative that the House allow an open amendment process to fix provisions that lock in irreversible harms.

As written, the bill undermines Tribal sovereignty and Treaty rights under the National Historic Preservation Act and the Clean Water Act; closes the courthouse doors so judges cannot halt harmful projects before the damage is done; creates “forever permit” loopholes that block future administrations from adopting health and environmental safeguards; accelerates development of data centers powered by natural gas; and weakens science-based protections for wildlife, public lands and waters, and Tribal lands. That is why concern over rushing this bill extends far beyond the environmental and conservation communities and we stand in solidarity with Tribal Nations, civil rights leaders including the NAACP and ACLU, state attorneys general and other state and local leaders, climate scientists, environmental justice organizations, historic preservationists, and public lands advocates, who are all calling on Congress to fix this bill.

Voters just delivered the largest wave election in a generation, giving House Democrats both the leverage and the responsibility to insist on regular order and, ultimately, legislation that strikes a better balance. Whether through a meaningful amendment process now or by negotiating a stronger bill in the next Congress, the House has the opportunity to deliver real permitting reform that lowers costs, reduces emissions, conserves natural resources, and protects the communities you represent. We urge you to fix the bill and oppose any vote on BAAJA unless it is amended to address the harmful provisions.

text:
Across the country, biogas capture facilities are recycling discarded food into renewable energy ─ and new research from the American Biogas Council (ABC) finds that the opportunity to do more is enormous.

404 U.S. facilities turn food waste into biogas for renewable energy. Recycling more food waste could provide energy for 1.5 million additional households.

WASHINGTON, DC, UNITED STATES, November 27, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- As Americans prepare Thanksgiving meals, stock their refrigerators and eventually clear their plates, much of the food that goes uneaten will end up discarded. But food that can't be eaten doesn't have to go to waste entirely. Across the country, biogas capture facilities are recycling discarded food into renewable energy ─ and new research from the American Biogas Council (ABC) finds that the opportunity to do more is enormous.

Food waste naturally produces biogas when the microorganisms in it break down the organic material. Biogas systems capture all the biogas to keep it from going into the air and use it to generate renewable electricity and heat, or be processed into renewable natural gas (RNG).

ABC's research team reports 404 operating facilities across 48 states that produce biogas from food waste. About 200 of these facilities operate at farms and wastewater treatment plants and combine food waste with manure or wastewater to capture biogas. Another 204 facilities make use of food waste alone, capturing approximately 36 billion cubic feet of biogas annually, and representing nearly $3 billion in capital investment.

ABC’s expanded research this year uncovered projects not previously included in its inventory. The increase of 73% over last year’s count reflects a more complete picture of the industry.

“America is literally throwing away enough renewable energy to power millions of homes,” said Patrick Serfass, Executive Director of the American Biogas Council. “The technology to make energy from food waste is already operating, but the potential to turn more of what we routinely discard into a valuable domestic energy resource is enormous.”

The facilities identified by ABC handle food waste from food manufacturers, grocery stores, restaurants and other sources. Some capture energy from food and beverage manufacturing. Others process consumer and retail food waste, including food that spoils, is rejected or remains unsold.

Of the 204 food-waste-only facilities, 161 process pre-consumer food waste, primarily wastewater from food processing and beverage manufacturing. Another 43 facilities handle retail and consumer food waste, capturing approximately 8.2 billion cubic feet of biogas annually.

Most facilities use their biogas to generate electricity and heat. In fact, 164 food-waste-only facilities produce power, heat or both. Another 38 upgrade biogas into RNG.

Food-waste biogas projects are getting larger and attracting more investment. The 42 facilities that have come online since 2020 account for 32% of the sector's annual biogas production and 45% of its total investment. On average, these newer projects capture nearly twice as much biogas as earlier projects and cost about three times as much to build.

The momentum continued in 2025, when seven new food-waste projects came online, all of which produce RNG. Together, they added more than twice the biogas capture capacity of any other year since 2020.

The potential to expand food-waste energy recovery is substantial. ABC estimates that if all 70 million tons of discarded food generated in the United States in 2024 were processed through anaerobic digestion, it could produce approximately 181 billion cubic feet of additional biogas annually—roughly five times the amount currently captured by the country's dedicated food-waste biogas facilities. That additional biogas represents approximately 113 million MMBtu of energy, enough to meet the annual energy needs of approximately 1.5 million U.S. households.

This holiday season, as Americans think about what happens to the food left behind, there's another part of the story worth knowing: some of it can help produce the energy we use every day.

Explore the ABC’s Food Waste Fast Facts, additional graphs, biogas project profiles, and more in the American Biogas Council Newsroom.

About the American Biogas Council

The American Biogas Council is the voice of the U.S. biogas industry, representing all companies working to recycle organic waste into clean, locally made energy and fertilizer. Biogas capture systems recycle waste, food scraps, manure, and wastewater, keeping communities safe and clean, and supporting local economies. The ABC’s mission is to maximize the economic and environmental benefits of biogas while advancing sustainable solutions for energy, agriculture, and waste management. Learn more at AmericanBiogasCouncil.org, on X @ambiogascouncil, Facebook, and LinkedIn.

title: West Virginia Challenges State Renewable Energy Credit Programs | Legal 500
description:
Key Takeaways West Virginia has filed three federal lawsuits challenging geographic restrictions on renewable energy credit (REC) eligibility in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and the District of Columbia.
A court decision requiring states to expand REC eligibility could impact REC supply and value, affecting the economics of renewable energy development.
The litigation raises broader questions about how states can promote local renewable energy development.
Other challenges have seen some success and led to changes in state renewable energy programs.
If West Virginia prevails in any of its challenges, states may be forced to rework REC eligibility in their programs and may seek alternative routes to incentivize in-state renewable energy development.
text:
On November 18, 2026, West Virginia filed separate lawsuits in the U.S. District Courts for the District of Columbia and the District of New Jersey challenging geographic restrictions on renewable energy credit (REC) eligibility under each state’s renewable portfolio standard (RPS) programs. The lawsuits follow a similar challenge West Virginia filed against Pennsylvania’s program in September 2026. These challenges pose a potential threat to aspects of each state’s RPS and REC programs, which could in turn impact REC markets and ratepayers.

Key Takeaways

West Virginia has filed three federal lawsuits challenging geographic restrictions on renewable energy credit (REC) eligibility in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and the District of Columbia.

The cases could have significant implications for renewable energy markets. A court decision requiring states to expand REC eligibility could impact REC supply and value, affecting the economics of renewable energy development.

The litigation raises broader questions about how states can promote local renewable energy development. Although courts have previously upheld certain geographic restrictions on REC eligibility, successful challenges could force states to rethink how they incentivize in-state renewable energy projects.

Analysis

West Virginia alleges that the programs violate the dormant Commerce Clause of the U.S. Constitution by restricting REC eligibility based on the location of generating facilities or their connections to specified electricity distribution or transmission systems. The D.C. and New Jersey lawsuits challenge restrictions on solar RECs (SRECs), while the Pennsylvania lawsuit also challenges restrictions on Tier II credits from energy resources such as waste coal, hydropower, and municipal solid waste. According to the complaints, these restrictions disadvantage out-of-state generators, including those in West Virginia, that would otherwise be able to sell RECs into these markets. West Virginia seeks declaratory and injunctive relief to remove the challenged restrictions and expand access to the affected REC markets.

Courts have previously rejected certain dormant Commerce Clause challenges to state RPS programs. In 2017, the Second Circuit upheld Connecticut’s program, which based REC eligibility on connections to the regional transmission grid rather than state borders. Other challenges have seen some success and led to changes in state renewable energy programs. For example, Massachusetts modified its geographic restrictions on long-term renewable energy contracts following litigation filed in 2010. The outcome of the current challenges will depend on the specifics of the challenged eligibility requirements, the justifications offered by the states, and the availability of less discriminatory alternatives.

The lawsuits follow several recent legal challenges to state energy and climate programs, including New York’s and Vermont’s Climate Superfund laws and California’s climate disclosure requirements. Separately, the U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments on October 5, 2026, in Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, concerning whether federal law precludes state-law climate damages claims brought by the City of Boulder and Boulder County, Colorado.

Renewable energy developers, REC buyers and sellers, utilities, and other market participants should monitor these cases. If West Virginia prevails in any of its challenges, states may be forced to rework REC eligibility in their programs and may seek alternative routes to incentivize in-state renewable energy development.

title: Permitting reform has driven a wedge into the U.S. climate movement - TribLIVE.com
description:
The U.S. climate movement is deeply divided over the permitting reform bill currently moving through Congress, fracturing the coalition that came together a few years ago to support former President Joe Biden’s signature climate law, the Inflation Reduction Act.
That’s despite it being sponsored by one of the Senate’s biggest climate hawks, Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island.
Climate advocates generally think permitting reform is needed to boost the nation’s clean energy build-out to meet growing energy demand and do it in a way that cuts energy-linked emissions.
This camp includes some prominent national and local environmental groups, tribal communities, current and former environmental regulators and more.
But it won’t be enough to overcome expected vetoes from Trump, dimming the chances of Democrats being able to pass their own version of permitting reform.
text:
The U.S. climate movement is deeply divided over the permitting reform bill currently moving through Congress, fracturing the coalition that came together a few years ago to support former President Joe Biden’s signature climate law, the Inflation Reduction Act.

Known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, the legislation would make it easier to build everything from data centers to fossil fuel pipelines to clean energy projects. After President Donald Trump endorsed the bill in early November, the Senate passed it. But with only a few weeks left in the congressional session, the bill’s fate in the House of Representatives is unclear.

Contributing to its uncertain fate are the opposing reactions from climate supporters. The broad coalition of Democratic lawmakers, companies, labor groups, scientists and advocates that backed the IRA is now splitting into different camps.

Just this week, more than 100 climate scientists and scholars published an open letter to the House urging members to vote no on the bill because it changes landmark environmental laws and would boost new fossil fuel projects. Meanwhile, three House Democrats who are vocal clean energy supporters — Sean Casten of Illinois and Mike Levin and Jared Huffman of California — came out against the bill’s current text. That’s despite it being sponsored by one of the Senate’s biggest climate hawks, Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island.

Different analyses of the bill have found enactment would lead to lower or higher power-sector emissions. But they more or less agree that it’s likely to help reduce household energy bills.

Climate advocates generally think permitting reform is needed to boost the nation’s clean energy build-out to meet growing energy demand and do it in a way that cuts energy-linked emissions. The current fault lines are over the potential for this bill to also boost fossil fuel and data center expansion while weakening tribal rights as well as laws that protect clean water, endangered species and historically important places.

Noah Kaufman, a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, said that on one hand, there are people who see permitting reform as “the single most important thing we can do for the climate.” This group includes a mix of renewable energy companies and labor organizations, as well as some climate and clean energy activists, Democratic lawmakers and former Biden administration climate leaders.

On the other side, Kaufman said, are people who see how this bill will alter environmental standards and boost fossil fuels and ask: How can you really call this a climate bill? This camp includes some prominent national and local environmental groups, tribal communities, current and former environmental regulators and more.

“I’m not really surprised that the clean energy industry and the environmental community aren’t on the same page in this particular case,” said Ethan Zindler, head of country and policy research at BloombergNEF. The clean energy industry’s top priority is “to maximize deployment of their own technologies,” he said, while environmental groups “will do a bit broader math, looking at overall plusses and minuses of any legislation.”

If this week is any indication, a growing number of groups have now done this calculation and decided to come out in opposition of the bill, at least in its current form. House Democrats are paying close attention.

“There’s a lot more going on in BAAJA than just streamlining the permitting system,” said Huffman in a video he recently posted on social media. “As drafted, this bill is the most sweeping rollback of environmental laws that we’ve ever seen.”

He wants the House to amend the bill — not vote on it in the current form, which is what House leadership is pushing for.

But it’s unclear whether there’s enough time in the lame-duck session to do that. “They’re fighting a ticking clock,” said Charlotte Jenkins, vice president at Capstone LLC, a global consulting firm based in Washington, DC. Although this is the closest a permitting reform bill “has ever gotten to becoming law,” she said, her team is “not as optimistic that this will pass in the House.”

In January, a new session of Congress will begin with Democrats holding sizable majorities in both chambers. But it won’t be enough to overcome expected vetoes from Trump, dimming the chances of Democrats being able to pass their own version of permitting reform. Whatever happens on the issue right now, the dynamics among environmentalists will no doubt shift once more.

Zindler said he doesn’t expect the rupture in the climate movement to be permanent: “When their top priorities overlap again, as they no doubt will on any variety of topics, I’d anticipate they’ll cooperate.”

description:

text:
Say what you want about the Tesla Cybertruck, but it's certainly going to find its way in the history books one way or another. While the vehicle has easily been one of the biggest flops in Tesla's history and has since led the company to stop producing it, the electric truck is now finding a second life in the used-car market. By sales volume, it's now one of the best-selling used cars in the U.S.

According to a report from iSeeCars.com, the Cybertruck is taking the top spot as the fastest-selling used truck, averaging 39.1 days on the market compared with the usual 65.5 days for a truck. Electric vehicles overall seem to be performing better than gas vehicles, with an EV averaging 45.6 days on the market versus 54.5 days for hybrids and 61 days for gas vehicles. The research was based on over 1.1 million sales of vehicles aged one to five years old sold in October 2026.

While some may not be surprised that EVs are more popular as gas prices fluctuate wildly, others may be surprised that a vehicle with so many major problems in its history is ranking so high. It may be head-scratching to see the Cybertruck as the fastest-selling vehicle, but that doesn't mean you should expect Tesla to revitalize it any time soon. The Cybertruck may have been the future when it launched, but Tesla has bigger ideas in store for now.

The Cybertrick may be the fastest-selling used vehicle right now, but that still hasn't stopped Tesla from deciding to wind down production starting in mid-2027. Musk has gone on record saying the decision let the company focus on the new Cybercab lineup — something that's already available at some surprising cost — though prices plunging by up to 48% in 2025 likely didn't help.

Originally set to launch in 2023, Tesla CEO Elon Musk planned for annual sales to hit around 250,000 units, though sales numbers for its first full sales year in 2024 hovered around the 30,000 mark. In 2025, SpaceX would be one of the largest purchasers of Cybertrucks, buying around $131 million in vehicles at list price, according to filings spotted by Reuters. During its lifetime, the vehicle also faced numerous controversies for its angular design and safety concerns.

For Tesla, the future likely will focus on autonomous vehicles like the Cybercab, which began offering rides to users in Austin, Texas, in September. However, since the launch of this service, Cybertrucks have been involved in at least eight reported collisions, with four at speeds of 5 mph or less and no injuries. While the technology may still be in its infancy, those interested in the Cybertruck may find this to be an opportune time to buy.

title: U.S. Loses Nearly 60% of Primary Energy | Wisevoter
description:
The U.S. consumed 34 quadrillion British thermal units of primary energy in 2025 to deliver 14 quads of electricity sales to end users, according to the Energy Information Administration.
Nearly 60% of the primary energy was lost in the process.
The players Energy Information Administration (EIA) The EIA is the statistical agency within the U.S. Department of Energy that collects and publishes official data on energy production, consumption and prices.
2025: The U.S. consumed 34 quads of primary energy and delivered 14 quads of electricity.
November 25, 2026: The EIA released its report on electricity energy losses.
text:
The U.S. consumed 34 quadrillion British thermal units of primary energy in 2025 to deliver 14 quads of electricity sales to end users, according to the Energy Information Administration. Nearly 60% of the primary energy was lost in the process.

Why it matters

The figures show that the largest source of energy waste sits in converting fuels such as coal, natural gas and petroleum into electricity rather than in moving power across the grid. Understanding where losses occur helps frame how much energy the country's electricity system uses to deliver each unit of power to homes and businesses.

The EIA reported 34 quadrillion British thermal units of primary energy consumed and 14 quads of electricity delivered in 2025, with about 95% of losses from fuel-to-electricity conversion. Coal plants use roughly 10,077 Btu of potential energy per kilowatthour of electricity output, compared with a constant heat content of 3,412 Btu per kilowatthour.

The players

Energy Information Administration (EIA)

The EIA is the statistical agency within the U.S. Department of Energy that collects and publishes official data on energy production, consumption and prices.

The details

Losses occur when fuels are burned to make heat that spins steam turbines, with energy escaping as heat to the environment along with unburned fuel and system efficiency limits. The EIA calculates conversion losses for coal, natural gas and petroleum plants by comparing energy consumed with electricity produced.

Timeline

2018 through 2022: Transmission and distribution losses averaged about 5%.

2025: The U.S. consumed 34 quads of primary energy and delivered 14 quads of electricity.

November 24, 2026: The EIA published a companion article on the captured energy approach.

November 25, 2026: The EIA released its report on electricity energy losses.

Related coverage

Data Centers

Nov. 20

Data Centers Strain U.S. Grid Equipment Supply

Energy

Nov. 21

U.S. Energy Storage Tops 200 GWh of Capacity

Energy

Nov. 25

Grid Transformer Shortages Loom by 2030

The Big Picture

The 2025 figures extend the EIA's loss-accounting method, which separates conversion losses at fossil-fueled plants from grid delivery losses that averaged about 5% from 2018 through 2022. This places the nearly 60% overall loss in the context of a conversion step that dominates waste, rather than the grid itself.

Because most primary energy is lost before reaching a home or business, the efficiency of power plants shapes how much fuel the country must burn to deliver the electricity households use. Electricity bills and energy policy both depend on how much of the fuel input becomes usable power.

The takeaway

Most energy lost in the U.S. power system occurs when fuels are converted into electricity, not when power travels along the grid. Readers interested in efficiency should look first at how plants turn fuel into electricity.
