text:
This week on Science Behind the Forecast, we’ll learn how Black Friday shopping can affect the weather. LPM’s Bill Burton talks about the effects with meteorologist Tawana Andrew.

This segment originally aired in November 2019. It’s been edited for clarity and length.

Tawana Andrew: It is Black Friday, so we're ready to shop, right?

Bill Burton: Bring on the deals! Weather can actually affect how and where we shop, right?

TA: Exactly. And in turn, where and how we shop can affect the weather, so that's something to keep in mind. USPS, the United States Postal Service, says that between Thanksgiving Day and New Year's Day, it's expected to make around 800 million deliveries. That's a lot of packages, and of course, the weather influences what we shop for. Warmer temperatures lasting into the winter can mean a lower demand for coats for certain stores. But also, you can have that blast of cold air, and then we warm up really quickly. That means that we could see a discount on fall and winter clothing when that kind of thing happens. So look for that if you see that in the forecast. Get those discounts, folks.

The National Retail Federation says that while retailers see their peaks during the holiday season, weather actually still has an impact overall, even online. Think about it: if you are snowed in, you're not going anywhere. You're not going to an actual store, so that means you're more likely to buy stuff online, or even be like, "Hey, can I order some pizza? Let the pizza guy drive in the snow.” All those things have an impact. One study found that the weather's impact on daily sales could be as high as 23% based on a store's location, and even jumped around 40% depending on the sale theme that a store may have. We have Black Friday as the busiest shopping day of the year, and then we also have Super Saturday, which is a Saturday before Christmas.

With billions of packages being shipped, we have to think about our carbon footprint. This is an estimate of the amount of greenhouse gasses that are created by our day-to-day activities. For the average U.S. citizen, it's about 16 tons of greenhouse gasses, and that is one of the highest rates in the entire world. Think about how you're shopping, because two-day shipping actually leaves a bigger carbon footprint than if you let it take its time and you are patient getting that package. One MIT study actually found that online shopping's carbon footprint is lower than shopping in an actual store because you're not using your gasoline cars to get there. But this lower footprint only exists when you don't use express shipping. No two day shipping from Amazon, people! So keep that in mind.

Also something to keep in mind is that the electronics we are buying could lead to pollutants if we don't recycle them properly. Because you know you're getting a new TV or whatever this year, and only 20% of electronic waste is actually recycled. That means all the stuff, the chemicals in it, is going to be leaching into our air or water.

Something that really shocked me is that a 2017 report showed that a garbage truckload of textiles, that's your clothes, is wasted every single second.

name: Congress
title: BAAJA: Can America build bigger and faster without sacrificing environmental laws?
authors: Ellis Juhlin, Nora Mabie and Nick Mott
description:
Provisions in BAAJA change existing policy to narrow which projects receive that kind of review, expand agency authority and shorten tribal consultation timelines.
It’s nothing new for tribal peoples.” — Nora Mabie BAAJA looks to change one of the country’s bedrock environmental protection laws: the National Environmental Policy Act.
Mark Mariano with the conservation and education organization Montana Wetlands and Waterfowl says wetlands are already threatened and BAAJA would worsen the problem.
That’s the trajectory we’re already at.” Despite making up just 4% of land cover in Montana, wetlands provide a variety of ecosystem services to humans and wildlife.
Like NEPA and NHPA, BAAJA limits the existing authority tribes and states have to intervene when a federal project could affect their waters.
text:
Typically, anytime state or federal dollars are involved in a major project, such as building a new road, pipeline or solar field, the agencies involved are required to consult with tribes whose land and resources may be affected. That kind of consultation, required through a provision of the National Historic Preservation Act, has meant tribes like the Blackfeet have been able to weigh in on projects including improvements to the St. Mary Canal and construction near Glacier National Park on ancestral homelands, among other things. Provisions in BAAJA change existing policy to narrow which projects receive that kind of review, expand agency authority and shorten tribal consultation timelines.

Tribes and tribal organizations nationwide, including the National Congress of American Indians, Native American Rights Fund and National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers, have condemned BAAJA, saying it threatens cultural heritage and tribal sovereignty.

Gheri Hall, co-director and deputy of compliance for the Blackfeet Tribal Historic Preservation Office, said that without consultation, “cultural sites can be permanently destroyed before we have the opportunity to identify, document and protect them.”

“There are so many cultural sites out there that we don’t even know exist,” Hall said. “So if we lose that information, it destroys evidence of where our ancestors lived, where they traveled, where they gathered plants. It destroys sacred places that are associated with our spiritual practices and traditions.”

When the government consults tribes on decisions that impact them, Hall said, the government is recognizing tribes’ unique status as sovereign nations. Weakening that process, she added, “diminishes our ability to protect the cultural heritage.”

While dozens of tribes oppose the bill, the Crow Tribe in southeast Montana is among the few in the country to publicly support it. Coal has long been an economic driver for the tribe, and while Crow Chairman Frank White Clay emphasized the importance of tribal participation in an October letter to several U.S. senators, he also wrote that red tape is slowing progress.

“For too long, overlapping federal reviews, bureaucratic delays, and unpredictable permitting timelines have hindered investment in Indian Country,” White Clay wrote.

Dean Nicolai, who chairs the Tribal Historic Preservation bachelor’s degree program at Séliš Ksanka Ql̓ispé University (formerly Salish Kootenai College), said he doesn’t believe lawmakers who claim the goal of the bill is to create jobs.

“It’s about money,” Nicolai said of BAAJA. “It’s just about corporations making more money. It’s nothing new for tribal peoples.” — Nora Mabie

BAAJA looks to change one of the country’s bedrock environmental protection laws: the National Environmental Policy Act. Passed in 1970, NEPA is often referred to as the “look before you leap” doctrine. It requires federal agencies to consider the environmental impacts of development before the agency makes decisions. BAAJA would limit the kinds of projects that require a NEPA review, narrow the scope of what is considered in an environmental analysis, and shorten the amount of time an agency has to complete that analysis.

“It makes NEPA a dead letter,” said Martin Nie, a natural resource policy professor at the University of Montana. BAAJA’s weakening of NEPA, he said, is one more erosion of the policy which has already been narrowed in scope in recent years.

“What we’ve seen over two years, is just this Gilded Age type of corruption and agency capture, and giveaways of our public lands to private interests,” Nie said. “That is the defining feature of this administration, and this bill does the same thing.”

The NEPA process is how the public knows what the potential impacts of a development project could be and where people can weigh in with concerns. “[NEPA] provides Montanans a seat at the table,” Nie said, “for everything from oil and gas leases, to timber sales to recreation development.”

In Montana, NEPA has had tangible impacts including with the expansion of Highway 93, which runs from the Bitterroot Valley through Flathead Valley and on to Eureka.

“That was originally proposed as a sort of mega highway,” Nie explained. “It was going to go through the refuges with no wildlife provisions. With tribal leadership using NEPA, we have all those overpasses along 93, and we had all the signage and a rerouting.”

The changes also included the addition of the prominent wildlife crossing built over the highway to help grizzly bears safely move across. The public comment that drove those changes couldn’t happen if NEPA changes as proposed by BAAJA.

The bill also limits how projects could be subject to judicial review, further preventing scrutiny of development. Nie said it could have devastating effects for years to come.

“Chances are an agency won’t have to do any NEPA analysis at all,” he said. “And if it does screw up its NEPA analysis, the project still moves forward.” — Ellis Juhlin

Supporters like the Pacific Legal Foundation say BAAJA would “prune our regulatory thicket” and make the Endangered Species Act “more transparent, predictable and efficient,” while environmental groups across the country have condemned the ESA rollbacks the permitting bill would legislate. For more than 50 years, the act has worked to stave off extinction for the country’s most imperiled species.

BAAJA’s ESA impacts are manifold, but potentially the largest comes in the form of consultation, according to Chris Westfall, senior government relations legislative counsel with Defenders of Wildlife. When a federal project proposes an action that could impact a threatened or endangered species — for example, a logging project that could harm elk or lynx — the party proposing it must consult with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. But BAAJA upends that half-century-old relationship.

“The bill is a solution in search of a problem,” Westfall said.

Approximately 90% of ESA consultations currently take less than two weeks to complete, according to a Defenders of Wildlife analysis. The remaining 10% take about two months. That doesn’t amount to meaningful delays in projects, Westfall argues.

Under new definitions in the bill, states can act as consultants instead of the federal government. Westfall says that will overwhelm state governments and create even lengthier review processes, creating more of a regulatory burden rather than reducing it. Worse yet, he argues, project sponsors might leverage that ability to seek state sign-off when the federal government might not greenlight a project.

“We worry that could be bad for wildlife across the board,” he said.

BAAJA also shortens the timespan the consultation process can be litigated, exempts highway projects entirely from ESA requirements, changes the definition of what constitutes the “best available science,” and institutes restrictions on updating permits when a project could impact more listed species than initially anticipated. Westfall said the overhaul fits in with bigger-picture rollbacks over the last two years, which sought to redefine “take” under the ESA.

“This is just another attack on the Endangered Species Act that works in tandem with those other attacks that we’ve seen from the administration,” he said. “It’s really infuriating.” — Nick Mott

BAAJA proposes several large changes to the Clean Water Act, another 1970s-era policy regulating pollution in waterways, everything from wetlands to rivers and streams to lakes. BAAJA changes sections of the CWA regarding water-quality certification and wetland permitting. The bill would remove or weaken protections for small wetlands under 2 acres and would make it easier for developers to drain or fill in wetlands of any size.

Mark Mariano with the conservation and education organization Montana Wetlands and Waterfowl says wetlands are already threatened and BAAJA would worsen the problem.

“If you weigh it all out and you’re losing protections on things that are already getting hammered,” he said, “the U.S. itself loses more than 60,000 acres of wetlands a year. That’s the trajectory we’re already at.”

Despite making up just 4% of land cover in Montana, wetlands provide a variety of ecosystem services to humans and wildlife. Mariano says Montana can’t afford to lose more.

“In western Montana, we have turned a spongy system historically into a flashy, more desert-like system,” he said. “As we get warmer and drier, our main reservoir of water is our snowpack, and it flows off the landscape as fast as possible. Wetlands slow that down, and they act as a sponge.”

Wetlands of any size hold water on the landscape longer for farmers and ranchers, and act like nature’s kidneys by filtering pollution, Mariano explained. “Water that spends time in a wetland can lose contaminants from industrial situations like we have here in Butte.”

When it comes to wildlife needs, Mariano said “a smaller wetland is better,” in that it creates habitat for ducks and geese to nest in, and places that migratory birds can rely on as critical stopover points as they cross the continent.

Like NEPA and NHPA, BAAJA limits the existing authority tribes and states have to intervene when a federal project could affect their waters. If a company wanted to build a dam or a pipeline in Montana, for example, the state could review whether or not that would impact water quality for a river or lake. If it had concerns, it could stop the project from certification.

According to an analysis from the Natural Resources Defense Council, the changes that would happen under BAAJA would make it more difficult for the state or a tribe to object. It would also allow water pollution permits to last up to 10 years, which some opponents say would further delay federal action on regulating pollution like PFAS, the forever chemicals that have already been found in unsafe levels in fish across Montana. — Ellis Juhlin

title: Your local drives through 2050 are being mapped now. Time is running out to weigh in.
authors: LIZ SWAINE, Staff, JILL PICKETT, Staff photographer
description:
A decision to be made on Dec. 18 will affect local motorists use of roadways for the next 23 years and beyond.
The most recent numbers from 2023 estimated that each day there were 1.7 million trips on local roads.
Over the past year, officials in Caddo, Bossier, Webster and DeSoto Parishes have been mapping out transportation needs through the year 2050 in an updated Metropolitan Transportation Plan, a document required by the federal government.

text:
A decision to be made on Dec. 18 will affect local motorists use of roadways for the next 23 years and beyond. Those will be trips in which drivers will either make good time or be delayed by traffic or route.

Local drivers have multiple roadway experiences per day. The most recent numbers from 2023 estimated that each day there were 1.7 million trips on local roads.

Over the past year, officials in Caddo, Bossier, Webster and DeSoto Parishes have been mapping out transportation needs through the year 2050 in an updated Metropolitan Transportation Plan, a document required by the federal government.

Without an MTP, the four-parish metro area will be out of luck on getting federal transportation dollars.

The transit needs are plentiful, and this document does not cover all of them. The 48 projects included in the draft MTP are deemed the most needed. To be included, there must also be a reasonable belief that they can be funded.

Ellen Soll of the New Orleans’ engineering firm Neel- Schaffer shared details of the draft document at the Nov. 20 North Louisiana Council of Government's Metropolitan Planning Organization meeting. This is the group that represents the four parishes in transportation planning.

Having a plan and a 20-year timeline is required by the federal government, she said, reiterating that the plan has to be “fiscally constrained,” meaning the $2 billion list includes projects “that we reasonably anticipate there will be money for.”

Now it's the public's turn

The clock is ticking on the public’s opportunity to comment on the MTP. The comment period ends on Dec. 9.

“When it comes to public engagement and outreach, there's a little bit of fatigue because there are so many efforts right now to really make this region a better place for people to live in,” said NLCOG's Director of Planning, Chris Petro. “We want to develop a plan that serves the public well, and we can be proud of.”

He encourages everyone to take a look at the draft plan, and send any comments they have about it.

Soll noted that since February there have been multiple in-person engagement events. They and an online survey drew a total of 316 comments from the roughly 400,000 people in the four-parish area.

Some of the road projects

The MTP projects are categorized into Stage 1 (2025-2030), with 29 projects, Stage 2 (2031-2040), 12 projects, and Stage 3 (2041-2050), seven projects.

A few of the Stage 1 projects include Bossier’s new east-west road, portions of The Port of Caddo-Bossier’s long-sought I-69 frontage road, a variety of Shreveport asphalt rehab projects, a new southbound through lane and dual left-turns at Airline Drive and I-220 in Bossier City, and ‘congestion improvements’ along a portion of Shreveport’s Kings Highway.

Stage 2 includes widening a portion of I-20 in Bossier City, widening a portion of north Market Street in Shreveport, and launching the reconstruction on the Linwood Bridge between Texas Avenue and Dalzell Street.

Stage 3 includes widening a portion of I-20 in Shreveport, widening Shreveport-Blanchard Hwy from Roy Road to I-220, and widening a portion of US 71 in Bossier.

In addition is a list of ‘Vision Projects’ that do not fit into projected funding, which include the I-49 inner city connector, a portion of I-69, and several major widening projects.

Petro said the projects come up first in planning, then federal or other dollars are identified, there are feasibility studies and then the projects are prioritized. In the new MTP, Bossier’s new east-west road is prioritized as project number one.

Decisions are hard, he said, because there are always more needs than money, but public input does matter and it has made a difference in the past. Comments from the public led to sidewalks at high-traffic bus stops and has influenced the design of a portion of Shreveport’s Kings Highway corridor.

Three issues have been top-of-mind among those giving remarks, said Soll. “People let us know they were really interested in maintaining existing infrastructure, providing and expanding reliable service, and of course improving project delivery and implementation,” she said of comments received to date.

A committee established to work on the MTP developed nine goals, she said: “Improving the highway system, improving infrastructure conditions and preservation, improving safety and security, improving system reliability and reducing congestion, improving access and increasing connections, protecting the environment, supporting land use and economic development, increasing multimodal options, and improving quality of life.”

name: Clean Energy
title: Further concessions to automakers would cost Canadians | Pembina Institute
description:
Largely missing from this conversation is what Canadians stand to lose if these regulations are weakened, and whether doing so would secure lasting jobs.
Flexibility is built into these regulations by design and the federal government has since given automakers additional flexibility.
What’s more, given Stellantis' previous commitments to maintain production in Canada, what assurances do Canadians have that further concessions will secure lasting jobs?
“We need to be thinking about the jobs Canada can create over the next decade as much as the jobs we’re trying to protect today.
Growing Canada's EV market supports jobs across the country in critical minerals, battery manufacturing, electricity generation and charging.
text:
TORONTO— ADAM THORN, clean growth director at the Pembina Institute, made the following statement in response to calls from the Ontario government to exempt Canadian automakers from vehicle pollution rules and other greenhouse gas regulations:

“There has been a lot of discussion this week about the cost of greenhouse gas (GHG) regulations to automakers, with calls for further exemptions to help keep automotive production in Canada. Largely missing from this conversation is what Canadians stand to lose if these regulations are weakened, and whether doing so would secure lasting jobs.

“We share the concerns about the future of Stellantis' Brampton assembly plant and the livelihoods of thousands of Canadian workers, but we're talking about weakening national policies that benefits millions of Canadians. This offers no guarantee that this will keep this one company manufacturing in Canada, and it does little to address the real threat facing automakers, the Trump administration's efforts to bring automotive manufacturing back to the U.S.

“The costs being cited this week warrant closer scrutiny, analysis from Clean Energy Canada puts industrial carbon pricing compliance costs for Ontario's entire automotive sector at less than $3 million in 2023.

“Just last month, Ottawa froze vehicle pollution rules at 2026 levels until 2030, exemptions being proposed this week would further limit Canadians' access to electric vehicle (EV) options at a time when affordability is a major concern. Our research released this week shows that Ontario drivers spend significantly less on fuel by driving an EV. A greater share of what they spend also stays in Ontario's economy. For every $100 spent on gasoline, more than $50 leaves the province, compared with about $10 of every $100 spent on charging an EV.

“We also have good reason to question whether further exemptions are necessary. Our modelling published in September shows that Canada's auto industry is capable of meeting even stronger vehicle emissions standards than those currently in place. Flexibility is built into these regulations by design and the federal government has since given automakers additional flexibility.

“Emission standards only apply to vehicles sold in Canada, not those built in Canada. Even with Canadian production commitments, much of the regulatory relief would apply to vehicles manufacture in the United States and elsewhere. The Ford government is calling for action that would be making it easier for automakers to sell imported vehicles with little guarantee this effort will protect domestic manufacturing. What’s more, given Stellantis' previous commitments to maintain production in Canada, what assurances do Canadians have that further concessions will secure lasting jobs?

“We need to be thinking about the jobs Canada can create over the next decade as much as the jobs we’re trying to protect today. Growing Canada's EV market supports jobs across the country in critical minerals, battery manufacturing, electricity generation and charging. With nearly 30% of new cars sold globally this year to be electric, weakening policies that support this growth leaves Canada — and auto workers — further behind.”

About Bruce Power Bruce Power is an electricity company based in Bruce County, Saugeen Ojibway Nation Territory, Ontario.
Bruce Power has worked hard to build strong roots in Ontario and is committed to protecting the environment and supporting the communities in which we live.
Formed in 2001, Bruce Power is a Canadian-owned partnership of TC Energy, OMERS, the Power Workers’ Union and The Society of United Professionals.
text:
Bruce Power has reached a key milestone for the Bruce C Project – a project that would build a long-term supply of clean and reliable nuclear electricity to support Ontario’s growing energy needs while driving the economy through privately funded investment and good-paying jobs.

The company has submitted the Bruce C Project Impact Statement and Licence to Prepare Site Application (LTPS) to the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada (IAAC) and the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC), the next step in the federally integrated Impact Assessment process to build up to 4,800 megawatts (MW) of nuclear capacity at the Bruce Power site.

Canada’s Nuclear Energy Strategy was released this year as part of the wider National Electricity Strategy, Powering Canada Strong, with the goal of doubling the country’s energy grid and build a low-carbon economy in less than 25 years. It stated that there is no credible plan to accomplish the goal without nuclear energy and the clean, reliable baseload power it provides.

The Impact Statement documents existing conditions, assesses effects of the project and provides proposed mitigation measures. Engagement with Indigenous Nations and communities, municipalities, and the public took place throughout the development of the Impact Statement and informed the assessment process and findings. Opportunities for engagement in this public process are ongoing through the IAAC, CNSC and Bruce Power, including a Bruce C livestream event Dec. 8 at 7 p.m.

“The filing of the Bruce C Project Impact Statement and Licence to Prepare Site application marks a major milestone for the project,” said James Scongack, Bruce Power’s Chief Operating Officer and Executive Vice-President. “The Bruce C Project represents a generational opportunity for Canada, Ontario, and our region and we are committed to ensuring that the benefits of the project are maximized while mitigating potential challenges, a commitment that is reflected throughout the Impact Statement. Thank you to all who engaged throughout this process. We look forward to continuing to engage as the project advances.”

Following an initial review from IAAC and CNSC, the submission will be posted for the public to view on the Bruce C Project registry page. The IAAC and CNSC will share more information regarding the public comment period in the weeks ahead.

The Ontario government is building the future of nuclear energy to power a more competitive, resilient and self-reliant economy, including the ongoing Life-Extension Project and Major Component Replacement Project of Bruce Power’s existing units, and the opportunities for new, large-scale builds such as Bruce C.

“Our government is making generational investments in Ontario’s energy future as electricity demand hits record levels. Ontario is proud to promote this achievement as we work to accelerate the development of the Bruce C nuclear expansion, bringing Ontario one step closer to its first large-scale nuclear project in more than 30 years,” said Stephen Lecce, Ontario’s Minister of Energy and Mines. “Nuclear is made-in-Canada, with 95 per cent of spending staying in our province and country. This project is key to meeting rising electricity demand, which is why Ontario is driving this project forward creating 18,900 jobs during construction and generating power for nearly five million families.”

An independent economic impact analysis published by the Ontario Chamber of Commerce earlier this year found that the large-scale Bruce C nuclear project would deliver lasting job creation, stimulate Ontario’s economy, and reinforce Canada’s long-term energy security for decades to come.

The Bruce C Project’s direct benefits would be concentrated in Ontario, contributing more than $217 billion to Ontario’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) during its 80-year lifespan; and would contribute $2.3 billion to the Clean Energy Frontier (Bruce, Grey and Huron Counties) regional GDP on an average annual basis.

The addition of up to 4,800 MW of energy production through the Bruce C Project would make Bruce Power the largest nuclear generator in the world with a capacity of 12,000 MW.

Bruce Power is Canada’s largest public-private partnership and its Life-Extension Program and Major Component Replacement Project is one of the country’s biggest privately financed electricity infrastructure projects in Canada.

Two-way communication is key to the process and Bruce Power is committed to receiving your comments and keeping you up to date as the Bruce C Project moves through the Impact Assessment process. For more information, visit the Bruce C Project webpage or email brucec@brucepower.com.

About Bruce Power

Bruce Power is an electricity company based in Bruce County, Saugeen Ojibway Nation Territory, Ontario. We are powered by our people. Our 4,200 employees are the foundation of our accomplishments and are proud of the role they play in safely delivering clean, reliable nuclear power to families and businesses across the province and cancer-fighting medical isotopes around the world. Bruce Power has worked hard to build strong roots in Ontario and is committed to protecting the environment and supporting the communities in which we live. Formed in 2001, Bruce Power is a Canadian-owned partnership of TC Energy, OMERS, the Power Workers’ Union and The Society of United Professionals. title: Preview 2027: Electrification high on EU agenda, as grids and power prices remain hurdles – CATF
description:
Lea Romm: Electrification will still be the big topic at the start of 2027, because it provides energy security for Europe.
The way forward for the EU as a global player is electrification, and setting this up for success will be very high on the agenda.
The second hurdle is high electricity prices.
Non-energy costs can make up as much as three quarters of the price of electricity in EU countries.
Electricity prices currently move up and down with geopolitical crises because of their link to the gas system.
text:
Lea Romm: Electrification will still be the big topic at the start of 2027, because it provides energy security for Europe. The EU still imports more than half of the energy it consumes, and much of this is fossil fuels. This is a problem for EU competitiveness and creates dependencies. The way forward for the EU as a global player is electrification, and setting this up for success will be very high on the agenda.

What are the big friction points, or major hurdles, that could come up in implementing electrification?

The first hurdle is infrastructure, which has been overlooked until now. There was a lot of effort over recent years to build out renewables, and that was fairly successful. But now the question is what we need to complement those renewables with – how do we bring storage into the system, and how do we connect renewables efficiently across the EU’s internal market? There’s a package of EU network-related proposals, the so-called grids package, on the way, but its first measures will only come into real effect in a few years, so we need to figure out what to do in the meantime to build out the infrastructure for electrification.

Cross-border projects are also genuinely difficult for investors because cost-benefit sharing isn’t straightforward – you’re negotiating with two countries and two sets of DSOs and TSOs. I’m hopeful the grids package will help here too, by setting out a common methodology for cost-benefit sharing, including a rule that transit countries which also benefit from a power line should contribute financially to the project. That could add some fairness to the system and help move more projects forward.

Are there other major frictions for European electrification?

The second hurdle is high electricity prices. Electricity in the EU is currently two to three times more expensive than in the US – a real disadvantage and an issue of competitiveness. There’s a major effort at EU level right now to bring prices down. The challenge is that a lot of gas still sits in the electricity system, and that depends on global gas markets, which are currently constrained. Even though Europe wasn’t heavily dependent on LNG before, it has now disconnected almost entirely from Russian pipeline gas and shifted to LNG markets – which exposes it directly to high global market prices. So at the moment, both gas-reliant industry and electrified industry suffers due to that. A clean power sector in Europe however makes the case for broad electrification, as it means more independence, less volatility, lower prices, wasting less energy through efficiency and producing fewer emissions.

These challenges often differ a lot depending on the country or region, but are there cross-border solutions?

The EU is currently proposing a legislative change to the electricity taxation rules – contested and heavily debated right now – that would set out a framework for energy taxation, which is normally a national competence, so member states aren’t thrilled about the EU proposing this. But the underlying idea is a high-level principle: electricity should not be taxed higher than gas, at most the same. Non-energy costs can make up as much as three quarters of the price of electricity in EU countries. In some member states, taxes make up around 18 percent of the electricity bill, so lowering that would be one lever to bring prices down.

Another lever is longer-term contracts for industry, which allow hedging against price volatility. Electricity prices currently move up and down with geopolitical crises because of their link to the gas system. One way to do this is by opening up Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) to more consumers, since at the moment these are mostly accessible only to very large ones. The EU has said in its Electrification Action Plan that it will explore mechanisms for this, and we at Clean Air Task Force work on ideas to de-risk long-term contracts so that small and medium consumers – including industrial ones – can access them, too, and get a predictable price. It likely won’t be the lowest price, maybe not as low as in the US, but at least a workable business case: you can plan and invest, knowing roughly what electricity will cost over the years you commit to. Right now, if you want to shift your business from fossil-fuel energy to electrified operations, you don’t even know what to expect, because you’re so exposed to the global market.

That price pressure isn’t just a problem for businesses but for citizens too. Looking at friction points for next year – there are major elections coming up. What role will this play? Will it speed up the solutions you mentioned, or derail them?

I think we’re at a critical point in the energy transition – we’ve made progress, but it’s not yet visible on consumers’ bills. That’s exactly the point where you need to keep pushing to bring the benefits through to consumers, but we’re losing some political momentum, and that’s a real problem across Europe.

Spain has elections coming up and might roll back some climate laws. France has a presidential election next year, essentially between a left-leaning and a right-wing candidate with very different energy agendas, which will shape policy going forward. And we shouldn’t forget there’s already a conservative, right-leaning majority in the European Parliament – and at the next European Parliament elections, that majority could grow further.

All of this will likely shape the agenda at a time the EU is reforming major elements of its climate and energy policy.

What do you mean?

The EU agreed in late 2025 to reduce emissions by 90 percent by 2040, but the open question is how to adjust the energy and climate targets and regulations to reach that goal. For example, there is an existing Renewable Energy Directive (RED) target for 2030, which will be updated. The question is whether it will increase, stay the same, or exist in a different form going forward. The EU wants to speed up this process to land an ambitious outcome before elections create more political headwinds.

This is part of a large package – known as the “governance package” or “post-2030 framework package” – which sets out important milestones for energy and climate policy. It was originally expected by the end of this year, but it hasn’t materialised.

What’s pending is the revision of the renewables directive and an impact assessment for the Electrification Action Plan. An indicative electrification target to increase electrification from today's 23 percent of energy use to 46 percent by 2040 was set with that plan in July, but whether it becomes binding is still open, and also depends on the assessment.

There’s also pressure from some member states to move away from “renewables” targets toward “clean energy” targets, which would give countries more flexibility – potentially including nuclear and other low-carbon sources alongside renewables. The real question in discussion is whether this should be a renewables-only target, an electricity-focused target, or a broader energy target?

All of that is now expected in the first quarter of 2027.

text:
Kia is offering $10,000 in Customer Cash on the 2026 EV9 Light RWD, lowering its $54,900 base price to $44,900 before destination. The offer has run since at least September and requires delivery by Jan. 4, 2027, and buyers may instead take 0% APR for 60 months with $5,000 in APR Bonus Cash.

Why it matters

The incentive lowers the upfront cost of one of Kia's electric SUVs for U.S. buyers at a time when competitors are also discounting EVs. Buyers must choose between the cash rebate and the financing offer, since the two cannot be combined.

The Light RWD carries an EPA-estimated 230-mile range and the Light Long Range 305 miles, with the long-range trim discounted from $57,900 to $47,900 with the cash. The offer is not available on leases.

The players

Kia

Kia is a South Korean automaker, a subsidiary of Hyundai Motor Group, that sells electric vehicles including the EV9 three-row SUV in the United States.

Lucid

Lucid Group is a California-based electric vehicle maker known for its luxury sedans and SUVs, including the Gravity model.

Volkswagen

Volkswagen is a German automaker and one of the world's largest car manufacturers, selling the ID.4 electric crossover in the United States.

The details

Buyers can take the $10,000 Customer Cash on the 2026 EV9 or choose 0% APR for 60 months with $5,000 in APR Bonus Cash, but Kia's terms say the offers cannot be combined unless specified. Competing offers include a $15,000 Black Friday Credit on the 2027 Lucid Gravity Touring and a $10,000 Customer Bonus on the 2026 Volkswagen ID.4 running through Nov. 30.

Timeline

Since at least September 2026: Kia begins offering $10,000 on the 2026 EV9.

Nov. 27, 2026: Black Friday EV9 cash offer is reported.

Nov. 30, 2026: Lucid and Volkswagen offers require delivery by this date.

Jan. 4, 2027: Deadline for taking delivery of an EV9 under the Kia cash offer.

Roadmap

Automakers are relying on steep cash incentives to clear electric vehicle inventory as buyers weigh EV prices against gasoline models. Kia, Lucid and Volkswagen are all using large rebates to compete for the same buyers this holiday season.

A buyer taking the $10,000 cash on the Light RWD pays $44,900 before destination instead of $54,900, but must forgo the 0% APR route. Those comparing financing should note the 0% offer equals about $832 per month on the $49,900 amount financed.

The takeaway

Comparing a cash rebate against low-APR financing can change the real cost of an EV, so run both numbers before signing. Confirm the delivery deadline and whether a lease is eligible, since this offer excludes leases.

title: New Oregon initiative targets 16,500 energy jobs by 2035 | Local | kdrv.com
description: A new statewide initiative is launching to help Oregonians find careers in the growing energy industry, including jobs that pay well and don't require a four-year degree.
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. — A new statewide initiative is launching to help Oregonians find careers in the growing energy industry, including jobs that pay well and don't require a four-year degree.

The Oregon Clean Energy Workforce Coalition, known as OCEWC, officially launched its "Do What You Love" campaign Nov. 13 at Portland Community College's Workforce Opportunity Center. According to OCEWC, more than 100 organizations joined together to help students, jobseekers and people considering career changes explore energy jobs and the training needed to pursue them.

The timing makes sense, given how much the industry is expected to grow. According to the Oregon Department of Energy's 2025 Oregon Energy Strategy, the state could gain 9,200 to 16,500 energy-sector jobs by 2035 — a 7% to 12% increase over 2024 employment. ECONorthwest also reports that Oregon energy workers earn about 37% more annually than the average Oregon worker.

"This tool is needed now because the energy sector in Oregon is changing rapidly," said Brooke Brownlee, executive director of OCEWC. "We have new technologies; we have decarbonization goals in the state that are requiring us to provide different types of energy than we have historically. All of that requires people."

Brownlee said the industry needs people with a wide range of skills, including those who may never have considered working in energy.

"We have data scientists, we have folks who work in environmental, we have folks who work with forests and trees," Brownlee said. "And so it really is an opportunity for basically anyone to come in and use their skills."

The initiative is designed for students, people considering career changes, workers in other industries, rural residents and people returning to the workforce after incarceration. Before Derek Thill joined Portland General Electric, he was building cabinets, and he eventually worked his way up from utility worker to journeyman lineman and now serves as a union business representative.

"You're going to make great wages, you're going to have excellent benefits, and you're going to learn what it's like to be in the electrical trade," Thill said. "And then you work your way from the ground up, and they'll train you, and you'll get paid the whole time you're doing it."

Ashley Yost was serving a five-year sentence at Coffee Creek Correctional Facility when she discovered the program. Now a second-year ironworker apprentice with Ironworkers Local 29, she has health benefits, retirement savings and a goal of buying her first home.

"I knew that was it. That was my chance to make something of my life, to do something positive, to turn this negative experience of prison into a whole lifestyle. And that was my way out," said Yost.

Brownlee hopes stories like Yost's will help others recognize opportunities they may not have imagined for themselves.

"And so making sure that we have those faces behind who is actually doing this work allows people to recognize and see themselves in the work," said Brownlee.

Many energy careers offer paid training and apprenticeships. Electricians, for example, can train through five-year paid apprenticeships and earn a median annual wage of $101,310, according to occupational data published by OCEWC.

Through the "Do What You Love" website, Oregonians can take a free five-minute Career Explorer Quiz that matches their interests and skills with six career types, access a free Introduction to Energy Jobs course and find information about training programs across Oregon, with Spanish-language resources also available. OCEWC aims to have 5,000 Oregonians complete the free introductory course by September 2027.

text:
This story was originally published by Michigan Advance. Sign up for their weekly newsletter at michiganadvance.com/subscribe

By Kyle Davidson, Michigan Advance

As data center proposals pop up across Michigan, concerns about the amount of energy and water used by hyperscale facilities across the country has been at the forefront of arguments against the projects.

With a facility under construction in Saline Township expected to use 1.4 gigawatts of electricity – roughly equivalent to the power usage of 1.2 million Michigan homes – and another in Van Buren Township expected to demand 1 gigawatt from the grid, environmental advocates have raised concerns over how the electricity demand from facilities like these will impact Michigan’s clean energy goals.

In 2023, the Democratic-led Michigan Legislature passed a series of clean energy bills, including legislation requiring Michigan energy companies to supply power from a portfolio of 100% clean energy resources – which can include nuclear energy and natural gas facilities using 90% effective carbon capture and storage technology – by 2040.

Along with the clean energy standard, the law also requires energy companies to secure 60% of their power from renewable sources including solar, wind, geothermal energy and the movement of water by 2035.

While the law has benchmark requirements for energy providers to build up their portfolio of renewable energy resources, organizations such as the Michigan Environmental Council have argued that increased energy demand from data centers could extend the lifespan of fossil fuel plants, and incentivize companies to build additional gas plants.

In a recent research brief, the nonpartisan Citizens Research Council of Michigan examined how data centers could impact the state’s efforts to meet that 60% renewable energy standard within the next nine years.

Currently, only about 13% of Michigan’s electricity is generated from renewable energy sources, the report notes.

The state is also facing separate challenges in building up its renewable resources, including ongoing legal challenges to the law around renewable energy siting, expiring tax credits from the federal Inflation Reduction Act, the growing cost of energy generation and the difficulties connecting energy resources to the grid.

The brief also noted that Michigan’s clean energy law was crafted in 2023, meaning policymakers hadn’t considered the possibility of rapid growth in electricity demand from hyperscale data centers when setting these goals. It also points to comments from the Data Center Coalition, an industry group, acknowledging that increased electricity demand from data centers “may challenge the utility’s ability to procure or develop sufficient clean energy sources, implicating statutory or regulatory clean energy and emissions reductions targets.”

Tax breaks come with a clean energy requirement

When Michigan lawmakers penned the bills creating the sales and use tax exemption for data centers, they included requirements for data center developers to procure 90% clean energy. However the brief explains that the law does not specify how data centers would demonstrate this, leaving certification of the clean energy requirement to the Michigan Strategic Fund.

Under the fund’s guidelines, a data center can meet the clean energy requirement by contracting with an electric utility that is “actively pursuing compliance” with Michigan’s clean energy law.

If the utility does not comply, the data center does not lose certification for the tax credit, the brief explains, noting that this effectively makes the 90% clean energy requirement a non-factor in meeting the requirements for a tax exemption. Considering the difficulty that new data center energy loads will impose on the utilities, the Citizens Research Council said that could prompt utilities to delay complying with the state’s clean and renewable energy requirements, through the law’s “off-ramp” provision.

Given that two utilities – DTE Energy and Consumers Energy – supply 90% of Michigan’s electricity, the Citizens Research Council examined each company’s plans for meeting the state’s renewable energy requirements.

Consumers Energy is already supplying power to a hyperscale data center, which the council defines as a facility using more than 100 megawatts at peak demand. Additional data center contracts are pending local approval.

In its most recent integrated resource plan, Consumers Energy acknowledged it must accommodate an additional 2,000 megawatts of electricity demand that it had not anticipated in its 2021 plan. It must do so while replacing 3,000 megawatts of fossil fuel generation as it retires the J.H. Campbell coal plant in Ottawa County and winds down operations at the Dan E. Karn Generating Plant in Bay County by 2031.

To meet that demand, Consumers plans to add 3,000 megawatts of solar energy generation and 1,200 megawatts of wind by 2031, continuing at a similar pace through 2041. The company expects to bring 17,500 megawatts of renewable energy online over the next 15 years, which its analysts say will allow it to meet the state’s clean and renewable energy benchmarks.

DTE Energy, meanwhile, is contracted to provide power to both the Saline Township and Van Buren Township data centers.

The Saline Township project includes an agreement for the data center to fund 1.4 gigawatts of 4-hour battery storage capacity, which would be owned by DTE. While battery storage is complementary to renewable energy use, the council notes that the batteries do not generate renewable energy.

In order to meet the state’s renewable energy portfolio standards while supplying power to the Saline Township data center, the council’s brief says DTE will need to bring more renewable energy resources online than previously planned.

As for the Van Buren Township project, Google, which is developing the data center, plans to ensure 40% of the power it receives will be generated by renewables. Google will also be funding 480 megawatts of energy storage and 1.6 gigawatts of renewable generation capacity, although the report said the renewable energy credits created by these sources will not be available to DTE.

In order to serve the Google data center and maintain compliance with the state’s renewable portfolio requirements, DTE estimates that it will need to increase its long-term renewable energy target by 10.8%, which will be funded by a surcharge on Google’s bill. According to the company, the Google data center will be funding 40% more renewable energy than it uses

In its briefing, the council noted that funding for renewable energy and battery storage from these two data centers is critical to DTE’s recently proposed Integrated Resource Plan.

While these agreements will help bring more renewables online, the Citizens Research Council said these data centers will also bring substantial, unanticipated energy load growth, creating a challenge for DTE to provide enough power for these energy loads while it works to retire 3 gigawatts of coal by 2032.

However, DTE expects to meet this challenge while complying with the state’s renewable portfolio requirements by building roughly 15 gigawatts of renewable generation, 4.5 gigawatts of battery storage, and two new natural gas plants for peak energy demand with a combined generation capacity of 2.1 gigawatts.

Renewable energy opportunities and risks

While the two utilities have provided plans to meet Michigan’s renewable energy requirements while supplying power to data centers, the Citizens Research Council does acknowledge concerns from environmental advocates that these companies would not need to develop a combined 3.5 gigawatts of new natural gas generation if they were not serving data centers.

Although it is theoretically possible to meet current and future energy demand with renewables alone, the council said that could prove difficult, and could be “unacceptably costly.” It notes that while fossil fuel energy generation can be turned on and off to meet demand, renewable energy is contingent on climate and weather.

Power transmission could also present a challenge, the council said, as redistributing energy generation from a few large fossil fuel plants to several smaller renewable sites could require a substantial investment into transmission infrastructure that would ultimately be paid for by energy customers.

According to the council, if Consumers and DTE did not plan to build this additional natural gas generation, they would need to build at least 10 gigawatts of additional renewable energy alongside additional battery storage and transmission infrastructure to make that power available where it is needed.

“Michigan’s utilities are obligated to meet Michigan’s renewable goals, but they are also obligated to do so without impairing reliability or incurring excessive costs,” the council’s brief stated.

Although DTE and Consumers plans appear to meet their regulatory obligations, the council said these plans may not reflect real-world constraints. While together the utilities have planned to build more than 30 gigawatts of solar generation and substantial wind and battery storage, the addition of solar alone would require 150,000 acres of land, or 235 square miles, the brief explains.

Identifying suitable land and securing leases from landowners will be difficult, the council states. It also notes that utilities may struggle to obtain project approvals and secure labor and materials at the required pace.

While the council set out to determine whether data centers would make it more or less difficult for Michigan to meet its 60% renewable energy standard, its final conclusion is complicated.

In the short term, the additional electricity demand from data centers will make it more difficult for Michigan utilities to meet the state’s renewable energy requirements by 2035, the council found. The projects will require a rapid expansion of renewable generation, while potentially increasing the reliance on natural gas.

Over the longer term, however, the data centers could help utilities meet those requirements by funding new renewable energy generation and battery storage. Contracts that allow data centers to reduce their electricity consumption during periods of high demand could also ease pressure on utilities.

However, the council cautioned that utilities may nevertheless need to delay compliance with the state’s renewable energy targets.

name: Texas American Energy
title: Expert on the permitting reform bill: boon for clean energy or environmental rollback?
authors: Reid Frazier | Allegheny Front, www.wesanews.org, reid-frazier-allegheny-front
description:
It’s either a needed boon for the clean energy buildout, or a giveaway to fossil fuel and data center companies that will gut protections for endangered species, Native American tribes, and local communities.
“I have struggled to answer it,” writes Paulina Jaramillo, in her newsletter Amped Up.
To understand the bill better, The Allegheny Front’s Reid Frazier with Paulina Jaramillo, Trustee Professor of Engineering and Public Policy at Carnegie Mellon University.
And especially for clean energy.
Why it matters for the clean energy transition is that our best renewable energy resources are spread around the country and are not necessarily close to where our electricity demand is.
text:
What’s inside the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, currently winding its way through Congress? It’s either a needed boon for the clean energy buildout, or a giveaway to fossil fuel and data center companies that will gut protections for endangered species, Native American tribes, and local communities. Or a bit of both, depending on who you ask.

The bill has divided many in the environmental movement. Proponents say it will make energy projects cheaper and easier to build, including renewable energy. They also say the bill makes data centers pay for the grid upgrades they need.

Opponents argue the bill guts protections for the environment and native lands by limiting public participation. And they fear it will speed construction of fossil fuel infrastructure.

BAAJA passed the Senate late Thursday, and now heads to the House of Representatives. The big question many have is: should Congress pass it?

“I have struggled to answer it,” writes Paulina Jaramillo, in her newsletter Amped Up. “Both the bill’s benefits and its costs are uncertain, and I cannot resolve that uncertainty.” Congress may soon pass the expansive bill, which would make it easier to build transmission lines, natural gas and oil pipelines, and other energy infrastructure.

To understand the bill better, The Allegheny Front’s Reid Frazier with Paulina Jaramillo, Trustee Professor of Engineering and Public Policy at Carnegie Mellon University.

Reid Frazier: For many years, people have talked about the need for permitting reform. What does this mean? And why is permitting a problem in the U.S.? And especially for clean energy.

Paulina Jaramillo: In order for the U.S. to build infrastructure, transmission lines, highways, pipelines, mining projects, there are some very structured permitting processes that the project developers have to go through. They have to meet environmental regulations, particularly, they have to go through the National Environmental Policy Act, which was first signed in 1970.

We have definitely seen over the last decades that building infrastructure, and especially linear infrastructure, like transmission lines, is very difficult. The permitting processes take a lot of time. There are a lot of lawsuits that happen as opposition arises to these projects. And so some of these projects really do take a long of time (to complete).

Why it matters for the clean energy transition is that our best renewable energy resources are spread around the country and are not necessarily close to where our electricity demand is.

So to be able to expand the generation and consumption of renewable energy resources, we need to build transmission lines that move that power from where it is to where we need it. The challenges of building transmission are very acute and significant and have posed a lot of barriers to really a much accelerated deployment that we need of these technologies.

Reid Frazier: So can you explain what this bill would do?

Paulina Jaramillo: The bill is huge; it’s over 400 pages long. It has a lot of provisions. In the big picture, it has a lot of provisions that are geared towards being able to build out the grid. And so things like giving authority to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to manage permitting of projects without having the Department of Energy first designate certain areas as corridors of transmission.

It also would require regional planning of transmission so that regions have to coordinate their transmission plans. And one of the things that is really good [in the bill] is that it could really accelerate the deployment of grid-enhancing technologies in existing corridors. Those are technologies that have been developed that could increase an existing transmission line’s capacity to deliver power, even though those projects are not building new transmission lines, deploying them requires permitting. This would ease some of those restrictions so that we could redo that of technology deployment.

Reid Frazier: What parts of the bill do you like and are worth passing?

Paulina Jaramillo: The grid technology, especially the transmission provisions, I think are really good. I think there are some reasonable timeline requirements for doing environmental review and for how long judicial review or basically how long opponents have to file lawsuits after a report like an environmental impact study is released.

I know that some environmentalists are worried about it, but I think some of those timelines are reasonable. We definitely cannot be having people sue six years after a review comes out. There’s funding associated with, so the authorizing, the bill authorizes funding to support permitting processes. So those are good things that I think will help the system.

Reid Frazier: What are some parts of the bill that give you pause?

Paulina Jaramillo: There are definitely some changes to the Clean Water Act and to the Endangered Species Act and to The National Historic Preservation Act that have [drawn] concerns.

I think the Clean Water Act changes are a serious concern. The way the bill is written, it would remove some authority from the states, and sometimes states are the ones that serve as a backstop when the federal government doesn’t act as it should. And so taking that power away could be a concern.

And then tribal organizations are really worried about the changes to some of these, especially the National Historic Preservation Act and the processes through which the agencies have to engage with tribes in doing these permits. And I think we need to take seriously the concerns of tribal members or of tribal organizations.

So when you look at the list, the list of concerns seems very long, whereas the list of things that are good by the bill, maybe it’s a little shorter. But that’s where I’m really struggling is, are the impacts of the transmission and the grid provisions large enough that we accept some of the costs associated with the environmental loss?

Reid Frazier: Where do you see the balance between having to build a lot of clean energy infrastructure and also having to balance out a lot of countervailing constituencies, like Native American tribes, environmental groups, local communities that might not often want to host a big renewable energy project? How do you see this balance working out?

Paulina Jaramillo: I think there are ways, there are interventions that we can put in place so that, yes, there are people who are going to live close to mining communities that are [going to be impacted]. But we can ensure that those mines are safe. And there are mechanisms to compensate those people for that added cost. But it’s not easy.

You do need the policies in place. And in this case, it allows us to build the infrastructure, but maybe diminishes a little bit our ability to protect those communities. That’s a true trade-off. And so that is why I haven’t really made up my mind fully [on the bill] because it is hard, as an environmentally conscious person, to give up on some of the environmental provisions.

But at the same time, I think climate change is our biggest challenge. And if we cannot address climate change, our water is not going be clean, our air is not going to be clean, our endangered species, we’re going to keep losing species.

I’ve been working on climate change for 20 years, and we’ve made progress. Emissions have decreased over, compared to what they were in 2005, but nowhere at the speed that we need them to. It’s just more time passes and we keep not moving forward at the speed that we [need]. So that weighs heavily on me.

name: Clean Energy
title: Who pays to clean up a coal mine? - Montana Free Press
authors: Ellis Juhlin, Jessica Plance, Nora Mabie, Nick Mott, Robert Chaney
description:
Mining companies are responsible for cleaning up after their coal mines, per Montana state and federal law.
In Montana, before mining can begin, a company must deposit money into a reclamation bond with the state Department of Environmental Quality.
DEQ sets reclamation bond amounts, the dollar figure a mining company has to put down in order to operate in the state.
Once mining activities are complete, the landscape must be restored through a process often referred to as mining reclamation.
Westmoreland Mining, a company operating three coal mines in the state, said DEQ violated federal law by not submitting the new guidelines to the federal Office of Surface Mining.
text:
This story is produced by Montana Free Press/Mountain Journal in collaboration with Grist as part of the Report for America Local News Initiative.

Mining companies are responsible for cleaning up after their coal mines, per Montana state and federal law. But that doesn’t always happen. They can go bankrupt or be unable to afford reclamation costs. At that stage, the responsibility falls to state or federal government agencies.

In Montana, before mining can begin, a company must deposit money into a reclamation bond with the state Department of Environmental Quality. It’s a financial guarantee that ensures the state can afford to reclaim a mine in the event that the mine operator cannot. DEQ sets reclamation bond amounts, the dollar figure a mining company has to put down in order to operate in the state.

“The best way to think of it is it’s an insurance policy,” said Eric Dahlgren, DEQ’s mining bureau chief. “It’s an insurance policy for the state of Montana to ensure that the mining disturbance is reclaimed.”

In July, the agency passed new calculation guidelines around how it sets those amounts. “It’s really there to ensure that if similar reclamation activities are performed at different mines, that we’re using comparable assumptions while also accounting for the site-specific conditions at each mine,” Dahlgren said.

Developing a coal mine, as well as the mining process itself, can clear a landscape of vegetation, dig up layers of soil and rock to access coal deposits, and remove groundwater or discharge mining waste into downstream waterways. Once mining activities are complete, the landscape must be restored through a process often referred to as mining reclamation.

It’s lengthy and expensive to restore a landscape after a coal-mining operation and the bond ensures the state has the funds to see the process through. Reclamation requirements are set under the federal Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act, passed in the 1970s, and carried out by state agencies in some states, including Montana.

Westmoreland Mining, a company operating three coal mines in the state, said DEQ violated federal law by not submitting the new guidelines to the federal Office of Surface Mining. In a 60-day Notice of Intent to Sue, which Westmoreland sent to DEQ on Oct. 15, the company wrote the changes to calculating bonding amounts “fundamentally alter how DEQ applies its approved bonding provisions.” Westmoreland said the guidelines are part of a new regulatory framework and must be submitted to the federal agency for approval. Last month, the mining company asked OSM to step in and stop DEQ from carrying out the new guidelines.

The Montana Mining Association, which represents Westmoreland, along with other mining companies in the state, submitted comments and concerns to DEQ over the new guidelines and sent a letter outlining its concerns to OSM. In the letter, the Mining Association also requested the federal agency exercise oversight to review and disapprove of DEQ’s calculations.

“A bond is supposed to be an honest estimate of what reclamation would cost, and these guidelines in our opinion do not achieve that and go far overboard,” Matt Vincent, the Mining Association’s executive director, said in a statement to Montana Free Press. DEQ’s estimates “can add up to millions of dollars more than the work would really cost,” he added.

Vincent said the Mining Association is supportive of bonding, but that overestimating bonds can hamstring funds.

“The question isn’t whether mines should be bonded,” he said. “They absolutely and positively should be. It’s how big the bond should be. Too small puts taxpayers at risk. Too big ties up millions of dollars that could go to jobs, operations, reclamation work, or even important projects for the communities in which the mines operate. Overbonding only makes Montana a harder place to keep mining.”

Emails obtained by Montana Free Press show OSM asked DEQ to address the Mining Association’s and Westmoreland’s concerns. In response, DEQ refuted the claims and said that because the guidelines are not a change to regulation, OSM’s request was not appropriate. The letter goes on to say that MMA and Westmoreland do not have the authority to ask the federal office to step in and review the guidelines.

“Westmoreland is attempting to misuse potential federal oversight to force DEQ to allow it to set its own bond and determine its own liability risk,” wrote DEQ, adding that Westmoreland’s intent is contrary to state and federal law.

A spokesperson for DEQ told MTFP that the agency does not comment on pending litigation.

Derf Johnson, deputy director of the mining industry watchdog group Montana Environmental Information Center, referred to the new guidelines as a “good step forward.”

“They added indirect costs associated with reclamation and inflation,” Johnson said. “Having these fixed amounts is part of where the state gets in trouble.”

There have been times in the past, he added, where the bond amount is less than the actual cost of reclamation, which can lead to the state using taxpayer dollars to clean up environmental damage.

“If you’re thinking about who should be responsible for that reclamation, that’s the businesses making the money off it,” Johnson said. “This is the cost of doing business. It shouldn’t be borne by taxpayers and that’s why we have this bonding system in place.”

The 60-day notice of intent to sue that Westmoreland filed will expire in mid-December. The company could sue DEQ after that, unless the federal Office of Surface Mining adjusts the guidelines.

text:
Surging electricity demand, artificial intelligence growth, and renewable energy expansion are rapidly transforming rural land use across the United States. During a panel discussion titled "At a Crossroads: How Data Centers, Solar, Wind, and Land Use Are Reshaping U.S. Agriculture," industry leaders examined how farmers, ranchers, and rural communities can navigate these competing pressures while protecting agricultural production and private property rights.

Moderated by Cyndi, the session featured Joby Young, executive vice president of the American Farm Bureau Federation; Greg Brophy, a farmer and representative with Renewable Energy Farmers of America (REFA); and Daniel Nibarger, strategic negotiator with Google.

Exploding Power Demand and the Push for Rural Land

After decades of relatively flat electricity consumption, the U.S. power grid is experiencing massive growth driven by artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and shifts in energy generation. According to Nibarger, AI and advanced digital tools have become essential decision-making partners in agriculture, requiring substantial backend data center infrastructure to process complex farm data.

For producers facing tight margins, offers to lease or sell acreage for solar panels, wind turbines, or data centers can be financially compelling. Brophy noted that during challenging commodity cycles—such as crop years 2015 through 2020 when he made no money farming—diversified revenue streams from energy projects can keep family operations afloat and help bring the next generation back to the farm.

"If you convert a field to solar, for instance, you may not be farming it any longer, but that's a temporary conversion," Brophy said, comparing the 30- to 35-year lifespan of a solar lease to the Conservation Reserve Program, after which land can return to agricultural production.

While the U.S. has lost roughly 300 million acres of farmland since 1950 while doubling food and fiber output, Brophy emphasized that he is far more concerned about permanent losses to urban and suburban sprawl than temporary energy leases.

Balancing Property Rights and Community Impact

Young noted that across the American Farm Bureau's 2,800 county chapters, land-use debates consistently center on balancing a landowner's private property rights against the broader interests of the surrounding community. Unlike temporary solar leases, data center developments typically represent permanent, one-way land conversions.

"We are for a balanced approach that takes all these factors into consideration—the benefits, the risks, the costs—and making sure that from a public policy perspective, whether at a local level or moving up to a state level and so forth, and in the national conversation, that it's one that balances all these things," Young said.

Young pointed out that while states like Virginia—home to more than 700 data centers—and Texas have navigated these developments for years, the rapid acceleration of projects has caught many rural counties off guard. More than 40 municipalities nationwide recently voted to enact restrictions or moratoria on data center construction as local officials work to catch up.

Infrastructure, Water, and "Good Neighbor" Commitments

When evaluating potential sites, Nibarger explained that Google prioritizes brownfield sites, industrial parks, and retired power plants—such as a converted coal plant in Jackson, Alabama—where high-voltage transmission infrastructure already exists.

To address rural concerns over water depletion, noise, and utility rate hikes, Nibarger outlined Google's "Good Neighbor Principles," which include funding its own energy infrastructure upgrades under clean transition tariffs so local ratepayers do not subsidize data center power. He also noted that Google no longer uses non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with government officials, allowing local leaders and residents to have open conversations early in the planning process.

Regarding water consumption, Nibarger stated that Google conducts deep hydrological studies and utilizes closed-loop hybrid and air-cooling systems—similar to a vehicle radiator—that recycle water rather than drawing continuously from local aquifers. In water-stressed regions or areas where municipalities need infrastructure support, the company also invests in upgrading local water treatment and stormwater drainage facilities.

"If you've seen a data center, then you've seen a data center," Nibarger said, emphasizing that every community engagement plan must be tailored to local needs, whether that means supporting 4-H and FFA programs in Kansas or addressing medical and infrastructure gaps elsewhere.

Preparing Farmers and Local Leaders for Negotiations

During the audience question-and-answer session, broadcasters—including Farm Director KC Sheperd of the Oklahoma Farm Report, who noted Google's active development in Stillwater, Oklahoma—raised questions about closed-loop water systems, turbine blade recycling, and setback distances.

Nibarger confirmed that Google relies on reclaimed gray water and storm runoff rather than potable water where possible, while Brophy noted that the wind industry and the National Energy Lab of the Rockies are actively developing fully recyclable turbine blades alongside alternative uses such as agricultural windbreaks and road-base aggregate.

As developers increasingly look to rural America for land and power, all three panelists urged farmers and county officials to be proactive rather than reactive.

"They only pass pie every so often, so if they're passing pie, you ought to get a piece," Brophy advised landowners, while urging them to hire experienced attorneys and consult organizations like REFA before signing long-term agreements with professional landmen.

Young echoed the call for early preparation, noting that local governments and residents must define their community priorities before developers arrive at the table.

"Every partner should go into this project, like many projects, treating farmers, treating that rural community as a partner, not an obstacle," Young said.
