title: Rivian Takes $1000 Off R1, BMW $3750 Off i5 And i4 Through Nov. 30 - EVXL
authors: Haye Kesteloo, H. Kesteloo, D. Kesteloo, EVXL Wire
description:
BMW has a $3,750 purchase credit on the i4 and i5 through the same Monday.
A BMW i5 charging at an IONNA Rechargery.
Image credit: BMW The larger numbers in circulation depend on who is buying.
Buyers of a 2027 i5 also get the $500 public charging credit EVXL reported on November 6.
Sources: Rivian, BMW USA, BMW Blog, Mercedes-Benz High-Power Charging, Mercedes-Benz High-Power Charging terms EVXL uses automated tools to support research and source retrieval.
text:
Rivian is taking $1,000 off any new R1S or R1T ordered from its inventory between Friday, November 27, and Monday, November 30. BMW has a $3,750 purchase credit on the i4 and i5 through the same Monday. Mercedes-Benz is discounting energy at its own fast chargers by 25% until January 3, for drivers of any car who pay by card.

None of the three was in EVXL’s Black Friday roundup on Wednesday, which covered 12 offers led by Polestar’s $25,000 cut. We checked these on the companies’ own websites on Friday, November 27.

Rivian’s $1,000 Needs An Order By Monday And Delivery By December 31

Rivian’s offer page gives $1,000 off a new 2026 or 2027 R1S or R1T ordered from inventory through its R1 Shop between November 27 and November 30. It applies to a purchase or a lease. The buyer has to complete the deal and take delivery by December 31.

Rivian says the discount can be combined with its other current offers, “as permitted by Rivian” in the fine print. Lucid’s Black Friday credits, by contrast, do not stack. The offer is limited to U.S. inventory, and Rivian says it can change or end it without notice. It names only the R1, not the R2.

BMW’s $3,750 Becomes $5,750 On An i5 Only For Returning Customers

BMW’s national offers page lists a $3,750 purchase credit off MSRP on the 2026 i4 eDrive40 and xDrive40, the 2026 i5 M60 and the 2027 i5 eDrive40 and xDrive40. It pairs the credit with 3.99% financing for up to 60 months. The Road Home Sales Event ends November 30.

A BMW i5 charging at an IONNA Rechargery. Image credit: BMW

The larger numbers in circulation depend on who is buying. BMW Blog, using dealer-bulletin data from CarsDirect, reports that a customer who has owned or leased a BMW in the last 12 months can add a $2,000 loyalty credit on the i5 and $1,000 on the i4. That makes $5,750 and $4,750. It also reports that the credits require financing through BMW Financial Services, so most cash buyers miss them, and that the loyalty money requires delivery by November 30. Those totals are not on BMW’s national page, and BMW’s offers vary by region and dealer, so confirm them with a dealer.

BMW Blog puts the 2027 i5 eDrive40 at $68,550 and the 2026 i4 eDrive40 at $59,250, both with destination. Buyers of a 2027 i5 also get the $500 public charging credit EVXL reported on November 6. The i4 is in its last model year before the Neue Klasse i3 replaces it.

Mercedes Takes 25% Off Charging, But Not With Plug & Charge

Mercedes-Benz High-Power Charging is taking 25% off energy at participating U.S. and Canadian stations from November 25 through January 3, 2027. The driver starts the session with a credit or debit card at the charger, scans the QR code on the screen and enters the code HOLIDAYCHARGE.

The terms exclude sessions started through Plug & Charge, third-party apps or roaming partners. Drivers whose cars use Plug & Charge have to tap the card before plugging in, the promotion page says. The discount applies to energy only, not to idle fees, parking fees or taxes. The terms set no requirement on the make of car.

Thirteen locations are excluded. Twelve are at Buc-ee’s travel centers in Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, South Carolina, Tennessee and Texas, and the thirteenth is at Mercedes-Benz USA’s headquarters in Sandy Springs, Georgia.

EVXL’s Take

These are the small offers of the weekend, and I’d read the deadlines before the dollar amounts. Rivian’s $1,000 is modest on a vehicle in the R1’s price range, but Rivian lets it stack with its other offers and gives you until December 31 to take delivery. BMW’s $5,750 is the number that will get repeated, and most shoppers won’t qualify for it. If you don’t already have a BMW in the driveway, your number is $3,750, and by BMW Blog’s account only if you finance through BMW. The loyalty money needs the car delivered by Monday.

I’d use the Mercedes discount. It asks for nothing but a card and a code, it runs through the whole holiday travel season, and it isn’t tied to owning a Mercedes. Tap the card before you plug in, or Plug & Charge will start the session at full price.

title: How Ebikes Could Transform the Way People Get Around Los Angeles
description:
Los Angeles is famous for its sunshine, beaches, entertainment industry, and sprawling neighborhoods.
Reducing Dependence on Cars for Everyday Trips One of the biggest opportunities for ebikes in Los Angeles is replacing short car journeys.
Making Los Angeles Hills Easier to Navigate Los Angeles is not completely flat.
Making Longer Urban Journeys More Accessible Los Angeles is geographically spread out.
However, e-bikes are not a complete solution to Los Angeles transportation challenges.
text:
Los Angeles is famous for its sunshine, beaches, entertainment industry, and sprawling neighborhoods. However, getting around the city is not always easy. Heavy traffic, long commuting distances, expensive parking, and dependence on personal vehicles make everyday transportation challenging for many residents.

For decades, cars have dominated transportation in Los Angeles. But that may gradually change as electric bicycles become a more practical option for commuting, shopping, recreation, and short-distance travel.

E-bikes offer something that traditional bicycles cannot always provide: the ability to travel farther and tackle hills without requiring the same level of physical effort. They also give residents more flexibility when choosing how to get around, particularly for trips that are too long to walk but too short to justify driving.

With improvements in cycling infrastructure, growing interest in sustainable transportation, and increasingly capable electric bikes, Los Angeles has an opportunity to make e-bikes a much bigger part of everyday urban mobility.

1. Reducing Dependence on Cars for Everyday Trips

One of the biggest opportunities for ebikes in Los Angeles is replacing short car journeys.

Consider a typical weekday. Someone might drive three miles to buy groceries, another two miles to visit a coffee shop, and four miles to meet a friend. Each journey may seem insignificant, but collectively, these short trips contribute to traffic congestion, fuel consumption, and parking demand.

An electric bicycle can handle many of these journeys without requiring a car.

For example, residents living in neighborhoods such as Silver Lake, Echo Park, Culver City, or Santa Monica may find an e-bike useful for visiting nearby businesses, commuting to local workplaces, or running errands.

Electric assistance also makes cycling more accessible to people who might otherwise avoid traditional bicycles because of distance, hills, or physical fatigue.

A rider can choose how much assistance to use, allowing them to arrive at work without necessarily needing a shower or a complete change of clothes.

This flexibility could make e-bikes particularly attractive to people who want to reduce their daily driving but are not ready to give up their cars entirely.

Rather than replacing every car journey, e-bikes can replace the trips where driving offers relatively little advantage.

2. Making Public Transportation More Convenient

Public transportation is an important part of Los Angeles mobility, but getting from a person’s home to a train station or from a station to their final destination can sometimes be inconvenient.

This is known as the first-mile and last-mile transportation problem.

An e-bike can help solve it.

For instance, someone living several miles from an E Line station could ride an electric bicycle to the station, continue their journey by train, and use another transportation option at the destination.

This combination can make public transportation more practical for people who do not live within comfortable walking distance of a station.

Los Angeles already has infrastructure supporting bicycle and public transportation connections.

According to LA Metro’s September 2026 transportation statistics, the regional bicycle network includes approximately 1,935 miles of bicycle facilities, including 77 miles of separated Class IV bicycle lanes. Metro Bike Share also operates 225 stations, with approximately 1,800 bicycles and 430,000 recorded rides in 2025.

These figures demonstrate that cycling is already becoming part of the region’s wider transportation system.

However, riders should understand the limitations of bringing their own electric bicycles onto public transportation.

Metro allows electric bicycles on trains if they are comparable in size to regular bicycles, subject to security inspection. However, motorized bicycles and bicycles weighing more than 55 pounds cannot be accommodated on Metro bus-mounted bicycle racks.

This is particularly relevant when considering a heavier model such as the Himiway D5 2.0 20″, which weighs approximately 80 pounds.

Its listed length is 70 inches, but its weight and wide tires can make station access and handling less convenient. Riders should check Metro’s current requirements before planning a train journey with this particular model.

For many commuters, a lighter electric bicycle or a shared bicycle at the destination may be more practical for public transportation connections.

3. Making Los Angeles Hills Easier to Navigate

Los Angeles is not completely flat.

Neighborhoods around Hollywood, Griffith Park, Silver Lake, and the Hollywood Hills include challenging climbs that can discourage people from commuting by traditional bicycle.

This is where electric assistance becomes especially valuable.

A conventional bicycle requires the rider to provide all the power needed to climb a hill. An electric bicycle supplements the rider’s effort, making uphill journeys more manageable.

For people who want additional climbing support, a 750w ebike can be an appealing option.

The Himiway D5 2.0 20″ provides a useful example. It features a 750W geared hub motor with 90Nm of torque, designed to provide electric assistance during acceleration and uphill riding.

Its 48V 15Ah battery offers 720Wh of capacity, giving riders additional flexibility for longer journeys.

The bike also features a Shimano eight-speed drivetrain. Riders can combine appropriate gearing with pedal assistance instead of relying entirely on the throttle when climbing.

This is important because electric assistance does not eliminate the physical demands of steep hills. Choosing the right gear, maintaining a steady pedaling rhythm, and managing battery consumption still matter.

For someone commuting through a neighborhood with several climbs, these features can make the difference between cycling regularly and continuing to drive.

4. Making Longer Urban Journeys More Accessible

Los Angeles is geographically spread out. Traveling between neighborhoods can involve considerable distances, especially when commuting across different parts of the city.

Traditional bicycles can be tiring over longer distances, particularly for people who are not regular cyclists.

E-bikes extend the practical distance many people are comfortable riding.

For example, a resident might use an electric bicycle to travel between home, a nearby shopping district, a recreational area, and a workplace without depending on a car for every journey.

Battery capacity is an important consideration when choosing an e-bike for this purpose.

The Himiway D5 2.0 20″ has a 48V 15Ah battery, equivalent to 720Wh. Himiway advertises a maximum pedal-assist range of up to 70 miles and a throttle range of up to 40 miles.

These are manufacturer estimates rather than guaranteed real-world distances.

Actual range depends on several factors:

Rider and cargo weight.

Terrain and elevation changes.

Pedal-assist level and throttle usage.

Tire pressure and road conditions.

Riding speed and frequent acceleration.

Temperature and battery condition.

For example, someone planning a 20-mile round trip through relatively flat neighborhoods may use considerably less battery than someone covering the same distance through steep hills with frequent stops.

The best approach is to test the bike on the actual commuting route and leave enough battery reserve for unexpected detours.

5. Making Everyday Cycling More Comfortable

Another reason e-bikes could become more popular in Los Angeles is comfort.

Some people avoid cycling because conventional bicycles can feel uncomfortable on uneven pavement, rough streets, and poorly maintained roads.

A comfortable electric bicycle can make everyday journeys more enjoyable and encourage people to ride more frequently.

The Himiway D5 2.0 20″ combines several features intended to improve riding comfort.

Its 20 × 4.0-inch fat tires provide a wider contact area than conventional narrow bicycle tires. Its full-suspension design includes a 90mm front suspension fork and 100mm rear suspension travel.

Together, these components help absorb some of the vibrations and impacts encountered on uneven surfaces.

The bike also includes a memory-foam comfort saddle, an adjustable stem, and a torque/cadence sensor system that allows riders to choose between different assistance experiences.

These features may appeal to people who want an electric bicycle for both commuting and recreational riding.

However, wide tires and full suspension also add weight and can increase rolling resistance compared with lightweight urban commuter bicycles.

The D5 2.0 20″ weighs approximately 80 pounds, so it is not an ideal choice for everyone, particularly riders who frequently need to carry a bicycle upstairs or lift it onto a vehicle.

Choosing an e-bike should involve considering the complete daily riding environment, not just motor power or battery capacity.

6. Supporting Local Businesses and Neighborhood Economies

E-bikes could also change how people interact with their neighborhoods.

When residents travel by car, they often focus on reaching a specific destination. Parking availability, traffic, and driving distances can discourage spontaneous stops at local businesses.

Cycling creates a different experience.

People riding through a neighborhood can more easily stop at independent coffee shops, restaurants, grocery stores, farmers markets, and other local businesses.

For example, an e-bike rider in Santa Monica might visit a local grocery store, stop for coffee, and continue to a nearby park without having to find a new parking space for every destination.

This type of mobility can encourage more neighborhood-level spending and make local commercial districts more accessible.

Electric bicycles equipped with practical storage options can also support everyday shopping.

The Himiway D5 2.0 20″ includes a rear rack with a listed capacity of up to 120 pounds. Riders can use compatible baskets or pannier bags to carry groceries, work equipment, and other everyday items.

Of course, cargo capacity should not be confused with the recommended load for every individual trip. Riders must stay within the manufacturer’s overall payload limits and secure cargo properly.

For many households, using an e-bike for small shopping trips could reduce the need to start a car for every errand.

7. Reducing Transportation Emissions and Improving Urban Living

Transportation is a major contributor to greenhouse gas emissions in the United States.

Electric vehicles have an important role in reducing transportation emissions, but electric bicycles offer another approach.

An e-bike requires substantially less energy to move a person than a typical passenger car. It also occupies less road and parking space.

When an electric bicycle replaces a car journey, it can reduce the emissions associated with that particular trip, including direct vehicle exhaust.

The environmental benefits are especially meaningful when people use e-bikes for routine journeys rather than purchasing one exclusively for occasional recreation.

E-bikes can also contribute to quieter neighborhoods and reduce demand for parking spaces.

Imagine a neighborhood where more residents cycle to nearby shops, workplaces, and public transportation stations.

Fewer short car journeys could mean less local traffic, less demand for parking, and a more pleasant street environment.

However, e-bikes are not a complete solution to Los Angeles transportation challenges. Their environmental benefits depend on actual car-trip replacement, electricity sources, battery manufacturing, and responsible battery disposal.

The biggest impact will come from making cycling a convenient and safe everyday transportation choice.

8. Better Cycling Infrastructure Is Essential

Even the most capable electric bicycle cannot solve every transportation problem.

One of the biggest barriers to e-bike adoption in Los Angeles remains road safety.

Many streets were designed primarily around motor vehicles. Riders may encounter fast-moving traffic, complicated intersections, parked cars, opening vehicle doors, potholes, and discontinuous bicycle lanes.

For e-bikes to become a mainstream transportation option, infrastructure improvements must keep pace with growing demand.

The Los Angeles Department of Transportation is working on bicycle infrastructure projects throughout the city, including improvements along the LA River, the Expo Line corridor, and streets with high rates of serious bicycle-related crashes.

Protected bicycle lanes, safer intersections, secure bicycle parking, and better connections between neighborhoods can make cycling more attractive to people who currently feel uncomfortable riding alongside traffic.

Education is equally important.

E-bike riders should understand traffic signals, turning procedures, safe following distances, and the differences between bicycle classes.

California recognizes three e-bike classifications:

Class 1: Pedal assistance only, stopping at 20 mph.

Class 2: Throttle-assisted operation, with assistance stopping at 20 mph.

Class 3: Pedal assistance only, stopping at 28 mph, with a speedometer.

California also prohibits riders under 16 from operating Class 3 e-bikes and requires helmets for all Class 3 riders. Riders under 18 must wear helmets on other e-bike classes as well.

The Himiway D5 2.0 20″ is advertised with a 750W motor, a thumb throttle, a default maximum speed of 20 mph, and adjustable speed settings. Because its specifications list multiple class configurations, buyers should verify the permanent classification label and the exact throttle and pedal-assist settings of their individual bicycle before using it on public roads.

A 28 mph setting alone does not establish Class 3 compliance. California Class 3 bicycles must provide pedal assistance rather than unrestricted throttle propulsion.

Riders should follow the applicable classification and local trail restrictions rather than assuming every bicycle path permits every type of e-bike.

9. How Los Angeles Residents Can Start Using E-Bikes

For people considering an electric bicycle, the easiest approach is to begin with one or two regular journeys rather than immediately replacing every car trip.

Here are some practical steps:

Start with a manageable route. Choose a relatively short journey to a grocery store, workplace, or nearby transportation station.

Check the bicycle infrastructure. Look for dedicated bike lanes and safer alternative streets. A slightly longer route with better separation from traffic may be preferable to the shortest route.

Choose a bike that matches your needs. Consider motor assistance, battery capacity, weight, comfort, cargo requirements, and storage space.

Practice before commuting. Become familiar with acceleration, braking, turning, and stopping before riding in busy traffic.

Protect your bicycle. Use a high-quality lock, choose secure parking, and avoid leaving an expensive e-bike unattended for extended periods.

Maintain the battery and brakes. Check tire pressure, inspect brake pads, and follow the manufacturer’s battery charging and storage recommendations.

These small decisions can make e-bike ownership more practical and help riders develop sustainable transportation habits.

title: Why homeowners who go electric have advantage - Finance & Commerce
description:
The Blueprint Census data show 7% of homeowners have solar panels, compared with 2.8% of renters.
Electric or plug-in hybrid vehicles are owned by 6.4% of homeowners versus 3.6% of renters.
And now homeowners have a new financial advantage that has nothing to do with equity or rising property values: electrification.
While using solar panels or an EV can help, the real financial advantage comes from using them together.
Getting more out of the same investment Say a homeowner installs solar panels to cut their electric bill.
text:
The Blueprint

Census data show 7% of homeowners have solar panels, compared with 2.8% of renters.

Electric or plug-in hybrid vehicles are owned by 6.4% of homeowners versus 3.6% of renters.

A $24,000 solar installation could pay for itself in approximately 10 years when paired with home EV charging.

Community solar subscriptions could reduce renters’ electricity bills by 5% to 15%, according to Columbia University’s Climate School dean.

Owning a home has long been one of the most effective ways to build long-term wealth. And now homeowners have a new financial advantage that has nothing to do with equity or rising property values: electrification.

Homeowners who take advantage of green energy to power their homes and cars can potentially save money on electricity bills and transportation costs. But for renters, this benefit might be out of reach.

Data recently released by the Census Bureau show that 6.4% of homeowner households have an electric or plug-in hybrid vehicle, compared with only 3.6% of renter households. Another Census finding shows that 7% of owner-occupied homes have solar panels, compared with 2.8% of renter-occupied homes.

While using solar panels or an EV can help, the real financial advantage comes from using them together.

Getting more out of the same investment

Say a homeowner installs solar panels to cut their electric bill. During the day, those panels might generate more electricity than the home needs, with the rest going back to the utility company.

The catch is that the utility might pay considerably less for that electricity than it charges customers to buy it back.

In California, for example, state regulators say compensation for excess solar electricity under the state’s newer billing system is generally lower than retail electricity rates.

That’s where owning an EV can pay off.

“The less your utility pays you for exported solar, the more it’s worth to keep that energy and put it in your car,” said Alexis Abramson, dean of Columbia University’s Climate School.

If you’re paying 20 cents per kilowatt hour to use electricity, for example, but the utility buys your excess solar-generated power for only 5 cents, you’re on the losing end of that trade. By using that electricity to charge up your EV, you could get an additional 15 cents of value per kilowatt hour.

Jesslyn Pei, a former infrastructure investment and asset management professional, estimated that a $24,000 solar installation could pay for itself in about 10 years if the homeowner uses the solar-generated electricity to charge an electric vehicle at home, assuming favorable conditions. Solar alone, she said, might take 13 to 14 years.

But if homeowners use the electricity they generate instead of selling it to the grid at a low rate, they can recoup the high upfront cost of a solar installation much more rapidly. “The more use cases for utilization, the shorter the payback period,” Pei said.

Making the numbers work

Of course, homeowners don’t necessarily have to make two expensive purchases at once to start saving money.

The Department of Energy says some EVs can add 2 to 5 miles of driving range per hour using an ordinary household outlet. For drivers with shorter commutes, that might eliminate the need for a more expensive charging installation.

Other opportunities include charging during cheaper overnight hours, checking utility discounts for EV owners and comparing the value of using solar electricity against selling it back to the grid.

But going electric isn’t automatically a good financial decision. Abramson cautioned that a shaded roof, an aging roof that may soon need replacing or particularly low electricity prices in a community can make solar a poor investment. Financing costs can also eat into any savings.

She recommended running the numbers with a local installer, including the cost of financing and any available state or local incentives, before committing to a system.

What about renters?

As renters by definition don’t own their properties, they’re usually limited in how they can modify them. For example, renters generally can’t install rooftop solar panels or home chargers without their landlord’s cooperation.

Other options might be available, however.

Abramson says community solar subscriptions can reduce electricity bills by 5% to 15%, with potentially greater savings for qualifying low-income households. Renters with an EV can benefit from workplace chargers, potentially cheaper overnight charging rates and buying an affordable used EV to lower the upfront cost.

More innovative solutions might be coming. Abramson pointed to plug-in balcony solar systems, which are gaining attention as a lower-cost alternative to traditional rooftop installations. They can be used with regular wall plugs and are portable. While not eliminating the benefit gap with homeowners, these types of options provide renters with choices.

Before spending thousands of dollars, homeowners should compare the total upfront costs against their expected annual savings, including financing expenses and any available incentives. They should also consider how long they plan to stay in the home. The longer you plan on staying put, the bigger the potential savings.

text:
Surging electricity demand, artificial intelligence growth, and renewable energy expansion are rapidly transforming rural land use across the United States. During a panel discussion titled "At a Crossroads: How Data Centers, Solar, Wind, and Land Use Are Reshaping U.S. Agriculture," industry leaders examined how farmers, ranchers, and rural communities can navigate these competing pressures while protecting agricultural production and private property rights.

Moderated by Cyndi, the session featured Joby Young, executive vice president of the American Farm Bureau Federation; Greg Brophy, a farmer and representative with Renewable Energy Farmers of America (REFA); and Daniel Nibarger, strategic negotiator with Google.

Exploding Power Demand and the Push for Rural Land

After decades of relatively flat electricity consumption, the U.S. power grid is experiencing massive growth driven by artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and shifts in energy generation. According to Nibarger, AI and advanced digital tools have become essential decision-making partners in agriculture, requiring substantial backend data center infrastructure to process complex farm data.

For producers facing tight margins, offers to lease or sell acreage for solar panels, wind turbines, or data centers can be financially compelling. Brophy noted that during challenging commodity cycles—such as crop years 2015 through 2020 when he made no money farming—diversified revenue streams from energy projects can keep family operations afloat and help bring the next generation back to the farm.

"If you convert a field to solar, for instance, you may not be farming it any longer, but that's a temporary conversion," Brophy said, comparing the 30- to 35-year lifespan of a solar lease to the Conservation Reserve Program, after which land can return to agricultural production.

While the U.S. has lost roughly 300 million acres of farmland since 1950 while doubling food and fiber output, Brophy emphasized that he is far more concerned about permanent losses to urban and suburban sprawl than temporary energy leases.

Balancing Property Rights and Community Impact

Young noted that across the American Farm Bureau's 2,800 county chapters, land-use debates consistently center on balancing a landowner's private property rights against the broader interests of the surrounding community. Unlike temporary solar leases, data center developments typically represent permanent, one-way land conversions.

"We are for a balanced approach that takes all these factors into consideration—the benefits, the risks, the costs—and making sure that from a public policy perspective, whether at a local level or moving up to a state level and so forth, and in the national conversation, that it's one that balances all these things," Young said.

Young pointed out that while states like Virginia—home to more than 700 data centers—and Texas have navigated these developments for years, the rapid acceleration of projects has caught many rural counties off guard. More than 40 municipalities nationwide recently voted to enact restrictions or moratoria on data center construction as local officials work to catch up.

Infrastructure, Water, and "Good Neighbor" Commitments

When evaluating potential sites, Nibarger explained that Google prioritizes brownfield sites, industrial parks, and retired power plants—such as a converted coal plant in Jackson, Alabama—where high-voltage transmission infrastructure already exists.

To address rural concerns over water depletion, noise, and utility rate hikes, Nibarger outlined Google's "Good Neighbor Principles," which include funding its own energy infrastructure upgrades under clean transition tariffs so local ratepayers do not subsidize data center power. He also noted that Google no longer uses non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with government officials, allowing local leaders and residents to have open conversations early in the planning process.

Regarding water consumption, Nibarger stated that Google conducts deep hydrological studies and utilizes closed-loop hybrid and air-cooling systems—similar to a vehicle radiator—that recycle water rather than drawing continuously from local aquifers. In water-stressed regions or areas where municipalities need infrastructure support, the company also invests in upgrading local water treatment and stormwater drainage facilities.

"If you've seen a data center, then you've seen a data center," Nibarger said, emphasizing that every community engagement plan must be tailored to local needs, whether that means supporting 4-H and FFA programs in Kansas or addressing medical and infrastructure gaps elsewhere.

Preparing Farmers and Local Leaders for Negotiations

During the audience question-and-answer session, broadcasters—including Farm Director KC Sheperd of the Oklahoma Farm Report, who noted Google's active development in Stillwater, Oklahoma—raised questions about closed-loop water systems, turbine blade recycling, and setback distances.

Nibarger confirmed that Google relies on reclaimed gray water and storm runoff rather than potable water where possible, while Brophy noted that the wind industry and the National Energy Lab of the Rockies are actively developing fully recyclable turbine blades alongside alternative uses such as agricultural windbreaks and road-base aggregate.

As developers increasingly look to rural America for land and power, all three panelists urged farmers and county officials to be proactive rather than reactive.

"They only pass pie every so often, so if they're passing pie, you ought to get a piece," Brophy advised landowners, while urging them to hire experienced attorneys and consult organizations like REFA before signing long-term agreements with professional landmen.

Young echoed the call for early preparation, noting that local governments and residents must define their community priorities before developers arrive at the table.

"Every partner should go into this project, like many projects, treating farmers, treating that rural community as a partner, not an obstacle," Young said.

Alongside the expansion of its manufacturing facilities, Andersen has been investing in new technologies and introducing AI into its production processes. These developments are designed to improve operational efficiency, streamline production and support a more responsive manufacturing operation.

One of the key benefits for customers is the introduction of same-day dispatch across Andersen's A2, A3 and Andersen Quartz home charger ranges. Customers placing an order before 11am on a working day can now have their charger in their chosen colour and specification dispatched that same day.

The expansion comes as Andersen continues to develop partnerships across the automotive, retail and design sectors, strengthening its position within the premium EV market. A further collaboration with English Heritage has brought distinctive heritage-inspired finishes to the Andersen range, demonstrating the brand's commitment to combining contemporary technology with considered design.

“We have seen considerable growth in demand for Andersen chargers over the past year, reflecting both the continued development of the EV market and the growing importance customers place on the design of products in their homes” said David Martell, CEO of Andersen EV. “Our investment in manufacturing at Stewartby is an important step in the next stage of Andersen's development. FAQ: 2027 Chevrolet Bolt and EVs Under $40,000 How much does the 2027 Chevrolet Bolt cost?
text:
The 2027 Chevrolet Bolt is back with a sticker that undercuts every other electric car in the rankings circulating today. Chevrolet’s own page lists a starting MSRP of $28,995 and calls the car “America’s most affordable.” CBT News, citing a Cars.com ranking, puts it first among 11 electric vehicles below $40,000, with a stated range of 262 miles. The headline version of that story, the cheapest new EV with 10 more under $40,000, is mostly right, though one part of it needs a caveat.

That caveat is the word “cheapest.” The sources we reviewed support a narrower claim: lowest in the rankings we checked. They do not prove it holds across every new EV sold in the US, and no outlet we found published a verified, manufacturer-confirmed list of all 10 rivals. This analysis separates what is confirmed from what is implied, and it shows where the 2027 Chevrolet Bolt lands against the competition on price, range, and charging. If you track battery chemistry, the Bolt’s LFP pack matches the chemistry covered in our look at a Tesla Model Y with 111,000 miles and 92% battery health.

We wrote this for readers who want the numbers behind the headline. Each figure below carries a named outlet, and anything we could not confirm is flagged. Our hardware coverage at shattered.io/hardware follows the same rule.

What Chevrolet and CBT News Actually Reported

Start with the primary source. Chevrolet’s official Bolt page carries the title “THE NEW 2027 BOLT” and shows a starting MSRP of $28,995, along with a “From: $27,600” line. The two numbers describe the same car at two points in the price build. The lower figure is the base price before destination. The higher one includes the $1,395 destination charge that The Weekly Driver and U.S. News both break out in their price tables.

CBT News published the story today, November 27, 2026, under a headline that says the Bolt returns as the cheapest new EV, with 10 more under $40,000. The article leans on a Cars.com ranking. That ranking lists 11 electric vehicles below the $40,000 line and puts the 2027 Chevrolet Bolt LT on top at $28,995 including destination. CBT News gives the Bolt’s range as 262 miles.

CarGurus backs up the price from a different direction. Its research page on electric cars under $40,000 lists the 2027 Chevrolet Bolt at $28,995 and opens its ranking with the Bolt at number one. Edmunds shows the same $27,600 base MSRP before destination. Chevrolet and three outlets, then, agree on the number that matters most. They disagree on how many cars sit below $40,000, which we cover further down.

One detail stays murky. The sources do not agree on when the Bolt arrived or returned, and we could not find a single clear date. U.S. News describes the car as on sale now at $27,600 plus the $1,395 destination fee. We treat availability as current and decline to assign a launch date.

2027 Chevrolet Bolt Price: LT and RS Trims

The $28,995 headline belongs to the LT trim. The Weekly Driver’s buyer overview lists a second trim, the RS, at $31,600 before destination and $32,995 with it. That makes the RS exactly $4,000 more than the LT once both carry the destination charge. Buyers who see “from $27,600” on a banner should add $1,395 before comparing with anything else.

The last two rows matter for shoppers who care about the $40,000 threshold. Even the RS, fully loaded with destination, leaves about $7,000 of headroom before dealer fees, options, taxes, and registration eat into it. That headroom is why a Bolt can stay inside a typical financing budget in a way the pricier Chevrolet Equinox EV, at $36,795, usually cannot.

Bolt Range, Battery and Charging Specs

Range and battery

Chevrolet lists an EPA-estimated 262 miles of range. The Weekly Driver adds the split: 262 miles combined, 294 in city driving, and 232 on the highway. The gap between city and highway figures is normal for a front-wheel-drive EV and tells buyers to expect closer to the 232-mile number on long interstate runs.

U.S. News reports that the lithium-iron-phosphate pack carries the same 65 kWh capacity as the car’s predecessor but now delivers up to 262 miles on a full charge. Same capacity, more range, tells us efficiency improved. LFP packs also tend to cost less per kilowatt-hour than nickel-based chemistries, which helps explain the price. Chevrolet has not, in the material we reviewed, published a cost breakdown, so treat that link as informed inference.

Charging and other specs

Edmunds lists a home charging time of 6.8 hours on a 240-volt circuit. For a car parked overnight, that means a full refill between a typical evening plug-in and morning departure. Edmunds also records front-wheel drive, five seats, 16.2 cubic feet of cargo space, a 3,776-pound curb weight, and a basic warranty of three years or 36,000 miles.

The sources we reviewed give no verified DC fast-charging peak rate and no complete 10-to-80% time for the Bolt. That is a real gap. Nissan, by comparison, says its Leaf charges from 10% to 80% in about 35 minutes, according to the CBT News piece. Until Chevrolet publishes a number we can check, we will not print one. Readers planning road trips should ask a dealer for the figure in writing.

Is the Bolt Really the Cheapest New EV?

Chevrolet calls the Bolt “America’s most affordable,” and CBT News frames it as the cheapest. Inside the rankings we reviewed, the claim holds. CarGurus puts the Bolt first. Cars.com, via CBT News, puts it first. ElectricVehiclesHQ also names the Bolt LT at $28,995 as the cheapest of its group. None of those pages shows a cheaper new EV.

Still, a ranking is not a census. These lists cover cars sold nationally with published prices. They can miss low-volume models, regional offers, and fleet-only trims. A discounted lease or an incentive can also make a pricier car cheaper to drive away. So the careful reading is that the Bolt has the lowest starting price in the lists we checked, and Chevrolet’s own claim stands as marketing language rather than an audited market fact.

Pricing basis creates a second trap. EVdataguys states that its prices are MSRP before options, destination fees, taxes, and incentives. CarGurus and Cars.com quote the Bolt with destination. A reader who compares a before-destination figure for one car with an after-destination figure for another can misjudge a gap by $1,000 or more. Always match the basis before declaring a winner.

The Other EVs Under $40,000: What Outlets List

CBT News names three rivals in the excerpt we could verify. The Kia EV3 Light ranks second at $31,385 with 221 miles of range. The Nissan Leaf comes in third at $31,565, with a range of 259 to 303 miles depending on trim. The Chevrolet Equinox EV starts at $36,795 and offers up to 319 miles. CarGurus adds the Tesla Model 3 at $38,630 and the Hyundai Kona Electric at $34,470. TrueCar lists the Toyota C-HR starting at $38,675.

We did not fill the range column where an outlet gave a number we could not tie cleanly to a model year. Leaving a cell honest beats printing a guess. Beyond these seven, the CarGurus page also covers the Fiat 500e, Toyota bZ, Subaru Uncharted, Hyundai Ioniq 5, Hyundai Ioniq 6, and Subaru Solterra in its headings, so the broader field is wide even though a single clean list of the other 10 is not available.

Price Per Mile of Range: Bolt vs EV3 vs Equinox EV

A sticker price alone says little about value. Dividing price by stated range gives a rough yardstick. The Bolt at $28,995 and 262 miles works out to about $111 per mile of range. The Kia EV3 at $31,385 and 221 miles comes to about $142. The Chevrolet Equinox EV at $36,795 and up to 319 miles lands near $115.

Two cautions apply. First, the Equinox EV figure pairs a base price with a best-case range, so it flatters the SUV. Second, EPA range measures energy use, not usefulness. A bigger vehicle gives you more cargo space and more seats. Even so, the arithmetic shows the Bolt matching the far larger Equinox EV on dollars per mile while costing $7,800 less up front, a gap of about 21% against the Equinox EV’s price.

The EV3 comes out worst on this yardstick, but it may still win on other terms such as interior space or driving feel. We have not driven either car for this piece, and we do not rank them on anything beyond published numbers.

Why the Count of EVs Under $40,000 Keeps Changing

The CBT News headline says 10 more under $40,000, which matches the 11-vehicle Cars.com ranking. Other outlets count differently. TrueCar titles its page “13 Best Electric Vehicles Under $40K for 2026 & 2027.” ElectricVehiclesHQ says 15 models clear the bar. Those differences come from model-year rules, trim-level counting, and whether destination is included.

When we scraped the TrueCar page today, its headings did not include the Bolt, which tells us the 13-car list was built around different inclusion rules or an older snapshot. Treat that as an observation about the page, not proof about the market. The takeaway: the number “10 more” describes one ranking, and a shopper’s real option count depends on which trims and model years they will accept.

Chevrolet’s Own Lineup and the Tesla Model 3 Squeeze

The most interesting competitor for the Bolt may sit on the same showroom floor. The Equinox EV starts $7,800 higher, so Chevrolet now sells an EV ladder with a clear price gap between a hatch and a crossover. That structure lets a dealer move shoppers up from the $28,995 entry point, though it also risks pulling some Equinox EV buyers down.

Tesla sits near the top of the sub-$40,000 range. CarGurus lists the 2026 Model 3 at $38,630, which is $9,635 above the Bolt. Put differently, the Model 3 costs about a third more than the Chevrolet. Listings for different model years show slightly different Model 3 prices across outlets, so confirm the exact year before comparing. Owners weighing long-term costs can also read our report on a Tesla Model 3 or Y battery replacement at about $12,000, since pack replacement exposure matters more as cars age.

Toyota’s C-HR at $38,675 and the Hyundai Kona Electric at $34,470 fill the middle of the list. Neither undercuts the Bolt. The Kona’s price sits $5,475 above the Chevrolet, while the C-HR sits $9,680 above it. In this field, only the Kia EV3 and Nissan Leaf land within roughly $2,600 of the Bolt, and both trail it on price.

Tax Credits and What a Buyer Actually Pays

The $28,995 figure is not an out-the-door price. It excludes sales tax, registration, dealer fees, and any options. It also excludes incentives, and that is where the picture gets fuzzy. The material we reviewed does not establish that the 2027 Bolt qualifies for the former federal clean-vehicle credit. Edmunds shows an “EV Tax Credits & Rebates” row with a “Check my eligibility” prompt rather than a dollar value.

That matters because shoppers often subtract a credit from the advertised price in their heads. Don’t. Verify eligibility under the rules in effect on your purchase date, and check state and utility programs separately. Leasing offers can also behave differently from purchase incentives. If a dealer quotes a monthly payment, ask for the full price, rebates, and fees on paper.

Charging costs deserve a line in the budget as well. A 6.8-hour home charge cycle favors owners with a garage or driveway. Apartment dwellers depend on public networks, and prices there swing widely. Our report on IONNA cutting Thanksgiving EV charging to $0.20 per kWh shows how a single promotion can reshape the cost of a fill-up for a few days, while ordinary rates stay higher.

Market Impact: What a $28,995 EV Does to Pricing

A sub-$30,000 electric car with 262 miles of range resets a reference point. For years, shoppers treated $35,000 as the floor for a mainstream EV with usable range. A listing near $29,000 pulls the conversation toward gas-car transaction prices, where buyers compare against compact crossovers rather than against other EVs. That is the real market impact, and it does not depend on whether the Bolt is literally the cheapest car in the country.

Rivals will feel pressure at the edges. The Leaf and EV3 sit within about $2,600 of the Bolt, so a modest incentive from either maker could close the gap. The Equinox EV, at $7,800 above, faces a harder choice: defend its price on size and range, or let Chevrolet’s own entry model absorb the budget buyers. We expect dealers to emphasize the combination of trim, range, and financing instead of the sticker alone.

Lower price points also mark a shift in how makers build cars. The Bolt’s LFP chemistry, discussed in U.S. News, reflects an industry move toward cheaper packs. Other low-cost entries are appearing worldwide. For one example of a cheap sedan taking a different route, see our report on the $17,175 VW sedan that is Level 2, not self-driving. Premium plug-in hybrids, by contrast, chase range differently, as our coverage of the Volvo XC60 T8 doubling its EV range to 78 miles shows.

Historical Context: The Bolt Name and Cheap EVs

The Bolt name is not new, and that shapes the story. U.S. News describes the 2027 car as the return of America’s most affordable EV, and it notes that the new pack matches its predecessor’s 65 kWh capacity. The return framing is why headlines treat this as a comeback rather than a debut. Our research did not surface verified details on the original car’s production history or recall record, so we leave those out.

What the sources do show is a market that has grown more crowded since. The CarGurus list now runs from the Bolt through the Leaf, Fiat 500e, Kona Electric, Toyota bZ, Subaru Uncharted, Ioniq 5, Equinox EV, C-HR, and Model 3. A buyer shopping under $40,000 today faces a long menu, even when exact model-year counts differ by outlet.

Pricing history for the Bolt itself also stays uncertain. We found conflicting timing information on when the 2027 car arrived, so we will not put a date on the return. That caution applies to any article that pins a precise launch day on the car without a primary-source citation.

What Remains Unconfirmed

Three claims in the headline sit outside our verified material. First, the assertion that the Bolt is definitively the cheapest new EV across the whole market. Second, any complete ranking of the “10 more” vehicles that rests on current official manufacturer pricing. Third, any specific date for the car’s arrival, because the sources conflict.

We also lack confirmed DC fast-charging figures, a verified tax-credit status, and manufacturer-published range for several rivals. Where outlets disagree, we used the more conservative number or left the cell blank. For instance, the 2026 Leaf shows $31,565 in CBT News and $31,535 at CarGurus, and charging time reads 35 minutes in the Nissan claim relayed by CBT News but 30 minutes in EVdataguys. Both pairs differ by trim or basis, and neither pair changes the ranking.

If you plan to buy, treat every price here as a starting point. Dealers set final prices, and manufacturers adjust MSRPs between model years. Confirm with Chevrolet or a dealer before you commit.

Four Predictions for the Next 12 Months

These are our analysis, not reported facts, and we hold them loosely.

Rivals respond with incentives, not list-price cuts. The Leaf and EV3 trail the Bolt by roughly $2,400 to $2,600, a gap that a lease deal or rebate can close without touching MSRP.

Charging speed becomes the main argument. With price roughly settled, shoppers will ask about the Bolt’s DC fast-charge time. Nissan already advertises its Leaf’s 35-minute 10-to-80% figure, so Chevrolet will face pressure to publish a comparable number.

Ranking counts keep shifting. As 2027 model-year prices post, outlets will add or drop cars from their under-$40,000 lists, and the “11” in today’s headline will not hold across publishers.

The Equinox EV gets repositioned. A $7,800 gap between two Chevrolet EVs invites a trim or pricing rethink, probably through packages instead of a headline price cut.

A fifth call is more cautious. If the federal credit question resolves in the Bolt’s favor, the car’s effective price could fall below anything else in these lists. If it resolves against it, the sticker price alone carries the story.

What Shoppers Should Do Before Visiting a Dealer

Start with a total-cost worksheet. Write down the LT or RS price with destination, then add tax, registration, and any dealer charges. Subtract only incentives you have confirmed in writing. Next, check your charging situation. A home 240-volt outlet turns the Bolt’s 6.8-hour charge time into a nightly routine. Without one, price your public charging against a gas car’s fuel bill.

Then compare trims on a like-for-like basis. An LT at $28,995 against an Equinox EV at $36,795 is a fair price comparison but an unfair space comparison. If you need cargo room and the 319-mile top range, the larger car may justify its $7,800 premium. If you commute under 100 miles a day, the Bolt’s range leaves ample margin.

Finally, ask three questions the published sources do not answer. What is the DC fast-charge peak and the 10-to-80% time? Which incentives apply to this exact VIN on this date? And what is the delivery timeline for the trim you want? Written answers protect you if the headline number shifts.

FAQ: 2027 Chevrolet Bolt and EVs Under $40,000

How much does the 2027 Chevrolet Bolt cost? Chevrolet lists a starting MSRP of $28,995 and a “From: $27,600” line. The Weekly Driver explains the difference as the $1,395 destination charge. The RS trim runs $32,995 with destination.

Is the Bolt the cheapest new electric car in the US? It is the cheapest in the rankings we reviewed, including Cars.com via CBT News and CarGurus. Chevrolet calls it “America’s most affordable.” No source we found proves it is the cheapest across every new EV sold, so treat the superlative as lowest-in-ranking.

What is the Bolt’s range? Chevrolet and CBT News list 262 miles, and The Weekly Driver gives 294 miles in the city and 232 on the highway. That range comes from a 65 kWh LFP battery, according to U.S. News.

Which other EVs cost under $40,000? The Cars.com ranking cited by CBT News counts 11 in total. Named examples include the Kia EV3 at $31,385, the Nissan Leaf at $31,565, the Chevrolet Equinox EV at $36,795, the Tesla Model 3 at $38,630 per CarGurus, and the Toyota C-HR at $38,675 per TrueCar. Counts differ by outlet.

Does the Bolt qualify for a federal tax credit? The sources we reviewed do not confirm it. Edmunds only offers a prompt to check eligibility. Verify the rules on your purchase date before subtracting any credit.

How long does home charging take? Edmunds lists 6.8 hours on a 240-volt circuit. We found no verified DC fast-charging peak rate or full 10-to-80% time for the Bolt, so ask Chevrolet for those figures.

text:
A Republican member of the House of Representatives from Suffolk County, Andrew Garbarino,

has with five other House GOPers, just broken with the Trump administration and called on another official

from Suffolk, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, to adhere to court rulings and reinstate $7 billion in grants

provided during the Biden administration for solar energy projects.

The grants are aimed at reducing the costs to install solar power for lower- and middle-income

consumers nationwide. The program cancelled by Zeldin, of Shirley, was named the Solar for All program.

Zeldin, charging it was a “boondoggle,” cancelled the program last year.

Garbarino and the other Republican House members, in their letter to Zeldin dated November 18, two

weeks after the Midterm election in which Garbarino, of Bayport, was re-elected (despite the national “Blue

Wave”) wrote: "Congress fully appropriated and obligated $7 billion in Solar for All funding.

Recently, two federal District Courts affirmed Congress’s intent that the Solar for All program be

fully implemented so that its widespread benefits can be realized nationwide.”

“Reinstating this program now represents an opportunity for EPA to lower energy bills at

a time when electric grids are under pressure from rising demand,” they declared.

According to a Newsday story about the letter, “A prompt restart of the Solar for All

program could bring first-year savings of more than $44.3 million for more than 60,000

households in New York, lowering their costs each by roughly 25%, or $738, according to

projections from the Environmental Protection Network, a group of former Environmental

Protection Agency employees that does independent analyses.”

Meanwhile, published recently in a highly respected science publication, Scientific

American, was a 10-page article headlined “Why Solar is Taking Over the World.”

The spread began: “Forty-seven years ago U.S. President Jimmy Carter stood grinning in

front of a set of 32 bulky solar panels. It was 1979, and the oil crisis had sent fuel costs

skyrocketing. Carter, in response, was making the White House an example of conservation and

alternative energy. ‘Solar power will not pollute our air or water,’ he said. ‘We will not run short

of it. No one can ever embargo the sun or interrupt its delivery to us.’”

“The panels were expensive and rudimentary by today’s standards. They cost roughly

$165,500 in 2026 dollars,” the piece continued, “and they didn’t even generate electricity; all

they did was heat water for things such as kitchen use. But Carter’s argument still resonates

today: in a global economy in which a single conflict can shut down shipments of millions of

barrels of fossil fuel overnight, the lure of the sun as a power source is inarguable.”

The Scientific American article went on: “And there’s no better deal on energy…‘Today

solar makes the cheapest electricity,’ says Walajabad S. Sampath, site director of the Center for

Next Generation Photovoltaics at Colorado State University.”

“Even before the U.S.-Iran conflict closed the Strait of Hormuz for months, causing

fossil-fuel prices to spike, solar was soaring,” it reported in its September issue. “Last year the

world added 600 terawatt-hours of solar photovoltaic energy…It was the first time that a

renewable source took the top slot in global supply growth. It was also the largest single-year

increase for any electricity-generation technology, according to the International Energy

Association.”

The problem in the U.S., said the article: “The Trump administration has been hostile to

solar power, cutting billions of dollars in funding.”

Still, as the next section of the article was headed: “Solar Is Now the Cheapest Way to

Produce Energy in Human History.” There were pages and pages of details.

However, even though costs of solar energy have plummeted and efficiencies of solar

panels (the amount of power they produce from sunlight) increased greatly, the costs for folks of

lower or moderate income can be problematic.

The important 30% federal residential solar tax credit for solar installations expired on

Dec. 31 of last year. In comparison, the many billions of dollars the federal government

provides annually in subsidies to the oil, gas, coal and nuclear industries continue. That’s no

problem for the Trump administration.

The cost for a solar installation since 2006 when we had 38 solar photovoltaic panels

installed on the roof of our house in Noyac is now half of what it was then.

So, so critical, once solar panels are installed, the sun sends no bills.

Still, reported the Scientific American piece: “Even in places where government support

is weak or has declined, such as the U.S., solar ‘will continue to be at a competitive price,’ says

Christopher Namovicz, an analyst at the U.S. Information Administration. Solar has now

irrevocably joined coal and natural gas as an inexpensive way to power the world.”

And unlike coal and gas, and, of course, oil—all fossil fuels that produce greenhouse

gases—solar energy doesn’t contribute to the global warming impacting the earth and life on it

more and more ever year. And unlike nuclear power, using solar energy cannot result in disasters

like the Three Mile Island, Chernobyl and Fukushima accidents, happening now nearly every

decade.

“The plummeting price over the past decade,” the Scientific American article went on, “is

also a result of advances on the production side: the materials are purer and the manufacturing

process is more precise. Scale has contributed as well. The Chinese solar industry is now highly

integrated and efficient, and larger factories can churn out panels at a lower cost per unit than

when solar was a niche industry with smaller production lines. The world—led by China—can

now produce enough solar modules in one year to generate a collective 1,405 gigawatts of

energy.”

It is encouraging that Garbarino and the other GOP representatives have broken with the

Trump administration on the Solar for All program.

The reaction, however, of the “Trump EPA” to the letter was not positive. It stated: “The

days of wasteful Biden-era boondoggles are over, and the Trump EPA is committed to being an

exceptional steward of taxpayer dollars.”

text:
Unbelievable. What could three Democratic Great Lakes senators possibly have been thinking on November 19, when the Senate approved the implausibly reckless industrial development bill known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act?

Elissa Slotkin and Gary Peters of Michigan, and Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota, all with near perfect records on the League of Conservation Voters scorecard of environmental votes, switched their allegiances and sided with unions and the Republican majority to pass and move the irresponsible lame-duck legislation to the House of Representatives, where it needs to die.

Here’s why. If enacted, the law will allow builders of major industrial and agricultural facilities to increase the scale of their operations and accelerate construction by 1) curtailing the reach of three of the country’s most consequential environmental statutes and 2) sharply limiting oversight by state and federal regulators.

In effect, the proposed jobs act would achieve in a single stroke of environmental antagonism what the Trump administration and five decades of anti-environmental rhetoric in Washington has so far not achieved. It would rewrite the authority of the 1970 National Environmental Policy Act, the 1972 Clean Water Act, and the 1973 Endangered Species Act in ways that shrink the rigor and time big projects are reviewed by agencies and the public.

The effect is particularly dangerous to the forested and water-rich states of the upper Great Lakes because it essentially sanctions more water pollution, more wetlands to be filled, more land to be developed, and more wild habitat to be disturbed.

This is no exaggeration. Under the terms of the proposal approved by the Senate, U.S. industry will be allowed to build new pipelines with scant oversight. Transmission lines can cross sensitive wetlands. Large livestock feeding facilities, which produce millions of gallons of raw manure, will be subject to permit oversight only once a decade. Mines will be allowed to open in wild regions, like Minnesota’s Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness. Even after an election when voters soundly rejected new data center construction, the jobs act would make it easier to approve and build data centers on private and federal land.

Proposal Unmasked As Dangerous

These outrageous consequences are what lawmakers clearly hoped they could disguise when the jobs act was quietly introduced on the last day of September. It was marketed as a bipartisan measure to modernize federal permitting, accelerate infrastructure construction, lower energy costs, and produce good jobs. Sponsors even attracted the acclaim of some environmental organizations by promising faster approvals for transmission lines to solar and wind power projects.

But in the days since the Senate vote, the astonishing consequences of the measure have come into much clearer focus. States and tribes, for instance, would no longer have authority to block projects that cause erosion, pollution, clear cutting, and other activities that harm watersheds. The Environmental Protection Agency could be barred from tightening limits on air emissions and discharges to water that respond to new conditions or scientific knowledge.

Another provision ends the authority of the Environmental Protection Agency to block big and damaging projects after they’ve been issued a construction permit by the Army Corps of Engineers. The EPA has always had that authority, and it’s been used sparingly to prevent really damaging projects – a mountaintop-removal coal mine in West Virginia in 2011, or mining in Alaska’s salmon-rich Bristol Bay watershed in 2023.

A third provision allows construction projects to fill wetlands without permits, and specifically speeds review and approvals for roads, pipelines, transmission lines and other infrastructure that cuts through forests and crosses wetlands. Lastly, developers of big geothermal, oil and gas, and mining projects can proceed without rigorous reviews of their effects on groundwater reserves.

Summed up, Congress is now considering a legislative I.E.D. purposely intended to blow up the core idea of federal environmental oversight. The great achievement of America’s program of natural resources protection is its capacity to subject potentially damaging projects to careful review and thoughtful approval by agency personnel and the public. Speed is not the central goal of environmental oversight. No, the central goal is ensuring the safety of people, animals, water, land, and plants.

Not nearly enough Americans are still alive who encountered the mess we made of our country. Before the U.S. enacted its foundational environmental laws in the last decades of the 20th century, industrial developers certainly completed their projects with speed. Our natural domain and human communities paid a steep price. Smog choked the air in Los Angeles and New York. Poisonous air emissions from steel manufacturing killed 20 people in Pennsylvania in 1948. Lake Erie was so contaminated with untreated municipal wastes that it was declared dead. Poisoned by pesticides, bald eagles nearly became extinct. Buried toxic chemical waste leaked into the homes of residents in upstate New York.

Say What?

That Congress is actually considering a measure to start a new era of industrial depredation indicates that Americans are insufficiently informed, or not actively valuing an environmental protection program that cleared our air, scrubbed our waters, and protected our wild habitats. The truth is that the nation is far safer and much more beautiful than it otherwise would have been had Congress not acted. And while the supporters of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act contend that environmental laws are impeding the economy, that’s a load of nonsense, too. The U.S. gross domestic product is almost four times larger than it was in 1970.

In pushing so hard to emasculate our nation’s environmental statutes, Congress is overlooking one of their principal assets: the capacity to adjust and flex with the evolution of industrial practices, new science, and changing conditions.

Consider that the basic premise underlying the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is that regulations hurt businesses. The debate about whether this is true dates to the 1980s when lawmakers considered how much should the United States spend to reduce environmental and public health risks. When Philip K. Howard published the “Death of Common Sense” in the mid-1990s, in which he argued that some rules produced absurd results for communities, national consensus emerged that reform was needed.

Toxic Cleanup Changes

One example was how the federal Superfund toxic cleanup law, designed to protect water and public health, was updated to enable cities to redevelop their old industrial sites. Before the change, the law required contaminated sites to be cleaned up to pristine levels, meaning virtually no detectable levels of poisons should linger after the work. But when city managers complained that cleanups were costing $20 million an acre, more than enough to discourage developers to get started, the rules were amended to allow some level of contamination to remain, particularly if the parcel was going to be rebuilt as something where people would not be exposed, like a parking lot for a new municipal building.

The Superfund update cut the steep cost of toxic cleanups, led to construction on old industrial sites, and helped stir the revival of U.S. cities in this century.

The history of Congressional consideration of environmental statutes is rich in similar work to adjust laws to meet new conditions without damaging natural resources. Just three years ago Congress approved changes to the National Environmental Policy Act to keep the length of environmental reviews manageable. Environmental assessments were limited to no more than 75 pages and no longer than one year. Full environmental impact statements, a more comprehensive review, are limited to 150 pages and two years to finish.

So there it is. Prima facie evidence that Congress is fully capable of adjusting environmental law when it’s needed. And that’s what needs to happen now.

Kill the lame-duck Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. It has few benefits and its risks to the environment and communities are dreadfully apparent. When the new Congress is seated next year, it has the chance to craft new provisions that more elegantly address whether there really are shortcomings in current law.

text:
Overview:

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 faces an uncertain path in the House, where a narrow Republican majority, procedural hurdles, competing legislative priorities and a limited congressional calendar could prevent the bill from advancing before the end of the year.

What’s next for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026?

Before I answer, a story. My mentor Forrest J. Gerard, Blackfeet, had a lot of legislative accomplishments over the years (Indian Finance Act, Indian Health Care Improvement Act and the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act) and he loved to tell stories about the ins and outs of how those laws were made. But he was also fond of showing what could be done to kill legislation.

To read more articles by Mark Trahant, go to: Marktrahant.substack.com

One of his favorite stories was about a bill to put a time limit on tribal land claims. The chairman of the Senate Indian Affairs Committee was then William Cohen of Maine, whose views had been shaped by land claims by the Passamaquoddy and Penobscot tribes in the 1970s. A settlement was reached in that case and it became law in 1980. Cohen then wanted a blanket time limit on all third-party claims by tribes (against states and private parties) and pushed through a measure to do just that. Tribes wanted changes and Cohen was in a rush.

When the bill got before the Senate, it was late in the calendar, and the only option left for the Cohen bill was unanimous consent. Gerard’s play was to have tribes call on Montana’s John Melcher. Once he signed on to the issue he was unmovable. The sponsors tried everything they could think of and nothing worked. So the bill died and when it came back in the next Congress there was a lot more tribal input.

That’s all to say that the calendar is now the best friend of folks trying to kill the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026.

Last week the Native American Rights Fund issued a legal analysis of what is now H.R. 2347.

“… a permitting reform bill designed to accelerate federal environmental reviews and project approvals. It proposes significant changes to the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, and National Historic Preservation Act, as well as energy permitting laws.

By shortening review timelines and narrowing what triggers a review, BAAJA would reduce federal oversight and opportunities for Tribal Nations to participate in decisions affecting their lands, waters, and cultural resources. It would also weaken Tribal consultation and make it harder to challenge harmful project approvals in court.”

Back to the calendar.

The House has about three weeks left and it has a busy agenda, including funding the government. The Republicans would love to get their farm bill through now, because a rewrite after January will mean a lot of Democratic priorities will rise to the surface (including restoring food benefits under the SNAP program.)

The Hill reports:

“… it won’t be an easy task for Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to wrangle his caucus, especially as he struggles to keep his own members in Washington long enough to get the work done.

“Attendance problems have already begun disrupting the House floor schedule. GOP leaders postponed a procedural rule vote Wednesday over absences and canceled Friday’s votes altogether. Twenty-one Republicans missed votes on Thursday morning, following 14 absences the previous day.

“Johnson will need near-unanimous support on any procedural rule if he decides to bring a bill to the floor via regular order, requiring most of his conference to be present as he juggles a razor-thin margin. The House this week took up bills under a fast-track process known as suspension of the rules, which requires a two-thirds majority for passage and is typically reserved for legislation with broad bipartisan support. Because those bills often attract significant Democratic backing, Republicans can afford absences without jeopardizing passage.”

Remember House Democrats vote against the rule as a matter of course.

So Johnson has two choices: Move the bill through the rules committee and regular order or try and get a suspension of the rules with requires a 2/3s vote.

And a strong Democratic opposition could stop bill either way (depending on how many Republicans show up to vote).

And if the House bill does get through, and it has any amendments, even a paragraph, then the measure it has to go back to the Senate for reconsideration. And then back to the House.

Why It Matters

Tesla Inc. added Kountoupes Denham Carr & Reid LLC to its federal lobbying roster in a new client registration signed Nov. 24. The Tesla lobbying filing lists the Energy/Nuclear issue area and describes the work as "Issues related to solar manufacturing and battery storage." ​

Tesla already lobbies in-house and through other firms. Its third-quarter reports came from Tesla in-house, Capitol Consulting Group LLC (District of Columbia), Rich Feuer Anderson, Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld LLP and Continental Strategy LLC. Cassidy & Associates Inc. filed a first-quarter termination for a Feb. 19 end date.

By the Numbers

The registration carries a $0 filing amount. Tesla's in-house reports show $650,000 for the third quarter, $650,000 for the second quarter and $760,000 for the first quarter. Third-quarter reports show $20,000 for Capitol Consulting, $40,000 for Rich Feuer Anderson, $60,000 for Akin Gump and $90,000 for Continental Strategy. Akin Gump's second quarter report shows $90,000, and Cassidy's termination filing shows $30,000.

The filing lists three lobbyists: Jonathan Gilbert (Principal), Lisa Kountoupes (President/Founder) and M.J. Kenny (Partner). Gilbert's covered experience is with Rep. Mike Levin (D-CA), whose office he served as chief of staff from April 1 through June 30. Kenny's is with Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL), where he was deputy floor director from Dec. 19 through Dec. 31, 2018. None of the three appears on Tesla's earlier filings.

Broader Context

The Solar Energy Industries Association says H.R. 1 ended the residential solar tax credit as of Dec. 31, 2025, set a July 4 construction-start deadline for utility-scale solar credits, and set no placed-in-service deadline for energy storage. The Federal Register shows Tesla notified the Foreign-Trade Zones Board on March 3 about expanding production at three California sites, including Megapack storage batteries and inverters.

Between The Lines

Rep. Chris Smith (R-NJ) told a July 15 Committee on Foreign Affairs hearing on supply chain dependency that he had introduced H.R. 2310, the Cobalt Supply Chain Act. He asked witnesses to look at it and "see if you can support it," and said he had asked Elon Musk and others about exploitation in the supply chain. Sen. Ed Markey (D-MA) posted on X on Feb. 20 that Tesla must stop using the name Autopilot.

Advertisement

Competitive Landscape

The firm also signed ClearPath Action for Conservative Clean Energy Inc. on Nov. 24 on science and technology. Stonepeak Partners LLC hired Cornerstone Government Affairs Inc. on Nov. 23 on natural resources and energy/nuclear. City Labs Inc. hired Artemis Group LLC on Nov. 20 on energy/nuclear.

The Bottom Line

Tesla is widening its outside lobbying bench on solar manufacturing and storage, adding a new firm to its existing in-house and outside lobbying.

We will get this province back on track, welcoming investment, creating jobs and supporting the services British Columbians depend on. B.C. is open for business again, and it’s going to become the fastest place in North America to permit an LNG facility.”

The new infrastructure will support NorthRiver Midstream’s plans to expand its West Doe Gas Plant northwest of Dawson Creek. To help make additional electricity capacity available sooner and secure billions of dollars in new investment, Neufeld has exempted BC Hydro from requiring a certificate of public convenience and necessity for substation and transmission upgrades in the South Peace region. The expansion, combined with other potential investments in northeastern B.C. unlocked by this exemption, represents more than $3 billion in collective investments.

The additional capacity will support the West Doe Gas Plant expansion’s connection to the BC Hydro system, enabling NorthRiver Midstream to proceed toward a final investment decision.

NorthRiver Midstream’s plans include increasing the West Doe Gas Plant’s processing capacity from 100 million to 400 million cubic feet per day, with an estimated capital cost of $500 million for the project.

Growing natural-gas production and processing are increasing demand for electricity in the region. Limited transmission capacity and uncertainty about when additional capacity will be available are preventing some industrial customers from making final investment decisions and advancing projects to construction.

BC Hydro’s South Peace System Reinforcement Project will address the constraint by upgrading the Dawson Creek and Bear Mountain substations, allowing the existing transmission lines between them to operate at a higher voltage. It will increase capacity without the need to build new transmission lines.

West Doe is one of several potential developments that could benefit from increased electricity capacity in the South Peace region. In addition to the West Doe expansion, the upgrades are expected to benefit other projects planned by NorthRiver Midstream, Tourmaline, ARC Resources and Shell, providing greater timeline certainty.

Together, the developments represent as much as $3 billion in industrial investment and support as much as 900 million cubic feet per day of additional upstream and midstream natural-gas capacity. The resulting industrial development is estimated to contribute as much as $8.8 billion in gross domestic product over the lifetime of the developments, while supporting hundreds of construction jobs and dozens of permanent industry jobs.

BC Hydro plans to begin work on the South Peace System Reinforcement Project transmission upgrades in 2028, with a 2030 in-service date. The project will enable two existing 12-kilometre, 138-kilovolt (kV) transmission lines between the Dawson Creek and Bear Mountain substations to operate at 230 kV. The work includes:

upgrading the Dawson Creek substation to operate at 230 kV

upgrading the Bear Mountain substation to operate at 230 kV

modifying the transmission line points of connection at the substations to enable the existing lines to operate at 230 kV

By making better use of existing transmission infrastructure, the South Peace System Reinforcement Project will help get more power to industry sooner, unlock private-sector investment and support new jobs and economic growth in northeastern B.C.
