title: Midterm Elections Reset The Policy Landscape: Takeaways For Businesses Operating And ...
description:
Congressional oversight will become a more significant consideration for businesses across sectors.
Businesses should distinguish among existing statutory obligations, final regulations currently in effect, pending rules and policy initiatives whose durability remains uncertain.
The midterm results do not diminish—and may indeed increase in certain areas- the role of state and local governments in shaping major investments.
Companies evaluating U.S. projects should therefore assess federal developments alongside state and local requirements, community impacts and incentive conditions.
Consistent, constructive engagement with relevant federal, state and local stakeholders will also remain important.
text:
The midterm elections will change the balance of power in Washington without changing control of the executive branch, creating a divided policy environment for businesses for at least the next two years. Congress is poised to take a more active role in oversight, funding and scrutiny of federal programs, while the Trump Administration will retain authority to pursue the administration’s existing regulatory and enforcement agenda.

For companies operating or investing in the United States, the practical consequence of this shift will likely not be a wholesale change in law, but a more complex environment in which infrastructure development, government incentives, and corporate decision-making may receive closer attention from Congress, and state regulators may play a greater role.

1. Congressional oversight will become a more significant consideration for businesses across sectors.

Changes in congressional leadership are expected to bring new oversight priorities, with energy, artificial intelligence and technology, financial services, digital assets, health care, telecommunications and government contracting among the likely areas of focus. While Congress does not have the power to prosecute, it does have broad power to investigate, particularly where potential legislation or federal funds are involved. Companies should assess now—before the new Congress takes office—whether they are likely targets of Congressional inquiry and consider developing proactive response plans.

2. Federal incentives remain available, but government-supported projects will likely face additional scrutiny.

We expect significant federal financing to remain available for energy projects, but those financing decisions will likely be of keen interest to the new Congress. Current Department of Energy priorities include nuclear energy, fossil fuels and geothermal development, some of which may continue to attract bipartisan support. The election nevertheless increases the prospect of congressional scrutiny of major funding decisions and award processes. Companies receiving or seeking federal support should maintain clear documentation demonstrating compliance with program requirements, technical milestones and funding conditions.

3. Environmental policy may face greater congressional scrutiny without an immediate change in existing law.

Federal environmental agencies remain under executive control and will likely continue pursuing the administration’s regulatory agenda. The new Congress, however, can influence implementation of that agenda through oversight and appropriations. Timing also matters: major federal rules finalized late in an administration may, depending on statutory requirements, become eligible for disapproval by the next Congress under the Congressional Review Act. Businesses should distinguish among existing statutory obligations, final regulations currently in effect, pending rules and policy initiatives whose durability remains uncertain.

4. State and local governments will remain consequential to development and investment decisions.

The midterm results do not diminish—and may indeed increase in certain areas- the role of state and local governments in shaping major investments. Data centers, manufacturing facilities, energy projects and other developments may depend on state regulation, local approvals, infrastructure commitments and economic development incentives. Companies evaluating U.S. projects should therefore assess federal developments alongside state and local requirements, community impacts and incentive conditions. Changes in Washington may garner the most headlines, but many decisions affecting project viability will continue to be made at the state and local level.

5. Corporate governance and compliance provide continuity amid policy uncertainty.

The election changes the political environment, not the underlying legal obligations businesses already face. Existing statutes remain in force, executive agencies retain their responsibilities, and many regulatory requirements will continue regardless of congressional priorities. However, given potential increased Congressional oversight and shifting political winds, companies working on projects involving government funding, major infrastructure or other public commitments should ensure accurate documentation of key decisions and that they are following their established processes for procurement and bidding, given the possibility that these decisions may later be scrutinized in hindsight by politically-motivated actors. Consistent, constructive engagement with relevant federal, state and local stakeholders will also remain important.

text:
MAN Truck & Bus has handed over 21 Lion’s City 18 E electric buses to VAG Nuremberg, equipped with battery packs manufactured at MAN’s local production site.

The vehicles, handed over on 27 November 2026, are the first MAN articulated electric buses featuring eight MAN BatteryPacks, with an installed capacity of 712 kWh and a range of up to 480 kilometres, the manufacturer announces in a press note.

The handover ceremony was attended by Bavarian Minister-President Markus Söder, Nuremberg Mayor Marcus König, VAG board member Magdalena Weigel and MAN CEO Alexander Vlaskamp.

With the latest delivery, battery-electric vehicles will account for almost 75% of VAG’s bus fleet, with the public transport operator targeting full fleet electrification.

VAG Nuremberg’s cooperation with MAN in the electric bus segment dates back to 2021, when the operator ordered 39 Lion’s City E buses. VAG subsequently expanded its zero-emission fleet with 46 Mercedes-Benz eCitaro in 2023 and a further batch of 31 eCitaro G in 2025, marking the milestone of 100 electric buses in its fleet in May of that year. On the infrastructure side, VAG selected Siemens in 2020 to equip its eBus port in Schweinau.

Meanwhile, on the industrial front, MAN completed construction of its battery manufacturing facility in Nuremberg in November 2024, officially launching series production in April 2025 with an initial annual capacity of 50,000 battery packs and a further €150 million investment announced for the production of next-generation battery modules.

MAN Lion’s City 18 E with 712 kWh battery capacity for Nuremberg

The 18-metre vehicles feature a new battery configuration consisting of eight MAN BatteryPacks produced at the manufacturer’s Nuremberg plant.

According to MAN, an analysis of around 6,500 routes carried out by MAN Transport Solutions as part of its e-mobility consultancy activities for public transport operators shows that the installed battery capacity can cover almost all typical urban bus rotations without intermediate charging.

MAN investing €500 million in its Nuremberg production site

The batteries equipping the newly delivered articulated buses are manufactured at the same industrial site where MAN has established its large-scale battery production activities, supported by the Free State of Bavaria.

The decision to establish series production of batteries in Nuremberg was taken in 2022. The facility now has a production capacity of up to 100,000 battery packs annually, MAN points out.

Since 2023, the site has also hosted the Campus Future Driveline, bringing together research institutions and industry partners in the development of powertrain technologies, with activities integrated into the wider TRATON R&D organisation.

In parallel, in 2025 MAN launched production in Nuremberg of its latest generation of diesel engines, used in the D30 PowerLion powertrain.

Overall, the manufacturer is investing 500 million euros in the further development of the Nuremberg site.

In brief

How many electric buses has MAN delivered to VAG Nuremberg? 21 MAN Lion’s City 18 E articulated buses.

What is the battery capacity of the new MAN electric buses? 712 kWh, distributed across eight battery packs, for a stated range of up to 480 kilometres.

Where are the batteries manufactured? At MAN’s Nuremberg plant, which has an annual production capacity of up to 100,000 battery packs.

What share of VAG’s bus fleet will be electric? Almost 75% following the latest delivery.

“Nowhere is MAN’s transformation as tangible as here in Nuremberg. Step by step, we have realigned our long-established powertrain site towards the mobility of the future,” said Alexander Vlaskamp, CEO of MAN Truck & Bus, adding: “Today, another chapter is added: batteries made in Nuremberg will in future be on the road in MAN electric buses on Nuremberg’s streets. The value creation stays local, which strengthens the city, Bavaria and Germany as an industrial location.”

name: American Energy
title: America cannot afford an FAA moment for its electric grid - Washington Examiner
description:
The Energy Department’s 2026 Draft National Transmission Needs Study identifies a pressing need for additional transmission capacity to maintain reliability, accommodate electricity demand, and relieve congestion.
Advanced transmission technologies can accomplish this.
Modern conductors can carry substantially more electricity using existing transmission towers.
Similarly, surplus interconnection service allows additional electricity generation or storage to utilize unused capacity at existing grid connections, subject to reliability reviews.
We cannot afford to let America’s electric grid experience its own FAA moment before deciding it’s time to act.
text:
The New York subway stopped. Businesses closed. Traffic signals went dark. Millions were left without air conditioning, refrigeration, or reliable communications.

Imagine something similar happening today, when even more of our economy depends on electricity and interconnected technologies.

In my role at the Abundance Institute, conversations with utilities, energy innovators and infrastructure developers reinforce a concerning reality: America’s aging transmission infrastructure faces growing demands that existing systems and regulatory frameworks are struggling to accommodate.

The Energy Department’s 2026 Draft National Transmission Needs Study identifies a pressing need for additional transmission capacity to maintain reliability, accommodate electricity demand, and relieve congestion. Aging equipment and barriers to infrastructure development threaten both reliability and affordability.

But building entirely new transmission lines isn’t our only option. We can get substantially more from the grid we already have.

Think of our electricity network as a highway system. When traffic increases, we don’t always need another interstate. Sometimes we can expand capacity by improving existing lanes and managing traffic more efficiently.

Advanced transmission technologies can accomplish this. Modern conductors can carry substantially more electricity using existing transmission towers. Dynamic line ratings use real-time weather conditions to determine how much electricity lines can safely carry. Advanced power flow controls redirect electricity around congested portions of the grid.

These aren’t futuristic concepts. The DOE’s 2026 Speed to Power through Accelerated Reconductoring and other Key Advanced Transmission Technology Upgrades initiative has selected projects expected to upgrade more than 1,500 miles of transmission lines and deploy grid-enhancing technologies across nearly 21,000 miles.

Similarly, surplus interconnection service allows additional electricity generation or storage to utilize unused capacity at existing grid connections, subject to reliability reviews.

Of course, America must also build more transmission, including stronger connections between regions. But how we build matters.

Competitive transmission policies can allow qualified developers to compete for projects, while merchant transmission enables privately financed infrastructure without automatically shifting financial risks onto ratepayers.

Congress also has an opportunity through the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act to improve permitting certainty, streamline federal reviews, and accelerate infrastructure development, including upgrades within existing transmission rights-of-way.

Not every growing electricity need requires another transmission line. Microgrids and bring-your-own-power arrangements can enable businesses to generate electricity locally, accommodating economic growth while reducing pressure on the broader grid.

These solutions share a common objective: increasing capacity, strengthening reliability, and protecting affordability.

Modernization, however, should never become a blank check for utilities. Regulators must ensure investments deliver measurable improvements and meaningful value for consumers.

The 2003 blackout demonstrated how quickly localized problems can become widespread emergencies. The FAA’s recent ground stop reminded us that aging infrastructure remains vulnerable, even as our dependence on it grows.

We have the technology, engineering expertise, and policy solutions to strengthen America’s electric grid.

TRUMP MUST NOT MISTAKE IRAQ’S MILITIA RESHUFFLE FOR IRAN’S RETREAT

America needs more transmission, but it also needs a smarter approach to the transmission it already has.

Waiting for a crisis to force modernization is an expensive and unnecessary gamble. We cannot afford to let America’s electric grid experience its own FAA moment before deciding it’s time to act.

Ryan Norris is a senior fellow for energy policy at the Abundance Institute.

name: Clean Energy
title: Workforce readiness as a constraint to green hydrogen deployment in the Southern Mediterranean
authors: Aly H. Abdelbaky, Rania A, Tarek A, Al-Attili, Abdelrahman Z, Al-Hijaj, Al-Salaymeh, Al‐Smadi, Mohammed Fawzi, Omar Aly
description:
RQ5: How can the perspectives of students, academic staff, and industry stakeholders be integrated into a structured framework for improving hydrogen workforce readiness in the Southern Mediterranean?
The study makes four principal contributions to the literature on hydrogen workforce development and energy-system transition.
Faculty members also identified core technical domains with any hydrogen education framework, including hydrogen safety, electrolysis processes, fuel cells, and storage systems.
The purpose of this section is to present the findings of all three groups of stakeholders, to analyze the shortcomings of the hydrogen education system and to propose ways of improving hydrogen education in the Southern Mediterranean.
Actionable policy implications The findings indicate that hydrogen workforce readiness cannot be improved through curriculum revision alone.
text:
Despite growing investments in green hydrogen infrastructure and increasing policy commitment across the Southern Mediterranean region, a critical enabling dimension remains underdeveloped: workforce readiness1,2. While national hydrogen strategies emphasize production capacity, export potential, and technological deployment, limited attention has been given to the human capital required to design, operate, maintain, and scale hydrogen systems3,4,5,6.

This creates a significant implementation problem. Green hydrogen projects cannot be deployed successfully through infrastructure investment, technological availability, and regulatory support alone. Hydrogen technologies require interdisciplinary competencies spanning electrochemical systems, safety engineering, power electronics, digital modeling, and system integration7,8,9,10,11. Recent experimental studies illustrate this breadth, ranging from the optimization of electrolyzer configuration and operating conditions for hydrogen-rich gas production to its integration into multi-fuel combustion systems for improving engine performance and emissions12,13. A shortage of suitably trained personnel may therefore delay project execution, increase operational costs, create safety risks, increase dependence on external expertise, and reduce the local economic benefits expected from national hydrogen strategies. However, existing educational and training ecosystems in the region are not adequately aligned with these emerging requirements. As a result, a disconnect is forming between policy ambition and implementation capacity14.

The absence of a sufficiently trained workforce introduces systemic risks, including project delays, increased operational costs, safety concerns, and reliance on external expertise15. These risks are particularly significant in developing regions where institutional capacity and industrial ecosystems are still evolving16,17,18,19,20. Therefore, understanding the nature and extent of workforce gaps is essential not only from an educational perspective but as a policy-relevant issue directly affecting the feasibility and scalability of hydrogen deployment21,22. Universities have increasingly played an active role in sustainability transitions, not only through research but also through operational energy management and carbon reduction strategies23,24.

This study addresses this challenge by examining the alignment between education, training systems, and industry needs, positioning workforce readiness as a critical constraint within the broader energy transition framework.

Green hydrogen, produced using renewable energy through water electrolysis, is a key decarbonization pathway due to its versatility and zero carbon emissions at the point of use25,26. Owing to its high energy density, green hydrogen is pivotal in the global net-zero agenda as it enables the decarbonization of hard-to-electrify sectors as well as supports large-scale energy storage27,28. In the Southern Mediterranean region, Jordan, Algeria, and Egypt have made long-term plans for hydrogen production and storage29,30,31,32. Jordan, with its high solar and wind potentials, strives for hydrogen adoption as it will help the country reach its national emission reduction goals by 203031,33. Algeria, particularly in the Saharan region, possesses high solar energy and benefits from a well-established export network, positioning the country for large-scale export to international markets, particularly to Europe34,35,36,37,38,39,40. On the other hand, Egypt targets to capture up to 8% of the world’s hydrogen market by 2040 through its national strategy41,42,43,44,45. These goals are supported by the country’s strategic geographic location and abundant solar and wind resources, which facilitate linking to Africa, Europe, and Asia through planned port infrastructure that facilitates hydrogen and ammonia export.

International comparative studies demonstrate that hydrogen-transition pathways differ substantially according to countries’ renewable resources, existing energy systems, technological capabilities, infrastructure, production costs, policy support, and strategic priorities. Kakran et al.46, in their comparison of the BRICS countries and the United States, showed that national hydrogen development is shaped by differences in production capacity, utilization pathways, storage, technological innovation, and government intervention. Similarly, Pal et al.47 identified distinct strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats affecting hydrogen deployment across the QUAD countries. These findings indicate that hydrogen strategies cannot be separated from their national institutional and socioeconomic contexts and that successful deployment requires coordinated development of technology, infrastructure, policy, and implementation capacity.

Yet, while technological, financial, and regulatory frameworks are advancing, skills development remains significantly behind48,49,50,51. Hydrogen technologies require specialized expertise spanning electrolysis systems, fuel cells, safety engineering, storage materials, power electronics, digital modeling, and system integration. Current education systems in the region do not adequately prepare graduates or retrain professionals to meet this demand.

Figure 1 outlines the research’s top-to-bottom workflow, moving from the problem context of a green hydrogen skills gap in the Southern Mediterranean to the aim, triangulated methodology, and core findings, culminating in the central insight that a structural misalignment necessitates a coordinated skills ecosystem.

Studies show a growing shortage in skilled workers along the hydrogen value chain52,53,54,55. As highlighted by The European Hydrogen Skills Strategy and other international efforts, transitioning to hydrogen-based energy systems will require new interdisciplinary workforce, skilled in production technologies, storage and transportation, safety, system modeling, and legal requirements52,53,54,55, from technicians to advanced researcher’s level56. In this context, the H2EDGE program aims to help students and educators by strengthening their technical and digital skills related to hydrogen technologies57.

Efforts in North Africa show persistent structural problems, including the lack of specialized hydrogen curricula, well trained educators, and limited lab infrastructure56,58,59,60. Global education platforms57,61,62,63 similarly emphasize barriers to scaling hydrogen education due to insufficient funding. At the same time, international roadmaps always prioritize R&D on hydrogen production efficiency, storage technologies, and system-level integration64,65,66,67.

Although previous studies and international initiatives have examined hydrogen technologies, policy frameworks, technical skills requirements, and individual education or training programmes, important gaps remain in the available literature. First, much of the existing work addresses workforce development conceptually or through policy and literature reviews rather than through direct empirical evidence from the principal stakeholders involved. Second, empirical studies commonly focus on only one group, such as students, educators, or employers, and therefore provide limited insight into the alignment of the complete education-to-employment pathway. Third, comparative evidence remains limited regarding how student readiness, university capacity, and industry expectations differ among Southern Mediterranean countries.

Consequently, it remains unclear whether students’ interests and learning experiences, universities’ institutional resources and teaching capabilities, and employers’ competency requirements are sufficiently aligned to support the emerging hydrogen economy. This gap is important because workforce readiness is not produced by one stakeholder in isolation. It results from the interaction of students, academic institutions, industry, accreditation bodies, and public-policy actors. A fragmented assessment of these actors may therefore overlook the structural causes of hydrogen-related skills shortages.

Against this backdrop, the Southern Mediterranean faces a critical mismatch between positive national hydrogen targets and the availability of skilled human capital, thus reflecting the need for tri-perspective evaluation.

More specifically, the study addresses the following research questions:

RQ1: What are the levels of awareness, interest, prior exposure, preferred learning modes, and career orientation toward green hydrogen among university students in Egypt, Jordan, and Algeria?

RQ2: To what extent are academic institutions prepared to introduce or expand hydrogen-related education in terms of curriculum relevance, faculty expertise, laboratory resources, and teaching methods?

RQ3: What technical, safety, digital, economic, and interdisciplinary competencies are considered most important by industry stakeholders for employment in the emerging hydrogen sector?

RQ4: What similarities and differences exist among Egypt, Jordan, and Algeria regarding hydrogen education readiness, practical-training capacity, perceived skills gaps, and opportunities for industry–academia collaboration?

RQ5: How can the perspectives of students, academic staff, and industry stakeholders be integrated into a structured framework for improving hydrogen workforce readiness in the Southern Mediterranean?

To answer these questions, the study applies a triangulated mixed-methods approach that combines quantitative survey analysis, qualitative evaluation of open-ended responses, and mapping of the regional education and training ecosystem. The three stakeholder groups are examined collectively to identify points of convergence, divergence, and structural misalignment across the talent-development pipeline.

The study makes four principal contributions to the literature on hydrogen workforce development and energy-system transition. First, it positions workforce readiness as a system-level constraint on hydrogen deployment rather than treating it only as an educational issue. By linking skills deficiencies to project implementation, the study highlights their potential effects on project timing, safety, cost, and reliance on external expertise.

Second, the study provides an integrated empirical assessment of three interdependent stakeholder groups: students as the future workforce, academic institutions as the primary providers of education and training, and industry stakeholders as employers and users of hydrogen-related competencies. This triangulated design enables the identification of misalignment across the complete education-to-employment pathway.

Third, the study provides a comparative assessment of Egypt, Jordan, and Algeria, allowing shared regional challenges to be distinguished from country-specific conditions related to educational capacity, practical training, and industry engagement.

Fourth, the study develops an evidence-informed “Golden Triangle of Employability” structured around industry–academia collaboration, experiential learning, and recognized certification. The framework translates the triangulated findings into a practical model for improving alignment between student preparation, institutional delivery, and labour-market requirements.

The paper is structured as follows. Section 2 reviews the regional hydrogen education and training context in Egypt, Jordan, and Algeria. Section 3 presents the research design, sampling, data collection, coding, and analytical procedures. Section 4 reports the stakeholder findings and country-level analyses. Section 5 interprets the three workforce gaps, develops the Golden Triangle of Employability, and presents policy implications. Section 6 concludes the study and outlines its limitations and future research directions.

This research examined skill gaps and training needs by collecting information from three key groups: students, academia, and industry professionals. The study followed a clear four-step process, which allowed for a thorough review of the topic.

The revised methodological framework is presented as a triangulated mixed-methods design. Quantitative data were obtained from closed-ended questionnaire items, while qualitative data were derived from open-ended responses and the mapping of regional education and professional-training provision. The three evidence streams were analysed separately and subsequently integrated to identify areas of convergence, divergence, and structural misalignment across the hydrogen workforce-development ecosystem.

The study followed four main stages: (1) research design and questionnaire development; (2) participant recruitment and data collection from students, academic staff, and industry professionals; (3) quantitative and qualitative analysis; and (4) triangulation and interpretation of the findings. Figure 2 presents the overall research design.

Research design

A convergent mixed-methods design was used. Quantitative and qualitative information was collected during the same general data-collection period and was analysed as complementary evidence. The quantitative component identified frequencies, response distributions, and differences across participant groups and countries. The qualitative component was used to explain the reasons underlying participants’ preferences, perceived barriers, training needs, and proposed forms of collaboration.

Triangulation was performed at the interpretation stage by comparing findings from:

students, representing potential entrants to the hydrogen workforce;

academic staff, representing curriculum developers and education providers; and.

industry professionals, representing employers, technical practitioners, and users of hydrogen-related competencies.

The purpose of triangulation was not to merge the three groups into a single homogeneous sample, but to determine whether their perspectives supported, contradicted, or complemented one another.

Study setting and participant recruitment

Participants were recruited from Egypt, Jordan, and Algeria because these countries have announced hydrogen-related ambitions and represent different stages of development in hydrogen policy, higher education, professional training, and industrial engagement. The number of participants from each country per survey type is listed in Table 5.

The study used a non-probability convenience sampling strategy. Participants were recruited through the researchers’ accessible institutional and professional networks across Egypt, Jordan, and Algeria. The questionnaires were distributed through participating universities and academic departments, professional contacts, industrial partners, and direct communication with eligible participants. Public online platforms and general email mailing lists were not used for participant recruitment.

Convenience sampling was selected because the study sought responses from accessible individuals with backgrounds relevant to green hydrogen workforce development, including engineering, energy, renewable energy, sustainability, maritime studies, manufacturing, transport, oil and gas, and related technical or professional fields. Participation was voluntary, and respondents were included based on their availability, willingness to participate, and eligibility for one of the three stakeholder groups.

Because participants were recruited through accessible institutional and professional networks rather than through random selection, the sample should not be considered statistically representative of the entire student, academic, or industrial populations of Egypt, Jordan, and Algeria. The findings should therefore be interpreted as an exploratory assessment of the views of relevant stakeholders rather than as nationally representative estimates.

Eligibility and inclusion criteria

Students were eligible to participate if they were enrolled in an undergraduate or postgraduate programme relevant to engineering, energy, renewable energy, environmental science, maritime transport, logistics, physics, water engineering, or another related technical discipline in Egypt, Jordan, or Algeria.

Academic staff were eligible if they were involved in teaching, research, curriculum development, laboratory supervision, programme management, or academic leadership in an engineering, energy, environmental, scientific, or related discipline.

Industry respondents were eligible if they had professional experience in energy, renewable energy, manufacturing, transport, maritime activities, oil and gas, construction, industrial management, technical operations, or a related sector.

Participation was voluntary. Responses were anonymous, and no personally identifiable or sensitive information was collected. Participants were required to provide informed consent before completing the questionnaire. Responses were excluded if it was a duplicate submission or from an ineligible country.

Student survey

A structured questionnaire was administered to 159 students across Egypt, Jordan, and Algeria. Respondents included students from mechanical engineering, energy engineering, maritime transport, environmental sciences, and other technical disciplines. The survey captured:

Familiarity with hydrogen technologies.

Interest in hydrogen courses.

Experience gaps (e.g., prior training).

Preferred learning modes.

Career aspirations.

Perceived barriers to participation.

Both closed-ended and open-ended questions were analyzed using descriptive statistics and thematic coding. A statistical analysis of the students’ fields of study and academic levels is summarized in Tables 6, 7 and 8. Free-text academic-year responses were standardized into undergraduate and postgraduate categories. Ambiguous responses were classified based on the stated programme, year, and field of study.

Academic staff survey

A second questionnaire was completed by 98 academic staff members representing various engineering and science disciplines. Data collection focused on:

Perceptions of hydrogen relevance in engineering curricula.

Curriculum priorities.

Institutional resource availability.

Faculty training needs.

Teaching methodology preferences.

Desired modes of industry collaboration.

Responses were analyzed for quantitative and qualitative insights. Table 8 illustrates the staff’s varied academic levels, while Table 8 summarizes their areas of expertise.

Free-text responses describing academic position, area of expertise, industry sector, and professional role were standardized using a predefined coding framework. Each respondent was assigned to one mutually exclusive primary category. For academic position, leadership titles such as Dean, Director, Vice President, or Head of Department were given precedence over academic rank. Remaining respondents were classified as Professor, Associate Professor, Assistant Professor, Lecturer, or Research and Teaching Staff according to their stated title. Spelling variants and equivalent titles were standardized before coding. Ambiguous responses were reviewed manually by the research team and assigned according to the closest stated role Table 9.

Free-text responses concerning areas of expertise were standardized into six mutually exclusive disciplinary groups: Energy and Renewables; Environmental and Climate Science; Electrical, Electronics and AI; Mechanical and Thermofluids; Chemical, Materials and Physics; and Other/Unspecified. Each respondent was assigned to one primary category based on the dominant or first clearly stated discipline. Where several related fields were listed, the most specific leading discipline was used. For example, “Thermofluids, Renewable Energy and Mechanical Systems” was classified under Mechanical and Thermofluids, whereas “Renewable Energy–Mechanical Engineering” was classified under Energy and Renewables because renewable energy was stated as the principal field.

Electrical engineering, electronics, power systems, mechatronics, control engineering, signal processing, artificial intelligence, and IoT were grouped under Electrical, Electronics and AI. Environmental engineering, climate science, water resources, hydrology, environmental chemistry, sustainability, and related fields were grouped under Environmental and Climate Science. Maritime, logistics, general policy, economics, and urban-planning responses that did not clearly belong to the five technical categories were classified as Other. Numeric or otherwise invalid expertise entries were also classified as Other/Unspecified.

Industry and training ecosystem mapping

Industry needs and training provision patterns were triangulated based on:

Documented professional training programs in the region.

Global education and skills frameworks.

National hydrogen strategies.

This mapping enabled identification of alignment and misalignment between educational offerings, student readiness, and industry skill demands. The main areas of work experience are grouped in Table 10, and their professional level and years of experience are summarized in Tables 11 and 12.

Free-text responses concerning stakeholders’ sectors were standardized into six mutually exclusive groups: Energy and Renewables; Industry and Manufacturing; Transport and Maritime; Academia and Civil Society; Oil and Gas; and Construction. Classification was based primarily on the respondent’s self-reported sector, with the organization and professional title used to clarify ambiguous or overlapping responses. Each respondent was assigned to one primary sector to avoid double counting.

Free-text professional titles were standardized into four mutually exclusive categories: Leadership, Management, Engineering and Technical Roles, and Academic/Other. Executive positions with organization-wide responsibility, including CEO, Managing Director, General Manager, Director, Vice President, Founder, and equivalent titles, were coded as Leadership. Positions involving responsibility for a department, project, region, or operational function were coded as Management. Engineering, operational, maintenance, design, safety, and technical-specialist positions were coded as Engineering and Technical Roles. Academic positions and titles that did not clearly fall within the preceding categories were coded as Academic/Other. Where a title contained more than one role, executive or managerial responsibility was given precedence over technical or academic rank to avoid double counting.

Years-of-experience responses were standardized into three ordered groups: 0–10 years, 11–20 years, and 21 years or more. Numerical values embedded in text, including expressions such as “30 years” or “26 ans,” were extracted and classified using the stated boundaries. Responses describing a starting year were converted to approximate experience using the survey year. Entries that described an area of work rather than a duration, or that contained no interpretable numerical information, were treated as missing or unclassifiable and were not assigned to an experience category.

Inferential statistical analysis

In addition to descriptive frequencies and percentages, inferential analyses were conducted to examine whether selected survey responses differed significantly across Egypt, Jordan, and Algeria. Country-level comparisons were undertaken separately for students, academic staff, and industry stakeholders because the three questionnaires were designed for different populations and did not use identical wording for all items.

The selected outcomes were converted into substantively meaningful binary categories. For example, student familiarity was classified as “familiar” when respondents selected “Know the basics” or “Very knowledgeable about it,” while the remaining responses were classified as limited or no familiarity. Positive interest, internship, certification, training, collaboration, and readiness outcomes were based on clear affirmative responses rather than combining “Yes” and “Maybe.”

Associations between country and survey response were assessed using Pearson’s chi-square statistic. Because some cells contained small expected counts, particularly in the industry sample, statistical significance was estimated using a Monte Carlo permutation procedure with 20,000 permutations. This approach avoids relying solely on the large-sample chi-square approximation when category frequencies are small.

Cramér’s V was reported as an effect-size measure, with larger values indicating stronger associations between country and response. All tests were two-sided, and statistical significance was evaluated at p < 0.05. Inferential analyses were performed. Country comparisons within the industry sample were interpreted cautiously because only six industry respondents were from Algeria. The tests should therefore be considered exploratory rather than nationally representative.

Ethics statement

All methods were carried out in accordance with relevant institutional guidelines and regulations for research involving human participants and with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The study protocol, participant recruitment procedures, and questionnaire-based survey methods were reviewed and approved by the Head of Port Said Branch, Arab Academy for Science, Technology and Maritime Transport (AASTMT), acting as the institutionally authorized approving authority for this minimal-risk academic research. No separate institutional ethics committee review was required under the applicable institutional procedure for this type of anonymous, minimal-risk questionnaire-based study.

The study involved voluntary and anonymous surveys administered to adult university students, academic staff, and industry professionals. No personally identifiable or sensitive information was collected. Informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to participation in the study.

This section presents the triangulated results from students, academic staff, and industry stakeholders across Jordan, Egypt, and Algeria. The findings highlight significant gaps in practical preparedness, institutional capacity, and alignment between educational programs and labor market needs.

Student findings

Students’ interest in learning about hydrogen technologies is high, with nearly 88% “interested” or “very interested” in learning about hydrogen technologies. Although interest was high, only 14.5% of respondents reported having substantial prior knowledge. This indicates a substantial gap between student interest and prior familiarity. The same disparity was evident in students’ practical exposure. About 62% said they had never worked with hydrogen technologies before, and 29% said they had taken part in related programs, most often through graduation projects, internships, or self-directed online courses. Additional 9.2% were aware of training opportunities but could not access them due to availability and cost. Overall, results show clear gap between growing interest and limited educational and training opportunities as shown in Fig. 3.

Additionally, many students strongly favored experiential learning, with a majority of 86% preferring project-based learning, and 88% willing to participate in internships offered in their schools. Professional recognition was also a reason why people wanted to take hydrogen-related classes, with up to 80.5% are likely to take courses for official certification. Blended learning was favored among 43.4% of people, 26.4% recommended hands-on fieldwork, 12.6% were for lab experiments, and 10% recommended simulation tools.

Furthermore, in terms of career interest, students showed various interests in different parts of the hydrogen value chain. Findings reported that 26.7% wanted to work in renewable or green energy, followed by 22.9% in engineering jobs related to hydrogen systems, safety, and storage, 16% were interested in research and development, 7.6% were interested in policy and management roles, and 6.1% were interested in maritime or logistics applications. Final-year students tended to focus on practical, job-ready paths like safety or operations roles. Students in earlier undergraduate years showed greater interest in technology and digital tools.Graduate students, on the other hand, showed greater interest in research, policy, and analytical skills.

Academic staff findings

The majority of surveyed faculty strongly favoured integrating hydrogen-related topics to engineering curricula, with 87% confirming the relevance of the topic and an important area of knowledge for future engineers. The respondent sample was highly experienced; with 69.4% of the participants holding positions as Professors or Associate Professors, and many had direct involvement in curriculum development. This gave additional credibility to the findings and highlights a strong academic justification for incorporating hydrogen-focused content into higher education programs. The key results are summarized in Fig. 4.

Despite this strong endorsement, many institutions remain insufficiently prepared to deliver effective hydrogen education. A significant 83% proportion of academic staff reported not having enough lab resources to teach hydrogen technologies well. Key challenged include that lack of proper equipment, such as electrolyzers, storage systems, and sensors, as well as limited simulation tools. Shortage of technical support and academic funding were frequently reported These limits reveal a structural resource gap that hinders universities from providing students and faculty with the practical, hands-on training they both consider essential.

Additionally, academic staff showed strong interest in enhancing their skills and expertise in hydrogen technologies, with 85% wanting specialized training to improve their teaching skills. Workshops to train trainers, internships for faculty in industry, and chances to work together on research projects were all popular ideas. This string willingness to engage in capacity building suggests that academic staff are well positioned to lead in advancements in hydrogen education, provided that they receive adequate training and support.

Moreover, regarding instructional approaches, most faculty preferred modern, experimental methods in line with international trends in engineering education, with 89% of people supporting project-based learning, real-world case studies, lab work, and modules backed by industry in hydrogen-focused curricula. Faculty members also identified core technical domains with any hydrogen education framework, including hydrogen safety, electrolysis processes, fuel cells, and storage systems. Additionally, digital competencies were widely recognized as important, with strong interest in adding modeling, simulation, and analytical tools alongside hands-on activities to help students understand systems better.

Industry stakeholder findings

Industry professionals’ insights, illustrated in Fig. 5, expressed concerns about the readiness of fresh graduates to meet the emerging demands of the industry, with 78% expressing doubts about graduates’ ability to handle hydrogen-related work, while 65% reported difficulty recruiting suitably skilled personnel for hydrogen projects. These responses highlight a clear and pressing skills shortage, indicating that educational institutions in the region have not adequately prepared graduates for employment in the rapidly hydrogen-powered industries.

The stakeholders, however, were very specific about the competencies required for workforce readiness, where hydrogen safety emerged as the most critical skill area due to handling, storing and systems risks. Additionally, the industry partners emphasized the importance of techno-economic evaluations, digital simulations, and system modeling along with hydrogen production, storage, and environmental impact. These requirements emphasize the multidisciplinary nature of hydrogen value chain, thereby requiring the workforce to possess a combination of engineering, analytical, and safety skills.

The findings further indicate a high level of industry readiness to collaborate with educational institutions, with 93% of the stakeholder’s willingness to support curricula design, training activities, and providing learning-by-doing opportunities for students. Preferred forms of collaboration include internships and site visits, co-development of capstone projects, guest lectures and technical workshops, as well as contributing to training programs leading to certification. Such engagement highlight the importance of close industry–academia partnerships in bridging the skills gap and ensuring alignment between educational outputs and workforce needs.

Moreover, stakeholders identified new job roles that are likely to be in high demand as the hydrogen sector in the region expands, including Hydrogen Systems Engineers, Electrolyzer Production Specialists, Hydrogen Safety Engineers, Infrastructure and Storage Engineers, Hydrogen Project Managers, and Techno-economic Analysts. These positions require a mix of technical skills, safety knowledge, economic knowledge, and digital modeling skills, reflecting that knowledge and skills are needed to support a mature hydrogen workforce.

Overall quantitative insights

Table 13 summarizes the key quantitative results of the survey across the three stakeholder groups. The data clearly confirms a strong orientation toward practical learning among students, recognition of project-based education by academics, and persistent concerns from industry regarding the shortage of qualified professionals.

As indicated in Table 13, students overwhelmingly value internships (88%) and hands-on projects (86%) as the most effective pathways to improve employability. Furthermore, their emphasis on digital skills such as MATLAB and HOMER highlights the demand for advanced simulation capabilities, confirming the growing importance of computational literacy in hydrogen-related education81.

From the academic perspective, the data show that 89% of faculty members advocate project-based learning, aligning closely with student preferences. However, the most significant barrier as reported by 83% of respondents is insufficient funding for laboratories as the primary challenge. This resource gap represents a major constraint on the ability of universities to deliver hands-on learning41.

Finally, industry perspectives reinforce the systemic mismatch, where 65% of employers report a shortage of qualified professionals, particularly in critical positions such as production engineers, safety officers, and systems integrators. These findings confirm that the hydrogen sector requires a diverse set of technical, safety, and interdisciplinary competencies, many of which remain underrepresented in current curricula67.

Overall qualitative themes

Beyond numbers, the survey highlights qualitative themes that converge around the concept of the Golden Triangle of Employability.

Collaboration: the recognition of the need for industry–academia partnerships is evidenced across all groups, including advisory boards, co-designed curricula, and joint projects. Such collaborations are identified as critical to aligning training with market realities82.

Practical Learning: The demand for laboratories, case studies, and internships is articulated by students, academics, and validated by industry stakeholders. This reflects a shared understanding that employability requires real-world contexts more than theoretical mastery83.

Certification: Both students and employers attach high value to formal certification in hydrogen-related skills. Certification thus emerges as a common ground between employability strategies and labor market recognition84.

These qualitative themes highlight that bridging the experience, implementation, and skills gaps is not only a question of resources but also of shared governance and accountability across universities, students, and industry actors.

Country-level descriptive and inferential analysis

Inferential analyses were conducted to determine whether selected findings differed significantly across Egypt, Jordan, and Algeria. Table 14 presents the country-specific affirmative-response rates, Monte Carlo permutation p-values, and Cramér’s V effect sizes.

The student results revealed statistically significant country-level differences in all four selected indicators. Familiarity with hydrogen technologies was highest among Egyptian students and lowest among Jordanian students. Interest in learning about hydrogen was high in all three countries but comparatively lower in Jordan. The same pattern was observed for internship interest and motivation associated with official certification. The corresponding Cramér’s V values ranged from 0.243 to 0.280, indicating modest but meaningful associations between country and student response.

A statistically significant country difference was also found in academic perceptions of the relevance of hydrogen education. Positive assessments were particularly high among the surveyed Algerian academic staff. This association produced the largest observed effect size, Cramér’s V = 0.375. However, the analysis did not find statistically significant country differences in perceived departmental resource shortages or interest in specialized faculty training. Resource constraints were widely reported across all three countries.

No statistically significant country-level differences were identified for the selected industry indicators. Perceptions of graduate readiness, definite willingness to collaborate with universities, and the importance of certification were not significantly associated with country. Nevertheless, these results must be interpreted cautiously because the Algerian industry subsample contained only six respondents, limiting the statistical power and reliability of cross-country estimates.

Overall, the inferential results show that some student and academic perceptions differ across national contexts, whereas institutional resource limitations and the principal industry concerns appear broadly shared.

To identify whether the aggregated regional findings concealed important national differences, selected indicators were examined separately for Egypt, Jordan, and Algeria. The analysis used 159 student responses, comprising 40 from Egypt, 69 from Jordan, and 50 from Algeria; 98 academic staff responses, comprising 28 from Egypt, 30 from Jordan, and 40 from Algeria; and 54 industry stakeholder responses, comprising 34 from Egypt, 14 from Jordan, and 6 from Algeria.

The Algerian industry results should be interpreted cautiously because they are based on only six respondents. Consequently, the observed percentages should not be treated as robust estimates of the wider Algerian industrial sector.

The purpose of this section is to present the findings of all three groups of stakeholders, to analyze the shortcomings of the hydrogen education system and to propose ways of improving hydrogen education in the Southern Mediterranean. The intention is not merely to present the data but also to provide a thorough understanding of the issues and to propose practicable solutions to them.

The triangulated findings indicate that workforce readiness is shaped by the interaction of three connected components: student preparation, institutional delivery capacity, and industry demand. Weakness in any one component reduces the effectiveness of the others. High student interest cannot be converted into occupational competence without appropriate curricula and practical training; institutional commitment cannot produce job-ready graduates without adequate infrastructure and industry engagement; and industry demand cannot be met if employers remain disconnected from curriculum design and training provision.

Accordingly, the central finding of this study is not simply that separate skills shortages exist. Rather, a structural misalignment is present across the full education-to-employment pathway. This interpretation provides the basis for the three-gap framework and the proposed Golden Triangle of Employability.

The inferential analysis demonstrates that the three countries should not be treated as completely homogeneous. Significant differences were observed in student familiarity, educational interest, internship interest, certification motivation, and academic perceptions of curriculum relevance. However, not every descriptive difference was statistically significant. In particular, departmental resource limitations and the selected industry indicators were broadly similar across countries.

Determining the disconnect: a three-part examination of the gaps

The triangulated analysis uncovered a persistent pattern of misalignment across the region. This approach reveals very basic issues in the hydrogen education ecosystem.

The first gap that stands out is the Student Experience Gap. University students have publicly expressed their interest in hydrogen technologies, which are one of the major areas of their future. However, this is often confounded with a lack of access to practical training, hands-on experience and a clearly defined, structured learning pathway. In fact, theory has fortunately been put above practice in their education.

The second gap that exists is the Academic Implementation Gap. Faculty recognize the fact that it is essential for their students to be trained in this new field, nevertheless, instructors’ efforts are constantly thwarted by the lack of lab facilities, outdated curricula, and limited opportunities for professional development. The provision of inadequate tools and resources is a major barrier to effective teaching.

Finally, and most importantly for the region’s economic future, a broadIndustry skills gap has been found. Industry stakeholders—who represent the primary employers of graduates—consistently perceive new graduates as insufficiently prepared for professional practice. Recurrent concerns were raised regarding deficiencies in key areas such as hydrogen safety regulations, techno-economic assessment of hydrogen projects, and system-level modeling capabilities, all of which are essential for real-world deployment. As a result, graduates often require extensive foundational training before they can contribute to industrial settings.

These three interrelated gaps form a bottleneck that hinders the development of hydrogen-ready workforce in a region with growth potential. This common problem needs a solution that everyone can agree on.

The three gaps are mutually reinforcing. Limited practical exposure contributes to weak graduate readiness. Weak institutional capacity restricts the ability of universities to address this lack of exposure. Limited industry participation reduces access to real projects, equipment, internships, and updated occupational requirements.

The relationship can be summarized as follows: students seek practical and recognized learning opportunities; universities support hydrogen education but face implementation constraints; and industry requires job-ready graduates but remains only partially integrated into formal education and training systems.

Therefore, addressing only one gap is unlikely to resolve the overall workforce constraint. Purchasing laboratory equipment without faculty development may result in underutilized facilities. Revising curricula without industry involvement may produce content that remains disconnected from occupational needs. Offering internships without structured learning outcomes may provide exposure without measurable competence development. A coordinated response is required across the three stakeholder groups.

Country-level differences

Although Egypt, Jordan, and Algeria share the broader challenge of aligning hydrogen ambitions with workforce capacity, the survey results indicate that the three national samples should not be treated as fully homogeneous. Differences were observed in student familiarity and engagement, academic perceptions of curriculum relevance, institutional resources, and industry assessments of graduate readiness.

These differences should not be interpreted as a ranking of national hydrogen readiness. The study used convenience sampling through accessible institutional and professional networks, and the country samples were unequal. The findings therefore represent patterns among the surveyed respondents rather than nationally representative estimates.

Jordan

The surveyed Jordanian students reported lower familiarity and lower affirmative engagement than their Egyptian and Algerian counterparts. Only 40.6% reported basic or advanced familiarity with hydrogen technologies. Nevertheless, 76.8% remained interested or very interested in learning about the subject, indicating that the main issue is not an absence of interest but comparatively limited prior exposure and access.

Definite interest in university-supported internships was 65.2%, and 68.1% stated that certification would increase their motivation. These proportions were lower than those observed in Egypt and Algeria, but they still represent a clear majority of the Jordanian student sample.

The academic data identify practical infrastructure as a particularly important challenge. Although 66.7% of Jordanian academics considered hydrogen relevant or extremely relevant, 96.7% described their departments as not equipped or only partially equipped. This was the highest reported resource limitation among the three academic samples.

Jordan benefits from international cooperation, transnational programmes, and green hydrogen and power-to-X training initiatives. However, the findings suggest that these strengths have not yet translated into sufficiently broad laboratory and practical-training capacity. In addition, 76.7% of academics expressed definite interest in specialized training, indicating continued demand for faculty development.

Among the Jordanian industry respondents, 42.9% considered graduates ready for hydrogen work and 64.3% expressed definite willingness to collaborate with universities. Certification was considered important or very important by 92.9%.

Jordan’s priority should therefore be to connect its international knowledge partnerships more directly to domestic laboratory development, faculty upskilling, technician training, and structured placements with relevant industrial and energy-sector organizations.

Egypt

The Egyptian student sample showed comparatively high familiarity with hydrogen technologies, with 70.0% reporting either basic or advanced knowledge. Student interest in further learning was also high at 95.0%, while 85.0% requested university-supported internships and 90.0% reported greater motivation where official certification was available.

These results suggest that the principal challenge in Egypt is not a lack of student demand. Rather, it is the conversion of strong interest and broad renewable-energy awareness into structured hydrogen-specific competence. Egypt has a large and diverse higher-education system, including numerous engineering and renewable-energy programmes, but the existing hydrogen provision remains fragmented across institutions.

The academic findings reinforce this interpretation. Although 67.9% considered hydrogen relevant or extremely relevant to current curricula, 82.1% reported that their departments were either not equipped or only partially equipped. At the same time, 92.9% expressed interest in specialized training or partnerships. This indicates that Egypt possesses significant educational scale and faculty willingness, but requires stronger coordination, laboratory access, curriculum specialization, and industry-linked delivery.

Only 23.5% of the Egyptian industry respondents definitely considered graduates ready for hydrogen work, while 67.6% expressed definite willingness to collaborate with universities. This combination suggests a clear opportunity: employers perceive a readiness gap, but many are willing to participate in closing it.

Accordingly, Egypt’s priority should be to convert its broad university base into a coordinated hydrogen skills system through shared laboratories, nationally aligned learning outcomes, industry-supported internships, faculty training, and recognized hydrogen micro-credentials.

Algeria

The Algerian student sample demonstrated strong educational interest. A total of 96.0% were interested or very interested in learning about green hydrogen, 88.0% requested university-supported internships, and 90.0% stated that official certification would increase their motivation. Familiarity was lower than in Egypt but remained above the Jordanian sample, at 58.0%.

Academic recognition of hydrogen education was particularly strong in Algeria. 95% of academic respondents considered hydrogen relevant or extremely relevant to engineering curricula. This may be consistent with the country’s emerging dedicated hydrogen programmes, industrial energy experience, and growing involvement of universities and major energy-sector actors.

However, strong recognition did not eliminate implementation constraints. A total of 82.5% of Algerian academics reported that their departments were either not equipped or only partially equipped. This indicates that policy and curricular interest are developing faster than the practical resources needed for delivery.

The Algerian industry sample showed high affirmative responses regarding graduate readiness and collaboration. However, these results were based on only six respondents and should not be interpreted as representative of Algerian industry. They are better treated as preliminary indications of positive engagement among the participating organizations.

Algeria’s priority should be to scale emerging hydrogen programmes beyond a limited number of institutions, expand laboratory and vocational-training capacity, and link its established oil, gas, and energy expertise to green hydrogen safety, electrolysis, renewable integration, storage, and export infrastructure.

Comparative interpretation

The three countries therefore face different versions of a common workforce-development challenge. Egypt has broad institutional scale and strong student demand, but hydrogen education remains fragmented and practical delivery requires greater coordination. Jordan benefits from international cooperation and specialized initiatives, but the surveyed institutions reported particularly severe laboratory limitations and students showed comparatively lower exposure. Algeria showed strong academic recognition and student interest, but its emerging programmes require wider coverage, resources, and further empirical validation of industry readiness.

Several commonalities are equally important. Most academic respondents in every country reported inadequate or only partial departmental resources. Strong support for certification was also observed among academic and industry respondents across all three national samples. These shared findings support regional cooperation in competence standards, certification, faculty development, and access to specialized practical facilities.

At the same time, national actions should differ according to context. Egypt requires coordination and scaling across a large higher-education system; Jordan requires stronger practical infrastructure and translation of international partnerships into local delivery; and Algeria requires expansion and consolidation of its emerging hydrogen education and industry-engagement mechanisms. Implications for workforce development

The emerging hydrogen economy demands a workforce equipped with diverse and highly specialized competencies, ranging from skilled technicians and engineers to safety specialists, data and simulation experts, and professionals versed in policy and regulatory frameworks. Addressing these requirements calls for a coordinated approach that brings together universities, industry partners, and government agencies. Such collaboration is essential not only to ensure that educational institutions can update curricula and strengthen practical training, but also to align national workforce strategies with the technical, safety, digital, and regulatory needs of a rapidly evolving sector. Developing a robust hydrogen workforce therefore hinges on sustained investment, targeted capacity building, and strategic partnerships that collectively support the formation of a competent and future-ready talent pipeline.

Industry stakeholders provided the most critical assessment of the skills landscape. The survey results confirm the existence of a growing demand for hydrogen expertise across energy, transport, and industrial sectors, yet employers consistently report that graduates are not adequately prepared for immediate integration into the workforce85.

Specifically, employers emphasize competencies in:

1. Safety – handling, storage, and compliance with regulations.

2. Technical expertise – operation and maintenance of electrolyzers, fuel cells, and related systems.

3. Techno-economic analysis – assessing the financial feasibility and scalability of hydrogen projects26.

4. Digital modeling and simulation – designing and optimizing hydrogen systems using advanced computational tools.

The “skills gap” is therefore multidimensional, spanning technical, safety, economic, and digital domains. The European Commission86 underscores that this gap poses a risk to Europe’s hydrogen ambitions, as the shortage of trained personnel could delay large-scale project deployment.

At the same time, the survey reveals high willingness of industry to collaborate with academia, where more than 90% of employers expressed readiness to offer internships, co-design curricula, and open industrial sites for student training. This openness represents a unique opportunity to bridge the gap through structured partnerships, where universities and industry co-create pathways for workforce development.

The findings suggest that workforce readiness functions as a binding constraint within the hydrogen system, comparable to infrastructure or financing limitations. Unlike traditional bottlenecks, however, workforce gaps are slower to resolve and require long-term institutional coordination. This positions human capital development as a strategic priority rather than a supporting activity in hydrogen policy.The Golden Triangle of Employability is supported by converging evidence from students, academic staff, and industry stakeholders and consists of three interdependent pillars: industry–academia collaboration, experiential learning, and certification. Students strongly favored internships, real projects, site visits, mentoring, hands-on training, and officially certified courses; academic staff similarly prioritized placements, joint research, curriculum co-development, faculty upskilling, project-based learning, laboratory work, and accredited learning; and industry respondents expressed willingness to collaborate through internships, research, mentoring, curriculum participation, field exposure, and continuing professional development. Together, these findings show that collaboration can align curricula with labour-market needs, experiential learning can convert theoretical knowledge into practical competence, and certification can provide visible and trusted recognition of that competence. However, certification should assess actual knowledge and skills, including safety, practical performance, digital modelling, system analysis, and techno-economic evaluation, rather than merely confirming attendance.

Implications for hydrogen deployment

The findings have implications extending beyond university education as summarized in Table 15. A hydrogen economy requires not only trained graduates, but also technicians, safety specialists, plant operators, project managers, regulatory experts, researchers, and professionals capable of conducting techno-economic and environmental assessments.

If workforce development continues to lag behind infrastructure planning, several consequences may arise.

Hydrogen projects may face delays during design, installation, commissioning, operation, and maintenance if competent personnel are unavailable. Even where equipment and finance are secured, implementation may be constrained by shortages in specialist labour.

Hydrogen production, storage, transportation, and use involve specific safety requirements. Insufficient competence in risk assessment, leakage detection, material compatibility, pressure systems, emergency response, and regulatory compliance may increase operational and public-safety risks.

A lack of local competence may require project developers to recruit international experts, import consultancy services, or provide extensive foundational training. This may increase project costs and reduce the share of economic value retained within the host country.

National hydrogen strategies often emphasize industrial development, local employment, technology transfer, and export potential. These benefits may not be fully realized if local workers and institutions are not prepared to participate across the value chain.

Technology transfer depends on the capacity of local engineers, researchers, technicians, and institutions to understand, adapt, operate, and improve imported technologies. Weak institutional and workforce capacity may lead to long-term dependence rather than sustainable local capability.

Hydrogen infrastructure may become underutilized or less effective if investment in physical assets is not accompanied by comparable investment in curriculum development, laboratories, faculty training, certification, and industrial placements.

These implications support the central argument that workforce readiness should be treated as a strategic component of hydrogen policy and project planning. Human-capital requirements should be assessed at the same stage as technology selection, financing, environmental approval, and infrastructure design Table 16.

The first pillar, industry–academia collaboration, is supported by evidence from all three groups. Students sought internships, mentoring, site visits, and participation in real research projects. Academic staff prioritized student placements, co-developed research, joint curriculum design, and faculty upskilling. Industry respondents indicated substantial willingness to collaborate through research, internships, expert exchange, curriculum participation, and continuing professional development. These findings indicate that collaboration is the principal mechanism through which labour-market requirements can be communicated to educational institutions and translated into relevant learning activities.

The second pillar, experiential learning, reflects the consistent demand for learning through application rather than classroom instruction alone. Among students, 105 of 159 gave a definite positive response to participating in hands-on projects or training, while a further 50 expressed conditional interest. In addition, 123 students requested internship or employment opportunities through their universities. Academic staff similarly preferred project-based learning, collaborative industry-linked projects, laboratory work, research projects, access to pilot plants, and internships. Industry respondents recommended field visits, real-project case studies, on-site training, laboratory experiments, and digital simulation. The convergence of these results indicates that practical competence must be developed through a combination of experimental, digital, project-based, and workplace learning.

The third pillar, certification, emerged as a shared mechanism for recognizing and communicating competence. A total of 128 students indicated that an official certificate would increase their motivation to enrol in a green hydrogen course. Accredited certification was considered valuable or extremely valuable by 95 of the 98 academic respondents. Similarly, 48 of the 54 industry respondents considered certification important or very important. These results suggest that certification can support student motivation, provide a reference for curriculum quality, and increase employer confidence in graduates’ capabilities.
