Industry–academia collaboration identifies and updates relevant competencies; experiential learning develops those competencies through applied activities; and certification verifies and communicates competence. Their interaction is expected to improve curriculum alignment, practical readiness, and employer confidence.

Actionable policy implications

The findings indicate that hydrogen workforce readiness cannot be improved through curriculum revision alone. The three identified gaps require coordinated intervention by governments, universities, accreditation authorities, industry, and funding organizations. Each actor has a distinct role in aligning education provision with the technical, safety, digital, and economic requirements of hydrogen deployment.

The recommendations below are derived from the triangulated findings. Students emphasized practical training, internships, and recognized certification; academic staff identified laboratory limitations, faculty-development needs, and the value of industry-supported teaching; and industry stakeholders highlighted graduate-readiness concerns, priority competence areas, and willingness to collaborate with universities.

Actions for national governments and ministries

National governments should integrate workforce-development targets directly into hydrogen strategies rather than treating skills as a secondary education issue. Hydrogen policy documents should identify the number and types of technicians, engineers, safety specialists, project managers, researchers, and regulatory professionals required at different stages of project development.

Specific actions should include:

1. Preparing national hydrogen skills roadmaps linked to planned production, storage, transport, industrial-use, and export projects.

2. Establishing an inter-ministerial hydrogen skills committee involving the ministries responsible for energy, higher education, technical education, labour, industry, and environment.

3. Allocating dedicated funding for hydrogen laboratories, faculty development, technician training, and shared practical facilities.

4. Including workforce-readiness requirements within public funding calls, industrial licences, and major hydrogen investment agreements.

5. Creating incentives for companies that provide internships, equipment access, staff training, guest instruction, and co-supervised student projects.

6. Supporting national databases that monitor hydrogen-related occupations, vacancies, competence shortages, and training provision.

These actions would help align infrastructure investment with the human-capital capacity required to operate and maintain the resulting systems.

Actions for universities and technical education providers

Universities should move from isolated hydrogen lectures or elective topics toward structured and progressive competence development. This does not necessarily require the immediate establishment of complete hydrogen degree programmes. Hydrogen content may instead be introduced through modular pathways embedded within electrical, mechanical, chemical, energy, environmental, maritime, and industrial engineering programmes.

Recommended curriculum areas include:

• hydrogen fundamentals and value chains;

• electrolysis and renewable-energy integration;

• fuel cells and end-use applications;

• hydrogen storage and transport;

• safety, risk assessment, and emergency response;

• materials and component compatibility;

• power electronics and system integration;

• modelling, simulation, and digital tools;

• techno-economic analysis;

• environmental and lifecycle assessment;

• standards, regulation, and certification; and.

• project management and market development.

Universities should map these areas to explicit learning outcomes and define the level of competence expected from technicians, undergraduate students, postgraduate students, and practising professionals.

Further actions should include:

1. Introducing project-based modules using regional hydrogen case studies.

2. Embedding internships, site visits, and industry-defined capstone projects within study programmes.

3. Developing low-cost modular training rigs, simulations, remote laboratories, and shared facilities where full-scale equipment is unaffordable.

4. Creating interdisciplinary teaching teams across engineering, economics, safety, policy, and environmental disciplines.

5. Establishing industry advisory boards that review curriculum content periodically.

6. Tracking graduate progression into hydrogen-related employment and using employer feedback to revise curricula.

Actions for accreditation and professional authorities

Accreditation bodies and professional organizations should define minimum competence standards for hydrogen-related education and short-course certification. These standards should focus on demonstrable outcomes rather than attendance or contact hours alone.

The competence framework should distinguish among:

• awareness-level knowledge;

• design and analysis competence;

• operational and maintenance competence;

• safety-critical competence;

• supervisory and project-management competence; and.

• advanced research and specialist competence.

Recommended actions include:

1. Defining minimum learning outcomes for hydrogen-related university modules and professional courses.

2. Developing stackable micro-credentials in areas such as hydrogen safety, electrolysis, storage, system modelling, and techno-economic assessment.

3. Requiring practical assessment for certificates claiming operational or safety competence.

4. Establishing procedures for periodic review as technologies, standards, and regulations evolve.

5. Supporting mutual recognition of certificates across the Southern Mediterranean where appropriate.

6. Involving universities, employers, professional bodies, and safety authorities in standard development.

A common competence framework would improve transparency for students and employers and reduce inconsistency among short courses and institutional certificates.

Actions for faculty development

The high level of academic interest in specialized training indicates that faculty development should be treated as a central implementation requirement. Curriculum reform cannot be effective where instructors lack access to updated technical knowledge, practical facilities, or industrial experience.

Recommended actions include:

1. Train-the-trainer programmes covering hydrogen production, storage, safety, system integration, simulation, and techno-economic assessment.

2. Short industrial secondments allowing academic staff to observe real project design, operation, maintenance, and safety procedures.

3. Joint teaching by academics and industry professionals.

4. International mobility and exchange programmes linked to specific curriculum-development outputs.

5. Access to shared teaching materials, simulation models, laboratory procedures, and regional case studies.

6. Small competitive grants for faculty-led teaching innovation and laboratory development.

7. Periodic competency renewal where staff teach safety-critical or rapidly evolving subjects.

Faculty-development programmes should require participants to translate training into concrete outputs, such as a revised module, laboratory activity, case study, assessment method, or industry-linked student project.

Actions for industry representatives

Industry involvement should progress from occasional guest lectures toward structured participation in workforce development. The survey findings indicate substantial willingness among participating industry stakeholders to collaborate with universities. This willingness can be converted into formal and measurable partnerships.

Industry actions should include:

1. Providing structured internships with defined learning objectives and supervisor evaluations.

2. Offering controlled access to sites, pilot facilities, equipment, operational data, and case studies.

3. Co-designing curricula and reviewing competence requirements annually.

4. Providing practising engineers and safety professionals as guest instructors or mentors.

5. Co-supervising graduation projects and applied research addressing real industrial problems.

6. Supporting faculty secondments and train-the-trainer activities.

7. Participating in practical assessment and certification panels.

8. Reporting emerging occupations, recruitment difficulties, and changing skill requirements to universities and government agencies.

Public-private agreements should specify the contribution expected from each partner rather than relying on informal commitments.

Public-private partnerships

Public-private partnerships can address the high cost of hydrogen laboratories and the fragmented nature of current training provision. Rather than requiring every university to purchase complete hydrogen systems, shared regional or national training centres may be established through combined public funding, university participation, and industry support.

Possible partnership models include:

• shared hydrogen laboratories serving multiple institutions;

• mobile demonstration and training units;

• virtual and remote-access laboratories;

• university-industry pilot plants;

• jointly funded training chairs;

• regional centres for hydrogen safety;

• industry-sponsored scholarships and placements; and.

• common digital platforms containing teaching materials, simulations, and case studies.

Such partnerships should include governance arrangements, access rules, maintenance responsibilities, safety procedures, and measurable training targets, these recommendation as listed in Table 17.

name: Clean Energy
title: From commitments to measurable action: how can manufacturing reduce its impact on nature
description:
With a global manufacturing footprint, we have a responsibility to reduce our impact on nature and help create safe conditions for people and wildlife to coexist.
As part of our Brighter Lives, Better World 2030 program, we have committed to making 100% of our manufacturing sites Low Nature Impact sites by 2030.
Nearly half of our manufacturing sites have achieved four out of six Low Nature Impact targets, while more than a third have reached three of the six.
Our Low Nature Impact initiative reflects our belief that environmental challenges must be addressed as they exist, as an interconnected system.
Signify’s Low Nature Impact program is a clear example of the kind of measurable, site-level action that can help reduce emissions, protect nature and create benefits beyond the factory gate.
text:
At our manufacturing site in Piła, Poland, recent wildlife monitoring revealed some unexpected night-time activity: at least six bat species use the area to feed on insects around the trees and factory lighting. It is a small but powerful reminder that industrial sites are part of local ecosystems. With a global manufacturing footprint, we have a responsibility to reduce our impact on nature and help create safe conditions for people and wildlife to coexist.

That responsibility is becoming increasingly material for business. More than half of the world’s GDP – approximately $44 trillion of economic value generation1 – is moderately or highly dependent on nature and its services. As ecosystems come under pressure, nature loss is reshaping how companies think about resilience, compliance and long-term value.

Awareness is growing, but meaningful corporate action still needs to accelerate. Frameworks such as the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures are helping companies better assess nature-related risks and dependencies, yet the World Benchmarking Alliance has found that many large companies still lack a full understanding of their impacts on nature, even as regulatory and investor expectations continue to rise.

From ambition to measurable action

This urgency is already driving practical and measurable change at Signify’s operational sites: from renewable electricity and solar installations to wastewater optimization, chemical substitution, water-use reduction, and waste-to-landfill targets.

As part of our Brighter Lives, Better World 2030 program, we have committed to making 100% of our manufacturing sites Low Nature Impact sites by 2030. While targets and transparent disclosure are essential, these measures alone are not enough to protect ecosystems, which is why we have translated nature ambitions into measurable operational targets. These targets include minimizing emissions to water, air and soil, water consumption, hazardous waste and waste to landfill across our global manufacturing footprint. By addressing these interconnected challenges, we are helping reduce pollution while advancing broader climate and biodiversity goals.

Progress across the manufacturing footprint

Manufacturing is where environmental commitments become operational reality. Setting these targets involved comprehensively examining our full manufacturing footprint to understand where we could make a real impact that would carry corporate-made targets through to on-the-ground reality integrated into everyday decision-making.

We already have strong momentum. Nearly half of our manufacturing sites have achieved four out of six Low Nature Impact targets, while more than a third have reached three of the six. Less than 0,5% of our waste goes to landfill. We are building on decades of environmental progress and scaling proven solutions across our global manufacturing footprint.

Our Low Nature Impact initiative reflects our belief that environmental challenges must be addressed as they exist, as an interconnected system. By reducing emissions, conserving water and minimizing waste, we are simultaneously strengthening the resilience of our operations while helping protect the ecosystems on which we all depend.

What this looks like in practice:

Renewable energy: deploying solar panel projects and battery energy storage systems to support the transition to lower-carbon manufacturing.

Energy efficiency: installing radiant heaters and heat-recovery solutions that reuse energy that would otherwise be lost.

Cleaner processes: upgrading pretreatment filter systems and chemical substitution to reduce chemical use and wastewater impact.

Air quality: chimney electro-filter improvements designed to reduce particulate emissions.

Waste and water: site-level actions to improve wastewater treatment, reduce hazardous waste and minimize landfill.

Site plans also show quantified actions, including solar panel installations expected to deliver 503 kWh and 893 kWh of solar energy and cut CO₂ emissions by 352 and 623 tons per year respectively, as well as boiler room modernization targeting a 2,099-ton annual CO₂ reduction and stack electro-filter installation designed to reduce PM10 emissions from an average of 67 to 17 mg/Nm.

Working with partners to scale impact

No company can address nature loss, pollution and climate resilience in isolation. Meaningful progress depends on collaboration between businesses, expert partners and civil society, combining operational action with scientific insight, accountability and shared learning.

For Signify, partnerships play an important role in strengthening the impact of our Low Nature Impact program by helping connect site-level environmental improvements with wider efforts to protect ecosystems, reduce pollution and support healthier communities. This is especially important when it comes to air quality, where reducing emissions at source can deliver benefits beyond our own operations.

Clean air is essential for healthy people, resilient communities and thriving ecosystems, but it cannot be delivered by policy alone. Businesses have a critical role to play by cutting pollution at source, embedding air quality into climate and nature strategies, and using their operational reach to accelerate practical solutions. Signify’s Low Nature Impact program is a clear example of the kind of measurable, site-level action that can help reduce emissions, protect nature and create benefits beyond the factory gate.

Clare Daly, Head of Private Sector Engagement, Clean Air Fund

Manufacturing as part of the solution

We will only see true progress on protecting nature when businesses move beyond generic commitments and become specific enough to manage, measure and improve. The next phase of corporate nature-action will be judged less by the promises companies make, and more by how clearly they can show where, how, and by how much they are reducing their impact.

For manufacturers, now is the time to embed nature into site planning, investment decisions and day-to-day operations, turning commitments into measurable progress for climate, nature and communities.

Drivers set out from Miami, Raleigh, New York, Minneapolis, Chicago, Houston, Tuscaloosa, Ellabell & West Point, GA, Woodcliff Lake, Mountain View & Big Bear, CA, Phoenix, Portland and Salt Lake City, crossing mountains, deserts and plains in every kind of weather, and charging at roughly 30% of IONNA’s over 220 locations along the way. Every route ended at the same place: IONNA’s newest Rechargery in Westminster, CA. The goal was simple: show that the great American road trip has gone electric.

Autocharge at IONNA, coming soon for Stellantis drivers and now available for Tesla drivers

A road trip only works when charging is simple for every driver, and as IONNA grows, its seamless experience grows as well. With Stellantis coming next month and Tesla available now, these drivers join owners of BMW, GM, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Toyota, Rivian, Ford, Porsche and Volvo EVs in plugging in and charging automatically at IONNA.

Presto is enabling Autocharge for Tesla drivers, exclusively at IONNA. No card, tap or extra steps. Just the frictionless charging experience they know, at up to 400kW. With this addition, IONNA’s Plug & Charge capabilities now extend to roughly two-thirds of EVs on the road today, reinforcing its commitment to open access for drivers of every brand.

Charging discounts at IONNA, coming in December for Stellantis BEV drivers

IONNA is also expanding its charging benefits for drivers of its founding automakers to include eligible Stellantis BEVs. Starting in December, all Jeep®, Dodge, Ram, and FIAT Battery-electric vehicle drivers will receive a 10% discount on charging at all IONNA Rechargeries. For drivers with an eligible connected services subscription, they will receive an additional 15% discount, increasing to a total of 25% off. The addition gives more drivers access to everyday savings as the IONNA network continues to grow.

Westminster: The IONNA Rechargery experience

At the end of the road trip, drivers arrived at a station showing the very epitome of what IONNA has to offer. The Westminster station, at 6260 Westminster Blvd., draws on lessons learned from the network’s original Rechargeries in Apex and Garner, N.C. It features 22 high-powered charging bays, indoor and outdoor lounge space, dedicated restrooms, Amazon’s Just Walk Out technology and additional amenities nearby. Purpose-built around IONNA’s core tenets, it makes EV charging an experience, not just a utility stop.

And it doesn’t stand alone. IONNA now has 16 full Rechargeries open or under construction in Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Georgia, Maryland, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio, Oregon, Texas and Utah. Each brings enhanced amenities, upgraded canopies & lighting, improved accessibility, customer spaces and retail, so drivers well beyond a handful of major cities can enjoy the full IONNA experience.

“Westminster is the embodiment of reliable, affordable, and convenient charging,” said Seth Cutler, CEO of IONNA. “It provides a comfortable place to wait and the amenities you’d expect from a great stop, all in one place. IONNA is building a quality charging experience at scale, and we will keep raising the bar until charging is no longer a barrier to EV adoption.”

title: 5 trends that will define 2027—and how to invest in them | Fortune
description:
Interest rates go even higher In 2024, it appeared that pandemic-era inflation had been tamed, and the Federal Reserve responded with a series of cuts to its benchmark interest rate.
But high interest rates are not bad for everyone.
Beneficiaries include individual savers, who can look forward to higher income, and big banks whose business involves lending money.

text:
Interest rates go even higher

In 2024, it appeared that pandemic-era inflation had been tamed, and the Federal Reserve responded with a series of cuts to its benchmark interest rate. This optimism didn’t last, however, and price shocks from tariffs and the Iran war led the Fed to boost rates in 2026. The central bank is expected to continue on this path.

This is glum news for homebuyers and the real estate industry, and for sectors including AI, which count on cheap credit to keep their businesses humming. But high interest rates are not bad for everyone. Beneficiaries include individual savers, who can look forward to higher income, and big banks whose business involves lending money.

While banks tend to earn more from loans when rates are higher, it is the “goliath” banks that do best in these environments, said Mike Mayo, head of U.S. large-cap bank research at Wells Fargo Securities. For 2027, Mayo said JPMorgan Chase (JPM) and Bank of America (BAC), in particular, appear poised for a strong year based on bullish guidance they have issued. But he cautions that high interest rates only act as a tailwind up to a point—and that a rapid series of hikes would put larger portions of the economy under strain, counteracting the positive effect of higher interest rates for banks.

Mayo dismissed concerns over new technologies, such as yield-seeking AI agents that could threaten the deposit base of the biggest banks such as Citigroup (C) and Wells Fargo (WFC). “The death of large banks has been exaggerated for 50 years,” he said. “Their deposit franchises have become bigger over time, and the reason is trust. Trust is more important than Big Tech.”

This trust in established financial institutions, along with big banks’ aversion to risk in general, are likely to serve the banks especially well at a time of mounting unease over cybersecurity—the result of a spate of recent incidents, including ones involving rogue AI agents. In this context, the “goliath” banks may draw investors looking for a safe and steady play.

And while their performance trailed the broader S&P 500 in 2026, the Big Four banks delivered on another attribute that investors value: large and reliable dividends.

AI, AI, and more AI

It’s been about four years since OpenAI’s launch of ChatGPT set off a massive rally in AI stocks. Some investors are getting jitters about the scope of the AI build-out amid fears that it’s a bubble—especially after the blue wave midterms elected a slew of Democrats on promises to rein in the AI industry. Still, the tech behemoths at the center of the boom—including Meta Platforms, Microsoft, and Amazon—are going full speed.

In this environment, looking for opportunities is not about deciding whether artificial intelligence is the future (spoiler alert: It is). The real question is which companies are positioned to succeed, no matter the pace of the AI build-out.

In this context, Bernstein senior analyst Stacy Rasgon likes the chipmaker Broadcom (AVGO) because its stock is “very, very cheap,” he told Fortune. The stock, like that of other chipmakers, sold off sharply in late 2026 as investors questioned how long the AI spending frenzy can last, even though earnings expectations remain strong.

Fellow chipmaker Nvidia’s shares took a major hit in November following revelations that its CEO, Jensen Huang, had acknowledged an affair, while the company opened an investigation into reports that he had been targeted by Chinese intelligence. Huang resigned from the company he cofounded four days later.

Applied Materials (AMAT) is another stock that may offer considerable upside. The company sells equipment to manufacture chips, positioning Applied Materials to benefit from infrastructure investments in advanced processors, memory, and chip packaging. “It’s very clear to me that we need a lot more equipment,” said Rasgon.

That doesn’t mean these companies won’t face potential headwinds in 2027. Arun Sundaram, an investment strategist at CFRA, points to potential energy bottlenecks and concerns that higher interest rates could make AI financing more expensive. He cites political pushback against data center construction as another potential obstacle—opposition that will only increase as Democrats, many of whom have been vocal critics of the AI industry, take power in Congress.

Still, analysts like Rasgon remain optimistic. He pointed to third-quarter earnings from Big Tech, which included more AI spending and a surge in cloud revenues. “As it turns out, a lot of these companies may be more profitable than people thought. They’re actually generating money,” he said. “From a fundamental level, we’ll probably see sustainability in spending … Whether or not sentiment from a stock standpoint is going to buy into that or not, I don’t know yet. But that’s going to be the key debate.”

A world at war

Most of our recommendations point you toward stocks or sectors to buy. When it comes to the defense industry in 2027 you might be well served to do the opposite: Stay on the sidelines. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine dragged into its fifth year in February 2026. That same month, the U.S. and Israel launched a war against Iran, triggering retaliatory attacks across the Middle East. By early summer, there was anxious talk in Washington, D.C., about depleted stocks of missiles and other munitions.

In such an environment, investors might expect the shares of large defense companies to be soaring. That’s not the case. Even as demand for weapons has grown and a slew of techy startups have entered the sector, the stock prices of the big military contractors known as the “primes”—including RTX, Northrop Grumman, and General Dynamics—have largely flailed. Only one of these companies, Lockheed Martin, outperformed the S&P. Shares of Boeing, which has a sizable division that sells to the military, lagged the index by 30%.

The reason for this lackluster performance is ongoing uncertainty over U.S. defense spending, said Peter Arment, a senior analyst at Baird. While the Pentagon and President Donald Trump are keen to pass a massive allocation for the military, it’s unclear where the money to pay for it would come from. Meanwhile, many in the incoming freshman class of Democrats vocally oppose Trump’s military policies.

While there is a tradition of bipartisan support for the military in Congress, this may not translate into a major defense bill in 2027, Arment said. Instead, lawmakers may rely on ad hoc measures that don’t include significant military spending.

The weight-loss boom, supersized

We’ve all heard the buzz about GLP-1s, the blockbuster category of drugs that are delivering dramatic results in treating obesity and Type 2 diabetes. In 2027, the medications—sold under brand names including Ozempic and Wegovy—are poised to reach even more patients as insurance coverage expands and pills offer an alternative to injections.

JPMorgan forecasts that the global market for incretin-based drugs, which include GLP-1s, will reach $200 billion by 2030. In the U.S., the bank predicts that the number of patients taking these drugs will jump from roughly 10 million in 2025 to 25 million by the end of the decade.

This rise will be driven in part by expanded Medicare access. The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge, which launched in July and runs through December 2027, offers certain weight-management drugs for $50 a month.

GLP-1 in pill form could draw more users, too. Novo Nordisk’s oral Wegovy won FDA approval in December 2025, followed by Eli Lilly’s Foundayo in April 2026. Both are taken daily and could appeal to people who have held off on the treatment because they don’t like injections.

Lilly (LLY) and Novo (NVO) stocks stand to benefit the most. Both sell injectable and oral weight-loss treatments, and have spent years building the manufacturing facilities needed to meet demand. Lilly has committed more than $50 billion to U.S. manufacturing since 2020. It would take years for smaller would-be rivals to reach this scale. That business “moat” should help Lilly and Novo hold on to their lead, Evan Seigerman, BMO’s head of health care research, told Fortune: “I think that those two are poised to really maintain the lion’s share of the market in 2027,” he said. “You don’t see anyone else coming to take that share.”

For investors looking for a picks-and-shovels play outside of the drugmakers themselves, West Pharmaceutical Services (WST) is an option. The company sells injectable-drug components like stoppers, plungers, and seals. Wall Street has taken notice: In November, Jefferies called the stock a buy and hiked its price target.

Solar is ready to shine

Those who assumed the solar sector was dead are missing out on one of the more surprising twists of 2027. Amid ongoing tensions in the Middle East, demand for energy is stronger than ever, and that is good news for solar power.

Solar companies are also poised to benefit from developers rushing to meet a key end-of-2027 deadline for federal clean-electricity tax credits. The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 established the clean-electricity tax credits, but President Donald Trump’s 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act accelerated their expiration. Projects that began construction after July 4, 2026, must be placed in service by the end of 2027; those that began construction on or before that date can qualify even if they come online later, subject to other requirements. The investment credit generally covers 30% of qualifying costs for projects, with additional bonuses available. Developers can alternatively claim a credit based on electricity production.

A rush by solar installers to meet the end-of-2027 deadline is likely to boost sales for First Solar (FSLR), which makes electricity-generating panels, and for Nextpower (NXT) and Array Technologies (ARRY), which sell tracking systems that help panels follow the sun.

Regardless of how many installers meet the solar tax credit deadline, overall energy consumption will rise in 2027. UBS projects this will lead to 310 gigawatts of combined U.S. solar and wind additions through 2030, driven partly by power-hungry data centers and industrial customers. Goldman Sachs forecasts global data center power demand will rise 220% from 2023 levels by 2030.

Natural gas could help meet that demand, but there has been a surge in orders for the gas turbines that power data centers, meaning delivery can take years. Case in point: GE Vernova, a leading maker of this heavy-duty machinery, was already taking orders for 2031 in July 2026.

Those long lead times could give solar an opening. Gregory Nemet, a professor at the University of Wisconsin, told Fortune that developers planning data centers in the next few years may choose solar if they cannot get these turbines. “That dynamic is pretty consequential to how fast solar grows,” Nemet said.

This article appears in the December 2026/January 2027 issue of Fortune.

title: What did COP31 deliver on super pollutants and health? - Clean Air Fund
description:
Amidst the headlines decrying the failure of this year’s negotiations, we saw glimmers of progress on areas like super pollutants, with emerging coalitions of the willing stepping up.
Action on super pollutants is an essential part of protecting our climate and improving our health.
These short-lived climate pollutants are responsible for nearly half of global warming to date.
Progress on super pollutants at COP31 COP31 reflected growing recognition that action on super pollutants, alongside reducing CO2, can deliver benefits four times faster than decarbonisation alone.
That said, the scale of the momentum on super pollutants is a real step-change.
text:
COP31 ended in gridlock and ultimately without agreement, as countries rightly refused a cover text that failed to mention fossil fuels. Amidst the headlines decrying the failure of this year’s negotiations, we saw glimmers of progress on areas like super pollutants, with emerging coalitions of the willing stepping up.

That’s why two main developments on clean air action stood out to me: stronger political and philanthropic backing for action on super pollutants – notably with a growing focus on black carbon – alongside a clearer recognition that health concerns can help drive more ambitious climate policy.

Action on super pollutants is an essential part of protecting our climate and improving our health. These short-lived climate pollutants are responsible for nearly half of global warming to date. Several are linked to lung disease and early death.

Progress on super pollutants at COP31

COP31 reflected growing recognition that action on super pollutants, alongside reducing CO2, can deliver benefits four times faster than decarbonisation alone.

At the High-Level Summit on Methane and Non-CO₂ Greenhouse Gases – co-hosted by Brazil, China, the United Kingdom and the COP31 Presidency – more than US$480 million in new philanthropic commitments were announced to accelerate action on methane and other super pollutants. A further US$25 million was announced for the Super Pollutant Country Action Accelerator, which will help seven additional countries with implementation by setting up national units embedded within governments that focus on super pollutant action.

As for black carbon, its impacts on ice and glacier melt drove it up the political agenda. Nepal’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Shisir Khanal, called for stronger international action on black carbon following the devastating glacier-related flooding his country experienced in August. This call to action emerged from a high-level event with several Asian countries championing action to protect glaciers. Alongside this, the Ministers of Environment from Bangladesh, Chile, Iceland, Monaco and Norway signed a statement drawing attention to the need to preserve the cryosphere and to reduce methane and black carbon emissions.

We also saw an expansion of the Peer Network for Sectoral Action on Black Carbon. Launched at COP30, this year Cambodia, Mexico and Panama joined, expanding the network to 12 countries. The Peer Network is helping member countries drive practical measures across key emitting sectors. For example, Nigeria has included action on agricultural burning and clean cooking in its national climate plan, while Uganda is developing a National Black Carbon Action Plan. We are pleased at Clean Air Fund to support this network with Clima Trust and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition.

But greater political attention has yet to translate into finance at the scale that is needed. Our latest State of Global Air Quality Funding report found that less than 1% of international development funding went to outdoor air quality projects in 2024. For super pollutants specifically, the funding gap remains particularly stark. Primary black carbon funding – where black carbon reduction is an explicit project objective – represented less than 1% of total air quality funding across 2020–2024. Finance explicitly targeting tropospheric ozone also remained negligible.

Growing recognition that health is central to climate action

The UN Climate Change Executive Secretary, Simon Stiell, noted at COP31 that “Health belongs at the heart of climate action.”

It was encouraging that the Climate & Health Funders Coalition announced it has awarded over two thirds of its original $300 million commitment, with a further $150 million committed this year; a sign of growing philanthropic momentum across climate and health.

More than 100 countries are now part of the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health, and Spain, France, Peru, Tuvalu, Ireland and Barbados launched a Political Declaration on a Healthy Transition committing the health sector to driving action. The declaration frames the move away from fossil fuels not only as a climate necessity, but an opportunity to improve health, strengthen economies and reduce inequality.

That framing is important. Climate negotiations can feel distant from people’s everyday lives, whereas polluted air, extreme heat and fossil fuel combustion have immediate health consequences. In our work at Clean Air Fund, we see how climate action can deliver benefits now, through cleaner transport, healthier homes, more reliable clean energy and fewer illnesses linked to air pollution.

What needs to happen after COP31?

The coalitions of the willing that emerged and grew at COP31 are an important path to progress – especially given how difficult the formal negotiations were – but they are not a substitute for the UNFCCC process and do not remove the need for deep CO2 reductions. That said, the scale of the momentum on super pollutants is a real step-change.

title: Why drivers want cheap, dumb cars again.
description:
So buyers have a simple question: Can’t the engineering and marketing geniuses of the auto industry make a new dumb car that’s also cheap?
But a hard pivot may be on the way, just as Gen Z and their craving for old-school cars comes of age.
Earlier this year, the carmaker debuted a new EV pickup, the Fathom, designed to offer affordability without compromising on technology features.
Ford sees the Fathom pickup as a way to offer cheap and nonannoying without having to lean into dumb.
If it can learn to embrace cheap and tolerate a bit more dumb, it could again.
text:
My 16-year-old son recently obtained his learner’s permit and is starting to have ideas about what he wants behind the wheel. In our driveway, we have a 2023 Fisker Ocean, which is an all-electric SUV with a solar panel on the roof, an enormous rotating center touch screen, and the ability to roll down all the windows and open the sunroof at the flip of a switch. There’s also a 2005 Honda Element, which can do none of those things. If it weren’t for an aftermarket audio unit, it wouldn’t even have Bluetooth capability.

My son always goes for the Element. In fact, he has elaborate plans for tricking it out down the road, with things like a wooden plank for sleeping on campouts. I should point out that he is part of what is supposed to be the first truly digitally native generation, yet his contempt for in-vehicle tech is something of a badge of honor.

He’s actually part of a significant trend. If you’ve driven a car produced in the past 20 years, you’ve definitely faced some struggles: fumbling through a complicated infotainment interface just to connect your phone, dealing with the annoying bings and boops if you’re maneuvering through a crowded parking lot or briefly drift out of a highway lane, wondering how much of your personal data that fancy new SUV is sharing with companies that want to sell you stuff. Automobiles have been “smart” for decades, and with self-driving technology and more advanced onboard computers, they’re getting smarter.

Cue the backlash. Like those tech-averse consumers who have ditched iPhones for flip phones, installed apps such as Blank Spaces that offer a stripped-down experience, or swapped their Apple and Android mobiles for minimalist alternatives from Light Phone or Punkt, an emerging cadre of drivers crave simple, throwback cars. Some of it is about price, some is sheer neurological overload. There’s also a paranoid fringe that sees high-tech vehicles as instruments of the surveillance state. Tucker Carlson brags that he ditched his modern Chevy pickup because it was spying on him. He now drives a defiantly disconnected model from 1987.

But it’s actually hard to find a reliable analog used car—one that rocks only an AM/FM radio and that might not even be equipped with AC. Automakers largely stopped making rudimentary vehicles back during the Clinton administration, mostly because an improved economy led customers to demand more features, and because larger and more profitable SUVs became popular. Precious few super-basic vehicles have survived, and the ones that have have usually racked up plenty of miles and have the scars to prove it. So buyers have a simple question: Can’t the engineering and marketing geniuses of the auto industry make a new dumb car that’s also cheap?

The auto industry is aware of my son’s opinions. Tucked in a 2026 report from QNX (a division of BlackBerry, which yes, is still around) analyzing “software-defined vehicles” is a surprising nugget: The report asked, could a “deliberately minimalist, low-tech vehicle, designed to limit digital features and connectivity” succeed? Almost 80 percent of the SDV experts surveyed said yes.

“I think it definitely points to some sentiment out there,” John Pelliccio, global product marketing director at QNX, told me. “Sometimes the tech is so in-your-face that it becomes difficult rather than supportive. I don’t want to go through seven different submenus to roll down my windows.”

He cautioned that the report surveyed views among SDV developers and wasn’t focused on consumers. QNX is also in the business of innovating with software platforms so that automakers can offer simpler and more intuitive user experiences. But he also acknowledged that consumers believe tech is making cars more expensive, a tricky issue to negotiate at a time when affordability is an issue that can swing national elections, and Silicon Valley is confronted by a public with torches and pitchforks.

The disconnect is real: Automakers are contending with a cranky, financially stressed-out public that wants to smash everything from GOP political careers to dashboard touch screens. Why, they ask, has crappy tech taken over the driving experience? The backstory is less straightforward than you might think. For decades, car companies installed unpopular technology largely because they didn’t want to surrender the data business to Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. Struggling to attract the best interface designers, they ended up lost in a forest of ornate decision trees (BMW, for one, was often criticized for creating an infotainment system that sent befuddled users into seemingly endless submenus).

But a hard pivot may be on the way, just as Gen Z and their craving for old-school cars comes of age. A company that’s going all-in on low-tech is Jeff Bezos–backed Slate Auto, an EV startup that broke cover in 2025 and expects to start delivering a $25,000 EV pickup by the end of this year (the pickup can also be converted to an SUV for an additional $5,000 to $7,000). The “Blank Slate” base vehicle has two seats, hand-crank windows, no infotainment, no speakers, and no exterior paint. If you want a red truck, you’ll have to get the polymer exterior wrapped in red. The vehicle has attracted a lot of attention for its no-frills philosophy and rock-bottom sticker price. The company says it has more than 180,000 reservations.

This contrasts dramatically with what carmakers were pushing just a few years ago. Inspired by Tesla, high-speed connectivity and over-the-air software updates were all the rage for a while there. Tesla owners boasted that they could go to sleep as an OTA update started and wake up to a new car the next morning. Auto-industry executives were dreaming of fresh business models that leveraged the massive amounts of data vehicles generate to offer lucrative subscription-based products. But it hasn’t always gone according to plan. Not to gang up on BMW, but in 2022 the company infamously experimented with charging owners to activate seat heaters. Customers revolted.

If the Slate truck takes off, it could create a dumb-car boom. YouTube influencer Marques Brownlee has already told his 1 million–plus subscribers that he likes the thing and considers it a good choice as a starter EV. Former Top Gear presenter James May took it out for a spin and offered an approving verdict. Motor Trend believes it could validate a niche. There’s no question that in short order, Slate has generated more positive buzz for a cheapskate pickup than Ferrari did when it rolled out a widely ridiculed first crack at an EV, the $615,000 Luce (designed by the man behind the iPhone, Jony Ive, no stranger to minimalism).

Not everyone is taking such an either-or approach. Ford thinks it can offer the best of both worlds. Earlier this year, the carmaker debuted a new EV pickup, the Fathom, designed to offer affordability without compromising on technology features. Kay Hart, general manager of Ford’s Model e electric division, told me that the company had to put itself in the mindset of a buyer concerned about affordability who thinks that a cheaper car equals one with fewer features.

“Our approach was to find out what our customers valued and figure out how we could bring that to the vehicle,” she said, pointing out that even the sub-$29,000 version of the Fathom is equipped with Ford’s hands-free, driver-assist tech, called BlueCruise. But she also said that Ford is aware of driver frustration when it comes to screen-based interfaces. “They are not looking to learn a new experience” when they slip into the driver’s seat, as she put it.

Ford sees the Fathom pickup as a way to offer cheap and nonannoying without having to lean into dumb. It helps to have enough industrial might to build the new pickup on a new EV engineering platform that is designed to reduce complexity and significantly lower costs. Slate, meanwhile, is subtracting by necessity and making that the core part of the marketing pitch. The critical question is whether Slate’s approach will be so successful that the big guys decide it’s worth abandoning decades of investments in automated paint shops, power windows, autonomous-driving systems, and dashboard-dominating touch screens that control everything from AC to interior lighting.

For the auto industry as a whole, making money on modest, “de-contented” vehicles is tough. That’s why Detroit favors large, fully loaded pickups and SUVs. Since the financial crisis, Ford and General Motors have reinvented themselves to be consistently profitable rather than chase market share; they’ve abandoned the sedan segment, where consumers have typically looked for starter vehicles like Toyota Corollas and Honda Civics. Automotive News reports that the average transaction for a new car has topped $50,000, a whopping $2,500 increase from a year ago.

A better bottom line is nothing to dismiss, but if it comes at the cost of losing first-time buyers, a carmaker has a long-term vulnerability. The classic example, of course, is the barebones Volkswagen Beetle. It first hit the U.S. in the late 1940s and early 1950s, when massive tailfinned cars ruled the roads (those flamboyant Chevy Bel Airs and Caddy Eldorados were the luxury SUVs of their era). The Beetle caught on, becoming a countercultural icon, selling more than 21 million units globally and reviving the German postwar economy.

It isn’t just curmudgeonly car enthusiasts jonesing for the raw thrill of driving an old Porsche who are setting the tone. Basically, what Gen Z wants is the right to get into a car, rev the engine, put on some music, and drive. The auto industry used to serve that more elemental desire quite well. If it can learn to embrace cheap and tolerate a bit more dumb, it could again.

text:
Federal investment will help Aurea Technologies Inc. build a third-generation portable wind turbine for consumer and defence use

November 27, 2026 · Dartmouth, Nova Scotia · Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency (ACOA)

Atlantic Canadian companies are developing energy technologies for demanding environments, from the deep wilderness to disaster zones.

Today, Braedon Clark, Member of Parliament for Sackville—Bedford—Preston, announced federal support to Aurea Technologies Inc. to develop and validate its next-generation portable wind energy products ($687,723 repayable).

The investment will help Aurea advance its third-generation turbine, a dual-use design for both everyday use, and the demands of defence and emergency operations. The company will also develop supporting AI software for its turbines.

The project includes building and testing at least 20 prototype turbines, preparing for pilots and adding in-house testing equipment, including a wind tunnel. This work will help Aurea prove its technologies, and bring its products closer to commercialization.

Today’s announcement further demonstrates the Government of Canada’s commitment to strengthening industrial capacity in strategic sectors, including defence and clean technology, while helping Canadian businesses compete globally.

The announcement was made on behalf of the Honourable Sean Fraser, Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and Minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency.

name: American Energy
title: Prioritising System-Wide Decarbonisation: Drax's 2026 Climate Transition Plan
description:
It connects our own decarbonisation plans with Drax’s role in leading the transformation of the UK’s energy system.
The GHG Protocol has raised concerns around supporting the uptake of renewable electricity and a new focus for temporal matching of renewable electricity generation and consumption.
This will enable the import of electricity at times when renewable electricity generation is high or in excess, then deploy electricity when demand – and cost – rises.
Alongside this, our assets can support wider energy system decarbonisation, helping to avoid emissions across the UK economy.
Drax’s 2026 Climate Transition Plan brings together these two priorities: supporting the wider transition and implementing the decarbonisation measures needed to deliver our own targets.
text:
Our mission is to lead the transformation of the UK’s energy system. As the UK moves towards a flexible system that balances reliable access, cost and environmental impact, what is required of power generators is changing and we are adapting our business to help lead that change.

Our strategy is to become a bigger, broader and more resilient integrated UK power company by growing capacity, operating with excellence and making the system work smarter. By investing in renewables and flexibility, and running our assets safely, reliably and efficiently, we aim to help build a more secure, affordable and lower-carbon energy system.

To this end, we have published our most comprehensive Climate Transition Plan to date, setting out a roadmap to achieve our Science Based Targets and support the wider transition to Net Zero. Our 2040 Net Zero targets were validated by the Science Based Targets Initiative (SBTi) this year, highlighting the ambition behind our long-term decarbonisation plans.

Our latest Climate Transition Plan sets out our climate ambitions and targets, and the actions, timings and investment needed to deliver them across our full portfolio. With a greater focus on the Transition Plan Taskforce principles of Ambition, Action and Accountability, it integrates our decarbonisation actions, climate-related risks and opportunities, and support for the wider economy’s transition. It connects our own decarbonisation plans with Drax’s role in leading the transformation of the UK’s energy system.

How Drax Supports Flexibility and Storage to Increase Renewable Electricity Uptake

Following the rapid growth of wind and solar construction in the UK over the past decade, the focus is increasingly on how flexible generation and storage can complement these sources and how the gaps in generation can be filled to provide 24-hour renewable power, with the aim of maintaining a reliable, increasingly renewable electricity system.

The GHG Protocol has raised concerns around supporting the uptake of renewable electricity and a new focus for temporal matching of renewable electricity generation and consumption. Drax’s plan puts flexible generation and storage at the centre of how we support the grid to ensure renewable electricity is available to meet demand, and four takeaways stand out:

A new low carbon Contract for Difference (CfD) has been signed for Drax Power Station to run from 2027 to 2031. The CfD will enable Drax Power Station to operate more flexibly, enabling the power station to provide renewable electricity when intermittent renewable sources are not able to generate.

Drax has been investing in battery energy storage systems (BESS) with fleet totalling 260MW once operational of long- and short-duration storage and flexible generation across three UK sites. The investment in BESS is also supported by a 40MW expansion at Cruachan pumped storage backed by an £80 million upgrade. This will enable the import of electricity at times when renewable electricity generation is high or in excess, then deploy electricity when demand – and cost – rises. This will reduce the reliance on fossil based flexible generation sources.

Drax also has three Open Gas Cycle Turbines (OCGTs), one of which is currently operational and two in development. They will provide flexible generation when renewable output falls and help maintain grid stability as more wind and solar power are added to the system. We are considering options for low-carbon generation with on option being use of the synchronous condenser, which can enable low carbon grid support where the turbines are spun using renewably generated electricity.

Drax’s acquisition of the BSIF has also added 0.9GW of solar and wind capacity, with a development pipeline of 2.9GW of new assets. This has provided Drax with a diverse portfolio of wind and solar assets to support Drax’s biomass, hydro, and BESS assets.

Drax will be able to optimise its asset base to provide renewable electricity when the wind is blowing and sun is shining, and when these intermittent renewables drop off, Drax can provide flexible renewable electricity through hydropower and biomass. This places Drax in a unique position within the UK energy market to be able to support the provision of 24-hour renewable electricity.

Growth in Drax’s portfolio of flexible and intermittent renewable assets may increase our absolute greenhouse gas emissions in the nearer term. Our commitment to reach Net Zero by 2040 remains unchanged, but delivering it will require us to address our own emissions as the portfolio grows. Alongside this, our assets can support wider energy system decarbonisation, helping to avoid emissions across the UK economy. These wider benefits are not a substitute for reducing our own emissions. Drax’s 2026 Climate Transition Plan brings together these two priorities: supporting the wider transition and implementing the decarbonisation measures needed to deliver our own targets.

description:

text:
MA, UNITED STATES, November 27, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — Senior Product Marketing Leader Turns Complex Food Industry Technology Into Clear, Meaningful Customer Value With a Focus on Safety, Traceability, and Sustainable Food Systems

Leominster, Massachusetts – Alison P. Shepard is a Senior Product Marketing Leader with 7+ years of experience in the food technology industry. She served most recently at a software-as-a-service company that builds solutions for the food industry. A tech-enabled sustainable food systems professional, she specializes in turning complex technical products and capabilities into clear, meaningful value for customers. Her work centers on product marketing, customer insights, food safety, and traceability. Through each of these areas, she helps strengthen the systems that support a safer and more sustainable food supply chain.

Alison brings broad experience across food technology, sustainability, customer success, and retail food supply chains. Before her current role, she spent nearly four years at a sustainability tech startup, where she advanced through sustainability, account management, and customer success roles. In that work, she partnered with major grocery retailers to reduce the environmental impact of food waste. Earlier in her career, she served as the Sustainability Team Lead at Whole Foods Market, conducting waste audits and helping departments shrink their environmental footprint. She also spent three years in Japan through the Japan Exchange and Teaching Program, working with the Tokyo Metropolitan Government and Shinjuku High School in education, translation, communications, and advocacy. She speaks both English and Japanese.

Alison holds a Master of Arts in Law and Diplomacy from The Fletcher School at Tufts University, where she concentrated on sustainable food systems, environmental law, and policy. She also earned a bachelor’s degree in international service from American University with a focus on Japan and East Asian policy, and a minor in Japanese language. She has continued to build her expertise through certifications that include Customer Research Certified at the Masters level and the Google Project Management Specialization.

Alison attributes her success to curiosity, creativity, and an active approach to managing her career. She makes a point of staying informed, exploring new ideas, and understanding how her work connects to the broader goals of her organization and industry. Colleagues know her as creative, solution-oriented, and highly collaborative, and she approaches her work by linking big-picture ideas with practical steps that produce measurable results. The best career advice she has received is to resist the temptation to over-explain. A skill that distinguishes good leaders, she has learned, is that they can identify what context is necessary for your team to make good decisions.

For young women entering the food technology field, Alison offers a message of confidence. She encourages them to recognize that they are more capable than they may realize. Rather than second-guessing their abilities, she urges them to believe in themselves and trust that they can achieve more than others may expect.

Alison sees the food industry facing growing pressures, including food safety issues, recalls, severe weather events, and risks tied to unsafe water in the supply chain. At the same time, she views these challenges as openings for those who remain proactive and prepared. In her view, the professionals who stay focused on protecting customers, consumers, and food safety will be best positioned to lead.

Empathy, purpose, and keeping the human element at the center of her work are the values that guide Alison most. She consistently asks why something matters and how it affects the people around her. Beyond her professional role, she is a member of the Women in Food Safety Organization and Phi Mu Fraternity Alumnae, and while she lived in Japan, she was the founding president of the Tokyo JET Organization.

From waste audits at a grocery store to marketing software that protects the food supply, Alison has built a career around innovation, sustainability, and food safety. She continues to strengthen systems that benefit both organizations and the communities they serve. Through her blend of technical insight, global experience, and genuine care for people, Alison P. Shepard is helping shape a safer and more sustainable future for the way the world produces and shares its food.

But the overall trend is clear: Solar is on the upswing in China, and that’s not changing anytime soon.
text:
See more from Canary Media’s ​“Chart of the Week” column.

Solar energy is poised to become the No. 2 source of electricity in China, capping off a remarkable ascent over the last decade.

Hydropower has historically been the runner-up on China’s grid — a distant second to coal, which provides more than half the nation’s electricity and is the key reason that China emits more carbon dioxide than any other country.

But solar energy, which China has been building at a remarkable pace, has climbed from less than 1% of the nation’s electricity generation a decade ago to more than 13% through this October. Hydro has provided just under 13% of China’s electricity in 2026.

The rise of solar — and wind — has helped China avoid burning even more coal in its power plants as energy demand rises. Coal power declined in the country last year, contributing to a slight drop in its overall emissions.

For China’s emissions to fall in line with what scientists say is necessary to avert the worst of climate change, it will need to bring a lot more solar online. The country’s solar installations are actually slowing this year compared to last, thanks to policy changes. But the overall trend is clear: Solar is on the upswing in China, and that’s not changing anytime soon.

title: Ford begins U.S. battery production for $28,350 electric pickup - Wilcox Newspapers
description:
Battery cells are now being manufactured at BlueOval Battery Park near Marshall for Ford’s planned Fathom electric pickup, which has a target starting price of $28,350.
Production is still increasing, but the first battery cells are already being supplied for prototype development.
Ford representatives said Fathom test vehicles are already on the road.
Ford representatives said this chemistry offers cost advantages and can be charged regularly to full capacity.
Ford representatives compared battery manufacturing’s cleanliness standards to those of food processing and medical device manufacturing.
text:
By Maggie LaNoue

contributing writer

A new, more affordable electric pickup is taking shape at Ford, bringing changes to the automobile industry. Battery cells are now being manufactured at BlueOval Battery Park near Marshall for Ford’s planned Fathom electric pickup, which has a target starting price of $28,350.

During a Nov. 18 media tour, Ford representatives described the facility as the first in the United States to produce lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells on a large scale for mainstream consumer vehicles. Production is still increasing, but the first battery cells are already being supplied for prototype development.

The truck is still in development, with production planned for 2027. Battery cells from Marshall are being sent to Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky for prototype work.

Ford representatives said Fathom test vehicles are already on the road. Photographs shown during the presentation depicted prototypes wrapped in blue material that concealed their exterior designs while development continues.

LFP batteries use iron and phosphate instead of the nickel and cobalt found in some other lithium-ion batteries. Ford representatives said this chemistry offers cost advantages and can be charged regularly to full capacity. Some battery-grade materials, however, remain difficult to source domestically.

Tracy Church, plant manager at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan, presented an overview to journalists. She explained that LFP technology originated in the United States decades ago. Ford manufactures the cells using technology licensed from Chinese battery manufacturer CATL. A second operation at the Marshall facility uses Ford’s own technology to assemble battery packs.

The plant encompasses approximately 2 million square feet. Visitors began the tour by putting protective coverings over their shoes. Safety glasses and high-visibility vests were also required.

Ford representatives compared battery manufacturing’s cleanliness standards to those of food processing and medical device manufacturing. Temperatures are maintained around 70 degrees, humidity is carefully controlled, and the plant guards against contamination by particles smaller than the thickness of a human hair.

The media tour included a presentation and a limited walk-around featuring manufacturing displays, rather than unrestricted access to the production floor. Photography was restricted during the tour.

Displays illustrated how battery ingredients are mixed into a thick substance called slurry, spread onto thin metal foil, compressed and cut. The prepared material is wound into tightly packed assemblies called jelly rolls. A guide compared the process to rolling up toilet paper, although the finished rolls are flattened. Two jelly rolls are placed inside each rectangular battery cell.

Journalists were invited to hold an inactive demonstration cell weighing approximately nine pounds. Each Fathom battery pack, mounted beneath the passenger compartment, will contain more than 100 cells.

Ford representatives said one of two cell production lines is operating, with output increasing gradually. At full capacity, each line is designed to manufacture approximately 2,400 cells per hour. Battery-pack production is expected to increase in spring 2027, ahead of planned vehicle production later that year.

Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer appeared after the tour and discussed the plant’s importance to surrounding communities. Of the projected 1,700 jobs, she said 70% were expected to be filled by Calhoun County residents. Ford representatives separately reported that more than 70% of the current workforce comes from the local area, including Marshall, Albion and Battle Creek.

“This technology is driving so much change globally,” Whitmer said. She also emphasized consumer choice, explaining that she plans to purchase an electric vehicle in the near future, while her husband intends to buy a gasoline-powered model.

Whitmer’s administration ends as the new year begins, but the plant’s expansion will continue under Michigan’s next governor.

Albion and Marshall already share important regional connections, from schools and health care to government services and transportation. Residents travel between the communities for work and essential services.

As BlueOval Battery Park expands production, its influence may extend well beyond Marshall. For Albion and the surrounding region, electric vehicles are one part of a changing economy whose effects will cross community boundaries.

text:
Energy ministers from Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) participating countries have stressed the importance of cooperation in advancing green transition and safeguarding energy security across the globe.

These priorities took center stage as the Fourth Belt and Road Energy Ministerial Conference wrapped up in east China's Qingdao on Friday. Held under the theme "Sharing innovation outcomes, advancing energy transition, building a secure future together," the two-day event brought officials together to translate those goals into action.

Discussions centered on innovation-driven energy transition, energy security and system resilience, and coordinated efforts toward a green, low-carbon transition across industrial and supply chains. During the conference, Wang Hongzhi, administrator of the National Energy Administration of China, said China is accelerating its new energy system. By 2030, China aims for a cleaner, low-carbon system, with a better energy mix, stronger resilience and more innovation.

"Kazakhstan is a big new exporter of the hydrocarbons to the Chinese market. The energy sector is the fundamental of our cooperation. We built a lot of projects in the renewable energy, in the processing of the raw materials. Chinese companies are taking a lot of works in Kazakhstan in building the energy infrastructure," said Yerlan Akkenzhenov, Minister of Energy of Kazakhstan.

"We think that China is leading the way to the transformation, that is sharing the advancement and the technology, also enhancing the cooperation between the members of the [Belt and Road] Initiative," said Al-Mutasim Ibrahim, Minister of Energy and Petroleum of Republic of Sudan.

The conference released a Blue Book on green, low-carbon transition and security resilience in developing countries. The Blue Book sets up a four-dimensional evaluation system and classifies developing countries into 16 energy-system types, offering tailored solutions in technology, policy, finance and smart digitalization.

"There is no single model for the energy transition. Countries need to set roadmaps based on their own conditions, balancing green and low-carbon goals, energy security, system resilience and economic affordability. In terms of the international cooperation, the Blue Book recommends expanding from project construction alone to broader areas such as planning consultation, standards alignment, digital and intelligent empowerment, and risk resilience enhancement, helping countries turn resource advantages into momentum for sustainable development," said Zhou Yi, director of China Electric Power Planning and Engineering Institute.

"New energy here is everywhere. Every household, when I go out of the big cities, I see even the farmers installing solar panels on their house, because now it's just basically cheaper. They are not only installing to use for themselves. They also sell it to grid. So basically, they earn money by using their roof. That's amazing," said Rafael Bekshentayev, head representative in China of EXia Energy Research Center, a Kazakhstan-based energy analytics, and research organization.

The conference also saw the formally established of the Governing Board of Belt and Road Energy Partnership, a multilateral energy cooperation platform under the BRI. The Belt and Road Energy Partnership has expanded to 35 BRI member countries, with its cooperation network bringing together nearly 300 enterprises.

title: Lighthouse | A welcome budget for infrastructure – but tough choices remain
description:
On clean energy, the government has refocused its investment policy to prioritise projects that lower bills for households and businesses.
How this connects to reaching the net zero target and the next carbon budget is unclear, but it suggests a move away from decarbonisation as the driving force behind energy policy.
The second notable theme was the move towards fiscal devolution, which will have implications for infrastructure investment.
The budget tied this to infrastructure delivery more explicitly than we have seen in the past.
Tough choices are inevitable, however infrastructure investment should not be viewed solely as a cost, but as investment in building a more sustainable future.
text:
But the chancellor also signalled some key shifts in infrastructure policy goals – particularly around energy. And there’s no doubt that some difficult decisions have been kicked into the Spending Review next year.

On clean energy, the government has refocused its investment policy to prioritise projects that lower bills for households and businesses. How this connects to reaching the net zero target and the next carbon budget is unclear, but it suggests a move away from decarbonisation as the driving force behind energy policy.

It wasn’t the only sign of a shift in priorities. While the NWF will get an additional £15.4bn, including £2bn for the Energy Wealth Fund, the chancellor directed the body to focus more on defence, critical minerals and artificial intelligence.

The second notable theme was the move towards fiscal devolution, which will have implications for infrastructure investment. The fiscal devolution roadmap positions these reforms as a ‘first step’ towards giving local leaders more control over locally generated revenues and a stronger incentive to support economic growth.

It builds on the direction set out in July’s Rewiring the State announcement, moving strategic authorities beyond a delivery role towards becoming longer-term investors in meeting the needs of their areas.

For infrastructure, this could see priorities being shaped regionally, with Whitehall setting strategic frameworks and local leaders taking on a greater role in investment and delivery decisions. More detail is expected in the government’s Rewiring the State Delivery Plan, due later this year.

Finally, there was acknowledgement of the need for more meaningful public engagement in infrastructure decision-making.

Notably, the chancellor responded to public pushback on new data centres by announcing a new covenant that sets tests developers must meet, including their contribution to impacted communities and the UK’s economic interests. In return for delivering local benefits, a ‘ministerial control centre’ will help developers connect their projects to the grid faster.

The ICE is clear that better engagement can speed up rather than slow down infrastructure delivery, and rebuild trust in the institutions that plan, fund and deliver it. It’s encouraging to see government wanting to move past the binary choice of ‘less or more consultation’ and focus on better and more representative engagement. The budget tied this to infrastructure delivery more explicitly than we have seen in the past.

It’s clear that the Burnham government recognises the role that infrastructure investment and certainty can play in driving economic growth, attracting private capital and improving people’s lives in all parts of the country.

The key test remains whether that recognition is backed by a clear plan for delivery and long-term commitment. Anything else risks undermining the clarity and certainty provided by the 10-Year Infrastructure Strategy and Infrastructure Pipeline – and the benefits to delivery that allows.

The sector will be looking for more detail in next year’s Spending Review and 10-year strategy refresh. Tough choices are inevitable, however infrastructure investment should not be viewed solely as a cost, but as investment in building a more sustainable future.

The ICE will continue to make the case for protecting investment in new and existing infrastructure.

text:
The global transition to renewable energy risks perpetuating economic inequalities between countries that control green technologies and those primarily involved in manufacturing them, according to new research involving the University of Manchester.

A study of the wind power industries in Brazil and India has found that, despite substantial investment in renewable energy and the development of domestic manufacturing capabilities, both countries remain dependent on foreign companies for key technologies and strategic decisions.

The researchers warn that establishing manufacturing facilities and creating jobs in developing countries does not necessarily ensure that they will benefit fully from the energy transition. Control over research and development (R&D), intellectual property and key components remains concentrated among established international manufacturers, particularly in Europe, North America and China.

Brazil has more than 7,000 onshore wind turbines and an installed capacity of 33GW. European manufacturers Siemens, Vestas and Nordex Acciona account for more than 80% of the country’s installed wind generation capacity. While Brazilian manufacturers have developed capabilities in producing components such as turbine blades and towers, they remain reliant on foreign companies for key technologies and design specifications.

India became the world’s third-largest wind market, with 56GW of installed capacity in 2025, but continues to import more than half of the gearboxes, generators and converters used in its wind turbines. Domestic companies also remain reliant on foreign licensing and overseas research partnerships.

Both countries have introduced policies to encourage domestic manufacturing and support national companies, but these have not been accompanied by comparable levels of technological independence.

The researchers distinguish between what they describe as the industry’s ‘brain activities’ – including R&D, strategic decision-making and gearbox capabilities – and its ‘muscle activities’, such as manufacturing components to specifications determined by international companies.

Developing technological capabilities

China provides a contrasting example, having developed its own technological capabilities and established domestic wind turbine manufacturers as major international players.

The researchers attribute this to a more coordinated industrial strategy, combining government direction, support for domestic companies and investment in innovation. China’s domestic market helped its manufacturers acquire the expertise needed to compete internationally.

The study suggests that countries seeking to benefit from the renewable energy transition need to look beyond the number of factories established or components manufactured domestically, and prioritise investment in research, innovation and technological capabilities.

“The transition to renewable energy is often presented as an opportunity for developing countries to build new industries, create jobs and benefit from the technologies of the future, but our research shows that manufacturing wind turbines and their components is not necessarily enough,” said Pritish Behuria.

“If countries do not also develop the capacity to control the technology, research and strategic decisions behind these industries, they risk remaining dependent on established international manufacturers.

“A genuinely just transition needs to consider not just where green technologies are manufactured, but who controls them and who captures the economic benefits.”

description:
