text:
By Environment+Energy Leader Editorial Staff

Definition

Power Purchase Agreement (PPA)

A power purchase agreement (PPA) is a long-term contract, typically 10 to 20 years, to buy electricity from a specific renewable energy project at a set price. A physical PPA delivers the power; a virtual PPA settles financially against a wholesale price. The contract also sets whether the buyer receives the project's renewable energy certificates (RECs).

Why this matters in 2027: The federal tax credits that kept U.S. wind and solar PPA prices down are ending for projects that did not start construction by July 4, 2026, unless they come online by the end of 2027, tariffs are pushing solar prices up, and electricity demand from data centers and industry keeps rising. At the same time, the GHG Protocol is rewriting the rules for how PPAs count toward Scope 2 claims. PPAs remain one of the strongest clean energy tools a large buyer has, but the price, the supply, and the accounting are all moving at once, which is why more organizations are evaluating them now.

Power Purchase Agreements: The Executive Takeaway

A PPA typically runs 10 to 20 years. A physical PPA provides electricity under the contract, while a virtual PPA settles financially against a wholesale power price. It can stabilize energy costs for the contracted volume and, when the contract transfers the project's renewable energy certificates, support a credible market-based Scope 2 claim. It is also a long-term financial obligation with real delivery, price, and accounting risk.

For executives, 2027 changes the math on three fronts. U.S. wind and solar projects that miss the federal tax credit deadlines may come with higher PPA prices, and new tariffs are already lifting solar offers. The GHG Protocol is rewriting how PPAs count toward Scope 2, and SBTi has proposed a February 1, 2027 cutoff for grandfathering existing contracts under its new net-zero standard. Before signing, know which credits the price assumes, who bears delivery and curtailment risk, and how the deal would hold up under stricter hourly-matching rules.

If you've spent any time in a sustainability strategy meeting in the last five years, you've heard the acronym. PPAs come up whenever the conversation turns to renewable energy procurement, Scope 2 targets, or the gap between what a company has committed to and what it's actually done. They're often described as the gold standard for corporate clean energy — which is true, with caveats — and just as often described in ways that make them sound more complicated, or simpler, than they actually are.

This explainer is for the sustainability director who keeps nodding along in those meetings and wants to stop. It's also for the energy manager who understands the mechanics but needs to explain them clearly to a CFO who controls the budget. We'll cover what a PPA is, how the different types work, who they make sense for, and where the real risks live — because there are real risks, and most vendor materials conveniently underplay them.

What Is a Power Purchase Agreement?

A power purchase agreement is a long-term contract between a company and a renewable energy generator — typically a wind farm, solar farm, or other clean energy facility — in which the company agrees to buy electricity at a fixed price over a set period, usually between 10 and 20 years.

That's the core of it. The company isn't buying solar panels or wind turbines. It isn't building anything. It's buying the output — the electrons, or more precisely, the contractual right to that output, and often the renewable energy certificates (RECs) that come with it. The contract specifies whether the buyer receives the project's RECs.

The fixed price is the point. Grid electricity prices fluctuate constantly, subject to fuel costs, weather, geopolitical shocks, and regulatory changes. A PPA lets a company lock in a rate today for energy it will consume years from now, which does two things at once: it can stabilize what the company pays for the contracted volume of power, and, when the contract includes the RECs, it creates a traceable, auditable link between the company's energy consumption and a specific renewable energy source.

For companies with net-zero commitments, science-based targets, or RE100 membership, that traceability is increasingly non-negotiable. Unbundled RECs — certificates sold separately from the electricity they represent, though they can still come from an identifiable project — have come under growing scrutiny from sustainability standard-setters. A PPA offers what an unbundled REC can't: a direct contractual relationship with a specific generator. When that generator is new, the buyer can also make a credible case that its contract helped get the project built, a quality known as additionality that stakeholders increasingly look for, even though current accounting rules do not require it.

How a PPA Actually Works: The Mechanics

The electricity grid doesn't work like a direct pipeline. When a wind farm in Texas generates power, it doesn't flow through a dedicated wire to a corporate headquarters in Ohio. It goes into the grid, mixes with everything else, and the company in Ohio draws from whatever the grid is supplying at that moment.

So how does a PPA create a meaningful clean energy claim?

Through the contract and the certificates. When a company signs a PPA with a wind farm, it agrees to pay a set price per megawatt-hour (MWh) for the farm's output over the contract term. If the contract transfers them, it also receives the RECs associated with that generation — one REC per MWh — and can retire eligible certificates to support its market-based Scope 2 claim under the GHG Protocol Scope 2 Guidance. The physical electrons may go anywhere on the grid; the retired certificates are what document the buyer's claim to that generation.

In a physical PPA, the generator delivers power directly to the buyer through a utility or transmission arrangement. A recent example: a 100 MW solar installation in Elkhart County, Indiana, is supported by a long-term physical PPA with Indiana Michigan Power, part of American Electric Power — one of two utility-scale facilities that added a combined 200 MW to the U.S. grid in early 2026.

In a virtual PPA (also called a financial PPA or VPPA), no power changes hands at all. The generator sells its power into the wholesale market, and the two parties settle the difference against the agreed fixed price, called the strike price. When the market price is below the strike, the buyer pays the generator the difference; when it is above, the generator pays the buyer. The buyer keeps buying electricity from its utility or retail supplier as before, so the VPPA works as a financial hedge on top of that bill, and how well it hedges depends on how closely the project's market price tracks what the buyer actually pays. In either structure, the buyer's clean energy claim depends on receiving and retiring the RECs, which the contract should spell out. VPPAs are the more common structure for corporate buyers who aren't in the business of managing power delivery.

Types of PPAs: A Quick Reference

PPA Types at a Glance

Who Should Actually Consider a PPA?

PPAs are not universally the right tool. They're the right tool for a specific profile of buyer, and being honest about that profile upfront saves a lot of time.

You're likely a good candidate if:

Your electricity use is large enough to justify a standalone utility-scale contract, with its legal, advisory, and credit requirements. Smaller buyers aren't shut out: on-site PPAs and aggregated deals that pool several buyers can work at lower volumes.

You have a board-level or publicly stated renewable energy or net-zero commitment that requires credible, auditable clean energy procurement.

You operate in a competitive electricity market, are open to a virtual PPA, or have the regulatory sophistication to navigate a sleeved or utility-mediated structure.

Your finance team has the tolerance for a long-term contract with some price risk exposure, and isn't looking for a capital-free, zero-risk solution.

You have at least one person — internally or through an advisor — who understands energy procurement well enough to evaluate contract terms and developer creditworthiness.

A PPA is probably not the right starting point if:

You're a smaller organization with modest energy consumption and limited procurement staff.

Your primary goal is a quick win for an ESG report rather than a durable, long-term emissions reduction strategy.

You operate primarily in regulated electricity markets where physical PPAs are restricted, and a virtual PPA's RECs wouldn't match the market your facilities are in.

One more thing worth saying here: a PPA is not a substitute for an energy strategy. As we've reported, most organizations have an energy plan — fewer have an energy strategy built on current infrastructure realities rather than grid conditions from three years ago. A PPA signed without that strategic context is a contract in search of a rationale.

The 2027 Market: Tax Credits, Prices, and Who Is Buying

The corporate PPA market is more complicated to navigate than it was even two years ago. Global corporate clean energy procurement fell 10% in 2025, to 55.9 GW, the first decline in nearly a decade, and Meta, Amazon, Google, and Microsoft accounted for 49% of the capacity announced. The biggest buyers are also changing what they buy: hyperscalers are blurring the line between buyer and producer, and a growing share of their contracts are for nuclear, geothermal, and other around-the-clock sources, which run on very different delivery timelines from wind and solar. As we've reported, multinationals are increasingly splitting their procurement strategies by region as policy diverges between the U.S., Europe, and Asia Pacific.

The tax credit cliff. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed July 4, 2025, ends the federal production and investment tax credits (Sections 45Y and 48E) for wind and solar projects unless they began construction by July 4, 2026, or are placed in service by December 31, 2027, and meet the other eligibility rules. Treasury guidance in August 2025 tried to make it harder to prove construction had begun, but a federal court vacated that guidance in June 2026, restoring the long-standing 5% safe harbor for establishing when construction began (our coverage). Projects that began construction in time generally have a four-year continuity safe harbor to come online. Wind and solar projects starting construction after 2025 also face restrictions on components and ownership tied to China and other "prohibited foreign entities." For buyers, the practical step is to ask which credits the developer assumed in its price and how it documented eligibility, because a project that loses its credit will need a higher price to stay viable.

Prices are rising. In the third quarter of 2026, LevelTen Energy reported North American solar PPA offers up 4.9% from the prior quarter and 6% from a year earlier, as developers priced in new Section 232 tariffs on polysilicon, wafers, cells, and modules that take effect December 4, 2026. Wind offers were flat for the quarter but up almost 14% from a year earlier, as federal permitting for wind projects slowed. These are developer offer prices, not signed deals, but they set the starting point for negotiations.

Smaller buyers have new ways in. For mid-market buyers without hyperscaler budgets and dedicated procurement teams, the market is tighter and less forgiving than when most long-term energy strategies were set. Aggregated deals help: groups of smaller buyers can now pool their demand into a single utility-scale contract. And companies with contracts signed in the 2010s are discovering that renewing a legacy PPA means pricing a very different power market.

The Benefits That Actually Hold Up

The Risks That Get Underplayed

This is the section most vendor materials skip. It's also the section where procurement teams learn the most expensive lessons.

This explainer is available for sponsorship. Learn more about partnering with us. Editorial content produced independently by Environment+Energy Leader

PPAs and Scope 2 Reporting: What You Need to Know

Under the GHG Protocol's current market-based Scope 2 accounting method, from its 2015 Scope 2 Guidance, a PPA qualifies as a valid instrument for reducing reported Scope 2 emissions if it meets the Scope 2 Quality Criteria. Those criteria require, among other things, that the certificates are tracked and retired by or for the buyer, are claimed only once, come from the same market where the electricity is consumed, and correspond to the period of consumption. They do not require additionality.

Unbundled RECs bought on the open market can meet these criteria too. What a PPA adds is traceability to a named project and, when the project is new, a credible role in getting it financed and built.

For companies reporting under the EU's CSRD, ISSB-based rules, California's SB 253, or voluntary frameworks like CDP, the quality and documentation of PPA-linked RECs has become an area of increasing scrutiny, and third-party assurance of Scope 2 is phasing in. Buyers should ensure their contracts clearly specify the REC delivery mechanism and retain documentation sufficient for third-party verification. Our corporate sustainability disclosure explainer covers which regimes apply.

The Scope 2 rules are being rewritten. The GHG Protocol is revising its Scope 2 Guidance, and the revision matters directly to PPA buyers. Its 2025 consultation proposed requiring hourly matching of clean energy to consumption and deliverability from the same grid region, and most respondents opposed both. In October 2026, the GHG Protocol proposed two market-based methods: a stricter method built on hourly matching and deliverability, and a second that keeps today's 2015 rules, possibly as a transition option. At a late-October workshop, the technical working group favored recommending incremental procurement and requiring companies to disclose its share. Procurement would count as incremental either through a long-term contract with the project's original buyer or while the plant is within an age limit, with about 15 years discussed. Timing, any transition period, and the treatment of existing contracts are all still open. The revision will feed a joint GHG Protocol–ISO corporate standard, with a consultation planned for the second quarter of 2027 and publication slated for the fourth quarter of 2028.

The proposed revisions are still under development, and the 2015 rules apply until a new standard takes effect. But a PPA signed today will still be delivering in the 2030s, so buyers should ask how a contract would score under the stricter method: whether the project is new, whether it sits in the same grid region as the load, and whether hourly generation data will be available. Contracts for local, new-build projects with hourly data are the ones least likely to lose value if the stricter method is adopted.

Companies with science-based targets have a nearer date to watch. The Science Based Targets initiative's Corporate Net-Zero Standard Version 2.0 takes effect February 1, 2027, with tighter rules on where and from which plants clean electricity can count. Companies can still submit targets under Version 1.3.1 through January 31, 2028. In November 2026, SBTi opened a consultation proposing that contracts signed before February 1, 2027 be grandfathered under Version 2.0, which makes the signing date of a deal now under negotiation more important than usual.

It's also worth noting that a PPA addresses Scope 2 emissions — purchased electricity — not Scope 1 or Scope 3. Companies with net-zero commitments will need additional strategies beyond PPAs to address their full emissions profile, including value-chain emissions covered in our Scope 3 explainer. And a delivery shortfall doesn't just create a budget problem — it reduces the zero-carbon supply a company can claim, requiring replacement RECs at current market prices that may be higher than when the PPA was negotiated.

text:
The US climate movement is deeply divided over the permitting reform bill currently moving through Congress, fracturing the coalition that came together a few years ago to support former President Joe Biden’s signature climate law, the Inflation Reduction Act.

Known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, the legislation would make it easier to build everything from data centers to fossil fuel pipelines to clean energy projects. After President Donald Trump endorsed the bill in early November, the Senate passed it. But with only a few weeks left in the congressional session, the bill’s fate in the House of Representatives is unclear.

Contributing to its uncertain fate are the opposing reactions from climate supporters. The broad coalition of Democratic lawmakers, companies, labor groups, scientists and advocates that backed the IRA is now splitting into different camps.

Just this week, more than 100 climate scientists and scholars published an open letter to the House urging members to vote no on the bill because it changes landmark environmental laws and would boost new fossil fuel projects. Meanwhile, three House Democrats who are vocal clean energy supporters - Sean Casten of Illinois and Mike Levin and Jared Huffman of California - came out against the bill’s current text. That’s despite it being sponsored by one of the Senate’s biggest climate hawks, Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island.

Different analyses of the bill have found enactment would lead to lower or higher power-sector emissions. But they more or less agree that it’s likely to help reduce household energy bills.

Climate advocates generally think permitting reform is needed to boost the nation’s clean energy build-out to meet growing energy demand and do it in a way that cuts energy-linked emissions. The current fault lines are over the potential for this bill to also boost fossil fuel and data center expansion while weakening tribal rights as well as laws that protect clean water, endangered species and historically important places.

Noah Kaufman, a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, said that on one hand, there are people who see permitting reform as “the single most important thing we can do for the climate.” This group includes a mix of renewable energy companies and labor organizations, as well as some climate and clean energy activists, Democratic lawmakers and former Biden administration climate leaders.

On the other side, Kaufman said, are people who see how this bill will alter environmental standards and boost fossil fuels and ask: How can you really call this a climate bill? This camp includes some prominent national and local environmental groups, tribal communities, current and former environmental regulators and more.

“I’m not really surprised that the clean energy industry and the environmental community aren’t on the same page in this particular case,” said Ethan Zindler, head of country and policy research at BloombergNEF. The clean energy industry’s top priority is “to maximize deployment of their own technologies,” he said, while environmental groups “will do a bit broader math, looking at overall plusses and minuses of any legislation.”

If this week is any indication, a growing number of groups have now done this calculation and decided to come out in opposition of the bill, at least in its current form. House Democrats are paying close attention.

“There’s a lot more going on in BAAJA than just streamlining the permitting system,” said Huffman in a video he recently posted on social media. “As drafted, this bill is the most sweeping rollback of environmental laws that we’ve ever seen.”

He wants the House to amend the bill - not vote on it in the current form, which is what House leadership is pushing for.

But it’s unclear whether there’s enough time in the lame-duck session to do that. “They’re fighting a ticking clock,” said Charlotte Jenkins, vice president at Capstone LLC, a global consulting firm based in Washington, DC. Although this is the closest a permitting reform bill “has ever gotten to becoming law,” she said, her team is “not as optimistic that this will pass in the House.”

In January, a new session of Congress will begin with Democrats holding sizable majorities in both chambers. But it won’t be enough to overcome expected vetoes from Trump, dimming the chances of Democrats being able to pass their own version of permitting reform. Whatever happens on the issue right now, the dynamics among environmentalists will no doubt shift once more.

Zindler said he doesn’t expect the rupture in the climate movement to be permanent: “When their top priorities overlap again, as they no doubt will on any variety of topics, I’d anticipate they’ll cooperate.”

text:
Reducing emissions in the automotive industry involves more than replacing combustion engines with electric drivetrains. Manufacturing processes, electricity consumption, and the materials used throughout the supply chain also contribute to a vehicle manufacturer’s environmental footprint.

Vietnamese electric vehicle manufacturer VinFast has detailed how its net-zero strategy addresses these challenges through industrial electrification, smart energy monitoring, renewable electricity, and battery energy storage. The company aims to achieve net-zero emissions by 2040 while expanding its electric mobility operations internationally.

For eeNews Europe readers, VinFast’s roadmap provides insight into how electric vehicle manufacturers are approaching energy management at the factory level, while also addressing the infrastructure requirements associated with commercial electric mobility.

VinFast’s Net-Zero Strategy and Smart Manufacturing

Approved in January 2025, VinFast’s climate roadmap centers on what the company calls its 3E Mission: Electrification, Energy Saving, and Energy Greening.

By 2030, VinFast plans to electrify equipment at its own production and business sites. The company also intends to introduce smart energy monitoring systems at its manufacturing facilities by 2028, allowing factory teams to identify opportunities to reduce electricity consumption across production lines and equipment.

At its manufacturing complex in Hai Phong, Vietnam, improvements to lighting and compressed air systems, adjustments to production robot operations, and other efficiency measures saved approximately 2.7 GWh of electricity in 2024, according to VinFast.

These measures correspond to an estimated reduction of 1,782 metric tons of CO₂ equivalent.

The company has also initiated a 30 MWp rooftop solar project at the facility. Its longer-term plans include integrating battery energy storage to support renewable electricity use and sourcing 100% of its electricity from renewable sources at all manufacturing plants by 2040.

Electric Buses and Charging Infrastructure

The transition to electric mobility also presents challenges beyond vehicle design, particularly for commercial fleet operators managing charging infrastructure, maintenance, and vehicle availability.

In October 2026, VinFast announced an initial agreement with NexMove, a joint venture between Transportation Management Services and Zeem Solutions, to introduce its electric buses to the US market.

NexMove plans to combine vehicles, charging, maintenance, and fleet operations under a single service agreement, with a proposed uptime commitment of 97%.

VinFast’s electric buses incorporate lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, fast charging capabilities, and driver assistance systems based on cameras and radar.

“Bringing VinFast electric buses to the United States marks an important next step in our long-term commitment to this market,” said Brian Finnerty, CEO of VinFast North America.

Demonstration vehicles will allow fleet operators to evaluate the technology at Zeem’s charging depots, with certified bus deliveries expected to begin in the first quarter of 2028.

Managing Emissions as Production Expands

VinFast reported greenhouse gas emissions exceeding 1.12 million metric tons of CO₂ equivalent in its 2022 baseline year. The company estimates that this figure could exceed 20 million metric tons if its existing production facilities in Vietnam reached their maximum registered capacity.

Against its 2022 baseline, VinFast aims to reduce Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 42% and Scope 3 emissions by 29% by 2030.

By 2040, the company intends to reduce total emissions by at least 85%, neutralizing the remaining emissions through carbon offsetting mechanisms.

As electric vehicle production expands, reducing emissions will depend not only on advances in battery and drivetrain technology but also on how manufacturers integrate industrial automation, energy monitoring, renewable generation, and energy storage into their production facilities.

More information is available at VinFast.

text:
CLARION, Pa. (EYT) — A small group of concerned residents has revived the name PEACE, asking Clarion County Commissioners to make data center standards a top priority as the county updates its Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance (SALDO).

Limestone resident Paul Linnan spoke on the group’s behalf during the public comment period of Wednesday’s commissioners meeting. The group, he said, is now called Protect Environment and Citizens Everywhere. The original PEACE fought a toxic waste proposal about 25 years ago and prevailed.

Linnan said the group hopes to inform and educate local municipalities about the potential negative impacts of data centers. Many municipalities share the interest, he said, but lack the resources to pass their own zoning ordinances setting standards for such facilities. They would like to rely on the county SALDO, which is currently being amended.

“We don’t want any other township or borough in the county or even in counties adjoining to find themselves in a position where all of a sudden it’s there, and they can’t do anything,” Linnan said.

He pointed to Homer City in Indiana County, which he said was caught off guard by a large development. He said facilities should be required to meet conditions such as setbacks and noise limits. He described a data center proposal discussed locally as not yet a firm plan, though one that contains elements of concern.

Linnan said he delivered a letter outlining the group’s concerns to the county planning commission about 10 days ago. The group also mailed a similar letter to all municipalities about six weeks ago, copying the commissioners. Commissioners Ted Tharan and Wayne Brosious said they had not received it. Linnan offered to hand-deliver a copy to Tharan’s office next week, and Tharan suggested he leave it with the chief clerk if he cannot find the commissioners.

Tharan acknowledged the county’s record on the issue, noting it was among the first in the state to adopt an ordinance on solar and wind. “You can’t prevent them,” he said of data centers, adding that any ordinance would aim to protect the county.

Linnan said three minutes was not enough time to cover such a significant issue, and he asked for a more informal setting to talk with the commissioners, noting the planning commission works for them. Tharan said he would like any such session to be a public meeting open to everyone and asked that attendees keep the conversation civil. Commissioner Braxton White called the matter a “huge issue” with many views to consider. Linnan said the group had come mainly to observe the process and would be better prepared when it returns in about two weeks. A meeting after Thanksgiving was discussed.

Along with the letter, Linnan gave commissioners a summary of what the group describes as the negative impacts of data centers, selected pages of a model ordinance from Physicians for Social Responsibility, a copy of the letter sent to all municipalities, and short articles from other agencies expressing concern. He said staff had never seen the municipal letter.

Electricity

According to the group’s summary, a typical U.S. household uses slightly more than 10,300 kilowatt-hours of electricity per year, and one megawatt of continuous power serves about 96 households annually. By that math, a 100-megawatt data center draws the equivalent power of 9,600 homes, while large hyperscale campuses (100 to 300 megawatts and up) can use the daily electricity equivalent of up to 2 million households.

Power generation

The group worries that new grid infrastructure costs will be passed to existing customers as higher monthly bills. Where the grid falls short, it says, facilities generate their own power, mainly from natural gas. Linnan said his household used 837 hundred cubic feet of gas last year, while the gas company serving the Homer City data center project will supply 640 million cubic feet per day. Supplying that much, he said, would take more than 200 wells at current rates, and burning the gas adds emissions that contribute to climate and health problems.

Cooling

Recent centers have drawn millions of gallons of fresh water daily from local sources, the summary says, with most of it evaporating and the rest discharged. Newer closed-loop systems would avoid daily draws, but the group says it has not yet been told which fluids would be used, how often they would be replaced, or the quality of what is discarded.

Noise and light

Data centers run around the clock, and backup generators, cooling towers and rooftop air handlers can send noise past property lines. The group says constant low-frequency noise can be heard or felt miles away. It cites reports from nearby residents of headaches, nausea, vertigo, sleep deprivation and ear pain, as well as frustration over constant lighting that disrupts daily life.

Land

Campuses can span several thousand acres, the group says. The Homer City site occupies the former coal-fired power plant footprint and has acquired, or is acquiring, up to 3,100 additional acres. Clarion Borough covers slightly more than 1,000 acres, so the group notes the Homer City site in Indiana County will be at least three times its size.

Jobs

The group says the jobs communities hope for often do not materialize locally. It argues that many construction jobs would go to workers from outside the area, and that once buildings are complete, only a few security and maintenance positions remain.

text:
Spain is preparing a new aid package of €200.4 million to strengthen domestic manufacturing of technologies related to renewables, storage, hydrogen, electricity networks, demand management and heat pumps.

The Ministry for Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge (MITECO) opened the public consultation on the regulatory framework and the call for FEDER STEP-ZERO , a program aimed at expanding the industrial and technological capacity associated with net zero emissions technologies.

The focus will be on manufacturing equipment, components and transforming essential raw materials , rather than subsidizing the deployment of commercially available facilities.

The scheme will be financed with ERDF 2021-2027 funds and will be managed by the Institute for Energy Diversification and Saving (IDAE).

Of the planned €200.4 million, €136 million would be allocated to the autonomous communities considered less developed , in line with the territorial criteria of the European funds.

The call for applications is structured into two programs.

The first will be aimed at the manufacture of specific products and components linked to STEP technologies and may cover the creation of new industrial plants, capacity expansions or innovative conversions of existing production lines.

Actions related to the deployment of commercially available technologies, batteries intended for mobility, and renewable generation or storage facilities will be excluded from this line.

The second program will focus on the innovative technological development of key products and components , in accordance with the list of strategic technologies established by the European Union.

Continuity after €459 million awarded by RENOVAL

STEP-ZERO takes over from the two calls of the RENOVAL program, financed through NextGenerationEU within the Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan.

In total, these lines made it possible to award €459 million to 73 projects linked to the manufacture of equipment and components for the energy transition.

The new scheme seeks to extend that strategy to segments where Spain and Europe still maintain a high dependence on third-party markets.

According to MITECO, Spain already manufactures more than 60% of the components of the solar photovoltaic value chain and practically 100% of the wind power value chain , although certain final products and specific parts continue to be concentrated outside the continent.

This highlights one of STEP-ZERO's main objectives: to gain local production capacity in strategic links , while developing new technological solutions.

The call also aligns with the European Commission's Clean Industry Pact and the Strategic Technologies Platform for Europe, which seeks to strengthen the bloc's industrial autonomy in sectors considered critical.

The MITECO proposes that the program contribute to improving energy security, modernizing the productive fabric and increasing the competitiveness of the industry associated with the transition.

Interested parties may submit observations and allegations during the public consultation phase until December 22, 2026 .

With this new package, Spain is shifting some of its public effort from installing new capacity towards manufacturing the equipment that will support the growth of renewables, storage, hydrogen and networks over the next few years.

text:
Highlights

Elevra Lithium has secured the final statutory permit for Carolina Lithium

The approval clears a regulatory hurdle but is not a construction decision

The annual meeting confirmed a sharper focus on Quebec and North Carolina

Elevra Lithium (ASX:ELV) Basic Materials Elevra Lithium Limited (ASX:ELV) 3.08 AUD +0.110 ↑ 3.704% , the dual-listed lithium miner formed through a recent merger and focused on North America, has received the final statutory permit for its Carolina Lithium Project in North Carolina, and followed that with an annual meeting that set out a narrower portfolio built around Quebec and the United States. As Elevra Lithium continues operating within the ASX 200, growing attention is also being directed towards ASX Lithium Stocks as companies across the sector navigate changing market conditions.

For readers following ASX today live coverage, Elevra Lithium remains a key name to watch.

The last permit in the stack

The state Division of Air Quality issued an air permit for the Gaston County project after a public comment period. It was the final statutory permit the company needed for a proposal that combines spodumene mining and lithium chemical processing at a single integrated site.

Management described the approval as a significant milestone. For a project that combines a mine and a chemical plant, closing out the permit list removes a key layer of regulatory uncertainty.

Scope of the Permit

The air permit does not amount to a green light for construction. The company has been clear that a build decision depends on a scoping study, local rezoning, project financing and a partner.

The scoping study is expected in the period to June of next year. Until then, Carolina remains a permitted but unfunded project, which is how the market is likely to value it.

Permitted projects do carry a premium over unpermitted ones, because the time and cost of approvals in the United States can be substantial. Even so, the value of that permit depends on whether the remaining commercial pieces can be assembled at a time when lithium prices are soft and capital for new chemical plants is scarce.

A partner for the chemical plant

Elevra intends to bring in a partner for the downstream processing stage. Its strategy centres on committing capital in, developing and operating mines, rather than running chemical conversion plants on its own.

That approach reflects a broader shift across the sector. Chemical conversion is capital-intensive and technically demanding, and many miners now prefer to share that risk with chemical companies or battery makers.

Among ASX Lithium Stocks, a partnership model for downstream processing has become a common way to reduce funding needs while keeping exposure to higher-value products.

AGM confirms a narrower portfolio

At its annual meeting, the company said it now operates under a single strategy following the merger. The meeting was framed around simplifying the business after a busy year of corporate activity.

The company has exited its Ewoyaa interest in Ghana, with that transaction closing in October, and has also parted with its Tabba pegmatite rights in Western Australia. Those moves free up resources for its core assets.

North American Lithium expansion underway

The core producing asset is North American Lithium in Quebec. Construction on a brownfield expansion began in June, with funding being delivered in stages.

Staging capital in this way allows the company to adjust spending if lithium prices weaken further. It also lets the market judge progress in smaller steps rather than on a single large commitment.

Moblan in the background

Elevra also has a majority interest in the Moblan Lithium Project in Quebec, which management said continued to advance during the year. Few details on milestones were given at the meeting.

Moblan provides another Quebec growth option, which could eventually share services and expertise with North American Lithium.

Market Position

That US listing is especially relevant for Carolina, as American policy settings favour domestic lithium supply for the electric vehicle sector.

US policy and local politics

Federal support for domestic battery materials has created a favourable backdrop for US lithium projects.

At the local level, rezoning remains a hurdle. Community views on a combined mine and chemical plant can influence how quickly approvals progress, regardless of state permits.

Risks to weigh

Lithium prices remain the biggest external risk. Chinese carbonate futures fell sharply this week, and a prolonged downturn would make it harder to attract a downstream partner or finance a new build.

Execution risk at North American Lithium is another factor, as the expansion must be delivered on time and on budget while the plant keeps producing.

Key Watchpoints

Progress on the North American Lithium expansion will be the main operating marker over the coming quarters. For Carolina, the key steps are the scoping study, rezoning and the search for a partner.

Any updates on Moblan's development pathway would also add clarity to the company's longer-term production profile.

text:
Lyra Energy, a joint venture (JV) between Scatec and Stanlib Infrastructure Investments, has commenced construction on the 126MW Noko solar power project in South Africa following financial close.

Scatec, which holds a 50% stake in Lyra Energy, will invest approximately $13m in equity in the Noko project.

The company also expects to generate around $100m in design and construction (D&C) revenues from the development.

Standard Bank, a long-term financing partner for Scatec in South Africa, is providing non-recourse debt for the project.

The Noko solar plant is scheduled to begin commercial operations in the first half (H1) of 2028.

Scatec CEO Terje Pilskog said: “Noko is the second project being realised through the Lyra platform and with our partners, Scatec is building a leader in the corporate PPA market in South Africa.

“Lyra has secured a diverse portfolio of private offtake agreements in South Africa, and Scatec is creating value in a highly capital-efficient way through our integrated business model in this deregulating market.”

In addition to the Noko project, Scatec has decided to withdraw its 288MW Mercury solar power project from South Africa’s Renewable Energy Independent Power Producer Procurement (REIPPP) programme and sell it to Lyra Energy.

The move aims to address increased demand from corporate offtakers seeking long-term supply agreements.

Construction for the Mercury project is expected to commence in the first half of 2027.

Scatec continues to provide construction, operational, and asset management services for these projects.

Scatec Sub-Saharan Africa EVP and GM Alberto Gambacorta said: “With these important milestones, Lyra is moving from proving its model to scaling it.

“South African businesses need reliable, clean power at competitive prices, and Lyra is well positioned to deliver it at the pace the market demands.”

Lyra Energy operates as a renewable electricity trading platform in the country, serving commercial and industrial customers through multi-year power purchase agreements (PPAs).

The company’s operating model involves acquiring projects developed by Scatec and initiating construction once adequate commitments from corporate energy buyers have been secured.

At present, Lyra Energy has two solar projects under construction with a combined capacity of 381MW and an additional 288MW project in its pipeline.

text:
Input

[Financial News] With the National Assembly reviewing an amendment to tax laws to establish a Domestic Production Tax Credit, the solar industry is calling for direct refunds and the transfer of tax credit rights to third parties to be allowed. Chinese-made products accounted for 69.3% of domestic solar module supply last year, but under the government’s proposal, domestic manufacturers with insufficient corporate tax liabilities would find it difficult to use the credits immediately, even if they increase production.

According to the government and industry on the 27th, the National Assembly’s Finance, Economy and Planning Committee Tax Subcommittee has been reviewing an amendment to the Restriction of Special Taxation Act, including the establishment of a Domestic Production Tax Credit, since the 23rd.

In August, the government announced in its tax reform plan that it would introduce a Domestic Production Tax Credit in six key sectors, including solar power, wind power, secondary batteries and semiconductors. Under the plan, an amount calculated by multiplying the production volume of eligible products directly produced and sold in Korea by a standard credit amount would be deducted from income or corporate taxes. The credit would be available through the end of 2036.

The government proposal includes a provision allowing credits unused in a given year to be carried forward for the next 10 years, but it does not include direct refunds or the transfer of credit rights. As a result, companies with insufficient corporate tax liabilities due to losses or other reasons would find it difficult to reduce their immediate production costs, even if they accrue credits.

The United States supports solar cells, modules and other products made domestically through the Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit (AMPC) under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). Companies that meet certain requirements can receive a direct refund of the credit or transfer it to a third party.

At a public briefing on the Korean Green Transformation (K-GX) strategy on October 7, President Lee Jae-myung proposed paying subsidies to loss-making companies upfront and deducting them from future tax credit amounts. The government is reportedly leaning against pursuing direct subsidies, having taken into account factors such as fairness and feasibility. However, the Ministry of Finance and Economy and the Ministry of Planning and Budget said on the 5th that a decision had not been made on whether to introduce them.

The expansion of Chinese products’ share of the domestic market is behind the solar industry’s emphasis on the effectiveness of the production tax credit.

According to data obtained from the Korea Energy Agency by Shin Jeong-hun of the Democratic Party of Korea (DPK), Chinese-made modules accounted for 2,601 MW, or 69.3%, of the 3,753 megawatts (MW) of solar modules supplied domestically last year, based on facility confirmations under the Renewable Portfolio Standard (RPS). The share of domestically made modules fell 47.7 percentage points in six years, from 78.4% in 2019 to 30.7% last year.

Investment in domestic mass production of next-generation solar cells is also tied to the design of the production tax credit. Industry, academia and research institutions in Korea are pursuing the development and demonstration of key processes for tandem solar cells, which combine silicon and perovskite to increase power-generation efficiency. The industry’s target for full-scale mass production is around 2029.

Some in the solar industry say that if direct refunds or the transfer of credit rights prove difficult to introduce, temporary purchase subsidies for domestically produced products or separate financial support programs should also be implemented.

An industry official said, “To maintain the domestic production base and invest in next-generation facilities, companies with insufficient tax liabilities should also be able to use the credit benefits immediately.”

IRVINE, Calif.
,
Nov. 26, 2026
/PRNewswire/ -- While some automakers have scaled back their North American EV ambitions, VinFast continues to view electric vehicles as essential to addressing climate change. In the U.S. and Canada, the company is focused on making EVs easier to purchase, charge and service while helping customers understand operating costs. Its broader strategy centers on building a network of vehicles, charging infrastructure and services that can support more drivers and fleets over time.
One of the latest steps came on October 6, 2026, when VinFast announced an initial agreement with NexMove at the APTA TRANSform & EXPO in Chicago to bring its electric buses to U.S. customers. NexMove, a joint venture between Transportation Management Services and Zeem Solutions, plans to bundle buses, charging, maintenance and operations in a single agreement. It intends to offer a 97% uptime service-level commitment, with certified bus deliveries expected to begin in the first quarter of 2028. The announcement followed VinFast's September 2026 franchise agreements for three U.S. dealerships in California and Pennsylvania.
Making electric mobility practical for fleets and drivers
For a transit agency, introducing electric buses requires decisions about depot charging, maintenance schedules and daily vehicle availability. NexMove's proposed service brings these elements together into one agreement. Ahead of certified deliveries, NexMove plans to place demonstration buses at Zeem's charging depots, where transit agencies and fleet operators can evaluate the vehicles firsthand. The demonstration units are intended for evaluation, with certified vehicles to follow on the planned delivery schedule.
VinFast's buses combine camera- and radar-based driver assistance, fast charging capabilities, lithium iron phosphate batteries and corrosion protection. The company reported that approximately
2,000
of its electric buses were operating in Vietnam at the time of the announcement. VinFast's experience in the market spans manufacturing, operations and maintenance, giving it firsthand knowledge of the demands fleet operators face when vehicles are in daily service.
"Bringing VinFast electric buses to the United States marks an important next step in our long-term commitment to this market," said Brian Finnerty, CEO of VinFast North America.
For households, the questions are more personal: How much will it cost to charge a vehicle each month? Where can it be serviced? What options are available at a price the buyer can afford? The franchise agreements in Redondo Beach and Tustin, California, and Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, expand access to sales and after-sales service. The company's U.S. certified pre-owned program gives buyers another option when weighing the upfront cost of an EV.
In Canada, VinFast offers a 10-year or 200,000-kilometre limited new-vehicle warranty on the VF 8, whichever comes first. Its online energy-cost calculator allows shoppers to compare estimated EV charging costs with the fueling costs of a gasoline vehicle over their expected mileage and ownership period. The comparison gives buyers a clearer picture of how an EV could fit their driving habits and household budget.
Annual EV charging costs can be 50% or more below gasoline fueling costs, depending on electricity rates, whether drivers charge at home or use public stations, driving habits, and vehicle efficiency. Coltura's Q3 2024 analysis estimated that U.S. EV drivers saved an average of 7.4 cents per mile on fuel. At 1,200 miles a month, that works out to about $90 a month, or nearly $1,100 a year if the same per-mile savings hold.
Why a long-term climate commitment matters as markets change
VinFast announced its transition to all-electric vehicle production at CES in Las Vegas in 2022. Just over two years later, it became Vietnam's best-selling vehicle brand in 2024, according to Vingroup's annual report. Its expansion into North America brings a different set of considerations, including where to build out sales and service operations, how to support charging infrastructure and how to help commercial customers integrate electric vehicles into their existing operations.
Incentives, regulations and customer demand can change while a factory upgrade or charging project is still in development. VinFast's 2040 net-zero goal provides a long-term framework for investments that take years to plan and implement. For example, the timing of an equipment replacement affects when a plant can shift more of its operations to electricity. The source of that electricity then affects the emissions associated with running the equipment. Decisions about materials and suppliers have a similar bearing on emissions across the value chain.
VinFast's emissions inventory illustrates why those decisions matter as production grows. The company calculated that its emissions exceeded 1.12 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) in its 2022 base year. In a separate scenario, VinFast estimated that emissions could exceed 20 million metric tons of CO₂e if its existing production operations in Vietnam reached their maximum registered capacity, excluding future factories. The estimate illustrates the importance of factoring energy efficiency, electricity sourcing and supplier emissions into plans for higher production.
How the 3E Mission puts the 2040 pledge into practice
VinFast signed The Climate Pledge on August 17, 2022, and announced its participation in September 2022. It was the first Vietnamese enterprise to sign the pledge, an initiative co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism. The company's stated goal is to reach net-zero emissions by 2040 across Scopes 1, 2 and 3, covering direct emissions from its operations, indirect emissions from purchased energy, and emissions across its wider value chain. Signatories commit to measuring and reporting greenhouse gas emissions regularly, reducing emissions and neutralizing the remainder.
In January 2025, VinFast's chairwoman approved the company's net-zero strategy through 2030, with a view to 2040. The strategy centers on the 3E Mission, which sets out how VinFast plans to change the equipment it uses, reduce the energy it needs and source cleaner power.
Electrification.
VinFast plans to electrify equipment at company-owned production and business sites by 2030. The roadmap also includes expanding access to charging and developing battery energy storage.
Energy Saving.
VinFast plans to introduce smart energy monitoring at manufacturing facilities by 2028. Monitoring production lines and major electricity-consuming equipment gives factory teams more detailed information on where energy is used and where operations can be made more efficient.
Energy Greening.
VinFast aims to use 100% renewable electricity at all its plants by 2040. Its roadmap includes rooftop solar, battery storage to support renewable power use, and work with suppliers on lower-emission materials.
VinFast's manufacturing complex in Hai Phong offers a practical example of what these priorities translate to on the factory floor. The company reported that upgrades to lighting and compressed-air systems, changes to how production robots operate, and other efficiency measures saved approximately 2.7 million kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2024, equivalent to an estimated 1,782 metric tons of CO₂e.
The company also said it initiated a 30-megawatt-peak rooftop solar project at the site. While the efficiency measures address how much electricity the plant needs, the solar project addresses the source of the electricity.
Against its 2022 baseline, VinFast aims to reduce Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 42% and Scope 3 emissions by 29% by 2030. By 2040, the strategy calls for cutting total emissions by at least 85% and neutralizing residual emissions of up to 15% through carbon offsetting mechanisms, which could include carbon credits. As VinFast serves more drivers and fleets, its reported emissions will show how far the company has progressed toward those targets across its operations, purchased energy and value chain.

title: Oregon slower than other states to OK green energy projects; now there's an alternative
authors: Penny Rosenberg / Oregon Journalism Project, Leo Heffron, Jaime Adame, Mike McInally, Ben Botkin, Alex Baumhardt, Oregon Capital Chronicle, Tyson Alger, Annie Aguiar, William L. Sullivan

text:
In February, the Oregon Legislature passed a bill that in essence said the state process for siting clean energy projects was too slow and allowed certain projects to bypass the state and go to the counties for approval.

As of this date, only two developers have made the switch, and they’ve already sailed through to approval.

But this does not portend well for a state that promised in 2021 utilities would be carbon-free by 2040.

“We are 47th in the nation for the production of new clean energy, partly because we make it harder to do than any other state,” state Rep. Mark Gamba, D-Milwaukie, wrote to a state agency in September. Gamba said he is looking to tighten the state’s process in the 2027 legislative session.

Shortening the process was the goal when lawmakers passed House Bill 4031 earlier this year. It gave some applicants a fast track by allowing them to skip state approval and instead apply directly to the counties where the renewable energy projects are proposed.

The main drivers behind the bill were the state’s long delays and Congress’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which set an expiration date on federal tax credits for clean energy projects.

County officials have proven they can usher an application through in less than half the time it takes the state’s Energy Facility Siting Council.

When it comes to green energy, Oregon talks a big game but mostly strikes out. A report released earlier this year by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Berkeley Lab looked at the states’ approval times for wind and solar projects. Oregon came in last place.

For the 19 states that offer a state approval apparatus, the report says “90% of projects obtained permit approval, most within a year or so of entering the process.”

But Oregon projects take, on average, 600 days to arrive at a decision — nearly double the time of other states studied — and can spend nearly as long in a preapplication stage.

After HB 4031 passed, the Oregon Department of Energy identified seven renewable energy projects in the pipeline that were eligible to switch to local jurisdictions. To date, only two have: a solar array in Morrow County and a 69-turbine wind farm in nearby Gilliam County. Both got signoff from their respective counties in September, a timeline counted in months, not years.

Brian Walsh, vice president of project development for MN8 Energy’s Well Springs Solar Project, estimates the switch from state to Morrow County jurisdiction shaved more than a year off the siting process. That represents “a tremendous savings for the project,” Walsh said, “and also keeps the price of power lower for those who buy the power and consume the power.”

Thirteen other clean energy projects did not qualify under HB 4031 for county approval and are currently making their way through the slog of the state’s process.

On Sept. 18, for example, the state Energy Facility Siting Council signed off on the Yellow Rosebush Energy Center, a solar farm to be built primarily in Wasco County. It had been originally pitched to the state back in 2023.

A polite word to describe the state of Oregon’s process would be “methodical,” said state Rep. John Lively, a Democrat from Springfield, who is retiring from the Legislature. He chaired the House Interim Committee on Climate, Energy, and Environment, which recommended passing HB 4031.

“At the local level, you’ve got local elected officials and staff that are in a position just to act much quicker,” Lively said. “Now, you can argue whether they’re as thorough as they should be or not. The reality is, they follow the code, so they’re doing what the code requires them to do. At the end of the day, not everybody wants these facilities. So, depending on the county and what they’re doing, there’s opposition.”

There was, in fact, little opposition to the two projects that have been pushed through county approval: none for Saddle Butte, and only one person went on the record against Well Springs.

In the end, Oregon counties are much more “streamlined” in their approach, said Ethan Kirkham, a Portland senior research analyst at Greenlight America, which helps proponents of clean energy advocate for projects at a grassroots level.

At the state, “it’s a much more exhaustive list of checking all these boxes, and you’ll often see projects going back and forth for one to three to four to five years,” Kirkham said.

Even if only one or two projects make it to completion in time to reap the tax benefit, Lively said, HB 4031 will have been worth it.

Though, he acknowledged, “it would be nice to see more.”

title: The U.N. Climate Talks Were a Disaster. But There's a Silver Lining. | The New Republic
authors: Mark Hertsgaard, Malcolm Ferguson, Ellie Quinlan Houghtaling, UNSHACKLED Greg Sargent, The New Republic Staff, DOUBLE BOGEY Harry Litman

text:
“Breakdown.” “Collapse.” “Failure.” Those were some of the words that media coverage used to describe last week’s COP31 U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. The talks ended in acrimony and finger-pointing after the nearly 200 participating nations could not reach consensus on how to advance the official mission of these annual summits: to protect humanity from “dangerous” amounts of man-made global warming.

Most news coverage also identified the main reason for the lack of consensus. As Reuters reported, Saudi Arabia “was at the forefront of resisting language on reducing reliance on fossil fuels,” even as “the European Union, several small island states, and other nations particularly vulnerable to climate change said they could not accept a text that failed to mention the oil, gas, and coal that scientists say drive global warming.”

Coming on the heels of a summer that featured 50,000 excess heat deaths across Europe and a glacial collapse in Nepal that killed at least 7,000 people and wiped out 10 percent of the country’s gross national product in minutes, the failure to highlight fossil fuels’ role in the climate emergency unleashed both derision and dismay. “A climate deal that leaves out fossil fuels is like a plan to quit smoking that never mentions cigarettes,” commented Katharine Hayhoe, the chief scientist at the Nature Conservancy.

Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister and COP31 co-president, opened the final day of talks by declaring that “a historic decision” was in the offing. What followed was historic all right, though not in the way Kurum hoped. This COP marked only the second time in the 31-year history of these summits that no final agreement (known in COP parlance as a “cover decision”) was published.

Yet a strong case can be made that COP31 was not a total failure, but a much-needed turning point toward more effective climate diplomacy going forward. “No deal is better than a deal that locks in failure,” said Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser and global engagement director for the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative. Bill Hare, chief executive at Climate Analytics, wrote in The Guardian that “the failure of COP31 in Antalya was a line-in-the-sand moment, a victory for multilateralism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no.”

COP31 vividly demonstrated what has been evident for years: Petrostates—including the U.S., which boycotted these talks for the second year in a row—will never willingly agree to leave fossil fuels behind. And they will exploit the COP tradition of consensus decision-making to delay action as long as possible.

By refusing at COP31 to keep playing along, the vast majority of the world’s countries were, to borrow from Beckett, no longer “waiting for Godot”—no longer waiting for petrostates to help rather than hinder the fight against climate breakdown. Instead, many of these countries are moving ahead on their own to do what both science and justice call for.

One of the few bright spots at COP31 was further growth of the Santa Marta coalition of countries that is committed to a global phaseout of fossil fuels. The coalition first took shape at COP30, where 87 countries wanted the final agreement to endorse developing a global “roadmap” to phase out oil, gas, and coal. But when Saudi Arabia and Russia led a handful of petrostates in refusing to consent, consensus decision-making meant that the endorsement of a roadmap was excluded from the agreement.

Undaunted, many of those countries met in April 2026 in Santa Marta, Colombia, to begin developing a roadmap themselves. Collectively, the countries that met in Santa Marta—a group that included Germany, the world’s third-largest economy; France, the sixth-largest; the United Kingdom, the seventh-largest; Brazil, the tenth-largest; and the Netherlands, the eighteenth-largest—amount to the biggest economic superpower on earth. Combine their GNPs and the total is larger than that of the U.S. Include California—whose governor, Gavin Newsom, said at COP31 that he backed the Santa Marta effort “100 percent”—and the coalition’s GNP is nearly as large as that of the U.S. and China put together.

If these countries can implement credible plans for transitioning away from fossil fuels to solar, wind, batteries, and other forms of clean energy, it would put governments and financial markets on notice that staying invested in fossil fuels will be a risky proposition that could leave them with trillions of dollars of stranded assets. This scenario became more plausible at COP31, as the coalition expanded to include not only California, the world’s fourth-largest economy, but also Spain, Ireland, Belgium, Finland, Denmark, Norway, Luxembourg, and Pacific island nations.

Petrostates’ obstructionism at COP31 also led to renewed calls to reform the decision-making process at future COPs. “COPs are designed to fail,” Juan Carlos Navarro, the minister of the environment for Panama, said in an interview with Covering Climate Now. Minutes earlier, Navarro had delivered the summit’s most piercing sound bite, telling a press conference that “we are being held hostage by the petroleum mafia.” In the interview, he explained that consensus decision-making means that “all it takes is one idiot to torpedo the entire process. If we don’t change direction, by the time we have COP61, the world will be five degrees [Celsius, or 9 degrees Fahrenheit] warmer.”

Panama plans to press this issue at the U.N. General Assembly, Navarro said. “Decisions at the COP should be made by simple majority, just like at the General Assembly,” he said, adding that “more and more countries” are coming around to this view. An effort within the U.N. to update the operating rules for COPs is another potential avenue for reform.

Such reform is not as unlikely as some observers seem to think. Chris Bowen, the climate minister of Australia and the co-president of COP31, acknowledged after the talks ended that consensus decision-making was partly to blame for the outcome. But Bowen misstated the relevant history when he asserted that “when COPs were created … [decision-making] was made consensus only.”

Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research, walked through the history in a LinkedIn post during COP31. How COPs would make decisions was initially discussed at the very first COP, held in 1995. A proposal was made to reach decisions by consensus if possible, but if “all efforts have been exhausted and no consensus reached,” then a two-thirds majority vote would serve as a last resort. “But oil producing countries opposed this, with support from U.S. oil lobbyists,” Rockström wrote.

The issue was left unresolved. Nevertheless, Rockström said at a CCNow Press Briefing, in subsequent years “a culture took hold … to operate under consensus,” though in fact “there is nothing hindering … the COP process to have majority voting today.”

How the various efforts to reform decision-making at U.N. climate summits unfold is a story worth watching—and covering. There would seem to be enough time to fix the process before COP32 takes place next November in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Doing so could make a world of difference.

description:
Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson wants a hard look at any combination of Tesla and SpaceX, and he said so on the record.
What the quote does establish is that the incoming head of the state’s top law office has publicly put the Texas attorney general Tesla SpaceX merger question on his agenda before taking the oath.
Why a Texas Attorney General Gets a Say Mergers in the United States face federal review first.
Parties negotiating a transaction have to plan for several reviewers with different incentives, and the Texas attorney general Tesla SpaceX merger question now sits among them.
If that happens, the Texas attorney general Tesla SpaceX merger question moves from hypothetical to live in a matter of weeks.
text:
Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson wants a hard look at any combination of Tesla and SpaceX, and he said so on the record. In a Bloomberg interview on November 12, 2026, Johnson told Bloomberg that “Any merger of companies of that consequence warrants tremendous scrutiny.” The Texarkana Gazette carried the story on November 27 under the headline “Texas’ next AG vows ‘tremendous scrutiny’ of Tesla-SpaceX deal.”

The comment arrives while the two Elon Musk companies weigh a possible tie-up. Reports from the Financial Times, relayed by Reuters, say each board has set up a review committee, a process we covered in our piece on the directors and committees handling the talks. Neither company has announced a deal. That gap matters for everything that follows, because a Texas attorney general reviewing a transaction that does not yet exist is working with a promise, not a case.

This analysis separates what Johnson said from what outlets have reported and from what remains unknown. It also explains what the Texas attorney general can realistically do, why a hardware-heavy merger of cars, batteries, rockets and satellites raises unusual questions, and how investors and suppliers should read the signal. Johnson is scheduled to take office in January 2027. No investigation has been announced.
