Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.

Add now

What Nathan Johnson Said About the Tesla-SpaceX Merger

The core of the story is one sentence. Johnson said any potential merger between Space Exploration Technologies Corp., the company commonly known as SpaceX, and Tesla Inc. would get close examination from his office. He framed the concern around the size of the companies involved, not around any specific term of a deal.

He also declined to discuss the specifics of a possible combination. That restraint is standard for an incoming prosecutor. An attorney general-elect does not hold the office yet, has no access to confidential filings, and risks tainting any later case by previewing conclusions. Johnson gave a posture, not a position.

According to the Texarkana Gazette’s account of the Bloomberg interview, Johnson also warned about the dangers of corporate concentration, and the outlet described Tesla and SpaceX as the state’s two most valuable companies. The same account says he plans to steer the office toward consumer protection and antitrust litigation, and that he praised outgoing Attorney General Ken Paxton’s work in those areas and intends to keep some of the lawyers who specialize in them. We treat those details as reported by the Gazette and not as separate confirmation.

The wording is worth reading closely. “Tremendous scrutiny” promises attention. It does not promise a lawsuit, a subpoena, or opposition. A prosecutor can scrutinize a deal and then wave it through. What the quote does establish is that the incoming head of the state’s top law office has publicly put the Texas attorney general Tesla SpaceX merger question on his agenda before taking the oath.

What Is Confirmed and What Is Not

Coverage of this story has blurred two very different kinds of claim. Some facts are on the record. Others come from unnamed people or from outlets summarizing other outlets. The table below sorts them so readers can see how thin the confirmed layer is.

The last three rows carry the most weight. Outlets including Business Insider, Yahoo Finance and The Next Web have repeated figures and structures attributed to reports. Neither company has confirmed any of them, so we do not repeat those numbers here as fact. A valuation that circulates through five headlines is still one unverified number.

Timeline: How the Talks Reached Texas

The Texas angle is only a few weeks old, but the underlying story has run longer. The sequence below draws on the outlets named in each row.

Note the order. Johnson spoke before the FT reported the director appointments, which means he was reacting to talk of a deal, not to a filing. The one hard date ahead is the swearing-in. Any enforcement action by Texas has to wait for that, and for an actual transaction to review.

Why a Texas Attorney General Gets a Say

Mergers in the United States face federal review first. Parties above certain size thresholds must notify the Federal Trade Commission and the Justice Department and then wait while the agencies decide whether to dig deeper. States sit beside that system, not under it. An attorney general does not need federal permission to investigate a deal that affects people in the state.

Texas has its own antitrust statute, the Texas Free Enterprise and Antitrust Act of 1983, and the attorney general can use civil investigative demands to compel documents and testimony. The attorney general can also sue in state court. Under the federal Clayton Act, states can seek injunctions against mergers that threaten competition, and the Supreme Court has long allowed remedies as sweeping as divestiture. Consumer protection law adds a second path, one that does not require proving a competition harm at all.

Where state power ends

A state cannot simply veto a private merger. It must persuade a judge. That requires a legal theory, evidence, and usually months of work. Johnson’s office would also face the political reality that both companies are major Texas employers and that a lawsuit would draw national attention. Scrutiny can be a negotiating lever as much as a prelude to litigation, and prosecutors often extract commitments without ever filing a complaint.

Those are general features of state enforcement, not predictions about Johnson. He has said nothing about which tools he would use, and the record shows no case open.

The Hardware Stakes: Cars, Batteries, Rockets and Satellites

This is a hardware story, and the hardware is what makes a merger review unusual. Tesla builds electric vehicles and energy storage. SpaceX builds rockets and runs a satellite network. The two do not compete head to head in any obvious product market, which is the usual trigger for a classic antitrust challenge.

So scrutiny would likely turn on other questions. Do shared suppliers, shared engineering talent and shared capital create advantages that rivals cannot match? Would a combined company tilt procurement of batteries, chips or launch services? Our coverage of the FCC’s clearance of a very large SpaceX satellite plan shows how fast the space side is scaling, and any merger would fold that capital appetite into a company that also sells cars.

These questions are our analysis. No regulator has put them in writing, and Johnson has not named any theory of harm. They matter because a state prosecutor looking for a hook in a non-competing merger usually reaches for vertical effects, labor markets, or consumer protection.

The consumer-facing hardware also matters. Tesla owners already face questions about repair and replacement costs, as we noted in our look at battery replacement pricing for the Model 3 and Model Y. A merged company with a larger balance sheet could change how those costs get absorbed or passed on, and consumer protection staff watch exactly that kind of shift.

Texas Is Home Turf for Both Companies

The Texarkana Gazette’s account describes Tesla and SpaceX as the state’s two most valuable companies. Tesla runs a major vehicle factory near Austin, and SpaceX launches Starship from its Gulf Coast site. Both have staked their futures on Texas land, Texas workers and Texas political goodwill.

That home-field status cuts two ways. It gives the state leverage, since a merger that reshapes a dominant local employer touches property tax rolls, utility demand, and the labor market. It also gives the companies leverage, because few governors or attorneys general want to be seen driving away headline employers.

Johnson’s remark reads in that light as a statement of independence. By saying the largest companies in his state do not get a pass, he positioned himself against the idea that proximity to power buys softer treatment. Whether he keeps that line once real documents arrive is the open question.

State AG vs Federal Agencies: A Competitive Comparison

Reviewers do not operate alone. A large deal can draw the FTC, the Justice Department, the Securities and Exchange Commission, foreign competition authorities, and state attorneys general at once. The table compares what each can do, in general terms, and where each stands in this case.

The comparison shows why a state can matter even when federal agencies stay quiet. Federal enforcement priorities change with each administration. A state prosecutor can pursue a deal that Washington clears, and the reverse is possible too. Parties negotiating a transaction have to plan for several reviewers with different incentives, and the Texas attorney general Tesla SpaceX merger question now sits among them.

Historical Context: Musk Deals and the Courts

Transactions between Musk-linked companies have drawn legal attention before. Tesla’s 2016 purchase of SolarCity, a company with ties to Musk’s family, produced years of shareholder litigation over whether the board had paid a fair price. That fight centered on governance and related-party dealing, not on competition law.

The lesson applies here. When one person has a major stake in both sides of a deal, the sharpest questions often concern process. Who negotiated for each side, were they independent, and did minority shareholders get a fair deal? The reported use of separate committees at each company looks designed to answer those questions in advance.

State prosecutors know that history. A review that begins with a look at how a deal was negotiated can reach the same conclusions as a competition case without needing a market definition. For a prosecutor who wants to show seriousness without overreaching, process questions are a lower-risk starting point than a structural challenge. They also keep the focus on documents, which a company can produce or withhold, rather than on contested economic theories.

Our earlier reporting on Donald Trump’s comments about protecting Musk showed how political context can shadow Musk-related stories. Johnson’s statement adds a new political dimension at the state level. Reporting on his remarks has noted that he is the incoming attorney general in a state where Musk’s companies are enormous, which is part of why the quote traveled.

Market Impact: What Investors and Suppliers Watch

A prospective state review adds timing risk to a deal that reports say both sides want done quickly. Electrek, citing the Financial Times, described a year-end target and a race to finish before a new Congress arrives. A state investigation that opens in January would run straight through that window.

For shareholders, the practical question is whether regulatory risk gets priced in. We cannot say how markets will react, and we have no verified stock move tied to Johnson’s remark. Our earlier piece on SpaceX shares falling and one analyst’s bid scenario shows how sensitive sentiment has been to merger chatter alone.

Suppliers and partners face a quieter version of the same uncertainty. Contracts for batteries, chips and structural components assume stable counterparties. A pending merger plus a possible state review raises questions about future volumes and pricing, though nothing in the record shows any supplier changing terms.

The takeaway: Johnson’s remark does not change the deal’s economics today. It changes the list of people who must be satisfied before it closes.

What Johnson’s Other Remarks Signal

The Bloomberg quote is not Johnson’s only recent statement about Musk. In a Politico report published November 20, Johnson said “Elon Musk will be held to the same standards as everyone else. Perhaps that’s a shift.” The sentence frames his approach as equal treatment, and the aside suggests he sees the past as different.

In the same coverage, Johnson described his job this way: “My job as attorney general is to uphold the law, protect consumers, and ensure fair competition, without bias or preference, and that’s what I’m going to do.” That language points to consumer protection and competition as the lenses, and to a deliberate effort to sound neutral.

The quoted material also records Johnson saying he holds no personal vendetta against Musk, a point he reportedly made in a separate interview with Texas Monthly. We leave the colorful phrasing in that interview to the original reports. What matters for analysis is the stated principle: opposition, if it comes, is meant to rest on law and competition, not personal feeling. That framing gives him cover to scrutinize and also gives the companies a rule to hold him to.

Where the Scrutiny Could Land

Johnson has not described a theory of harm, so any list of possible targets is informed speculation. Based on how state attorneys general have handled large deals between non-competitors, four areas stand out.

Vertical effects. A merged company that supplies its own launch, satellite and vehicle needs could squeeze outside suppliers or rivals who rely on the same services.

Labor markets. Combining two of the state’s largest engineering employers could reduce options for specialized workers in the Austin and Gulf Coast regions.

Consumer protection. Warranty terms, pricing practices, data handling and driver-assistance claims fall under state consumer law regardless of merger status.

Governance and disclosure. Related-party dealing between companies sharing a controlling figure invites questions about whether minority holders and the public got full information.

None of these has been raised by Johnson. They represent the questions a careful prosecutor would likely ask first, and they explain why a deal with no direct product overlap can still draw scrutiny.

Five Predictions for the Next Few Months

These are our judgments, labeled as such. They rest on how similar situations have played out and on the reported timeline, not on inside knowledge.

No Texas action before the swearing-in. Johnson cannot open a formal matter until he holds office in January 2027, so expect talk and not subpoenas before then.

The first move will be informal. Letters, meetings and requests for voluntary information usually precede compulsory demands, especially when a deal is unsigned.

Federal review will frame the timeline. If the companies announce a deal, the federal premerger process sets the clock, and Texas will decide whether to move with it or ahead of it.

The companies will court the office early. Parties facing a prospective state review often brief the attorney general before announcing, to avoid surprises.

Process disclosures will matter most. Expect pressure for detail on how the committees were run, because independence is the strongest answer to governance concerns.

For readers following the hardware side of these companies, our hardware coverage hub tracks the chips, batteries and satellites behind the story.

What to Watch Next

Four signals will tell readers whether the scrutiny is rhetoric or the start of a case. The first is whether either company confirms a deal, since there is nothing to review without one. The second is whether Johnson names specific concerns once he takes office. The third is whether his office hires or retains antitrust specialists, as the Gazette’s account says he intends to do. The fourth is whether federal agencies appear in the story at all.

Bloomberg reported earlier in November that an announcement could come as soon as December, according to Electrek’s summary. If that happens, the Texas attorney general Tesla SpaceX merger question moves from hypothetical to live in a matter of weeks. If it does not, Johnson’s quote stays what it is today: a firm statement about a deal that has not been signed.

The honest summary is short. One official has promised attention. No investigation exists. No deal is confirmed. Everything else is reporting, and readers should weigh it that way.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Nathan Johnson?

Nathan Johnson is the Texas Attorney General-elect. He is scheduled to take office in January 2027, succeeding Ken Paxton, according to the Texarkana Gazette’s account of his Bloomberg interview.

What exactly did Johnson say about Tesla and SpaceX?

On November 12, 2026, he said that “Any merger of companies of that consequence warrants tremendous scrutiny.” He said he would closely examine any potential merger between SpaceX and Tesla and declined to discuss specifics.

Has Texas opened an investigation?

No. No investigation has been announced. Johnson has not taken office, and the reviewed reporting does not show a formal state review, lawsuit or demand for documents.

Have Tesla and SpaceX agreed to merge?

Not according to either company. Outlets including TechCrunch, Reuters and Electrek report that boards formed review committees and that talks are ongoing, but no agreement, value, closing date or structure has been confirmed.

Can a state attorney general block a merger?

Not on its own. A state can investigate and sue under state and federal antitrust law, but it must persuade a court. Prosecutors also often negotiate commitments in place of litigation.

Why would a merger of non-competing companies draw scrutiny?

Reviewers can look beyond direct competition. Vertical effects on suppliers, labor market concentration, consumer protection issues and governance questions can all arise, especially when one person is closely tied to both companies. These are general enforcement patterns, not charges Johnson has made.

When could a Tesla-SpaceX deal be announced?

Reports attributed to Bloomberg and the Financial Times point to a year-end target, with an announcement possible as soon as December. Those timelines are unconfirmed, and neither company has committed to a date.

text:
Last week, the Senate passed a bipartisan permitting reform bill that supporters say could lower costs by speeding approvals for major energy, housing and internet infrastructure projects, but the measure is facing opposition from some House Democrats and environmental advocates who warn it could weaken environmental protections.

The Senate approved the bill, officially titled the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (or BAAJA), by a bipartisan vote of 62-33 on November 19, before lawmakers left Washington for the Thanksgiving holiday.

RELATED STORY | Texas regulators are resuming environmental permits for data centers

Supporters argue the measure would help address lengthy permitting delays that can hold up new infrastructure projects for years and increase costs.

“There’s about $1.1 trillion worth of projects that are awaiting approval right now across the country,” Republican Sen. John Hoeven of North Dakota told the Scripps News Group, shortly before the bill's passage. “This permitting reform gets those projects going.”

The legislation seeks to shorten the approval process for major projects, including by addressing lengthy environmental reviews and litigation.

Joe Lippino-Esposito, the director of federal policy for the Pacific Legal Foundation, a libertarian law firm that supports passage of BAAJA, told Scripps News that prolonged legal challenges have long prevented projects from swiftly moving forward.

“What it's doing is it's taking away the never-ending litigation of people who just want to stop every project just for the sake of stopping every project,” Lippino-Esposito said.

A report from the Pacific Legal Foundation found it takes an average of 29 years to open a new mine in the United States, the second-longest timeline in the world.

“If you have something, like a mine, that's taking 29 years to develop, that means you're not getting a lot of them online and getting them started,” Lippino-Esposito said. “So when you have less supply, you have higher costs. It's just a simple economics problem in a lot of these cases.”

But some Democrats and environmental advocates are urging House lawmakers to reject the legislation, citing concerns about environmental protections and a lack of input from Native American tribes.

“The risks and downsides of this bill are not worth it,” Democratic Congresswoman Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico said at a virtual press conference opposing the bill's passage, held earlier this week.

RELATED STORY | Elon Musk's record $474 million election bet backfires in Texas

Stansbury told the Scripps News Group she wants changes to the legislation and opposes the measure in its current form. Among her concerns is its potential effect on Mount Taylor in New Mexico, a site considered sacred by several Native American tribes.

“The administration is proposing to open a uranium mine on Mount Taylor,” Stansbury said. “This bill could expedite the permitting process and take away the rights permanently of our tribes to protect the most sacred mountain that has been protected for thousands of years.”

Stansbury questioned whether speeding infrastructure projects was worth that risk.

“Why would we take the risk of allowing a few extra transmission projects to go through for the permanent destruction of a sacred site,” she added. “It is not worth it. The risk is not worth it.”

The bill could pass the House without Democratic support if nearly all Republicans back it.

The bill is expected to come up for a vote when Congress returns next week.

text:
HANOI, VIETNAM – Media OutReach Newswire – 27 November 2026 – VinEnergo has officially broken ground on a 126 MWp solar power plant in Sagay City, Negros Occidental, Philippines. The project marks the first to be implemented under the cooperation framework between VinEnergo and the Philippine Department of Energy (DOE) on the development of renewable energy solutions integrated with energy storage systems, representing a tangible step forward in VinEnergo’s commitment to investing in and advancing clean energy in the country.

The groundbreaking ceremony was attended by Mr. Lai Thai Binh, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Vietnam to the Philippines; Mr. Rafael Leo M. Cueva, Mayor of Sagay City; Mr. Narciso L. Javelosa Jr., Vice Mayor of Sagay City; and representatives of local government authorities.

Previously, VinEnergo and the Philippine Department of Energy signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to establish a framework for cooperation in developing clean energy sources, laying the foundation for the research and implementation of large-scale energy projects across the country. A key focus of the cooperation is the development of renewable energy projects integrated with energy storage systems, with a targeted renewable energy capacity of more than 20 GW and the potential to deliver up to 5 GW of baseload power to the Philippine national grid. The 126 MWp Sagay Solar project represents the first concrete step in advancing this cooperation, while paving the way for broader collaboration between VinEnergo and leading energy companies in the Philippines.

The 126 MWp Sagay Solar project is being developed in partnership with SunAsia Energy, a Philippine renewable energy company. The project features the innovative Solar on Stilts solution, which utilizes elevated solar panel structures to maximize space efficiency and optimize land use while generating clean electricity.

The project forms part of a broader 422 MWp portfolio jointly developed by VinEnergo and SunAsia Energy, comprising three projects in Macabebe, Sagay, and Silay. This portfolio underscores VinEnergo’s long-term commitment to working with local partners to unlock the Philippines’ renewable energy potential and contribute to the country’s energy transition.

Commenting on the project, Ms. Sharon S. Garin, Secretary of Energy of the Philippines, said: “We welcome VinEnergo’s investment in the Philippine energy sector. The 126-megawatt-peak (MWp) Sagay Solar Power Project represents an important addition to the Philippines’ growing renewable energy capacity and our continuing efforts to strengthen national energy security. By harnessing our indigenous renewable energy resources, projects such as this help diversify our energy mix, reduce dependence on imported fuels, and lessen our exposure to volatility in international energy markets.”

Mr. Nguyen Anh Khoa, Chief Executive Officer of VinEnergo, said: “We believe that the energy transition is about more than simply expanding clean power generation; it is about building a sustainable energy system capable of supporting each country’s long-term development ambitions. For VinEnergo, the 126 MWp Sagay Solar project holds particular significance as the first concrete step in our strategic cooperation with the Philippine Department of Energy. It demonstrates our commitment to translating strategic cooperation into tangible projects that deliver real value. By bringing together our project development capabilities, technological expertise, and strong partnerships with local stakeholders, VinEnergo aims to make a lasting contribution to strengthening energy security, unlocking the Philippines’ renewable energy potential, and shaping a greener, more reliable, and sustainable energy future for the country.”

Looking ahead, VinEnergo plans to further develop a portfolio of power generation projects in the Philippines with a total capacity of up to 5 GWp of baseload power, integrating renewable energy sources with battery energy storage systems (BESS) to support a 24/7 renewable energy model capable of meeting baseload demand. Between 2027 and 2029, the company will progressively advance investment preparations and move eligible projects toward construction and groundbreaking, while continuing to explore new partnership opportunities. These efforts form part of VinEnergo’s long-term investment strategy in the Philippines, contributing to national energy security and the country’s green transition.

With a long-term development vision and as part of the Vingroup ecosystem, VinEnergo aspires to become a comprehensive green energy investor and developer, delivering clean, reliable, and efficient energy solutions while contributing to the global energy transition.

Hashtag: #VinEnergo

The issuer is solely responsible for the content of this announcement.

About VinEnergo

As Vingroup’s green energy company, VinEnergo is focused on developing technological and manufacturing capabilities in renewable energy, energy storage, and electricity transmission and distribution infrastructure. Through continuous improvements in product standards and the expansion of its project implementation capabilities, VinEnergo aims to become a competitive provider of green energy solutions in international markets.

For more information, please visit: https://vinenergo.com

About SunAsia Energy

SUNASIA ENERGY INC. develops renewable energy projects in the Philippines, focusing strongly on solar energy. Since 2013, the company has partnered with local and international organizations to advance solar initiatives nationwide, including the 60 MW solar power project in Toledo, Cebu.

Building on its experience in large-scale solar development, the company expanded into floating solar development, recognizing the potential of water-based solar infrastructure to complement land-based renewable energy projects. Since 2019, SunAsia has operated a floating solar testbed on Laguna Lake, strengthening its technical expertise and gaining insights into the unique engineering and environmental conditions associated with deploying solar technology on water. These efforts support the development of larger projects that contribute to the Philippines’ energy security and clean energy objectives

title: The European Parliament Brings the EU One Step Closer to a Sound Investment Policy
description:
This could soon change thanks to the forthcoming European Competitiveness Fund that will become active from 2028.
Yesterday, the European Parliament cemented its support to a robust fund.
With the European Competitiveness Fund (ECF), the Commission proposed a new instrument to support Europe’s industry and deliver on its Clean Industrial Deal.
Scaling-up strategic clean technologies Over the years, the EU has developed a broad range of funding instruments, but they still largely focus on supporting research and developments.
They should listen to more than 75 businesses that also highlighted the importance of a well-resourced European Competitiveness Fund in the next EU budget.
text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

Being locked-in a race for technological leadership with China and the US, the EU lacks focus, coordination and financial firepower to transform its industry, ensure long-term prosperity while reaching its climate objectives.

This could soon change thanks to the forthcoming European Competitiveness Fund that will become active from 2028. Yesterday, the European Parliament cemented its support to a robust fund. Today, EU leaders meet and need to secure an adequate budget for the ECF to deliver.

Since the launch of the US Inflation Reduction Act in 2022, Europe has developed several strategies, masterplans and policy initiatives to build a compelling industrial policy. Still, they largely failed to deliver on focus, coordination and financial firepower.

With the European Competitiveness Fund (ECF), the Commission proposed a new instrument to support Europe’s industry and deliver on its Clean Industrial Deal. Yesterday, the European Parliament voted on rules that would make the proposal even stronger.

A bigger budget

MEPs raised the ECF’s overall budget by €30 billion to €264 billion. Crucially, they boosted the envelope for clean energy and industrial decarbonisation to €40 billion, with €4 billion earmarked specifically for clean-tech manufacturing.

MEPs backed a budget of €40 billion for InvestEU, including €15 billion specifically for clean energy and industrial decarbonisation. Through budgetary guarantees, debt and equity, InvestEU aims to collect private capital for higher-risk domestic manufacturing projects that would otherwise fail to reach a final investment decision. This extra €29 billion in additional guarantees compared to the Commission’s proposal could unlock over €300 billion in total mobilised investment.

The Parliament also earmarks €10 billion for the Critical Raw Materials Centre (CRM Centre). The Centre is poised to secure resilient and sustainable critical raw material supply chains for Europe by investing in strategic projects. Securing budgetary resources via the ECF is a crucial step for success.

Scaling-up strategic clean technologies

Over the years, the EU has developed a broad range of funding instruments, but they still largely focus on supporting research and developments. Yet, every year the EU falls further behind China in terms of manufacturing of key technologies, such as batteries. This is because the existing funding programmes neglect the critical and capital intensive scale-up period. Many new market entrants do not survive due to technological risk, insufficient access to risk capital and foreign competition.

Europe does spend substantial money to support industry, both via European funds and at the national level under slow-moving state aid schemes. However, many of the support schemes are spread out widely across technologies without enough focus and clear priorities.

This makes sense for funding early research to steer innovation. For scaling this is different. Today, we know which technologies we need to produce in the next 5 to 10 years to cut emissions and retain leadership, starting with clean transport: the battery value chain, zero-emission vehicles, clean aviation and maritime technologies and e-fuels.

To deliver on the green transition, European funding must be decisively redirected toward the development of strategic clean industries and essential technology value chains. T&E estimates that manufacturing of clean transport technologies alone requires at least €39 billion public funding per year by 2030. Broader decarbonisation needs — industrial heat, buildings, and cleantech deployment — require significantly more.

European cleantech innovators too often stall in the “valley of death” between R&D and commercial production. The Parliament’s text tackles this directly by mandating “ramp up” support for projects that strengthen critical value chains and reduce foreign dependencies — backed by a dedicated €4 billion envelope for clean technologies like battery cell manufacturing. Finally, the EU will be able to deploy production aid — a model that has proven impactful in other jurisdictions like the US.

Time for governments to follow suit

The Parliament has set out a far bolder industrial vision than EU governments who so far largely stuck to the Commission’s narrower draft.

One immediate test will decide whether the ECF will make a difference in the future. EU heads of states and governments who meet today for a special summit must reverse the heavy cuts inflicted on the ECF in recent Council negotiating drafts. They should listen to more than 75 businesses that also highlighted the importance of a well-resourced European Competitiveness Fund in the next EU budget.

Designing a smart new industrial investment tool means little if leaders starve it of cash. They must back a Competitiveness Fund with the budget to match its ambition.

text:
QINGDAO, China, Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Report from iQingdao:

The Fourth Belt and Road Energy Ministerial Conference concluded in Qingdao this week, bringing together energy ministers and senior representatives from partner countries under a partnership that now counts 35 member states and a cooperation network of nearly 300 enterprises. The gathering marked a shift from framework-building to institutional implementation, with the host city itself serving as a working case study in rapid renewable deployment.

Under the theme "Sharing Innovation Outcomes, Advancing Energy Transition, Building a Secure Future Together," the conference featured a main forum, multiple parallel sessions covering artificial intelligence in energy and natural gas cooperation, and technical visits. The inaugural meeting of the partnership's Governing Board was held during the event, alongside the release of a joint ministerial statement emphasizing energy security and green transition. Over the past decade, cumulative installed new energy capacity in Belt and Road partner countries has quadrupled to more than 600 GW, while cumulative energy cooperation investment and engineering contracts have exceeded 3.33 trillion yuan, reflecting the partnership's steady evolution from dialogue platform to project pipeline.

Qingdao's selection as host reflected its own domestic energy trajectory. Renewable energy now accounts for over 61% of the city's installed power capacity, with new energy sources surpassing traditional generation to become the largest electricity source. Under State Grid Qingdao's planning, the city aims to expand new energy capacity from 8.33 million kilowatts to 21.5 million kilowatts by the end of the 15th Five-Year Plan period, raising its share to 72%. The city's coastal geography, port infrastructure and manufacturing base have also made it a natural testbed for offshore wind, hydrogen and smart-grid pilot projects linked to the broader partnership agenda.

"For our international audience, the message from Qingdao is clear: energy cooperation is not just about policy — it's about projects, technology, and shared green growth," the conference script stated. "From this city, the road ahead is green — and it's open to all."

The Belt and Road Energy Partnership connects energy ministers and senior representatives from partner countries to advance green energy transition, energy security, and concrete project collaboration. It currently comprises 35 member states and facilitates engagement among nearly 300 participating enterprises, with working groups focused on areas including renewable energy, hydrogen, smart grids and capacity building.

text:
The World Bank Group has approved financing to help India strengthen its bond markets to support long-term infrastructure investment and create more and better-paying jobs, with a focus on clean energy, electric mobility, public transport, and urban systems. The initiative, called the Unlocking Private Capital for Long-Term Infrastructure Financing and Bond-Market Transformation (UPLIFT) Project, is designed to mobilize private capital for infrastructure that can help sustain employment and growth over decades.

The package includes a $30 million loan and a $470 million guarantee from the World Bank’s International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), complemented by a $20 million grant from the Livable Planet Fund. The Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA) is proposing a separate $1 billion guarantee to help mobilize international capital and expand lending capacity for clean energy.

Why infrastructure finance is difficult

India needs to invest about 10% of gross domestic product (GDP) in infrastructure each year to sustain high economic growth and job creation, according to the World Bank. The World Bank estimates a financing gap of about 5% of GDP—roughly $160 billion annually.

A key challenge is the mismatch between long-term infrastructure needs and the typical investment horizons of banks, which often focus on short- to medium-term lending. The World Bank also points to credit-rating requirements that can limit access to bond markets for some infrastructure issuers, despite the availability of long-term capital from pension, insurance, and provident funds.

The UPLIFT Project and how it works

Under UPLIFT, India’s National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development (NaBFID) will operate a Credit Enhancement Facility. The facility provides partial credit guarantees to infrastructure bond issuers, aiming to raise bond ratings, reduce borrowing costs, and extend repayment periods to better match the operating lives of the financed assets.

The World Bank says the Credit Enhancement Facility is expected to help mobilize about $1.8 billion in private capital. It also projects support for over 1,800 megawatts (MW) of renewable energy capacity through credit-enhanced bond issuances.

Expected market outcomes

The World Bank stated that UPLIFT will support bond markets with at least 11 issuers reaching capital markets, and about $2.5 billion in credit-enhanced bond issuances. It frames the approach as improving access to long-term financing for infrastructure projects that can be developed and owned by Indian investors.

Project task team leaders Tushar Arora and Laurent Gonnet described the underlying goal as increasing long-term financing for infrastructure built in India and owned by Indian investors, tied to job creation for Indians.

Funding structure and parallel planning

In addition to World Bank support, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) is considering providing a $30 million loan and a $470 million guarantee, according to the World Bank’s press release. MIGA’s proposed $1 billion guarantee is also expected to help mobilize international capital and expand its clean energy-related lending capacity.

Paul Procee, World Bank Acting Country Director for India, said India’s long-term savings can be better deployed through bond markets to build infrastructure such as roads, power lines, and transit systems.

Implications for jobs and clean energy investment

By targeting the bond-market constraints that affect long-term infrastructure financing, UPLIFT seeks to create a more predictable channel for private investment into sectors linked to jobs and growth. The World Bank’s focus areas—clean energy, electric mobility, public transport, and urban systems—connect infrastructure financing to broader development priorities, including energy transition, productivity, and urban services.

Why This Matters

The UPLIFT announcement highlights a growing emphasis in development finance on using guarantees and credit enhancement to unlock private capital for long-horizon infrastructure. For NGOs and civil society organizations working alongside government and development banks, the project’s focus on cleaner energy and transport systems also underscores the importance of long-term planning and financing mechanisms that can sustain investment beyond grant cycles.

The use of a credit enhancement facility implemented through a national development bank offers a potential model for strengthening local capital market infrastructure while aligning incentives for private issuers and investors. It may also raise practical questions that organizations often monitor in comparable programs, including how credit support affects transparency, affordability, and the inclusion of affected communities as infrastructure projects are scaled.

Key Details

Initiative/Programme: Unlocking Private Capital for Long-Term Infrastructure Financing and Bond-Market Transformation (UPLIFT) Project

Lead organization: National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development (NaBFID) (Credit Enhancement Facility)

World Bank Group support: IBRD $30 million loan and $470 million guarantee; Livable Planet Fund $20 million grant

Additional guarantee proposed: MIGA is proposing a $1 billion guarantee to mobilize international capital for clean energy

Geographic focus: India

Target groups: Infrastructure bond issuers; private investors; renewable energy and related infrastructure sectors (clean energy, electric mobility, public transport, urban systems)

Expected reach/outcomes (as stated): mobilize about $1.8 billion in private capital; support over 1,800 MW of renewable energy capacity; at least 11 issuers reaching capital markets; about $2.5 billion in credit-enhanced bond issuances

Duration/timeline: Not specified in the provided source

Why This Matters

For NGOs and development professionals, the UPLIFT financing package illustrates how development finance institutions increasingly use guarantees and credit enhancement to address market failures in long-term infrastructure funding. The emphasis on bond-market transformation can affect how infrastructure projects are financed and may influence downstream outcomes such as energy access, job creation, and transport services.

The project’s implementation through a national development bank also signals an approach aligned with localization and building domestic capability in capital market tools. Civil society organizations may find it relevant to track how credit support translates into real investment flows, investor participation, and the inclusion of communities affected by renewable energy, mobility, and urban infrastructure development.

text:
The partnership launched in July 2025 has involved more than 130 companies. The virtuous combination of public finance and industry expands investment and internationalization opportunities, including for smaller companies across the supply chain

Rome, November 27th, 2026 – More than 130 financing applications worth a total of 100 million euros, of which 17.5 million euros have already been disbursed. These are the results of the Memorandum of Understanding signed in July 2025 between SIMEST, the CDP Group company supporting the international growth of Italian businesses, and Enel, a leading integrated player in the global power and renewables markets.

The figures confirm the effectiveness of a partnership that translates companies’ development needs into tangible investment and growth opportunities, both in Italy and international markets: 131 companies have been involved, all with revenues below 250 million euros, including 28 large companies and Mid-Caps, 100 SMEs and 3 micro-enterprises. These figures highlight the agreement’s ability to reach the entire supply chain, fostering growth across the full value chain, from larger operators to smaller businesses.

The initiative also has a significant geographical footprint, involving companies spread across numerous Italian regions, with particularly strong participation from Lombardy (53), Lazio (16), Emilia-Romagna and Veneto (14 each), and Tuscany (9). It therefore represents not only financial support, but also a model of cooperation that connects the development needs of a major industrial supply chain with the expertise, potential and ambitions for growth and internationalization of the companies within it.

The agreement is part of the “Filiere d’impatto” (“Impact Supply Chains”) program, through which SIMEST, in line with the strategic guidelines of the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, supports the growth and competitiveness, including in Italy, of companies belonging to the supply chains of leading Italian companies, including Enel, by providing integrated financial solutions for their supply chains.

The partnership also complements Enel Oltre, the Group’s Supplier Development Program, which aims to strengthen the competitiveness of its industrial ecosystem by fostering the growth of partner companies and enhancing their contribution in terms of innovation, quality, cost efficiency, sustainability and social impact. The figures demonstrate the effectiveness of the Filiere d’impatto program: in 2026 alone, companies in Enel’s supply chain submitted 81 financing applications worth a total of more than 65 million euros.

Under the Memorandum, SIMEST provides companies in the supply chain with dedicated financial instruments to support their investment programs and internationalization strategies, facilitating access to new growth opportunities in international markets.

The partnership generates value throughout the entire supply chain. The companies involved operate in sectors that are strategic to Italy’s energy and industrial system, ranging from mechanical engineering and electromechanics to machinery, plant engineering and transport. This wealth of expertise and specialization represents a key asset for strengthening the competitive positioning of Italian companies and supporting their international expansion.

Enel is a multinational power company and a leading integrated player in the global power and renewables markets, present in 27 countries worldwide.

At global level, it is the largest renewable player, the foremost electricity distribution network player by number of grid customers served and the biggest retail operator by customer base[1].

Enel generates electricity with more than 93 GW of total capacity. Enel Green Power, the Group’s renewables arm, has a total capacity of over 68 GW and a generation mix that includes wind, solar, geothermal, and hydroelectric power, as well as energy storage facilities, installed in Europe, the Americas, Africa, Asia, and Oceania.

Enel Grids, the Group’s global business line dedicated to the management of the electricity distribution service worldwide, delivers electricity through a network of 1.9 million kilometers with around 70 million end users connected to its distribution grids. Enel Commercial is the Group’s arm dedicated to customers around the world with the aim of effectively providing products and services based on their energy needs and encouraging them towards a more conscious and sustainable use of energy. It provides electricity, gas and integrated services to around 54 million customers globally including households, enterprises, industries and public administrations. In addition, it offers flexibility services aggregating 11.3 GW and has more than 35,600 owned public charging points for electric mobility.

[1] Enel’s leadership in the different categories is defined by comparison with FY2025 data and results of relevant comparable listed companies, excluding those with predominant state control.

IRVINE, Calif.
,
Nov. 26, 2026
/PRNewswire/ -- While some automakers have scaled back their North American EV ambitions, VinFast continues to view electric vehicles as essential to addressing climate change. In the U.S. and Canada, the company is focused on making EVs easier to purchase, charge and service while helping customers understand operating costs. Its broader strategy centers on building a network of vehicles, charging infrastructure and services that can support more drivers and fleets over time.
One of the latest steps came on October 6, 2026, when VinFast announced an initial agreement with NexMove at the APTA TRANSform & EXPO in Chicago to bring its electric buses to U.S. customers. NexMove, a joint venture between Transportation Management Services and Zeem Solutions, plans to bundle buses, charging, maintenance and operations in a single agreement. It intends to offer a 97% uptime service-level commitment, with certified bus deliveries expected to begin in the first quarter of 2028. The announcement followed VinFast's September 2026 franchise agreements for three U.S. dealerships in California and Pennsylvania.
Making electric mobility practical for fleets and drivers
For a transit agency, introducing electric buses requires decisions about depot charging, maintenance schedules and daily vehicle availability. NexMove's proposed service brings these elements together into one agreement. Ahead of certified deliveries, NexMove plans to place demonstration buses at Zeem's charging depots, where transit agencies and fleet operators can evaluate the vehicles firsthand. The demonstration units are intended for evaluation, with certified vehicles to follow on the planned delivery schedule.
VinFast's buses combine camera- and radar-based driver assistance, fast charging capabilities, lithium iron phosphate batteries and corrosion protection. The company reported that approximately
2,000
of its electric buses were operating in Vietnam at the time of the announcement. VinFast's experience in the market spans manufacturing, operations and maintenance, giving it firsthand knowledge of the demands fleet operators face when vehicles are in daily service.
"Bringing VinFast electric buses to the United States marks an important next step in our long-term commitment to this market," said Brian Finnerty, CEO of VinFast North America.
For households, the questions are more personal: How much will it cost to charge a vehicle each month? Where can it be serviced? What options are available at a price the buyer can afford? The franchise agreements in Redondo Beach and Tustin, California, and Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, expand access to sales and after-sales service. The company's U.S. certified pre-owned program gives buyers another option when weighing the upfront cost of an EV.
In Canada, VinFast offers a 10-year or 200,000-kilometre limited new-vehicle warranty on the VF 8, whichever comes first. Its online energy-cost calculator allows shoppers to compare estimated EV charging costs with the fueling costs of a gasoline vehicle over their expected mileage and ownership period. The comparison gives buyers a clearer picture of how an EV could fit their driving habits and household budget.
Annual EV charging costs can be 50% or more below gasoline fueling costs, depending on electricity rates, whether drivers charge at home or use public stations, driving habits, and vehicle efficiency. Coltura's Q3 2024 analysis estimated that U.S. EV drivers saved an average of 7.4 cents per mile on fuel. At 1,200 miles a month, that works out to about $90 a month, or nearly $1,100 a year if the same per-mile savings hold.
Why a long-term climate commitment matters as markets change
VinFast announced its transition to all-electric vehicle production at CES in Las Vegas in 2022. Just over two years later, it became Vietnam's best-selling vehicle brand in 2024, according to Vingroup's annual report. Its expansion into North America brings a different set of considerations, including where to build out sales and service operations, how to support charging infrastructure and how to help commercial customers integrate electric vehicles into their existing operations.
Incentives, regulations and customer demand can change while a factory upgrade or charging project is still in development. VinFast's 2040 net-zero goal provides a long-term framework for investments that take years to plan and implement. For example, the timing of an equipment replacement affects when a plant can shift more of its operations to electricity. The source of that electricity then affects the emissions associated with running the equipment. Decisions about materials and suppliers have a similar bearing on emissions across the value chain.
VinFast's emissions inventory illustrates why those decisions matter as production grows. The company calculated that its emissions exceeded 1.12 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) in its 2022 base year. In a separate scenario, VinFast estimated that emissions could exceed 20 million metric tons of CO₂e if its existing production operations in Vietnam reached their maximum registered capacity, excluding future factories. The estimate illustrates the importance of factoring energy efficiency, electricity sourcing and supplier emissions into plans for higher production.
How the 3E Mission puts the 2040 pledge into practice
VinFast signed The Climate Pledge on August 17, 2022, and announced its participation in September 2022. It was the first Vietnamese enterprise to sign the pledge, an initiative co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism. The company's stated goal is to reach net-zero emissions by 2040 across Scopes 1, 2 and 3, covering direct emissions from its operations, indirect emissions from purchased energy, and emissions across its wider value chain. Signatories commit to measuring and reporting greenhouse gas emissions regularly, reducing emissions and neutralizing the remainder.
In January 2025, VinFast's chairwoman approved the company's net-zero strategy through 2030, with a view to 2040. The strategy centers on the 3E Mission, which sets out how VinFast plans to change the equipment it uses, reduce the energy it needs and source cleaner power.
Electrification.
VinFast plans to electrify equipment at company-owned production and business sites by 2030. The roadmap also includes expanding access to charging and developing battery energy storage.
Energy Saving.
VinFast plans to introduce smart energy monitoring at manufacturing facilities by 2028. Monitoring production lines and major electricity-consuming equipment gives factory teams more detailed information on where energy is used and where operations can be made more efficient.
Energy Greening.
VinFast aims to use 100% renewable electricity at all its plants by 2040. Its roadmap includes rooftop solar, battery storage to support renewable power use, and work with suppliers on lower-emission materials.
VinFast's manufacturing complex in Hai Phong offers a practical example of what these priorities translate to on the factory floor. The company reported that upgrades to lighting and compressed-air systems, changes to how production robots operate, and other efficiency measures saved approximately 2.7 million kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2024, equivalent to an estimated 1,782 metric tons of CO₂e.
The company also said it initiated a 30-megawatt-peak rooftop solar project at the site. While the efficiency measures address how much electricity the plant needs, the solar project addresses the source of the electricity.
Against its 2022 baseline, VinFast aims to reduce Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 42% and Scope 3 emissions by 29% by 2030. By 2040, the strategy calls for cutting total emissions by at least 85% and neutralizing residual emissions of up to 15% through carbon offsetting mechanisms, which could include carbon credits. As VinFast serves more drivers and fleets, its reported emissions will show how far the company has progressed toward those targets across its operations, purchased energy and value chain.

HALLSVILLE, Texas (Nov. 19, 2026) – Community leaders, elected officials and economic development partners gathered today at the Hallsville Energy Hub to learn more about SWEPCO’s growing investments in generation, operations and critical energy infrastructure across East Texas.

The event follows a significant project milestone. Regulatory commissions in Arkansas, Louisiana and Texas have now approved the Hallsville Natural Gas Plant project, with all three commissions determining the project is in the public interest and completing the project’s regulatory review process.

The Hallsville Energy Hub brings together generation, logistics, operations and workforce resources that support customer reliability and future energy needs throughout the region. The site includes SWEPCO’s Regional Distribution Center and the Hallsville natural gas generation facility currently under construction.

“The Hallsville Energy Hub represents our commitment to investing in East Texas while building the infrastructure needed to serve customers and communities for decades to come,” SWEPCO President and COO Brett Mattison. “This project reinforces our long-term commitment to the region by supporting economic development, attracting future investment and helping ensure East Texas has the energy infrastructure needed for continued growth.”

Guests toured the site, which will also feature SWEPCO’s Regional Distribution Center, received construction updates and learned more about how Hallsville is becoming a strategic center for generation, operations and logistics supporting SWEPCO’s three-state service territory.

When announcing the issuance of the orders from the three state commissions, finding the projects were in the public interest Lynn Ferry Nelson, SWEPCO vice president of regulatory affairs shared her thanks to regulators.

“We appreciate the confidence the three state commissions have placed in these projects and their recognition of the value to the public,” Ferry-Nelson said. “This is an important step forward for our customers and communities.”

State leaders have also highlighted the importance of the Hallsville investment.

“Texas must have reliable power that is there when we need it,” wrote Texas Sen. Bryan Hughes, in a prepared statement. “SWEPCO is giving us that. They’re expanding energy production for the future, repurposing existing facilities in East Texas, and using clean, reliable natural gas as the power source. I’m grateful for these investments to support our economy and the grid.”

The Hallsville Natural Gas plant is expected to begin serving customers in late 2027 and represents an important part of SWEPCO’s long-term strategy to meet growing energy needs, strengthen reliability and support economic development across the region.

Mattison shared how this work is creating jobs, adding to the tax rolls and contributing meaningful value to the economy of East Texas.

The Steering Column

Cars are getting more expensive. Are we thinking too big?

As affordable cars disappear, Fiat and Toyota are exploring smaller, cheaper alternatives. But are they practical?

AJC

By McKynzie Steward – Cox Automotive

1 hour ago

In last week’s Steering Column, we wrote about the disappearing affordable new car, but recent announcements from Toyota and Fiat offer a glimpse of an unconventional alternative.

Their latest vehicles are tiny, relatively simple and limited to 25 mph. One is electric. The other is a pickup.

Neither could replace most Americans’ everyday transportation, but both raise an interesting question: Have cars become so expensive that it’s time to reconsider how much vehicle we really need?

Fiat Topolino: A $15,000 alternative to a conventional car

The Fiat Topolino is the little low-speed vehicle that could.

This microcar is almost guaranteed to draw attention wherever it goes. At first glance, it might resemble a stylish golf cart rather than a traditional automobile. But its arrival in the U.S. market raises questions about its practicality.

Because the Topolino is classified as a low-speed vehicle, or LSV, it’s subject to different safety requirements than conventional cars. LSVs are limited to 25 mph and generally restricted to roads with speed limits of 35 mph or less.

The 2026 Topolino wasn’t street legal in the United States, topping out at 19 mph. However, for 2027, the Topolino officially qualifies as an LSV title after Fiat raised its top speed to 25 mph.

This microcar is almost guaranteed to draw attention wherever it goes. At first glance, it might resemble a stylish golf cart rather than a traditional automobile. But its arrival in the U.S. market raises questions about its practicality.

Because the Topolino is classified as a low-speed vehicle, or LSV, it’s subject to different safety requirements than conventional cars. LSVs are limited to 25 mph and generally restricted to roads with speed limits of 35 mph or less.

The 2026 Topolino wasn’t street legal in the United States, topping out at 19 mph. However, for 2027, the Topolino officially qualifies as an LSV title after Fiat raised its top speed to 25 mph.

This two-seat electric car measures just over 8 feet long. It offers up to 46 miles of range and can be recharged through a standard household outlet. Pricing starts at $13,995, or $14,985 including the mandatory destination fee.

The Topolino has already proven popular in parts of Europe, attracting buyers for short urban trips and local commuting.

If your daily commute includes short trips on neighborhood streets or within a small community, the Topolino could be surprisingly useful. If your commute requires regular highway travel, however, its limitations become impossible to ignore.

Toyota revives Scion — but not as we remember it

Fiat isn’t alone in experimenting with smaller vehicles.

The revival of Toyota’s Scion brand brings another LSV for 2027, but not the kind of vehicle many might expect.

Scion originally targeted younger, budget-conscious buyers with inexpensive conventional cars. The new Scion serves a different purpose.

Rather than offering a lineup of inexpensive commuter cars, Toyota is using the revived brand to explore niche mobility solutions.

The first addition: the KEI-01 — a tiny pickup truck inspired by Japanese kei trucks. It’s just over 11 feet long, with a 660cc gasoline engine, four-wheel drive and a top speed of 25 mph.

Toyota isn’t targeting first-time buyers or commuters with this vehicle. Instead, the automaker sees potential for farmers, construction crews or commercial fleets that need utility but not necessarily a large pickup truck.

It will be assembled in Indiana beginning in the second half of 2027. Toyota has not announced a price, and retail sales aren’t guaranteed: The truck will initially be available only through a limited fleet-focused pilot program.

Could you actually drive one around Atlanta?

The idea of tiny vehicles sounds fun. The practical reality is more complicated.

Low-speed vehicles are legal to drive in Georgia and are allowed on roads with a speed limit of 35 mph or less.

That works well in certain environments. Resort towns, retirement developments, campuses and beach towns often have road networks that accommodate slow vehicles. In those places, a Topolino could perform many of the same tasks as a golf cart with more comfort and added weather protection.

The challenge arises when you leave those communities.

Most Americans use major roadways or highways where LSVs aren’t permitted. A Topolino isn’t an option for many drivers because their daily commute includes roads where the vehicle isn’t legally permitted to travel.

A Topolino might fit naturally in a community like Peachtree City, where golf cart transportation is already well established. It makes considerably less sense for someone whose daily drive involves I-285.

Is this really an affordability solution?

A vehicle priced around $15,000 seems like a great deal compared with most new cars. But if a family still needs a full-speed vehicle for work, school and travel, the Topolino could become an added expense.

Small vehicles may not solve the affordability problem for most households, but they could help certain businesses cut costs.

For most American households, an LSV simply isn’t practical as the only vehicle.

Maybe the answer isn’t another car

The Topolino and Scion KEI-01 won’t solve America’s car affordability problem. Most drivers need something that travels faster than 25 mph, and neither is a practical family vehicle. But they challenge an assumption that has shaped the American market for decades: Bigger, faster and more capable is always better.

Maybe the next breakthrough in affordable transportation won’t be a cheaper version of what we’re driving today. Maybe it will be something entirely different.

text:
Experts warn Ontario residents could lose longstanding rights to challenge environmental decisions under proposed legislation that would also change how local electricity utilities are governed. They say the bill could weaken public accountability and leave opportunities to expand smaller-scale clean energy untapped as the province prepares for growing electricity demand.

The Building Ontario Faster Act, 2026, known as Bill 140, would remove key public rights under the 1993 Environmental Bill of Rights through Schedule 8 and change utility governance under Schedule 16. The province says the reforms would reduce regulatory burdens, strengthen utility management, and support infrastructure development.

The legislation comes as Ontario’s local electricity distributors face growing investment pressures. The Electricity Distributors Association projects up to $120 billion in infrastructure investment over the next 25 years, according to a provincial advisory panel. The estimate, which the panel has not independently verified, highlights the scale of potential spending as utilities prepare for rising demand.

Mark Winfield, a professor at York University and co-chair of its Sustainable Energy Initiative, argues Bill 140 would weaken environmental accountability while missing an opportunity to expand the role of local utilities in solar generation, battery storage, and electricity demand management.

In a November 16 submission to legislators, Winfield described the proposed environmental changes as a “near de facto repeal” of the Environmental Bill of Rights.

The proposed changes would eliminate public rights to appeal certain environmental approvals, request government reviews and investigations, and pursue legal action to protect public resources. They would also reduce requirements for public notice and comment on environmental policies and regulations.

Richard Lindgren, counsel with the Canadian Environmental Law Association (CELA), said eliminating appeal rights would leave residents without comparable protections under other provincial environmental laws. Challenging decisions could instead require costly court proceedings.

CELA cited a 2025 case in which Grassy Narrows First Nation successfully challenged a water-taking permit for a proposed gold mine. The Ontario Land Tribunal revoked the permit after identifying risks of environmental harm.

Phil Pothen, counsel with Environmental Defence Canada, said in an interview with The Mix that advance public notice allows communities and journalists to scrutinize environmental decisions before they take effect. He warned that shifting notices to Ontario’s Regulatory Registry, as proposed, could remove mandatory consultation requirements for many environmental policies and regulations.

“It’s the mandate that matters,” Pothen said, adding that voluntary disclosure cannot provide the same accountability.

The proposed utility reforms raise separate questions about municipal control and electricity costs. Schedule 16 would exclude municipal officials and employees from voting positions on utility boards and introduce new governance and capital planning requirements.

The province says the changes would help distributors prepare for growing demand and future investment needs. Former Ontario environmental commissioner Dianne Saxe and Winfield have raised concerns that the reforms could pave the way for privatization of municipally-owned utilities, although Bill 140 does not itself authorize their sale.

Winfield argues the reforms also fall short of establishing a broader role for local distribution companies (LDCs) in developing distributed energy resources, including rooftop solar, batteries, and programs that shift electricity consumption away from peak periods.

A 2022 study commissioned by Ontario’s Independent Electricity System Operator (IESO) estimated [pdf] that distributed resources could provide between 1.3 and 4.3 gigawatts of achievable summer peak-demand capacity by 2032, depending on market conditions and policy support.

The study identified substantial cost-effective potential, but found that barriers to adoption could limit deployment. It recommended improving market participation, procurement opportunities, and compensation for the electricity services distributed resources provide.

The findings come as Ontario turns to electricity imports from the United States to address temporary supply constraints. The IESO has secured 600 megawatts of winter capacity from New York-based Alpha Generation, whose power production portfolio relies heavily on fossil fuels, while four reactors at the Pickering nuclear station undergo refurbishment. The six-month agreement began November 1.

Schedule 16 would allow temporary licencing exemptions for certain distributed energy projects, but Winfield argues that broader regulatory changes are needed to help local utilities develop and coordinate these resources.

He said that without a stronger role for local utilities in distributed energy development, the province risks continuing to favour large, centralized projects over alternatives that could help manage demand and reduce future infrastructure costs.

Bill 140 remains under legislative committee review, while public comments on the province’s electricity distribution reforms are open until November 30. The province was contacted for comment on November 10 and 13 but had not responded by publication time.
