title: India's plan to take on China is gathering speed but Donald Trump is not amused
description:
The move raises questions about Washington's push to shift supply chains away from China while challenging India's manufacturing incentives.
Its Section 45X advanced manufacturing production credit offered tax incentives for manufacturing eligible components such as solar modules, battery cells and critical minerals in the US.
India's manufacturing ambitions fit into that strategy.
It also argues that Indian industrial policies are creating capacity that hurts American producers in third-country markets.
India's manufacturing expansion cannot be judged simply by the number of factories or the value of goods produced.
text:
Synopsis

The Trump administration's Section 301 investigation has put India's PLI schemes and Make in India programme under scrutiny, proposing tariffs of up to 25% on Indian goods. The move raises questions about Washington's push to shift supply chains away from China while challenging India's manufacturing incentives. With trade negotiations nearing completion, the proposed tariffs could become a key bargaining tool.

India wants to become an alternative to China in global manufacturing. Washington has long encouraged companies to diversify their supply chains away from Beijing, particularly in strategic sectors such as electronics, semiconductors and solar equipment.

But when India uses subsidies and industrial incentives to build precisely those capabilities, the Trump administration sees a problem. Its latest Section 301 investigation has put India's flagship Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes and Make in India programme under the scanner, with proposed tariffs of up to 25% on Indian goods. The contradiction is difficult to miss: America wants manufacturing supply chains to move out of China, just not necessarily into India on terms that make Indian industry more competitive.

Also Read: PLI, Make in India under US scanner as Washington proposes 25% tariffs on Indian goods

The problem with India's manufacturing ambitions

The US Trade Representative's latest investigation accuses India of creating structural excess manufacturing capacity through government intervention. Its list of concerns includes Make in India, the PLI programme and the broader Self-Reliant India initiative. Washington argues that these policies channel public resources and financing into manufacturing, creating production capacity that would not emerge under normal market conditions.

The investigation also points to India's policies on steel, solar equipment, healthcare and information and communications technology. It cites India's relatively high investment-to-GDP ratio, the low share of labour in manufacturing, persistently unprofitable firms and trade surpluses with the US as evidence of structural distortions.

Live Events

You Might Also Like:

India, China and others aren't taking Trump's latest tariff salvo lying down

Also Read: Trump's new tariff tantrum for India, China can run into a legal and political minefield

The USTR has proposed tariffs of up to 25% on Indian imports, excluding certain goods and existing Section 301 duties. The proposed rate could fall to 17% if the two countries reach a reciprocal trade agreement. India, meanwhile, has rejected the central allegation, maintaining that it has no structural excess capacity in any sector.

Washington's own industrial policy is no different in principle

The irony becomes sharper when America's own industrial policy is examined. The Biden administration's CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 committed $52.7 billion towards semiconductor research, manufacturing incentives and related programmes. This included $39 billion in manufacturing incentives and $11 billion for semiconductor research and development. It also introduced a 25% investment tax credit for qualifying semiconductor manufacturing facilities.

The Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), also enacted in 2022, went further. Its Section 45X advanced manufacturing production credit offered tax incentives for manufacturing eligible components such as solar modules, battery cells and critical minerals in the US. The legislation was explicitly designed to bring clean-energy manufacturing and associated supply chains onto American soil. These were not merely incentives to encourage research. They were intended to influence where companies invested and manufactured.

You Might Also Like:

From India to Vietnam: Why some firms are rethinking the China-plus-one strategy

The Trump administration has also hardly been reluctant to use tariffs for industrial protection. In 2018, Trump imposed 25% tariffs on steel imports and 10% on aluminium under Section 232, citing national security concerns. His administration also imposed tariffs on imported solar panels and washing machines under Section 201 safeguards. The tariffs on Chinese goods under Section 301 followed soon after.

The current administration is continuing that approach. The difference, apparently, is that Washington considers its own industrial interventions necessary for national security and economic resilience while treating similar efforts by trading partners as market distortions.

There is a legitimate distinction between the American and Indian schemes in their design, scale and implementation. But the broader principle is remarkably similar: governments are using public money and trade barriers to build domestic manufacturing capabilities. Calling one industrial policy strategic and another unreasonable raises questions about the consistency of Washington's position.

The China alternative that America wants, but on its terms

This is particularly awkward given America's own China strategy. Washington has spent years trying to reduce dependence on Chinese manufacturing, especially in semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, solar equipment and critical minerals. Encouraging companies to diversify production away from China has been a central objective of its economic security agenda.

India's manufacturing ambitions fit into that strategy. PLI was designed partly to attract multinational companies looking for alternatives to Chinese production bases. Apple's expanding manufacturing presence in India, including through its contract manufacturers, is a prominent example of how this shift is unfolding.

Yet the USTR's investigation specifically flags India's growing imports and foreign investments from non-market economies, particularly China. It also argues that Indian industrial policies are creating capacity that hurts American producers in third-country markets.

This creates a peculiar situation. India is being criticised for building manufacturing capacity even as the US wants global companies to diversify their supply chains away from China. If India cannot expand production without attracting accusations of excess capacity, the alternative manufacturing destination Washington wants to promote becomes harder to develop.

There is another complication. American companies benefit from access to Indian manufacturing and a large domestic market. Higher tariffs could make Indian exports less competitive in the US, potentially weakening the very investment ecosystem that Washington's China diversification strategy should encourage.

PLI's record is mixed, but hardly evidence of a manufacturing glut

The November 13 NITI Aayog assessment offers a useful reality check against the sweeping American allegations. As of March 2026, PLI had attracted investments of ₹2.40 lakh crore, generated production worth ₹22.66 lakh crore and created 8.49 lakh jobs. The government had disbursed ₹35,354 crore in incentives against a total scheme outlay of ₹1.91 lakh crore.

The scheme had achieved 76% of its full-tenure investment target and 64% of its production target. Employment achievement, however, stood at just 28% of the full-tenure target. These numbers show that PLI has stimulated manufacturing activity but has not yet delivered evenly across all its objectives.

Large-scale electronics manufacturing has emerged as a particularly strong performer. Its ₹34,193-crore allocation has helped expand mobile manufacturing, production, exports and employment. Pharmaceuticals and telecom have also recorded encouraging outcomes.

The picture is less impressive in sectors such as advanced chemistry cell batteries and advanced electronic components, where investments are still moving through capacity creation and commissioning. Automobiles, auto components and speciality steel also need to improve on employment, exports and domestic value addition.

That last point matters. India's manufacturing expansion cannot be judged simply by the number of factories or the value of goods produced. The extent of domestic component manufacturing, technology absorption and integration into global supply chains will determine whether the country becomes a genuine manufacturing alternative to China or merely an assembly base dependent on imported inputs.

The NITI Aayog report itself stresses the need for deeper MSME participation and stronger domestic supply chains. It also notes that nearly 70% of targeted segments are on track. This is hardly a picture of an economy awash with idle manufacturing capacity. It is one of an industrial policy still being implemented, with significant gaps to close.

A trade negotiation dressed up as an industrial dispute?

The timing of the American action also deserves attention. The Section 301 investigation covers 14 economies, including China, the European Union, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan. India is therefore not being singled out in isolation. But the proposed 25% tariff makes it one of the most heavily targeted economies in the exercise.

More importantly, Washington has explicitly linked the proposed tariff to the ongoing bilateral trade negotiations. The rate could fall to 17% if India reaches an agreement that addresses American concerns. This gives the investigation an unmistakable negotiating dimension. GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava has argued that excess capacity is being used as a pretext to push countries towards trade agreements favourable to the US.

Reuters reported on November 27 that Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal had said the India-US trade deal was nearing completion, with the pathway towards finalisation taking shape. That makes the proposed tariff a significant bargaining instrument at a particularly sensitive moment.

India does have homework to do. Its high import dependence for critical components, uneven domestic value addition and limited manufacturing employment are genuine weaknesses. PLI also needs tighter performance monitoring to ensure public incentives translate into durable competitiveness rather than subsidised production.

But Washington cannot credibly argue that government support for manufacturing is inherently unreasonable while maintaining its own extensive subsidy architecture and using tariffs to shield domestic producers. India is not asking for a free pass. It is seeking the same policy space that major industrial economies have long used to build their manufacturing strengths.

The larger question is whether America genuinely wants a stronger manufacturing partner outside China or simply wants supply chains relocated without creating a serious competitor to its own industries. Trump's latest move suggests that the distinction matters considerably in Washington.

text:
As Washington seeks to protect its industries from cheaper foreign competition, African economies face a difficult balancing act: benefiting from affordable Chinese products and industrial investment without undermining their own manufacturing ambitions.

The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China, India, Japan, South Korea and the European Union, following an eight-month investigation into industrial overcapacity.

According to the Office of the US Trade Representative, Washington concluded that industrial policies and other practices in the affected economies had encouraged excess manufacturing capacity at the expense of American commercial interests.

ADVERTISEMENT

China faces proposed tariffs of up to 20% on many products, alongside existing duties dating back to Trump’s first administration. The measures remain subject to public consultation and have not yet taken effect.

The announcement comes despite recent efforts by Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to stabilise relations ahead of the January 10 expiration of their existing trade truce.

Beijing has rejected Washington’s accusations, arguing that the competitiveness of Chinese exports reflects its industrial strengths rather than unfair trading practices.

Reuters reported that Washington’s latest measures also place pressure on China’s trading partners, particularly economies where Chinese manufacturers have established production facilities.

Although no African country is directly targeted by the latest proposals, the continent’s growing commercial relationship with Beijing leaves it vulnerable to shifts in global trade flows.

ADVERTISEMENT

Sean Gallup/Getty Images

Africa’s widening trade imbalance with China

Data from China’s General Administration of Customs, compiled by the University of International Business and Economics, showed that Chinese exports to Africa increased by 24.5% to $202.98 billion between January and September 2026.

Chinese imports from Africa rose by 18.5% to $109.13 billion, bringing bilateral trade to $312.11 billion, an increase of 22.3% compared with the corresponding period of 2025.

The continent’s trade deficit with China stood at approximately $93.84 billion during the period.

ADVERTISEMENT

The trend builds on a record-breaking year in 2025, when China-Africa trade reached $348 billion and the continent recorded a $102 billion trade deficit with Beijing.

The latest figures predate Trump’s November tariff proposals, but they illustrate an existing imbalance that could become more pronounced if Chinese manufacturers encounter greater restrictions in Western markets.

China’s economic challenges are also contributing to the shift. Weak domestic consumption and a prolonged property market downturn have increased the importance of overseas markets to Chinese manufacturers.

Africa, Southeast Asia and Latin America offer alternative destinations for products facing intensifying competition and trade restrictions elsewhere.

China’s commercial influence across Africa has already surpassed that of the United States.

ADVERTISEMENT

An August 2026 report by the US Congressional Research Service showed that China’s goods trade with sub-Saharan Africa was worth four times that of the United States in 2025.

However, the composition of that trade remains heavily uneven. While Africa predominantly supplies China with minerals, crude oil and other commodities, Beijing exports machinery, vehicles, electronics and other manufactured products to the continent.

This imbalance has implications beyond trade statistics. African countries that export raw materials but import higher-value finished products capture a smaller share of the economic benefits associated with manufacturing, including skilled employment, technological development and industrial investment.

Business Insider USA

South Africa and the growing pressure on local industries

ADVERTISEMENT

South Africa, Africa’s most industrialised economy, provides an important example of the competing interests at play.

The country recorded $53.6 billion in bilateral goods trade with China in 2025, compared with $22.7 billion with the United States.

Unlike several African economies that rely predominantly on commodity exports, South Africa has an established industrial base, including automotive manufacturing, steel production and engineering.

Its automotive industry is particularly exposed to changes in international trade policy because it relies on both domestic vehicle sales and access to overseas markets.

An expansion of competitively priced Chinese vehicle imports could benefit South African consumers while placing additional pressure on established manufacturers and their local suppliers.

ADVERTISEMENT

The steel industry faces similar challenges.

September 2026 research by Rhodium Group found that China’s economic slowdown and excess steel production were weighing on global ferrous metal prices, affecting South Africa’s earnings from iron and chromium ore.

However, the consequences of China’s changing economy are not uniform across Africa.

While weaker demand for traditional commodities presents challenges for oil exporters such as Angola, the expansion of China’s clean energy industries is supporting demand for copper and cobalt from the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Chinese machinery, solar panels and other industrial equipment also offer potential benefits to African businesses by reducing the cost of production and improving access to technology.

ADVERTISEMENT

For countries struggling with electricity shortages and expensive industrial infrastructure, affordable renewable energy equipment could strengthen manufacturing competitiveness rather than weaken it.

The policy challenge is therefore not simply whether African governments should restrict Chinese imports, but whether they can distinguish between products that support domestic production and those that threaten the viability of local industries.

Sweeping import restrictions could increase costs for consumers and businesses, while unrestricted competition could make it harder for emerging manufacturers to establish themselves.

BI Africa

From consumer markets to manufacturing hubs

ADVERTISEMENT

While South Africa illustrates the competitive pressure facing established industries, Morocco offers an example of how African economies could capitalise on the restructuring of global manufacturing supply chains.

The North African kingdom has positioned itself as an automotive manufacturing hub, using its proximity to Europe, industrial infrastructure and preferential trade arrangements with major Western markets to attract international investors.

Chinese interest in Morocco’s electric vehicle and battery industries reflects a broader effort by manufacturers to diversify production beyond their home market.

For African economies, attracting manufacturers seeking alternative production locations could create employment, encourage technology transfer and increase exports of higher-value products.

However, establishing factories in Africa does not automatically guarantee unrestricted access to American or European markets.

ADVERTISEMENT

Washington’s latest trade investigations extend beyond China to economies that have attracted Chinese manufacturing investment, highlighting the growing scrutiny of international supply chains.

Rules governing the origin of products could become increasingly important, particularly where factories rely heavily on imported Chinese components or undertake limited processing before exporting finished goods.

African countries seeking to benefit from manufacturing relocation would therefore need to develop local supply chains rather than simply serve as assembly or transit points for Chinese products.

Beijing, meanwhile, has taken steps to strengthen its commercial relationship with the continent.

In May 2026, China extended its zero-tariff policy to all 53 African countries with which it maintains diplomatic relations, offering African exporters broader access to the world’s second-largest economy.

ADVERTISEMENT

The policy could support agricultural exports, including South African citrus fruits and wine, Kenyan coffee and avocados, and cocoa products from West Africa.

But removing tariffs addresses only one of the barriers limiting African exports.

Unreliable electricity, expensive financing, insufficient processing facilities and transport bottlenecks continue to constrain the ability of many African businesses to compete internationally.

The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) provides another potential opportunity. By reducing barriers to trade within the continent, it could allow manufacturers to serve larger markets, develop regional supply chains and reduce dependence on imported finished goods.

Ultimately, Africa’s economic interests extend beyond whether Washington or Beijing gains an advantage in the global trade confrontation.

ADVERTISEMENT

The more consequential question is whether African economies can use intensifying international competition to expand their own productive capacity.

Without significant investment in manufacturing, infrastructure and regional supply chains, the continent risks remaining a major destination for the very industrial output that the United States is seeking to keep out of its market.

text:
VinFast VF 8 & VF 9 All-Electric SUVs

VinFast

An electric bus partnership in the U.S. and expanded sales and service options for drivers show how VinFast is putting its electric mobility strategy into practice. The company's published climate roadmap outlines how it plans to reduce emissions as the business grows.

IRVINE, Calif. , Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- While some automakers have scaled back their North American EV ambitions, VinFast continues to view electric vehicles as essential to addressing climate change. In the U.S. and Canada, the company is focused on making EVs easier to purchase, charge and service while helping customers understand operating costs. Its broader strategy centers on building a network of vehicles, charging infrastructure and services that can support more drivers and fleets over time.



One of the latest steps came on October 6, 2026, when VinFast announced an initial agreement with NexMove at the APTA TRANSform & EXPO in Chicago to bring its electric buses to U.S. customers. NexMove, a joint venture between Transportation Management Services and Zeem Solutions, plans to bundle buses, charging, maintenance and operations in a single agreement. It intends to offer a 97% uptime service-level commitment, with certified bus deliveries expected to begin in the first quarter of 2028. The announcement followed VinFast's September 2026 franchise agreements for three U.S. dealerships in California and Pennsylvania.

Making electric mobility practical for fleets and drivers

For a transit agency, introducing electric buses requires decisions about depot charging, maintenance schedules and daily vehicle availability. NexMove's proposed service brings these elements together into one agreement. Ahead of certified deliveries, NexMove plans to place demonstration buses at Zeem's charging depots, where transit agencies and fleet operators can evaluate the vehicles firsthand. The demonstration units are intended for evaluation, with certified vehicles to follow on the planned delivery schedule.

VinFast's buses combine camera- and radar-based driver assistance, fast charging capabilities, lithium iron phosphate batteries and corrosion protection. The company reported that approximately 2,000 of its electric buses were operating in Vietnam at the time of the announcement. VinFast's experience in the market spans manufacturing, operations and maintenance, giving it firsthand knowledge of the demands fleet operators face when vehicles are in daily service.

"Bringing VinFast electric buses to the United States marks an important next step in our long-term commitment to this market," said Brian Finnerty, CEO of VinFast North America.

For households, the questions are more personal: How much will it cost to charge a vehicle each month? Where can it be serviced? What options are available at a price the buyer can afford? The franchise agreements in Redondo Beach and Tustin, California, and Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, expand access to sales and after-sales service. The company's U.S. certified pre-owned program gives buyers another option when weighing the upfront cost of an EV.

In Canada, VinFast offers a 10-year or 200,000-kilometre limited new-vehicle warranty on the VF 8, whichever comes first. Its online energy-cost calculator allows shoppers to compare estimated EV charging costs with the fueling costs of a gasoline vehicle over their expected mileage and ownership period. The comparison gives buyers a clearer picture of how an EV could fit their driving habits and household budget.

Annual EV charging costs can be 50% or more below gasoline fueling costs, depending on electricity rates, whether drivers charge at home or use public stations, driving habits, and vehicle efficiency. Coltura's Q3 2024 analysis estimated that U.S. EV drivers saved an average of 7.4 cents per mile on fuel. At 1,200 miles a month, that works out to about $90 a month, or nearly $1,100 a year if the same per-mile savings hold.

Why a long-term climate commitment matters as markets change

VinFast announced its transition to all-electric vehicle production at CES in Las Vegas in 2022. Just over two years later, it became Vietnam's best-selling vehicle brand in 2024, according to Vingroup's annual report. Its expansion into North America brings a different set of considerations, including where to build out sales and service operations, how to support charging infrastructure and how to help commercial customers integrate electric vehicles into their existing operations.

Incentives, regulations and customer demand can change while a factory upgrade or charging project is still in development. VinFast's 2040 net-zero goal provides a long-term framework for investments that take years to plan and implement. For example, the timing of an equipment replacement affects when a plant can shift more of its operations to electricity. The source of that electricity then affects the emissions associated with running the equipment. Decisions about materials and suppliers have a similar bearing on emissions across the value chain.

VinFast's emissions inventory illustrates why those decisions matter as production grows. The company calculated that its emissions exceeded 1.12 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) in its 2022 base year. In a separate scenario, VinFast estimated that emissions could exceed 20 million metric tons of CO₂e if its existing production operations in Vietnam reached their maximum registered capacity, excluding future factories. The estimate illustrates the importance of factoring energy efficiency, electricity sourcing and supplier emissions into plans for higher production.

How the 3E Mission puts the 2040 pledge into practice

VinFast signed The Climate Pledge on August 17, 2022, and announced its participation in September 2022. It was the first Vietnamese enterprise to sign the pledge, an initiative co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism. The company's stated goal is to reach net-zero emissions by 2040 across Scopes 1, 2 and 3, covering direct emissions from its operations, indirect emissions from purchased energy, and emissions across its wider value chain. Signatories commit to measuring and reporting greenhouse gas emissions regularly, reducing emissions and neutralizing the remainder.

In January 2025, VinFast's chairwoman approved the company's net-zero strategy through 2030, with a view to 2040. The strategy centers on the 3E Mission, which sets out how VinFast plans to change the equipment it uses, reduce the energy it needs and source cleaner power.

VinFast's manufacturing complex in Hai Phong offers a practical example of what these priorities translate to on the factory floor. The company reported that upgrades to lighting and compressed-air systems, changes to how production robots operate, and other efficiency measures saved approximately 2.7 million kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2024, equivalent to an estimated 1,782 metric tons of CO₂e.

The company also said it initiated a 30-megawatt-peak rooftop solar project at the site. While the efficiency measures address how much electricity the plant needs, the solar project addresses the source of the electricity.

Against its 2022 baseline, VinFast aims to reduce Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 42% and Scope 3 emissions by 29% by 2030. By 2040, the strategy calls for cutting total emissions by at least 85% and neutralizing residual emissions of up to 15% through carbon offsetting mechanisms, which could include carbon credits. As VinFast serves more drivers and fleets, its reported emissions will show how far the company has progressed toward those targets across its operations, purchased energy and value chain.

Per-Vehicle Consumer Tax Credits: US vs South Korea

Per-vehicle tax credits and purchase incentives have become important tools for governments to encourage electric vehicle (EV) adoption, reduce emissions, and shape the automotive industry's future. However, countries like the United States and South Korea are now adopting different approaches to EV financial support, reflecting changing priorities in their respective automotive markets.

US Government Ends Federal EV Tax Credits

The US government previously offered substantial financial incentives to consumers purchasing eligible electric vehicles. Under the federal Clean Vehicle Tax Credit programme, buyers of qualifying new EVs could receive tax credits of up to $7,500, while eligible used EV purchases could receive up to $4,000. These incentives helped reduce the upfront cost of electric vehicles and encouraged consumers to consider switching from conventional petrol and diesel cars.

CompareCars

However, the federal consumer clean vehicle tax credits were discontinued for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, following legislative changes. The decision marks a significant shift in America's EV policy, as consumers can no longer rely on the previous federal tax benefits when purchasing eligible electric vehicles.

South Korea Considers Support for Domestic EVs

South Korea, meanwhile, is exploring additional financial support to strengthen its domestic EV manufacturing industry amid growing competition from Chinese automakers. Chinese electric cars are gaining popularity due to competitive pricing, expanding model choices and growing international reach, putting pressure on established Korean manufacturers.

One proposal under consideration is a tax credit for electric vehicles manufactured and sold within South Korea. Unlike the earlier US consumer-focused incentive, the proposed Korean measure appears to be aimed at supporting local production, improving the competitiveness of domestic automakers and encouraging buyers towards locally manufactured EVs. However, the proposal is still under discussion and has not been finalised.

text:
QINGDAO, China, Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Report from iQingdao:

The Fourth Belt and Road Energy Ministerial Conference concluded in Qingdao this week, bringing together energy ministers and senior representatives from partner countries under a partnership that now counts 35 member states and a cooperation network of nearly 300 enterprises. The gathering marked a shift from framework-building to institutional implementation, with the host city itself serving as a working case study in rapid renewable deployment.

Under the theme "Sharing Innovation Outcomes, Advancing Energy Transition, Building a Secure Future Together," the conference featured a main forum, multiple parallel sessions covering artificial intelligence in energy and natural gas cooperation, and technical visits. The inaugural meeting of the partnership's Governing Board was held during the event, alongside the release of a joint ministerial statement emphasizing energy security and green transition. Over the past decade, cumulative installed new energy capacity in Belt and Road partner countries has quadrupled to more than 600 GW, while cumulative energy cooperation investment and engineering contracts have exceeded 3.33 trillion yuan, reflecting the partnership's steady evolution from dialogue platform to project pipeline.

Qingdao's selection as host reflected its own domestic energy trajectory. Renewable energy now accounts for over 61% of the city's installed power capacity, with new energy sources surpassing traditional generation to become the largest electricity source. Under State Grid Qingdao's planning, the city aims to expand new energy capacity from 8.33 million kilowatts to 21.5 million kilowatts by the end of the 15th Five-Year Plan period, raising its share to 72%. The city's coastal geography, port infrastructure and manufacturing base have also made it a natural testbed for offshore wind, hydrogen and smart-grid pilot projects linked to the broader partnership agenda.

"For our international audience, the message from Qingdao is clear: energy cooperation is not just about policy — it's about projects, technology, and shared green growth," the conference script stated. "From this city, the road ahead is green — and it's open to all."

The Belt and Road Energy Partnership connects energy ministers and senior representatives from partner countries to advance green energy transition, energy security, and concrete project collaboration. It currently comprises 35 member states and facilitates engagement among nearly 300 participating enterprises, with working groups focused on areas including renewable energy, hydrogen, smart grids and capacity building.

text:
I was excited when I first heard it was possible. It’s something different—a new challenge.

More than anything, we’re happy that Toyota believes in us, our team members and the quality we produce here. One of TMMI’s strengths is the passion and can-do attitude our team members bring to the plant. On a unique project like this, that is a big strength.

Our team is ready for the challenge. I’m excited to see what this could open up.

On a kei truck, the engine sits directly beneath the floor—essentially, you are sitting right on top of it. Unlike a passenger car, there is not enough space to work from inside the cabin, so before the engine is installed, operators enter through the opening and install parts around the roof.

Kei trucks have been part of work and daily life in Japan for decades, and their basic layout has been carried forward over the years. As a result, some distinctive production methods remain in use today.

That is why I felt it was important to work with the actual vehicle and pass on the hands-on techniques that come with it.

The first thing that amazed me was the size. I knew it was a small truck, but here we are used to seeing big vehicles like the Tundra. It looked like a little toy.

On the trim side, I learned every part—how it goes on and how to hold it. You know the basics, but then every little thing is just a little different. It’s all the same, but different.

For this project, we wanted to start small and keep the launch as lean as possible, using off-the-shelf equipment and manual work wherever we could.

What worried me was whether a team so experienced in high-volume production would be comfortable with that approach—and whether they could adapt to building such a small vehicle.

This is a very unique project—nothing I’ve experienced before. In some ways, it feels like taking the old Tundra we used to build here and shrinking it down. On the chassis side, for example, you have leaf springs in the rear and rear-wheel drive.

We haven’t dealt with some of those structures here in a long time, so for me it feels a little like going back in time.

The radiator was a real surprise. It was so small that we could pick it up by hand without an assist. That kind of difference in weight is harder to understand in a digital environment.

Seeing the actual vehicle helped us understand what we need to think about differently because it’s a smaller vehicle, and what we can approach the same way we do today.

For the rear window glass, you fit a weather strip around the glass and run a rope through it to help pull the glass into the body.

At Daihatsu Kyushu, they were using a special jig made by modifying an off-the-shelf tool to feed the rope through the weather strip. We’ll need the same kind of tool at TMMI, so on the last day they gave me one to bring back.

text:
On November 16, the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) signed a subscription agreement with South Asia Growth Fund IV, LP, a private equity fund newly established and managed by GEF Capital Partners, LLC (GEF), a pioneer among fund management companies that invest in enterprises to address the climate solutions in India. A signing ceremony was held in Mumbai, India, on November 26, attended by Ms. Sato Hitomi, Consul-General of Japan in Mumbai, Mr. Takeshita Masataka, Deputy Director General of Private Sector Partnership and Finance Department of JICA, Mr. Raj Pai, Co-Founder & Managing Partner of GEF Capital Partners and other distinguished guests.

JICA will invest USD 45 million in the Fund alongside private investors and development finance institutions, including the International Finance Corporation (IFC). Through this investment, JICA will contribute to India's decarbonization efforts and the growth of clean energy-related industries. The investment is also expected to contribute to the strengthening of supply chains through enhanced collaboration between Indian and Japanese companies.

India's rapidly growing economy continues to drive a significant increase in energy demand. At the same time, the country remains heavily dependent on coal-fired power generation and is the world's third-largest emitter of greenhouse gases. While the Government of India has set a goal of achieving net-zero by 2070 and has pursued a long-term transition toward a low-carbon economy, substantial private sector investment is needed to accelerate the deployment of clean energy and energy-efficiency solutions.

The Fund will invest in companies that contribute to climate change mitigation and adaptation across a range of sectors, including renewable energy, electric vehicles, energy-efficiency technologies, next-generation water management, sustainable agriculture and food systems, green buildings, and circular economy businesses. Particular emphasis will be placed on manufacturing and engineering companies operating in the clean energy and energy-efficiency sectors.

This investment is also expected to become the Private Sector Investment Finance project in line with the Government of Japan's initiative, “Partnership on Wide Energy and Resources Resilience Asia (POWERR Asia)” and the Government of Japan and World Bank Group’s framework, “Dynamic Response for Invigorating Value Chains and Energy Security (DRIVE)”. By fostering the development of clean energy supply chains and strengthening access to critical resources, the project will contribute to enhancing energy security and supply chain resilience. GEF has an established track record of fostering partnerships between fast-growing Indian manufacturing and engineering companies contributing to climate solutions and Japanese companies seeking to expand their business presence in India. Through this investment, JICA will promote Japanese companies' development of business opportunities in India while contributing to the strengthening of supply chains for clean energy-related products and promotion of decarbonization in India.

text:
Shanghai, China - Nov. 26, 2026 - Sludge is an important by-product of wastewater and sewage treatment. As cities expand their wastewater infrastructure, the volume of sludge requiring treatment and disposal also becomes an important part of urban environmental management.

For SUS ENVIRONMENT, sludge treatment is closely connected with its broader waste-to-energy and low-carbon eco-industrial park model. Instead of treating sludge as an isolated waste stream, the company integrates sludge treatment and disposal with waste-to-energy, energy recovery, and other solid waste management facilities.

What Is Sludge Treatment?

Sludge treatment generally involves reducing the volume of sludge, improving its handling characteristics, and preparing it for subsequent treatment or disposal.

Within SUS ENVIRONMENT's service system, sludge treatment and disposal form part of its integrated environmental management business. Sludge treatment facilities are incorporated into its low-carbon eco-industrial parks, alongside waste-to-energy, food waste treatment, and construction waste treatment facilities.

Its project portfolio includes dedicated sludge treatment capacity. The Nanning Shuangding Circular Economy Industrial Park has a sludge disposal capacity of 620 tonnes per day, while the Qingdao Xiaojianxi Eco-industrial Park has a municipal sludge treatment capacity of 500 tonnes per day.

Sludge Drying and Energy Recovery

One of the important connections between sludge treatment and waste-to-energy is energy utilization.

SUS ENVIRONMENT's low-carbon eco-industrial park concept is based on the circulation of materials and energy. Waste heat generated from waste-to-energy processes can be reused for sludge drying, kitchen waste fermentation, and medical waste sterilization.

This creates an energy cascade within the industrial park.

Instead of allowing waste heat from a waste-to-energy plant to remain underutilized, the heat can be directed toward other treatment processes. Sludge drying therefore becomes part of a wider energy circulation system.

The concept is particularly relevant to integrated waste management because municipal solid waste and sludge are often generated simultaneously in urban areas, but traditionally may be handled through separate treatment systems.

Qingdao Xiaojianxi: Coordinated Treatment of Waste and Sludge

The Qingdao Xiaojianxi Eco-industrial Park is one of the clearest examples of SUS ENVIRONMENT's integrated sludge treatment approach.

The park has a domestic waste treatment capacity of 2,250 tonnes per day and a municipal sludge treatment capacity of 500 tonnes per day.

The sludge treatment process includes a receiving bin, storage bin, disc dryer, dry sludge bin in the waste bunker, sludge grab bucket, and waste feed hopper. This process connects sludge drying with the waste-to-energy treatment system.

The configuration illustrates the role of sludge drying as a bridge between sludge treatment and subsequent thermal treatment.

Rather than developing sludge treatment as a completely separate chain, the project allows sludge to be prepared and incorporated into the broader waste treatment system.

Nanning Shuangding: A Different Sludge Treatment Configuration

The Nanning Shuangding Circular Economy Industrial Park demonstrates another configuration.

The project has a domestic waste treatment capacity of 2,250 tonnes per day, an organic waste treatment capacity of 600 tonnes per day, and a sludge disposal capacity of 620 tonnes per day.

The sludge treatment process includes a receiving bin, disc dryer, dry sludge temporary storage, transport truck, and waste feed hopper.

The configuration shows that sludge treatment can be designed according to the specific conditions of an eco-industrial park. Rather than applying one identical process to every project, different treatment units can be arranged according to the characteristics of the waste streams and the overall infrastructure.

Sludge Treatment as Part of a Low-Carbon Eco-Industrial Park

SUS ENVIRONMENT's low-carbon eco-industrial park model goes beyond waste disposal.

The concept is based on the circulation of materials and energy. Waste-to-energy plants form the core of the system, while other facilities can use recovered energy or participate in the recycling of materials. Waste heat can be used for sludge drying, while combustible residues from solid waste treatment can be returned to the incineration process where appropriate.

This creates a dual circulation system centered on waste-to-energy.

From a sludge treatment perspective, the model creates a direct connection between municipal solid waste treatment and sludge management. Waste-to-energy provides an energy source, while sludge treatment becomes one of the downstream applications within the industrial park.

Sludge Treatment and Equipment Manufacturing

SUS ENVIRONMENT's sludge treatment capabilities are supported by its broader equipment manufacturing and engineering capabilities.

Its Wuxi Fangling equipment manufacturing base covers sewage treatment, sludge treatment, flue gas treatment systems, and moving incinerators.

This combination allows sludge treatment equipment to be considered alongside the other systems required for an integrated environmental project.

SUS ENVIRONMENT also provides investment, construction, and operation services for waste-to-energy projects. The company has invested in, constructed, and operated projects with a combined domestic waste processing capacity approaching 120,000 tonnes per day.

For large-scale eco-industrial parks, the ability to combine equipment, engineering, project management, and operations can be important when multiple treatment facilities need to operate as one integrated system.

Connecting Sludge Treatment with Sewage Treatment

Sludge treatment and sewage treatment are naturally connected because sludge is one of the important by-products generated through wastewater treatment.

This connection is reflected in SUS ENVIRONMENT's broader environmental technology and equipment portfolio. Its Wuxi Fangling manufacturing base covers both sewage treatment and sludge treatment systems.

Within a low-carbon eco-industrial park, this relationship can extend further.

Sewage treatment manages wastewater, sludge treatment handles the resulting sludge stream, and waste-to-energy can provide an energy source for sludge drying. When these systems are planned together, the treatment chain can extend from wastewater management to sludge treatment and ultimately to energy recovery.

Sludge Treatment within Integrated Solid Waste Management

SUS ENVIRONMENT's integrated solid waste management services combine waste-to-energy with sludge treatment, district heating, environmental remediation, and resource recovery within low-carbon eco-industrial parks. As of December 2025, the company had invested in and developed more than 90 low-carbon eco-industrial parks worldwide, with total domestic waste treatment capacity approaching 120,000 tonnes per day. Its technologies and equipment had been applied in more than 300 waste-to-energy facilities globally.

The company's project portfolio provides examples of this integrated approach.

Xi'an Gaoling has a waste treatment capacity of 2,250 tonnes per day and integrates waste treatment, renewable energy generation, district heating, sludge treatment, and environmental control technologies.

Nanning Shuangding combines domestic waste, organic waste, and sludge treatment within the same circular economy industrial park.

Qingdao Xiaojianxi combines domestic waste treatment with municipal sludge treatment.

Together, these projects demonstrate how sludge treatment can be incorporated into different types of integrated environmental infrastructure.

From Sludge Disposal to Resource and Energy Circulation

The development of modern sludge treatment requires more than simply finding a final disposal route. Treatment systems increasingly need to consider volume reduction, energy consumption, environmental control, and connections with other waste streams.

SUS ENVIRONMENT's approach places these considerations within its low-carbon eco-industrial park model.

Waste-to-energy provides a source of recovered heat. Sludge drying provides a pathway for using that heat. Other waste streams can be treated through dedicated facilities, while the entire park can operate as a coordinated environmental management system.

This approach also reflects SUS ENVIRONMENT's evolution from a waste-to-energy technology and equipment provider into an integrated environmental governance service provider. Its business combines waste-to-energy with environmental investment, key equipment, EPC, operation, and environmental remediation.

A Systematic Approach to Sludge Treatment

Sludge treatment is becoming an increasingly important component of modern urban environmental infrastructure. For projects that combine wastewater, municipal solid waste, organic waste, and energy recovery, the treatment of sludge can be planned as part of the overall system rather than as an isolated process.

SUS ENVIRONMENT's project experience demonstrates several approaches to this integration. Qingdao Xiaojianxi connects municipal sludge treatment with waste-to-energy, while Nanning Shuangding incorporates dedicated sludge disposal capacity within a larger circular economy industrial park. Xi'an Gaoling further demonstrates the integration of sludge treatment with waste treatment, renewable energy generation, and district heating.

Through these projects and its broader equipment, engineering, investment, and operation capabilities, SUS ENVIRONMENT positions sludge treatment within a wider integrated environmental management framework.

For cities seeking to develop more coordinated waste and environmental infrastructure, this model connects sludge treatment with waste-to-energy, energy recovery, sewage treatment, and resource circulation—supporting the development of low-carbon eco-industrial parks and more integrated urban waste management systems.

About us

SUS ENVIRONMENT is the world's largest provider of waste incineration equipment and technology, and one of the world's top three waste-to-energy investors and operators. As of December 2025, it operates 11 global management centers and has invested in and constructed over 90 waste-to-energy plants, with a daily municipal solid waste processing capacity of nearly 120,000 tonnes and annual green power generation of approximately 20,000 GWh. Its equipment and technologies are deployed in over 300 waste-to-energy plants worldwide, covering a daily capacity of more than 300,000 tonnes of municipal solid waste. SUS ENVIRONMENT is committed to advancing solid waste management and low-carbon clean energy solutions to create a cleaner and more sustainable living environment.

title: Pakistan's Roadmap to Green Mobility - Minute Mirror
description:
Pakistan’s transition towards sustainable transportation has become an economic, environmental and industrial necessity rather than simply a technological choice.
Its scope covers two-wheelers, three-wheelers, passenger vehicles and commercial transportation, alongside charging infrastructure, battery manufacturing, supply-chain development and recycling.
These projections highlight the relationship between electric mobility and Pakistan’s broader economic stability.

The 2025–2030 framework builds upon these earlier initiatives by presenting a broader vision of transportation electrification and domestic industrial development.
text:
Pakistan’s transition towards sustainable transportation has become an economic, environmental and industrial necessity rather than simply a technological choice. With rising petroleum imports, deteriorating urban air quality and increasing pressure on foreign exchange reserves, the country needs a comprehensive strategy to modernise its transport sector. The New Energy Vehicle (NEV) Policy 2025–2030, introduced by the Ministry of Industries and Production, offers an opportunity to accelerate this transformation through electric mobility, indigenous manufacturing, technological innovation and investment in supporting infrastructure. Its success, however, will depend on the government’s ability to translate ambitious policy objectives into financially viable and measurable outcomes.

The policy sets an ambitious target of achieving 30 per cent of new vehicle sales through new energy vehicles by 2030, increasing to 50 per cent by 2040, with the longer-term objective of transitioning towards zero-emission road transport by 2060. Its scope covers two-wheelers, three-wheelers, passenger vehicles and commercial transportation, alongside charging infrastructure, battery manufacturing, supply-chain development and recycling. This broader approach recognises that electric mobility requires an integrated industrial ecosystem rather than merely replacing conventional vehicles with imported electric alternatives.

According to the Pakistan Economic Survey 2023–24, the country consumed approximately 16.7 million tons of oil, with nearly 77 per cent attributed to the transport sector. Growing economic activity, urbanisation and a young population are likely to increase transportation demand further. Reducing dependence on imported petroleum could therefore provide substantial economic benefits. The NEV Policy estimates potential savings of approximately USD 0.95 billion in oil imports by 2030, equivalent to 1.823 million tons of oil equivalent. It also projects a reduction of 4.5 million tons in carbon emissions and annual healthcare-related savings of approximately USD 405 million.

These projections highlight the relationship between electric mobility and Pakistan’s broader economic stability. Lower petroleum imports could improve the balance of payments, reduce pressure on foreign exchange reserves and strengthen energy security. Nevertheless, replacing petroleum imports with imported batteries, semiconductors, electric motors and other critical components could create new external dependencies. Developing domestic manufacturing capabilities and technology partnerships must therefore remain central to the policy’s implementation.

Pakistan’s electric mobility journey is not entirely new. The National Electric Vehicle Policy introduced by the Ministry of Climate Change in 2019 sought to promote electric vehicle adoption, reduce fuel imports, encourage investment and create export opportunities. Subsequently, the draft Electric Vehicles and New Technology Policy 2020 emphasised industrial development, employment generation and environmental sustainability. The 2025–2030 framework builds upon these earlier initiatives by presenting a broader vision of transportation electrification and domestic industrial development.

An important strength of the new policy is its recognition of infrastructure as a prerequisite for market expansion. Charging stations, battery-swapping facilities and reliable electricity connections are essential to consumer confidence. Initial investment should prioritise major urban centres, industrial zones, motorways and national highways before extending coverage to smaller cities and rural communities. Public-private partnerships can help mobilise investment, provided that commercial regulations, land-use arrangements and electricity tariffs remain transparent and predictable.

Battery technology represents another strategic dimension. Pakistan must avoid becoming excessively dependent on imported battery systems and a single technological pathway. Investment in lithium-ion battery manufacturing, research into sodium-ion and solid-state technologies, and the development of electric motors and power electronics could strengthen domestic industrial capacity. Universities, research institutions and private manufacturers should collaborate to develop technical expertise, promote technology transfer and establish commercially viable local production.

Fiscal incentives, reduced import duties, tax concessions and targeted subsidies can accelerate initial adoption. However, these measures must be based on realistic economic assessments rather than open-ended government expenditure. Incentives should encourage genuine localisation, investment in research and development, employment generation and technology transfer. A transparent regulatory framework would also provide investors with the confidence required to commit long-term capital to the emerging industry.

Environmental sustainability must remain a fundamental consideration throughout this transition. Electric vehicles produce no tailpipe emissions, but their overall environmental footprint depends on electricity generation, battery manufacturing and end-of-life disposal. Pakistan should therefore integrate the NEV Policy with its renewable energy and electricity-sector strategies. Solar and wind energy can support charging infrastructure, while smart charging arrangements can help manage electricity demand and avoid unnecessary pressure on the national grid. This integration is particularly important for ensuring that electrification delivers genuine reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.

The policy also offers opportunities for employment generation and skills development. Domestic vehicle assembly, battery production, charging infrastructure, software development, maintenance and recycling can create new employment avenues for technical graduates and skilled workers. However, affordability remains a major challenge. Higher initial vehicle prices, limited charging facilities and uncertainty regarding battery replacement costs could discourage middle- and lower-income consumers. Accessible financing, affordable vehicle models and public awareness programmes will be necessary to broaden participation.

Pakistan must also establish a comprehensive framework for used battery management. Electric vehicle batteries contain valuable recoverable materials, but improper disposal can create environmental hazards and fire risks. Regulations should cover battery collection, transportation, second-life applications, recycling and safe disposal. Manufacturers and importers should share responsibility through extended producer responsibility arrangements. Domestic recycling facilities could simultaneously reduce environmental risks and create opportunities for recovering valuable industrial materials.

Effective implementation requires institutional coordination, reliable information and continuous performance assessment. Federal and provincial governments, manufacturers, energy suppliers, financial institutions, regulators and consumers must work within clearly defined responsibilities. A centralised NEV database should monitor vehicle registrations, charging facilities, electricity consumption, investment, manufacturing capacity and market demand. Performance indicators should also measure employment generation, battery recycling, petroleum import savings and actual emissions reductions.

Artificial intelligence and machine learning can further strengthen policy planning. Predictive models, including neural networks and Long Short-Term Memory networks, can analyse vehicle sales, income levels, fuel prices, electricity tariffs and consumer preferences to forecast adoption patterns. Such systems could help identify infrastructure requirements, regional demand and potential supply-chain bottlenecks. However, technological forecasting must be supported by accurate data and effective institutional decision-making.

A phased implementation strategy would make the transition more manageable. The initial phase should establish charging infrastructure, technical standards, public awareness and targeted financial incentives. The second should prioritise domestic manufacturing, technology transfer, industrial investment and battery recycling. The final phase should focus on affordable mass adoption, competitive local production, research and development and wider infrastructure coverage.

Pakistan’s NEV Policy also supports several United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 7 on clean energy, SDG 9 on industry and innovation, SDG 11 on sustainable cities and SDG 13 on climate action. However, achieving these objectives will require more than policy declarations and ambitious numerical targets. Fiscal discipline, institutional accountability, technological preparedness and sustained private-sector participation must underpin the entire process.

Ultimately, electric mobility should be viewed as an instrument of economic transformation, not simply a change in vehicle technology. Pakistan has an opportunity to reduce its petroleum dependence, strengthen industrial competitiveness, generate skilled employment and improve environmental conditions. The real test of the NEV Policy will be whether its vision translates into affordable vehicles, reliable infrastructure, indigenous technological capacity and measurable economic and environmental gains.

text:
Maintaining production in Italy is a challenge due to increasing costs and competition, the European head of carmaker Stellantis said on Thursday, calling for greater cooperation between industry, government and local authorities.

Emanuele Cappellano said Stellantis was investing over €5 billion ($5.5 billion) in research and development in Italy over the next five years, with 14 models being produced and another nine to be added by 2030, while spending more than €7 billion annually in purchases from local suppliers.

He said such figures confirmed the group's commitment to the country, though it was being made "more and more complex" by a difficult and constantly evolving context. Fiat and Alfa Romeo are among the Stellantis brands.

Cappellano cited rising production costs linked to current global conflicts, an increasingly competitive market due to rising vehicle imports and the costs associated with the electric transition. "Under these conditions, ensuring the continuity of production that Italy needs becomes a daily challenge," he was quoted as saying during a conference in Verona by a company spokesman.

Stellantis is Italy's sole major automaker and its production in the country remains well below historical levels despite a slight recovery this year from the sharp downturn of 2025, when output fell 20 per cent to about 380,000 vehicles, its lowest level in decades and roughly half the volume produced in 2023. To support local production, Cappellano urged Italy to focus on curbing energy costs and cutting red tape, while adding Stellantis was holding talks with the European Union authorities on "pragmatic solutions" that address both environmental and industrial goals.

He said discussions on European local-content requirements and CO2 rules had shown promising progress in recent weeks and could result in new regulations by next spring.

title: A sweeping permitting reform bill is headed to the House. Critics want to stop it
description:
The Senate passed a bipartisan permitting reform bill that supporters say will pave the way for much needed infrastructure projects.
But critics argue it will do so at the expense of the environment, tribes and public lands.
They want the House to either fix or reject the bill before the year ends, as NPR's Rachel Treisman reports.
But critics say it would weaken bedrock environmental and historic preservation laws, including by limiting input from tribes and the public.
The bill passed last week with only one amendment by a vote of 62 to 33.
text:
JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:

With just weeks left in its term, Congress could reshape the country's physical landscape for generations. The Senate passed a bipartisan permitting reform bill that supporters say will pave the way for much needed infrastructure projects. But critics argue it will do so at the expense of the environment, tribes and public lands. They want the House to either fix or reject the bill before the year ends, as NPR's Rachel Treisman reports.

RACHEL TREISMAN, BYLINE: Last week, the Senate passed a bill that aims to speed up the approval process for federal infrastructure and energy projects, from wind turbines to data centers. It's called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, and it's nearly 500 pages long.

XAN FISHMAN: This isn't just, like, a mushy, middle, moderate, do-nothing bill. Like, it's actually a big-deal bill.

TREISMAN: Xan Fishman leads the energy program at the Bipartisan Policy Center.

FISHMAN: At its heart, it's about trying to take a permitting system which has just grown out of proportion and make sure that it's protecting the environment but getting to a yes or no answer in a reasonable amount of time.

TREISMAN: Supporters of the bill say it will improve America's aging grid while creating jobs and lowering electricity bills. But critics say it would weaken bedrock environmental and historic preservation laws, including by limiting input from tribes and the public.

WESLEY FURLONG: From our perspective, there are no pros. There are only cons.

TREISMAN: Wesley Furlong is a senior staff attorney with the Native American Rights Fund. He says tribes were not consulted about the bill, even though it threatens their lands and sovereignty.

FURLONG: It will fundamentally change the federal government's relationship with Indian tribes in a really negative way.

TREISMAN: The bill was introduced in the Senate at the end of September. Critics say lawmakers didn't give it the time or debate it deserved in the lead-up to the midterms.

FURLONG: And then they come back, and the first thing that they do the Monday after the election is vote on this bill.

TREISMAN: The Senate first voted to bypass the committee markup process, skipping hearings and rewrites. The bill passed last week with only one amendment by a vote of 62 to 33. It now heads to the House. President Trump has said he will sign it. It's also backed by an unusual alliance of energy companies, big tech, some Democrats and a mix of labor and environmental groups.

SARAH GONZALEZ-ROTHI: People see a very slim chance to address a very urgent issue, and they think they've found the way to do it.

TREISMAN: Sarah Gonzalez-Rothi served as the senior director for water at the White House Council on Environmental Quality under President Biden. She opposes the bill, as do hundreds of climate, tribal, public health, historic preservation and civil rights groups.

GONZALEZ-ROTHI: I think the way they've come up with doing it is looking at rose-colored glasses at text that, if they are wrong, has such severe consequences that it could actually make things worse.

TREISMAN: For example, the bill would make data centers cover their own energy costs, but critics say it could make it easier to build data centers on public lands. And as Furlong says it has provisions that would make it harder to challenge or change permits once they're issued.

FURLONG: Courts can't really stop these projects, and future administrations can't stop them, and so as soon as they are permitted, we are stuck with them forever.

TREISMAN: The House could vote in the days after Thanksgiving. Some key Democrats have already said they oppose the bill, but it's not clear if they have the support or time to revise it before Congress adjourns on January 3.

Rachel Treisman, NPR News. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

text:
MARKHAM, Ontario--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- While some automakers have scaled back their North American EV ambitions, VinFast continues to view electric vehicles as essential to addressing climate change. In the U.S. and Canada, the company is focused on making EVs easier to purchase, charge and service while helping customers understand operating costs. Its broader strategy centers on building a network of vehicles, charging infrastructure and services that can support more drivers and fleets over time.
One of the latest steps came on October 6, 2026, when VinFast announced an initial agreement with NexMove at the APTA TRANSform & EXPO in Chicago to bring its electric buses to U.S. customers. NexMove, a joint venture between Transportation Management Services and Zeem Solutions, plans to bundle buses, charging, maintenance and operations in a single agreement. It intends to offer a 97% uptime service-level commitment, with certified bus deliveries expected to begin in the first quarter of 2028. The announcement followed VinFast’s September 2026 franchise agreements for three U.S. dealerships in California and Pennsylvania.
Making electric mobility practical for fleets and drivers
For a transit agency, introducing electric buses requires decisions about depot charging, maintenance schedules and daily vehicle availability. NexMove’s proposed service brings these elements together into one agreement. Ahead of certified deliveries, NexMove plans to place demonstration buses at Zeem’s charging depots, where transit agencies and fleet operators can evaluate the vehicles firsthand. The demonstration units are intended for evaluation, with certified vehicles to follow on the planned delivery schedule.
VinFast’s buses combine camera- and radar-based driver assistance, fast charging capabilities, lithium iron phosphate batteries and corrosion protection. The company reported that approximately 2,000 of its electric buses were operating in Vietnam at the time of the announcement. VinFast’s experience in the market spans manufacturing, operations and maintenance, giving it firsthand knowledge of the demands fleet operators face when vehicles are in daily service.
“Bringing VinFast electric buses to the United States marks an important next step in our long-term commitment to this market,” said Brian Finnerty, CEO of VinFast North America.
For households, the questions are more personal: How much will it cost to charge a vehicle each month? Where can it be serviced? What options are available at a price the buyer can afford? The franchise agreements in Redondo Beach and Tustin, California, and Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, expand access to sales and after-sales service. The company’s U.S. certified pre-owned program gives buyers another option when weighing the upfront cost of an EV.
In Canada, VinFast offers a 10-year or 200,000-kilometre limited new-vehicle warranty on the VF 8, whichever comes first. Its online energy-cost calculator allows shoppers to compare estimated EV charging costs with the fueling costs of a gasoline vehicle over their expected mileage and ownership period. The comparison gives buyers a clearer picture of how an EV could fit their driving habits and household budget.
Annual EV charging costs can be 50% or more below gasoline fueling costs, depending on electricity rates, whether drivers charge at home or use public stations, driving habits, and vehicle efficiency. Coltura’s Q3 2024 analysis estimated that U.S. EV drivers saved an average of 7.4 cents per mile on fuel. At 1,200 miles a month, that works out to about $90 a month, or nearly $1,100 a year if the same per-mile savings hold.
Why a long-term climate commitment matters as markets change
VinFast announced its transition to all-electric vehicle production at CES in Las Vegas in 2022. Just over two years later, it became Vietnam’s best-selling vehicle brand in 2024, according to Vingroup’s annual report. Its expansion into North America brings a different set of considerations, including where to build out sales and service operations, how to support charging infrastructure and how to help commercial customers integrate electric vehicles into their existing operations.
Incentives, regulations and customer demand can change while a factory upgrade or charging project is still in development. VinFast’s 2040 net-zero goal provides a long-term framework for investments that take years to plan and implement. For example, the timing of an equipment replacement affects when a plant can shift more of its operations to electricity. The source of that electricity then affects the emissions associated with running the equipment. Decisions about materials and suppliers have a similar bearing on emissions across the value chain.
VinFast’s emissions inventory illustrates why those decisions matter as production grows. The company calculated that its emissions exceeded 1.12 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) in its 2022 base year. In a separate scenario, VinFast estimated that emissions could exceed 20 million metric tons of CO₂e if its existing production operations in Vietnam reached their maximum registered capacity, excluding future factories. The estimate illustrates the importance of factoring energy efficiency, electricity sourcing and supplier emissions into plans for higher production.
How the 3E Mission puts the 2040 pledge into practice
VinFast signed The Climate Pledge on August 17, 2022, and announced its participation in September 2022. It was the first Vietnamese enterprise to sign the pledge, an initiative co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism. The company’s stated goal is to reach net-zero emissions by 2040 across Scopes 1, 2 and 3, covering direct emissions from its operations, indirect emissions from purchased energy, and emissions across its wider value chain. Signatories commit to measuring and reporting greenhouse gas emissions regularly, reducing emissions and neutralizing the remainder.
In January 2025, VinFast’s chairwoman approved the company’s net-zero strategy through 2030, with a view to 2040. The strategy centers on the 3E Mission, which sets out how VinFast plans to change the equipment it uses, reduce the energy it needs and source cleaner power.
Electrification. VinFast plans to electrify equipment at company-owned production and business sites by 2030. The roadmap also includes expanding access to charging and developing battery energy storage.
Energy Saving. VinFast plans to introduce smart energy monitoring at manufacturing facilities by 2028. Monitoring production lines and major electricity-consuming equipment gives factory teams more detailed information on where energy is used and where operations can be made more efficient.
Energy Greening. VinFast aims to use 100% renewable electricity at all its plants by 2040. Its roadmap includes rooftop solar, battery storage to support renewable power use, and work with suppliers on lower-emission materials.
VinFast’s manufacturing complex in Hai Phong offers a practical example of what these priorities translate to on the factory floor. The company reported that upgrades to lighting and compressed-air systems, changes to how production robots operate, and other efficiency measures saved approximately 2.7 million kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2024, equivalent to an estimated 1,782 metric tons of CO₂e.
The company also said it initiated a 30-megawatt-peak rooftop solar project at the site. While the efficiency measures address how much electricity the plant needs, the solar project addresses the source of the electricity.
Against its 2022 baseline, VinFast aims to reduce Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 42% and Scope 3 emissions by 29% by 2030. By 2040, the strategy calls for cutting total emissions by at least 85% and neutralizing residual emissions of up to 15% through carbon offsetting mechanisms, which could include carbon credits. As VinFast serves more drivers and fleets, its reported emissions will show how far the company has progressed toward those targets across its operations, purchased energy and value chain.
