title: Bridging the Grid: Solar, Storage, and Natural Gas Solutions - Mexico Business News
description:
Q: What specific shifts in industrial demand and grid reliability in Mexico motivated RER Energy’s expansion into multitechnology solutions that incorporate natural gas?
Furthermore, when a facility utilizes natural gas alongside industrial thermal processes—such as steam or chilled water—we can implement cogeneration systems.
We then evaluate natural gas to cover baseload or high-density power needs where there is no more available from the grid.
We are seeing tremendous demand for maximizing on-site solar capacity, paired with growing adoption of battery energy storage systems.
Battery storage protects against those costly disruptions, while natural gas complements the system in critical high-demand corridors.
text:
Q: Could you briefly introduce RER Energy Group, explain your history in the energy sector, and describe the company’s core focus in Mexico and the United States?

A: RER Energy Group specializes in providing renewable energy solutions for the commercial and industrial sectors across Mexico and the United States, with a primary focus on on-site self-consumption and energy storage. We have been operating in Mexico for 11 years, marking our 11th anniversary this September, and we have 76 years of history in the United States.

A defining characteristic of our company is continuous transformation in response to market needs and emerging opportunities. We originally operated as a utility in Pennsylvania, and when the renewable energy boom began in the United States between 2005 and 2008, we shifted our business model to focus on clean energy. In Mexico, we were among the pioneers in medium-scale commercial and industrial distributed generation.

Alongside guiding major corporations through their energy transition, we have been actively involved in the regulatory landscape through industry associations and ongoing dialogue with government authorities to help shape a viable framework for self-consumption.

Q: What specific shifts in industrial demand and grid reliability in Mexico motivated RER Energy’s expansion into multitechnology solutions that incorporate natural gas?

Mexico is experiencing a significant power shortage, particularly in the northern region, where industrial demand is surging and natural gas is most abundant.

Companies nearshoring to Mexico frequently find that grid electricity is unavailable. Our answer starts with solar and battery storage, which are the lowest-cost energy available and the fastest to install. When a plant runs around the clock and its roof or land cannot host enough solar and storage to cover that demand due to the generation curve or physical space, natural gas complements the system, ideally through cogeneration, so the plant can keep operating while government grid infrastructure catches up.

For any energy technology to be viable in our industry, several factors must align. In 2015, when we first began operating in Mexico, solar panel costs were significantly higher and return on investment took six, seven, or even eight years, meaning companies adopted solar primarily for environmental rather than financial reasons.

Today, solar projects routinely achieve payback periods of under two years, while battery storage achieves payback in three to four years purely from energy savings—and even faster when additional applications are stacked. Economics is always the first driver. The second factor is a clear regulatory ecosystem that gives clients long-term certainty, which has evolved favorably over the past year to support self-consumption. The third is overcoming market hesitation, as industrial leaders move past traditional habits after seeing proven results from their peers. The fourth—and arguably most urgent—factor is operational necessity.

Q: How do you explain to plant managers and CFOs that on-site natural gas and hybrid microgrids act as a bridge rather than a contradiction to their long-term ESG commitments?

A: We asked ourselves that exact same question internally before offering gas-based solutions, because our core philosophy is centered on renewable energy and helping companies reduce their carbon footprint toward net-zero goals.

Our approach is to maintain alignment with those sustainability goals by always prioritizing a hybrid energy mix. Whenever we integrate natural gas, we seek to combine it with renewable components such as solar photovoltaics and battery storage rather than relying solely on fossil fuels.

Furthermore, when a facility utilizes natural gas alongside industrial thermal processes—such as steam or chilled water—we can implement cogeneration systems. By capturing and reusing those existing thermal resources to generate electricity, companies maximize energy efficiency, reduce their overall carbon intensity, and stay competitive without halting operations.

Q: How do financing and contracting models such as Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) and Energy-as-a-Service (EaaS) enable industrial facilities to deploy custom hybrid solutions without heavy upfront capital expenditure?

A: We maintain a highly flexible approach because we serve very different client profiles. On the one hand, we work with cash-rich companies that prefer to invest their own capital directly to maximize long-term returns. For those clients, our focus is on delivering creative, safe, and high-quality technical engineering adapted to their specific site conditions and operational infrastructure.

On the other hand, many companies prefer not to tie up capital in energy assets so they can allocate those resources toward core business growth, such as purchasing new production machinery or opening additional plants.

For these clients, we structure zero-upfront-cost contracts—including PPAs, Energy-as-a-Service agreements with shared savings that remain off the balance sheet, and leasing schemes—typically spanning 7, 10, 15, or up to 20 years. In all of these models, we supply more reliable electricity at a lower cost than CFE or alternative suppliers, generating immediate net savings from day one. We have also seen the Mexican market mature substantially in this regard.

Q: Which industrial sectors are feeling interconnection bottlenecks most acutely, and how are they using on-site generation to keep new production lines on schedule?

A: In short, virtually every sector is affected, though the severity depends heavily on geographic location. Mexico’s core challenge lies in electricity transmission and distribution. While initiatives such as Plan México and financial vehicles like Fibra E are moving in the right direction to fund grid expansion, building thousands of kilometers of transmission lines and new substations takes years—especially given global lead times for electrical equipment.

If we look at who is experiencing the greatest impact across the board, it is industrial park developers. It is deeply frustrating for developers to have fully urbanized land or build-to-suit facilities ready for incoming manufacturers, only to lose or delay tenants due to a lack of power capacity.

As a result, industrial park developers have become highly sophisticated in energy management—understanding kilowatts, kVA requirements, natural gas integration, and complex multi-party financing structures involving the park developer, generator, financier, and end user. Regulatory tools introduced over the past year, such as the self-consumption framework allowing on-site generation up to 20MW, have become vital mechanisms for unlocking capacity and keeping projects on schedule.

Q: As multinational manufacturers accelerate nearshoring plans in Mexico, what are the most common blind spots engineering teams encounter when projecting electrical loads?

A: The biggest challenge for incoming engineering teams is accurately forecasting their operational ramp-up. When a foreign manufacturer enters a region where grid capacity will not be available for five to seven years, they typically plan a phased expansion—for instance, installing 2MW in the first year, scaling to 5MW, and eventually reaching 10MW. While they may model operations on a sister plant in another country like Vietnam, they cannot always predict with 100% certainty how market demand will evolve in North America.

That lack of load predictability directly affects infrastructure sizing and permitting. When applying for generation permits, companies must commit to specific capacity thresholds, though recent regulatory updates have introduced helpful flexibility. Beyond permitting, engineering teams must account for the total cost of ownership from the initial feasibility stage. Accurate load projections are critical for sizing natural gas volumes, negotiating molecule supply and price hedging, allocating rooftop or ground space for solar arrays, and properly dimensioning battery storage banks.

Q: What criteria does RER evaluate to determine whether a client is best served by pipeline natural gas, virtual pipeline delivery (LNG/CNG), or a standalone solar-plus-storage solution?

A: Everything starts with the client’s operational profile and commercial location strategy. Once we understand their consumption curve and target regions, we map out the expected cost per kilowatt-hour and kilowatt of capacity based on local solar irradiation and existing infrastructure.

Our first priority is always to deploy as much solar and battery storage as technically and spatially feasible. Solar and storage represent the lowest-cost energy and the fastest solution to install, particularly because Mexico benefits from exceptional solar irradiation per square meter across almost the entire country.

We then evaluate natural gas to cover baseload or high-density power needs where there is no more available from the grid. If pipeline gas is not available directly at the site, extending pipeline infrastructure or transporting LNG or CNG via virtual pipelines adds logistical costs that increase the unit cost of energy. We carefully model those variables to ensure the resulting tariff remains below utility grid rates; if transportation costs push the price above grid power, the project loses bankability, as the client would face the risk of grid electricity becoming cheaper in the future.

Q: What is RER Energy Group’s commercial roadmap for expanding hybrid generation and storage in the near term, and what is your growth outlook toward 2030?

A: Self-consumption is undeniably the central pillar of our commercial roadmap. We are seeing tremendous demand for maximizing on-site solar capacity, paired with growing adoption of battery energy storage systems. Beyond standard economic applications—such as time-of-use tariff arbitrage and peak shaving—batteries play a critical role in ensuring power quality and operational continuity. In several industrial regions, seasonal grid instability causes frequent voltage flickers and brief outages.

For sensitive sectors like food and beverage manufacturing, where high-temperature ovens and continuous production lines operate near 100% capacity, even a momentary flicker can shut down equipment, forcing plants to discard ruined products, sanitize machinery, and lose valuable production hours. Battery storage protects against those costly disruptions, while natural gas complements the system in critical high-demand corridors.

Looking ahead, this year is already shaping up to be a historic milestone for RER Energy Group, and we have mapped out an accelerated growth trajectory through 2030 and 2031. With competitive technology economics, a supportive regulatory framework for self-consumption, and an urgent industrial need for reliable power, all the fundamentals are aligned for sustained expansion.

Q: How are emerging sectors like artificial intelligence and data centers reshaping energy demand in Mexico, and how is RER supporting these facilities?

A: Artificial intelligence is driving an unprecedented surge in global energy and water demand through the rapid expansion of data centers, and traditional power supply is simply not growing at the same pace. That widening gap between supply and demand will push the industry toward increasingly creative solutions and rapid technological evolution over the next two to three years. Microgrids are one of those innovations that will help data centers reach their goals.

For us, staying competitive means continuously updating our capabilities and working closely with regulators so that policy frameworks keep pace with new technologies. Across our portfolio, we have more than 250MW installed, and we are actively supporting data center developers in evaluating optimal locations from an electrical standpoint alongside water and telecommunications requirements. Specifically, we help them to find the right location with grid-connected energy and develop on-site self-consumption generation, and engineer ultra-reliable power continuity systems.

Unlike conventional facilities, data centers cannot tolerate even a fraction of a voltage flicker, making power protection and operational continuity critical areas where our solutions add significant value.

SHERIDAN, Wyo., Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The global lithium-ion battery market is valued at USD 209 billion in 2026 and is projected to reach USD 368.3 billion by 2031, an increase of roughly 76% over the forecast period (2026–2031), according to a new study by Wissen Research.

Three shifts explain the demand. The first is cheaper chemistry. The second is heavier vehicles: global electric truck sales exceeded 400,000 units in 2025, doubling year on year, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). The third is the grid: the IEA reports that 108 GW of battery storage capacity was added globally in 2025, roughly 40% more than in 2024. Together with passenger cars, where about one in four cars sold worldwide in 2025 was electric, they pushed global electric vehicle battery demand to around 1.2 TWh in 2025, up nearly 30% from the year before.

The constraint is cost and concentration, not demand. China accounted for more than 80% of global battery cell production in 2025, and battery pack prices there were 30% lower than in North America and 35% lower than in Europe. That gap is driving a wave of localization, and it is shaping the strategies of the industry's leading manufacturers.

LFP Moves from Alternative to Default

The most important change inside the battery is chemistry. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries accounted for more than 55% of global electric vehicle battery deployment in 2025, up from nearly half in 2024, and for more than 90% of stationary storage installations, according to the IEA. The reason is cost. LFP battery packs were on average more than 40% cheaper per kilowatt-hour than nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) packs in 2025, and LFP prices fell by more than 15% in 2025 while NMC prices fell by less than 5%. LFP also avoids nickel and cobalt in the cathode, which removes exposure to those price swings and adds thermal stability.

NMC is not going away; it remains relevant where higher energy density matters. Newer chemistries are advancing alongside. Sodium-ion batteries are moving closer to production as a lower-cost option that performs better in cold climates, and solid-state batteries and silicon anodes are in development to address charging performance, material availability, and safety. The report notes that competitive differentiation increasingly depends on cost per kilowatt-hour, cycle life, safety, charging speed, and manufacturing yield.

Trucks and the Grid: Demand Moves Beyond Passenger Cars

Electric trucks are now the fastest-growing major vehicle category for battery demand. Global sales of electric heavy freight trucks rose from approximately 84,000 in 2024 to 230,000 in 2025, electric truck sales in Europe increased 40% to nearly 17,000 units, and one in four trucks sold in China in 2025 was electric. Battery-swap-capable trucks represented around 15% of China's electric truck sales. Trucks accounted for approximately 8% of global EV battery deployment in 2025, up from less than 5% in 2024. The product response is visible: in September 2026, CATL launched its TECTRANS II commercial-vehicle battery at IAA Transportation 2026, supporting a driving range of up to 1,000 km and megawatt-level fast charging.

Battery energy storage systems (BESS) are the other growth engine. Utility-scale systems accounted for approximately 87 GW of the 108 GW added globally in 2025, and the price of battery storage has fallen by more than 90% between 2010 and 2025. About 90% of new battery storage projects in 2025 were for energy shifting, up from roughly 40% in 2015, meaning batteries are increasingly used to store electricity when it is cheap and release it when it is needed. In the United States, the Energy Information Administration estimates 18.2 GW of new utility battery installations in 2025. CATL reported a 30.4% share of global energy-storage battery shipments in 2025, showing how leading EV battery makers are diversifying beyond cars.

Localization Becomes the Strategy

With China's cost advantage in place, manufacturers elsewhere are building closer to customers. Panasonic Energy started mass production at its Kansas factory in July 2025, targeting around 32 GWh of capacity in North America. India announced an incentive program of ₹18,100 crore aimed at 50 GWh of advanced lithium-ion cell production. And the latest agreements, covered below, tie European and North American battery capacity to Chinese and Korean cell makers, automakers, and energy-storage integrators.

What's Fueling Growth in the Lithium-Ion Battery Market

Electric vehicle batteries: Global demand for EV batteries reached around 1.2 TWh in 2025, growing nearly 30% from the previous year.

Large-scale energy storage: U.S. utilities added 10.3 GW of new battery storage capacity in 2024, and utility-scale batteries are supporting grid stability as renewable generation grows.

Commercial transport electrification: Electric truck demand surged in 2024 and sales doubled in 2025, increasing battery consumption in freight transport.

Government support for local manufacturing: India's ₹18,100 crore incentive program targets 50 GWh of advanced lithium-ion cell production and wider manufacturing investment.

Investment in large-scale production: Capacity is being added across Asia, Europe, and North America, including Panasonic Energy's Kansas factory.

Renewable energy storage: Growing need to store renewable electricity is supporting demand for lithium-ion systems in utilities, commercial buildings, and data centers.

Challenges Facing the Lithium-Ion Battery Market

Cost and profitability are the central pressures. Regional pack-price gaps hurt manufacturers in North America and Europe, and many leading battery material producers have operated at a loss since 2023. Cathode active materials account for approximately 40–50% of NMC cell production costs and 25–30% for LFP, which makes materials pricing critical. Higher lithium prices in early 2026 are expected to affect production costs, investment decisions, and competitiveness, and the IEA's Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2025 projected that announced mining projects could meet only around 60% of lithium requirements in 2035 under its stated-policies scenario.

Building new factories is hard. Battery manufacturers generally need production yields above 90% to compete, which makes defect reduction, automation, and process optimization essential, and a new plant requires large investment, qualified labor, stable raw material supply, and time to reach production efficiency. The collapse of a Swedish cell manufacturer shows how difficult it is to control defects while expanding several supply-chain stages at once. Supply-chain concentration, raw material price swings, recyclability requirements, and the localization of manufacturing remain the industry's defining issues.

Recent Strategic Developments in the Lithium-Ion Battery Market

In September 2026, Gotion High-tech Co., Ltd. of China agreed to invest €1.1 billion for a 49% stake in Volkswagen's Valencia battery plant in Spain. Volkswagen's PowerCo also planned to invest €470 million in Gotion's facilities in Slovakia and Morocco, strengthening European LFP battery manufacturing and supply-chain capabilities.

In September 2026, LG Energy Solution, Ltd. of South Korea signed a master supply agreement with Canadian energy storage integrator Eneon to supply North America-manufactured, LFP-based energy storage systems. The agreement supports regional battery supply chains, as the company plans to expand its global energy storage production capacity to more than 60 GWh.

In September 2026, Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL) of China launched its TECTRANS II commercial-vehicle battery at IAA Transportation 2026. The battery supports a maximum driving range of up to 1,000 km and megawatt-level fast charging, strengthening CATL's portfolio for electric heavy-duty trucks and long-distance commercial transportation.

In August 2026, Samsung SDI Co., Ltd. of South Korea signed an agreement with General Motors to jointly develop next-generation prismatic battery cells for future electric vehicles. The company also acquired GM's stake in their Indiana joint venture, making the facility its first wholly owned plant in North America and preparing it for energy storage battery production.

Three of the four announcements are about making batteries closer to customers, and the fourth is about the heaviest vehicles on the road.

LFP batteries held the largest share by battery type in 2025, supported by cost advantages, growing EV adoption, and extensive use in stationary storage. China continued to dominate LFP cathode material production and technical expertise.

The IEA reports that the market value of recycled battery metals grew nearly elevenfold between 2015 and 2023, and that recycling recovered more than 40% of available nickel and cobalt feedstock and around 20% of lithium feedstock in 2023. It expects end-of-life EV and stationary storage batteries to account for more than 90% of available recycling feedstock by 2050.

text:
WASHINGTON, November 25, 2026 — The World Bank Board of Executive Directors has approved a financial package of $800 million to support Uzbekistan’s reforms aimed at creating more and better-paid jobs, strengthening the role of the private sector, and advancing a greener and more inclusive economy. The program is expected to support an equivalent of 275,000 additional jobs over 2029–2031, building on earlier progress in the country.

The World Bank says the reforms are designed to widen opportunities for women, farmers, and businesses across Uzbekistan. Implementation will support policy measures across labor and social protection, the business environment, digital connectivity, energy markets, agricultural resilience, trade procedures, and energy efficiency.

Background: jobs and competitiveness alongside inclusion and greener growth

Uzbekistan has been pursuing economic reforms to boost employment, attract private investment, and integrate more fully into global markets. The new support package links those priorities with measures intended to improve protections for vulnerable groups, increase women’s participation, and reduce environmental and climate risks.

The World Bank describes the approach as policy support to enable the government to carry out reforms in multiple sectors, rather than a single-sector intervention. It also sets out specific targets for digital access, energy service delivery, and agricultural insurance coverage by 2028.

Key reform areas supported by the World Bank package

According to the World Bank press release, the government will be supported to implement policy measures in six connected areas.

More economic opportunities for women and stronger social protection

The program focuses on expanding social insurance, including maternity and temporary sickness benefits. It also includes strengthening mechanisms for safer and more respectful workplaces, and professionalizing social work to improve service quality for vulnerable people and families.

A more competitive private sector

To increase space for private business, investment, and innovation, the World Bank support includes continued reforms of state-owned enterprises and strengthening the framework for fair competition. The goal is to help create conditions for more job creation through a more competitive private sector.

A more connected digital economy

The package supports modernization of rules for secure cross-border data flows so businesses can use digital technologies, cloud services, and international digital platforms, while maintaining safeguards for personal data. By 2028, the program aims to support 500,000 additional broadband users, including 250,000 women.

Modern and reliable energy services

The reforms seek to improve the rules and institutions governing electricity and natural gas markets and to create opportunities for private investment. By 2028, the program targets that 15% of electricity customers will be served through privately operated distribution networks.

Greater resilience for farmers

The World Bank support includes expanding agricultural insurance to better protect farmers and livestock producers against droughts, floods, extreme weather, and other risks. The release states a target to expand insurance coverage to 35% of farmers and livestock producers by 2028.

Faster and easier trade

The package also supports modernization and digitalization of trade procedures, including strengthening Uzbekistan’s trade single window and simplifying border processes. The World Bank links these steps to easing the cost of international trade and to Uzbekistan’s WTO accession process.

Cleaner and more energy-efficient growth

Finally, the reforms include improving energy efficiency standards for buildings and encouraging businesses to invest in cleaner technologies. The program aims to mobilize $10 million in private energy-efficiency investment and support the expansion of distributed renewable energy capacity to 3,000 MW by 2028.

What the approval means for implementing reforms

The World Bank approval was made by its Board of Executive Directors on November 25, 2026. The release does not specify the identities of implementing agencies or partner organizations beyond the government and the World Bank, but it outlines a multi-sector policy agenda supported through the $800 million package.

Why the development approach matters for services and livelihoods

For civil society organizations and development practitioners, the package reflects a blended reform agenda: it combines labor and social protection with measures intended to strengthen private-sector competitiveness, expand digital connectivity, and improve energy access. Its inclusion of agricultural insurance targets and trade facilitation measures also connects economic growth to risk management and market access—areas that can affect livelihoods and resilience.

The World Bank’s targets for broadband adoption by gender and for insurance coverage among farmers are also relevant to equity goals, while energy and efficiency measures align with broader environmental and climate resilience priorities.

Key Details

Initiative or programme: World Bank support for Uzbekistan’s reforms for jobs and a greener, private-sector-led growth

Lead organization: World Bank (World Bank Board of Executive Directors)

Partners: Uzbekistan government (partners beyond the government not specified in the provided source)

Funding amount: $800 million

Geographic focus: Uzbekistan

Target groups: Women; farmers and livestock producers; businesses (including private businesses); electricity customers

Duration or timeline: Reforms support expected to create an equivalent of 275,000 additional jobs over 2029–2031; several targets set for by 2028

Expected reach or outcomes (selected targets): Support 500,000 additional broadband users including 250,000 women by 2028; expand agricultural insurance coverage to 35% of farmers and livestock producers by 2028; 15% of electricity customers served through privately operated distribution networks by 2028; mobilize $10 million in private energy-efficiency investment; expand distributed renewable energy capacity to 3,000 MW by 2028

Why This Matters

The World Bank’s $800 million package signals how major development financing is increasingly bundling economic competitiveness with inclusion and resilience outcomes. For NGOs and development professionals, the emphasis on women’s access to jobs and broadband, expansion of agricultural insurance, and modernization of trade and digital rules highlights areas where civil society can engage on implementation quality, safeguards, and service delivery effectiveness.

The multi-sector reform design also suggests potential opportunities for partnerships around social protection systems, workplace standards, and rural risk management. The specific by-2028 targets provide reference points for monitoring and advocacy as Uzbekistan advances reforms in energy, digital connectivity, and trade facilitation.

text:
What's next for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026?

Before I answer, a story. My mentor Forrest J. Gerard, Blackfeet, had a lot of legislative accomplishments over the years (Indian Finance Act, Indian Health Care Improvement Act and the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act) and he loved to tell stories about the ins and outs of how those laws were made. But he was also fond of showing what could be done to kill legislation.

To read more articles by Mark Trahant, go to: Marktrahant.substack.com

One of his favorite stories was about a bill to put a time limit on tribal land claims. The chairman of the Senate Indian Affairs Committee was then William Cohen of Maine, whose views had been shaped by land claims by the Passamaquoddy and Penobscot tribes in the 1970s. A settlement was reached in that case and it became law in 1980. Cohen then wanted a blanket time limit on all third-party claims by tribes (against states and private parties) and pushed through a measure to do just that. Tribes wanted changes and Cohen was in a rush.

When the bill got before the Senate, it was late in the calendar, and the only option left for the Cohen bill was unanimous consent. Gerard's play was to have tribes call on Montana's John Melcher. Once he signed on to the issue he was unmovable. The sponsors tried everything they could think of and nothing worked. So the bill died and when it came back in the next Congress there was a lot more tribal input.

That's all to say that the calendar is now the best friend of folks trying to kill the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026.

Last week the Native American Rights Fund issued a legal analysis of what is now H.R. 2347.

"… a permitting reform bill designed to accelerate federal environmental reviews and project approvals. It proposes significant changes to the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, and National Historic Preservation Act, as well as energy permitting laws.

By shortening review timelines and narrowing what triggers a review, BAAJA would reduce federal oversight and opportunities for Tribal Nations to participate in decisions affecting their lands, waters, and cultural resources. It would also weaken Tribal consultation and make it harder to challenge harmful project approvals in court."

Back to the calendar.

The House has about three weeks left and it has a busy agenda, including funding the government. The Republicans would love to get their farm bill through now, because a rewrite after January will mean a lot of Democratic priorities will rise to the surface (including restoring food benefits under the SNAP program.)

The Hill reports:

"… it won't be an easy task for Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to wrangle his caucus, especially as he struggles to keep his own members in Washington long enough to get the work done.

"Attendance problems have already begun disrupting the House floor schedule. GOP leaders postponed a procedural rule vote Wednesday over absences and canceled Friday's votes altogether. Twenty-one Republicans missed votes on Thursday morning, following 14 absences the previous day.

"Johnson will need near-unanimous support on any procedural rule if he decides to bring a bill to the floor via regular order, requiring most of his conference to be present as he juggles a razor-thin margin. The House this week took up bills under a fast-track process known as suspension of the rules, which requires a two-thirds majority for passage and is typically reserved for legislation with broad bipartisan support. Because those bills often attract significant Democratic backing, Republicans can afford absences without jeopardizing passage."

Remember House Democrats vote against the rule as a matter of course.

So Johnson has two choices: Move the bill through the rules committee and regular order or try and get a suspension of the rules with requires a 2/3s vote.

And a strong Democratic opposition could stop bill either way (depending on how many Republicans show up to vote).

And if the House bill does get through, and it has any amendments, even a paragraph, then the measure it has to go back to the Senate for reconsideration. And then back to the House.

title: Avantus and PG&E sign 20-year Buttonbush solar deal - MarketScale
description:
Avantus has signed 20-year power purchase agreements with Pacific Gas and Electric for the first two phases of its Buttonbush Solar Center in western Kern County, California.
Three Kern projects, three battery ratios Avantus already has two projects in Kern County that make a handy comparison.
Aratina 1, which began commercial operations in July, pairs 200 MW of solar with 500 MWh of storage.
Aratina 2, next to it and still under construction, will add 150 MW of solar and 452 MWh of storage, according to the company's announcement.
At 3,200 MWh, Buttonbush 1A and 1B would hold far more storage than Aratina 1, with 500 MWh, and Aratina 2, with 452 MWh.
text:
Avantus has signed 20-year power purchase agreements with Pacific Gas and Electric for the first two phases of its Buttonbush Solar Center in western Kern County, California. Buttonbush 1A and 1B add up to 800 MW of solar and 3,200 MWh of battery storage, an estimated $3 billion build that the San Diego developer announced on November 17. Avantus says the combined output is enough to power approximately 381,000 homes each year.

Beyond the price tag and the jobs, the battery number is the more useful one. Avantus ranks the agreements among California's biggest utility-scale solar and storage offtake contracts signed so far, and the way the deal is sized shows what kind of power PG&E wants to lock in for two decades.

Three Kern projects, three battery ratios

Avantus already has two projects in Kern County that make a handy comparison. Aratina 1, which began commercial operations in July, pairs 200 MW of solar with 500 MWh of storage. Aratina 2, next to it and still under construction, will add 150 MW of solar and 452 MWh of storage, according to the company's announcement.

Do the arithmetic and Buttonbush carries 4 MWh of battery for every megawatt of solar, against 2.5 at Aratina 1, which makes the deal look like a contract for evening power with solar as the fuel. Aratina 2 sits in between, at roughly 3 MWh per megawatt by the same math. In other words, each newer project puts more storage behind its panels.

Avantus CEO Cliff Graham described the purpose the same way. In the announcement, he said Buttonbush would keep low-cost solar flowing into the evening, when the sun goes down and demand peaks. PG&E's Gillian Clegg, vice president of energy policy and procurement, said the projects will be among the largest clean energy resources in the utility's portfolio and will help it meet growing demand across its service area for the next 20 years.

Graham also linked the scale of the deal to cost. In his view, a PG&E commitment this large reflects California's need for clean power with steady reliability and predictable pricing. Clegg framed it in terms of customers, saying the projects would supply them with clean power that is affordable and dependable over the next two decades. Read those remarks alongside the 4-to-1 ratio and the picture gets clearer: PG&E appears to be buying predictability as much as megawatts, meaning solar output shifted into the evening on terms fixed now for 20 years.

The ratio has a limit. The announcement gives storage in megawatt-hours but not the batteries' power rating in megawatts, so 4 MWh per solar megawatt describes how much stored energy sits behind the panels, not how many hours the batteries run at full output. Three projects from one developer also don't make a market trend. They're one company's sizing choices, and the latest choice leans hard toward stored energy.

Farmland, tax revenue and local backing

Avantus will build the projects on water-stressed farmland, and it presents that as a way to help meet the state's groundwater requirements. Farmers get long-term lease income from fields that would otherwise need scarce water, and that water stays available for other crops in the region.

Graham listed "steady income for local landowners" among the county benefits, alongside union jobs and new tax revenue. The setup turns a groundwater constraint into a land-use decision. Fields that would otherwise compete for scarce water earn lease income instead, which suggests water policy is doing part of the siting work here, not just grid access and sunshine.

The public-finance side is also large. Over the projects' operating life, Avantus estimates they will produce hundreds of millions of dollars in local property taxes, money that would go toward county public services. The Business Journal in Fresno, which reported on the deal the day it was announced, opened with the jobs: approximately 900 union construction jobs, then permanent operations and maintenance jobs that Avantus says will last for decades.

For scale, Aratina 2 supported up to 300 jobs at its construction peak. The two figures aren't measured the same way, since one is a peak headcount and the other a project estimate. Even so, they suggest Buttonbush sits in a different weight class from Avantus's earlier Kern builds on labor as well as on storage.

Chapman called it one of the most significant energy projects in Kern County. Labor and county officials backed it as well. Brian Holt, business manager and financial secretary of IBEW Local 428, said the union has worked with Avantus for about 15 years, and Kern County Supervisor David Couch of District 4 pointed to union jobs and local tax revenue. At the state level, Alex Jackson, executive director of American Clean Power-California, said the agreement "demonstrates the scale of investment needed" to meet California's growing electricity demand.

A 20-year owner with a growing credit line

Avantus intends to keep ownership of Buttonbush 1A and 1B and run both projects itself, operating as an independent power producer that supplies clean electricity to California's grid.

That choice puts Avantus, not a buyer, in charge of the 20 years of operations the PG&E contracts cover. The company has been building the balance sheet and the team for that job.

Avantus has increased its corporate credit facility to $1.28 billion and added five new lenders. Avantus is backed by KKR and EIG and says its development pipeline of solar with integrated storage could serve more than 10 million Americans.

The credit line has grown fast. The $1.28 billion figure builds on a $1.05 billion facility Avantus closed in August 2026, which itself doubled the $522 million facility put in place in July 2024. The company links each expansion to its independent power producer strategy across California and the Desert Southwest.

Leadership has moved the same way. Avantus appointed Kim Anderson as chief financial officer to oversee financial strategy and help scale its operating platform alongside its development portfolio. She brings more than 25 years across energy, power and infrastructure in public and private markets. Together with the credit line, the hire suggests a company preparing for the long owner-operator years that a deal like Buttonbush implies, not only for the development phase.

Reading the next solar and storage offer

Buttonbush gives large power buyers and utility procurement teams a public reference point for how much storage a developer will put behind solar on a long contract. For buyers in California weighing solar-plus-storage supply, three questions follow from this deal:

What is the storage in MWh per megawatt of solar, and how does it compare with the 2.5-to-4 range in Avantus's own Kern projects?

What is the battery power rating in megawatts, so the length of evening delivery can be worked out?

Who owns and operates the asset over the full contract term?

The next step is a CPUC review of the two agreements. If the commission approves them, construction would be expected to start in 2027, with commercial operation expected in 2029. Graham's remarks stressed speed, arguing that families and businesses will feel the benefits sooner when projects like this come online faster. At 3,200 MWh, Buttonbush 1A and 1B would hold far more storage than Aratina 1, with 500 MWh, and Aratina 2, with 452 MWh.

text:
HANOI, VIETNAM – Media OutReach Newswire – 27 November 2026 – VinEnergo has officially broken ground on a 126 MWp solar power plant in Sagay City, Negros Occidental, Philippines. The project marks the first to be implemented under the cooperation framework between VinEnergo and the Philippine Department of Energy (DOE) on the development of renewable energy solutions integrated with energy storage systems, representing a tangible step forward in VinEnergo’s commitment to investing in and advancing clean energy in the country.

The groundbreaking ceremony was attended by Mr. Lai Thai Binh, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Vietnam to the Philippines; Mr. Rafael Leo M. Cueva, Mayor of Sagay City; Mr. Narciso L. Javelosa Jr., Vice Mayor of Sagay City; and representatives of local government authorities.

Previously, VinEnergo and the Philippine Department of Energy signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to establish a framework for cooperation in developing clean energy sources, laying the foundation for the research and implementation of large-scale energy projects across the country. A key focus of the cooperation is the development of renewable energy projects integrated with energy storage systems, with a targeted renewable energy capacity of more than 20 GW and the potential to deliver up to 5 GW of baseload power to the Philippine national grid. The 126 MWp Sagay Solar project represents the first concrete step in advancing this cooperation, while paving the way for broader collaboration between VinEnergo and leading energy companies in the Philippines.

The 126 MWp Sagay Solar project is being developed in partnership with SunAsia Energy, a Philippine renewable energy company. The project features the innovative Solar on Stilts solution, which utilizes elevated solar panel structures to maximize space efficiency and optimize land use while generating clean electricity.

The project forms part of a broader 422 MWp portfolio jointly developed by VinEnergo and SunAsia Energy, comprising three projects in Macabebe, Sagay, and Silay. This portfolio underscores VinEnergo’s long-term commitment to working with local partners to unlock the Philippines’ renewable energy potential and contribute to the country’s energy transition.

Commenting on the project, Ms. Sharon S. Garin, Secretary of Energy of the Philippines, said: “We welcome VinEnergo’s investment in the Philippine energy sector. The 126-megawatt-peak (MWp) Sagay Solar Power Project represents an important addition to the Philippines’ growing renewable energy capacity and our continuing efforts to strengthen national energy security. By harnessing our indigenous renewable energy resources, projects such as this help diversify our energy mix, reduce dependence on imported fuels, and lessen our exposure to volatility in international energy markets.”

Mr. Nguyen Anh Khoa, Chief Executive Officer of VinEnergo, said: “We believe that the energy transition is about more than simply expanding clean power generation; it is about building a sustainable energy system capable of supporting each country’s long-term development ambitions. For VinEnergo, the 126 MWp Sagay Solar project holds particular significance as the first concrete step in our strategic cooperation with the Philippine Department of Energy. It demonstrates our commitment to translating strategic cooperation into tangible projects that deliver real value. By bringing together our project development capabilities, technological expertise, and strong partnerships with local stakeholders, VinEnergo aims to make a lasting contribution to strengthening energy security, unlocking the Philippines’ renewable energy potential, and shaping a greener, more reliable, and sustainable energy future for the country.”

Looking ahead, VinEnergo plans to further develop a portfolio of power generation projects in the Philippines with a total capacity of up to 5 GWp of baseload power, integrating renewable energy sources with battery energy storage systems (BESS) to support a 24/7 renewable energy model capable of meeting baseload demand. Between 2027 and 2029, the company will progressively advance investment preparations and move eligible projects toward construction and groundbreaking, while continuing to explore new partnership opportunities. These efforts form part of VinEnergo’s long-term investment strategy in the Philippines, contributing to national energy security and the country’s green transition.

With a long-term development vision and as part of the Vingroup ecosystem, VinEnergo aspires to become a comprehensive green energy investor and developer, delivering clean, reliable, and efficient energy solutions while contributing to the global energy transition.

The issuer is solely responsible for the content of this announcement.

About VinEnergo

As Vingroup’s green energy company, VinEnergo is focused on developing technological and manufacturing capabilities in renewable energy, energy storage, and electricity transmission and distribution infrastructure. Through continuous improvements in product standards and the expansion of its project implementation capabilities, VinEnergo aims to become a competitive provider of green energy solutions in international markets.

For more information, please visit: https://vinenergo.com

About SunAsia Energy

SUNASIA ENERGY INC. develops renewable energy projects in the Philippines, focusing strongly on solar energy. Since 2013, the company has partnered with local and international organizations to advance solar initiatives nationwide, including the 60 MW solar power project in Toledo, Cebu.

Building on its experience in large-scale solar development, the company expanded into floating solar development, recognizing the potential of water-based solar infrastructure to complement land-based renewable energy projects. Since 2019, SunAsia has operated a floating solar testbed on Laguna Lake, strengthening its technical expertise and gaining insights into the unique engineering and environmental conditions associated with deploying solar technology on water. These efforts support the development of larger projects that contribute to the Philippines’ energy security and clean energy objectives

text:
Marshall County voted in 2025 to ban solar projects for two years, and Clark County passed a 2025 ordinance with a setback that disqualified nearly half of one landowner's farm from a solar lease. Utility-scale solar energy boomed across Indiana in 2025 even as county-level restrictions multiplied.

Why it matters

Because zoning power in Indiana largely sits with county officials, solar siting depends on local votes rather than a uniform state standard. The state does not track how many projects or megawatts county bans have kept off the grid, leaving the statewide impact unmeasured.

Abandoned Marshall County projects would have brought 350 megawatts onto the grid, and Clark County's 2025 ordinance disqualified nearly half of one landowner's farm from a solar lease. The Indiana state government does not track how many projects or megawatts county bans have kept off the grid.

The players

Geenex

A solar developer that worked through the Marshall County zoning process in 2024 for projects later abandoned.

Clark County Board of Zoning Appeals

The county body that oversees zoning appeals, where member Bob Ellison resigned one month after taking the role.

The details

Counties decide solar projects through local zoning processes, and opposition has been voiced at county meetings that were moved to larger venues to accommodate crowds. Legislation to consolidate state authority over solar siting failed to become law in 2021 and 2025.

Timeline

2014-08-06

Jim McCune died, leaving 800 acres of Marshall County farmland to his daughters.

2019: Geenex approached the McCune sisters with a solar lease offer.

2020: A solar company approached Clark County landowners before the pandemic.

2021: State legislation to consolidate solar siting authority failed.

2024: Marshall County's zoning process for two solar developers occurred.

Related coverage

Elections

Nov. 25

Rural Coalition Wins 16 Indiana Legislative Seats

Government

Nov. 25

Rokita Won't Rule Out 2028 Challenge to Braun

Family

Nov. 17

Lawmaker Drafts Bills to Aid Disability Families

Legal Context

Indiana's 2021 and 2025 attempts to consolidate state authority over solar siting both failed to become law, leaving county zoning as the controlling mechanism. Wisconsin and Michigan, by comparison, grant their states greater control over siting decisions.

Residents in counties with solar bans or restrictive ordinances may find that landowners cannot lease land for solar development for the duration of the restriction. Landowners weighing a lease should check their county's current zoning rules before signing.

The takeaway

Solar siting in Indiana is decided county by county, so landowners and residents should track local zoning votes that may change what can be built on nearby land.

description:

text:
Lisa Desjardins:

Let's delve more into one national issue that fell under the radar during this year's midterm elections, climate change.

Even though it did not play a major role on the campaign trail, with Democrats commanding wins nationwide, including at the state level, some environmental groups are convinced that more substantive action is just around the corner.

William Brangham explains.

William Brangham:

For the environmental community, the last two years have been dark ones. The Trump administration has rolled back many of the ways that the U.S. tries to address the dangerous warming of our planet, everything from closing major research centers to blocking renewable energy projects.

But my next guest argues that the blue wave that swept the midterms could mark a major change in policy.

Caroline Spears is the executive director of an advocacy group called Climate Cabinet, which promotes and supports candidates who back climate action.

Caroline Spears, so nice to have you on the program.

In this election, my understanding is, you were focused on something like 120-something races. Your candidates won over 100 of those races. Am I right, though, that, in a lot of those races, the issue of climate change, per se, was not really spoken about or on the ballot?

Caroline Spears:

Yes, well, William, what we know was on the ballot clearly was cost.

I was knocking doors in Bucks County just a few weeks before the election. Bucks County is a critical kind of battleground district that people across the country watch every year to figure out what's going to happen. And what I heard directly from people on the doors is that their utility bills were rising, gas prices were up. That was a primary concern on voters' minds.

We also know that clean energy is fast to grid and cheap to grid. It can lower people's bills and lower costs, especially as gas prices have been through the roof. So you're right, it wasn't kind of a top line, but there were clean energy moments kind of throughout the campaign that were interesting to see.

William Brangham:

So, gas prices, utility bills, the sort of affordability suite of issues, you're arguing, are and were climate change issues, but they maybe weren't called that much.

Caroline Spears:

Yes, and that makes sense, right?

Like, when you think about something like home insurance or property insurance, that's home insurance and property insurance, but we know that one of the reasons those prices have been going up so much over the last few years is because of climate disasters and climate-fueled disasters across the country. So that's really what we have seen across the country.

William Brangham:

When you are looking, as an organization, to promote and pick certain candidates to promote, what are the metrics you're using? Are you looking for people who are advocates for the issue or they're in locations where they can have an impact?

Caroline Spears:

Both.

The first thing we really look for is, is this person running for an office that has a big impact on our ability to build clean energy jobs and solve climate change? So that's the first piece. But the second piece we're really looking for is track record. Do they have a track record, whether they had a previous position before and they voted to expand solar access in that space?

Were they working at the neighborhood level to make sure people could take climate action into their own hands locally?

William Brangham:

So you win over 100 of the 120 races you're targeting. What are some of the states and locations or individuals that you think, aha, these are really going to be powerful for us going forward?

Caroline Spears:

There's a few places that really come to mind to me.

The first has to be the state of Arizona, which has so much solar potential, but it's really bad policies that have held the state back. So I'm really excited to see a change in leadership in the state of Arizona.

In particular, there's a senator there named Senator Sundareshan who actually was in water and energy law before she ran for office, and now she's going to be president of the Senate next year. So that's one of the reasons I'm really optimistic about the next two years is, we have people who are experts on these topics that people have said they really care about and can bring solutions to the table as well.

William Brangham:

Everyone that followed this election knows how central the issue of data centers were to this election. Do you think that there was a climate connection? Or were the candidates that you were backing making a climate connection to data centers?

Caroline Spears:

Generally, what we have heard about data centers are, what voters are really talking about was cost and also economic anxiety.

I think data centers are a physical manifestation of some of the broader economic anxieties that we have, with additional tie-in of people are thinking, is this raising my utility bill? Is this why my utility rates have gone up so much in the last few years?

There was a candidate named Peter Hubbard who ran last year for the Public Service Commission in Georgia. He had to run again this year. But he's now going to be in the majority at the Georgia Public Service Commission. He's already said that he's really thinking about how to lower people's bills with clean energy.

William Brangham:

What about the skeptics who might argue, unless you change federal policy, state level is only going to be piecemeal, because the federal government has its ability, as we have seen, to block renewable energy projects in multiple states, and that there might be a lot of promises made, but states and localities might have a hard time delivering on those promises?

Caroline Spears:

I would actually flip that on its head. I think that's the wrong way to look at energy policy.

We have 50 states, and each of them has an enormous role in our ability to actually build energy projects and build the clean energy economy. I know this. I used to work in the solar industry, and I saw our projects kind of live or die by state policies at the governor, at the PUC, and the state legislature level.

That's going to continue. And the last piece on that is, states pass policy at a rate of five times that of the federal government. I think everyone watching knows that the federal government can be slow and dysfunctional. And so states are really where we can stop and make progress -- make some progress on this over the next couple of years.

William Brangham:

Caroline Spears, executive director of Climate Cabinet, thank you so much for being here.

Caroline Spears:

Thanks for having me.

text:
German automotive component supplier MAHLE has introduced a Park & Charge pilot for vehicle manufacturers that pairs autonomous parking with wireless charging for drivers and fleet operators, including car rental companies, logistics providers and delivery services.

The system utilises the vehicle camera and algorithms without requiring sensors, by identifying parking spaces equipped with charging infrastructure it guides the vehicle over a ground-mounted charging pad using the Differential Inductive Positioning System (DIPS), a standard set by SAE International.

Once positioned, the system initiates energy transfer up to 11 kW at an efficiency exceeding 92 percent, while supporting bidirectional charging to return electricity from the vehicle to the power grid.

MAHLE is evaluating the technology alongside the BMW Group in a BMW iX3 and has converted a combustion engine test facility in Stuttgart into a test bench rated for capacities up to 30 kW to validate object detection in the air gap, magnetic field measurements, and coil integration across vehicle architectures including the BMW Neue Klasse platform.

Dr. Marco Warth, Vice President of Corporate Research and Advanced Engineering at MAHLE, said, “Wireless charging has the potential to make electric mobility much easier in everyday life. Key to acceptance is high efficiency, maximum ease of use, the ability to automate the process, and seamless integration into existing vehicle and infrastructure concepts. With our Park & Charge pilot, we are taking the next step by laying the foundation for an automated charging process that not only enhances convenience for users but also opens up new application opportunities for fleet operators.”

“By setting up this state-of-the-art system test bench in a former combustion-engine test cell, we are making transformation tangible. Through the close integration of development, software engineering, validation, and maintenance, we bring together our full expertise within a single team and deliver end-to-end solutions, from system know-how to the final product,” added Dr. Warth.

Detroit Engineered Products (DEP), developer of the DEP MeshWorks and DEP AIWorks platforms, has entered into a Talent Development Partnership with IntelliNXT Learning & Technologies (IntelliNXT) to build a pipeline of Computer-Aided Engineering (CAE) talent in India.

As per the agreement, IntelliNXT will design and deliver a training programme in association with DEP to develop participants' skills in CAE and DEP MeshWorks, a platform used by engineering teams to build element models from CAD data, parameterise them, and run optimisation studies.

Delivered through sessions, labs and projects, the curriculum will also introduce engineering workflows enabled by artificial intelligence (AI), an area where DEP AIWorks combines machine learning with simulation to shorten product development cycles. IntelliNXT will assess participants, certify graduates, and coordinate placement activities with DEP by recommending candidates based on assessment performance, streamlining recruitment and onboarding for the software developer.

Radha Krishnan, Founder & President, DEP, said, “Industry-ready engineers are the foundation of every successful CAE adoption. Partnering with IntelliNXT lets us bring DEP MeshWorks to a new generation of engineers in India and build a lasting talent pipeline.”

Karaiadiselvan, Chief Mentor, IntelliNXT Learning & Technologies, said, “Access to DEP MeshWorks lets us train our learners on a tool that industry actually uses, and helps companies find job-ready talent.”

Hindustan Zinc, in collaboration with the Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IIT Madras), has unveiled a three-wheeler prototype fitted with an approximately 1 kWh zinc-air battery acting as a range extender.

The partners presented the prototype during the IIT Madras Energy Summit 2026 in the presence of Praveen Chakravarthy, Member of Parliament (Rajya Sabha), Amarendu Prakash, CEO and Whole-time Director, Hindustan Zinc, IIT Madras Dean (ICSR) Prof. Manu Santhanam and project lead Dr. Aravind Kumar Chandiran from the Department of Chemical Engineering.

Initiated in 2024, the research partnership has progressed from laboratory testing to vehicle demonstration under Hindustan Zinc's HZL 2.0 growth strategy. The vehicle utilises a dual-battery architecture in which the zinc-air unit supplies nearly 10 percent of the vehicle's energy requirements during operation, while a lithium-ion battery handles acceleration and power demands. Operating with a water-based electrolyte, zinc and oxygen from the air, the technology leverages India's zinc reserves to advance energy storage capabilities.

Amarendu Prakash said, “At Hindustan Zinc, we are constantly exploring opportunities to expand the applications of zinc and unlock greater value from this versatile metal. With zinc being abundantly available in India, there is an opportunity to explore indigenous energy storage solutions that can contribute to the vision of Viksit Bharat. Our collaboration with IIT Madras reflects our commitment to translating scientific research into practical applications, creating new demand avenues for zinc and strengthening its role in the global clean energy transition.”

Prof. V. Kamakoti, Director, IIT Madras, said, “Energy is the major focus of discussion globally, be it artificial intelligence, agriculture all the way to advanced manufacturing. Ensuring generation, storage and distribution of energy from different sources, specifically the renewable ones is the most important topic for research, development and commercialisation. Our collaboration with Hindustan Zinc is yet another important effort towards this goal.”

Chinese automotive and technology company XPENG has launched public test rides for its Next Generation Pilot (NGP) driver-assistance system at its retail store at 10 boulevard Gouvion-Saint-Cyr in Paris, becoming the first automaker from China to offer such trials from a retail location in Europe.

Following its participation alongside Tesla in the Autonomous Lab programme at the 2026 Paris Motor Show, the initiative allows customers to book drives in city traffic and intersections while the company conducts testing and localisation ahead of a rollout planned for 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and market readiness.

Powered by XPENG's VLA 2.0 architecture, the NGP system sits within a technology stack that includes Turing AI chips, world foundation models and integrated software and hardware across electric vehicles, robotaxis and robots. title: A sweeping permitting reform bill is headed to the House. Critics want to stop it - NPR
description:
The Senate passed a bipartisan permitting reform bill that supporters say will pave the way for much needed infrastructure projects.
But critics argue it will do so at the expense of the environment, tribes and public lands.
They want the House to either fix or reject the bill before the year ends, as NPR's Rachel Treisman reports.
But critics say it would weaken bedrock environmental and historic preservation laws, including by limiting input from tribes and the public.
Rachel Treisman, NPR News.
text:
Transcript

JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:

With just weeks left in its term, Congress could reshape the country's physical landscape for generations. The Senate passed a bipartisan permitting reform bill that supporters say will pave the way for much needed infrastructure projects. But critics argue it will do so at the expense of the environment, tribes and public lands. They want the House to either fix or reject the bill before the year ends, as NPR's Rachel Treisman reports.

RACHEL TREISMAN, BYLINE: Last week, the Senate passed a bill that aims to speed up the approval process for federal infrastructure and energy projects, from wind turbines to data centers. It's called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, and it's nearly 500 pages long.

XAN FISHMAN: This isn't just, like, a mushy, middle, moderate, do-nothing bill. Like, it's actually a big-deal bill.

TREISMAN: Xan Fishman leads the energy program at the Bipartisan Policy Center.

FISHMAN: At its heart, it's about trying to take a permitting system which has just grown out of proportion and make sure that it's protecting the environment but getting to a yes or no answer in a reasonable amount of time.

TREISMAN: Supporters of the bill say it will improve America's aging grid while creating jobs and lowering electricity bills. But critics say it would weaken bedrock environmental and historic preservation laws, including by limiting input from tribes and the public.

WESLEY FURLONG: From our perspective, there are no pros. There are only cons.

TREISMAN: Wesley Furlong is a senior staff attorney with the Native American Rights Fund. He says tribes were not consulted about the bill, even though it threatens their lands and sovereignty.

FURLONG: It will fundamentally change the federal government's relationship with Indian tribes in a really negative way.

TREISMAN: The bill was introduced in the Senate at the end of September. Critics say lawmakers didn't give it the time or debate it deserved in the lead-up to the midterms.

FURLONG: And then they come back, and the first thing that they do the Monday after the election is vote on this bill.

TREISMAN: The Senate first voted to bypass the committee markup process, skipping hearings and rewrites. The bill passed last week with only one amendment by a vote of 62 to 33. It now heads to the House. President Trump has said he will sign it. It's also backed by an unusual alliance of energy companies, big tech, some Democrats and a mix of labor and environmental groups.

SARAH GONZALEZ-ROTHI: People see a very slim chance to address a very urgent issue, and they think they've found the way to do it.

TREISMAN: Sarah Gonzalez-Rothi served as the senior director for water at the White House Council on Environmental Quality under President Biden. She opposes the bill, as do hundreds of climate, tribal, public health, historic preservation and civil rights groups.

GONZALEZ-ROTHI: I think the way they've come up with doing it is looking at rose-colored glasses at text that, if they are wrong, has such severe consequences that it could actually make things worse.

TREISMAN: For example, the bill would make data centers cover their own energy costs, but critics say it could make it easier to build data centers on public lands. And as Furlong says it has provisions that would make it harder to challenge or change permits once they're issued.

FURLONG: Courts can't really stop these projects, and future administrations can't stop them, and so as soon as they are permitted, we are stuck with them forever.

TREISMAN: The House could vote in the days after Thanksgiving. Some key Democrats have already said they oppose the bill, but it's not clear if they have the support or time to revise it before Congress adjourns on January 3.

Rachel Treisman, NPR News.
