title: Open Source Tool Estimates European Electric Truck Charging Infrastructure Investment Costs
description:
The deployment of heavy-duty charging infrastructure occurs against stringent European Union decarbonization mandates aimed at freight transportation.
Despite the operational suitability of electric freight, physical charging infrastructure rollouts face severe grid integration and capacity bottlenecks.
Under the European Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation, member states are legally obligated to install a minimum of 3.6 megawatts of dedicated truck charging capacity at regular 60-kilometer intervals along core trans-European road networks by 2030.
Subject of Research: Capital investment cost modeling for European heavy-duty battery-electric vehicle charging depots Article Title: CHARGE-IT: Investment cost estimation tool for charging infrastructure of heavy-duty vehicles Article References: Ferraro, D., Gil Ribeiro, C., & Thakur, J.
CHARGE-IT: Investment cost estimation tool for charging infrastructure of heavy-duty vehicles.
text:
A research team from KTH Royal Institute of Technology in collaboration with commercial vehicle manufacturer Scania AB has developed an open-source, web-based simulation model named CHARGE-IT to estimate the upfront capital investment required for heavy-duty battery-electric vehicle charging infrastructure across Europe. Documented by researchers Davide Ferraro, Carolina Gil Ribeiro, and Jagruti Thakur, the software addresses a significant analytical gap in commercial fleet electrification by modeling fifteen distinct physical and civil cost components from the medium-voltage utility grid connection directly to the dispenser plug. Operating through an interactive browser interface, the tool calculates complete balance-of-system expenditures using component pricing benchmarks calibrated in 2024 euros derived from industrial equipment catalogs, supplier price sheets, published literature, and interviews with nine European industry professionals. By evaluating site-specific electrical constraints, physical layouts, and depot operating parameters, the model provides fleet operators, infrastructure developers, and transport planners with transparent financial estimates before initiating capital-intensive civil construction or utility grid interconnection requests.

The deployment of heavy-duty charging infrastructure occurs against stringent European Union decarbonization mandates aimed at freight transportation. Heavy-duty vehicles represent roughly six percent of total greenhouse gas emissions across the European Union and account for more than one-quarter of all road transport emissions despite comprising only a minor fraction of the overall vehicle fleet. To curb these sectoral emissions, the European Union’s Fit for 55 legislative package establishes binding fleet-wide carbon dioxide reduction targets for newly registered heavy-duty vehicles, demanding reductions of 45 percent by 2030, 65 percent by 2035, and 90 percent by 2040 relative to historical baselines. Because battery-electric trucks generate zero tailpipe emissions, commercial vehicle manufacturers and freight operators are incentivized to transition directly away from diesel powertrains. Falling battery pack production costs have enabled electric trucks to become technically viable across diverse freight duty cycles, with market research indicating that commercial fleet operators will predominantly favor overnight depot charging regimes to exploit predictable parking schedules and cheaper off-peak electricity tariffs.

Despite the operational suitability of electric freight, physical charging infrastructure rollouts face severe grid integration and capacity bottlenecks. A standard long-haul battery-electric truck incorporates an on-board traction pack storing between 300 and 800 kilowatt-hours of electrical energy, meaning that a medium or large logistics depot charging dozens of commercial vehicles simultaneously can demand multiple megawatts of instantaneous electrical capacity from the distribution network. Under the European Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation, member states are legally obligated to install a minimum of 3.6 megawatts of dedicated truck charging capacity at regular 60-kilometer intervals along core trans-European road networks by 2030. While Europe possessed approximately 10,000 public truck charging points in 2023, regional networks must expand to roughly 300,000 operational points by the close of the decade, requiring a cumulative capital deployment estimated at seven billion euros. Existing commercial depots rarely possess sufficient spare electrical capacity, and acquiring distribution grid upgrades involves protracted administrative permitting, engineering design, and utility interconnections that frequently span multiple years.

Prior computational tools and academic literature have left capital expenditure calculations for heavy-duty European depot stations largely unaddressed. Existing software platforms broadly fall into three categories that bypass the specific balance-of-plant capital needs of European fleet depots. One class of software evaluates the levelized cost of charging, such as the open-source lcoc-ldevs model developed for United States passenger cars, European country-level models that omit utility grid interconnections, and policy calculators focused exclusively on dynamic electricity bills. A second group includes simulation environments from the United States Department of Energy EVI-X suite, including EVI-FAST, datafev, and EV-EcoSim, alongside commercial microgrid tools like HOMER and XENDEE, which model charging demand profiles, dispatch schedules, or levelized distributed generation without generating bottom-up capital equipment breakdowns. Finally, static published literature provides component breakdown tables that are either roughly a decade old, confined to North American light-duty passenger vehicles, or structured as non-reusable regional case studies that omit interactive station design capabilities.

To overcome these limitations, CHARGE-IT is implemented as an open-source Python application utilizing the Streamlit framework, structured into a clean three-layer software architecture. The presentation layer, spanning approximately 995 lines of code in app.py, collects seventeen user configuration variables via an interactive widget form, dynamically re-rendering the graphical interface and exporting tabular results to Excel spreadsheets or structured PDF project summaries. The orchestration layer, contained in utils/calls.py across roughly 325 lines of code, runs validation routines including medium_requirement and hard_requirement to evaluate whether the local grid can absorb the planned charging demand, subsequently executing case_definition to classify the project and compute_all_costs to coordinate the downstream financial subroutines. The underlying computational layer, implemented in utils/cost.py across roughly 490 lines of code, houses the fifteen dedicated cost functions mapping physical dimensions, electrical ratings, and site characteristics into euro expenditures based on lookup tables and fitted analytical equations that users can inspect and modify.

The model requires fourteen numerical parameters and three categorical inputs to characterize a station’s electrical, spatial, and mechanical design. Charger specifications include the total dispenser count, individual dispenser power ratings ranging between 10 and 350 kilowatts, the electrical load power factor, and a simultaneity factor denoting the maximum proportion of installed charger capacity operating concurrently from the utility grid. Sizing calculations begin by computing the planned apparent load in kilovolt-amperes, calculated as the simultaneity factor multiplied by charger count and power rating, divided by the load power factor. Comparing this apparent load against the facility’s existing utility connection capacity automatically assigns the project into one of four standardized installation categories. Type 1 represents facilities where existing grid capacity fully satisfies charging demand; Type 2 applies where minor low-voltage connection upgrades bridge the deficit; Type 3 denotes sites requiring a supplemental medium-voltage connection alongside an existing transformer; and Type 4 indicates locations lacking electrical infrastructure, requiring a complete medium-voltage substation buildout from scratch.

The computational engine calculates specific physical sizing parameters before executing the fifteen cost functions. The required intermediate engineering calculations size alternating current and direct current conductors, transformer ratings with user-defined percentage safety margins, and modular rectifier units sized in 200-kilowatt blocks using ceiling integer division. Low-voltage and direct-current cabling costs scale linearly with electric current and physical trench distance at 0.276 euros per ampere-meter, while medium-voltage alternating-current cables are priced via an exponential function of current multiplied by distance. Low-voltage distribution cabinets scale linearly with current, whereas central rectifiers cost 44,400 euros per 200-kilowatt module for chargers rated at or above 40 kilowatts. Sized transformers, medium-voltage switchgear, and surge arresters are evaluated using voltage-indexed and apparent-power catalog lookup tables. Civil works and soft costs are incorporated via linear empirical regressions for charger engineering planning and site installation based on unit count and power capacity, combined with surface preparation rates set at 45.2, 55.2, or 150.6 euros per square meter.

The authors validated the computational model across nine empirical case studies situated at commercial truck stops and parking facilities across Germany, Italy, and the United Kingdom. Candidate locations were identified through spatial cross-referencing between established heavy-duty truck parking facilities and high-power Combined Charging System dispensers registered in the Open Charge Map database to ensure nearby medium-voltage grid availability. Evaluated cases spanned all four installation categories, encompassing installations ranging from three 200-kilowatt dispensers at an Italian facility with 650 kilovolt-amperes of existing capacity to forty 20-kilowatt plugs at a German site with only 50 kilovolt-amperes of supply. Total investment figures exhibited pronounced variance depending on electrical infrastructure requirements, ranging from approximately 20,000 euros per dispenser plug for expansive Type 1 installations with abundant surplus grid headroom to more than 80,000 euros per plug for compact Type 4 projects burdened by complete greenfield medium-voltage substation construction.

Across all evaluated scenarios, specific capital investment measured in euros per installed kilowatt dropped sharply as facility capacity expanded, although fixed equipment costs established an irreducible financial baseline. In Type 1 configurations, direct-current dispensers, power rectifiers, and electrical installation labor constituted the majority of project expenditures, with specific capital costs declining from over 1,500 euros per kilowatt for 10-kilowatt chargers to below 800 euros per kilowatt for 150-kilowatt units. Conversely, Type 4 projects required substantial upfront expenditures for utility transformers, medium-voltage switchgear, specialized cabling, and civil trenching, causing specific capital costs to level off at approximately 1,000 to 1,100 euros per kilowatt. When comparing Type 1 and Type 4 installations at equivalent power levels, the resulting expenditure discrepancy was attributed to medium-voltage electrical hardware accounting for roughly 60 percent of the cost gap and specialized installation labor comprising the remaining 40 percent.

The resulting modeling architecture equips commercial fleet operators, distribution system operators, and infrastructure planners with a rapid method to evaluate capital trade-offs prior to project commitment. By adjusting simultaneity factors, operators can analyze managed charging configurations that avoid costly medium-voltage substation buildouts by capping coincident peak demand. Furthermore, the tool operates complementarily with operational scheduling frameworks such as FleetRL, enabling comprehensive life-cycle assessments spanning capital expenditure and ongoing charging energy costs. As noted in the study published in SoftwareX, future expansions of the codebase are planned to incorporate levelized cost of charging algorithms, permitting lead-time estimation models across regulatory jurisdictions, support for emerging Megawatt Charging System hardware standards, and regional fleet deployment planning capabilities to support Europe’s statutory commercial transport electrification targets.

Subject of Research: Capital investment cost modeling for European heavy-duty battery-electric vehicle charging depots

Article Title: CHARGE-IT: Investment cost estimation tool for charging infrastructure of heavy-duty vehicles

Article References: Ferraro, D., Gil Ribeiro, C., & Thakur, J. (2026). CHARGE-IT: Investment cost estimation tool for charging infrastructure of heavy-duty vehicles. SoftwareX, 36, Article 103192. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.softx.2026.103192

text:
In Kakinada, on India’s eastern coast, an existing ammonia and urea complex is being converted into a large-scale renewable ammonia production facility, becoming one of the world's largest green ammonia and green hydrogen production facilities.

The project will use renewable electricity to produce green hydrogen through electrolysis, before combining that hydrogen with nitrogen to create green ammonia. Once fully operational, the facility is expected to produce one million tonnes of renewable ammonia annually and avoid approximately two million tonnes of CO₂ emissions each year.

Green ammonia is becoming increasingly important because it connects renewable electricity and hydrogen with industrial applications that can be difficult to decarbonize through direct electrification alone. Green hydrogen provides the essential building block, while converting it into ammonia creates a versatile product that can serve as a lower-carbon feedstock for industries such as fertilizers and chemicals, as well as an energy carrier with potential applications in shipping and power generation.

Producing green ammonia begins with green hydrogen. At Kakinada, pressurized alkaline electrolysers will use renewable electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. The hydrogen will subsequently be used in the ammonia-production process, creating an alternative to conventional ammonia production based on fossil fuels. The project is being developed through two electrolyser phases of approximately 640 MW each.

However, supplying renewable electricity to the site is only part of the challenge. Electrolysers operate on controlled direct current, while the plant’s electrical network supplies alternating current. Before that electricity can support hydrogen production, it must therefore be transformed to the required voltage and then converted from AC to DC. At this interface between renewable power and the electrolysis process, rectifier transformers become a critical part of the electrical system.

Working in collaboration with Hubei Green Power, Hitachi Energy is supplying 64 rectifier transformers, each rated at 15.58 MVA and 33 kV, for integration into the rectifier power-supply system. Green Power will integrate the transformers into the complete power-conversion equipment before the system is delivered to the Kakinada project.

The transformers adapt the incoming AC electricity to the operating requirements of the rectifier system. The rectifiers then convert that electricity into the controlled DC power required by the electrolysers. Together, these technologies enable renewable electricity to reach the hydrogen-production process in a usable and controlled form.

The Kakinada project demonstrates how renewable electricity can be converted into green molecules for industrial use. The combination of renewable generation, energy storage, large-scale electrolysis and ammonia production creates a pathway from clean power to applications where direct electrification may not always be practical.

Within this wider ecosystem, the rectifier transformers provide an essential connection between the electrical network and the electrolysers. By helping deliver power at the voltage and in the form required for electrolysis, the Hitachi Energy solution supports the production of green hydrogen and, ultimately, renewable ammonia at scale.

The project also illustrates the importance of collaboration across the value chain. By combining Hitachi Energy’s transformer expertise with Green Power’s power-conversion system capabilities and the wider project partners’ electrolysis and ammonia-production technologies, the Kakinada facility can help advance lower-carbon industrial production and the development of an international renewable-ammonia supply chain.

title: Q&A: How host countries can strike better deals with cleantech manufacturers | News
description:
Sahay tells Dialogue Earth why the Cleantech Manufacturing Foreign Direct Investment database is important.
Understanding what drives investment can help countries make better choices as they try to transition away from fossil fuels, he explains.
Tim Sahay: We tracked every single solar manufacturing plant, wind manufacturing plant, battery manufacturing plant and EV manufacturing plant that is owned by a foreigner.
That creates powerful political coalitions inside countries that want to go green and act on climate.
And we are now also seeing the benefits of acting on climate in the form of local jobs, local profits, local political interests, local labour unions.
text:
China’s green technologies have become a modern obsession. But solar panels, wind turbines and batteries are not the only things moving around the world from China. The factories that make them are spreading too.

As China’s domestic market has become saturated and new trade barriers limit direct access to key markets, businesses have looked overseas for opportunities and taken their manufacturing with them. This is reshaping not just local economies but also national industrial strategies and global climate policies.

Tim Sahay, co-director of the Net Zero Industrial Policy Lab at Johns Hopkins University in the United States, has been following this money with his colleagues. They have built a database that tracks trends in global clean technology investment since 1996.

Sahay tells Dialogue Earth why the Cleantech Manufacturing Foreign Direct Investment database is important. Understanding what drives investment can help countries make better choices as they try to transition away from fossil fuels, he explains.

The interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Dialogue Earth: Could you describe what you did for this work?

Tim Sahay: We tracked every single solar manufacturing plant, wind manufacturing plant, battery manufacturing plant and EV manufacturing plant that is owned by a foreigner.

There are a lot of factories being built, but people don’t know quite where. They don’t know how much capital is being invested, by whom, in what places, and why. There are over 1,000 such FDI factories, adding up to about US$435 billion in pledged capital in 66 destination countries.

And people have a vague sense that, well, China is the leader, but they don’t know precisely when China became the leader or which countries are attracting Chinese firms to build their own cleantech manufacturing base.

These are all important questions for the future of climate politics, for the future of climate and development, for how industries get social licence to operate in different parts of the world. They matter for this clean technological revolution that is reshaping not just every country’s electricity and factories but also ownership, profits and control.

And you found this huge leap in investment after 2017?

Yes, and that is the most staggering finding, the scale of this build-out after 2017.

Before 2017, there used to be green FDI. But it was built by the winners of the 20th-century manufacturing world. The Japanese, Germans and Americans were building plants overseas in other countries, but it was just a handful — of the order of a few billion dollars a year.

“

‘The green component of overall global FDI was about 2 per cent before 2017. Since then, it has become 20 per cent.’

Tim Sahay, co-director of the Net Zero Industrial Policy Lab.

And what happens after 2017 is immense change in the amount of plants being built overseas. In our dataset, we are tracking over 650 plants that have been built just in the last five years alone, with a surge especially in battery and EV factories.

Whenever you have big numbers like these, you want to know as a share of what? And what we found is the green component of overall global FDI used to be about 2 per cent before 2017. Since then, it has become 20 per cent of all of the manufacturing activity happening overseas.

And who is behind that massive jump? Is it mainly driven by Chinese FDI?

First, in the early 2010s, it was the US, Japan and Germany. China passing its big industrial policies in 2015 — the Made in China policy — really focused and honed in on batteries and EVs in particular.

When we get to the 2020s and during the pandemic, China puts in another enormous surge of investment into solar, wind, EVs and batteries, and you get this enormous domestic industrial boom inside China. By 2022, those same companies are now leaping out and building factories outside the country.

China ends up becoming about 40 per cent of our dataset, which is about US$130 billion of investment outside China.

And what is motivating where in the world investments go?

There are four big buckets of motivations for firms to build plants outside their home country.

The first is they are attracted to large consumer markets. That’s exemplified by the United States becoming the largest destination for foreign-owned factories. But it’s also true for large developing countries like Brazil or India that are receiving a lot of factories.

The second big reason is third-market access, if that destination country has an existing trade relationship with the United States or Europe in the form of a free-trade agreement. Morocco, Korea, Oman. Those factories are not being built to sell an EV or a battery to Moroccans. Morocco is a production base, an export base to access the European market or the American market.

The third one is that companies want to be close to raw materials. And if a country has raw material power — which many developing countries do have — then they can basically tell foreign investors, “We are not going to give you access to our raw mineral ores unless you build us a processing factory.. That is exemplified by Indonesia, which has bargained its vast nickel reserves in exchange for battery factories and nickel-processing facilities, again from the Chinese and the Koreans.

Lastly, there is the industrial policy of host countries themselves, who are trying to attract these foreign companies to set up shop with attractive subsidies in order to meet their own climate and development goals.

You said the database will help people see what kind of deals are being struck. How can they use that information?

One of our primary reasons was a benchmarking so that countries can avoid a race to the bottom, and instead have a race to the top in terms of standards that they impose on foreign investors in return for subsidies.

You can have very extractive outcomes, where there are very few local jobs being created, environmental standards are not met, labour standards are not met. Essentially, the companies get a free pass, a special economic zone or an industrial park, and they do precious little for the country’s own development or its own workers or its environment. That’s a race to the bottom.

The developmentalist outcome is a race to the top outcome, where countries compare what companies are doing, and what standards are being set by other countries, and benchmark themselves against them.

Is there an example of how that can work?

Spain versus Hungary.

CATL, the largest battery manufacturer in the world, built up a factory in Spain that is a 50-50 joint venture with a European automaker, Stellantis. The Spanish were able to negotiate their subsidies in return for requirements on technology transfer, domestic workers, R&D in Spain and local firms’ participation in the supply chain.

The Hungarians under Viktor Orbán essentially created a special economic zone, absolutely a race to the bottom, to attract CATL and Korean battery manufacturer Samsung. They essentially said you can do whatever you want with very low environmental standards, which provoked an enormous social protest movement in Hungary.

Knowing what the same company, CATL, is doing in two different places is important. What I would want is our database to be used by development planners, industrial policymakers, unions and environmental advocates to hold these companies to account and to hold their governments to account.

What do you think the investment that you’re seeing means for our ability to combat climate change?

It is unambiguously good that more and more countries are now participating in a global green industrial build-out, making climate and development, climate and prosperity work together instead of against each other. That creates powerful political coalitions inside countries that want to go green and act on climate.

And we are now also seeing the benefits of acting on climate in the form of local jobs, local profits, local political interests, local labour unions. And so that is entrenching climate in the politics of countries and in their development and growth models, which is just unambiguously good.

title: IFC, EAAIF, Ninety One Commit USD 88.6 Million To Clean Power In Ghana's Manufacturing Hub
description:
EAAIF and Ninety One commit USD 18.15 million in senior secured debt as part of a USD 60.6 million co-financed debt package with IFC and IDA.
The commitment comprises USD 15.65 million from EAAIF and USD 2.5 million from Ninety One’s Africa Credit Opportunities strategy.
IFC led the financing for the USD 88.6 million project’s first phase, providing a direct loan of USD 24.2 million and partnering with EAAIF, Ninety One, and the World Bank’s International Development Association (IDA) to mobilise the remaining USD 60.6 million debt package.
LMI Holdings’ USD 28 million equity investment completed the total financing package.
The project offers a model for transition finance in sub-Saharan Africa by enabling backward integration for LMI Holdings and supporting the decarbonisation of Ghana’s main industrial manufacturing hub.
text:
EAAIF and Ninety One commit USD 18.15 million in senior secured debt as part of a USD 60.6 million co-financed debt package with IFC and IDA.

The USD 88.6 million project will finance a 100MWp solar PV plant in Dawa as Phase 1 of an intended 200MW project, delivering cleaner, lower-cost power to more than 95 industrial tenants across Ghana’s key industrial zones in Dawa and Tema.

The transaction is structured as a corporate facility with LMI Holdings’ subsidiaries, Solar for Industries Ltd (SFI) and Enclave Power Company Ltd (EPCL), helping expand private power generation and distribution in Ghana.

The Emerging Africa & Asia Infrastructure Fund (EAAIF), a Private Infrastructure Development Group (PIDG) company managed by Ninety One, has announced a USD 18.15 million loan commitment to locally owned conglomerate LMI Holdings through its subsidiaries, Solar for Industries Ltd (SFI) and Enclave Power Company Ltd (EPCL). The facility will support the development and operation of a 100MWp ground-mounted solar PV plant in Dawa, Ghana, supplying lower-cost clean energy to more than 95 energy-intensive manufacturers in the Tema Free Zone.

The commitment comprises USD 15.65 million from EAAIF and USD 2.5 million from Ninety One’s Africa Credit Opportunities strategy. SFI is a newly formed special-purpose vehicle dedicated to solar generation, while EPCL is LMI’s main operating utility. As Ghana’s first and only licensed private electricity distributor, EPCL helps reduce state off-taker risk and offers a privately led utility model for Africa’s clean energy transition.

IFC led the financing for the USD 88.6 million project’s first phase, providing a direct loan of USD 24.2 million and partnering with EAAIF, Ninety One, and the World Bank’s International Development Association (IDA) to mobilise the remaining USD 60.6 million debt package. LMI Holdings’ USD 28 million equity investment completed the total financing package.

The 100MWp solar facility is expected to generate 129.5 GWh annually in Phase 1. EPCL will wheel the power approximately 40 kilometres across the national grid under a Transmission Service Agreement (TSA) to the Tema Free Zone, supplying more than 95 industrial tenants across the Tema Free Zone and Dawa Industrial Zone.

The project offers a model for transition finance in sub-Saharan Africa by enabling backward integration for LMI Holdings and supporting the decarbonisation of Ghana’s main industrial manufacturing hub. With exports accounting for approximately 35% of Ghana’s GDP, stable, lower-cost solar power for key exporters in sectors including cocoa, cement, and steel will help reduce indirect greenhouse gas emissions, strengthen corporate green credentials, and support Ghana’s export competitiveness.

The project also supports Ghana’s Renewable Energy Master Plan, which aims to increase the share of renewables in the national generation mix to 10% by 2030. It also aligns with PIDG’s 2023–2030 Strategy, which prioritises climate finance, market transformation, and private capital mobilisation across emerging markets.

Martijn Proos, Co-Head of Emerging Market Alternative Credit, Ninety One, the fund manager of EAAIF, said: “This transaction highlights EAAIF’s commitment to financing transition infrastructure that accelerates green growth and delivers affordable, reliable power to Ghana’s manufacturing heartland.”

Mr. Kojo Aduhene, Founder, Chairman, and CEO of LMI Holdings, said: “Following the success of our 16.8MWp Helios Solar rooftop project in Tema, we are privileged to be part of this structural evolution in Ghana’s power and energy sector by effectively demonstrating how private innovation can drive the nation’s sustainable economic development.”

name: Congress
title: A sweeping permitting reform bill is headed to the House. Critics want to stop it - NPR
description:
The Senate passed a bipartisan permitting reform bill that supporters say will pave the way for much needed infrastructure projects.
But critics argue it will do so at the expense of the environment, tribes and public lands.
They want the House to either fix or reject the bill before the year ends, as NPR's Rachel Treisman reports.
But critics say it would weaken bedrock environmental and historic preservation laws, including by limiting input from tribes and the public.
Rachel Treisman, NPR News.
text:
Transcript

JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:

With just weeks left in its term, Congress could reshape the country's physical landscape for generations. The Senate passed a bipartisan permitting reform bill that supporters say will pave the way for much needed infrastructure projects. But critics argue it will do so at the expense of the environment, tribes and public lands. They want the House to either fix or reject the bill before the year ends, as NPR's Rachel Treisman reports.

RACHEL TREISMAN, BYLINE: Last week, the Senate passed a bill that aims to speed up the approval process for federal infrastructure and energy projects, from wind turbines to data centers. It's called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, and it's nearly 500 pages long.

XAN FISHMAN: This isn't just, like, a mushy, middle, moderate, do-nothing bill. Like, it's actually a big-deal bill.

TREISMAN: Xan Fishman leads the energy program at the Bipartisan Policy Center.

FISHMAN: At its heart, it's about trying to take a permitting system which has just grown out of proportion and make sure that it's protecting the environment but getting to a yes or no answer in a reasonable amount of time.

TREISMAN: Supporters of the bill say it will improve America's aging grid while creating jobs and lowering electricity bills. But critics say it would weaken bedrock environmental and historic preservation laws, including by limiting input from tribes and the public.

WESLEY FURLONG: From our perspective, there are no pros. There are only cons.

TREISMAN: Wesley Furlong is a senior staff attorney with the Native American Rights Fund. He says tribes were not consulted about the bill, even though it threatens their lands and sovereignty.

FURLONG: It will fundamentally change the federal government's relationship with Indian tribes in a really negative way.

TREISMAN: The bill was introduced in the Senate at the end of September. Critics say lawmakers didn't give it the time or debate it deserved in the lead-up to the midterms.

FURLONG: And then they come back, and the first thing that they do the Monday after the election is vote on this bill.

TREISMAN: The Senate first voted to bypass the committee markup process, skipping hearings and rewrites. The bill passed last week with only one amendment by a vote of 62 to 33. It now heads to the House. President Trump has said he will sign it. It's also backed by an unusual alliance of energy companies, big tech, some Democrats and a mix of labor and environmental groups.

SARAH GONZALEZ-ROTHI: People see a very slim chance to address a very urgent issue, and they think they've found the way to do it.

TREISMAN: Sarah Gonzalez-Rothi served as the senior director for water at the White House Council on Environmental Quality under President Biden. She opposes the bill, as do hundreds of climate, tribal, public health, historic preservation and civil rights groups.

GONZALEZ-ROTHI: I think the way they've come up with doing it is looking at rose-colored glasses at text that, if they are wrong, has such severe consequences that it could actually make things worse.

TREISMAN: For example, the bill would make data centers cover their own energy costs, but critics say it could make it easier to build data centers on public lands. And as Furlong says it has provisions that would make it harder to challenge or change permits once they're issued.

FURLONG: Courts can't really stop these projects, and future administrations can't stop them, and so as soon as they are permitted, we are stuck with them forever.

TREISMAN: The House could vote in the days after Thanksgiving. Some key Democrats have already said they oppose the bill, but it's not clear if they have the support or time to revise it before Congress adjourns on January 3.

Rachel Treisman, NPR News.

title: Cranberries With a Side of Solar - Mother Jones
authors: Sarah Shemkus, Nick Lund, Julian Spector, Maddie Oatman, Dan Friedman, Sophie Hurwitz, Rachel Santarsiero, Marianne Szegedy-Maszak, Julia Métraux, Mariana Duran

text:
This story was originally published by Canary Media and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

It’s cranberry season in southeastern Massachusetts. At bogs throughout the region, growers are collecting the ruby-red berries destined for holiday cakes, juice bottles, and cans of jellied sauce. At two farms, however, the harvesting process looks a little different: Pickers are navigating equipment around metal poles in the shade of solar panels.

The two bogs are the first in the country—perhaps the world—to grow cranberries beneath an operating solar installation. This fall marks the second season cranberries have been harvested from beneath the panels.

“We are literally proving it can be done,” said Prateek Tare, co-founder and executive vice president of Distributed Energy Infrastructure. His company constructed the two projects—a 4.4-megawatt array paired with a 13.5-megawatt-hour battery in the town of Kingston, and a 1-MW solar array in neighboring Plymouth.

Solar development is a major part of Massachusetts’ plan to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2050. The state has offered solar incentives since 2001, evolving and expanding them over the decades to drive even more development.

However, the question of where to site solar projects has become a major point of contention in the densely populated and heavily wooded state. Building on rooftops and parking lots in developed areas can increase costs and limit generation capacity. But proposals for arrays on previously undeveloped land often spark protests from locals worried about the character of their community and environmental groups opposed to disrupting ecosystems. Using pre-cleared farmland has potential, but raises concerns about taking agricultural acres out of production. Many of these same dynamics are at play in communities across the US.

One of the solutions Massachusetts has been encouraging is agrivoltaics, or dual-use solar, which involves building solar panels above active agricultural operations. This strategy, which is gaining traction nationwide, allows farmland to be used for energy generation even as livestock graze or crops flourish beneath the elevated arrays.

In 2018, Massachusetts became the first state to offer a financial boost to dual-use solar projects like these. The state’s solar incentive program pays participants a set rate for every kilowatt-hour of electricity they generate; an array with a capacity between 1 MW and 5 MW currently gets a base rate of 23.17 cents. Agrivoltaic projects get an extra 9 cents per kilowatt-hour.

That can be enough money to attract developers interested in leasing land for solar arrays or, less commonly, buying property outright with an agreement to keep it in agricultural use. Farmers who agree to lease are also generally paid for their services maintaining the landscape around the panels and poles.

In Kingston and Plymouth, clean energy developer Greenbacker Renewables bought the land, which had been home to cranberry-growing operations for decades, from farmers who were ready to get out of the business. Greenbacker then worked with Distributed Energy Infrastructure to build the arrays, and hired Iain Ward, a solar consultant and longtime cranberry farmer in the area, to manage the growing operations. Both projects use a community solar model, selling power to customers interested in the lower prices and environmental benefits offered by renewable energy.

Solar can be particularly advantageous for cranberry farmers in Massachusetts, which grows more of the fruit than any state other than Wisconsin. While sheep farms and cornfields can often be sold to housing or commercial developers, cranberry bogs are protected wetlands: Even if they go out of production, they cannot be built on. Not all bogs are well placed to connect to the grid, but for those that are, solar panels can be a financial lifeline.

“This is a farm viability opportunity,” Ward said.

Figuring out how to build a solar array over a cranberry bog was a unique puzzle, Tare said. The first challenge was the foundations. For most solar arrays, the foundation goes 8 to 10 feet into the ground, he said. But in a cranberry bog, you have to go well past that to find ground solid and stable enough to hold the pilings. It took some trial and error to find the right machine to sink piles that deep. Wiring couldn’t be buried in the boggy ground, so it had to be hung overhead.

“You’re trying to figure it out from a farmer’s perspective,” said Tare, who worked closely with Ward on the design of the two projects.

The resulting installations have photovoltaic panels mounted 10 feet off the ground on an axis that allows them to tilt throughout the day to follow the sun. Pilings are spread farther from each other than standard so that harvesting equipment can be moved freely through the bog.

These successes in Kingston and Plymouth have led to more agrivoltaic opportunities for Tare’s company, including arrays in apple orchards, a cattle pasture, and a Christmas tree farm. Preliminary work is also underway at another bog.

Meanwhile, a stalled cranberry solar project in the nearby town of Carver could be resuscitated. Five years ago, a different pair of bogs there were set to become the nation’s first cranberry agrivoltaic operations. The arrays were built, and crops are growing beneath them, but the company behind the developments went bankrupt before they could get up and running. Today, the new bog owner has ​“every intention to finish them,” Ward said.

“They’re not a failure,” Ward said. ​“There is an opportunity for them to be finished.”

Tare expects future cranberry projects to get easier each time, as the company carries forward the lessons it learns. Though momentum has been slow so far, Ward expects development to accelerate soon. “It is picking up steam, and the lessons learned have been significant,” he said. ​“When you change a paradigm it takes a little time.”

name: North Carolina American Energy
title: US midterms and mining policy: oversight risks and takeaways for project teams
description:
US midterm elections in 2026 are expected to leave core mining policy—permitting, public land management, tariffs and critical mineral financing—largely unchanged, while sharply increasing congressional scrutiny of how tools like Defense Production Act Title III, DOE Loan Programs Office facilities, EXIM and DFC funding are allocated.
Oversight committees are preparing GAO-backed reviews of expedited authorities, Pentagon equity stakes in rare-earth producers, and structures such as EXIM’s US$12 billion “Project Vault”, with a focus on conflicts of interest, beneficial ownership and technical readiness.
Mining companies receiving federal support, operating on BLM lands, or involved in Latin American, African or Central Asian critical mineral ventures should expect hearings on FPIC, tribal consultation, NEPA emergency reviews and China-linked midstream exposure.
The focus on NEPA, BLM and FAST-41 in this piece aligns with several other US critical minerals items in our coverage where permitting timelines, rather than geology or capex, are now the primary gating factor for lithium and copper projects in states like Idaho and North Carolina.
Mention of Latin America, Africa and Central Asia alongside US agencies such as EXIM and DFC reflects a pattern in our critical minerals coverage where US-backed finance is increasingly directed to overseas graphite, cobalt and rare earths supply, potentially diluting capital available for purely domestic projects.

name: EVs
title: Can electric vehicles work in Nigeria? - New African Magazine
description: The removal of subsidies may make electric vehicles a more attractive option for Nigerian drivers, but the industry still has to confront several structural challenges to succeed. A four-year-old company is betting on a comprehensive approach.
text:
On May 29, 2023, as part of a raft of reforms introduced by the then newly elected Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, subsidies on fuel products in Nigeria were removed.

This was a profound economic shock for motorists in the oil-rich nation who had become accustomed to paying less than market rates for petroleum products. In the event, however, it may well turn out that the death of petroleum subsidies may give life to an electric vehicle boom in Africa’s most populous country and its third-largest economy.

Electric vehicles are, for now, a minority pursuit in Nigeria. Of the 720,000 vehicles that are (mostly) imported into the country every year, only about 1% are electric, according to the Rocky Mountain Institute, an energy non-profit based in the US.

However, a local ecosystem of sorts is evolving. From assembly and charging stations to battery swapping, local companies, some with foreign partners, are slowly building capacity to support the growth of the market.

Among them is Qoray Mobility & Energies, which is attempting to address the question from a wider perspective. It is not enough, they contend, for the cars to be available. “Clean tech in Africa scales when it becomes affordable and financeable, not when it becomes more advanced,” says Olabanjo Alimi, the founder.

That is indeed the central question that companies trying to put electric vehicles on Nigeria’s roads must confront. For potential users in Nigeria and indeed other African countries, the calculus rests on whether they can pay for the cars and whether there is a support system of charging solutions and after-sales service that can support their use.

That is the challenge that Qoray is building its business model around. “The vehicles are the visible part. The business is the software and the financing underneath,” Alimi says. That will be an important differentiator in the emerging market for electric mobility in a West African economic powerhouse.





Qoray is not entering an empty field. Already, Spiro has made its mark as one of Africa’s largest electric-mobility companies, combining vehicle manufacturing, battery swapping and financing. Its Nigerian operations are part of a much broader continental strategy, with the company investing heavily in manufacturing and swapping infrastructure.

MAX offers another model. The Lagos-based mobility company has evolved from motorcycle ride-hailing and vehicle subscription into a wider platform incorporating electric vehicles, fleet management, battery swapping, charging and financing. It has attracted significant international capital to expand its fleet and infrastructure.

Then there are the companies addressing the opportunity purely from the manufacturing side. Innoson Vehicle Manufacturing is developing locally assembled electric models, while SAGLEV and JET Motor are building domestic EV assembly capacity. Other companies are concentrating on charging, battery swapping or renewable-energy infrastructure.

The competitive landscape is itself a demonstration of the immense potential that the market has. It also means Qoray cannot win simply by putting more electric vehicles on Nigerian roads.

The company began life in 2024, initially signing with Chinese manufacturers and launching what it describes as Nigeria’s first commercial EV charging station. In 2024, it expanded its charging infrastructure, started assembling electric tricycles and financed solar projects. By 2025, the company says it had assembled 2,000 electric tricycles locally and deployed more than 2,000 EVs overall.

The company also reports having mobilised more than ₦20bn ($15m) in clean-energy and sustainable-mobility assets and installed more than 7MWh of decentralised solar systems, remarkable results for a relatively young company.

Rather than merely selling vehicles, it is attempting to build a comprehensive system that holds the hands of consumers from buying through the life of the vehicle. “You cannot sell EVs without places to charge them,” Alimi points out.

Payment is also another crucial piece of the jigsaw in selling new technologies in Africa. There are some pioneers that Qoray can learn from, however. Solar companies such as Sun King and M-KOPA demonstrated that affordable payment models and customer data can be as important as the solar panels themselves. Qoray is attempting to apply a similar logic to mobility.

An important part of Qoray’s proposition is its Superdash platform, which enables digital payments, financing and collections. The idea is to give financiers more data than they typically have when lending to car buyers.

A driver without a formal credit history may still generate a predictable daily income. If the vehicle is connected to a digital platform that records its earnings and repayment behaviour, the lender has more information with which to assess the risk.

“We build the technology that makes an unbankable sector bankable,” Alimi says of the Superdash platform. He argues that data can build the bridge between the financier and the borrower who may not meet conventional standards of scrutiny but nevertheless has the income that makes him a worthy risk.

“Data is what turns an asset nobody wants to finance into one a bank will fund. With real-time visibility and revenue assurance, we can finance a ₦4m electric 3-wheeler for someone with zero credit history. They repay over 2-3 years from daily earnings, while earning 3-4x the national minimum wage. That’s how we turn riders into owners and how we make them real stakeholders in the energy transition story,” Alimi explains.

If the model works at scale, its significance could extend beyond EVs, but that proposition still has to be proven. Success will not merely be about how many vehicles Qoray has deployed, but how many are generating revenue, whether repayments are made on time, what default rates look like and how much it costs to recover a vehicle when a customer fails to pay. Those are the metrics that will determine whether Qoray’s financing proposition is genuinely disruptive.



There is also the matter of electricity. Nigeria’s notoriously unreliable power supply means that charging electric vehicles is a more complex and expensive exercise than it should be. Qoray appears to have addressed this in its business model. It is combining solar energy generation, storage and charging into a comprehensive system that keeps cars on the road.

Battery swapping is also another option that it supports, particularly for motorcycles and three-wheelers. Instead of waiting for a battery to charge, a driver can exchange a depleted battery for a charged one and return to work within minutes. This is important, especially for commercial drivers who have to remain on the road to meet their sales targets and make their repayments.

While Qoray and others in the nascent sector can deploy these innovations, a lot will also depend on the policy environment in which they operate. Operators may thus welcome the government’s efforts, including the proposed Electric Vehicle Transition and Green Mobility framework, which includes incentives for EV users and investors, including tax and duty measures, support for charging infrastructure and provisions aimed at developing domestic vehicle and battery manufacturing.

The government has also expanded its Presidential Initiative on Compressed Natural Gas to include electric vehicles, signalling an openness to include electric mobility firmly in its overall transport strategy.

If there is one country to emulate, it is Ethiopia, which has become today the fastest-growing market for electric vehicles on the continent, outpacing many European peers. In 2024, more than 60% of new cars sold in Ethiopia were fully electric.

It is said that 5% of cars are electric today in the country, well ahead of global averages. But it is on two wheels where the biggest change is taking place, and this is prevalent throughout the continent. Spirio, for example, aims to build an EV ecosystem across the continent, starting on two wheels.

For Qoray and the other players in the sector, this could be a flip in their ambitions, which they have in abundance.  Alimi says the company wants two out of every ten EVs in Nigeria to be Qoray-powered within five years, while also considerably scaling up their distributed solar installations.

Achieving that would require the company to move into an entirely different league. It would also need significantly more capital, increased manufacturing capacity, a nimble commercial operation and enhanced partnerships with financial institutions to support buyers.

Alimi, however, is determined and committed. “Africa must build its own solutions. “Nobody is coming to save us,” he says. It is a refreshing, if not completely original, take, but in the end, it is the results that will matter. As he himself recognises, in the EV industry, building the vehicles is often the easy part. The real task will be to make clean technology affordable and achievable in a largely informal economy. And they are only just getting started with that.

text:
Texas A&M engineering students are building next-generation vehicles in the four-year EcoCar Innovation Challenge. The competition is underway in Atlanta, Georgia, where the Texas A&M team is working on a 2026 Jeep hybrid.

Why it matters

The program gives students hands-on experience with real vehicles through a real-world development process guided by industry professionals. It also prepares a new generation of engineers for the automotive workforce as the industry shifts toward electrified vehicles.

The EcoCar Innovation Challenge spans four years and includes students from 20 universities working on a 2026 Jeep hybrid. The source does not report the team's competition standings or the vehicle's measured performance.

Students work with real vehicles through a development process guided by industry mentors, including Jon Darrow of Stellantis' North American Tech Center. Students also tackle off-road scenarios as part of the challenge.

title: If politicians really want to cut heating bills they need to trust in green energy - The Conversation
description:
In a 2025 global Ipsos survey, 64% of adults said failing to act on climate change would hurt future generations.
And in 2026 around 60% of American adults think global efforts will not be enough to avoid the worst effects of climate change.
But very few politicians make the point that the cost-of-living crisis would be much worse without green policy.
This year, green energy investment is expected to reach US$2.2 trillion (£1.68 trillion) – almost double the investment in fossil fuels, and double the global investment in artificial intelligence.
And the consequences of climate change, such as flooding and high temperatures, are among the top reasons people leave their home countries.
text:
This year’s United Nations climate summit, Cop31, ended in Antalya without a deal.

It appears that the world’s politicians and policy makers have collectively moved on from building a global coalition against climate change, just as its effects are becoming impossible to ignore.

Yet the public have not stopped worrying. In a 2025 global Ipsos survey, 64% of adults said failing to act on climate change would hurt future generations.

And in 2026 around 60% of American adults think global efforts will not be enough to avoid the worst effects of climate change.

But perhaps the biggest hurdle to making more climate-friendly changes is the current cost-of-living crisis. It appears to be politically difficult to tell cash-strapped voters to be more environmentally friendly.

Opponents of policies tackling climate change, including British and European right-wing parties and Donald Trump, seem to have effectively persuaded a majority of the public that it is impossible to make climate-friendly choices and keep your bills down. In 2026, 62% of the UK public expected net zero – Britain’s route to climate neutrality – to increase their bills in the short run.

Read more: Cop31: Why the UN climate summit ended in victory for fossil fuel producing nations

Voters often tend to overestimate how much they would lose from a carbon tax, and to underestimate how much others care.

But despite this, people are starting to notice that climate action cannot be blamed for an economic and environmental crisis fuelled by gas and petrol prices.

The 62% share of voters who think net zero increases their bills is the lowest on record. And 51% expect net zero to be good for the economy in the long run – only 24% think it will hurt it.

Politicians are right to be careful about what voters will accept. French president Emmanuel Macron has learned the hard way, after ten years of public protests, that taxing petrol is unpopular. In Milan, some voters owning polluting cars said they were likely to vote for the far right when the city banned their vehicles from the city centre.

But very few politicians make the point that the cost-of-living crisis would be much worse without green policy.

Cost-of-living crisis is a fossil fuel crisis

In 2021, Russia supplied around 40% of the EU’s pipeline gas imports. Scrambling to replace these imports with liquefied gas from Qatar and the US has sent energy prices through the roof.

Because of its past dependency on Russian fossil fuels, Europe now pays around ten times more than the US for the same quantity of gas. These high prices have hurt the economy and pushed up inflation.

Every unit of electricity generated by wind turbines, solar panels and nuclear power plants cuts consumer bills.

Those resources saved £5.9 billion in gas imports for the UK at the start of the Iran conflict when shipping was blocked through the Strait of Hormuz. Every time no gas is needed to produce electricity, prices come down.

Significant economic damage can be caused by ignoring this. It has been clear for some time now that the future is made of electric cars and batteries. Yet European carmakers still lobby for a perpetual delay of the transition.

This strategy is costing jobs today, having transformed Europe’s leading carmakers into global laggards.

And it also hurts consumers. The world’s cheapest electric cars are made in China. EU efforts to protect what remains of its car industry using tariffs mean they cost consumers 45% more.

Britain has so far avoided the extra cost. But the EU is pushing it to impose similar tariffs.

Business is investing in green energy

But global investors are not as backward-looking as governments. This year, green energy investment is expected to reach US$2.2 trillion (£1.68 trillion) – almost double the investment in fossil fuels, and double the global investment in artificial intelligence. More than 90% of large-scale renewable investment in 2025 was cheaper than the cheapest fossil fuel alternative.

The same self-interested approach could apply to ordinary citizens.

An electric car costs less to run than a petrol one. But delays in the transition mean there are still too few charging points to make it practical for everyone.

Another factor is that in England, for instance, road congestion is taking an increasing toll on the economy, and this primarily affects motorists. Even in the US, where public transport accounts for less than 1% of journeys, when subways are not working, these few passengers switching to the car increase road congestion by 47%.

Pro-car lobbies do try to block investment in walkable cities and public transport. Will they take responsibility for the projected 85% increase in British road congestion by 2040?

Migration is very high on voters’ list of concerns, higher than any other in some British polls. And the consequences of climate change, such as flooding and high temperatures, are among the top reasons people leave their home countries. Without international cooperation on issues like water and energy, the flow of people wanting to escape poverty to live in less affected countries is likely to go up.

We live in an ageing world, and it appears that people are increasingly scared of change. The global mood feels protectionist and as crises accumulate, many want to put their own country first.

Very few environmental activists or politicians seem to speak to these instincts.

But green electricity makes you independent from foreign dictators, global cooperation should make migration more manageable, and many of our current problems come from ignoring climate change, not from trying to address it.

name: EPA
title: States split over EPA's proposal to drop greenhouse gas rules for power plants
description: States are divided over the Trump administration’s proposal to repeal remaining greenhouse gas standards for power plants, while medical groups warn of public health dangers.
text:
Illinois will not participate in the federal government’s sc…

Before the turkeys went into the oven, hundreds of local run…



States are divided over the Trump administration’s proposal to repeal remaining greenhouse gas standards for power plants, while medical groups warn of public health dangers.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency released a proposal that contends it doesn’t have the authority to regulate power plant greenhouse gas emissions to address global climate change concerns. This would rescind the agency’s own findings in 2015 that it had the authority to do so under a section of the Clean Air Act.

If finalized and upheld by courts, the move would repeal remaining power plant greenhouse-gas emissions regulations for fossil fuel-fired electric generating units. The agency said it aims to maintain affordability and reliability of energy supplies.

It follows a final EPA rule that went into effect Monday that partially repeals 2024 emissions standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants as well as requirements that states develop related plans.

The proposed rule would go even further. A comment period for that measure closed earlier this month, generating over 165,000 comments, including from states, health and environmental groups, and private citizens. States, public health and environmental groups have also filed legal challenges to the EPA’s rollbacks.

Some states said the EPA’s regulatory authority over fossil fuel emissions is overreach and would harm their economies, while others said such federal regulations are needed as states, tribes and local governments grapple with the health and costs of air pollution and climate change.

In a joint comment submitted last week, the attorneys general of 22 mostly Democratic-leaning states plus Washington, D.C., and officials from New York City, Denver, Chicago and California’s Bay Area wrote that climate change is costly to state and local governments and imposes public health dangers.

In the over-160-page letter, the states pointed to a consensus study report from the National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine last year that concluded that human activity-initiated greenhouse gas emissions will lead to more climate change, “with the severity of expected change increasing with every ton of greenhouse gases emitted.”

The attorneys general wrote that EPA is pushing its proposal despite such “unequivocal evidence, and the increasingly devastating climate harms” that state and local governments experience. They added that the proposal “has no basis in fact or law, would result in large-scale emission increases that will harm the States and Local Governments, and is an unlawful abdication of EPA’s responsibility under the Clean Air Act to protect public health and welfare.”

But the attorneys general of West Virginia and 24 other largely Republican-leaning states  contended that the proposal “properly reverses course on past EPA attempts to reshape the Nation’s electricity-generating sector.”

It would “allow States to secure affordable, reliable, and environmentally responsible energy for their residents,” they added.

North Dakota, which signed on to that letter, also submitted its own comment saying it strongly supports the supplemental proposal. The state noted that it has a specific interest in the issue, since it collects a coal conversion tax when power is generated from coal within the state, which then helps pay for school districts and other government services.

The National Tribal Air Association, an organization of 162 tribes focused on air quality management policies and programs for American Indian and Alaska Native tribes, groups that have been disproportionately affected by emissions, submitted a comment opposing EPA’s actions.

“Many fossil fuel-fired electric generating units are located on or near American Indian and Alaska Native communities, and Tribes and Tribal members may disproportionately bear the public health and environmental consequences of the increased greenhouse gas and other emissions that this proposal would permit,” the association wrote.

Carrie Jenks , executive director of the Environmental & Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, noted that some ongoing court cases may affect the EPA rules. Jenks also said that states that support EPA’s authority to regulate greenhouse gases are typically the ones that also support their own authority to regulate them within their own programs.

“Then there are groups of states that want EPA’s authority to be limited, if not eliminated,” adding that others argue that states can’t regulate their own sources of greenhouse gases.

Over 70 medical and public health organizations also submitted comments in opposition to the rollbacks. The groups included the American Medical Association, the American Lung Association, and several state American Academy of Pediatrics chapters, who argued the changes would harm the health of children and other vulnerable groups.

“Children, older adults, people who work outside, individuals with preexisting health conditions or who are pregnant, low-wealth communities and communities of color often experience disproportionate health harms stemming from climate change and extreme weather events,” the groups wrote .

Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassanein@stateline.org .

Three shifts explain the demand. The first is cheaper chemistry. The second is heavier vehicles: global electric truck sales exceeded 400,000 units in 2025, doubling year on year, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). The third is the grid: the IEA reports that 108 GW of battery storage capacity was added globally in 2025, roughly 40% more than in 2024. The constraint is cost and concentration, not demand. LFP Moves from Alternative to Default

The most important change inside the battery is chemistry. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries accounted for more than 55% of global electric vehicle battery deployment in 2025, up from nearly half in 2024, and for more than 90% of stationary storage installations, according to the IEA. The reason is cost. LFP battery packs were on average more than 40% cheaper per kilowatt-hour than nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) packs in 2025, and LFP prices fell by more than 15% in 2025 while NMC prices fell by less than 5%. LFP also avoids nickel and cobalt in the cathode, which removes exposure to those price swings and adds thermal stability.

NMC is not going away; it remains relevant where higher energy density matters. Newer chemistries are advancing alongside. Sodium-ion batteries are moving closer to production as a lower-cost option that performs better in cold climates, and solid-state batteries and silicon anodes are in development to address charging performance, material availability, and safety. The report notes that competitive differentiation increasingly depends on cost per kilowatt-hour, cycle life, safety, charging speed, and manufacturing yield.

Trucks and the Grid: Demand Moves Beyond Passenger Cars

Electric trucks are now the fastest-growing major vehicle category for battery demand. Global sales of electric heavy freight trucks rose from approximately 84,000 in 2024 to 230,000 in 2025, electric truck sales in Europe increased 40% to nearly 17,000 units, and one in four trucks sold in China in 2025 was electric. Battery-swap-capable trucks represented around 15% of China's electric truck sales. Trucks accounted for approximately 8% of global EV battery deployment in 2025, up from less than 5% in 2024. Battery energy storage systems (BESS) are the other growth engine. Utility-scale systems accounted for approximately 87 GW of the 108 GW added globally in 2025, and the price of battery storage has fallen by more than 90% between 2010 and 2025. About 90% of new battery storage projects in 2025 were for energy shifting, up from roughly 40% in 2015, meaning batteries are increasingly used to store electricity when it is cheap and release it when it is needed. Electric vehicle batteries: Global demand for EV batteries reached around 1.2 TWh in 2025, growing nearly 30% from the previous year.

Challenges Facing the Lithium-Ion Battery Market

Cost and profitability are the central pressures. Regional pack-price gaps hurt manufacturers in North America and Europe, and many leading battery material producers have operated at a loss since 2023. Cathode active materials account for approximately 40–50% of NMC cell production costs and 25–30% for LFP, which makes materials pricing critical. Higher lithium prices in early 2026 are expected to affect production costs, investment decisions, and competitiveness, and the IEA's Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2025 projected that announced mining projects could meet only around 60% of lithium requirements in 2035 under its stated-policies scenario.

Building new factories is hard. Battery manufacturers generally need production yields above 90% to compete, which makes defect reduction, automation, and process optimization essential, and a new plant requires large investment, qualified labor, stable raw material supply, and time to reach production efficiency. The collapse of a Swedish cell manufacturer shows how difficult it is to control defects while expanding several supply-chain stages at once. Supply-chain concentration, raw material price swings, recyclability requirements, and the localization of manufacturing remain the industry's defining issues.

title: Pat Woods questions cost of New Mexico clean energy mandates - Albuquerque Journal
description:
A family asks those questions before any big purchase.
Yet New Mexico is charging ahead with one of the most expensive undertakings in state history without clear answers to either.
What will it take, through 2050, to build the power plants, power lines and batteries these mandates require?
How much of that is new cost the mandates create?
Why should families pay for Big Tech?
text:
What will it cost, and who will pay?

A family asks those questions before any big purchase. A farmer asks them before buying a tractor. Yet New Mexico is charging ahead with one of the most expensive undertakings in state history without clear answers to either.

I have spent decades in agriculture, and nobody values clean air, clean water and healthy land more than the people who make a living from it. But caring about the environment is not the same as signing a blank check.

State law requires our largest utilities to be 100% carbon-free by 2045, and rural co-ops by 2050. State rules call for 82% of new cars delivered to New Mexico dealers to be zero-emission by 2032, with quotas for commercial trucks too. These deadlines look less like engineering and more like activism. They were championed by advocates of a radical Green Agenda who set the goal first and left the cost for later.

So I've asked the administration and the Legislative Finance Committee for a plain accounting before lawmakers commit New Mexicans to more. The questions are simple.

How much will it cost? What will it take, through 2050, to build the power plants, power lines and batteries these mandates require? How much of that is new cost the mandates create?

What happens to my electric bill? Public Service Company of New Mexico customers have already seen two rate increases in a year and a half, about $12.46 a month for the average home. Even Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham has warned of "dramatically rising energy prices." What will bills look like for families, farms and co-op members in five years, and in 25?

Who else pays? What will it cost taxpayers to replace state vehicles and highway equipment? What will it cost the trucker, the delivery company and, if farm equipment is next, the farmer?

Will the lights stay on? What does it cost to keep power reliable in a July heat wave or a January cold snap, when demand peaks and the sun and wind don't cooperate?

Why should families pay for Big Tech? Data centers and other big new users should cover the grid costs they create. Even the governor's own energy council agrees.

Is there a cheaper way? Smarter use of off-peak power and faster permitting could save ratepayers money while still protecting our water, tribal sovereignty and private property.

If the mandates' backers are confident in their plan, they should welcome these questions. If the numbers hold up, show us. But if the answer is higher bills, shakier power and less competitive businesses, all to meet a deadline set on a political timeline, New Mexicans deserve to ask: Is that really worth all of this?

Good intentions are not a budget. Before Santa Fe locks families into decades of payments, the people making those payments deserve to see the bill.
