In Yemen, a World Bank-backed off-grid program provided solar systems to households and critical facilities and benefited almost 800,000 people during its first phase.
Survival Solar Is Not Yet an Energy System It would be easy to present Syria’s numbers as an uncomplicated renewable-energy success.
text:
Most power systems are built from the center outward. A government plans power stations. A utility signs fuel contracts, builds transmission lines and connects households. Large investors finance assets expected to operate for decades. The model assumes a state capable of making decisions, enforcing contracts and protecting infrastructure.

In fragile and conflict-affected countries, those assumptions can disappear before electricity demand does.

Syria offers a striking alternative. Solar panels now cover rooftops around the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus and are increasingly visible across Aleppo and other cities. This is not the result of a carefully executed national energy-transition strategy.

It is what happens when households stop waiting for the power system to recover. According to the latest IRENA capacity statistics, Syria’s off-grid solar capacity increased from 249 MW in 2022 to 2,060 MW in 2025. That is an eightfold increase in three years. Around a quarter of Syrian households are estimated to own some form of solar equipment.

The growth reveals an overlooked advantage of renewable energy. Solar is not only becoming cheaper than conventional generation. It can be deployed in pieces small enough to function when the institutions normally responsible for energy supply do not.

A Solar Panel Does Not Need a Functioning Utility

A new gas or coal plant is not merely a generator. It requires fuel imports or domestic production, creditworthy buyers, pipelines or ports, large construction contracts, transmission capacity, and a state capable of protecting the entire chain.

A rooftop solar system requires a panel, inverter, wiring, and usually a battery. That does not make it simple or universally affordable. But it radically lowers the minimum viable scale of investment. A household can purchase one panel. A shop can add enough capacity to run refrigerators and lights. A clinic can power medicine storage and communications. A village can build a mini-grid without waiting for a national transmission project. Related: Goldman Sachs Sees U.S. Natural Gas Demand Surging on Data Center Boom

Each installation is small. Collectively, they can become a power fleet. This is what happened in Syria. Years of war, sanctions, fuel shortages, damaged infrastructure and economic collapse reduced state electricity to only a few hours per day in many areas. The country now generates less than one-fifth of its pre-war electricity, while roughly two-thirds of the grid is damaged or requires major repair.

Yet household electricity investment did not stop. It changed technology and scale. Solar’s share of Syrian generating capacity has consequently become significant, even if its share of actual generation is lower and difficult to measure. Planned gas-fired plants may reduce renewables’ percentage of total capacity as the national system is rebuilt. They will not remove the panels already installed or the economic logic behind them.

Once people have experienced producing their own electricity without buying diesel every day, returning entirely to dependence on an unreliable utility becomes unlikely.

Lebanon Shows This Is a Regional Pattern

Neighboring Lebanon followed a similar path after its financial and electricity sectors collapsed.

Decentralized solar capacity increased from roughly 90 MW in 2020 to around 1,200–1,300 MW by 2024. Homes, businesses and municipalities combined panels with batteries to escape long blackouts and expensive neighborhood diesel generators.

Again, the solar boom did not initially represent a well-managed transition. It represented private adaptation to public failure.

But emergency investment changed the country’s energy economics permanently. Solar companies, installers, equipment importers and maintenance networks expanded. Consumers learned to manage batteries and time their demand. A technology once treated as supplementary became basic infrastructure.

The pattern extends beyond the Levant. In Yemen, a World Bank-backed off-grid program provided solar systems to households and critical facilities and benefited almost 800,000 people during its first phase. In conflict-affected Goma in the Democratic Republic of Congo, a 1.3-MW solar mini-grid continued supporting water, communications and businesses when other electricity supplies failed during the city’s violent takeover.

These are not substitutes for peace, functioning government or national infrastructure. They are ways of delivering energy before all three arrive.

Survival Solar Is Not Yet an Energy System

It would be easy to present Syria’s numbers as an uncomplicated renewable-energy success. They are not.

Many Syrian families cannot afford solar. Complete household systems reportedly cost thousands of dollars in a country where incomes are extremely low. Wealthier families obtain electricity, refrigeration, internet access, and cooling, while poorer households remain dependent on a weak grid or dangerous improvised equipment.

Quality also varies. Weak regulation creates markets for inferior panels, unsafe wiring, counterfeit equipment, and batteries with short lifetimes. Lead-acid batteries create health and waste risks when recycling is informal. Individual systems often curtail valuable midday electricity because households cannot sell it to neighbors or feed it into a functioning network.

Decentralization can therefore produce resilience without equity and capacity without coordination.

The answer is not to replace rooftop solar with another centralized fossil system. It is to organize the distributed assets that already exist.

The Next Power Grid May Be Built From the Rooftops Inward

Syria and Lebanon now have the foundations of a bottom-up electricity system. The next step is moving from isolated household systems to neighborhood and community networks.

Mini-grids can connect solar owners with households that cannot afford complete systems. Shared batteries can store surplus electricity more efficiently than thousands of poorly utilized individual units. Schools, water pumps, clinics and telecommunications can act as anchor customers, giving developers predictable demand and improving essential services.

This requires more institution-building than the first rooftop boom. Governments or local authorities need technical standards, licensing rules, consumer protection and tariffs that allow operators to recover investment without exploiting captive customers. Systems must be designed so they can eventually interconnect with a restored national grid rather than becoming incompatible electrical islands.

Development finance can accelerate the shift. Instead of concentrating support only on large generation plants, donors can provide guarantees, results-based finance and affordable credit for certified household systems, productive-use equipment, mini-grids and batteries. Aggregating thousands of small installations can turn assets too small for conventional project finance into investable portfolios.

National infrastructure still matters. Syria needs repaired transmission, stable utility-scale generation and professional system operation. New gas plants may provide dispatchable power during reconstruction, while larger solar and wind projects can reduce fuel exposure.

The future is not centralized or decentralized. It is a hybrid system in which national grids provide scale and balancing while distributed renewables provide speed, resilience and local access.

Modularity Is a Form of Energy Security

Large power projects work best where institutions are strong. Small renewable systems matter most where they are not.

A central power station can be disabled by a fuel shortage, damaged transmission line or political decision. Thousands of rooftop systems are harder to stop simultaneously. They require no continuous fuel convoy and can be repaired, expanded and replaced one component at a time.

That resilience has value far beyond carbon reduction.

Syria’s rooftop revolution was born from failure, not climate policy. It should never be used to excuse the collapse that made it necessary. But it demonstrates that the energy transition can reach places conventional infrastructure finance considers uninvestable.

Solar did not wait for Syria’s grid to return.

The task now is to make sure nobody has to wait for a private rooftop to receive electricity.

title: Meeting the growing global demand for sustainable aviation fuels - Bruegel
description:
Even at this early stage, the global SAF market is valued at more than €4 billion .
Governments are setting SAF requirements In 2025, SAF supplied 0.6 percent of global aviation fuel demand, up from 0.1 percent in 2021 (Figure 1).
Figure 1: Global sustainable aviation fuel production, million tonnes (Mt) undefined Source: Bruegel and Rhodium Group based on IATA factsheet of June 2026, ‘Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF)’, https://www.iata.org/en/iata-repository/pressroom/fact-sheets/fact-sheet-sustainable-aviation-fuels/.
SAF investment has grown, but technology rollout remains slow Global SAF investment has grown rapidly since 2018.
Figure 2: Global SAF investment, $ billions, 2024 prices undefined Source: Bruegel and Rhodium Group based on the Clean Investment Monitor.
text:
Conflict in the Middle East and the disruption it is causing to oil shipments and refining have, among other things, pushed up jet fuel prices, renewing interest in alternatives, particularly sustainable aviation fuels (SAF). These fuels could in principle reduce aviation’s dependence on oil and its associated emissions. Aviation accounted for about 2 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions in 2024 (Mobir et al, 2026), with 40 percent of the sector’s emissions coming from long-haul flights, though they make up for just 5 percent of flights worldwide (Teoh et al, 2024).

SAF is the main alternative to fossil jet fuel, especially for long-haul routes . Its feedstocks are biomass, waste or captured carbon dioxide rather than fossil energy sources. Burning SAF still generates emissions, but from feedstocks that have recently absorbed carbon from the atmosphere, which can substantially reduce lifecycle emissions. SAF can be blended with conventional jet fuel.

A growing number of governments require, or plan to require, rising shares of SAF use at airports and for regional flights, although questions remain about its cost and environmental impact. SAF production has risen significantly, but it still made up only 0.6 percent of global jet fuel consumed in 2025. Even at this early stage, the global SAF market is valued at more than €4 billion .

Here, we present data on investment in SAF production facilities worldwide, showing that investment grew rapidly between 2018 and 2024 before slowing. Four-fifths of present production capacity has been built since 2018. Unlike other clean technologies, production is spread out geographically. However, it is concentrated on one technology route (hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids, HEFA), future growth of which may be constrained by limited waste oil and fat feedstock availability. Further growth will require other production pathways to reach commercial maturity.

Governments are setting SAF requirements

In 2025, SAF supplied 0.6 percent of global aviation fuel demand, up from 0.1 percent in 2021 (Figure 1). The International Air Transport Association (IATA) projects that SAF will continue to grow in 2026, reaching 2.4 million tonnes of production, roughly 0.8 percent of global jet fuel production . Government requirements and voluntary commitments drive almost all this growth in demand, as SAF costs an estimated two to five times more than conventional jet fuel (EASA, 2026a) .

Figure 1: Global sustainable aviation fuel production, million tonnes (Mt)

undefined

Source: Bruegel and Rhodium Group based on IATA factsheet of June 2026, ‘Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF)’, https://www.iata.org/en/iata-repository/pressroom/fact-sheets/fact-sheet-sustainable-aviation-fuels/.

The European Union has the strictest SAF obligations. The EU ReFuelEU Aviation regulation (Regulation (EU) 2023/2405), which also applies in Switzerland and Norway, requires fuel suppliers to increase the share of SAF delivered to airports from 2 percent of all aviation fuel in 2025 to 6 percent in 2030 and 70 percent in 2050, with a sub-target of 5 percent for synthetic SAF (produced from hydrogen and captured carbon dioxide) by 2035. The EU exceeded its 2025 target, at a SAF share of 2.79 percent (EASA, 2026b). The EU also allocates free carbon allowances, tradable via the EU emissions trading system, to airlines to cover part of the price difference between SAF and conventional jet fuel. The United Kingdom has similar rising minimum shares for SAF, high penalties for non-compliance and price guarantees for domestic production. Japan, South Korea, Brazil and Singapore are all debating or introducing SAF obligations .

The United States and China have no requirements. Instead, the US supports production through tax credits that run until 2029, although the maximum credit for SAF fell by more than 40 percent in 2026. To qualify, feedstocks must originate in North America . In China, adoption and certification are voluntary .

SAF investment has grown, but technology rollout remains slow

Global SAF investment has grown rapidly since 2018. A total of $22 billion has been invested across 240 projects tracked by the Clean Investment Monitor . To measure ongoing investment in SAF production (Figure 2), we spread investment values evenly over the duration of facility construction. Actual annual investments grew from $150 million in 2018 to nearly $5 billion at a peak in 2024, but slowed in 2025.

Figure 2: Global SAF investment, $ billions, 2024 prices

undefined

Source: Bruegel and Rhodium Group based on the Clean Investment Monitor. Note: total facility capex, including co-produced renewable diesel, spread over construction periods; operating and under-construction projects only.

While investment has slowed, new SAF production projects continued to be announced in the first half of 2026, representing over two million tonnes of annual SAF capacity in Brazil, the US, the UK, Belgium, Denmark and France. Existing production capacity is substantially underutilised, with 1.9 Mt produced in 2025 compared to 7.3 Mt of capacity (our estimate). Many plants can switch output from SAF to renewable diesel and favour the latter because road transport policy makes it more profitable. This weakens the current investment case for new projects.

SAF production is geographically widespread

SAF production is concentrated in the US, China and Europe, each accounting for about a quarter (1.6-1.9 million tonnes) of operational global capacity. Most of the remaining capacity is in the rest of Asia. Planned projects could spread production further, particularly to Brazil, Canada, Australia and Oman.

Figure 3: SAF production capacity by geography and project status, million tonnes of SAF

undefined

Source: Bruegel and Rhodium Group based on Rhodium Clean Investment Monitor. Note: assumes 40 percent production of SAF from flexible HEFA facilities, where the split between SAF and renewable diesel or other clean fuels is not specified. Excludes speculative/intended facilities, feasibility studies and cancelled facilities.

About 2.5 million tonnes in additional SAF production capacity is expected from projects that were under construction as of the second quarter of 2026. The largest share of capacity under construction – about 850,000 tonnes – is in China, followed by Brazil (370,000 tonnes). Europe has 250,000 tonnes currently under construction from projects in Germany, Portugal, Romania and Spain. An additional 115,000 tonnes is expected from five projects currently under construction in the US.

The outlook for SAF production is significantly more geographically diversified than for solar panels, wind turbines and batteries manufacturing, for which China’s share is greater than 75 percent and as high as 90 percent (Figure 3). By contrast, China accounts for only 16 percent of SAF capacity, when under-construction and announced projects are accounted for. The US and Europe would be home to the largest shares of SAF production capacity, 32 percent and 22 percent, respectively. However, SAF production relies upon feedstock supply, and in this respect, concentration risks might still develop. For example, in 2025, 85 percent of EU SAF feedstocks originated outside the EU, with China accounting for 61 percent of the total (EASA, 2026b).

Figure 4: Regional distribution of global production capacity, including planned capacity

undefined

Source: Bruegel and Rhodium Group based on Rhodium Clean Investment Monitor. Note: the figure includes capacities that are operational, under construction and announced.

SAF feedstocks must move beyond used oils and fats

While SAF production is geographically diverse, it is technologically concentrated. Almost all (95 percent) of operational and under-construction SAF capacity globally uses the hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA) route, which converts oils and fats, mainly used cooking oil and animal fats, into jet fuel (Figure 5).

Figure 5: Global SAF production capacity by technology and status

undefined

Source: Bruegel based on Rhodium Clean Investment Monitor.

HEFA-based production can grow further, but ultimately the supply of used oils and fats is limited. Projections suggest that meeting global SAF targets for 2030 would require at least twice as much used cooking oil than can be collected in the US, Europe and China combined . In Europe, planned HEFA-based SAF capacity of 3.9 million tonnes by 2035 is roughly twice what estimated regional feedstocks could supply (SkyNRG and ICF, 2026). Better collection can increase waste supply but will still hit limits (IATA, 2025).

For SAF to grow further, pathways that use other feedstocks will need to develop (Figure 5). Alcohol-to-jet (AtJ) converts alcohols such as ethanol into jet fuel. A first commercial-scale plant in the US began production in 2025 . Ethanol supply chains are already well established for biofuel for road transport. Production using biomass Fischer-Tropsch (FT) synthesis can convert agricultural and forestry residues or parts of municipal waste into jet fuel .

Biomass-based SAF (including from waste) can reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions because the carbon released during combustion was previously absorbed by plants. These lifecycle savings depend on what would otherwise happen to the feedstock and the land used to grow it . In an extreme illustrative case, clearing a forest to grow fuel crops has disastrous biodiversity and climate consequences (Fargione et al, 2008). Certain animal fats and other biomass are already used in other markets, meaning diverting them to produce SAF would increase demand for substitutes and cause indirect land-use change and greenhouse gas emissions.

Substantial potential nevertheless remains in ‘low-risk’ wastes and residues, such as municipal organic waste and forestry residues, that can be collected sustainably, with limited competition from other uses. Taken together, maximising use of all the biomass resources available for HEFA, AtJ and biomass-FT would increase feedstock availability substantially. For example, low-risk feedstocks in the EU could support enough SAF production to meet 26 percent of the region’s jet-fuel demand by 2035 (O’Malley and Baldino, 2024).

Environmental and social risks make robust sustainability rules and their enforcement essential as SAF production expands. EU SAF obligations, for example, exclude food- and feed-crop fuels from blending targets and require eligible biofuels to meet sustainability and lifecycle emissions-saving criteria. Reliable checks on feedstock origin are also needed to prevent virgin vegetable oils being passed off as used cooking oil (T&E, 2024, 2025).

Finally, power-to-liquid (PtL), or synthetic SAF, combines hydrogen with captured carbon dioxide. This avoids biomass feedstock constraints but is currently the most expensive route. Production requires large volumes of low-carbon electricity to produce hydrogen, which can account for two-thirds or more of production costs. Carbon dioxide can be captured from industrial sources, biogenic sources or directly from the atmosphere . Globally, just 0.124 million tonnes of capacity is under construction (Figure 5).

Overall, future growth in SAF use and production depends on bringing alternative production technologies to commercial scale and maintaining government support to bridge the cost gap with fossil jet fuel. Across all pathways, SAF plants also produce valuable co-products including diesel, naphtha and liquefied petroleum gases. Sales of these products improve the economics of SAF production.

name: Clean Energy
title: BAAJA: Can America build bigger and faster without sacrificing environmental laws?
authors: Ellis Juhlin, Nora Mabie, Nick Mott, Robert Chaney, Victoria Eavis
description:
Due to the sluggish pace of permitting, bill proponents argue that big, ambitious projects sometimes take years and have sky-high price tags.
Below, we break down what BAAJA means for four pieces of legislation that shape federal projects in Montana.
Provisions in BAAJA change existing policy to narrow which projects receive that kind of review, expand agency authority and shorten tribal consultation timelines.
Mark Mariano with the conservation and education organization Montana Wetlands and Waterfowl says wetlands are already threatened and BAAJA would worsen the problem.
Like NEPA and NHPA, BAAJA limits the existing authority tribes and states have to intervene when a federal project could affect their waters.
text:
A sprawling bill that passed the Senate last week is set to overhaul arguably the least sexy aspect of government regulation: permitting. But critics say it could have enormous impacts on Montana’s environment that could be hard to reverse.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA (pronounced “Baja,” as in the peninsula) for short, aims to speed up the permitting process for federal projects — including on public land — whether for mines, data centers or renewable energy. Due to the sluggish pace of permitting, bill proponents argue that big, ambitious projects sometimes take years and have sky-high price tags.

But opponents worry it comes with too many sacrifices that could hurt the country’s wildlife and waterways, and roll back both public input and tribal involvement in federal decisions. In its 417 pages, BAAJA targets the country’s bedrock environmental laws, which were created decades ago to check development that was wreaking havoc on our natural places.

“It’s really just a rollback of the ideals of the ‘60s and ‘70s that people should get to have a voice in the process of these things,” said Deborah Sivas, a professor of environmental law at Stanford University.

Sivas argues that BAAJA strikes at the heart of democratic participation. The bill’s sweeping changes cut the ability of the public to participate in and challenge federal decisions, particularly on the grounds of their environmental impacts.

Both Montana senators voted for the bill. Outgoing U.S. Sen. Steve Daines said on X the bill will “deliver major wins for Montana” and “boost critical projects that create good-paying Montana jobs and strengthen made-in-Montana energy.”

Fourteen Democrats voted for BAAJA in the Senate. But its path forward is less clear in the House of Representatives. BAAJA is one of several pieces of legislation lawmakers are scrambling to pass before a new Congress is sworn in early next year. If the House, which is on recess until Dec. 1, amends the bill, it would need to go back to the Senate for approval.

Below, we break down what BAAJA means for four pieces of legislation that shape federal projects in Montana.

1. The National Historic Preservation Act and threats to tribal sovereignty and cultural heritage

Typically, anytime state or federal dollars are involved in a major project, such as building a new road, pipeline or solar field, the agencies involved are required to consult with tribes whose land and resources may be affected. That kind of consultation, required through a provision of the National Historic Preservation Act, has meant tribes like the Blackfeet have been able to weigh in on projects including improvements to the St. Mary Canal and construction near Glacier National Park on ancestral homelands, among other things. Provisions in BAAJA change existing policy to narrow which projects receive that kind of review, expand agency authority and shorten tribal consultation timelines.

Tribes and tribal organizations nationwide, including the National Congress of American Indians, Native American Rights Fund and National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers, have condemned BAAJA, saying it threatens cultural heritage and tribal sovereignty.

Gheri Hall, co-director and deputy of compliance for the Blackfeet Tribal Historic Preservation Office, said that without consultation, “cultural sites can be permanently destroyed before we have the opportunity to identify, document and protect them.”

“There are so many cultural sites out there that we don’t even know exist,” Hall said. “So if we lose that information, it destroys evidence of where our ancestors lived, where they traveled, where they gathered plants. It destroys sacred places that are associated with our spiritual practices and traditions.”

When the government consults tribes on decisions that impact them, Hall said, the government is recognizing tribes’ unique status as sovereign nations. Weakening that process, she added, “diminishes our ability to protect the cultural heritage.”

While dozens of tribes oppose the bill, the Crow Tribe in southeast Montana is among the few in the country to publicly support it. Coal has long been an economic driver for the tribe, and while Crow Chairman Frank White Clay emphasized the importance of tribal participation in an October letter to several U.S. senators, he also wrote that red tape is slowing progress.

“For too long, overlapping federal reviews, bureaucratic delays, and unpredictable permitting timelines have hindered investment in Indian Country,” White Clay wrote.

Dean Nicolai, who chairs the Tribal Historic Preservation bachelor’s degree program at Séliš Ksanka Ql̓ispé University (formerly Salish Kootenai College), said he doesn’t believe lawmakers who claim the goal of the bill is to create jobs.

“It’s about money,” Nicolai said of BAAJA. “It’s just about corporations making more money. It’s nothing new for tribal peoples.” — Nora Mabie

2. The National Environmental Policy Act and public participation

BAAJA looks to change one of the country’s bedrock environmental protection laws: the National Environmental Policy Act. Passed in 1970, NEPA is often referred to as the “look before you leap” doctrine. It requires federal agencies to consider the environmental impacts of development before the agency makes decisions. BAAJA would limit the kinds of projects that require a NEPA review, narrow the scope of what is considered in an environmental analysis, and shorten the amount of time an agency has to complete that analysis.

“It makes NEPA a dead letter,” said Martin Nie, a natural resource policy professor at the University of Montana. BAAJA’s weakening of NEPA, he said, is one more erosion of the policy which has already been narrowed in scope in recent years.

“What we’ve seen over two years, is just this Gilded Age type of corruption and agency capture, and giveaways of our public lands to private interests,” Nie said. “That is the defining feature of this administration, and this bill does the same thing.”

The NEPA process is how the public knows what the potential impacts of a development project could be and where people can weigh in with concerns. “[NEPA] provides Montanans a seat at the table,” Nie said, “for everything from oil and gas leases, to timber sales to recreation development.”

In Montana, NEPA has had tangible impacts including with the expansion of Highway 93, which runs from the Bitterroot Valley through Flathead Valley and on to Eureka.

“That was originally proposed as a sort of mega highway,” Nie explained. “It was going to go through the refuges with no wildlife provisions. With tribal leadership using NEPA, we have all those overpasses along 93, and we had all the signage and a rerouting.”

The changes also included the addition of the prominent wildlife crossing built over the highway to help grizzly bears safely move across. The public comment that drove those changes couldn’t happen if NEPA changes as proposed by BAAJA.

The bill also limits how projects could be subject to judicial review, further preventing scrutiny of development. Nie said it could have devastating effects for years to come.

“Chances are an agency won’t have to do any NEPA analysis at all,” he said. “And if it does screw up its NEPA analysis, the project still moves forward.” — Ellis Juhlin

3. Wildlife and the Endangered Species Act

Supporters like the Pacific Legal Foundation say BAAJA would “prune our regulatory thicket” and make the Endangered Species Act “more transparent, predictable and efficient,” while environmental groups across the country have condemned the ESA rollbacks the permitting bill would legislate. For more than 50 years, the act has worked to stave off extinction for the country’s most imperiled species.

BAAJA’s ESA impacts are manifold, but potentially the largest comes in the form of consultation, according to Chris Westfall, senior government relations legislative counsel with Defenders of Wildlife. When a federal project proposes an action that could impact a threatened or endangered species — for example, a logging project that could harm elk or lynx — the party proposing it must consult with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. But BAAJA upends that half-century-old relationship.

“The bill is a solution in search of a problem,” Westfall said.

Approximately 90% of ESA consultations currently take less than two weeks to complete, according to a Defenders of Wildlife analysis. The remaining 10% take about two months. That doesn’t amount to meaningful delays in projects, Westfall argues.

Under new definitions in the bill, states can act as consultants instead of the federal government. Westfall says that will overwhelm state governments and create even lengthier review processes, creating more of a regulatory burden rather than reducing it. Worse yet, he argues, project sponsors might leverage that ability to seek state sign-off when the federal government might not greenlight a project.

“We worry that could be bad for wildlife across the board,” he said.

BAAJA also shortens the timespan the consultation process can be litigated, exempts highway projects entirely from ESA requirements, changes the definition of what constitutes the “best available science,” and institutes restrictions on updating permits when a project could impact more listed species than initially anticipated. Westfall said the overhaul fits in with bigger-picture rollbacks over the last two years, which sought to redefine “take” under the ESA.

“This is just another attack on the Endangered Species Act that works in tandem with those other attacks that we’ve seen from the administration,” he said. “It’s really infuriating.” – Nick Mott

4. CWA and Wetlands

BAAJA proposes several large changes to the Clean Water Act, another 1970s-era policy regulating pollution in waterways, everything from wetlands to rivers and streams to lakes. BAAJA changes sections of the CWA regarding water-quality certification and wetland permitting. The bill would remove or weaken protections for small wetlands under 2 acres and would make it easier for developers to drain or fill in wetlands of any size.

Mark Mariano with the conservation and education organization Montana Wetlands and Waterfowl says wetlands are already threatened and BAAJA would worsen the problem.

“If you weigh it all out and you’re losing protections on things that are already getting hammered,” he said, “the U.S. itself loses more than 60,000 acres of wetlands a year. That’s the trajectory we’re already at.”

Despite making up just 4% of land cover in Montana, wetlands provide a variety of ecosystem services to humans and wildlife. Mariano says Montana can’t afford to lose more.

“In western Montana, we have turned a spongy system historically into a flashy, more desert-like system,” he said. “As we get warmer and drier, our main reservoir of water is our snowpack, and it flows off the landscape as fast as possible. Wetlands slow that down, and they act as a sponge.”

Wetlands of any size hold water on the landscape longer for farmers and ranchers, and act like nature’s kidneys by filtering pollution, Mariano explained. “Water that spends time in a wetland can lose contaminants from industrial situations like we have here in Butte.”

When it comes to wildlife needs, Mariano said “a smaller wetland is better,” in that it creates habitat for ducks and geese to nest in, and places that migratory birds can rely on as critical stopover points as they cross the continent.

Like NEPA and NHPA, BAAJA limits the existing authority tribes and states have to intervene when a federal project could affect their waters. If a company wanted to build a dam or a pipeline in Montana, for example, the state could review whether or not that would impact water quality for a river or lake. If it had concerns, it could stop the project from certification.

text:
As a kid in Cincinnati, Tom Jorling’s parents told him to stay away from the Ohio River. These days, he says, the same water that was too contaminated to touch is filled with luxury boats.

“Now I go back there, and you think you’re in Nantucket,” he said.

Jorling helped write the laws that made that happen, drafting the Clean Air Act and the Clean Water Act as counsel for Republicans on the Senate Public Works Committee in the 1970s. Those years were intense, he said, but unusually collaborative and productive, with lawmakers on both sides of the aisle backing major policy change.

This year, another group of lawmakers is pushing forward a similarly transformative, bipartisan bill: an effort to revise bedrock environmental laws, including the Clean Water Act, to reform the permitting system. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which passed in the Senate last week and now faces a fight in the House, is meant to speed up energy projects by reducing red tape.

Trending

Jorling says those pushing the bill forward are leaving behind decades of progress.

“They’re turning a blind eye to the success that [the Clean Water Act] had, and then trying to claim that the provisions of these successful laws are preventing things, which I don’t believe they are,” he said.

Proponents of permitting reform say it takes too long to build energy projects. On the left, lawmakers are thinking about the solar, wind and batteries that could help transition the grid away from climate-warming fossil fuels and the power lines that could carry that electricity across the country. On the right, wins for gas pipelines, power plants and mines are fueling support, along with the Trump administration’s push for “energy dominance.” Affordability concerns have allowed legislators to unite forces.

Jorling is sympathetic to the idea of permitting reform. After helping to create the Clean Water Act, he joined the Environmental Protection Agency and later led New York’s Department of Environmental Conservation. He also worked in the private sector in environmental affairs at International Paper.

He said he saw firsthand how “bureaucracies can gum up the process.” He said he would support permitting reform that required decisions to be made more quickly. But changing federal environmental regulations, he said, would be more ideological than effective, especially because so much permitting happens at the state and local levels.

“It’s the local permitting and approvals that are the problem, and they’re using the guise of the federal government to try and put limitations on those state bodies or local government bodies in order to bypass them,” he said. “I’m not sure how that’s consistent with old-time Republican or conservative orthodoxy.”

The bill would make changes to a host of environmental laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act. The section changing the Clean Water Act has concerned some Democrats, who say it could degrade the environmental gains of the past five decades.

The Clean Water Act made it illegal to discharge pollution into waters without a permit. The law also requires states, territories and tribes to maintain water quality standards. Under the Clean Water Act, citizens can sue polluters or the EPA for failing to carry out their responsibilities under the law.

The permitting reform bill would establish firm timelines for reviews that apply to infrastructure running across bodies of water. It would also limit states and tribes to only consider water quality issues spelled out in the law when issuing Clean Water Act certifications. Transmission lines and gas pipelines would only need reviews of specific pollution discharge points, not the full range of the project.

Jorling said during the development of the Clean Water Act, lawmakers wanted to protect states’ authority in the permitting process and ensure that the federal government didn’t override that authority. The law allows states to set more restrictive standards than the federal government.

Jorling said provisions protecting states’ rights were “strongly advocated by Republicans.”

“Now to hear Republicans basically trying to limit or control the states’ rights is quite surprising,” he said.

The permitting bill also would double the amount of time pollution discharge permits are valid, from five years to 10 years. Jorling called that “unnecessary,” saying the reason for the five-year term was to encourage periodic upgrades as technology improves.

“It’s another effort to lock in substandard performance,” he said. “I just find that sort of baffling, because industry always says, ‘Well, we want to do the best we can with the best technology.’”

The bill would also create a 150-day statute of limitations for lawsuits that have to do with pollution from dredging or filling wetlands or water bodies, and limit lawsuits so they can only be filed by those who have commented on a project during the public comment period on the issue they are suing over.

Jorling said the change seemed like an effort to protect the EPA from legal issues.

“I’m suspicious that they’re trying a backdoor way of relaxing the requirements,” he said.

The permitting bill’s sponsors have defended its provisions, saying the changes to the Clean Water Act are common-sense solutions to the ways that law can get in the way of development, and won’t gut environmental protections.

“Gas pipelines and transmission lines have both fallen victim to state politics on occasion,” Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island) said in a floor speech on the bill. “The changes in this subsection are designed to focus states on the Clean Water Act essential: ensuring water quality.”

But some Democrats have pushed back on the Clean Water Act changes. Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vermont) voted against the bill, saying one of his concerns was its effect on clean water resources. He filed amendments that were not included in the bill that would have protected states’ abilities to consider a wider range of effects to water.

In the House, Rep. Maxine Waters (D-California) noted her concern over the way the Clean Water Act provisions could limit communities’ ability to challenge projects or provide input. Rep. Mike Levin (D-California) said the bill would limit California’s ability to protect its water.

Whitehouse has said the bill would help push the clean energy transition forward, paving the way for more renewables moving more quickly onto the grid. But when it comes to the Clean Water Act provisions, Jorling said he didn’t know of any renewable energy projects that required a Clean Water Act permit and called the argument that law holds renewable energy back a “political ploy.”

“I don’t think the Clean Water Act is much of a barrier,” he said.

title: 10 States With Extra Registration Fees for Hybrids - NewsBreak
description:
Several US states impose special registration fees or road usage charges on certain hybrid and alternative-fuel vehicles.
Arkansas Arkansas is among the states that impose additional registration charges on certain hybrid and electric vehicles.
Hybrid owners should understand that registration costs can include more than the standard annual vehicle registration charge.
Registration charges can change through legislative updates, so relying on older fee schedules may lead to inaccurate cost estimates.
Colorado Colorado has introduced additional registration charges for certain vehicles that use alternative energy sources.
text:
Hybrid vehicles have become a popular choice for drivers seeking better fuel economy and lower fuel expenses. These vehicles combine a gasoline engine with an electric motor, reducing their reliance on traditional fuel. However, owning a hybrid can come with additional costs that buyers may not expect.

Several US states impose special registration fees or road usage charges on certain hybrid and alternative-fuel vehicles. These charges help replace revenue traditionally collected through gasoline taxes. The rules, fee amounts, and vehicle classifications differ by state, making it important for buyers to understand local registration requirements before purchasing a hybrid.

1. Arkansas

Arkansas is among the states that impose additional registration charges on certain hybrid and electric vehicles. The state collects special fees from qualifying vehicles to help maintain transportation infrastructure and compensate for reduced gasoline tax revenue.

Hybrid owners should understand that registration costs can include more than the standard annual vehicle registration charge. Depending on the vehicle’s classification, an additional alternative-fuel fee may apply.

Arkansas has historically used separate fee categories for hybrid and fully electric vehicles. These categories reflect differences in how vehicles consume fuel and use electricity.

The additional charge helps support road maintenance, highway improvements, and other transportation projects. Gasoline-powered vehicles contribute to these expenses through fuel taxes collected whenever drivers purchase petrol.

Hybrid vehicles generally use less gasoline than conventional cars. This means their owners may contribute less through traditional fuel taxes, creating a funding gap for transportation departments.

Drivers purchasing a hybrid in Arkansas should check the latest requirements through the Arkansas Department of Finance and Administration. Registration charges can change through legislative updates, so relying on older fee schedules may lead to inaccurate cost estimates.

Before completing a vehicle purchase, buyers should also determine whether their particular model qualifies as a conventional hybrid or plug-in hybrid. Vehicle classification can affect the registration requirements and applicable charges.

2. Colorado

Colorado has introduced additional registration charges for certain vehicles that use alternative energy sources. These charges help fund transportation projects and account for the reduced gasoline tax contributions associated with more fuel-efficient vehicles.

The state collects transportation-related fees through its vehicle registration system. Hybrid and electric vehicle owners may encounter additional charges beyond the standard registration expenses, depending on their vehicle classification.

Colorado uses several transportation funding mechanisms to maintain highways, bridges, and local roads. These expenses remain necessary regardless of whether drivers use gasoline, electricity, or a combination of both.

Traditional vehicles contribute to road funding through state fuel taxes. Hybrid vehicles generally purchase less gasoline, which can reduce their contribution to these revenue streams over time.

The additional registration charges help distribute transportation funding responsibilities across different categories of vehicle owners. This approach allows the state to collect revenue from drivers who rely less heavily on gasoline.

Hybrid owners should review Colorado’s Department of Revenue vehicle registration information before estimating their annual ownership expenses. The applicable charges can depend on the vehicle’s fuel classification and registration details.

Buyers should also distinguish between standard hybrids, plug-in hybrids, and fully electric vehicles. These categories may receive different treatment under state transportation fee rules, making accurate classification important.

description:

Araceli Becerril, Corporate Responsibility Director, L'Oréal Groupe Mexico, adds that integrating social inclusion with environmental stewardship underpins the group's L'Oréal for the Future framework.
The corporate milestones come as consumer goods manufacturers in Mexico accelerate circular packaging transitions ahead of stricter federal environmental compliance rules.
L'Oréal Groupe structured its Mexican sustainability initiatives across four operational pillars: Circular Economy and Waste Recovery.

text:
L'Oréal Groupe reported progress on its sustainability strategy in Mexico, confirming its two local plants operate on 100% renewable energy to produce over 420 million units annually, alongside 84 refillable products and social programs supporting over 46,000 jobs nationwide.

___

L'Oréal Groupe reported key milestones in its environmental and social sustainability strategy in Mexico, confirming that its two domestic manufacturing plants operate with 100% renewable energy to produce more than 420 million units annually. Presented during the company's sustainability forum in November 2026, the results highlight expanded refillable packaging portfolios, salon waste recovery, and workforce inclusion programs that support more than 46,000 jobs nationwide.

"Our history of more than six decades in Mexico reflects absolute confidence in its people, its talent, and its resilience," says Deborah Armstrong, CEO, L'Oréal Groupe Mexico, during the event cited by Valor Compartido. "We reaffirm our long-term vision in the country, committed to continuing to boost the local industry and leading by example in sustainability, demonstrating that the well-being of society and caring for the planet go hand in hand."

According to a 2025 socioeconomic assessment conducted by consultancy Asterès and cited by L'Oréal, every direct job generated by the company in Mexico supports 15 additional positions across its value chain, totaling over 46,000 direct, indirect, and induced jobs after 64 years of local operations. Araceli Becerril, Corporate Responsibility Director, L'Oréal Groupe Mexico, adds that integrating social inclusion with environmental stewardship underpins the group's L'Oréal for the Future framework.

The corporate milestones come as consumer goods manufacturers in Mexico accelerate circular packaging transitions ahead of stricter federal environmental compliance rules. As previously reported by Mexico Business News, Mexico's General Law of Circular Economy, published in the Official Gazette of the Federation (DOF) on Jan. 19, 2026, introduces extended producer responsibility (EPR), requiring manufacturers and importers to register packaging with the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (SEMARNAT) and finance end-of-life recovery.

Within personal care and beauty categories, refillable packaging has emerged as a primary mechanism to reduce virgin material consumption and retain customer loyalty. According to Mexico Business News, L'Oréal Groupe launched the third edition of its Join the Refill Movement campaign in June 2026 across 18 brands, offering 84 refillable products in Mexico, including formats that reduce plastic consumption by 60% in haircare and cut glass and plastic use by 74% and 63%, respectively, in fragrances.

Simultaneously, L'Oréal has expanded its industrial footprint in Mexico to strengthen regional manufacturing and export capacity. As documented by Mexico Business News, the company allocated more than US$80 million through 2026 to expand production lines at its facilities in San Luis Potosi and Mexico City, where its San Luis Potosi plant serves as a strategic export hub.

L'Oréal Groupe structured its Mexican sustainability initiatives across four operational pillars:

Circular Economy and Waste Recovery. Beyond its 84 refillable stock-keeping units (SKUs), the Hairstylists for the Future program—implemented across 60 beauty salons—has collected nearly 600kg of human hair for environmental remediation, helping clean 440,000L of water and avoiding 2.6t of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions.

Clean Energy and Water Stewardship. Both Mexican manufacturing facilities operate exclusively on renewable electricity while advancing water preservation initiatives highlighted in the company's locally produced Sense of Purpose: Planet institutional campaign, filmed in locations including Las Estacas, Morelos.

Workforce Training and Scientific Inclusion. Under the Beauty for a Better Life program, more than 6,200 women have received technical training in hairstyling and makeup, while the For Women in Science initiative has awarded grants and institutional backing to more than 124 Mexican female researchers.

By aligning industrial decarbonization and circular packaging with supplier value-chain employment, L'Oréal aims to meet global 2030 sustainability targets while adapting to evolving regulatory standards in Mexico.

text:
Brazil and India have built major wind energy industries, but they remain reliant on overseas companies for crucial technology and decision-making

The global shift towards renewable energy risks creating a new divide between countries that control green technology and those left doing the manufacturing, according to new research involving The University of Manchester.

A study examining the wind power industries in Brazil and India finds that, despite building substantial domestic manufacturing capabilities and investing heavily in renewable energy, both countries remain dependent on foreign companies for some of the industry's most valuable technologies and strategic decisions.

Instead, control over research and development (R&D), intellectual property and key components continues to be concentrated among established international manufacturers, particularly in Europe, North America and China.

The findings raise questions about whether the global transition to clean energy will reproduce existing economic inequalities, with wealthier countries retaining control of the most profitable and technologically advanced parts of the industry.

Key findings:

Brazil has more than 7,000 onshore wind turbines, with an installed capacity of 33 gigawatts, but foreign manufacturers dominate its market.

European manufacturers Siemens, Vestas and Nordex Acciona account for more than 80% of Brazil's installed wind generation capacity.

Brazilian manufacturers have developed capabilities in producing components such as turbine blades and towers but remain reliant on foreign companies for key technology and design specifications.

India became the world's third-largest wind market, with 56GW of installed capacity in 2025, but continues to import more than half of the gearboxes, generators and converters used in its wind turbines.

Both countries have introduced policies to encourage domestic manufacturing and support national companies, but these have failed to establish comparable levels of technological independence.

China provides a contrasting example, having developed domestic technological capabilities and established its own companies as major international players.

The researchers distinguish between manufacturing wind turbine components and controlling the technologies that determine how they work.

They describe research and development, strategic decision-making and gearbox capabilities as the industry's 'brain activities', giving companies control over technological development and the direction of the industry. Other activities, such as manufacturing components to specifications set by international companies, are characterised as 'muscle activities'.

In Brazil, domestic manufacturers produce components including blades and towers, but international manufacturers retain control over important design specifications. In India, domestic companies have developed manufacturing capabilities but remain reliant on imported technology, foreign licensing and overseas research partnerships.

The study contrasts Brazil and India with China, which has developed major wind turbine manufacturers and its own technological capabilities.

The researchers point to China's more coordinated industrial strategy, combining government direction, support for domestic companies and investment in innovation. Its domestic market helped national manufacturers acquire the expertise needed to compete internationally.

They argue that countries seeking to benefit from renewable energy must look beyond the number of factories established or components manufactured domestically, and prioritise investment in research, innovation and technological capabilities.

The findings highlight the need to consider not just where green technologies are manufactured, but who controls them and captures their economic benefits.

“The transition to renewable energy is often presented as an opportunity for developing countries to build new industries, create jobs and benefit from the technologies of the future, but our research shows that manufacturing wind turbines and their components is not necessarily enough” said Pritish Behuria. “If countries do not also develop the capacity to control the technology, research and strategic decisions behind these industries, they risk remaining dependent on established international manufacturers. A genuinely just transition needs to consider not just where green technologies are manufactured, but who controls them and who captures the economic benefits."

The research, Winds of Peripheralisation: Production Injustices in Brazil and India, was published in Environmental Politics

BASF and JGC passed the performance test run of HiPACT® at INPEX’s Kashiwazaki Hydrogen Park

CO2 capture and compression costs expected to be reduced by up to 35% based on estimates

Supports INPEX’s production of lower-emission energy sources that do not emit CO2 at the point of use

BASF and JGC Corporation (JGC) have passed the performance test run (PTR) of HiPACT®, a high-pressure regenerative CO2 capture technology co-developed by the two companies, contributing to the start-up of INPEX Corporation (INPEX)’s blue hydrogen and ammonia demonstration plant in Kashiwazaki City, Japan. Injection of the separated CO2 commenced in August 2026. INPEX is one of Japan’s largest exploration and production (E&P) companies, engaged in the development and operation of oil and gas projects worldwide.

HiPACT® is used for CO2 separation and capture, enabling more efficient CO2 injection. By releasing CO2 off gas above atmospheric pressure, HiPACT® based on engineering estimates, is expected to reduce CO2 capture and compression costs by up to 35% compared with conventional technologies, thanks to its high-temperature durability and CO2 absorption performance. As CO2 can be stored underground in an energy-saving manner, the technology is designed to enhance the benefits of Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS).

Lawrence Loe, Director, OASE® Gas Treating Excellence, Intermediates Asia Pacific, BASF, said, “We are proud to support INPEX in bringing this landmark blue hydrogen and ammonia project to life. It’s not only an important step towards Japan’s net zero roadmap, but also another key reference plant for our advanced HiPACT® gas treating technology co-developed with JGC.”

As Japan’s first project to integrate the entire process from production to utilization of hydrogen and ammonia, this demonstration plant is designed to produce approximately 700 tons of blue hydrogen annually. Of this, 600 tons will be supplied for power generation at hydrogen-fired facilities in the Kashiwazaki Hydrogen Park, providing electricity within Niigata Prefecture. The remaining 100 tons will be converted into approximately 500 tons of blue ammonia annually and supplied to customers within the prefecture. Roughly 5,500 tons of CO2 per year generated as a byproduct are expected to be captured and injected underground for reduced atmospheric emissions using CCS technologies. The project’s hydrogen and ammonia production and CO2 capture are subsidized by the Japanese governmental organization New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO). The joint research for the evaluation and implementation of subsurface storage of CO2 is conducted with Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (JOGMEC).

text:
A family in Oshawa say their first electric car has been a good vehicle, but they now have concerns that charging it could be potentially dangerous.

Brooke and Will Hepburn purchased a 2027 Chevrolet Bolt in June of this year.

In September, when Brooke got home from work and plugged it in to charge, she said she felt a sudden shock when she moved the charging cable on the ground.

“I just wanted to straighten it before I closed the door, so I came over and moved it, and that’s where I got the shock,” Brooke recounted.

She said initially it felt like a sharp sting, and then the pain got worse.

“That pain immensely changed. It felt almost like a flame on my finger, and it turned into a shock going up my arm,” she said.

Brooke made it into her home, but then collapsed on the floor in pain.

“She was on the ground rolling around, holding her finger, screaming, and gasping,” said Will.

They went to the hospital, and Brooke had an EKG to check her heart. While she was told she was fine to go home, she still felt a tingling sensation for days afterward.

“The immense pain wore off in 24 hours, but the nerve pain lasted for about a week,” said Brooke.

While a charger came with their home, which was built in the past few years, they upgraded it to the charger that was specially made for the Chevrolet Bolt. It was installed by a licenced electrician, and they said they had certification showing the install was done correctly.

General Motors sent an engineer to the family’s home to do an inspection of the charging system.

A spokesman for GM told CTV News, “GM Canada takes every report of a potential safety concern seriously. We investigated this customer’s report, including an inspection of the charging equipment, and found no evidence of a malfunction, defect, or broader issue with the charging system. We remain in contact with the customer and will continue to work with her directly.”

How to set CP24 as your preferred source on Google

How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

CTV News also reached out to the Electrical Safety Authority, and a spokesperson said, “ESA is not aware of EV charger shocks being a common or pervasive issue, and we do not have data indicating that this is a broader trend.”

“As with any electrical equipment, proper installation and use are important. Homeowners installing EV charging equipment should ensure the equipment is approved for use in Ontario and compatible with the vehicle and electrical system, hire a Licensed Electrical Contractor (LEC) to complete the installation, and ensure a notification (permit) is filed with ESA for the electrical work. In addition, the device should be maintained in good working order, and cords should be checked regularly for wear and tear,” the spokesperson added.

The Hepburns wanted to return the EV but were told that was not an option.

GM did offer to replace the charging cable with a new one, but the family says they’d rather change back to a gas-powered car.

“Switching to a gas vehicle, which we know doesn’t have the ability to shock us or shock our children, is the only thing that will make my wife feel safe,” said Will.

name: Clean Energy
title: Premier Ford is trying to mislead Canadians on Industrial Carbon Pricing
authors: Keith Brooks, Keith Brooks Programs Director
description:
The claim that industrial carbon pricing “will force companies [in the automotive sector] that build in Canada to pay out billions in non-compliance costs” has no basis in fact.
This isn’t the first time that premiers, including Premier Ford, have intentionally misled Canadians on carbon pricing.
Ontario’s industrial carbon pricing system is weaker than the federal program, meaning that polluters pay less in this province than in those where the federal backstop applies.
ABOUT ENVIRONMENTAL DEFENCE (environmentaldefence.ca): Environmental Defence is a leading Canadian environmental advocacy organization that works with government, industry and individuals to defend clean water, a safe climate and healthy communities.
– 30 – For more information or to request an interview, please contact: Scott Cooper, Environmental Defence, media@environmentaldefence.ca
text:
Statement by Keith Brooks, programs director, Environmental Defence

Toronto | Treaty Lands and Territory of the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation, and the traditional territory of the Anishinaabeg, the Haudenosaunee, and the Wendat – Premier Ford’s announcement today on industrial carbon pricing and auto manufacturing is shameful. This is the premier’s latest attempt to mislead Ontarians and Canadians and weaponize climate policy. The claim that industrial carbon pricing “will force companies [in the automotive sector] that build in Canada to pay out billions in non-compliance costs” has no basis in fact.

The Canadian Climate Institute estimates that the entire auto sector paid only $3 million in compliance costs in 2023 and slightly more in 2024. There is no foreseeable future where these costs reach the levels suggested by the Premier. Moreover, the idled assembly plant in Brampton would have paid nothing in compliance costs since there is no production, no emissions, and no output.

This isn’t the first time that premiers, including Premier Ford, have intentionally misled Canadians on carbon pricing. He and other premiers attacked the consumer carbon price relentlessly and intentionally omitted the fact that the monies raised by the federal carbon charge were returned to families, and 80 per cent of households ended up better off thanks to the charge. Their attack on that climate policy was ultimately successful, so it’s not hard to understand why they would seek to do the same again. But facts are facts.

We are very much supportive of keeping automotive manufacturing in Ontario and of the view that the sector should pivot to manufacturing and assembling electric vehicles to keep pace with global trends. The tariffs pose an unacceptable threat to the sector and should be fought with vigour. But when it comes to addressing costs within Ontario’s purview, rising electricity costs are the real threat, as outlined in a recent letter from the Association of Major Power Consumers in Ontario warning of price spikes. This is an issue that has been flagged by Environmental Defence and others, on multiple occasions.

More Information:

Ontario publishes data related to its Emissions Performance Standard which shows that the automotive sector’s compliance obligation was for 44,278 tonnes in 2023 and 43,551 tonnes in 2024. In 2023, the industrial price was $65/tonne and in 2024 it was $80/tonne.

This means that, in 2023, the compliance obligation was $2.8 million and in 2024, it was $3.2 million, though the sector paid slightly different amounts due to rules around banking and trading permits.

All of the money collected by Ontario under the Emissions Performance Standard is given back to the companies that pay the fees, and is earmarked for GHG reduction.

Ontario’s industrial carbon pricing system is weaker than the federal program, meaning that polluters pay less in this province than in those where the federal backstop applies.

Ontario’s electricity costs have been rising and are anticipated to rise again in the near future due to an over-reliance on gas and nuclear power while sidelining wind and solar power. Wind and solar are the cheapest sources of new electricity generation in the world, including in Ontario.

BMW is expected to reveal the electric M3, known internally as the ZA0, at CES 2027 in Las Vegas in January, though the company has not confirmed the venue. Production is expected to begin at BMW's Munich plant in 2027.

Why it matters

The ZA0 would mark BMW's move to a fully electric version of its performance M3 sedan, as the G80 M3 combustion model is expected to end production in 2027. A next-generation combustion M3 is projected to follow around mid-2028.

BMW's preliminary figures put the ZA0 at 838 hp and 885 lb-ft of torque from four motors, with a 0-to-62-mph target under three seconds and DC fast charging up to 420 kW. BMW has not published an official quarter-mile time or top speed.

The players

BMW

BMW is a German automaker headquartered in Munich, known for its performance M division and luxury vehicles.

The details

The ZA0 uses four electrically excited synchronous motors, one per wheel, and includes simulated gear changes and six selectable driving stages. BMW has tested the car at Miramas, the Nürburgring, and on public roads in California.

Timeline

January 2027: Expected world reveal at CES 2027 in Las Vegas.

February to late summer 2027: G80 M3 builds expected to wrap up, depending on market.

2027: Expected start of ZA0 production at the Munich plant.

Mid-2028: Projected arrival of the next-generation G84 combustion M3.

Roadmap

The electric ZA0 extends the M3 nameplate from the G80 combustion generation into full electric propulsion, marking a shift for one of BMW's core performance models. The next combustion M3, the G84, is projected to follow around mid-2028, suggesting BMW is running electric and combustion versions in parallel.

Buyers interested in the electric M3 should expect a reveal in early 2027 and production later that year, so the car is unlikely to be available to order before then. The published range targets differ, with BMW's WLTP goal of roughly 404 miles above MotorTrend's EPA-cycle estimate of roughly 300 miles.

The takeaway

Because the ZA0 is still unrevealed and key performance figures are preliminary, the official specifications and pricing will matter more than the early targets. Readers comparing range should note that WLTP and EPA estimates are measured differently.

What happens next

BMW is expected to reveal the ZA0 at CES 2027 in Las Vegas in January 2027, with production at the Munich plant expected to begin later that year.

description:

text:
An industry-backed “permitting bill” approved by the US Senate would gut key clean water protections with changes that would do little to speed up the development of major energy projects, advocates warn.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (Baaja) passed the Senate 62-33 and is now being debated in the House. The Baaja is a “permitting reform” bill that aims to reduce the time it takes federal agencies to approve major energy and infrastructure projects, like power lines, fossil fuel pipelines, natural gas plants and datacenters.

But the legislation also includes provisions that would make it more difficult for states to put in place protections against water pollution, double the amount of time between automatic reviews of water pollution permits, and reduce transparency around the types and levels of water pollution.

More than 50 groups in communities impacted by Pfas “forever chemical” water pollution have come out against the bill, warning that they would suffer further if the legislation is approved because it would weaken some of the few mechanisms in US law that regulate the chemicals’ discharge. The law would “put us in more danger”, said Emily Donovan, co-founder of the Clean Cape Fear advocacy group in Wilmington, North Carolina, where drinking, surface, and ground water is polluted by discharge from a nearby Pfas factory.

“We already see how hard it is for the [Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)] to [regulate] Pfas,” Donovan said. “What frustrates us is we don’t need to make it harder.”

Baaja has drawn wide industry support, including among trade groups like the American Chemistry Council and American Petroleum Institute. It is opposed by virtually every major US environmental group because it would eliminate some foundational environmental protections.

The bill’s supporters say the cost is worth it because it will allow energy projects to be built faster, and hasten the transition to clean energy. Opponents say industry is using the need to transition to clean energy as cover to ram through a range of unnecessary changes to water laws that do nothing to improve energy permitting.

“BAAJA is a handout to the oil and gas industry, while doing very little to solve the permitting problems being used to justify those changes,” the Clean Water Action advocacy group, which is lobbying against the law, said in a statement. “Congress is trading away protections for states, tribes, wetlands and streams even though those protections are largely unrelated to the years-long delays at the center of the permitting debate.”

Among other changes, the bill would allow industry to sue to undo the EPA’s guidance for states on water pollution discharge. The EPA currently develops criteria that states use to limit discharge into waterways. The agency does this without issuing a formal rule, and the criteria cannot easily be challenged in court.

The Baaja would require a formal rule-making process, which would slow the clean water criteria issuance by several years, and open it to lawsuits. The criteria are used by states to develop limits on Pfas water pollution, and the change would shift more responsibility onto states that are largely under-resourced and unable to meet the challenge, Donovan said.

Another provision would change the EPA’s mandatory review of water pollution permits from five years to 10 years. The EPA uses this review mechanism to require polluters to track their Pfas and other water pollution.

Donovan pointed to the Pfas pollution in North Carolina to highlight how the provision would prolong the public’s exposure to dangerous chemicals. North Carolina regulators in 2019 put in place a health advisory limit of 140 parts per tn (ppt) for GenX, one of the main Pfas compounds polluting the state’s waterways. By 2022, the EPA established a health advisory of 10 ppt.

Advocates fear that the extended review period for pollution permits from five to ten years would create a scenario in which a company issued a water permit in 2020 may continue to pollute at higher levels for much longer.

“Imagine not being able to make a change for 10 years despite that the science is showing that a chemical is more toxic than originally thought – that’s what terrifies and frustrates us,” Donovan said. The transition to clean energy does not need to sacrifice clean water, she added.

“We can get clean energy without having to cause cancer,” Donovan said.
