title: Fastest-Growing Business Sectors in India 2026: Where Companies Are Investing
description:
India pulled in roughly $72 billion in energy-transition investment in 2025, according to BloombergNEF’s India Transition Factbook 2026.
The fastest-growing business sectors in India 2026 are no longer limited to IT services and consumer goods.
Companies are using AI to automate back-office work, answer customer queries, read business data and trim operating costs.
A September 2026 Business Standard report, citing Jefferies research, says India’s space economy could reach roughly $40 to 45 billion by 2030.
The fastest-growing business sectors in India 2026 are drawing money because of real shifts in demand, government backing, technology adoption and rising domestic consumption.
text:
India pulled in roughly $72 billion in energy-transition investment in 2025, according to BloombergNEF’s India Transition Factbook 2026. That single number says a lot about where corporate India is heading. The fastest-growing business sectors in India 2026 are no longer limited to IT services and consumer goods. Capital is moving into chips, clean power, data centres, electric mobility and defence, and the money is coming from Indian conglomerates, startups, private equity funds and foreign investors alike.

The reasons are fairly easy to see. A large middle class keeps spending more. Digital infrastructure now reaches small towns. The workforce is skilled and cheap relative to most rivals, and global companies want a second manufacturing base outside China. Together, these factors have made several of the fastest-growing industries in India attractive at the same time, something that rarely happens.

For a founder, a CXO or an investor, knowing which emerging business sectors in India deserve attention is practical, not academic. It shapes where you place capital, which markets you enter and which partnerships you chase. Below is a sector-by-sector look at the high-growth industries of 2026, the companies already active in them and the business investment opportunities India offers within each.

Quick Glance

This table sums up the emerging sectors for investment in India covered above.

1. Artificial Intelligence and Technology

AI is probably one of India’s most talked-about fastest-growing sectors, and for once the talk has money behind it. Companies are using AI to automate back-office work, answer customer queries, read business data and trim operating costs. Demand for generative AI, machine learning, cloud services, cybersecurity and enterprise automation is rising together.

The big Indian IT names, including Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Wipro and HCLTech, are building out AI practices for overseas clients. Smaller startups are going narrower, building products for healthcare, education, financial services and retail. On the policy side, the IndiaAI Mission has an approved outlay of ₹10,371.92 crore to support the country’s AI ecosystem.

Where companies are investing:

Generative AI and enterprise automation

AI-powered software and business intelligence

Cloud computing and cybersecurity

Machine learning and data analytics

AI infrastructure and GPU computing

Business opportunity: AI consulting, automation services, SaaS platforms, AI-led marketing tools and specialised software development are strong entry points for both entrepreneurs and established technology firms.

2. Renewable Energy and Clean Technology

Energy security and the push to cut fossil fuel dependence have made renewables one of the most important emerging sectors for investment in India. Solar, wind, green hydrogen, battery storage and energy management systems are all drawing fresh capital, helped along by rising power demand from factories, offices and data centres.

BloombergNEF’s India Transition Factbook 2026 also points to heavy future funding needs for solar and wind capacity. Adani Green Energy, Tata Power, NTPC Green Energy and ReNew Energy Global are among the companies expanding capacity.

Where companies are investing:

Utility-scale and rooftop solar

Wind energy projects

Green hydrogen production

Battery energy storage systems

Transmission and distribution for renewable power

Commercial and industrial energy solutions

Business opportunity: Smaller players can look at solar installation, energy audits, rooftop solar maintenance, battery storage solutions and renewable energy consulting.

3. Electric Vehicles and Battery Manufacturing

Electric mobility in India is building speed, though unevenly. Two-wheelers and three-wheelers lead the way because they suit crowded cities and last-mile delivery fleets. Carmakers, battery producers, charging companies and startups are all putting money in, and some are looking at battery recycling, battery management systems and vehicle financing too.

The main names include Tata Motors, Mahindra & Mahindra, TVS Motor, Bajaj Auto, Ather Energy and Ola Electric. Government support for electric mobility and local manufacturing is helping firms build domestic supply chains. Battery costs, patchy charging networks and buyer affordability are still real hurdles, though.

Where companies are investing:

Electric two-wheelers and four-wheelers

Lithium-ion battery manufacturing

EV charging infrastructure

Battery swapping technology

Battery recycling and material recovery

Fleet electrification and mobility services

Business opportunity: EV dealerships, charging stations, battery maintenance, recycling units and electric fleet management are workable options for small and mid-sized businesses.

4. Semiconductor and Electronics Manufacturing

Chips go into phones, laptops, cars, telecom gear, factory machines and defence systems, and India still imports most of what it needs. That dependence is why semiconductor manufacturing has become a strategic priority and one of the high-growth industries to watch in 2026.

An EY-IESA report released in September 2026 projects that India’s semiconductor market will grow from about $64 billion in 2026 to $200 billion by 2035. The Semicon India Programme and its second phase, Semicon 2.0, are backing fabrication and supply chain development. Tata Electronics, Micron Technology, CG Power and Kaynes Technology are among the firms involved.

Where companies are investing:

Semiconductor fabrication facilities

Chip packaging and testing

Electronic components manufacturing

Printed circuit boards (PCBs)

Semiconductor design and research

Industrial electronics and equipment

Business opportunity: Component manufacturing, electronics assembly, testing services, industrial equipment supply and specialised engineering work all stand to gain as the sector expands.

5. Data Centres and Cloud Infrastructure

Every AI model, UPI payment and online order needs somewhere to run. That is pushing data centres to the front of the list of business investment opportunities in India. Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad, Pune and Delhi-NCR are the main hubs, mostly because of connectivity, power access and existing business clusters.

JLL’s India Data Centre 2026 Mid-Year Report puts national capacity at around 1.6 GW in mid-2026 and expects it to reach 6 GW by 2029. It estimates that about $110 billion will be needed by then. Global tech firms, cloud providers and infrastructure developers are all lining up to expand.

Where companies are investing:

Hyperscale and colocation data centres

Cloud computing infrastructure

Server and networking equipment

Data centre cooling systems

Power backup and energy management

Cybersecurity and data management

Business opportunity: Construction, electrical equipment supply, cooling technology, network infrastructure and specialised maintenance offer room for B2B businesses.

6. Healthcare, Pharmaceuticals and Health Technology

Healthcare stays on the list of growing industries in India because the demand base keeps widening. Incomes are rising, cities are expanding and people expect better medical care than their parents did. Money is flowing into hospitals, drug manufacturing, medical devices, diagnostics, health insurance and digital health platforms.

India also supplies generic medicines and vaccines to many countries, which gives the pharmaceutical side a global footprint. Meanwhile, healthtech startups are working on access, particularly outside the metros. Apollo Hospitals, Max Healthcare, Sun Pharmaceutical Industries, Cipla and Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories cover different parts of this ecosystem.

Where companies are investing:

Hospitals and specialised healthcare facilities

Diagnostic laboratories

Pharmaceutical research and manufacturing

Medical devices and equipment

Telemedicine and digital health platforms

Health insurance and patient management software

Business opportunity: Diagnostic centres, medical equipment distribution, healthcare software, specialised clinics and pharma supply-chain services can work for new entrants.

7. Defence, Aerospace and Space Technology

Defence production and aerospace now sit inside India’s wider industrial growth plan. The push for domestic manufacturing and self-reliance has opened the door for private companies, which were largely shut out of this space for decades. The same is happening in space, where private firms now work on satellites, launch vehicles, earth imaging, navigation and communication systems.

Skyroot Aerospace, Agnikul Cosmos, Pixxel and Digantara are among the startups building in different corners of the space ecosystem. A September 2026 Business Standard report, citing Jefferies research, says India’s space economy could reach roughly $40 to 45 billion by 2030.

Where companies are investing:

Defence equipment and components

Aircraft and aerospace manufacturing

Drones and unmanned aerial vehicles

Satellite technology

Rocket and launch vehicle development

Space-based data and communication services

Business opportunity: Precision engineering, component manufacturing, drone services, electronics, specialised software and defence supply-chain partnerships suit Indian businesses with technical depth.

8. Financial Technology and Digital Payments

UPI changed how Indians pay, and it changed how small businesses collect money. Corner shops, service providers and local merchants now take digital payments as a matter of routine. Fintech companies are using that base to move into lending, wealth management, insurance technology and financial automation.

PhonePe, Razorpay, Paytm, CRED and Groww each work in a different slice of India’s digital finance market, which is why fintech remains among India’s fastest-growing sectors.

Where companies are investing:

Digital payment platforms

Lending and credit technology

Insurtech and wealth management

Financial automation software

Fraud detection and cybersecurity

Financial services for MSMEs

Business opportunity: Payment integration, financial software, merchant solutions, accounting automation and fintech consulting benefit from rising digital adoption.

9. Advanced Manufacturing, Chemicals and Industrial Automation

Companies want to produce more at home, spread their supply chain risk and sell abroad. Make in India and production-linked incentive (PLI) schemes are encouraging exactly that. On factory floors, firms are bringing in robotics, smart sensors, industrial IoT and automated production lines to raise output and cut waste.

NITI Aayog’s August 2026 report on making India a global manufacturing hub identifies chemicals, textiles, telecom equipment and solar photovoltaic manufacturing as high-potential industries.

Where companies are investing:

Industrial robotics and automation

Specialty chemicals

Textile and technical textile manufacturing

Telecom and networking equipment

Solar panel and component manufacturing

Industrial packaging and machinery

Business opportunity: Industrial packaging, machinery distribution, automation consulting, specialty chemical production and component manufacturing serve steady B2B demand.

10. Logistics, Warehousing and Supply Chain Management

E-commerce, organised retail, manufacturing and trade all need goods to move faster and cost less. That has made logistics one of the quieter but more dependable growing industries in India. Firms are building modern warehouses, adopting automated inventory systems, adding cold storage and linking transport networks. Quick commerce has added pressure for fulfilment centres in the right locations.

Delhivery, Blue Dart, Mahindra Logistics, TCI Express and Allcargo Logistics are among the major operators.

Where companies are investing:

Industrial and commercial warehousing

Cold storage and temperature-controlled logistics

Automated inventory management

E-commerce fulfilment centres

Freight forwarding and transportation

Supply-chain technology platforms

Business opportunity: Regional warehousing, packaging, cold-chain logistics, third-party logistics (3PL) and last-mile delivery are open to smaller businesses.

11. Agritech and Food Processing

Agriculture still carries a large share of the Indian economy, but it is slowly picking up technology. Agritech and food processing aim to raise yields, cut wastage and connect farmers to bigger markets. Companies are putting money into precision farming, agricultural drones, farm management software, preservation, packaging and organised food supply chains.

Demand for packaged food, ready-to-eat products and processed farm goods is also encouraging investment in processing infrastructure. DeHaat, Ninjacart and BigHaat are some of the names in India’s agritech ecosystem.

Where companies are investing:

Precision agriculture and farm automation

Agricultural drones and monitoring technology

Food processing facilities

Cold storage and preservation

Agri-supply chain platforms

Packaged and ready-to-eat food products

Business opportunity: Food processing units, farm equipment rental, farm-to-business supply chains, packaging and storage facilities look promising, especially for firms serving regional markets.

What Is Driving Business Investment in India in 2026?

No single factor explains why these high-growth industries are expanding together. Five forces keep showing up.

Government policy and incentives. Make in India, PLI schemes, the IndiaAI Mission and semiconductor programmes are backing local manufacturing, technology development and infrastructure.

Consumer demand. Higher incomes, urbanisation and changing habits are lifting demand for healthcare, digital services, electric vehicles, packaged goods and organised retail.

Digital adoption. Businesses of every size are moving to AI, cloud tools, automation and digital payments to work faster and serve customers better.

Supply-chain diversification. Global companies are looking at India as a place to manufacture and source, which opens doors for domestic suppliers and industrial firms.

Infrastructure spending. Roads, railways, ports, power networks, logistics hubs and industrial corridors are making it easier to do business across the country.

Conclusion

India’s economic shift is opening up opportunities across technology, manufacturing, infrastructure, healthcare and consumer industries. The fastest-growing business sectors in India 2026 are drawing money because of real shifts in demand, government backing, technology adoption and rising domestic consumption.

AI, renewable energy, electric vehicles, semiconductors and data centres deserve the closest watch, since each one feeds growth in several other industries. Healthcare, logistics, fintech, food processing and industrial automation, meanwhile, give businesses a way to serve India’s expanding domestic market.

For entrepreneurs and established companies, the real opportunity is not simply being present in a hot sector. It lies in finding a specific customer problem, building a better answer to it and running the business in a way that lasts. As manufacturing capacity and digital infrastructure keep growing, these are India’s fastest-growing sectors and should stay central to business activity and investment for years to come.

name: Texas Environment
title: EPA Proposes Texas and Utah Clean Air Act Plans - CASRAI
authors: Gabriel Nieves Castro, CASRAI Editorial Board
description: The EPA proposed Clean Air Act rules approving the Texas SO2 attainment plan for Navarro County and revising Utah Cache County vehicle inspection standards.
text:
On November 26, 2026, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency issued proposed Clean Air Act rules approving the Texas attainment plan for the Navarro County sulfur dioxide nonattainment area alongside vehicle inspection revisions in Utah’s Cache County, establishing enforceable industrial emission limits and compliance benchmarks that directly impact regional atmospheric research, dispersion modeling validation, and university environmental health monitoring.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) issued multiple State Implementation Plan (SIP) decisions under 40 CFR Part 52, led by Document 2026-24033 for Texas and Document 2026-24036 for Utah. In Document 2026-24033 (Docket ID EPA-R06-OAR-2024-0069), EPA Region 6 proposed approving the Texas attainment demonstration for Navarro County under the 2010 1-hour primary National Ambient Air Quality Standard for sulfur dioxide of 75 parts per billion (ppb). Submitted by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) on October 24, 2022, the plan establishes enforceable emission limitations, a comprehensive point-source inventory, reasonably available control measures, and an attainment demonstration based on AERMOD dispersion modeling.

Concurrently, under Document 2026-24036 (Docket ID EPA-R08-OAR-2026-4555), EPA Region 8 proposed approving the Utah Cache County inspection and maintenance program revision submitted on February 28, 2025. This action amends Utah Administrative Rule R307-110-36 to incorporate local updates from the Bear River Health Department (BRHD), granting testing exemptions for emergency vehicles and establishing a parts unavailability waiver. The EPA also issued companion SIP proposals for Maryland (Document 2026-24042) and Virginia (Document 2026-24043), advancing regional Clean Air Act compliance infrastructure.

The Texas plan resolves sulfur dioxide (SO2) emissions from the Arcosa Lightweight Streetman Plant, an expanded shale aggregate facility contributing over 99% of modeled SO2 in the Navarro County nonattainment area. Codified under 30 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) Chapter 112, Subchapter G, the rules require a dedicated wet scrubber stack meeting Good Engineering Practice (GEP) height and enforce a 222 pounds per hour (lbs/hr) SO2 limit on kiln Emission Point Number E3-1. Compliance is verified via Continuous Emissions Monitoring Systems (CEMS) under 40 CFR Part 60.

In Utah, the Cache County inspection and maintenance (I/M) revisions address emissions testing administered by the Bear River Health Department air quality and vehicle maintenance division under BRHD Regulation No. 2013-1. The revisions update inspection station definitions, exempt 102 active emergency vehicles out of 124,718 registered vehicles (0.08% of the fleet), and create Appendix G procedures allowing waivers when replacement emissions components are discontinued or unavailable. A Clean Air Act Section 110(l) demonstration confirmed these changes do not interfere with maintaining the fine particulate matter (PM2.5) standard.

Projected point-source emissions in Navarro County fall from 3,493.10 tons per year in 2019 to 972.36 tons per year in 2026, delivering an annual reduction of 2,520.74 tons (72.2%).

The Navarro County nonattainment designation stems from the 2010 1-hour SO2 standard. Ambient data from the Richland Southeast 1220 Road monitor (AQS ID 48-349-1081) recorded a 2017–2019 design value of 165 ppb, leading EPA to designate the area nonattainment in 2021.

To demonstrate attainment, state scientists modeled emissions using AERMOD, archived in the TCEQ Navarro County dispersion modeling archive . Incorporating five years (2016–2020) of surface meteorology from Corsicana Municipal Airport, Shreveport upper-air data, and a 6 ppb background from the Midlothian OFW monitor, the modeling yielded a maximum predicted 5-year design value of 73.8 ppb, beneath the 75 ppb NAAQS. Recent ambient monitoring at the Richland station confirmed compliance, with measured levels dropping from 165 ppb to 16 ppb.

AERMOD modeling illustrates the critical role of environmental modelling and software tools in simulating complex atmospheric transport. Similarly, ensuring continuous industrial monitors and ambient analyzers produce reliable compliance data requires traceable sensor calibration protocols and rigorous quality assurance.

EPA technical evaluations highlighted that Texas successfully combined enforceable emission limits with operational flexibility through Alternate Means of Control (AMOC) provisions. Facilities seeking alternative operating limits must demonstrate through dispersion modeling that ambient concentrations will remain below the 73.8 ppb attainment ceiling.

Industrial representatives noted that installing wet scrubbers and certified CEMS requires substantial capital investment and multi-year engineering. Environmental health analysts underscored that lowering ambient SO2 protects vulnerable populations from severe bronchoconstriction and asthmatic attacks. Demonstrating compliance in Navarro County validates the Clean Air Act’s cooperative framework, proving targeted point-source controls can clean airsheds effectively.

The EPA’s proposed rule approvals carry direct implications for academic research programs, campus facilities, and environmental health offices:

Publication in the Federal Register on November 27, 2026, initiates a 30-day public comment window ending on December 28, 2026. Comments on the Texas plan should reference Docket ID No. EPA-R06-OAR-2024-0069, while comments on the Utah program should cite Docket ID No. EPA-R08-OAR-2026-4555.

Texas faces a statutory attainment date of April 30, 2026. With scrubbers operational and monitored values at 16 ppb, EPA Region 6 expects to issue final approval in early 2027. Following final action, these limits become permanently enforceable within the federally approved SIP.

title: 'The hour is late': Energy deal still elusive as holidays loom - AOL UK
description:
Dated Oct. 16, the Eversource letter says the annual cost of state clean energy programs topped $1.46 billion for Eversource electric ratepayers in 2026.
The utility didn't mention the Mass Save energy efficiency program by name in the letter and didn't take a position on the House's proposed cut.
Eversource Director of Residential Energy Efficiency Katherine Peters called the Mass Save program "one of the best partnerships that I can think of."
The report also said that Mass Save programs to reduce electricity and fossil fuel use have generated $38.4 billion in total benefits between 2011 and 2024.
The six conferees tasked with negotiating energy legislation first met on July 29.Cusack said Wednesday that they met Tuesday and plan to meet again next week.
text:
BOSTON (SHNS) - The fate of energy legislation in Massachusetts is still unresolved in closed-door legislative talks, which the Senate's lead negotiator this week called "still very viable but problematic" and his House counterpart described as "progressing."

The outlook follows Eversource's letter to energy negotiators last month, in which it wrote that its electric customers already pay more than enough for clean energy programs — counting $326.5 million a year in energy efficiency spending among the total — days before it publicly celebrated energy efficiency program Mass Save. On Tuesday, the utility drew a distinction between cutting the program's existing budget, as the House has proposed, and taking a look at what future budgets may entail.

Lawmakers have been negotiating a complex and contentious energy proposal for months, as energy costs and affordability have been a focus on Beacon Hill for more than a year. Gov. Maura Healey started the conversation before the 2026 gubernatorial race got off the ground; now she's headed into her second term and residents are into the heating season without legislative action to ease the burden of energy costs.

Sen. Mike Barrett, Senate chair of the Telecommunications, Utilities and Energy Committee, spoke with alarm to the Boston Globe about the Eversource letter last week, and on Tuesday called it "destabilizing to have a 20-page missive land in the middle of a sensitive negotiation between the House and Senate."

His House counterpart, Rep. Mark Cusack, said he knew of Eversource's concerns and that conferees have received around 70 letters from different stakeholders about the proposals.

"To pick one out and have a temper tantrum is bizarre to me. This is standard procedure. It's not an earth-shattering move that is going to derail our talks," Cusack said.

Eversource said the letter "followed months of active engagement on these topics."

The House passed its energy bill (H 5151) in February, proposing to cut the Mass Save energy efficiency program by $1 billion, and the Senate passed its own bill (S 3166) on July 1, proposing instead to phase out the Gas System Enhancement Program. Both chambers say their energy bills will save ratepayers billions over the long term.

Barrett wouldn't comment directly on negotiations with the House when asked if he thinks they'll reach an agreement by Jan. 5, but said, "The hour is late and the holidays loom."

Cusack's reply to the same question: "Yes."

"No matter what deadline you make, you always feel the pressure coming up to it. But we're still five weeks out. I still feel good about it," Cusack said. He characterized swirling opinions about negotiations as "par for the course, the parlor game of Beacon Hill gossip. It's certainly not new to me."

Dated Oct. 16, the Eversource letter says the annual cost of state clean energy programs topped $1.46 billion for Eversource electric ratepayers in 2026. The company said "$1.4 billion in annual ratepayer funding is more than sufficient to meet the Commonwealth’s energy transition goals, and yet the legislation currently contemplated by the Conference Committee asks for even more." The utility didn't mention the Mass Save energy efficiency program by name in the letter and didn't take a position on the House's proposed cut.

"I think there's an important distinction between making a cut to a current budget, especially as we approach the last year of the budget for the current three-year plan, and the conversation around what future budgets should look like," Eversource spokesperson William Hinkle said Tuesday.

Mass Save's existing three-year budget cycle runs through 2027 and is funded at $4.5 billion.

"I think it's pretty clear that if you made a significant cut to the current budget at this time, that would pose very serious challenges for the programs, the contractor and workforce community that delivers these solutions, and create significant issues over the balance of this term," he continued. "Ultimately what exactly that level lands at, that's a policy decision."

Cusack said, "The utilities make money off the program, so they're not going to criticize it." In February he described the House's proposed reduction as "a one-year pause" and the cut as "focused on the administrative and marketing budgets, which are bloated."

Healey did not directly answer repeated questions at a September press conference about her stance on the proposed cuts, instead promoting her "all-of-the-above" energy approach. After being pressured to answer a final time, she said, "Look, I filed my legislation, and I'll leave it at that. I asked the Legislature to act on my legislation."

Mass Save users at a State House event last month pointed to time and cost savings they say the program provides them. Eversource Director of Residential Energy Efficiency Katherine Peters called the Mass Save program "one of the best partnerships that I can think of."

"I think we need to keep in mind what those real on-the-ground results are, even as we have the policy discussion about where we might go with programs in the future," Peters said.

National Grid Director of Customer Energy Management Amy Vavak pointed to a Sept. 30 analysis from independent nonprofit American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy, which reported that Mass Save programs reduced Massachusetts natural gas imports by 8% in 2024, saving over $406 million that year. The report also said that Mass Save programs to reduce electricity and fossil fuel use have generated $38.4 billion in total benefits between 2011 and 2024.

A municipal impact study issued in September 2025 by the state auditor's office reported that its Division of Local Mandates found "significant disparities in the distribution of Mass Save incentives, where residents of some higher-income municipalities received more than they contributed and residents of many lower-income municipalities contributed more than they received."

The six conferees tasked with negotiating energy legislation first met on July 29.Cusack said Wednesday that they met Tuesday and plan to meet again next week.

Barrett said that he and Cusack "are getting along splendidly." Cusack characterized their relationship as "fine" and "friendly," adding, "We don't get in fights, we don't yell at each other."

text:
On Nov. 19, the U.S. Senate passed a bill that aims to speed up permitting for energy infrastructure projects.

The 62-33 vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) included support from pro-environment Democratic senators like Sheldon Whitehouse from Rhode Island.

The legislation would ease development for renewable energy and transmission lines, but environmental organizations warn it will also fast-track fossil fuels by undermining environmental regulations.

“A technology-neutral fast track in the hands of an administration openly hostile to clean energy is not a bargain. It is a one-way ratchet for fossil fuels,” Brad Campbell, CEO of the Conservation Law Foundation, said in a statement.

Currently, new U.S. infrastructure projects must comply with bedrock environmental laws including the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, and National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). If BAAJA becomes law, those environmental hurdles will become easier to clear.

Fewer projects would require NEPA review, the time frame for environmental assessments would be shorter, and the window to sue over approved projects would shrink. Consultation on potential impacts to endangered species would also be shortened.

Proponents of the bill say those changes would ease renewable energy development and lower U.S. carbon emissions.

“BAAJA is a big step forward in our fight against climate change,” Whitehouse, who co-sponsored the bill, wrote on social media. “The bill lowers emissions by 1.5 gigatons through 2040.”

However, the weakened environmental review would also apply to fossil fuel projects and data centers. In an open letter, more than 120 scientists urged the House of Representatives to reject the bill.

On land, BAAJA could lower barriers for oil, gas and mining projects on public and tribal lands. Several Native American organizations have condemned the bill.

At sea, BAAJA would “roll back ocean and wildlife protections, opening the door to more offshore oil and gas drilling, more pollution, and greater threats to marine life,” U.S.-based NGO Oceana said in a statement.

Section 1401 of the bill, also known as the “project certainty” provision, would bar agencies from making changes to permits once they’ve been granted.

“Once issued, these approvals would be nearly impossible to revisit in the future, even if they were expedited, legally flawed, or if new science uncovers serious harm,” Oceana said in a statement.

Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, founder of Finafinau, an environmental NGO based in American Samoa, told Mongabay by email that she welcomes economic development but not at the cost of jeopardizing American Samoa’s existing ocean-based economy. The U.S’s first-ever offshore critical mineral lease sale took place off America Samoa on Nov. 19, the same day BAAJA cleared the Senate.

“If progress requires weakening environmental protections, diminishing Indigenous voices, and asking communities with limited political power to shoulder disproportionate risks, then perhaps we need to reconsider our definition of progress,” she said.

The House of Representatives is expected to vote on the legislation next week.

title: Tensions Flare In Rural Indiana As Counties Decide On Solar Without State Oversight
description:

At first glance, solar projects seem like a win-win for rural counties and Indiana’s electric grid alike.
Anti-solar signs have cropped up along Indiana county roads, and in several Indiana counties, the pushback against solar has led to bullying and harassment, threats and intimidation and a slew of county-wide bans or restrictions on solar development.

This article originally appeared on Indianapolis Star: Tensions flare in rural Indiana as counties decide on solar without state oversight
text:
By Sophie Hartley

Indianapolis Star, USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect

MARSHALL COUNTY – When Jim McCune passed away on Aug. 6, 2014, he left nearly 800 acres of Indiana farmland and forest to his two adult daughters. Darla Harrington and Rhonda McCay, both married with families of their own, named the Marshall County farm in honor of the man who taught them how to pick rock and love thy neighbor.

The sisters, however, can’t farm it.

As their father developed health issues and medical bills piled on, he retired, sold much of the pricey equipment necessary for modern farming and rented out the land to a close friend. After inheriting the land, Harrington and McCay continued to lease it, generating a small income. But they worry a time will come when it won’t be easy for their children, who will one day split the land six ways, to hold on to it.

In 2019, Harrington thought she had found a lifeline that would preserve McCune Farm’s future. A solar company came knocking. Geenex, a utility-scale solar developer, wanted to lease several hundred acres of the land in a multi-decade agreement. Harrington and McCay hoped the lease would bring in more than enough revenue to persuade their children to keep the land.

Then the rest of Marshall County found out.

That’s when “all hell broke loose,” Harrington said. Anti-solar sentiment quickly devolved into harassment, threats and ostracization. The dream of steady solar income that could have sustained the farm for upwards of 30 years evaporated almost overnight.

At first glance, solar projects seem like a win-win for rural counties and Indiana’s electric grid alike. Through lucrative leases that often span decades, solar farms have helped rural farmers retire, pay down medical debt and keep land in the family as the agricultural industry faces staggering declines.

Solar power, which converts sunlight into electric currents, is the cheapest form of electricity for ratepayers. It’s also a timely solution to meeting rising electricity demand. Solar is considered the fastest form of power to deploy, from breaking ground to putting additional megawatts on the grid.

Despite the charms of sunshine-fueled electricity, utility-scale solar farms can be difficult to build in some parts of Indiana. Multiple projects across several counties have been shut down abruptly, sometimes after vicious fights that leave communities bruised and weary.

When two solar developers in Marshall County, including Geenex, worked through the county zoning process in 2024, anti-solar opposition erupted with vehemence. Crowds showed up at county meetings, which were eventually held in auditoriums and church sanctuaries to accommodate everyone (and inspire respectful language, one pastor said before a nearly four-hour meeting at the Plymouth Wesleyan Church).

In 2025 the county voted to ban solar projects for two years, dashing the McCune sisters’ hopes. But they lost more than money; relationships with many of their community members, including one of their father’s closest friends, were left fractured.

“The things they said about my sister and I, how we’re just wanting money and our dad is rolling over in his grave. It’s very hurtful. We admired our dad. We love him. And people were saying we were making decisions that would have hurt him,” Harrington said, shaking her head in disbelief. “Every time we made a decision or did research, it was, ‘How can we honor him? How can we keep the land?’”

Concern over solar often stems from unverified claims, disagreement over property rights and deeply personal feelings regarding how rural Indiana counties are changing. Anti-solar signs have cropped up along Indiana county roads, and in several Indiana counties, the pushback against solar has led to bullying and harassment, threats and intimidation and a slew of county-wide bans or restrictions on solar development.

Unlike Wisconsin and Michigan, where state government has substantial control over where and when large energy projects can set up shop, the power of zoning in Indiana largely sits with county officials, some of whom have been forced to make consequential decisions about Indiana’s electricity grid while staring down community in-fighting.

“We’re in a time of growing energy demand, and we needed megawatts on the grid yesterday,” said Topher Anderson, the director of programs and operations at the Indiana Conservative Alliance for Energy. “These local fights that are all being regulated at the county level determine the future of our state. It’s a huge opportunity and roadblock right now that’s made it really difficult.”

Vitriol and acrimony abound statewide

Utility-scale solar energy boomed across Indiana in 2025, but not every county is amenable to this form of energy generation. Threats of violence cropped up after local government meetings in Noble County last year, prompting County Commissioner Anita Hess to vote against a county-wide solar moratorium. Because the moratorium would likely bring more public debate, Hess said she voted against the measure to avoid creating an “arena for more of these types of threats.” Solar opposition led to death threats against county commissioners in Knox County, according to a local news station. As the solar debate heightened in Clark County, a Board of Zoning Appeals member, Bob Ellison, resigned one month after taking the role, citing personal attacks against his family. Harrington said one person threatened her physical safety one night after a county meeting.

‘Everyone is just nasty’

Kerri Vaughn, a landowner in Clark County, understands the skepticism about renewable energy. What she doesn’t quite comprehend is how the debate becomes quite so ugly.

A solar company approached Vaughn and her husband before the pandemic. The lease they offered to sign would provide nearly $80,000 annually, which could help pay off nearly $300,000 that the family accrued in medical debt after Vaughn went through treatment for breast cancer.

Still, Vaughn said, they were not interested: “We’ve always been conservative. We have always felt like the Green New Deal was kind of shoved down our throats.”

Plus, Vaughn had heard that solar could be dangerous for human and environmental health, lower nearby property values and harm agricultural communities. But when the pandemic left Vaughn and her husband with plenty of time on their hands, they decided to do some research – just to make sure they were right. They read about solar’s positive economic impact on rural economies and how the projects can let farmland rest, leaving the soil in better shape.

Vaughn’s research, however, did not prepare her for how her county would respond to the proposed project. As anti-solar opposition grew, she saw neighbors get bullied online, watched videos targeting her directly and learned to brace for county meetings.

“When you go into these meetings, and I’ve had to stand in front of their group because there weren’t any seats, you could hear them whispering, ‘What a piece of’ – you know. About me,” Vaughn said.

And the outcry didn’t just impact her, Vaughn said; she thinks it swayed county officials.

“Everyone is just nasty, trying to scare you out of it. Most of these [zoning officials] are appointed. They did not sign up for this, and it scares them. And they just fold,” she said.

The county passed an ordinance in 2025 that restricted how developers could design solar projects. It included a setback that disqualified nearly half of Vaughn’s farm from the solar lease. She was bewildered.

“If this was turned down for a legitimate reason, okay. That’s totally fine. But I have yet to hear anything legitimate,” Vaughn said.

Solar opponents explain their stance in a variety of ways.

Some worry about the future of Indiana farmland, despite a clause in many leases guaranteeing thorough removals after the life of the project. Others theorize about chemical leaks and property right infringement. And some detractors cite their frustration with the aesthetic effect of solar panels.

Counties have the authority, but do they have the right resources?

Despite Indiana’s desire to increase energy generation and keep electricity affordable, solar projects that could address both goals have gotten harder to build.

The state does not keep data on how many solar projects or megawatts have been kept off the grid by county bans or ordinances, according to Indiana Energy Secretary Suzanne Jaworowski.

The projects abandoned by developers in Marshall County would have brought 350 megawatts on the grid. Orion’s Idlewild Project, which would have leased the Vaughns’ land, was designed to produce nearly 500 megawatts. With renewable energy off the table, power generation that is slower to build and more dangerous for human and environmental health – such as coal, natural gas and backup diesel generators – becomes the fallback.

State officials say they want to see more solar energy on the grid, which would mean fewer moratoriums.

“As energy demand grows, we need more generation on the grid, not less,” Jaworowski wrote in a statement to IndyStar. “Moratoriums on solar or any other energy source undermine reliability, create unnecessary barriers to investment, limit future supply, and can ultimately increase costs for consumers. The path to energy affordability is growth, competition, and investment in new generation, not bottlenecks.”

But the energy secretary demurred when asked if the power of siting should be in the hands of the state, not the counties.

“The state respects local decision-making and does not impose a one-size-fits-all mandate,” Jaworowski said.

In both 2021 and 2025, legislation attempting to consolidate state authority over siting failed to become law. Nor do most energy experts endorse handing this power entirely to the state and taking away local control. Still, many believe the current system isn’t serving Indiana farmers or the grid.

Anderson, of ICAE, doesn’t want to see authority stripped away from counties, but he’s not sure that every county is governing appropriately. To thread the needle of supporting local government and supporting landowner rights, Anderson would like the state to compile a database of research and relevant information that county commissioners with little or no energy expertise can lean on to make sound zoning decisions.

Brian Flory, a program director with Solar United Neighbors, has traveled across Indiana, sitting in zoning meetings and meeting with landowners. He’s seen communities struggle with overwhelming decisions about siting solar and wind, as well as battery storage and data centers. Despite witnessing some contentious debates, Flory said he and his colleagues don’t want to see authority stripped from county government. Rather, they want counties to have more resources.

“Local control definitely needs to be a part of the solution. I think that is also a place where the state needs to step in and provide more clarity for counties and developers and for local groups, chambers of commerce, just for everybody to have a clear sense of the rules of the road,” Flory said. “Currently we don’t have that.”

When counties erupt into chaos, the noise may also drown out a very real concern of some opposed to solar farms, Flory said. The pain of watching rural life transform as solar becomes the preferred crop is not easy to express in a county zoning meeting.

“There is a deeply held emotional concern to a changing way of rural life, and there is a way to honor and acknowledge that experience,” Flory said. “But then there’s the social media stuff. And the derision. Those things all intermix really easily.”

For Harrington and her sister, solar power was a way to hold on to that heritage longer, even as the modern world encroaches. Now, the sisters are not entirely sure what they will do. They discussed selling the land after losing the prospect of the solar lease but ultimately decided to keep holding on to it for their father’s sake. At least for now.

“His name ends with us,” Harrington said. “We just feel that if we sell, that’s the end of his legacy. His name will be gone. And that saddens me. I want it to go on.”

Sophie Hartley is an IndyStar environment reporter. You can reach her at sophie.hartley@indystar.com or on X at @sophienhartley. IndyStar’s environmental reporting is made possible through the generous support of the nonprofit Nina Mason Pulliam Charitable Trust.

text:
The talks in Antalya ended without agreement on a cover decision, and African countries left without clarity on how adaptation finance would be tripled. Yet Parties recognised sustainable industrialisation and local value addition as part of a just transition and reached an understanding on how countries would shape future trade and climate dialogues.

How just is a transition that cuts emissions while leaving intact the economic structures that constrain development? African countries have set ambitious climate targets in their nationally determined contributions (NDCs). They are equally ambitious about industrialising, reducing poverty and improving livelihoods. The test of COP31 is whether its outcomes help them pursue those ambitions together.

1. The Just Transition Work Programme was extended, while the mechanism’s design remains open

Parties extended the UAE Just Transition Work Programme for three years and recognised sustainable industrialisation, economic diversification and local value addition as part of nationally determined just transitions. They agreed to operationalise the Just Transition Mechanism in phases, with its functions and operating arrangements to be negotiated in 2027. COP31 just transition text

The transition away from fossil fuels is increasing demand for minerals used in batteries and renewable energy technologies. But whose supply security are we talking about? If mineral partnerships leave African countries dependent on exporting raw materials while processing and manufacturing take place elsewhere, the transition risks creating new forms of economic dependence. International cooperation should help African countries participate in the industries their resources make possible. That means financing reliable and affordable power, transport and skills, supporting technology transfer and building regional value chains through the African Continental Free Trade Area.

At the High-Level Ministerial Round Table on Response Measures in Antalya, Zimbabwe’s Minister of Environment spoke about processing minerals and making batteries at home. UNU-INRA’s November 2026 policy brief What Zimbabwe Keeps records an early step. From January to September 2026, lithium sulphate made in Zimbabwe earned about US$191 million of US$2,159 million in lithium export earnings: about 8.8 cents of each lithium dollar. This gives Zimbabwe a baseline for tracking domestic processing. The next test is whether processing more lithium at home raises the share of each export dollar that stays in Zimbabwe and creates jobs that pay above the applicable minimum wage.

2. Adaptation finance remains unresolved

Parties agreed to continue work on the indicators for the Global Goal on Adaptation, while discussions on national adaptation plans made limited progress. African negotiators called for adaptation finance to triple to at least US$120 billion a year by 2035. COP31 left open how that finance would be delivered and how Parties would track whether it reaches the people it is meant to protect.

“You cannot triple a number nobody has written down,” says Dr Richard Munang, Director of UNU-INRA. “A baseline has two ends. One counts what was promised and sent. The other counts what arrived and protected someone. The promise will be believed when it carries both.”

African countries’ climate and development ambitions need to be matched by finance. The Paris Agreement reflects the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities. Under Article 9.1, developed countries are required to provide finance to help developing countries mitigate and adapt to climate change.

Unilateral trade-related climate measures can push financial flows in the opposite direction. A carbon border charge can raise revenue in a developed market while African exporters absorb part of the cost. Buyers can pass traceability costs down to smallholders. This shifts part of the cost of climate action onto developing economies and can erode the export earnings and public revenues they need to invest in adaptation and their own transitions. Climate ambition should not come at the expense of the economic capacity needed to deliver it.

3. No deal on response measures as Rule 16 pushes talks to June 2027

Climate policies adopted in one country can affect other economies by changing production costs, influencing investment and shaping employment. The proposed 2027 work programme omitted the dedicated activity on assessing cross-border impacts (Activity 6 of the Response Measures Forum). The draft decision did not secure consensus, and the item was carried forward under Rule 16 for renewed consideration in June 2027.

One model study, by the African Climate Foundation and the London School of Economics, puts the cost of the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) to Africa at about 0.91% of GDP, roughly US$25 billion at 2021 levels (ACF and LSE, 2023). A separate UNCTAD study estimated that CBAM would cut global emissions by about 0.1% (UNCTAD, 2021). These projections show why countries need to assess cross-border impacts before measures are introduced and track what happens once they take effect. Better data and stronger national capacity would help identify which sectors face higher costs, how jobs and public revenues are affected, and where opportunities for cleaner production and local value addition are emerging.

4. No dedicated trade and climate agenda item, but Parties secured a role in guiding future dialogues

The proposal for a dedicated trade and climate change agenda item did not secure agreement. Parties reached a procedural understanding that they would determine the form, format, process and reporting of the dialogues and the 2028 high-level event. The next dialogue, at the June 2027 talks in Bonn, gives countries an opportunity to bring sector-specific evidence into the discussion.

The international trade system should give African countries room to industrialise and grow their economies so they can invest in climate action. Article 3.5 of the UN Climate Convention provides a basis for that discussion. It calls for an open trading system that supports sustainable development and says climate measures, including unilateral ones, should avoid arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination and disguised restrictions on trade.

In 2022, Ghana exported 62% of the cocoa it produced to the EU. In 2025, the EU imported €2.63 billion in cocoa and cocoa preparations from Ghana. UNU-INRA’s analysis puts that at about 23 times the value of Ghanaian goods covered by CBAM. The scale of the cocoa trade makes implementation of the EU Deforestation Regulation a priority for Ghana. If buyers pass the cost of plot-level mapping and verification down the supply chain, smallholders with limited access to finance and technical support may struggle to retain access to European buyers. The next dialogue should examine how producers can meet environmental requirements while protecting their livelihoods.

5. The Antalya Pact exposed a gap between transition ambition and finance.

Parties did not reach consensus on the proposed cover decision. Some called for stronger language on transitioning away from fossil fuels. Parties also differed over the role of renewables in the proposed electrification goal and whether the emphasis on carbon capture, utilisation and storage could prolong fossil fuel use.

Some developed countries called for a faster transition away from fossil fuels. At the same time, public climate finance pledges for developing countries fell by more than 70% in 2026. The final draft omitted the call to triple adaptation finance to at least US$120 billion a year by 2035.

The terms of finance matter alongside its volume. In Mozambique’s Zambézia programme, the World Bank agreed to pay US$5 per tonne for 10 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in emissions reductions, with 70% of projected net payments earmarked for community projects. The agreed price and planned share give communities two figures against which they can track what actually reaches them. By mid-2025, the programme’s own report showed about 89 cents of each five-dollar tonne had reached communities. Counting what arrives is how a promise becomes a payment.

The proposed “35 by 35” target aimed to raise electricity’s share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035. Around 600 million people in Africa lack access to electricity. For the continent, electrification should expand access to electricity and clean cooking, power productive economies and support industrial transformation.

From Antalya to Addis — Africa’s COPFrom Antalya to Addis — Africa’s COP.

COP32 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, will be Africa’s COP. Hosting it gives African countries, researchers, workers and producers an opportunity to shape the agenda around what a development-led transition requires. At COP31, UNU-INRA provided technical support to the African Group of Negotiators on trade and climate change and contributed technical inputs on response measures and just transitions.

The second Global Stocktake is a chance to assess whether developing countries are receiving the finance, technology and capacity-building support they need to participate in the transition. National roadmaps for transitioning away from fossil fuels can apply a similar test. Alongside emissions reductions, they should track what happens to jobs, public revenues and productive capacity, and whether economies become more diversified and resilient.

On trade, this means counting what is at stake product by product. On adaptation finance, it means tracking what was promised and sent, what arrived and whom it protected. On just transition, it means asking how many cents of each mineral dollar stay in the producing country through wages, local procurement and public revenue. That is the keep rate, a measure UNU-INRA uses across African case studies.

“Value added is not value kept,” says Dr Munang. “A transition is just when the share of each mineral dollar kept at home goes up, and the jobs it creates pay above the minimum wage. Africa is not poor. Africa is uncounted.”

The 15 March 2027 call for submissions on the Just Transition Mechanism gives UNU-INRA an opportunity to bring evidence from those case studies into the design of the mechanism. The keep rate offers one way to track progress, alongside evidence on whether jobs pay above the applicable minimum wage and where processing and manufacturing take place. As the green transition gathers pace, how much of the value it creates will stay in Africa, and who will benefit?

title: Ineos Grenadier Is Officially Becoming An American-Made Off-Roader - CarBuzz
description:
The Ineos Grenadier is about to make its biggest move yet.
When Ineos Automotive first launched its rugged Grenadier SUV and Quartermaster pickup truck, it needed somewhere to build it.
But that plant led to a big problem for Ineos Automotive, because 70% of the brand's customers are located in the US.
The company said that it is working to make sure the sale won't end Grenadier and Quartermaster production.
Could it be a big enough deal to ensure Ineos Automotive continues?
text:
The Ineos Grenadier is about to make its biggest move yet. The UK-based and French-built off-roader with the spirit of the Defender and fully-modern mechanicals is coming to America. A new factory is coming that will assemble the Grenadier and Quartermaster in the US for the first time.

Now the challenge will be to make it happen in time to make the company a success.

When Ineos Automotive first launched its rugged Grenadier SUV and Quartermaster pickup truck, it needed somewhere to build it. The first plan was to put it together at a brand-new factory in Wales, but a year later that was axed. Ineos bought the former Smart car plant in Hambach, France, and started production in late 2022.

But that plant led to a big problem for Ineos Automotive, because 70% of the brand's customers are located in the US. The Quartermaster was subject to the 25% tariff known as the Chicken Tax that hits every pickup imported from outside of North America into the US.

When that stacked with the Trump tariffs on vehicles imported from the EU, Ineos had to raise prices. Originally, the Grenadier went up $3,800, and the Quartermaster was up $9,000. Those prices have fallen slightly as preliminary deals on tariffs were made, but the situation is still far from stable and a new announcement on vehicle tariffs is expected from the White House in early December.

Building a plant in the US won't be cheap, but it will exempt Ineos from both the 25% Chicken Tax and any EU import tariffs. It appears to have a plan to skirt retaliatory tariffs on US-built models as well.

Can Ineos Open A New Plant In Two Years?

The automaker has lined up a buyer for its old plant. Ineos announced that it is in "exclusive negotiations" to sell the French factory to Chinese automaker BYD. The company said that it is working to make sure the sale won't end Grenadier and Quartermaster production. If the negotiations are successful, it says, the two will be built there "for the medium term."

It might have to keep that European production because of some sales it has already made. Ineos has orders from the Italian Army and the Austrian Government, and is in what it calls advanced discussions with other European and NATO forces. It's unclear if they'd be thrilled by the idea of buying American.

Ineos has not announced where its new US factory will go. The automaker said that it had shortlisted possible sites, but it will have to decide in a hurry. Ineos said it plans to make the final announcement in the next few months, and it plans to start building vehicles in 2028.

That's an incredibly fast turnaround. For reference, VW brand Scout, which plans to build electric and range-extender trucks and SUVs in South Carolina, first announced its plant location in 2023. Production-ready vehicles aren't expected to get to customers before 2028. Ineos has the same end goal, but is starting three years behind.

CarBuzz Insight – Why This Matters:

An Ineos Quartermaster could suddenly become thousands cheaper for American buyers, and even for an $86,000 luxury pickup, that's a big deal. Could it be a big enough deal to ensure Ineos Automotive continues? That's the question.

The move is also a win for an administration that's been looking to bring back auto manufacturing, not to mention the hundreds of workers at whatever location Ineos chooses. But, with Ineos being a niche builder and a manufacturing site not even picked out yet, consider us skeptical about American-made Grenadiers until construction or renovation on a facility actually begins.

text:
Prashant Verma, Sub-Editor, ELE Times

Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) is an emerging technology enabling bidirectional power transfer by pairing the power station with the vehicle’s charging port to charge the battery in electric vehicles (EV) and supply power to the public electricity grid using bidirectional charging, power electronics, and two-way digital communication.

The primary purpose of introducing V2G technology is to balance electricity supply and demand on the power grid by using EV batteries as a source of power to be supplied to the grid. While supplying power to the public electricity grid, the user receives financial compensation and grid service rewards, depending upon local utility programs and regulations.

Understanding Vehicle-to-Grid Technology: How Does it Work?

​V2G is not the only technology that transfers power back to the source to balance source availability and consumption demand. Other available technologies that transfer power back to the source include Vehicle-2-Home (V2H) and Vehicle-2-Load (V2L). The concept of energy flow during power transfer is the same: the power distributor acts as a source and the consumer acts as a consumer.

Given below is a list that explains how V2G works.

Grid Monitoring & Signals: Grid operators monitor the balance between electricity demand and supply continuously from central control centres using real-time grid frequency, automated telemetry, and demand forecasting.

Two-Way Power Conversion: The bidirectional power conversion placed inside the charging station converts alternating current from the grid into direct current to charge an EV and reverses its functionality to charge the grid (power station) by converting DC current from the battery into grid-synchronised alternating current.

Smart Charging and Discharging: This is the core technology in V2G supported by bidirectional power electronics, battery controls, communication protocols, backend management software that coordinate together to supply power to an EV during surplus availability and draw power from an EV during a shortage of power supply.

Aggregation & Control: Aggregation decides the charging and discharging capacity while transferring power in both directions from source to consumer, whereas control manages the direction of flow of energy with time and amount between the vehicle and the grid, considering electricity demand, battery conditions, and user requirements.

For a practical explanation, consider vehicle-to-home (V2H) charging technology, where an electric scooter is charged by solar energy through solar panels during daytime, when the supply is abundant and power is drawn from the scooter during the evening when the demand is excessive through appropriate grid connection and utility arrangements.

Bidirectional Power Electronics: The Technology Behind V2G

Power electronics play a very important role in transferring power between the grid and an electric vehicle. These are bidirectional converters, inverters, and switches placed on both electric vehicles and the grid, controlling the flow of electricity by regulating the frequency, phase, and voltage in real-time. Transferring power between the grid and an EV also involves converting current from AC to DC because the power grid and EV batteries operate on different types of electrical current.

Below is a list of scenarios where current conversion takes place in V2G technology along with components utilized:

Level 1 & Level 2 Charging: Power is supplied from the grid to an EV and AC is converted into DC in this case using an EV On-Board Charger (OBC). Power is supplied directly from the charging station to EV’s onboard charger.

DC Fast Charging (Level 3): AC is converted to DC while transferring power from the grid to EV using step-down and conversion equipment.

Wireless Charging: Power flows from grid to an EV and conversion of electricity involve AC into high-frequency AC or AC to DC using ground pad and vehicle receiver pad.

AC V2G: In this state, the current flows from an EV to the grid and conversion of current is from DC to AC using EV Bi-Directional On-Board Charger.

Vehicle-to-Load (V2L): The energy stored in an EV’s battery is supplied to external components like mobile phones and power backup devices. The current is converted from DC to AC by an EV On-Board Inverter.

Silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) wide-bandgap semiconductors could improve bidirectional Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) charging performance by reducing switching and conduction losses. Their wide-bandgap properties enable higher switching frequency, reducing the size of passive components such as capacitors, inductors, and filter components inside the bidirectional chargers, and lowering thermal losses while charging and discharging an electric vehicle.

How V2G Can Support Renewable Energy and Grid Stability

Generation from solar and wind energy is variable. When renewable generation is available and not all of it is required to meet the electricity demand at that moment, rather than disconnecting the power from the grid and increasing the amount of energy that is wasted, this excess energy is stored in the electric vehicles’ batteries. When the demand increases, or renewable generation falls below the required level, the stored power can be transferred back into the power grid.

V2G Can Support Electricity Networks Through Several Applications

Peak Shaving: Hourly electricity demand typically peaks at certain times of the day. Utilities can utilize EV batteries connected to the grid to supply more electricity during peak demand hours, alleviating the power distribution.

Frequency Regulation: To ensure stability, an electricity network keeps a consistent frequency level by constantly matching generation to demand. When composed of aggregated EV batteries, the grid can send a control signal to increase or decrease electricity consumption.

Renewable Energy Integration: EV batteries can store excess solar and wind energy and discharge it back to the grid when there is little to no generation.

Demand Response: Demand response can be used by utilities/energy aggregators to motivate EV owners to charge/discharge vehicles according to tariff rates and grid needs.

According to the International Energy Agency’s Global EV Outlook 2026, V2G and smart charging could be used as a means to lower peak demands, reduce grid congestion, and minimize required grid investment.

V2G vs V2H vs V2L: Understanding the Difference

Even though these technologies all use vehicle-to-vehicle or vehicle-to-infrastructure power transmission, they are not used for the same purpose.

Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G): Sends electricity from an EV battery to the public electricity grid.

Vehicle-to-Home (V2H): Provides power back to the home from stored vehicle energy, possibly acting as a backup supply or to lower energy bills.

Vehicle-to-Building (V2B): Delivers electricity to commercial buildings, office buildings or other facilities.

Vehicle-to-Load (V2L): Delivers energy from an EV is used to power external electrical devices, tools and equipment.

For example, the energy stored in an EV battery can run a laptop, electrical lights, or small appliances via V2L. Power can be supplied to the home through V2H in case of a power outage (if the car supports backup operation and is compatible with the home electrical system).

V2G advances that concept by enabling electric vehicles to connect directly with the public electricity grid. Using bidirectional charging infrastructure, vehicles can feed electricity back to the grid and can provide other energy management services.

Conclusion

Vehicle-to-Grid is a key step toward integrating electric mobility with the electricity ecosystem. It offers bidirectional charging and is an example of an enabler of “EVs to Grid” applications, such as balancing renewable energy penetration, peak shaving, ancillary services for grid stability, etc.

But V2G is not just about deploying a bidirectional charger; it requires aligning progress across power electronics hardware, battery management, communication protocols, cybersecurity, grid protection, and energy management software.

As the adoption of electric vehicles and the deployment of renewables increase, V2G might give a new purpose to electric cars, in addition to travel. With the right technology, commercial frameworks and regulatory incentives, parked cars could play an important role in a more flexible and resilient grid.

text:
Deutsche Welle (DW) published a report on November 26, 2026 titled “From power cuts to bike theft: Africa’s EV test.” Its core finding is simple and awkward for the industry: electric vehicles in Africa face a real-world exam in which the grid, the street and the wallet all grade the technology at once. Nigeria wants electric vehicles to dominate its roads by 2050, yet frequent blackouts, few charging stations and high costs stand in the way.

The DW piece ranges across four markets. Uganda is promoting electric motorcycles partly because tracking technology makes them harder to steal. Ethiopia is leaning on hydropower to support one of Africa’s fastest-growing EV markets. India, included as a comparison case, is converting diesel trucks through electric retrofits. Each story points at the same hardware question: what has to sit in the battery pack, the charger and the tracker before drivers trust the switch?

This analysis unpacks what DW reported, what the hardware implications look like, and where the evidence stops. We also flag what the available material does not say, because the source gave no sales figures, battery specs or theft statistics. Charging hardware is a live topic elsewhere too, as our report on Hyundai’s slow-charger plan for Korea shows. The African picture runs on very different constraints.
