What DW Reported on Africa’s EV Test

DW’s framing treats the continent’s electric vehicle transition as a test rather than a rollout. That word choice matters. A rollout implies a plan moving through predictable stages. A test implies that something might fail, and that the failure modes are different from the ones seen in Europe, China or North America.

The confirmed points from the story are narrow but useful. Nigeria has set a 2050 ambition for EV-dominated roads. Frequent blackouts, thin charging coverage and high costs are named as obstacles. Uganda is pushing electric motorcycles, with tracking technology cited as a theft deterrent, while privacy concerns and limited charging infrastructure remain unresolved. Ethiopia’s hydropower supports a fast-growing market. India’s diesel truck retrofits round out the picture.

Anything beyond those points is outside the verified record. DW’s summary, as available to us, did not include named vehicle models, companies, prices, battery capacities, charging times or theft counts. We keep this article inside those limits. Where we offer analysis, we label it as analysis, and where a number would be convenient, we leave it out.

That restraint is itself a finding. The public conversation about African EV adoption often leans on large projections and glossy launches. A story that centres on blackouts and bike theft pulls attention back to the unglamorous layer where adoption is won or lost. A driver who cannot charge at home, or who loses a vehicle to theft, does not care about a 2050 target.

Nigeria’s 2050 Target and the Blackout Problem

Nigeria’s stated goal is for electric vehicles to dominate its roads by 2050. That is a long runway, roughly 24 years from today. The distance suggests officials view the shift as a generational change in the vehicle fleet rather than a near-term sales race.

The obstacles DW lists are physical and financial. Frequent blackouts undermine the basic promise of an electric vehicle, which is that you can refuel from the wall. If the wall is unreliable, the vehicle owner needs a second plan, such as a generator, a battery buffer or a public charger with its own backup. Each workaround adds cost, and cost is already on the list of barriers.

Few charging stations compound the problem. Public charging networks work as a chicken-and-egg system. Drivers wait for chargers, and operators wait for drivers. In a market where grid supply is shaky, a charging operator carries extra risk, because uptime depends on power that may not arrive.

High costs close the loop. DW did not publish price points in the material we reviewed, so we cannot quote the gap between an electric vehicle and a petrol equivalent. The direction of the argument is clear enough: when upfront prices stay high and charging stays patchy, the economic case for switching weakens for most households and fleet operators.

A 2050 target can still do useful work. It signals to importers, assemblers and energy planners that policy will eventually lean toward electrification. Whether that signal arrives early enough to shape investment decisions in the next few years is a separate question, and one the DW report leaves open.

Why Charging Hardware Matters More Than Battery Size

Debates about electric vehicles often fixate on battery capacity and range. The African test inverts that priority. When the grid fails unpredictably, charging reliability matters more than the biggest possible pack. A vehicle with modest range that can charge dependably beats a long-range vehicle that sits idle during an outage.

Grid-tied charging versus buffered charging

A standard grid-tied charger is the cheapest option and the most exposed to outages. A buffered charger pairs the connection with a stationary battery or solar input, so it keeps working when the grid drops. The second design costs more, but it fits the Nigerian reality DW describes. Whether such systems are being deployed at scale in any of the four markets is not stated in the report.

Pricing signals from other markets

Charging economics vary widely between regions. Our coverage of IONNA’s Thanksgiving charging discount in the United States shows how operators in mature markets use price promotions to manage demand. That tactic assumes plentiful, reliable supply. Operators facing blackouts have a different lever to pull, which is availability itself.

The takeaway for hardware makers is plain. In markets with weak grids, charger resilience, local power buffering and low-cost installation are sellable features. Peak charging speed, the number most marketing leans on, drops down the list.

Uganda’s Electric Motorcycles and the Theft Angle

Uganda’s approach starts from a different vehicle class. Electric motorcycles, rather than cars, are being promoted, and DW says part of the appeal is that tracking technology makes them harder to steal. Two-wheelers are widely used for transport in many African cities, so a push in this category reaches a large slice of daily trips even if car ownership stays low.

The theft angle is a clever reframing. Electrification usually gets pitched on fuel savings or emissions. Here, a built-in connected tracker becomes a security feature. For an owner whose motorcycle is also a livelihood, protection against loss can matter as much as running costs.

That logic depends on the tracker working in real conditions. A tracking module needs power, a data connection and a way to alert the owner or a response service. Each of those dependencies is a possible weak point. A tracker that loses signal in a dead zone, or one that a thief can disconnect, offers less deterrence than the sales pitch implies.

DW’s summary gave no theft statistics for Uganda, so we cannot say how much the trackers reduce losses. The claim, as reported, is that the technology makes bikes harder to steal. We present it as the stated rationale for promotion, not as measured performance.

The wider hardware lesson is that connectivity is moving from luxury to baseline. Even a low-cost electric motorcycle now carries a communications module in this model of adoption. That raises the bill of materials, but it also opens a path to fleet management, remote diagnostics and, as the next section covers, serious privacy questions.

Privacy Concerns When Your Bike Tracks Itself

DW identifies privacy concerns as an unresolved issue in Uganda. The tension is easy to describe. The same tracker that helps recover a stolen motorcycle also records where the owner goes, when, and how often. Whoever controls that data holds a detailed picture of a person’s daily life.

The report, as available to us, did not name the companies operating the tracking systems or the rules governing the data. We therefore cannot say who stores location histories, how long they keep them, or who can request access. Those gaps are exactly what privacy advocates tend to flag in any connected-vehicle program.

Good design can narrow the risk. A tracker can limit location reporting to cases where the owner marks the vehicle as stolen. It can store data on the device rather than a remote server. It can give owners a clear way to see and delete their own records. None of these measures is confirmed for Uganda, but they are the standard questions buyers and regulators should ask.

The privacy question also shapes trust, which shapes adoption. If riders believe the tracker serves a lender, an employer or the state more than themselves, some will resist it or try to disable it. A theft deterrent that owners defeat on purpose protects no one.

Ethiopia: Hydropower Behind a Fast-Growing Market

Ethiopia is the optimistic case in DW’s reporting. The story says hydropower is supporting one of Africa’s fastest-growing electric-vehicle markets. That is a meaningful pairing. An electric vehicle is only as clean and as dependable as the electricity behind it, and a country with abundant hydropower starts with a clear supply advantage.

The report did not provide sales figures, so we cannot size that growth or compare it with any other country. We also lack vehicle models, charger counts or pricing for Ethiopia. What we can say, on DW’s authority, is that the market is among the continent’s fastest-growing and that hydropower is part of the reason.

The Ethiopian example highlights how much the energy mix drives the EV story. Nigeria’s blackouts and Ethiopia’s hydropower sit at opposite ends of the same spectrum. A country does not need a perfect grid to start electrifying transport, but it needs enough dependable generation that charging does not become a daily gamble.

For hardware suppliers, markets like Ethiopia are early indicators. They show which products sell when the power question is partly answered. If cheap, reliable generation exists and adoption still lags, then price and charger access are the remaining barriers. If adoption surges, that suggests the supply of power was the bigger constraint all along.

India’s Retrofit Route for Diesel Trucks

DW also covers India, where diesel trucks are being converted through electric retrofits. The inclusion makes sense as a comparison. Retrofitting skips the purchase of a new vehicle and instead swaps the powertrain of an existing one, which can lower the capital hurdle for operators who already own a fleet.

The report, as available to us, gave no conversion costs, truck counts or payback periods. We cannot say how many trucks have been converted or at what price. The reported fact is the practice itself: diesel trucks becoming electric through retrofit work.

Retrofits raise their own hardware questions. A converted truck needs a battery pack sized for its duty cycle, a motor and controller matched to the load, and a charging plan for the depot. Freight work punishes weak components, because a truck that cannot deliver on time costs its owner money every hour it sits.

The approach could matter for African markets that already import large numbers of used vehicles. A retrofit pathway offers one way to electrify the fleet that exists rather than waiting for fleet turnover. Whether regulators and mechanics in Nigeria, Uganda or Ethiopia would back such a route is not addressed in the DW material, so we treat it as a reasonable question and nothing more.

Four Markets Compared: What Is Confirmed

The table below sets out the confirmed points from DW’s report, market by market. It deliberately includes only what the fact sheet supports. Blank spaces in the public record show up as “not provided” rather than estimates.

Two patterns stand out. First, the obstacles named are infrastructural and financial, not technological. Nobody in the story argues that the vehicles do not work. Second, the solutions on offer are tailored to local constraints, from motorcycle trackers to hydropower to retrofits. No single model is being copied across the continent.

Hardware Impact: Batteries, Chargers and Trackers

For a hardware-focused audience, the DW story points to three product categories that carry the most weight in these markets: battery systems, charging equipment and connected security modules. We offer the following as analysis rather than reported fact, since the source gave no component-level detail.

Batteries. Heat, rough roads and uneven charging habits stress battery packs. Durable thermal management and tolerance for irregular charging rank above peak energy density when owners cannot count on a stable supply. Packs that can be swapped or repaired locally would also ease the cost burden.

Chargers. Resilience beats speed. Chargers that tolerate voltage swings, ride through short outages or pair with solar and storage fit the conditions DW describes. Our report on VW’s bidirectional charging scheme in Europe shows one possible direction. A vehicle that can feed power back to a home turns the battery into a backup source, which is a potentially valuable idea where blackouts are routine. Nothing in the DW report says this is happening in Africa today.

Trackers. Uganda’s approach turns a communications module into a core feature. Low power draw, tamper resistance and a clear data policy decide whether such a module protects owners or just adds cost and risk.

Taken together, these needs favour modular, repairable and locally serviceable designs. A product that works in a showroom in a mature market may fail on a Kampala back road or during a Lagos outage. Suppliers who treat the African test as a design brief, not an afterthought, stand a better chance of winning.

Market Impact: Who Gains and Who Waits

With no sales or investment figures in the verified material, we cannot put a dollar value on any of this. We can describe where the pressure and the opportunity likely sit, based on the obstacles DW names.

Importers and assemblers face a policy signal in Nigeria’s 2050 goal but little clarity on near-term incentives. Charging operators face a hard business case in places where grid supply is unreliable. Motorcycle makers and fleet operators in Uganda may see the fastest returns, since a two-wheeler is cheaper to electrify and the theft angle adds a selling point. Truck owners, in markets like India, can use retrofits to cut the capital outlay of going electric.

Government policy shapes all of it. Other countries have moved to support electric vehicles through targeted measures, as our piece on Korea’s EV support plan as Chinese-made cars gain share illustrates. African governments face a different fiscal position and cannot always match that kind of support. Policy choices about import duties, charging standards and grid investment will matter more than any single product launch.

The risk for buyers is lock-in to products that do not fit local conditions. The risk for investors is backing infrastructure that outpaces vehicle demand or the other way round. The DW story, by naming blackouts and thin charging coverage first, suggests that infrastructure is the constraint to watch.

Competitive Comparison: New Builds, Retrofits and Two-Wheelers

The four stories in DW’s report amount to four competing strategies for electrifying transport. The table compares them on qualitative terms. It contains our analysis of trade-offs, not reported measurements.

The last row sits outside DW’s story and appears for context only. Other emerging markets have floated local battery production. Our coverage of a proposed EV battery plant in the Philippines shows how regional governments weigh that route. We make no claim that a similar plant exists in the African markets DW covered.

The strategies are not mutually exclusive. A country could pair a two-wheeler push with retrofit programs and long-term car targets. The strongest plans will probably match each vehicle class to the weakest link it can fix, whether that is theft, capital cost or fuel expense.

Historical Context: Why Africa’s Transition Looks Different

Earlier waves of technology adoption in Africa offer a useful lens, though we offer it as interpretation. Mobile phones spread widely partly because they skipped the need for fixed-line infrastructure. Many users leapfrogged straight to wireless service. Advocates sometimes hope electric transport can follow a similar pattern, bypassing fuel-station networks.

The analogy has limits. A phone needs a few watt-hours a day and a connection. A vehicle needs far more energy, which means it leans heavily on the electricity grid. The very obstacle DW highlights in Nigeria, unreliable power, shows why transport electrification cannot copy the phone story without solving supply first.

Elsewhere, electric vehicle adoption often started with generous incentives, dense urban charging and stable grids. African markets lack some of those ingredients. They bring other advantages, such as a large base of two-wheeler users, a culture of vehicle repair and conversion, and in places like Ethiopia, abundant renewable generation.

That mix explains why the DW lineup looks so varied. Each country is playing the hand it holds. A 2050 horizon for Nigeria, motorcycle trackers in Uganda, hydropower in Ethiopia and retrofits in India all reflect local starting points rather than a shared blueprint.

What Remains Unconfirmed

The DW material available to us leaves out a lot, and it is worth listing the gaps plainly. No specific vehicle, company, product, person, price, performance specification, sales figure, charging time, battery capacity or theft statistic was provided. No on-record quotation from a named speaker was included either.

Readers should therefore treat any figure they see attached to this story with caution unless it carries a clear source. Claims about the size of Ethiopia’s market, the number of motorcycles sold in Uganda or the price of a retrofit may exist elsewhere, but they are not part of what we verified here.

We also do not know the scope of the DW report’s reporting. It may draw on interviews, site visits or official statements that its summary does not detail. We have not seen those underlying materials, so we do not characterise them. For the same reason, this article includes no expert quotes. We would rather publish none than invent a voice.

The practical advice is to watch for follow-up reporting that fills in the numbers. Government statements, utility data and company disclosures would all help turn a promising narrative into a measurable one.

Five Predictions for Electric Vehicles in Africa

The following forecasts are our analysis, built on the obstacles and strategies DW describes. They are not reported facts and carry no confirmed timelines beyond Nigeria’s stated 2050 goal.

Two-wheelers lead the visible gains. Electric motorcycles cost less to build and charge than cars, and the theft angle gives them an extra selling point. Expect them to show progress before passenger cars do.

Charger resilience becomes a headline feature. Where blackouts persist, products that pair charging with storage or solar will outsell products that only chase speed.

Privacy rules move up the agenda. As connected trackers spread, pressure will build for clear data-retention and access policies. Companies that publish those rules early will earn trust.

Retrofits spread to more vehicle types. The truck conversions DW describes in India may inspire similar programs for buses and delivery vans in markets with large used-vehicle fleets.

Grid investment decides the pace. Nigeria’s 2050 target will stay aspirational unless power supply improves. Progress on blackouts will be the best leading indicator for vehicle adoption.

We will revisit these calls as new data appears. For wider coverage of batteries, chargers and related components, see our hardware section.

FAQ: Electric Vehicles in Africa

What is Nigeria’s goal for electric vehicles?

According to DW, Nigeria wants electric vehicles to dominate its roads by 2050. The report names frequent blackouts, few charging stations and high costs as the main obstacles.

Why is Uganda promoting electric motorcycles?

DW reports that electric motorcycles are being promoted partly because tracking technology makes them harder to steal. Privacy concerns and limited charging infrastructure remain unresolved, according to the same report.

What role does hydropower play in Ethiopia?

DW says hydropower is supporting one of Africa’s fastest-growing electric-vehicle markets in Ethiopia. The report summary we reviewed gave no sales numbers, so the size of that growth is unconfirmed.

How does India fit into the story?

The DW story covers India’s diesel trucks being converted through electric retrofits. It serves as a comparison point for how existing vehicles might be electrified without buying new ones.

Are there confirmed prices, battery specs or theft statistics?

No. The material we verified did not include specific vehicles, companies, prices, performance specifications, sales figures, charging times, battery capacities or theft statistics. We have kept those details out of this article.

Why do blackouts matter so much for EV adoption?

An electric vehicle depends on the grid for fuel. If power cuts are frequent, owners cannot charge reliably and need backup systems, which raises costs. That is why DW lists blackouts among Nigeria’s biggest obstacles.

What should hardware buyers and suppliers watch next?

Watch for resilient charging hardware, repairable battery packs and tracker modules with clear data policies. Also track official statements on grid investment, since power supply sets the pace for adoption.

text:
The Treasury Department aimed to issue a final rule on the 45Z biofuel producer tax credit in November 2026, and the final version is expected to be published in December. The credit, established under the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, applies to renewable fuels produced and sold from 1 January 2025.

Why it matters

The rule will set how biofuel producers prove lower carbon intensity, including the use of renewable energy certificates tied to the same year and region as the electricity consumed. The final version is expected to remain in line with earlier agency guidance, and it could add clarity on tolling arrangements and interactions with other tax credits such as 45V.

The 45Z rule requires generating facilities behind renewable energy certificates to have a commercial operations date no more than 36 months before the first taxable year of a qualifying fuel, and fuels must meet a carbon intensity threshold of 50. The Department of Energy's GREET model did not incorporate the IRA updates until 2025, and it remains unclear how that delay will affect producers' ability to document earlier facility dates.

The players

U.S. Department of the Treasury

The federal department responsible for tax policy and the agency issuing the final 45Z biofuel producer tax credit rule.

U.S. Department of Energy

The federal department whose GREET model is used to measure fuel lifecycle emissions and which did not incorporate the IRA updates until 2025.

The details

The One Big Beautiful Bill required changes to the 45Z credit, including a requirement that fuel feedstocks come from the United States, Mexico or Canada. A fuel is excluded from 45Z if it is produced from another fuel for which a 45Z credit is allowable.

Timeline

1 January 2025: The 45Z credit begins to apply to fuels produced and sold from this date.

February 2026: The proposed 45Z rule was released.

November 2026: The Treasury aimed to issue the final 45Z rule.

December 2026: The final 45Z rule is expected to be published.

First quarter of 2027: Other Treasury guidance documents have been postponed to this period.

Ethanol Output Rises to 1.129 Million Barrels

Legislative Policy

Roadmap

The 45Z credit was created by the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 and later modified by the One Big Beautiful Bill, which added feedstock sourcing limits for the United States, Mexico and Canada. The final rule is the Treasury's step in translating those statutory changes into operating standards for biofuel producers.

Biofuel producers will need to document renewable energy certificates and facility operating dates to qualify for the 45Z credit under the final rule. The rule's treatment of tolling arrangements and interactions with other credits such as 45V could affect how producers structure their operations and financing.

The takeaway

Producers planning around the 45Z credit should track the final rule in December, since the guidance will determine how renewable energy certificates and facility dates must be documented. Remaining Treasury guidance is delayed to 2027, so some compliance details may stay unsettled for months.

What happens next

The Treasury is expected to publish the final 45Z rule in December 2026, and other guidance documents are postponed to the first quarter of 2027.

name: Detroit and Evs
title: Ford, China, EV technology and the fight against the coming jobs massacre
description:
The “national security” rhetoric is a cover for preparations for war against China, not a defense of jobs.
The working class must not line up with either section of the ruling class in this dispute.
Whatever faction prevails in the current dispute, the working class faces a coming onslaught on jobs and working conditions.
The struggle over Ford and China is a struggle over who will bear the costs of a technological revolution, trade war and militarism.
The ruling class, in all its factions, intends that the working class should bear them.
text:
A bitter conflict is unfolding within the American ruling class over the relations of the US automakers—above all Ford—with their Chinese rivals and suppliers. At its center is a question that the corporate press and the political establishment are determined to keep from the working class: the enormous labor-saving character of the new technology that China has developed in electric vehicle production, and the fact that, under capitalism, this technology is being deployed as a weapon against jobs and living standards.

Ford has established a complex web of ties to Chinese industry. It licenses battery technology from CATL, the world’s largest battery maker, for its battery production in the United States, including at its Marshall, Michigan plant, which began making cells in October. It has agreed to build vehicles for Geely at its underused plant in Valencia, Spain, beginning in 2028, and it maintains relations with BYD, the Chinese automaker that has overtaken the Western giants in EV technology and cost. Ford continues to produce the Lincoln Nautilus in China.

Ford CEO Jim Farley has been blunt about the reason. It is impossible, he has argued, for the global automakers to compete without utilizing the most advanced technological developments made by Chinese automakers, particularly in the simplification of EV body assemblies. Chinese manufacturers have pioneered “gigacasting” and related techniques that replace dozens or hundreds of stamped and welded parts with a handful of large castings, drastically reducing the number of parts, assembly stations and labor hours required to build a vehicle.

This is not a matter of “unfair subsidies” or “cheating,” as the protectionists allege. It is a genuine technological revolution. And it was driven, in significant measure, by a strategic calculation made by the Chinese ruling elite after the 2003 US invasion of Iraq: the recognition that China’s dependence on imported oil, and the threat that the United States could cut off those supplies, required a crash program to electrify transport. The result is a body of production technology that is enormously labor-saving—and therefore, in the hands of capital, enormously job-destroying.

The scale of the threat to jobs is documented in the industry’s own figures. Ford is converting its Louisville Assembly Plant to build the Fathom electric pickup truck, which will reportedly sell for under $30,000 and hit the market in late 2027. Based on its Universal EV Platform, it will use 20 percent fewer parts and 40 percent fewer assembly stations and cut assembly time by 15 percent, with the highest level of automation in final assembly of any Ford plant globally.

Former Ford CEO Jim Hackett stated that EVs would require “30 percent fewer labor hours per car.” Volkswagen’s top labor representative said an electric powertrain has a sixth of the components of a combustion engine, and that a battery plant needs a fifth of the workforce of an engine plant. The International Workers Alliance of Rank-and-File Committees has warned that the transition threatens to eliminate half or more of all auto jobs in the US within five to ten years.

This is the real content of the dispute now raging in Washington. Farley’s position—that Ford must integrate Chinese technology to survive—has come under ferocious attack from sections of the Trump administration, from anti-China hawks in the Democratic Party such as US Senator and ex-CIA agent Elissa Slotkin, and from the United Auto Workers apparatus.

In September, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy sent Farley a letter expressing “profound concern” over Ford’s ties to CATL, Geely and BYD, demanding an acceleration of the decoupling from Chinese supply chains. Ford dismissed the letter as a “wrongheaded attempt to capture headlines,” and Trump intervened to declare Ford a “GREAT American company.” The UAW, for its part, has urged Congress to keep the House Select Committee on China in place and to enact a permanent statutory ban on Chinese automakers, co-authored by Slotkin and Republican Senator Bernie Moreno. UAW President Shawn Fain has called Chinese-owned production “a slap in the face to America” and invoked the slander of Chinese “slave labor.”

The conflict reproduces, in the auto industry, the struggle over Nvidia’s commercial relations with Chinese chipmakers analyzed in the WSWS perspective “The Huang affair, the AI bubble and the divisions within the American ruling class.” There, the ouster of CEO Jensen Huang after a campaign by the New York Times and sections of the intelligence agencies, followed by his reinstatement, exposed a deep rift within the ruling class over whether to exclude China from advanced technology or to tie Chinese developers to American hardware. Here, the same division appears as a fight between those sections of capital—represented by Ford and, fitfully, by Trump—that seek to profit from Chinese technology, and those—the Democratic hawks, the intelligence agencies, the union bureaucracy—that demand its exclusion in the name of “national security.”

Neither position has any progressive content. Both serve American imperialism, which regards China’s economic and technological development as an intolerable challenge to its hegemony. The “national security” rhetoric is a cover for preparations for war against China, not a defense of jobs. The dispute turns only on the pace and method of a shared drive to confront China: Ford cannot abruptly sever its links to Chinese technology without disrupting production, while Washington seeks to force a faster reorganization of supply chains around the strategic requirements of US imperialism.

Developments this week demonstrate the interconnectedness of trade war and military confrontation with China. On Wednesday, the Trump administration announced it was preparing new tariffs on China along with other countries in the EU and Asia for allegedly subsidizing industrial production and flooding global markets with cheaper goods that undercut US producers.

At the same time, the Wall Street Journal reported that administration officials are in preliminary talks with GM, Ford, Magna International and other auto and auto parts manufacturer about supplying motors and other components to domestic drone makers, which lack the capacity to meet expected demand in a market the Pentagon estimates could reach $20 billion to $30 billion annually. Earlier this year, GM CEO Mary Barra told investors the company’s defense unit, which already produces military vehicles and components for Lockheed Martin’s Patriot Missile System, would produce double-digit profit margins in coming years.

As usual, the Neanderthals in the UAW apparatus are staking out the most right-wing and nationalist position on the economic and military conflict with China. Trump went out of his way at a press conference last week to praise Shawn Fain’s support for the administration’s trade war measures.

The UAW’s nationalism revives the ugliest traditions in the union’s history—the “Buy American” campaigns and the smashing of Japanese cars of the late 1970s that formed the background to the 1982 murder of Vincent Chin. Today, the UAW’s anti-Chinese campaign goes hand-in-hand with suppressing resistance to mass layoffs and the conversion of auto plants for war. Fain has repeatedly held up as a model the World War II-era “Arsenal of Democracy,” i.e., the alliance of the UAW with the Roosevelt administration and the automakers to build tanks, planes and bombs, which included a ban on strikes against the war profiteerers.

The purpose of this chauvinism is to tell autoworkers that they share a common interest with the corporations that are restructuring production at their expense, and to redirect their anger away from Ford and GM, and against workers in China.

The working class must not line up with either section of the ruling class in this dispute. The workers of the United States have no interest in defending Ford, GM and Stellantis against Chinese manufacturers, and Chinese workers have no interest in the ambitions of the Chinese ruling elite. The answer to the trade war, the industrial mobilization and the drive to war is the unity of workers in the United States, China, Mexico, Canada and throughout the world against every capitalist government.

This requires a clear understanding of the technology at the center of the conflict. The simplification of EV body assemblies—the reduction of parts, stations and labor time—is a progressive development of the productive forces. Under capitalism, it is being used to throw workers onto the unemployment line, to intensify speedup and to drive down wages. But the same technology, placed under the control of the working class, could be used to shorten the workweek, to lessen burdensome and dangerous labor, and to guarantee a high standard of living for all.

That is the socialist program. The auto industry must be taken out of the hands of the corporations and placed under public ownership and workers’ democratic control, so that the transition to electric vehicles is carried out through a massive improvement of workers’ living standards and working conditions, not at their expense. If EVs require less labor time to produce, then reduce hours and increase pay.

Whatever faction prevails in the current dispute, the working class faces a coming onslaught on jobs and working conditions. Ford’s own third-quarter report boasts of rising profits, achieved through “stronger product mix” and work to “control our costs”—the language of layoffs, speedup and the extraction of ever more surplus value from a shrinking workforce. The company has announced or carried out roughly 14,000 job cuts across North America, Europe and India since 2022. Across the industry, Nissan is eliminating 20,000 jobs, and Volkswagen is preparing to eliminate up to 100,000. The Democrats, who owe their congressional majorities to a wave of opposition to war and social inequality, have made clear that their central priority upon taking power in January will be the escalation of the drive to secure American global dominance—not the defense of jobs.

The UAW bureaucracy will not defend the workers. It has collaborated in eliminating hundreds of thousands of jobs, closing scores of plants and imposing tiered wages and temporary employment for decades. Its function is to discipline the workforce and to channel opposition into the dead end of nationalism and war. Workers must build rank-and-file committees in every plant, independent of and in opposition to the corporatist UAW apparatus, uniting across plants, companies and borders through the International Workers Alliance of Rank-and-File Committees.

The struggle over Ford and China is a struggle over who will bear the costs of a technological revolution, trade war and militarism. The ruling class, in all its factions, intends that the working class should bear them. The task of the working class is to answer with a program of its own: no layoffs, no plant closures, full income and benefits for all affected, international unity against the trade war and the drive to war, and the socialist reorganization of the auto industry under public ownership and workers’ control. This is the only answer to the nationalist poison of “American manufacturing” and the only road to a future in which the immense productive powers now being developed are placed at the service of humanity.

text:
Latin America’s copper, energy and mineral resources could play a growing role in supplying the global artificial-intelligence build-out, as data centers and electrification drive demand for power and raw materials.

But for investors, it’s less about whether Latin America has the resources than whether governments can turn them into viable projects.

“We are going through an acceleration in energy demand growth. We need every possible energy source available,” Michele Della Vigna, head of natural resources research for Goldman Sachs, told CNBC. “Ultimately, what drives economic growth is energy,” he added.

Ben Kumar, head of strategy for wealth, investment and public policy at 7IM, suggested Latin America could benefit, given the physical materials needed for AI equipment and data centers. “We are currently neutral in the short term, but if the materials and mining cycle continues, we could see this moving to positive in a few months,” he said.

Where the investment case is strongest

The investment case varies across the region. Chile has copper; Argentina is expanding oil and gas exports; and Brazil has abundant renewable power and significant rare earth reserves.

Chile’s copper sector illustrates both the supply potential and the constraints to expanding supply. Copper production fell 8.5% in the first nine months of 2026, according to the state copper commission Cochilco, as lower ore grades, maintenance, and operational disruptions constrained supply.

But demand for refined copper is set to grow 1.6% this year and 2% next year, according to the International Copper Study Group. Supply is struggling to keep pace with demand from expanding electricity grids.

Chile’s copper commission has raised its 2027 price forecast to $5.95 a pound, from $5.10. Codelco, the state-owned copper producer, may also have scope to increase supply, including through proposed public-private partnerships.

Rafael Ch, partner and senior analyst for Latin America and emerging markets at Signum Global Advisors, sees demand continuing to grow. “As countries expand electricity grids, they need more copper regardless of which power source they choose,” he said.

The scale of the opportunity will depend in part on how quickly energy demand grows. Goldman Sachs forecasts that global power demand for data centers will grow by 170% by 2030. The IEA projected in April that global data center electricity consumption would rise from 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030.

Turning resources into investment

Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty Images

The investment case also depends on whether the region can capture more value from the resources it produces. Latin America and the Caribbean refined only 26% of the copper they mined in 2025, according to the IEA.

“Cautious optimism is justified and there will be massive critical mineral demand,” said Monica de Bolle, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.

“But improving refining capacity will be crucial to capture more of that value,” she added.

Some projects have already secured financing. Chilean explorer Marimaca Copper Corp selected a preferred lender for a $400 million debt facility to build a mine on Oct. 28. The funding will go towards developing an open-pit mine in the north of Chile that will produce 50,000 metric tons of refined copper annually. Production is expected from 2029.

Argentina shows the other side of the opportunity: strong oil and gas resources, but insufficient infrastructure to get more production to global markets.

“I see an opportunity in the infrastructure that gets Argentine oil and gas to market. A producer in Vaca Muerta can have excellent wells and still struggle to expand exports without pipeline capacity and access to ports.

That gives investors a reason to look at transport and export infrastructure alongside production,” Rafael Ch, partner and senior analyst for Latin America and emerging markets at Signum Global Advisors, added. Vaca Muerta is Argentina’s vast shale basin.

Argentina is also attracting investment in drilling and export infrastructure. International capital markets have reopened to investment in drilling and pipelines in Argentina. That investment has already driven the build-out of a pipeline and port. Argentina will then be able to export far more crude oil. Chevron and American oil tycoon Harold Hamm have also increased their investments in Argentina.

Brazil’s case rests partly on its renewable-heavy power mix. About 89% of the country’s electricity was generated from renewable sources in 2025, according to the country’s Ministry of Mines and Energy.

“That puts Brazil in a strong position to benefit as AI and data centers drive up demand,” Stephanie Link, chief investment strategist and portfolio manager at Hightower Advisors, told CNBC.

But while Brazil has the world’s second-largest reported rare-earth reserves, its estimated mine production is far smaller than China’s. USGS estimates put Brazil’s output at 2,000 metric tons in 2025, compared with China’s 270,000 metric tons. Brazil’s reserves are estimated at 11 million metric tons by the USGS, second only to China’s 44 million metric tons.

For investors, the gap between Brazil’s vast reserves and limited current production is both the opportunity and the execution risk.

Saul Loeb | Afp | Getty Images

The risks to watch

For investors, the policy question is whether governments can make projects viable and keep them on track.

Luis Costa, Citi’s global head of emerging markets strategy, said governments need to offer incentives, particularly in the early stages of projects, because infrastructure lags the region’s resource wealth. He also stressed that support must last: infrastructure projects can take several years to develop.

The World Bank’s Latin America and the Caribbean Economic Update for 2026 projects growth for the region of 2.2%, and highlights the “restricted fiscal space, sticky inflation and high borrowing costs.”

“The economic policy and fiscal policy needs to get in line as markets are globally becoming more sensitive to fiscal stories,” said Costa.

Brazil will need to establish fiscal credibility to attract investment, particularly if higher public spending puts additional pressure on debt and borrowing costs. “If investors doubt the government can stabilize public debt, companies’ long-term financing costs could stay high even as the central bank lowers its policy rate,” Ch added.

With Argentina set for national elections in October 2027, political continuity will also matter for energy investment. “A return to tighter currency controls or persistent deficits would make companies more likely to delay projects, even in an oil field with attractive economics,” said Ch.

Tomas Cuesta | Getty Images News | Getty Images

Pro-business President Javier Milei faces a tight race for re-election, though a change in leadership would not necessarily undermine medium- to long-term investment.

“There is also the possibility of a pragmatic Peronist ticket emerging, which markets would be satisfied with,” said Nicolas Jaquier, emerging-market fixed-income portfolio manager at Ninety One.

For those governing across Latin America, policies to unlock its wealth of resources will be key for it to emerge as a winner from the AI demand boom.

“Supply chain security is becoming more and more relevant, and if commodities take off Latin America can be a clear and obvious winner,” said Kumar.

title: Is a Victory For Lula a Victory for the Environment? - Rosa-Luxemburg-Stiftung
description:
Nevertheless, many projects jeopardising the environment and Indigenous communities are still being pushed forward – including some funded by European countries such as Germany.
Niklas Franzen: In the lead-up to this year’s presidential elections in Brazil, people mobilised en masse for President Lula, securing his victory.
The Limits of Lula’s Environmental Record Outside of Brazil, President Lula is often seen as a politician devoted to environmental protection.
This initiative ended up being the catalyst for one of the largest mobilisations of Indigenous communities.
Can you provide a concrete example of what role Germany could play in this?
text:
Brazil’s presidential elections resulted in a defeat for the far right. Nevertheless, many projects jeopardising the environment and Indigenous communities are still being pushed forward – including some funded by European countries such as Germany.

In this interview, Verena Glass from Rosa Luxemburg Foundation’s Sao Paolo office discusses Lula’s election victory, the far right’s continuing influence in Congress, and what Germany’s interest in Brazilian energy and rare-earth deposits means for climate protection and for Indigenous rights.

Niklas Franzen: In the lead-up to this year’s presidential elections in Brazil, people mobilised en masse for President Lula, securing his victory. How was the election for you?

Verena Glass: Brazil is known for its large social movements and strong trade unions. These groups have often been able to mobilise the public and get people out onto the streets. In this year’s second round of voting, however, the traditional left-wing groups were not at the forefront, calling on people to protest. It was ordinary citizens who were afraid of a return to fascism.

The election became about defending a democratic system that would have been under severe threat had the far right returned to power. Social media helped to mobilise precisely those people who had never been politically active.

The atmosphere was initially more subdued in the run-up to the first round.

Yes, before the first round, there was a prevailing sense of apathy and many simply did not vote. But just before the run-off, the mood changed – many felt that they had an important role to play and that they could actually make a difference with their vote. One example of this is the migrant workers from the Northeast who organised ride shares to help people return to their home towns and vote.

Which groups were particularly effective in their mobilisation?

Marginalised groups, I’d say. In other words, the groups who were attacked most under Bolsonaro’s government. Indigenous peoples, Quilombola communities — descendants of escaped enslaved people — and members of traditional communities.

Many people believed that there would be devastating consequences if Flávio Bolsonaro were elected, and this led to historic levels of grassroots organisation. You can even see very moving videos online of Indigenous people travelling hundreds of kilometres by boat in order to cast their vote.

The Limits of Lula’s Environmental Record

Outside of Brazil, President Lula is often seen as a politician devoted to environmental protection. And indeed, his government has managed to make some progress, by reducing deforestation in the Amazon for instance. What’s your assessment of the role he plays in Brazilian environmental policy?

His government has absolutely made progress. The establishment of the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples was an important step. Aside from that, Lula made advances in the designation of Indigenous territories.

Even in the Amazon, where there is a significant Indigenous population, the far right has become increasingly influential.

However, it must also be said that the National Congress is currently very conservative, with very strong representation from the far right. This means that extremely harmful laws have been passed, such as the so-called Marco temporal das terras indígenas (“the temporal marker for Indigenous land”) based on a ruling by the Supreme Court, which decided that Indigenous people only had rights to land that was in their possession when the current Brazilian constitution was passed in 1988.

That ruling and related laws largely brought the demarcation of Indigenous territories to a halt. And even in the Amazon, where there is a significant Indigenous population, the far right has become increasingly influential.

What have been the consequences of this?

Although many Indigenous areas are currently protected, they are under enormous pressure to open up from the mining industry, for example. The prospect of opening up Indigenous territories to mining is very real. One major source of leverage in this situation is the discussion around rare-earth elements (REEs) and critical minerals, which are needed for the energy transition.

Lula has emphasised the central role of REEs again and again.

What Lula is really saying is, “We will exploit rare-earth elements ourselves.”

When Lula says, “The rare-earth elements belong to us,” that does not mean that he wants to leave them all in the ground. What he’s really saying is, “We will exploit them ourselves.”

But to be fair, we must admit that Lula is under a lot of pressure from the business sector. Brazil is deeply in debt and depends on income from its raw materials. The whole world is competing for resources, and Brazil certainly does not want to fall behind.

Last year I met Edinho da Silva, the leader of the Workers’ Party (PT), in Berlin and spoke with him about the controversial offshore oil drilling near the mouth of the Amazon River. At the time he told me, “A country with as much poverty as Brazil cannot forgo potential sources of wealth.” What’s your take on this argument?

This particular project is absolutely preposterous, given the enormous repercussions it would have.

While people talk about environmental protection and decarbonisation, Brazil is still banking on petroleum as a source of energy. According to the government, petroleum represents an indispensable source of income, even despite the considerable social and ecological consequences.

If Brazil continues to be a country that primarily exports raw materials, this situation will never change. We need to start thinking about a different economic model.

Bolsonarismo Is Not Dead Yet

Flávio Bolsonaro lost the election, but many right wing politicians will still occupy seats in Parliament. It’s even expected that the new Congress will be the most conservative in Brazil’s history. What does that mean for the country’s political development?

We are currently witnessing a strong rollback since the National Congress has revamped and weakened environmental legislation. Numerous amendments are affecting laws that previously protected forests and the people who live in them.

The process unfolds as follows: Congress passes legislative amendments, Lula vetoes individual provisions, but Congress proceeds to override these vetoes.

As for the social movements and communities whose rights are being threatened and violated, how strong do you think they actually are?

One of Lula’s decrees provided for three large rivers that flow through Indigenous lands to be opened to privatisation and appropriation by the mining and agricultural industry. These rivers were to be privatised and made available to these economic sectors, with the ultimate goal of expanding their capacity to transport raw materials and agricultural products from the region.

This initiative ended up being the catalyst for one of the largest mobilisations of Indigenous communities. Over the course of 33 days, Indigenous activists occupied the premises of agribusiness company Cargill, successfully pressuring Lula to revise his decree.

Energy and Resources for the Global North

And what role does the Global North – Germany for example - play in all this?

German companies want to secure their share of Brazil’s REE deposits.

Just last month, a discussion meeting was held by the German-Brazilian Chamber of Industry and Commerce. The message from Germany was quite clear: we must invest heavily in this sector, otherwise it will be left to the Chinese.

At the beginning of Lula’s term, German politicians were practically lining up to have talks with Brazil, constantly pointing out the country’s central role in global environmental protection. How sincere is Germany’s commitment to environmental protection? Is it just a form of political marketing?

Three or four years ago, one of the world’s boldest visions for the future was the possibility of storing and exporting green hydrogen. At the time, green hydrogen was thought of as the largest energy source of the future.

In Germany, this sparked a lot of interest in Brazil, especially in local wind farms that generate green energy.

However, the technology didn’t continue to develop as quickly as expected. This shifted Germany’s interest to REEs.

Brazil has mastered the art of disregarding obligations to local communities.

At the same time, I also think that Germany has historically maintained a relatively consistent position on environmental issues. Germany is not one of the countries that deny climate change, and this is reflected in the Amazon Fund for example, one of the country’s most important development projects.

However, the current German government is very conservative, with political leadership focused more on the war in Ukraine and other developments within Europe right now. This may be an indication that relations with Brazil have lost some of their importance.

What could be the role of the International Labour Organization’s (ILO) Convention 169, which was ratified by Germany in 2022 and guarantees a whole host of rights for Indigenous and traditional communities?

ILO Convention 169 mandates that Indigenous, traditional and Quilombola communities be included in a consultation process. The state must carry out consultations with these communities in order to determine if a given undertaking is acceptable and viable for them.

Still, Brazil has mastered the art of disregarding this obligation.

Can you provide a concrete example of what role Germany could play in this?

Let’s imagine that the German federal government invests in a wind farm project in Brazil.

This wind farm produces clean, sustainable, and renewable energy. However, the project also has considerable consequences for the nearby fishing villages.

Before German money can flow into this project, the federal government would first have to require that certain conditions be met. They would have to ask whether the local population was actually consulted. If not, no money could be invested in the project.

In other words, it must be ensured that projects funded by German taxpayers are implemented under conditions that are environmentally sound and socially just.

title: India got nearly $31 billion in climate and sustainability funding—where did the money go?
description:
India has attracted nearly $31 billion in climate and sustainability equity funding since 2021, but more than 90% of the money has gone into just two sectors — power and low-carbon fuels, and transport — highlighting how investment remains concentrated in areas with more established business models.
The report, titled India’s Climate & Sustainability Moment: Capital, Opportunity and the Road Ahead, analysed equity investments in companies with a significant presence in India.
Transport received another $9.5 billion, taking the combined investment in the two sectors to about $28.5 billion.
Despite attracting nearly $31 billion since 2021, India will need far more capital to meet its climate and sustainability commitments.
The report estimates that India could require $22 trillion-$24 trillion in investments between 2026 and 2070, or roughly $500 billion a year, against current annual climate investment of about $135 billion.
text:
India has attracted nearly $31 billion in climate and sustainability equity funding since 2021, but more than 90% of the money has gone into just two sectors — power and low-carbon fuels, and transport — highlighting how investment remains concentrated in areas with more established business models.

A report by the Indian Venture and Alternate Capital Association (IVCA) and Boston Consulting Group (BCG) found that power and low-carbon fuels attracted about $19 billion, while transport drew another $9.5 billion between 2021 and October 2026.

The report, titled India’s Climate & Sustainability Moment: Capital, Opportunity and the Road Ahead, analysed equity investments in companies with a significant presence in India. The data was compiled from deals tracked by Tracxn and Venture Intelligence, with duplicate transactions removed. Debt financing and initial public offerings were excluded.

Where did the money go?

Power and low-carbon fuels attracted the largest share, at about $19 billion. The category includes renewable energy and other technologies supporting India's shift towards cleaner power.

Transport received another $9.5 billion, taking the combined investment in the two sectors to about $28.5 billion. According to the report, both benefited from early policy support that helped make investments commercially viable.

Funding for other sectors was considerably smaller. Manufacturing and waste attracted about $1 billion each, while agriculture received roughly $1 billion. Other climate and sustainability segments together drew around $500 million.

Why did investors favour these sectors?

Capital largely flowed to areas where policy support, market demand and the prospect of commercial returns came together, the report said.

In power, long-term power purchase agreements, renewable-energy auctions and other policy measures helped give investors greater visibility on returns. Transport benefited from policies supporting electric vehicles, battery manufacturing and cleaner mobility.

Renewable power and electric mobility have increasingly become commercially viable, while areas such as energy storage, green hydrogen, bioenergy and recycling continue to face funding constraints and need policy support to scale up, the report said.

Despite attracting nearly $31 billion since 2021, India will need far more capital to meet its climate and sustainability commitments.

The report estimates that India could require $22 trillion-$24 trillion in investments between 2026 and 2070, or roughly $500 billion a year, against current annual climate investment of about $135 billion.

text:
“If the grid goes down, or something really bad happens, like a natural disaster or a cybersecurity attack on infrastructure, you need to keep the lights on,” U.S. Rep. Betty McCollum said. “You need to keep the drinking water safe.”

McCollum was among those who celebrated the opening of the center’s 6,000-square-foot expansion.

“St. Thomas should not look the same today as it did 10 years ago, 25 years ago, 100 years ago, because the needs of the world are changing,” President Rob Vischer said at the ribbon-cutting ceremony on Oct. 21.

The Center for Microgrid Research started in the basement of what is now the Engineering Design Center with two students, a desk pulled from the university recycling center and a small microgrid system they were working to get fully operational.

Today, Mahmoud Kabalan, Bright.Green Director of the Center for Microgrid Research and an associate professor of electrical engineering in the College of Engineering, leads a team of about 25 researchers and students. The center’s electrical systems have a combined capacity of roughly 3 megawatts, enough to power an estimated 3,000 to 5,000 homes.

“This building that we are in today will usher in a new kind of power engineering research, education and workforce training,” Kabalan said.

Under Kabalan’s leadership, the center has secured more than $35 million in funding from sources including the National Science Foundation, Minnesota Department of Commerce and U.S. Army Engineer Research and Development Center. State and federal investments, university support and philanthropy, including support from electrical engineer and entrepreneur Jason Bright, helped make the expansion possible.

“The idea behind a Center for Microgrid Research is to help the nation modernize its electrical grid, to make it more resilient, more robust,” College of Engineering Dean Don Weinkauf said.

The expanded facility moves research beyond computer models into full-scale testing. Its first floor can support up to 45,000 pounds, accommodating electric buses and container-sized grid systems. An outdoor equipment yard includes a grid-level battery energy storage system and load bank, with additional power equipment in the basement.

The facility also allows researchers to test how energy technologies from different companies can work together, including electric vehicles, battery storage, fuel cells, solar arrays and generators.

“How do you get products from different companies and make them work together?” Kabalan said. “That is the trillion-dollar question.

St. Thomas serves as the lead organization in an applied research partnership with the U.S. Army that also involves Virginia Tech, North Carolina State University, MIT Lincoln Laboratory, Cal Poly and Texas A&M. The work supports the Army’s goal of making every installation a microgrid by 2035 while moving emerging technologies toward real-world applications.

Kabalan said the work is “advancing our nation’s research agenda and training its future workforce.”

The research also has civilian applications. Local governments and nonprofit organizations seek guidance from the center, while growing electricity demand from artificial intelligence and data centers is creating new questions about how power is generated and distributed.

McCollum described the expansion as “a big step toward greater energy security and workforce here in Minnesota.”

St. Paul Mayor Kaohly Her, who helped carry state funding for the project while serving in the Minnesota House of Representatives, also pointed to its workforce potential.

“As a city, we need to grow the businesses that rely on this energy,” Her said. “Then our ability to foster those businesses and to grow here becomes all the more viable for us.”

Vischer said the center reflects the university’s larger responsibility to put its expertise to work on changing societal needs.

“If we want to always be discerning how our expertise, our resources, our traditions, our mission connect with the needs of the world,” Vischer said, “we’re going to have initiatives like the Center for Microgrid Research.”

LGMG has unveiled the VTH150 electric-wheel mining dump truck at bauma CHINA 2026, which the company describes as the first electric-wheel drive system powered by permanent magnet synchronous motors. LGMG says its electric haulers cut energy use by up to 20% against fuel-powered trucks.

The release, as issued by LGMG

LGMG Unveils VTH150 Electric-Wheel Mining Truck at bauma CHINA 2026

The debut comes as LGMG marks ten consecutive years as the global sales leader in off-highway mechanical-drive wide-body dump trucks.

SHANGHAI, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — LGMG today unveiled its VTH150 electric-wheel mining dump truck at bauma CHINA 2026. Built to haul heavy loads around the clock in large open-pit mines, the VTH150 features what LGMG describes as the world’s first electric-wheel drive system powered by permanent magnet synchronous motors (PMSMs).

A Decade of Leadership in Purpose-Built Mining Trucks

LGMG entered the wide-body dump truck market in 2012 with trucks engineered from the ground up for mining. Field research guided improvements in payload capacity, structural strength, reliability and operator comfort on long shifts.

In August 2026, Frost & Sullivan published its independent study of the global off-highway mechanical-drive wide-body dump truck market, confirming that LGMG had led worldwide sales in the category for ten consecutive years.

Electric-Wheel Drive for Heavy Haulage

The VTH150 takes LGMG into the high-capacity electric-wheel mining truck segment. Its PMSM drive is more efficient, more compact and easier to service. LGMG can take its electric-wheel technology from prototype to full-scale production in-house.

LGMG introduced hybrid mining trucks in 2019 and began producing fully electric models in 2020. Its lineup now includes hybrid, fully electric and methanol-powered mining equipment.

LGMG’s mining truck portfolio uses in-house modular electric drives and vehicle controls to adjust power output as conditions change. These technologies can cut energy use by up to 20% versus conventional fuel-powered mining trucks.

LGMG is also developing its own drive-by-wire chassis technology and collaborating with autonomous driving specialists to demonstrate driverless haul trucks under a range of operating conditions. The projects are helping mines automate haulage and coordinate truck movements more precisely.

Linking Haulage, Power and Mine Operations

LGMG will continue to develop electric drives, electronic controls and battery systems. The company is also advancing microgrids that combine solar power, energy storage and charging, along with digital platforms for managing mine operations.

LGMG aims to bring trucks, charging infrastructure and mine management systems together so operators can run their sites more efficiently, cut operating costs and move toward lower-emission operations.

title: Shaking EV Manufacturing Base Demands Domestic Tax Credit
description:
If the domestic production base for completed vehicles falters, the ripple effects on suppliers and regional economies would be severe.
This is not merely a competition between vehicle models but a grave warning to our manufacturing base and industrial ecosystem.
Japan has introduced a tax incentive system to promote domestic production in strategic sectors, offering a 400,000 Japanese yen tax credit per EV produced and sold domestically.
In South Korea, the introduction of a domestic production tax credit for EVs has become a key legislative agenda.
The National Assembly and government must act swiftly, heeding the industry’s urgency and the imperative of shared growth, to decisively introduce domestic production tax credits.
text:
For a nation’s economy to endure external pressures and sustain long-term growth, it must have a robust manufacturing base as its foundation. South Korea, a resource-poor country, owes its rise to an economic powerhouse to the manufacturing capabilities built through decades of labor on the front lines.

Among these, the automotive industry stands as the backbone of our manufacturing sector, encompassing a vast network of related industries and jobs. It intertwines with steel, materials, batteries, electronics, and software, forming an ecosystem that supports countless first-, second-, and third-tier small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and regional communities. If the domestic production base for completed vehicles falters, the ripple effects on suppliers and regional economies would be severe.

Recently, the domestic and global automotive markets have faced intense competition from Chinese electric vehicles (EVs). From January to September this year, Chinese EVs—such as Tesla and BYD models produced at the Shanghai Gigafactory—accounted for 43.5% of newly registered passenger EVs in South Korea. In contrast, domestic EVs fell to 48.7%, dropping below the 50% mark. Analysis shows that the rate at which Chinese EVs are encroaching on the domestic market is the third-fastest globally. Meanwhile, South Korea’s trade deficit with China in the automotive sector reached over 4.2 billion dollars from January to October, the largest on record. This is not merely a competition between vehicle models but a grave warning to our manufacturing base and industrial ecosystem.

Major economies are responding urgently. The United States and the European Union are protecting their automotive industries through high tariffs and supply chain policies. Japan has introduced a tax incentive system to promote domestic production in strategic sectors, offering a 400,000 Japanese yen tax credit per EV produced and sold domestically. Despite differing circumstances and methods, governments worldwide share a common urgency to safeguard domestic production and employment.

In South Korea, the introduction of a domestic production tax credit for EVs has become a key legislative agenda. While the government’s August tax reform proposal included credits for battery production, EVs were excluded. However, lawmakers from both ruling and opposition parties have since proposed new bills for discussion. Given the fiscal constraints, scope of eligibility, potential overlaps with existing support, and compliance with trade norms, a meticulous design is needed to balance the policy’s intent with its fiscal impact.

To ensure effectiveness, the system must also address on-the-ground conditions and fairness. Key considerations include setting appropriate credit levels and limits, whether to include export volumes alongside domestic sales—as Japan does—to support factory operations, and how to extend benefits to low-profit companies and their supply chains. The government must carefully navigate between fiscal sustainability and the urgent needs of the manufacturing sector.

Protecting the manufacturing base cannot be the responsibility of a single entity. Only when domestic factories operate stably, with benefits flowing to SMEs, regional jobs, and improved working conditions, can sustainable growth take root. A virtuous cycle—where large corporations, SMEs, and regions mutually reinforce one another—will strengthen the economy’s resilience.

Policymaking cannot afford delays. The experiences of the UK, where a weakened automotive base has led to decline, and Germany, which faced turmoil during industry restructuring, demonstrate that reviving a collapsed production ecosystem and supply chain requires immense cost and time. The National Assembly and government must act swiftly, heeding the industry’s urgency and the imperative of shared growth, to decisively introduce domestic production tax credits.

text:
Honda is trusting the more than 5,000 workers at its Lincoln, Alabama plant with its next big bet, a hybrid V6. The company is investing $462 million in the plant, which builds the Pilot, Passport, Ridgeline, and Odyssey, and adding 200 new jobs along with a dedicated hybrid V6 assembly line.

For shoppers, that line means hybrid versions of Honda's biggest SUVs and its pickup are on the way. Here is what the investment means for the people who build them and for the families who drive them.

Inside Honda's $462 Million Alabama Plant Investment

Honda will use the $462 million to boost production of all four models built in Lincoln and to add an assembly line for the new hybrid V6, according to Ward's Auto. The investment is expected to create 200 new jobs.

Once the upgrades are complete, Honda expects to build multiple models on the same assembly line. That flexibility lets the plant shift production as demand for hybrids grows.

The Ridgeline is first in line, as Honda prepares the third-generation Ridgeline. Today's truck uses a 3.5-liter V6, and some have called the Ridgeline the last true V6 pickup.

The Pilot and Passport are likely to get the hybrid V6 too, either as the only powertrain or as an option. That would bring hybrid power to every vehicle built in Lincoln except the Odyssey.

The Alabama Workers Behind the Pilot and Ridgeline

Honda's Lincoln plant opened in 2001 and covers 4.9 million square feet. It is Honda's largest plant by both employment and production volume.

More than 5,000 people work there today, and the plant can build 340,000 vehicles and 340,000 engines a year. That engine experience is a big reason the hybrid V6 line is going to Alabama.

Nearly 15 percent of the Honda and Acura vehicles built since 2001 have come from Lincoln, according to Honda. Few plants anywhere can match that track record.

Ward's reports the plant generated $8.5 billion in economic impact for Alabama in 2024. Counting Tier 1 suppliers, the total rises to $11.7 billion and 47,000 direct and indirect jobs in the state.

Those numbers represent thousands of families, from the assembly line to the supplier shops around it. The new investment builds on decades of work by the people who already make Honda's biggest vehicles.

What a Hybrid V6 Pilot and Ridgeline Could Mean for Buyers

Today's AWD Pilot is rated at 21 mpg combined, while the Toyota Grand Highlander Hybrid is rated at 34. That gap has pushed some families toward Toyota, as in one Phoenix family's Pilot vs Grand Highlander Hybrid decision.

A hybrid V6 would help Honda close that gap while keeping the power Pilot and Ridgeline owners expect for towing. Honda has not released power or fuel economy figures yet.

Pilot owners tend to keep their SUVs for a long time. That shows in stories like a 2017 Pilot owner asking whether it will last forever.

Ridgeline owners already pay attention to fuel-saving technology. That includes federal scrutiny of the Ridgeline's start-stop system.

Why Honda Is Investing in Hybrids

Alabama is not Honda's only hybrid investment. Earlier this month, the company committed $3 billion to a new Ohio plant that will start building hybrids in 2029.

Honda plans to launch 15 hybrid models by 2030. The 2028 CR-V will be hybrid only, and there are clear reasons Honda is making that move.

Across the industry, automakers are leaning toward hybrids for several reasons.

Fast charging is not yet as widespread as it needs to be.

Even fast charging takes longer than filling a gas tank.

EVs are still expensive for many buyers.

Range anxiety remains a concern.

Federal EV tax credits ended in September 2025, leaving fewer incentives to buy EVs.

Hybrids serve as a bridge. Drivers do not need to change how they drive or worry about charging, and refueling works the same as with a gas vehicle.

Even plug-in hybrid owners do not have to plug in, though doing so saves more gas. That flexibility is a big part of the appeal.

Toyota has already made several popular models hybrid only, and Honda is following. Genesis, a brand that has invested heavily in EVs, also just added two hybrids to its lineup.

Honda's lineup is changing in other ways, too, including reports that the Honda Element will return. Here is what to expect from the 2028 CR-V.

For buyers, the next few years will bring more hybrids and, in some cases, fewer gas-only choices. For the workers in Lincoln, it means 200 new teammates and a new engine to build, and that is good news for the families who depend on the plant.

Would a hybrid V6 Pilot or Ridgeline be on your shopping list?

text:
Europe should soon start building substantial capacities of long-term energy storage based on hydrogen to secure supply in a fully renewables-based future energy system to get through prolonged ‘dark doldrum’ periods (“Dunkelflaute”) with little wind or sunshine, said researchers from the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin).

While today’s battery storage can help supply European demand during more frequent shorter periods of low renewables feed-in, other options are needed for longer Dunkelflaute events. In the current energy system, conventional power plants based on coal, gas or nuclear energy ensure supply during such periods, and Germany has begun tendering new gas power plants which are supposed to be converted to run on green hydrogen later.

In future, surplus renewable electricity could be used to produce hydrogen, which would be stored underground in cavern storage facilities, and converted back into electricity when required, the researchers said.

This process is set to remain costly and the researchers argued it is unlikely to happen without state support. “It is hardly worthwhile for private investors to maintain storage capacity designed to cope with extreme dark doldrum periods, as it is likely that such capacity would only very rarely be utilised to full capacity,” said author Wolf-Peter Schill. Targeted state-backed risk-hedging and support instruments would be needed to build out such storage capacity, and the researchers argued Germany should include them in the capacity market the government plans to introduce for the period after 2032.

DIW said that it is difficult to estimate the exact future demand for hydrogen-based long-term storage, as there are considerable uncertainties regarding the development of future electricity generation needs, as well as regarding alternative storage options. “However, this analysis suggests that the European energy system may require long-term storage capacities amounting to several hundred terawatt-hours,” the researchers wrote, pointing to especially long dark doldrums.

The German government is betting on green hydrogen as a key element of its energy transition. While the direct use of electricity is set to power the majority of applications – from EVs and heat pumps to home appliances and many manufacturing processes – some industrial production requires very high temperatures that electric systems currently struggle to deliver at a scale and a price that makes it competitive for industry use. Hydrogen will also be needed as a feedstock in the chemical sector, as a fuel in aviation, and to stabilise the power grid during longer periods of little wind and sunshine.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Sino-American Silicon Products and United Renewable Energy are moving ahead with their joint US expansion plans to build a solar module factory in Texas.

The companies announced the plan in July and established a subsidiary, Taiwan Solar Assure, to carry out the project. A contract with Fascore Construction will cover design and construction of the factory, with spending capped at NT$630 million (US$20 million), according to UDN Money.

The first phase will give the facility capacity to manufacture solar modules with a combined rated output of one gigawatt (GW), or 1 billion watts, per year. Mass production is scheduled to begin in the third quarter next year.

For context, a power plant with a capacity of 1 GW can generate 1 gigawatt-hour of electricity in one hour. This is enough to meet the annual power needs of about 876,000 households, according to Carbon Collective.

United Renewable Energy Chairman Hung Chuan-hsien (洪傳獻) previously said the US solar market has an annual demand of 40-50 GW, of which approximately 35 GW comes from buyers seeking non-China supply chains. This creates room for domestic manufacturers to expand their presence in the market.

The Texas factory will primarily produce solar modules for large-scale ground-mounted solar projects. It will also offer products for rooftop installations, residential solar systems, and AI data centers.

Solar modules, also known as solar panels, are a key component of solar power systems. They contain interconnected cells that convert sunlight into electricity, according to the Industrial Safety and Health Association and Hengs Technology.

The two companies bring different areas of expertise to the partnership. Sino-American Silicon Products spun off its semiconductor wafer manufacturing business into a separate subsidiary, GlobalWafers, in 2011, and has since focused on materials and energy, including solar cell and module production, according to Pocket Securities.
