text:
Now that Democrats are set to take power on Capitol Hill, the lame duck G.O.P.-controlled Congress is trying to push through its remaining priorities before time is up. That includes an enormous bill to overhaul federal permitting rules that passed the Senate last week with the help of 14 Democrats. The legislation, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, is heading to the House in what is likely to be a make-or-break vote.

Backed by oil and mining companies, the chemical and plastics industries, renewable energy businesses, Beltway think tanks, tech trade groups, hard-hat unions and some climate groups, the bill is a bipartisan effort to speed up development of all kinds. Large solar and wind farms, transmission lines, roads and other transportation projects, mines and pipelines would get easier paths to approval. According to its Democratic supporters, the measure is an affordability bill that will help lower energy costs and greenhouse gas emissions.

The problem is that, in seeking to speed up industrial development, the bill severely weakens core environmental laws that for generations have helped prevent pollution of lakes and rivers, conserved unique landscapes, protected tribal heritage and brought endangered species back from the brink. If the bill passes the House and is signed into law by President Trump, it would reduce public participation in federal government decision-making and free the Trump administration to reward its friends and allies with more lucrative deals on our treasured public lands. It could transform the places where Americans hunt, fish, camp, work and explore.

The targets of the bill include the National Environmental Policy Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, the Endangered Species Act and the Clean Water Act. According to the coalition behind permitting reform, litigious green groups use these laws to mount frivolous lawsuits that hamper the construction of critical infrastructure, including clean energy.

A recent paper by legal experts at the University of Utah and the University of Texas, Austin, examined the truth of such assertions. They found that in the case of the National Environmental Policy Act, “Neither the volume of litigation under NEPA nor the relief granted suggests that litigation is anywhere near crisis levels. The number of infrastructure projects challenged, in particular, is modest, and the likelihood of projects being enjoined is even smaller.”

Nevertheless, the permitting bill strips away much of NEPA’s remaining power. Right now, if the government fails to adequately and transparently conduct environmental reviews before authorizing major projects, including energy projects on public lands, citizens can sue to block them until they follow the law. This gives citizens and civil society groups a voice to influence federal decisions, and has helped reduce the destructive effects of oil and gas drilling on wildlife in Wyoming, prevented ill-conceived logging in national forests and lessened the threat of mining waste contaminating drinking water. It has also been used in lawsuits against Mr. Trump’s vanity projects.

But the Senate bill severely restricts the public’s ability to use the courts to enforce NEPA, making it nearly impossible for citizens to meaningfully ensure that government-authorized projects comply with the law before they proceed. NEPA will likely become a dead letter.

The permitting bill weakens core provisions of the Endangered Species Act, legislation that has helped keep the gray wolf, the grizzly bear, the American alligator and many other species from going extinct in the Lower 48. The proposed legislation exempts certain federally approved projects from having to comply with the Endangered Species Act’s environmental review component — one of the law’s most important safeguards. It also allows the federal government, with certain ground rules, to delegate key functions of the law to the states, many of which have been hostile to its mandates.

Will Wyoming do robust endangered species reviews for oil and gas projects it depends on for a significant share of its state budget? Will Florida do rigorous reviews for real estate developments backed by the governor’s wealthy donors? The permitting bill is not only a recipe for harm; it will create a regulatory patchwork that will be difficult for the public to track or challenge. And wildlife, including panthers and polar bears, may suffer the consequences.

Or consider a provision in the bill that pertains to the 1872 Mining Act and recent judicial decisions that have restricted the ability of mining companies to dump waste on public land. The permitting bill could allow these companies greater leeway to claim public lands for construction of waste dumps, and possibly roads, pipelines and power lines. This could result in widespread harm to biodiversity, water quality and recreational and cultural resources.

The bill’s “project certainty” provisions would also make it exceedingly difficult for a future administration to roll back the authorizations that the Trump administration locks in over the next two years. If the administration approves oil projects and mines in fragile ecosystems — for instance, a potential copper-sulfide mine in the watershed of Minnesota’s hugely popular Boundary Waters wilderness — future presidents might have little recourse to stop or materially alter those projects.

The bill could also make it easier for the Trump administration to build data centers on public lands, which Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who is heavily invested in A.I., has signaled he wants. This could mean more roads, as well as enormous complexes requiring huge quantities of water, on land owned by all Americans.

The bill’s prospects are uncertain in the House, where there are Republicans who may not want to return to Washington to vote and progressive Democrats who oppose it. Any efforts by the House to substantially soften the bill’s blows against federal environmental laws would likely fail, however.

The bill is in large part a sweeping deregulatory effort that supporters say could make electricity cheaper and speed the country’s transition away from fossil fuels. But the trade-offs are too great: President Trump will probably take full advantage of weakened environmental laws to cement his favored projects on public lands, further degrading America’s shared open spaces. Is that what the country just voted for?

More than 400 young people and jobseekers explored opportunities in one of the UK's fastest-growing sectors as University College Birmingham hosted a major Clean Energy Jobs Fair bringing together government, industry and education.

The event saw young people from schools and colleges across the region meet leading employers and discover the jobs, skills and training pathways being created as the UK transitions to clean energy.

Hosted at University College Birmingham by Professor Rosa Wells, Deputy vice-chancellor (FE College Principal, Apprenticeships & STEM), and David Paulson, Executive Dean Business School, the fair also welcomed Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, Local Energy and Jobs Minister Martin McCluskey and West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker.

Around 400 15 to 18-year-olds from local schools and colleges attended the fair, alongside 50 young people not currently in education, employment or training (NEET), with visitors able to speak directly to employers about jobs, apprenticeships, training and future careers.

Organisations represented included National Grid, Energy Systems Catapult, British Gas, Octopus Energy, Daikin, Rolls-Royce SMR and Hitachi Energy.

The Clean Energy Careers Fair gave young people the opportunity to engage directly with employers in a growing sector and see the routes available through education, apprenticeships, skills training and employment.

Among those representing National Grid was Nathan Rodrigues. Originally a culinary arts student at University College Birmingham, he returned to campus to help the next generation explore opportunities in the sector as a talent acquisition business partner for the energy company.

Nathan said: “I left school with a real passion for food and thought there was no better place to come than UCB, I loved my time here and it holds a special place in my heart.

“Since then, I switched my career and ended up in recruitment. Now I’m involved in looking after the National Grid’s Early Careers programme.

“It’s a really exciting programme that works with students from universities, colleges and schools, to find the next generation of talent.”

For University College Birmingham, the event brought together several strands of its work, from further and higher education, apprenticeships and STEM to employer partnerships, technical education and the development of skills for emerging industries.

Professor Rosa Wells said: “We are proud to host the Clean Energy Jobs Fair alongside our Green Skills Advisory Panel, bringing government, industry and education together to help people across the West Midlands seize the opportunities of clean energy.

“University College Birmingham is committed to developing the skilled workforce this transition demands, working with employers to create clear routes through further and higher education into rewarding careers.”

That skills challenge is particularly significant in the West Midlands. More than 20,000 people already work in the region's clean energy sector, with that figure expected to more than double over the next decade, according to West Midlands mayor Richard Parker.

The fair also coincided with another significant development for the University, as University College Birmingham announced new Innovate UK funding to expand battery manufacturing skills training through its Battery Manufacturing Skills Pathway (B-MSP).

text:
China is leveraging its dominance in clean technologies to expand partnerships with developing countries, promising to help them not only decarbonize but also strengthen energy security and economic development.

That was the message from Thursday’s Belt and Road energy meeting in Qingdao, which brought together ministers and officials from dozens of nations involved in the Chinese global infrastructure and investment program. China stands ready to work with other countries to bolster their energy transitions, but won’t dictate how other governments go about it, said Wang Hongzhi, head of China’s National Energy Administration.

“In the volatile energy landscape, no country can isolate itself,” Wang said. “We will respect differences in resource endowment and development stage, and support each country in pursuing a transition path suited to its own conditions.”

Energy has sat at the heart of President Xi Jinping’s Belt and Road Initiative since its launch in 2013. An early emphasis on infrastructure like pipelines, power stations and transmission lines has increasingly shifted toward solar panels, wind turbines, batteries and grids.

That hasn’t meant abandoning fossil fuels. Wang declared “the trend toward a green and low-carbon transition is irreversible,” even as he pledged that China would step up oil and gas exploration and diversify imports over the next five years. The combination encapsulated Wang’s broader message: countries should keep moving toward cleaner energy without sacrificing security or economic development along the way.

Climate Breakdown

This week’s gathering follows shortly after the breakdown of COP31 climate talks in Turkey, underscoring the strains facing global cooperation on climate and energy. In Qingdao, the prescription was to keep the transition moving while putting greater weight on security, affordability and development.

“In a crisis, the answer is not to pause the transition, but to adjust the balance and to keep moving forward,” said Adnan Amin, chair of the World Energy Council.

For their part, developing nations said they were seeking more than energy infrastructure. Ministers said they also wanted help with technology transfers and developing local manufacturing and workforce skills.

“For us, the energy transition must be a tool for industrial development,” said Kgosientsho Ramokgopa, South Africa’s minister of electricity and energy.

Still, reliable electricity was at the heart of many countries’ appeals, some of them quite direct, to the Chinese agencies and companies represented at the event. In South Sudan, just 8% of the population has access to electricity, said Minister of Petroleum Awow Daniel Chuang, who portrayed the country’s vast undeveloped energy resources as an investment opportunity.

“We invite the big Chinese companies that are working in oil and power, like PowerChina, China Energy and Huawei, to come to South Sudan and build our dams, build our solar farms, build our wind turbines and geothermal energy,” he said.

While most leaders steered clear of politics in their speeches, Iranian Energy Minister Abbas Ali Abadi excoriated the US and Israel for attacking civilian and energy infrastructure, and called on all countries and international organizations to condemn such strikes.

“Electricity is not merely a commodity,” he said. “It is the foundation of daily life, health, education and human security.”

text:
While the dust has barely settled on the Democrats' big midterm showing, lawmakers still have business to get done before a new US Congress takes office in 2027: namely, a permitting reform bill with rare cross-party support that could accelerate clean energy or fossil fuels — or both, depending on who's asked.

Permitting reform might sound like a snooze. But the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) could have far-reaching consequences for the country's energy mix, household utility bills and climate goals.

BAAJA, which is backed by US President Donald Trump, has already cleared the Senate and now faces a vote in the House of Representatives. DW breaks down what's in the bill, the political fight playing out on the sidelines and what it could mean for consumers' pockets and the US energy transition.

What does the bill do?

Before many new solar farms, wind projects or power plants can connect to the electricity grid, they must first pass through an arduous and complex permitting process.

Getting the green light for an energy project can often take years and requires permits from multiple government agencies. If it manages to overcome those hurdles, a legal challenge can easily stop new infrastructure in its tracks.

The nearly 500-page bill aims to overhaul that process. It would speed up environmental reviews, simplify the planning and construction of power transmission lines, make permits harder to revoke and require the growing number of data centers to pay for grid upgrades they need.

The bill is mostly technology-agnostic. So, the same reforms that would make it easier to build a lot of green energy infrastructure quickly could, in theory, be used to speed up oil and gas projects whose carbon emissions are warming the planet.

That's what's made BAAJA controversial, with some Democrats saying permitting reform is needed to get energy bills down and others saying they support provisions, like building more transmission lines required for transporting green energy, but not the whole package.

Would the bill cut emissions or raise them?

It's hard to estimate, and there's a lot of contradictory information out there.

The Rhodium Group, an independent research firm, found the bill would lower US greenhouse gas emissions in every scenario it ran, by up to 4% in 2040 compared with no bill. This is a fraction of the emissions reductions targets the US dropped when it withdrew from Paris climate accord this year.

Purdue University engineer Kevin Kircher reached the opposite conclusion. His analysis, which has not been peer-reviewed, estimates that domestic emissions would rise by about 2%, mostly because he assumes the bill would boost US fossil fuel production.

The difference comes down to a bet about what the bill ends up speeding up more: renewables and the power lines to carry them, or fossil fuels. That depends on which administration is issuing the permits.

Under Joe Biden's administration, for instance, renewables got a boost but since Trump took office, his administration has favored fossil fuels and spent billions paying developers to give up their offshore wind leases.

What would it mean for US household energy bills?

The White House Council of Economic Advisers, a team of economists that advises the president, estimates it would eventually cut the average household's electricity bill by $178 to $251 (€162 to €229) a year.

The logic is that long permitting delays discourage investment in infrastructure, which drives up prices. But that estimate considers only one part of the bill, faster environmental reviews, and doesn't say when the savings would arrive.

Independent analyses also found a drop in electricity prices for consumers, though a more modest one. The Rhodium Group estimates the bill's passage would save the average household $41 to $66 a year by 2035. That's largely because new transmission lines would let cheaper power reach customers and the costs of expanding the grid for data centers would no longer be passed on to households.

Critics point to the fact that those savings are relative. Electricity demand from data centers is expected to push up prices regardless, and permitting reform would only slow that rise rather than reverse it.

Oil Change International, an advocacy group that opposes the bill, argues households will still end up paying more for energy than they do now, especially if the bill mainly speeds up gas projects, since US gas prices are expected to rise sharply over the next decade.

What do environmentalists say about it?

Most major US environmental groups oppose the bill as written, including the Natural Resources Defense Council, League of Conservation Voters and Earthjustice. The Sierra Club called it "fundamentally flawed."

Much of the criticism focuses on provisions making federal permits harder to revoke.

"It would prevent a future administration from reconsidering a prior administration's flawed decisions to authorize activities such as Arctic drilling, deep seabed mining, or development of data centers on public lands," Earthjustice wrote in a critique.

The reverse is also true. That provision also makes it harder for an administration to come in and halt clean energy projects, as Trump did with offshore wind.

Opponents warn the bill could weaken protection for water and habitats, and limit environmental lawsuits. One area that environmental groups praised is the overhaul of how transmission lines are planned and approved.

That matters because the windiest and sunniest places in the US are often far from the cities that need power, and building long-distance power lines to connect them can take a decade or more.

Still, many critics say they would rather wait until Democrats control Congress in January and pass a version more focused on clean energy. Though that approach is risky, any bill would still require Trump's signature to become law.

title: Mayor of the West Midlands new taskforce targets jobs and growth in battery sector
description:
A new taskforce has been set up by Richard Parker, Mayor of the West Midlands, to supercharge the region’s ambition to become a European leader in battery manufacturing and technology.
Richard Parker, Mayor of the West Midlands, said: “There’s a huge opportunity in the fast-growing battery market and we must move quickly if we are to make the most of this.
“Put all that together and there’s no doubt that we can become one of Europe’s leading centres for battery manufacturing and technology.
It’s one of the key growth sectors in the West Midlands Growth Plan and provides a huge industrial base to build on.
The Battery Reindustrialisation Taskforce will support the UK’s wider battery strategy.
text:
A new taskforce has been set up by Richard Parker, Mayor of the West Midlands, to supercharge the region’s ambition to become a European leader in battery manufacturing and technology.

The Mayor has appointed Dr Roisin Hopkins, managing executive at HORIBA MIRA, to chair the Battery Reindustrialisation Taskforce, bringing together regional and national leaders from industry, research and policy making.

The group has met for the first time to start setting out the region’s proposition for batteries that builds on current capabilities in manufacturing, research, infrastructure and skills development.

A clear plan will be developed to attract new investment and focus on the development of sites, infrastructure, skills and supply chains needed to harness opportunities in a range of sectors. These include electric mobility, industrial and transport, consumer products, grid and network storage, and specialist defence, maritime and aerospace.

The taskforce will consult investors, business and industry representatives, skills providers and infrastructure partners before presenting the vision and plan to the Mayor in Spring 2027.

Richard Parker, Mayor of the West Midlands, said: “There’s a huge opportunity in the fast-growing battery market and we must move quickly if we are to make the most of this. I’ve given my taskforce a clear instruction: come up with a plan to win global investment. That's the big prize and it will bring thousands of highly skilled, well-paid jobs to our region.

“We already have a headstart as one of Europe’s strongest manufacturing bases, while world-leading research and innovation is already happening at the MTC, UKBIC, HORIBA MIRA and Warwick Manufacturing Group. And we’ve also got our first ready-to-go site at GreenPower Park, with planning permission in place and power grids being installed through the Investment Zone programme.

“Put all that together and there’s no doubt that we can become one of Europe’s leading centres for battery manufacturing and technology. That’s an exciting prospect for everyone.”

Taskforce chair, Dr Roisin Hopkins, said: “I'm pleased to be taking on the chair role at an important time for both the West Midlands and the UK battery sector. My ambition is that the taskforce brings industry, government and academia together to define where the region can lead, better connect our existing strengths, understand future demand and create the conditions needed for investment and growth. Ultimately, I want us to deliver a practical, evidence-based plan that helps secure high-value jobs and establishes the West Midlands as a critical part of the UK's battery future.”

Setting up the Battery Manufacturing Taskforce is one of the ways the Mayor is accelerating the West Midlands Reindustrialisation Blueprint to turn more research and innovation into companies that scale, manufacture and employ people in the region.

Advanced manufacturing and engineering already employs around 270,000 people. It’s one of the key growth sectors in the West Midlands Growth Plan and provides a huge industrial base to build on.

The Mayor is already backing the electrification of the all-important automotive sector with £50m to help businesses capitalise on new opportunities in growing supply chains. That’s already paying off with electric sports car maker Longbow Motors set to start production here in 2027.

Through the £50m Local Innovation Partnership, the Mayor is also investing in new technologies for future mobility and clean energy - both key markets for batteries.

The Battery Reindustrialisation Taskforce will support the UK’s wider battery strategy. Its full membership is: West Midlands Combined Authority; Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade; Office for Investment; Coventry City Council; UKRI/Innovate UK; Advanced Propulsion Centre; Ministry of Defence; National Wealth Fund; Warwick Manufacturing Group; Manufacturing Technology Centre; The Economic Intelligence Unit; HORIBA MIRA, EVTEC Group; Bruderer; West Midlands Growth Company.

description: The debut comes as LGMG marks ten consecutive years as the global sales leader in off-highway mechanical-drive wide-body dump trucks.
text:
The debut comes as LGMG marks ten consecutive years as the global sales leader in off-highway mechanical-drive wide-body dump trucks.
SHANGHAI
,
Nov. 25, 2026
/PRNewswire/ -- LGMG today unveiled its VTH150 electric-wheel mining dump truck at bauma CHINA 2026. Built to haul heavy loads around the clock in large open-pit mines, the VTH150 features what LGMG describes as the world's first electric-wheel drive system powered by permanent magnet synchronous motors (PMSMs).
A Decade of Leadership in Purpose-Built Mining Trucks
LGMG entered the wide-body dump truck market in 2012 with trucks engineered from the ground up for mining. Field research guided improvements in payload capacity, structural strength, reliability and operator comfort on long shifts.
In August 2026, Frost & Sullivan published its independent study of the global off-highway mechanical-drive wide-body dump truck market, confirming that LGMG had led worldwide sales in the category for ten consecutive years.
Electric-Wheel Drive for Heavy Haulage
The VTH150 takes LGMG into the high-capacity electric-wheel mining truck segment. Its PMSM drive is more efficient, more compact and easier to service. LGMG can take its electric-wheel technology from prototype to full-scale production in-house.
LGMG introduced hybrid mining trucks in 2019 and began producing fully electric models in 2020. Its lineup now includes hybrid, fully electric and methanol-powered mining equipment.
LGMG's mining truck portfolio uses in-house modular electric drives and vehicle controls to adjust power output as conditions change. These technologies can cut energy use by up to 20% versus conventional fuel-powered mining trucks.
LGMG is also developing its own drive-by-wire chassis technology and collaborating with autonomous driving specialists to demonstrate driverless haul trucks under a range of operating conditions. The projects are helping mines automate haulage and coordinate truck movements more precisely.
Linking Haulage, Power and Mine Operations
LGMG will continue to develop electric drives, electronic controls and battery systems. The company is also advancing microgrids that combine solar power, energy storage and charging, along with digital platforms for managing mine operations.
LGMG aims to bring trucks, charging infrastructure and mine management systems together so operators can run their sites more efficiently, cut operating costs and move toward lower-emission operations.

The visit comes just two weeks after RWE and KKR confirmed a £12 billion investment to jointly deliver the Vanguard West and Vanguard East offshore wind projects.
The long-term presence of the Vanguard projects is expected to support economic activity in Lowestoft, Great Yarmouth and the wider East of England for decades to come.
Beyond supporting investment in port infrastructure, RWE and KKR are focused on ensuring the Vanguard projects deliver lasting benefits for communities across the East of England.
The Vanguard projects build on RWE's longstanding presence in the East of England.
text:
RWE, in partnership with Associated British Ports and Clarksons Port Services, today welcomed the Minister of State for Energy to the Port of Lowestoft’s Eastern Energy Facility (LEEF), as they announce plans to establish facilities to support the Vanguard West and East projects at the site. The visit highlighted how RWE and KKR’s Vanguard projects will benefit local businesses, workers and young people across the region.

The visit comes just two weeks after RWE and KKR confirmed a £12 billion investment to jointly deliver the Vanguard West and Vanguard East offshore wind projects. RWE is working with Associated British Ports (ABP) and Clarksons Port Services (CPS) to finalise agreements to use the Port of Lowestoft for the projects’ long-term operations and maintenance.

This builds on the announcement to use LEEF as the base for construction of the projects, which is expected to start in early 2027. During the three-year construction period, it is estimated1 that the projects will create and support over 2,800 jobs, both directly and indirectly through the supply chain. Once the projects are fully operational in 2030, they are expected to directly support more than 300 long-term, skilled jobs including wider opportunities for local businesses providing services such as vessel maintenance, port operations, crew transfers and supplies.

The long-term presence of the Vanguard projects is expected to support economic activity in Lowestoft, Great Yarmouth and the wider East of England for decades to come. Together, once fully operational Vanguard West and East will have a combined generating capacity of 2.8 gigawatts (GW), enough to generate the equivalent electricity needed to power more than all the homes in the East of England.2

Energy Minister Michael Shanks said: “Britain’s clean energy future is being built in towns like Lowestoft, drawing on generations of industrial expertise and creating opportunities for the next generation. Lowestoft will be home to one of Britain’s biggest offshore wind projects, ensuring the benefits of Vanguard's £12 billion investment are felt locally for decades to come."

Tom Glover, UK Country Chair at RWE, said: "The £12 billion investment in Vanguard West and East offshore wind farms represents a major commitment to the UK's clean energy future, and we’re delighted that Lowestoft will play a vital role in turning that investment into reality. Today's visit was a fantastic opportunity to showcase the expertise, infrastructure and skills that already exist here, and the opportunities that major offshore wind projects can create for local businesses, workers and young people.

"RWE has a proud history in the East of England, and we're excited to be building on that through these projects. Working jointly with KKR, and with ABP, CPS and our local partners, we want to ensure these projects make a lasting contribution to the region's economy while helping deliver the secure, affordable energy the UK needs."

Julian Walker, Chief Commercial Officer and Regional Director at ABP, said: "ABP was proud to host the Energy Minister at the Port of Lowestoft in partnership with RWE and Clarksons, and to show how our collective investment in energy, port and supply chain infrastructure is turning offshore wind ambition into jobs and opportunity for local communities.

"Our £35 million investment in LEEF, together with RWE's intended long-term commitment to the Port and Clarksons' new facilities, is strengthening the supply chain needed to deliver Vanguard West and East. Lowestoft has the location, infrastructure, marine expertise and established offshore energy cluster to support these projects through construction and into decades of operation."

Steve Smith, Director, Clarksons Port Services, said: "It was a privilege to welcome the Minister to Lowestoft and showcase the facilities that will support the Vanguard projects for decades to come. Seeing the scale of the new warehouse and operational infrastructure first-hand demonstrates the long-term commitment being made to the region and the role Lowestoft will play in supporting one of the UK's most significant offshore wind developments. Together with RWE and ABP, we are proud to be helping provide the infrastructure and operational expertise that will underpin investment, skilled employment and economic activity across the East of England."

With preparations accelerating ahead of offshore construction, due to start in early 2027, the Minister's visit highlighted the important role Lowestoft will play in delivering the projects, as well as the wider opportunities they could create for the regional economy.

During the visit, the Minister joined representatives from RWE, ABP and CPS at the port's Lowestoft Eastern Energy Facility (LEEF), where he toured the facilities and met apprentices and teams working on the project, hearing first-hand about the skills, expertise and infrastructure that will help deliver the projects and support the region's growing offshore wind industry.

Beyond supporting investment in port infrastructure, RWE and KKR are focused on ensuring the Vanguard projects deliver lasting benefits for communities across the East of England.

The projects’ long-standing regional skills and employment programme is helping train the next generation of skilled workers. In 2026 alone, it has reached nearly 2,000 primary and secondary school pupils and more than 750 higher education students, while offering apprenticeships and work experience to young people across the region.

The Vanguard projects build on RWE's longstanding presence in the East of England. RWE has operated its Scroby Sands offshore wind farm from nearby Great Yarmouth for more than 20 years, while its Great Yarmouth gas-fired power station recently completed the largest overhaul in its history, supporting its continued operation well into the next decade..

title: BYD discusses investments in Brazil's Minas Gerais state, focusing on lithium processing ...
description:
BYD is expected to formalize a letter of intent for investments in Minas Gerais in January 2027.
In addition to the possibility of building a vehicle factory, the talks include industrial processing of lithium extracted in the state.
Lithium processing could increase the value of Brazilian production Lithium is an important raw material for rechargeable batteries used in electric vehicles and energy storage systems.
After extraction, the material must undergo industrial processing to meet the chemical specifications required by battery manufacturers.
Despite talks with Minas Gerais, the company has not yet announced where it will build its new commercial vehicle factory.
text:
The Chinese automaker is expected to sign a letter of intent with the Minas Gerais government in January 2027. The incoming administration’s priority is to attract investment to process lithium from the Jequitinhonha Valley and expand the electric-vehicle supply chain.

BYD is expected to formalize a letter of intent for investments in Minas Gerais in January 2027. A report published by Brasil Mineral on November 25, 2026, said the understanding was reached at a meeting between executives from the Chinese automaker and representatives of the incoming state government.

In addition to the possibility of building a vehicle factory, the talks include industrial processing of lithium extracted in the state.

However, no final decision has been made on whether to proceed with the projects.

Minas Gerais aims to process lithium from the Jequitinhonha Valley

The meeting took place in São Paulo on November 24, with Governor-elect Cleitinho Azevedo and representatives of BYD Brazil in attendance.

Executives present included Tyler Li, the company’s president in Brazil, and Alexandre Baldy, senior vice president.

According to Governor-elect Luís Eduardo Falcão, setting up an automotive plant is a secondary consideration in the current talks.

The priority, therefore, is to develop a lithium processing and beneficiation plant.

The incoming administration also plans to attract investment in other activities:

Battery manufacturing;

Renewable power generation;

Production of fast-charging equipment;

Development of the electric mobility industry.

With this proposal, the incoming government aims to increase Minas Gerais’s share of the industrial stages that follow mining.

BYD holds mineral rights covering 852 hectares in Minas Gerais

The Chinese automaker’s interest in Brazil’s mineral resources did not begin with the recent talks.

In February 2025, Reuters reported that BYD had acquired mineral rights covering 852 hectares in Coronel Murta, in the Jequitinhonha Valley.

The acquisition took place in late 2023 through its subsidiary, BYD Exploração Mineral do Brasil.

At the time of the report, however, the company was still conducting geological research and had no operating revenue.

Other international companies are also exploring the region’s mineral potential. In September 2026, a Canadian mining company identified 12 new rare earth exploration targets in Lithium Valley, with indications of elements that are strategic for various industrial sectors.

However, holding mineral rights does not guarantee that an area will become a commercial mine.

Lithium processing could increase the value of Brazilian production

Lithium is an important raw material for rechargeable batteries used in electric vehicles and energy storage systems.

However, mining is only one stage of this supply chain.

After extraction, the material must undergo industrial processing to meet the chemical specifications required by battery manufacturers.

China currently has a strong presence in these processing stages.

As a result, establishing processing facilities in Brazil could increase the country’s role in producing battery materials.

Other South American countries are also seeking to expand the industry. In Argentina, for example, Eramet is considering a US$350 million investment to increase the capacity of a lithium plant.

In Minas Gerais, however, decisions on the technology, production capacity and investment still depend on negotiations with the Chinese manufacturer.

Minas Gerais also competes for a R$1 billion electric vehicle factory

Another area of negotiations involves a new BYD facility that would manufacture electric commercial vehicles.

Minas Gerais, São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro are competing for the project, which has an estimated investment of R$1 billion and the potential to create about 2,000 jobs.

The expected start of operations under discussion is between 2028 and 2029.

Meanwhile, the automaker is expanding its industrial presence in Bahia. The company is also preparing to launch the BYD Dolphin GT, a flex-fuel hybrid model slated for production in Camaçari.

Despite talks with Minas Gerais, the company has not yet announced where it will build its new commercial vehicle factory.

In addition, the estimated R$1 billion investment is not related to the lithium processing project, which still has no publicly disclosed budget.

Letter of intent expected to be signed in January 2027

The next stage of negotiations is expected to take place after January 6, 2027, the scheduled inauguration date for the governor-elect.

In addition to signing the document, the transition team is preparing a mission to China to learn about the electric mobility supply chain and discuss potential partnerships.

For now, however, the letter of intent represents only a preliminary step in the negotiations.

BYD has not yet confirmed the municipality that would host the lithium plant, the investment amount, its production capacity or the expected number of jobs.

description:
The Trump administration on Wednesday gave SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a long-lofty goal of Elon Musk’s rocket company, in a move that has raised both skepticism and alarm among some scientists.
The world's richest man has long vowed to form vast, solar-powered data centers in space to help run AI tools on Earth.
Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and author, called the prospect of launching a million satellites into space to create data centers “a fantasy."
In its ruling, the FCC maintained that SpaceX's proposed Starmind constellation operates consistently with its orbital debris rules.
The American Astronomical Society, satellite communication company Viasat and Amazon-owned Kuiper Systems were among those who called on the regulator to deny SpaceX's proposed data centers in space.
text:
The Trump administration on Wednesday gave SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a long-lofty goal of Elon Musk’s rocket company, in a move that has raised both skepticism and alarm among some scientists.

The U.S. Federal Communications Commission lauded its authorization as a historic first amid the artificial intelligence race. It said that SpaceX's one million “orbital compute modules” (forming a data center constellation called “Starmind”) would process massive amounts of data that would be used back on Earth — and bring humans closer to harnessing “the full power of the sun.”

“America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who was appointed by Republican President Donald Trump, said in a statement. He added that Wednesday's move “opens a bold new frontier.”

A lengthier authorization order published by the FCC noted that the company must deploy at least “one authorized space station” by 2033 — and then gradually add more and more through 2040. Musk welcomed the decision over social media.

The world's richest man has long vowed to form vast, solar-powered data centers in space to help run AI tools on Earth. But scientists and industry experts have stressed enormous technical and financial obstacles, as well as a host of environmental concerns.

Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and author, called the prospect of launching a million satellites into space to create data centers “a fantasy."

“It’s not going to happen,” he said Wednesday.

Proponents of data centers in space argue that capturing the sun’s energy would ease pressure on power grids and cut demand for sprawling computing warehouses on Earth (and resources like water needed to cool them). Space seems to offer a solution because it is cold, but it is also a vacuum, trapping heat inside objects much like a thermos. Becker explained that there are “basic physical limits” to otherwise radiating that heat out — and sending lots of smaller satellites could potentially carry the necessary material combined, but it would be expensive and difficult.

He and others also point to additional risks, such as atmospheric pollution through launches and reentries, as well as possible in-orbit collisions that could impact other essential satellites.

“You could end up with a cascading set of space junk collisions,” said Becker, noting such crashes could create “a cloud of debris” in the low Earth orbit — where many weather and telecommunication satellites are also found.

In its ruling, the FCC maintained that SpaceX's proposed Starmind constellation operates consistently with its orbital debris rules. It also acknowledged that it had received a “substantial number” of public comments leading up to its authorization Wednesday, including petitions to deny SpaceX's request. But the regulator maintained that deploying the satellites “serves the public interest” — and said that it dismissed topics that it didn't have authority over, such as environmental concerns.

The American Astronomical Society, satellite communication company Viasat and Amazon-owned Kuiper Systems were among those who called on the regulator to deny SpaceX's proposed data centers in space.

In a statement Wednesday, the AAS said it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC's decision. The organization said that SpaceX's proposed position of data centers in low Earth orbit would undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and “the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky.”

“The proposed constellation involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects," AAS said, noting that “these satellites would therefore be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky.”

Becker echoed that sentiment. “It also is pollution of the night sky to the naked eye,” he said.

Viasat, Amazon, SpaceX and the FCC did not immediately respond to The Associated Press’ requests for further comment Wednesday.

description:
The House is preparing to vote next week on a bipartisan permitting bill that would speed construction of energy projects and power lines, as environmental objections and Republican attendance could complicate its path to President Donald Trump.
It would give federal regulators more authority over interstate power lines and generally protect approved permits from later revocation.
Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., one of four Senate negotiators, urged swift House action after the vote.
The House vote could turn on attendance.

text:
The House is preparing to vote next week on a bipartisan permitting bill that would speed construction of energy projects and power lines, as environmental objections and Republican attendance could complicate its path to President Donald Trump.

The House Rules Committee has scheduled a meeting on the Senate amendment to H.R. 2347 for Monday, Nov. 30. Roll Call reported that Republican leaders plan to bring the measure to the floor under a rule. The House would have to approve that rule before voting on the bill. No floor vote time has been announced.

The Senate's vote record shows it passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 on Nov. 19, 62-33. Fifteen members of the Democratic caucus voted yes. Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., were the only Republicans to vote no.

The Senate-passed legislation would change federal reviews and permitting under the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, and National Historic Preservation Act. It would give federal regulators more authority over interstate power lines and generally protect approved permits from later revocation.

Another provision would make large data centers bear the costs of grid upgrades needed to serve them. Supporters say faster construction of power plants and transmission lines would help meet rising electricity demand. Critics say shorter reviews and limits on lawsuits could leave communities fewer ways to challenge projects.

In January, Trump said technology companies should cover data center power costs instead of shifting them to households.

The White House has endorsed the permitting legislation. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., one of four Senate negotiators, urged swift House action after the vote. In her statement, Capito said: "I have spent years trying to achieve bipartisan compromise on legislation that gets our nation back to building, and the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is the culmination of those efforts."

The House vote could turn on attendance. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., urged Republicans to return after absences forced leaders to shelve a procedural vote last week. Democrats won control of the House in the midterm elections and take over in January, leaving Republicans a narrow window to act.

Democrats are divided. Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., said in his statement: "BAAJA fails to eliminate the economic disincentives stacked against cheaper energy and weakens critical environmental laws that keep dirtier energy sources offline."

Rep. Mike Levin, D-Calif., said the transmission provisions could help clean energy but opposed the bill without changes. In his statement, Levin said: "But in the end, taking the current deal would mean giving up protections we may never win back in exchange for gains that aren't guaranteed either."

The Senate did not adopt a negotiated amendment addressing tribal consultation and data center provisions after an objection during floor debate. House changes would require another Senate vote. Passage without changes would send the bill to Trump.

title: What is the US permitting bill and would it actually help the climate? - DW.com
description:

text:
While the dust has barely settled on the Democrats' big midterm showing, lawmakers still have business to get done before a new US Congress takes office in 2027: namely, a permitting reform bill with rare cross-party support that could accelerate clean energy or fossil fuels — or both, depending on who's asked.

Permitting reform might sound like a snooze. But the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) could have far-reaching consequences for the country's energy mix, household utility bills and climate goals.

BAAJA, which is backed by US President Donald Trump, has already cleared the Senate and now faces a vote in the House of Representatives. DW breaks down what's in the bill, the political fight playing out on the sidelines and what it could mean for consumers' pockets and the US energy transition.

What does the bill do?

Before many new solar farms, wind projects or power plants can connect to the electricity grid, they must first pass through an arduous and complex permitting process.

Getting the green light for an energy project can often take years and requires permits from multiple government agencies. If it manages to overcome those hurdles, a legal challenge can easily stop new infrastructure in its tracks.

The nearly 500-page bill aims to overhaul that process. It would speed up environmental reviews, simplify the planning and construction of power transmission lines, make permits harder to revoke and require the growing number of data centers to pay for grid upgrades they need.

The bill is mostly technology-agnostic. So, the same reforms that would make it easier to build a lot of green energy infrastructure quickly could, in theory, be used to speed up oil and gas projects whose carbon emissions are warming the planet.

That's what's made BAAJA controversial, with some Democrats saying permitting reform is needed to get energy bills down and others saying they support provisions, like building more transmission lines required for transporting green energy, but not the whole package.

Would the bill cut emissions or raise them?

It's hard to estimate, and there's a lot of contradictory information out there.

The Rhodium Group, an independent research firm, found the bill would lower US greenhouse gas emissions in every scenario it ran, by up to 4% in 2040 compared with no bill. This is a fraction of the emissions reductions targets the US dropped when it withdrew from Paris climate accord this year.

Purdue University engineer Kevin Kircher reached the opposite conclusion. His analysis, which has not been peer-reviewed, estimates that domestic emissions would rise by about 2%, mostly because he assumes the bill would boost US fossil fuel production.

The difference comes down to a bet about what the bill ends up speeding up more: renewables and the power lines to carry them, or fossil fuels. That depends on which administration is issuing the permits.

Under Joe Biden's administration, for instance, renewables got a boost but since Trump took office, his administration has favored fossil fuels and spent billions paying developers to give up their offshore wind leases.

Advertisement

What would it mean for US household energy bills?

The White House Council of Economic Advisers, a team of economists that advises the president, estimates it would eventually cut the average household's electricity bill by $178 to $251 (€162 to €229) a year.

The logic is that long permitting delays discourage investment in infrastructure, which drives up prices. But that estimate considers only one part of the bill, faster environmental reviews, and doesn't say when the savings would arrive.

Independent analyses also found a drop in electricity prices for consumers, though a more modest one. The Rhodium Group estimates the bill's passage would save the average household $41 to $66 a year by 2035. That's largely because new transmission lines would let cheaper power reach customers and the costs of expanding the grid for data centers would no longer be passed on to households.

Critics point to the fact that those savings are relative. Electricity demand from data centers is expected to push up prices regardless, and permitting reform would only slow that rise rather than reverse it.

Oil Change International, an advocacy group that opposes the bill, argues households will still end up paying more for energy than they do now, especially if the bill mainly speeds up gas projects, since US gas prices are expected to rise sharply over the next decade.

What do environmentalists say about it?

Most major US environmental groups oppose the bill as written, including the Natural Resources Defense Council, League of Conservation Voters and Earthjustice. The Sierra Club called it "fundamentally flawed."

Much of the criticism focuses on provisions making federal permits harder to revoke.

"It would prevent a future administration from reconsidering a prior administration's flawed decisions to authorize activities such as Arctic drilling, deep seabed mining, or development of data centers on public lands," Earthjustice wrote in a critique.

The reverse is also true. That provision also makes it harder for an administration to come in and halt clean energy projects, as Trump did with offshore wind.

Opponents warn the bill could weaken protection for water and habitats, and limit environmental lawsuits. One area that environmental groups praised is the overhaul of how transmission lines are planned and approved.

That matters because the windiest and sunniest places in the US are often far from the cities that need power, and building long-distance power lines to connect them can take a decade or more.

Still, many critics say they would rather wait until Democrats control Congress in January and pass a version more focused on clean energy. Though that approach is risky, any bill would still require Trump's signature to become law.

text:
India’s automotive industry needs to move beyond manufacturing scale and focus on technology ownership, higher research and development (R&D) investments and localisation of critical components, industry leaders said on Thursday.

Speaking at a Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) event, Vivek Vikram Singh, managing director and CEO of Sona Comstar, and Tarun Mehta, co-founder and CEO of Ather Energy, said electrification, software, electronics and changing global supply chains are reshaping the automotive industry.

The shift calls for greater investments in engineering, product development and indigenous technologies, they said.

"The vehicle is becoming a computer on wheels. It has so much more intelligence than it ever used to. There is so much connectivity, and the problem is that the ecosystem for connectivity and intelligence is what we don't actually own," Singh added. The industry needs to move beyond being an assembly base and develop products and technologies in India, with greater emphasis on emerging technologies. While the country has established capabilities in mechanical engineering and hardware, it needs to strengthen its position in areas that are increasingly shaping the value of modern vehicles.

To further scale the ecosystem, the industry demands active participation from micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and needs to grow and invest in better equipment, talent, training and professional management. "We can't have a few people who will take R&D seriously, and for everyone else, it's an event. Once a year, you'll have an event, you showcase three things you made in that year, spend half a per cent of your revenue on it and say, 'we are also doing that'. It won't work," he said.

EV transition reshaping automotive value chains The two-wheeler manufacturer said the automotive industry is undergoing several simultaneous changes, with electrification, software and electronics transforming not only how vehicles are developed but also where value is created and which countries emerge as global leaders.

"The biggest thing that hit us when we started building a vehicle, and we started recruiting people from the industry, is that 8 per cent of the bill of material for a scooter has not existed in the last seven years," Mehta said.

The transition to electric mobility has fundamentally changed the component ecosystem, requiring OEMs and companies to rethink product development, supplier partnerships and technology roadmaps. It demonstrates the extent to which the supply ecosystem has changed with the emergence of electric two-wheelers, specifically in areas such as batteries, electronics and software.

"In almost every case, Indian suppliers and Indian ecosystems were not just competitive; they were generally just the better option," he said. However, Mehta said the next challenge is to move beyond manufacturing products towards becoming leaders in the technologies and engineering that shape them. He highlighted the distinct requirements of Indian consumers, particularly in the two-wheeler segment, where affordability, performance and everyday usability need to be balanced. "Our market itself can inspire and incentivise R&D and innovation," Mehta said.Supply-chain rethink strategies Mehta also called for a fundamental rethink of supply-chain strategies, particularly as geopolitical disruptions and uncertainties around energy, shipping and raw materials expose vulnerabilities in globally integrated manufacturing networks.

He said the traditional automotive manufacturing model, built around just-in-time inventory, limited supplier diversification and concentrated manufacturing locations, may not be adequate in the current environment. "Supply-chain resilience is not just a procurement issue. It is a manufacturing capability and increasingly a strategic question," he said. He called for diversification across three areas: technology, partners and geographical locations. Manufacturers may need to work with multiple suppliers and maintain parallel technology options rather than depending on a single source. Mehta said the changing nature of electric vehicles is also requiring a shift in relationships between original equipment manufacturers and component suppliers. On the broader energy transition, the leaders said alternative fuels such as ethanol, CNG, biofuels and hybrids have a role in reducing emissions and India's dependence on imports. However, Singh cautioned against confusing these solutions with the industry's long-term destination. "We shouldn't confuse the bridge for the destination. I still believe all of these technologies are bridges to get to the final goal," Singh said.

title: Detroit Auto Show speeds toward 2027 with a new driver | Howard
description:

Detroit has an opportunity to be part of an evolution.” The economic impact of hundreds of millions of dollars generated by activity around the Detroit Auto Show directly impacts downtown businesses, including clothing shops, restaurants, bars, hotels and museums.
“The Detroit Auto Show is so important to our city,” Phillip said.

text:
Lincoln Phillip swims with sharks — literally.

His scuba diving experience might be perfect preparation to be the chair of the 2027 Detroit Auto Show during this time of dynamic change and transition. He’s fearless.

“We’re not quitters, and we don’t turn and cut and run when things get tough. They have been. We have ebbs and flows in the city,” he told me. “We had the EV mandate, which had to pivot from internal combustion engines over to electric vehicles and back again, a significant financial burden on manufacturers. We just want to make an exciting show. Detroit has been on the rise.”

Phillip is dealer-operator of Rochester Hills Chrysler Jeep Dodge Ram and BMW Motorcycles of Detroit in Rochester Hills. He steps into a key role following the unexpected departure of executive director Sam Klemet in April.

The planning team is spending hundreds of hours putting together a 10-day event scheduled to run from Jan. 14 through Jan. 24. Phillip, who enjoys hunting and flying in his off time, is committed to keeping the Motor City in the fray as critics continue to predict the demise of auto shows globally.

“I’m just a car guy,” said Phillip, who has lived in Michigan for two decades, having left a law career in New York to return to his wife’s home state and pursue a new dream. Playing a key role with the auto show is part of his vision for investing in the city.

“I want to build on the momentum we started to accumulate last year,” Phillip said. “I feel like this show was in a state of decline. The energy was measurably reignited last year. We want to have a successful show — impactful to the stakeholders and viable for everyone. We want people to want to participate. This is the fabric of this city, from little shops that create art to support the industry to cars themselves.”

'Evolution'

Having commitments from Ford Motor Co., Stellantis NV and General Motors Co. is huge, Phillip said: “We don’t anticipate the show will return to what it was, but we can reimagine it. We need to show the world. We’re celebrating 120 years of motoring heritage and what it means to be built in Detroit. We have to look to the future. Nothing is as it once was. Detroit has an opportunity to be part of an evolution.”

The economic impact of hundreds of millions of dollars generated by activity around the Detroit Auto Show directly impacts downtown businesses, including clothing shops, restaurants, bars, hotels and museums.

“The Detroit Auto Show is so important to our city,” Phillip said. “People need to recognize the why. We’re all working in this together.”

He said he anticipates exciting products at the show, based on conversation with Stellantis. And the sights Phillip saw at the Paris Motor Show last month inspired him to look at a different kind of energy flow, he said: “We are the comeback city. People have counted Detroit out. And the city keeps reinventing itself.”

The motto this year: “There is only one Motor City.”

Diving, flying and following a dream

Phillip calls himself a diehard motorhead whose friends thought he was having a breakdown when he decided to leave Manhattan for Michigan. Now he would live nowhere else. “It’s just beautiful.”

He may be flying his Cessna 182 RG Skylane to Charlevoix or diving in the Maldives or Mexico or Costa Rica or Nicaragua. He has encountered Orca whales. Or maybe he’s out hunting pheasant or quail. His wife Lara is a retired attorney who volunteers on behalf of children with autism. Their daughter is a law student at Howard University in Washington, D.C.

“I was in the food and wine business in New York,” Phillip said. “I worked in restaurants while finishing (law) school. My wife suggested that I try the auto business — and that’s where this journey began. I started with a Chrysler dealer there in Manhattan. I thought the car business was so much sexier, far more alluring, than the practice of law.”

Phillip worked briefly in employment law on the plaintiff’s side. His wife was a commercial litigator for three decades managing international and white-collar crime cases.

“My advocacy for dealer interests led me here,” Phillip said. “It’s overwhelming.”

He points to Detroit’s iconic motto “speramus meliora: resurget cineribus,” which translates from Latin to "We hope for better things; it will rise from the ashes.” These were the words of Father Gabriel Richard, a Catholic priest who came to Detroit in the 1700s after fleeing the French Revolution. He was credited with helping the city rebuild after the Great Fire of 1805 that caused much of the city to burn.

Extreme loss and resurrection have long been a pattern in Detroit.

'New energy'

When Phillip’s not attending planning meetings in these final weeks before the Detroit Auto Show at Huntington Place in downtown Detroit, he may be spotted riding his motorcycle through the city. Rod Alberts, former executive director of the Detroit Auto Dealers Association, is advising operations this year.

“Lincoln and his team are bringing fresh ideas and new energy to the Detroit Auto Show,” Alberts said. “Their focus is on delivering a spectacular experience in January that thrills our attendees and creates meaningful value for our automakers and partners. This is the right team to build on the show’s success in 2027 and shape its future.”

Investing in the city is essential to the Detroit Three, said Mark Truby, chief communications officer at Ford. “It’s the Motor City, and we’re proud to call Detroit home. It’s only natural for Ford to play our part in making the show memorable. Auto shows are evolving, but Detroit will always be an important place to bring people together and celebrate our industry.”

text:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) — As federal, state and city officials respond to a 403,000-gallon fuel leak at H-POWER, the company that operates the West Oʻahu facility has also faced environmental and community concerns at sites on the continent.

Reworld, the nation’s largest waste-to-energy operator, runs the H-POWER plant under a contract with the city. Mayor Rick Blangiardi has said he intends to terminate the contract, which is worth $70 million a year and expires in 2032. He acknowledged that finding a replacement would not be easy.

“We knew nothing about this,” Blangiardi said of the leak. “It’s beyond just being angry about this. I feel like we’ve let the community down in a way that I never fathomed that we would.”

Jacob Wallace, a waste industry expert and senior reporter at Waste Dive has written about the H-POWER spill.

“I was surprised that it took several months to inform the public about this leak,” Wallace said. “It’s not something I’ve seen in the past.”

Incidents in Ohio and Connecticut

Last October, a chemical leak at a Reworld waste management facility in Avon, Ohio, forced evacuations and shut down nearby stores. Officials said the company was neutralizing a chemical when the incident occurred.

“The smell was terrible. I don’t know if my throat hurts from it or not,” one person said at the time.

“We noticed a large release of a vapor cloud of some sort — light in color — so we called the hazmat team,” said one official.

In Bristol, Connecticut, noise from a Reworld plant prompted complaints from residents. The health department fined the company roughly $35,000 for noise violations. Earlier this year, Reworld said it had taken extensive steps to address those concerns.

“It’s not a consistent noise. It’s almost like someone revving their engine over and over again. Like, ‘vrmmm and vrmmm,’” said Francis Pickering, a Southington, Connecticut, resident.

Opposition to incineration in Pennsylvania

A Philadelphia City Council committee voted last week to end the city’s disposal contract with Reworld in an attempt to force the company’s plant in Chester to shut down. Opponents cheered and held signs reading “Incineration kills” and “We Deserve Clean Air.”

“There are various issues that can come with burning waste. The biggest thing is the emissions that come out of the stack and through the air,” Wallace said.

Wallace said the EPA has updated regulations recently to capture more of the particulate matter, lead, and cadmium that can be released by burning waste, but communities have not necessarily felt safer.

He added, “So we’ve seen in various cities around the country, community opposition to continuing to operate these facilities.”

H-POWER operator options

Wallace said relatively few companies are equipped to operate facilities like H-POWER.

“There aren’t a lot of companies set up to operate a facility like this. There’s about 57 large municipal waste incineration facilities in the country and Reworld operates more than 30,” he said.

In a statement about its Honolulu contract, Reworld said it is “committed to the City and County of Honolulu as well as the ongoing operations of H-POWER” and intends “to work collaboratively with the city to address their concerns.”

text:
SALT LAKE CITY — Danielle Knight grabbed some signs and walked around Sugar House.

"We are going to be canvassing some local businesses about the Community Clean Energy Program," Knight told FOX 13 News.

Watch: 16 Utah communities will get power from renewable sources for $4 a month extra on their bills

16 Utah communities will get power from renewable sources for $4 a month extra on their bills

Knight, a volunteer with the Sierra Club of Utah, walked into Tea Zaanti to meet with the owner and make a pitch to pay a little extra on a power bill.

"Your business is going to be automatically opted in," Knight explained at the counter. "How that’s going to impact your business? You’re going to see a 5% increase on your bill."

Notices have started going out to residents and businesses in 16 communities across Utah, letting them know about an extra $4 per month on a residential power bill to pay for the Community Clean Energy Program. It took years to craft through legislation and community organizing, but city councils and county commissions had to vote to opt into the program (after initially expressing interest, three cities' elected bodies voted not to participate further). The Community Clean Energy Program ensures that an entire area's electricity will come from renewable sources of energy like solar and wind.

"Folks may have seen an envelope in the mail that said Rocky Mountain Power and mentioned a clean energy fee," said Glade Sowards, who works on the program for Salt Lake City and the Utah Renewable Communities Agency.

The 16 communities participating — which includes some larger cities like Salt Lake City, Ogden, Millcreek, Holladay, Midvale, Park City and Moab — represent about 25% of Rocky Mountain Power's total customer base in Utah. Luis Miranda with the Sierra Club of Utah said it is community driven; residents organized and pushed their city councils and county commissions to get on board.

"For the first time? We have a choice of where we can get our electricity from," Miranda said.

As the program rolls out, the electricity dedicated to the 16 communities will phase out fossil fuel sources and increase renewable ones like solar and wind (nuclear and geothermal are not part of the program yet). The program is expected to be fully built out by 2030. Rocky Mountain Power declined to comment, saying it only facilitates the program that is run by the Utah Renewable Communities and member cities.

"It helps us with our air quality challenges in Utah, we have those. It helps us with economic development, a lot of that potentially in rural Utah where they could use the shot in the arm for that kind of benefit and then just helping us, we’re a fast growing state we need all the energy we can get and the next batch of energy that comes is clean energy," Sowards told FOX 13 News.

Residents and businesses in the participating communities are automatically opted in. Currently, people can choose to opt out without paying any termination fee. But a coalition of environmental groups are now working to persuade people to stay in the program.

"We know energy prices keep going up, but something like this goes directly to bringing new, renewable energy options onto the grid for those communities," said Carmen ValDez with the Healthy Environment Alliance of Utah. "We’re not seeing those programs coming through Rocky Mountain Power or any of our energy resources on their own, at this level."

Miranda said getting people to stay with the program and pay the extra $4 a month involves educating them about its benefits.

"Once you explain it people are like, 'Wait a second, $4? It’s community led? And you get renewable energy? It actually doesn’t sound that bad,'" Miranda told FOX 13 News. "Don’t get me wrong, affordability is a very serious issue. Right now, costs and inflation are high. But still we know the future is going to require us to transition to clean energy."

At Tea Zaanti, it wasn't that hard of a sell.

"I guess from our standpoint, I mean, we’re not going to notice anythingm right? Not going to be a glitch or anything, right?" the owner asked Knight.

"Right," she replied.

The business owner decided to stick with the clean energy program and even allowed a sign to be displayed out front to encourage others to stay with it.

text:
As we move forward with this transition, we have to make sure consumers can benefit along the way

— Kristian Ruby, Secretary General of Eurelectric

DUBLIN, IRELAND, November 26, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — Europe’s power suppliers are committing to help consumers manage electricity costs and reap the benefits of electrification. As Eurelectric’s Retail Committee gathers in Dublin to exchange views on measures to address energy prices, it issues a paper urging policymakers to cut the policy-driven cost of electricity, target support to energy-poor households and safeguard competitive retail markets.

Europe’s shift towards a secure, decarbonised energy system will require significant investment in clean generation, grids, flexibility and storage. At household level, electrification also comes with upfront costs, from switching to electric vehicles and heat pumps to investing in batteries and other technologies.

“Europe needs to massively invest in electrification to achieve energy independence and a more efficient energy system over time” said Kristian Ruby, Secretary General of Eurelectric.

“As we move forward with this transition, we have to make sure consumers can benefit along the way” he added.

Against this backdrop, Eurelectric is publishing a new paper setting out how suppliers can support customers through the transition and where action from governments is needed to make it fair and affordable. The discussion comes at a timely moment, as energy affordability and electrification feature prominently on Ireland’s EU Presidency agenda.

“As the main interface between millions of households and the electricity market, we are committed to helping consumers navigate the transition” said John MacNamara, Chief Executive Officer of the Electricity Association of Ireland ahead of the meeting in Dublin.

“Support can take many forms, from providing clear information and supporting energy efficiency to making electrification easier and enabling customers to participate more actively in the electricity system,” he said.

However, easing pressure on consumers will also require action from Member States and policymakers. The paper highlights three areas for action:

1. First, tax electricity fairly by removing non-energy-related costs from electricity bills and rebalancing taxes and levies away from electricity. Despite being the cleanest and most efficient form of final energy, electricity is disproportionately taxed in many Member States. Where fiscal space allows, Eurelectric calls for electricity taxes and levies to be reduced to minimum permitted levels, alongside targeted exemptions for consumers in energy poverty where necessary.

2. Second, governments should tackle energy poverty through targeted social policies and structural measures, focusing support on households that need it most rather than intervening broadly in electricity markets. Ireland’s Energy Engage Code is highlighted in the paper as an example of a national approach designed to support a fair and equitable market for consumers and suppliers.

3. Third, policymakers should remove barriers to market-based supply prices. Competitive prices and effective price signals are needed to reward flexibility, encourage efficient consumption and allow consumers to participate more actively in the electricity system.

India’s advanced chemistry cell (ACC) battery manufacturing capacity is expected to reach 47–48 GWh by the end of 2026, strengthening the country’s domestic electric vehicle battery ecosystem. According to Dr Hanif Qureshi, Additional Secretary, Ministry of Heavy Industries, India has already achieved approximately 40 GWh of manufacturing capacity.

Speaking at the CII Future of Mobility in India Conference 2026, Dr Qureshi highlighted the progress made towards the government’s 50 GWh ACC battery manufacturing target.

India Moves Closer to 50 GWh Battery Manufacturing Target

Dr Qureshi stated that an additional 7–8 GWh of manufacturing capacity is expected to become operational by the end of this year.

Key highlights include:

Current capacity: Approximately 40 GWh.

Expected addition: 7–8 GWh by December 2026.

Year-end projection: 47–48 GWh.

Government target: 50 GWh of ACC battery manufacturing capacity.

This expansion reflects growing investments in India’s domestic battery manufacturing industry.

PLI Scheme Encourages Wider Industry Participation

The government’s Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for ACC battery manufacturing has played an important role in attracting investments.

Although only three applicants were selected under the PLI scheme, Dr Qureshi noted that several companies outside the programme are also preparing to enter battery manufacturing.

This indicates that government incentives are encouraging broader industry participation beyond the selected beneficiaries.

Strengthening India’s EV Supply Chain

Expanding domestic battery manufacturing is crucial for reducing India’s dependence on imported battery cells.

Higher local production capacity could help:

Reduce dependence on imported battery cells.

Strengthen the domestic EV supply chain.

Improve long-term battery cost competitiveness.

Attract investments in advanced battery technologies.

Support India’s electric mobility ambitions.

With manufacturing capacity expected to approach 48 GWh by the end of 2026, India is making significant progress towards its 50 GWh target and building a stronger foundation for its electric vehicle industry.
