title: 'The hour is late': Energy deal still elusive as holidays loom - State House News Service
description: The fate of energy legislation in Massachusetts is still unresolved in closed-door legislative talks, which the Senate's lead negotiator this week called "still very viable but problematic" and his House
text:
STATE HOUSE, BOSTON, Nov. 25, 2026.....The fate of energy legislation in Massachusetts is still unresolved in closed-door legislative talks, which the Senate's lead negotiator this week called "still very viable but problematic" and his House counterpart described as "progressing."

The outlook follows Eversource's letter to energy negotiators last month, in which it wrote that its electric customers already pay more than enough for clean energy programs — counting $326.5 million a year in energy efficiency spending among the total — days before it publicly celebrated energy efficiency program Mass Save. On Tuesday, the utility drew a distinction between cutting the program's existing budget, as the House has proposed, and taking a look at what future budgets may entail.

Lawmakers have been negotiating a complex and contentious energy proposal for months, as energy costs and affordability have been a focus on Beacon Hill for more than a year. Gov. Maura Healey started the conversation before the 2026 gubernatorial race got off the ground; now she's headed into her second term and residents are into the heating season without legislative action to ease the burden of energy costs.

Sen. Mike Barrett, Senate chair of the Telecommunications, Utilities and Energy Committee, spoke with alarm to the Boston Globe about the Eversource letter last week, and on Tuesday called it "destabilizing to have a 20-page missive land in the middle of a sensitive negotiation between the House and Senate."

His House counterpart, Rep. Mark Cusack, said he knew of Eversource's concerns and that conferees have received around 70 letters from different stakeholders about the proposals.

"To pick one out and have a temper tantrum is bizarre to me. This is standard procedure. It's not an earth-shattering move that is going to derail our talks," Cusack said.

Eversource said the letter "followed months of active engagement on these topics."

The House passed its energy bill (H 5151) in February, proposing to cut the Mass Save energy efficiency program by $1 billion, and the Senate passed its own bill (S 3166) on July 1, proposing instead to phase out the Gas System Enhancement Program. Both chambers say their energy bills will save ratepayers billions over the long term.

Barrett wouldn't comment directly on negotiations with the House when asked if he thinks they'll reach an agreement by Jan. 5, but said, "The hour is late and the holidays loom."

Cusack's reply to the same question: "Yes."

"No matter what deadline you make, you always feel the pressure coming up to it. But we're still five weeks out. I still feel good about it," Cusack said. He characterized swirling opinions about negotiations as "par for the course, the parlor game of Beacon Hill gossip. It's certainly not new to me."

Dated Oct. 16, the Eversource letter says the annual cost of state clean energy programs topped $1.46 billion for Eversource electric ratepayers in 2026. The company said "$1.4 billion in annual ratepayer funding is more than sufficient to meet the Commonwealth’s energy transition goals, and yet the legislation currently contemplated by the Conference Committee asks for even more." The utility didn't mention the Mass Save energy efficiency program by name in the letter and didn't take a position on the House's proposed cut.

"I think there's an important distinction between making a cut to a current budget, especially as we approach the last year of the budget for the current three-year plan, and the conversation around what future budgets should look like," Eversource spokesperson William Hinkle said Tuesday.

Mass Save's existing three-year budget cycle runs through 2027 and is funded at $4.5 billion.

"I think it's pretty clear that if you made a significant cut to the current budget at this time, that would pose very serious challenges for the programs, the contractor and workforce community that delivers these solutions, and create significant issues over the balance of this term," he continued. "Ultimately what exactly that level lands at, that's a policy decision."

Cusack said, "The utilities make money off the program, so they're not going to criticize it." In February he described the House's proposed reduction as "a one-year pause" and the cut as "focused on the administrative and marketing budgets, which are bloated."

Healey did not directly answer repeated questions at a September press conference about her stance on the proposed cuts, instead promoting her "all-of-the-above" energy approach. After being pressured to answer a final time, she said, "Look, I filed my legislation, and I'll leave it at that. I asked the Legislature to act on my legislation."

Mass Save users at a State House event last month pointed to time and cost savings they say the program provides them. Eversource Director of Residential Energy Efficiency Katherine Peters called the Mass Save program "one of the best partnerships that I can think of."

"I think we need to keep in mind what those real on-the-ground results are, even as we have the policy discussion about where we might go with programs in the future," Peters said.

National Grid Director of Customer Energy Management Amy Vavak pointed to a Sept. 30 analysis from independent nonprofit American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy, which reported that Mass Save programs reduced Massachusetts natural gas imports by 8% in 2024, saving over $406 million that year. The report also said that Mass Save programs to reduce electricity and fossil fuel use have generated $38.4 billion in total benefits between 2011 and 2024.

A municipal impact study issued in September 2025 by the state auditor's office reported that its Division of Local Mandates found "significant disparities in the distribution of Mass Save incentives, where residents of some higher-income municipalities received more than they contributed and residents of many lower-income municipalities contributed more than they received."

The six conferees tasked with negotiating energy legislation first met on July 29.Cusack said Wednesday that they met Tuesday and plan to meet again next week.

Barrett said that he and Cusack "are getting along splendidly." Cusack characterized their relationship as "fine" and "friendly," adding, "We don't get in fights, we don't yell at each other."

Ella Adams is a reporter for the State House News Service and State Affairs Pro Massachusetts. Reach her at ella.adams@statehousenews.com .

text:
Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan on the 26th, a day before the government’s announcement of measures to strengthen electric vehicle (EV) competitiveness, reiterated the need for support, stating, “We must approach this from the perspective of enhancing the competitiveness of our domestic EV manufacturers” in relation to domestic production tax credits.

This comes as major countries like the U.S. and the European Union (EU) raise trade barriers against Korean-made vehicles, while domestic discussions on support measures for EV competitiveness face last-minute challenges within the government.

◇Pain Continues Despite Impending Announcement of EV Competitiveness Strengthening Measures

Minister Kim, attending a plenary session of the National Assembly’s Trade, Industry, Energy, SMEs, and Startups Committee on the same day, said, “Companies also have a rational direction to use government support in ways that benefit partner firms and consumer welfare,” in response to Democratic Party of Korea lawmaker Lee Un-ju’s criticism. Lee had pointed out, “EVs are not just an automotive issue but an industry linked to all sectors, including upstream and downstream industries. I don’t understand why there is debate over introducing domestic production tax credits when this seems like the last opportunity.”

The domestic production tax credit system reduces corporate taxes for companies that produce and sell products domestically based on production volume. The automotive industry has demanded that EVs be included in the credit system to counter the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) and other countries’ domestic production incentives, as well as low-cost pressure from Chinese EVs.

Industry circles had high expectations that the “EV Competitiveness Strengthening Measures” scheduled for announcement on the 27th would include production tax credits for EVs.

However, the Ministry of Finance and Economy, the tax authority, has adopted a cautious stance toward providing tax credits to the completed vehicle industry, which already has large-scale domestic production facilities. The origin of batteries, which account for about 40% of EV prices, has also emerged as a contentious issue.

During a National Assembly tax subcommittee meeting on the 23rd, the Ministry of Finance and Economy opposed tax support for EVs, stating, “There are concerns about significant administrative inefficiencies in setting the scope of production costs.” The subcommittee ultimately failed to reach a conclusion.

Vice Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyoung-il, also speaking to reporters on the same day, acknowledged, “The government understands that the next 2–3 years are a golden time for the EV market transition,” but added, “The introduction of tax credits is a matter to be decided after comprehensively evaluating the industry’s efforts, such as enhancing its own competitiveness and fostering partnerships with parts suppliers.”

The automotive industry argues that tax credits of around 4 million Korean won per vehicle are necessary to overcome higher production costs compared to China and maintain domestic production and employment. They claim the tax benefits will be used to lower vehicle prices and strengthen the competitiveness of parts suppliers.

◇Rising Trade Barriers for Korean Vehicles Abroad

Overseas, protectionist movements for domestic automotive industries are intensifying. The EU is pushing for the Industrial Acceleration Act (IAA), which grants subsidies and preferential treatment to locally produced EVs, while also introducing import quotas (safeguards) on hybrid vehicles from Korea, China, and Japan starting next month.

The U.S. is imposing a 15% tariff on Korean vehicles to encourage domestic investment and production. Japan provides tax credits of 400,000 Japanese yen per domestically produced EV and has revised its purchase subsidy criteria to favor its domestic industry starting this year.

In contrast, export-dependent Korea lacks meaningful trade barriers or purchase subsidy differentiations for foreign EVs. Meanwhile, Chinese EVs are increasingly dominating the domestic market. According to the Korea Automobile & Mobility Association (KAMA), Chinese EVs accounted for 43.2% of the domestic EV market from January to October this year. The trade deficit with China in the same period nearly doubled to 4.2306 billion dollars compared to the same period last year.

There are concerns that if Korea loses its home market to Chinese EVs amid rising trade barriers in key export markets, it could lead to reduced vehicle production, worsening management conditions for small and medium-sized parts suppliers, and employment contraction.

text:
The Texas and Louisiana Gulf Coast is home to a massive array of petrochemical operations, from LNG or liquefied natural gas export terminals, to oil refineries, to plastic production plants. Along with encroachment into residents’ communities, comes air and water pollution — as well as a much higher than average cancer rate — hence the nickname for the region, “Cancer Alley.”

In 2000, native Louisianan Anne Rolfes founded and today still directs the Louisiana Bucket Brigade, named for an easy to use air monitoring system. In the past quarter century, her organization has worked on a variety of health and environmental issues, all related to hazards linked to the state’s petrochemical industry.

Between The Lines’ Melinda Tuhus spoke to Rolfes about the worsening pollution and health conditions in the region, and how a bill currently moving through Congress, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, would have an even more devastating impact on her state and community.

ANNE ROLFES: We work to protect our home, Louisiana, from horrible industrialization projects like SpaceX, carbon capture, liquefied natural gas, refinery expansions, chemical plants, data centers. And unfortunately, it has gotten worse in the last 25 years. Our state doesn’t seem to understand that there are completely different ways to grow an economy and ways that actually would result in shared prosperity without ruining our home.

MELINDA TUHUS: Anne Rolfes, the Senate just passed BAAJA or BAHA, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, also known as the Energy Permitting Bill. All but two Republicans and many Democrats voted in favor. In exchange for faster permitting for both clean and dirty energy projects, the bill would decimate NEPA, the National Environmental Policy Act, which since 1970 has given standing to people directly impacted by transportation, energy and other projects to object and speak up for their own interests. It would also reduce protections under the Clean Water Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the Endangered Species Act. The bill will now go to the House, which will take it up after the Thanksgiving break. Should it pass the House, and it will certainly be signed by President Trump, how do you see it impacting your work?

ANNE ROLFES: Well, let’s be really clear. We need NEPA. We need the Endangered Species Act. We need all of these federal laws to protect us, right? There’s no question about that. I mean, this is a catastrophe, and it’s a massive giveaway on the part of a bunch of politicians who should see that this election was just about, in part, about stopping corruption just like this, about stopping data centers. And so what are the Democrats doing? They’re voting, or what are some of the Democrats doing, I should say, and what all the Republicans are doing. They’re voting in laws that would make it more easy to build, easier to build data centers and other horrible ideas. And then who’s going to get blamed for that? The Democrats will. And if this law does pass, they should be blamed because this is a tragedy. It’s also though really important to know that in Louisiana, those laws often don’t work for us.

We are absolutely a sacrifice zone. We do not get the enforcement by the EPA. Even when we have Obama or Biden in the White House, we are neglected. Certainly Biden was better than Obama. Obama was a disaster down here. You just didn’t have protections for people. What you do have is a lot of photo ops when there’s a Democratic president. They come down here, take pictures with communities in the firing lines of pollution, but you don’t have vigorous protection. And so what we are hoping happens is that this horrible law does not pass, and furthermore, that we can go take the next step and get the EPA to do its job here in Louisiana and around the South and other neglected areas.

MELINDA TUHUS: Now the whole country is a sacrifice zone since Lee Zeldin, the head of the Environmental Protection Agency, sees his job as terminating its work.

ANNE ROLFES: Yeah, there’s no comparison between what the South experiences and the rest of the country. I mean, that is also our own doing because we have terrible laws. We have elected officials who don’t protect us. But yes, of course, this horrible law would open up the country to unbridled industrialization. And I think it’s really important to use that word. It’s not development, it’s destruction. So it should be called industrialization. Just to say we need federal protection, we need strong federal laws. And here in Louisiana, there’s a lot we’re doing to protect ourselves. We’re challenging, for example, the public financing of some of these projects. We’ve exposed the secrecy. We’re challenging some of what we believe are the illegal ways they’re moving public money around. So we’re active. We are winning in some cases. We don’t want to project the idea that we’re sitting around here wringing our hands, and yet these federal laws are really important.

They’re foundational.

MELINDA TUHUS: Is the Louisiana Bucket Brigade working with other like-minded groups in Louisiana to have a bigger impact on these industrial projects?

ANNE ROLFES: Yes, always. We always work in partnership. Right now, one of our principal partner is a group called Rural Roots Louisiana, which is comprised and led by and founded by people from Ascension Parish, which is the region targeted for so much of our current governor’s industrialization fantasies.

To register your views on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) that will soon be voted on by the U.S. House, call: (877) 796-1949 to be connected to your member of Congress.”

title: Payne: Charging around town in the Kia EV3 bot - The Detroit News
description:
Sounds like my 2027 Kia EV3 tester.
On Mound Road, I pushed the DRIVE MODE appendage on the steering wheel and triggered SPORT.
Toggle the tool on the steering wheel and set cruise control.
Just don’t compare it to, say, a subcompact, gas-powered Kia Seltos SUV that is more practical, more trip-friendly.
Seize the square steering wheel on entry, and the EV3 cabin is a wonderfully upscale for a subcompact droid.
text:
STERLING HEIGHTS — Wookipedia describes R2-D2 as a battery-operated astromech outfitted in white, silver and blue, a robot on wheels equipped with tool-tipped appendages for utilitarian tasks. Sounds like my 2027 Kia EV3 tester.

Call it EV3-SUV3. It’s a cutie with purpose.

On Mound Road, I pushed the DRIVE MODE appendage on the steering wheel and triggered SPORT. WHOOOOSH! The droid surged forward, its all-wheel-drive system gripping the turf toward my destination.

Toggle the tool on the steering wheel and set cruise control.

Toggle the rocker switch appendage to control speed.

Activate the regen appendage on the steering column to slow down.

As the soon-to-be-most-affordable non-pickup EV in the U.S. market (after the limited-run Chevrolet Bolt exits), the $31,385 Kia subcompact hatchback is a futuristic-looking, well-endowed, affordable unit with lots of utility even as it comes up short compared to more sophisticated robots like the Bolt and King Tesla Model 3.

Indeed, next to a comparable, $49K all-wheel-drive Model 3, my $45K AWD tester boasts more style and utility while offering less software sophistication. Just don’t compare it to, say, a subcompact, gas-powered Kia Seltos SUV that is more practical, more trip-friendly.

The Tesla is a lean, aerodynamic C-3PO next to the boxy EV3-SUV3 droid. They make a good odd couple. Right down to its smooth rocker panels and single interior screen, the Tesla is iPhone simple. Nominated for both World Car of the Year and North American SUV of the Year, the Kia is Nintendo Switch-chunky by comparison, with lots of body cladding and twin instrument/infotainment displays under its hoodless, 25-inch dash screen.

Kia has poached heavily from European design houses, but its style reminds of Cadillac with that dash display and vertical light signature in front/back.

Heading to Zmash Padel in Sterling Heights, I opened the rear hatch, toppled the rear seats and threw in my racquets and laptop bags. In my Model 3, I would use the frunk’s deep well to store my laptop bag for security. Alas, the EV3 is equipped with a much smaller frunk, useful for charging adapters.

Sub-storage is available too, but sadly it’s not occupied by a spare tire (get one) but by a tangle of charging cords.

With its punchy torque, EV3 has potential as a hot hatch, my favorite (as readers of this column know) vehicle niche.

Hit the pavement for a road trip, however, and hot hatchin’ is confined to interstate merges. ZOT! I merged onto the I-696 racetrack with authority. Merge into backroads twisties in Oakland County (or further north in Gaylord County’s M-32 two-lane), however, and EV3’s big battery weighs it down. If you want an EV hot hatch, cross over to the Hyundai side of the aisle for an Ioniq 5 N.

The Kia, true to its brand, is happy to give you a boulevard cruiser.

It hits the market at the same time as the 2027 Seltos, which illustrates why EVs are a niche market. The Seltos (that I recently reviewed) boasts better range, interior room and ease of use. If your shopping list is exclusively EVs, the Kia makes a compelling case.

With its Tesla-friendly NACS port, the Kia is road-ready for an American landscape littered with reliable Tesla Superchargers. However, not all Tesla chargers are compatible with Kias.

“Hey, Kia. Navigate to Charlevoix, Michigan,” I barked, and the native navigation system routed me north for a 250-mile, 4.3-hour journey — about 40 minutes longer than a gas car due to two charging stops on the way.

Two stops, Payne? But the EV3 has 300 miles of range in ECO mode.

Yes, but unlike gas cars that can fill a tank in three minutes, EVs like to operate between 20-80% of charge. Keep filling over 80% and the charge slows to a crawl. Thus two stops. But beware Tesla stations.

That’s because the EV3 can only use Teslas Gen 3 and 4 Superchargers — not the Gen 2 stations on many Michigan roads. Like the Bay City Supercharger on the road to Charlevoix.

The good news is that non-Tesla chargers have proliferated in recent years and Bay City has plenty of alternatives nearby. Tesla’s proprietary network will give you a wealth of information about surrounding attractions like restaurants and shopping while you wait. In the Kia, you’ll have less information about the area around you while you wait 20 minutes to charge.

ZOT! You’re back on the interstate after a charge. With hands on the wheel, please.

Where Tesla and Chevy Bolt both offer hands-free driving (the Bolt is the cheapest hands-free driver in the market), the Kia is content with lane-centered adaptive cruise Remove your hands from the wheel for more than 15 seconds and EV3-SUV3 will beep at you to put your hands back on the wheel.

Seize the square steering wheel on entry, and the EV3 cabin is a wonderfully upscale for a subcompact droid.

The stubby tool-tipped appendage on the right steering column would make R2-D2 proud. It contains the starter button, FORWARD/NEUTRAL/REVERSE gears, and a PARK button on its tip. It opens up acres of console real estate which Kia puts to good use with phone chargers, two (adjustable to container size) cupholders, and open and closed storage bins.

My favorite VW Golf GTI is tight in the back seat (though with me flogging it through the twisties, passengers should be wary). The EV3’s boulevard-cruising nature is more passenger-friendly, but its rear seat is less roomy than a GTI — or Model 3, for that matter. Just tell the front passengers to skooch up.

Turning left at the Michigan Turn on Mound to Zmash, I pulled the regen appendage, pulled my foot off the accelerator, and the electric motor immediately slowed EV3 to a crawl. One-pedal driving is an EV specialty and the Kia allows multiple adjustments depending on your preference.

I backed into a parking space, removed my racquet bag, then reached for the rear door handle for entry to put the back seat back to its upright position. No door handle.

Because it’s cleverly located in the C-pillar. Love these hatchback droids.

text:
In a tight vote, Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court has ruled in favour of ending the government’s contract with Luma Energy following a controversial legal battle with the private power company.

The five-to-four ruling made public on Wednesday envisions a one-year transition period.

Power outages have continued to dog the Caribbean island since Hurricane Maria inflicted vast damage to power infrastructure in 2017, leading to years of bitter recriminations over financial and policy autonomy in the US territory.

The San Juan government sued Luma nearly a year ago, following up on a campaign promise made by Governor Jenniffer Gonzalez to cancel the contract.

Luma has faced protests for years from Puerto Ricans, who raised concerns about the cost and quality of its services.

Gonzalez said her administration would seek a new company within the year awarded by the court. She assured that transmission and distribution operations would not revert to Puerto Rico’s Electric Power Authority, from which Luma had initially taken over in 2021.

She blamed Luma for “constant interruptions” and “unnecessary outages”, asserting they have enough funds to provide proper service, as she accused the company of driving the cost of electricity in the territory to record highs.

Meanwhile, a federal control board that oversees the island’s finances issued a statement saying its immediate concern is the continuity of power services.

“The Puerto Rican government’s decision to terminate the contract creates enormous uncertainty at a time when the people and businesses of Puerto Rico look for stability,” the board said, noting that there is no “clear plan or successor company in place”.

But Gonzalez rejected those concerns, bluntly saying, “There will be no chaos.”

Tensions in court

With the narrow ruling came allegations that judges had been pressured to vote in favour of cancellation.

Judge Angel Colon Pérez, who voted against the cancellation, asserted that the final ruling stemmed from “an excessive eagerness to satisfy a capricious request from the leader currently in power”, in an apparent reference to the governor.

However, Judge Roberto Feliberti Cintron, who was part of the majority vote, sharply denied the allegations.

“We do not bow to external pressures, we do not yield to intimidation, nor do we allow smear campaigns to influence the exercise of our judicial function,” Cintron wrote. “Our obligation is to the Law, Justice, the People, and our conscience.”

Luma also commented on the allegations.

“In light of the serious allegations that have been raised publicly regarding attempts to influence the Court, we reiterate our call for an immediate, rigorous, and transparent investigation,” it said.

The company said in a statement on Wednesday that it disagrees with the court’s decision but will respect the judicial process and is “carefully evaluating all available legal alternatives”.

text:
Ten brands surpassed the 51.4% average vehicle brand loyalty in 2025

New vehicle brand loyalty reached a five year high in 2025, improving to 51.4%. The increase in loyalty is a bright spot in an otherwise challenging year for the U.S. auto industry, with disruptions coming from affordability barriers and changing fuel preferences.

Our analysis draws on LexisNexis® Risk Solutions proprietary data and industry sources. We examine the forces shaping automotive loyalty, the impact of EV (electric vehicles) adoption, and the strategies manufacturers should use to retain customers.

Industry Overview

Brand loyalty rates: For calendar year-end 2025, 51.4% of customers purchased a new vehicle from the same brand as the one(s) they already owned. The brand loyalty rate increased 0.4 percentage point from 2024. Ten brands surpassed the industry average, showing resilience in consumer loyalty.

Affordability and retention: High transaction prices and rising maintenance costs are slowing sales and jeopardizing long-term retention. Migration to EVs presents a challenge to the traditional dealer service model and is forcing manufacturers to rethink post-sale experiences. Alternate fuel vehicles are now replacing gas 6x more frequently than in 2020—growing from 3% of vehicle replacements to 18%. The industry must now compete on meeting vehicle owners’ expectations throughout the ownership cycle, not just on vehicle features and price.

Brand Loyalty Trends

Toyota leads: Toyota closed 2025 as the brand leader, posting a 60.2% loyalty rate. Stronger hybrid retention played a big role, with loyalty among those owners climbing 2.5 percentage points to 60.1%.

Tesla's challenge: After years taking number one or two positions, Tesla slipped to third place, with a 55.9% loyalty rate. More Tesla owners are exploring rival EV options, with Tesla loyalty dropping from 98% in 2020 to 78% in 2025 among those replacing their EV with another EV.

Fuel type dynamics: Preference for gasoline vehicles has been falling. That trend was interrupted in October when federal EV tax credits expired. Gas loyalty snapped back from a historic low of 79.7% in September to 84.9% in November.

Influencing Factors

Slower transition to electric vehicles: U.S. consumers are transitioning to EVs more slowly than expected, as the future looks unpredictable after policy changes, shifts in emissions standards and incentive rollbacks. EV brand loyalty dropped from 53.1% last year end to 51.3% in 2025.

Rise in vehicle prices: Average new vehicle prices crossed $50,000 in September, with incentives dropping to 6.5% of Average Transaction Price—the lowest since mid-2024, according to Cox Automotive. However, rising costs did not deter owners from re-purchasing with their brands. Two of the largest segments finished 2025 with the highest brand loyalty rates in years: Large Pickup (54.8%) and Compact SUV (53.0%) were both up a percentage point from last year.

Methodology

LexisNexis Risk Solutions analyzed U.S. consumers’ vehicle purchases and garages using proprietary linking technology and the LexID® unique identifier. Loyalty was measured by matching purchased vehicles against vehicles customers already had in their garages. A loyalty rate above 50% indicates strong brand retention.

Conclusion & Recommendations

Auto manufacturers must address affordability, adapt to supply chain disruptions, and improve post-sale experiences. As EV adoption reshapes loyalty dynamics, brands that deliver thorough value and address retention challenges early will be best positioned for long-term success.

text:
WASHINGTON, November 25, 2026: The World Bank Group's Board of Executive Directors today approved financing to help India strengthen its bond market for infrastructure and draw greater private capital, thus enabling more and better-paying jobs by expanding clean energy, electric mobility, public transport, and urban systems.

The Unlocking Private Capital for Long-Term Infrastructure Financing and Bond-Market Transformation (UPLIFT) Project is supported by a a $30 million loan and a $470 million guarantee from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) complemented by a $20 million grant from the Livable Planet Fund. The Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA) is proposing to support through a $1 billion guarantee to mobilize international capital and expand its lending capacity for clean energy. Together, the World Bank Group will help India attract both domestic and international private capital for sectors critical to jobs and growth. In parallel, the Asian Development Bank is considering providing a $30 million loan and a $470 million guarantee.

India needs to invest about10 percent of GDP in infrastructure every year to sustain high economic growth and create more jobs. That leaves a financing gap of about 5 percent of GDP, or roughly $160 billion annually. Infrastructure needs funding for decades, but most banks lend for the short and medium term. Pension, insurance, and provident funds, that have long-term capital, are often held back by strict credit-rating requirements.

The UPLIFT Project will help close this gap. The National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development (NaBFID) will run a Credit Enhancement Facility that offers partial credit guarantees to infrastructure bond issuers. This should raise their ratings, lower borrowing costs, and extend repayment periods to match the life of the assets.

The Canadian dealerships would give Canadian buyers local sales and service access as the brand prepares for its first customer deliveries. The planned Ontario-produced batteries also tie Scout's Canadian presence to domestic battery manufacturing.

Scout Motors plans seven Canadian dealerships, three in the Toronto area, two in Montreal, one in Ottawa and one in Vancouver. Canadians can reserve a vehicle with a refundable $150 deposit, and about 85% of reservations are for range-extender models.

Scout Motors

Scout Motors will operate the Canadian dealerships as workshops handling both sales and service. Its new Blythewood, South Carolina, plant is nearing completion, and teams are welding, painting and assembling validation units of the Traveler SUV and Terra pickup.

text:
I think it’s safe to say that Americans are weirdly excited about the Ford Fathom.

Despite being a very basic and unexciting pickup truck, the thing is trending, like, every few weeks. It’s usually because it’s cheap: the starting price will be $29,945. But this time, it’s because of its battery.

However, that battery is related to the Ford Focus’s affordability. It all comes back to that. The Fathom will utilize Ford’s new Universal EV Platform, which basically copies Tesla by introducing a unicasting element to the new assembly process. Fewer parts and fewer steps make it so cheap.

That assembly also includes a brand-new battery production process.

Ford’s unique (semi-Chinese) batteries

Earlier in the week, Ford apparently gave some journalists a tour of its new Blue Oval Battery Park in Michigan. And MotorTrend reported on what they saw, claiming it’s “unlike most other EV batteries available in America.”

First, the Fathom uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells in its lithium-ion batteries. That’s because the materials needed for LFP batteries are cheaper than those for the nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) batteries most automakers use. The Fathom will join the Kia EV3, Chevrolet Bolt, and Tesla Model 3 RWD in a fleet of affordable vehicles using LFP cells. But Ford licensed its LFP cell technology from the Chinese company CATL. Yes, despite Ford continuously claiming that China is going to destroy the American car industry.

While LFP batteries are heavier than NMC batteries, the Ford Fathom knows it has to use as few cells as possible to ensure it’s below $30,000. Engineers have been working to improve the Fathom’s aerodynamics as much as possible, reducing drag so they can shrink the battery pack while still meeting their range goals. According to MotorTrend, this process has made the Fathom $1,300 cheaper.

Next, the battery has to store as much energy as possible while ensuring the vehicle is strong and stiff. This balance has made the Fathom’s battery similar to the packs used in supercars like the Ferrari F50 and Aston Martin Valkyrie, which transfer loads from one side of the vehicle to the other.

The battery will also be located in the cabin floor underneath the passenger. Carpets and front seats will go on top. Then, the pack will be raised from underneath and bolted into place. This will reduce the amount of parts needed, further reducing costs.

Inside the factory

Green Cars was also on that factory tour, and they went further into the plant itself. Over 1,000 pieces of equipment from CATL were brought to the Marshall plant and there are dozens of CATL employees working on-site for three months to train Ford’s local staff. By the end of 2026, 800 people will be working there. At full production, that number will rise to 1,700 employees.

There’s definitely room for it. The factory is about a mile long and has two main areas. First, the cell manufacturing plant, which has two production lines, then the calendering. The plant keeps about four hours of inventory on hand, so production will continue even if there’s a hiccup in the system.

Once both lines are ramped up and at full production, they will produce 40 cells per minute. That’s 4,800 cells per hour. This should be happening by the fourth quarter of 2027, about a year from now.

title: NEPA By the Numbers: What Triggers NEPA Reviews? - Clean Air Task Force
description:
Key Findings Federal funding is the dominant NEPA trigger for decarbonization-related reviews—9,210 of 20,725 reviews (44.4%).
The Department of Energy’s (DOE) grant and loan portfolio generates more decarbonization-related NEPA reviews than any other federal nexus in the dataset.
Figure 1: Federal Funding Triggers 44% of All Decarbonization NEPA Reviews – More Than Any Other Federal Nexus Funding-triggered reviews are almost entirely categorically excluded Projects that are triggered by federal funding are almost always categorically excluded.
Figure 2: Funding-Triggered Reviews Are Almost Entirely Categorically Excluded (99%) NEPA triggers are unevenly distributed across NEPA review processes NEPA triggers are unevenly distributed across CEs, EAs, and EISs (Figure 3).
Figure 6: Common Grant-Scale Federal Funding Amounts Conclusion More than two in five decarbonization NEPA reviews (44.4%) are triggered by federal funding — and those reviews are almost entirely categorically excluded (99%).
text:
Key Findings

Federal funding is the dominant NEPA trigger for decarbonization-related reviews—9,210 of 20,725 reviews (44.4%). The Department of Energy’s (DOE) grant and loan portfolio generates more decarbonization-related NEPA reviews than any other federal nexus in the dataset.

But funding-triggered reviews are almost entirely categorically excluded— 99% of reviews for decarbonization technologies are completed through categorical exclusions (CEs). Removing federal funding as a trigger for NEPA would therefore mostly eliminate determinations that already conclude in days or weeks, and consequently would not significantly speed those reviews.

The triggers that result in more substantial reviews are federal land- and permit-related, not funding-related. Reviews triggered by federal land access or federal permits generate proportionally far more environmental assessments (EAs) and environmental impact statements (EISs).

There are clear patterns in review triggers. Reviews in the dataset for transmission projects are most commonly triggered by the federal power marketing administrations, which build, own, and operate transmission lines; certain technologies (carbon capture, hydrokinetic, energy storage) are the most funding-driven; and solar and onshore wind are mostly funding-triggered, with Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land access the clear second trigger.

Introduction

The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) is a foundational environmental law that has, for more than fifty years, ensured that federal agencies consider the environmental impacts of a proposed major federal action. NEPA requires federal agencies to consider the reasonably foreseeable environmental impacts of their activities, integrate those considerations into agency decision making, and enhance public transparency in the decision-making process.

A NEPA review is required when agencies undertake “major Federal actions significantly affecting the quality of the human environment.”1 Common triggers include federal grants and loans, the issuance of permits (e.g., environmental permits and the rights of way on federal lands), and actions taken by a federal agency itself (e.g., to upgrade a federal building).

The scope of what actions should trigger a NEPA review has been the subject of debate and legislation. In the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 (FRA), a major federal action was defined as “an action that the agency carrying out such action determines is subject to substantial Federal control and responsibility.”2 The FRA definition also listed certain activities that do not qualify as a major federal action, including when the federal government provides funds but does not control project outcomes, provides general revenue sharing funds, and provides loans or loan guarantees without “sufficient control and responsibility over the subsequent use of such financial assistance or the effect of the action.”3

More recent proposals suggest narrowing the scope of the actions that would trigger a NEPA review still further, including to:

Set a dollar threshold over which funding would trigger a NEPA review (proposal from the CEQ guidance template)4

Exempt the provision of federal funding (including through grants, loans, and loan guarantees) from a NEPA review entirely (proposal from the SPEED Act of 2025 and Problem Solvers Caucus,5 which was later included in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026)

Exempt projects from a NEPA review if they are also reviewed under “functionally equivalent” federal, state, or Tribal statutes (Problem Solvers Caucus, also included in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026)

However, there exists no research to date on how often various NEPA triggers apply across federal actions, making it unclear if proposed reforms would have any beneficial impact. Research on NEPA has historically been hindered by federal data management practices: NEPA documents are scattered across numerous agency databases, often in machine-unreadable formats that lack basic metadata and other identifiers, and some documents (e.g., categorical exclusion determinations) are not always published as a matter of routine.

The National Environmental Policy Act Text Corpus (NEPATEC) 2.0 dataset, developed as part of the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory’s (PNNL) PermitAI project, is a substantial step toward remedying this situation. The NEPATEC 2.0 dataset contains more than 120,000 NEPA documents from 60,000 reviews prepared by more than 60 different agencies. Nearly 21,000 of these reviews involve decarbonization technologies and nearly 11,000 involve fossil fuel technologies, which are the primary focus of our research. Most records in the NEPATEC 2.0 dataset span the period from 2000 through 2025, with a handful of records from as early as the 1980s. Reviews involving decarbonization technologies mostly span from 2010 through 2025, with a handful of projects recording dates from earlier in the 2000s.

This analysis, part of an ongoing series, uses the NEPATEC 2.0 dataset as a basis for analyzing which NEPA triggers apply to a suite of 20,725 decarbonization-related environmental reviews, thereby adding data-driven evidence to this policy conversation.

Methodology

Scope and trigger definitions

The analysis covers all 20,725 decarbonization projects in NEPATEC 2.0. Each is assigned one primary trigger — the federal nexus that brought it under NEPA:

Classification approach and caveats

Triggers were classified by a five-tier pipeline that starts with deterministic agency-to-trigger mappings and hand-labeled examples, then escalates through regex extraction on titles, document text, and purpose-and-need sections, and finally to machine-learning classification for genuinely ambiguous cases. The pipeline resolved 20,642 of 20,725 projects (99.6%); the remaining 0.4% are confirmed NEPA actions whose trigger could not be reliably identified from available text. Several caveats apply:

Triggers are assigned by priority rules when multiple nexuses exist, so secondary triggers (e.g., a funded project on federal land) are not counted here

Unknowns concentrate among EAs and EISs, whose longer documents are harder to classify conservatively

NEPATEC 2.0 contains substantially complete EA and CE data from only BLM and DOE, so these results may not be able to be fully extrapolated to all federal agencies

The scope of this fact sheet is limited to decarbonization-related reviews7

Results

Funding is the most common review trigger

Federal agency funding is the most common trigger, responsible for at least two in five of all decarbonization NEPA reviews (44.4%)(Figure 1). Land access is the second most common NEPA trigger (18.3%), followed by the power marketing administrations and TVA (17.1%) and direct federal action (15.3%), the latter dominated by DOE’s own facilities and laboratories.

Figure 1: Federal Funding Triggers 44% of All Decarbonization NEPA Reviews – More Than Any Other Federal Nexus

Funding-triggered reviews are almost entirely categorically excluded

Projects that are triggered by federal funding are almost always categorically excluded. Of the 9,210 reviews in the dataset that exist because of a federal grant or loan, 99% were categorically excluded. Of the remaining 1%, 116 escalated to an EA and just 22 to a full EIS (Figure 2).

Figure 2: Funding-Triggered Reviews Are Almost Entirely Categorically Excluded (99%)

NEPA triggers are unevenly distributed across NEPA review processes

NEPA triggers are unevenly distributed across CEs, EAs, and EISs (Figure 3). Most CEs are triggered by funding — DOE’s energy grant and loan programs generate a high volume of low-complexity actions. EAs show the most balanced mix. EISs skew toward land, PMA/TVA, and permits: the larger, more contested projects tend to be sited on public land, federally built, or federally licensed.

Land- and permit-triggered projects require more substantial reviews more often — 14% and 46%, respectively, are EAs or EISs. Projects that require a permit are the most striking: two in five permit-triggered reviews (40%) are full EISs, by far the highest EIS rate of any trigger. And in absolute terms, federal land access produced 308 EISs — more than any other nexus — even though the land class is less than half the size of the funding class. The gradient is consistent: the further a federal hook moves from writing a check toward authorizing ground disturbance or licensing a facility, the more intensive the review it generates.

Figure 3: NEPA Trigger Type by Review Process

Department jurisdiction shapes the trigger mix

Department patterns follow jurisdiction (Figure 4): DOE projects are largely funding-triggered (with sizable PMA and direct-action shares from the power administrations and national laboratories housed within DOE); Interior (primarily BLM) skews toward land; Agriculture (Forest Service) mirrors Interior at smaller scale (though Forest Service coverage in the dataset is scarcer than for BLM and DOE).

Figure 4: NEPA Trigger Distribution by Federal Department

Technology mirrors the same nexus logic

Technology patterns reflect the same nexus logic (Figure 5). The most funding-driven technologies are carbon capture (91%) and hydrokinetic (91%), with the other renewables catch-all category (89%) and energy storage (86%) just behind. Carbon capture and hydrokinetic technologies enter the NEPA process almost exclusively through DOE’s grant programs, because they have to date rarely been sited on federal land or required a federal license. Solar and onshore wind are also mostly funding-triggered (74% and 55%), but land (BLM rights-of-way) is a substantial second nexus (17% and 24%). Transmission is the mirror image — the lowest funding share of any technology (9%) and the highest PMA/TVA share (48%), because those agencies build and maintain federally-owned and operated lines. Hydropower and nuclear stand out for their permit shares (17% and 42%), driven by FERC licensing of non-federal dams for the former and Nuclear Regulatory Commission licensing for the latter.

Figure 5: Primary NEPA Trigger by Energy Technology

Few documents disclose a funding amount, and those that do skew small

For funding-triggered projects, we also extracted the dollar amounts where documents state them, though most NEPA documents do not report an award figure and therefore it is difficult to draw strong conclusions. The distribution in Figure 6 therefore describes typical award sizes among reviews that disclose them (5% of reviews), not the full portfolio. With that caution, the extracted amounts show most disclosed grant-scale awards falling in the tens of thousands to low millions of dollars, with loan guarantees and cooperative agreements reaching far higher.

Figure 6: Common Grant-Scale Federal Funding Amounts

Conclusion

More than two in five decarbonization NEPA reviews (44.4%) are triggered by federal funding — and those reviews are almost entirely categorically excluded (99%).

In most cases, the federal funding trigger does not add significant time to project reviews. The reviews that are most robust tend to be EAs and EISs for projects on federal land, federally built transmission, and federally licensed facilities.

Two caveats bound these conclusions. The trigger classes that generate the heaviest reviews are also the smallest — only 319 decarbonization reviews are permit-triggered, and 53 are property transactions — so process shares for the rare classes rest on far fewer projects than the funding figures and should be read with corresponding caution. And because each project is assigned a single primary trigger, projects with several federal hooks — a funded project on federal land, a licensed dam that also received a grant — are counted once, understating how often the heavyweight nexuses are in play. Both limitations trace to the same root: nothing in the NEPA process requires an agency to clearly record why NEPA applied. Building trigger identification into NEPA metadata — a structured field naming the federal nexus, or all of them when several apply, captured at the time of review — would replace after-the-fact classification like ours with an authoritative record, just as the CEQ NEPA and Permitting Data and Technology Standard would do for timelines.

The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) is a foundational environmental law that has, for more than fifty years, ensured that federal agencies consider the environmental impacts of a proposed major federal action. NEPA requires federal agencies to consider the reasonably foreseeable environmental impacts of their activities, integrate those considerations into agency decision making, and enhance public transparency in the decision-making process.

Clean Air Task Force (CATF) has conducted research over the years, delving into complex questions about NEPA’s role in clean energy infrastructure deployment. For technologies like transmission and offshore wind, NEPA is often scapegoated as a primary cause of infrastructure delays and cancelations. But we found that longer permitting timelines are typically not driven by NEPA requirements themselves, but rather a lack of federal agency leadership and prioritization of transmission, and, crucially, insufficient support for agency coordination, cooperation, and capacity. When done effectively, NEPA can actually improve environmental decision making and overall permitting efficiency by providing a coordination mechanism among federal agencies.

However, NEPA research is hindered greatly by lack of data availability and transparency. NEPA documents are scattered across numerous agency databases, often in machine-unreadable formats. This began to change with the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory’s PermitAI project and the release of its NEPATEC 2.0 dataset, which contains more than 120,000 NEPA documents from 60,000 reviews. This dataset standardizes and categorizes data across categorical exclusions, environmental assessments, and environmental impact statements for the first time, making them accessible for analysis.

CATF and data scientist Kasey Zapatka partnered to conduct first-of-a-kind analyses on this dataset to better understand NEPA and its impact on project outcomes.

NEPA by the numbers: Investigating how NEPA functions across a range of federal actions involving energy infrastructure

Given the historically limited amount of publicly available data on NEPA and its impact on project outcomes, our initial analysis of this new dataset sheds light on important trends in agency use of different types of NEPA documents and the initial effects of recent statutory reforms. This report summarizes our first phase of results from a planned series analyzing this new NEPA data corpus.

NEPA by the Numbers: New Insights on Environmental Reviews for Energy Infrastructure

NEPA by the Numbers Fact Sheet

A deeper dive

After our initial assessment of the dataset, the research team used more advanced data analysis techniques to dig into specific topics of interest to policymakers, developers, analysts, and other key stakeholders. We focused this research on three topics: NEPA triggers, NEPA timelines, and significance determinations, and analyzed provisions of Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) through the lens of this work.

What triggers NEPA reviews?

The scope of what actions should trigger a NEPA review has been the subject of debate and legislation. This analysis investigates what triggered a suite of 20,725 decarbonization-related environmental reviews, adding data-driven evidence to the policy conversation for the first time.

How long do reviews actually take?

The time for agencies to complete reviews has dominated discussion and policy debates in recent years, however, the lack of comprehensive data on NEPA review timelines means the evidence record is dominated by anecdotes, hindering informed policy discussions. This analysis expands on previous research by including all reviews in the NEPATEC 2.0 database (~60,000).

Where NEPA draws the line: Determinations of significance

A single word — “significant” — can determine how long a project takes to get through environmental review. This analysis provides the first systematic look at how federal agencies make significance determinations for decarbonization projects.

description:

text:
Texas made more electricity from wind in 2025 than Iowa, Oklahoma, and Kansas combined. Its 130.1 billion kilowatt-hours came to 28% of all the wind power generated in the United States.

The ten states below are ranked by U.S. Energy Information Administration figures for wind generation over the full 2025 calendar year. Together they produced about three-quarters of the nation's wind power. In three of them, wind made more than 40% of the state's electricity. In western Kansas, wind payments even helped buy a school district a new football grandstand.

1. Texas

Drive Interstate 20 into West Texas and the turbines start lining the mesas on both sides of the highway. Sweetwater and surrounding Nolan County had more than 1,400 of them as of the city's 2021 count. The nearby Roscoe Wind Complex alone spreads 627 turbines across four counties and roughly 100,000 acres. It was the largest wind farm in the world when it was completed in 2009, and by 2023 it had paid more than $92 million in local taxes, according to the Texas comptroller.

Sweetwater is also where Texas State Technical College trains wind technicians, in what the Texas Tribune described in 2024 as the only program in the state developed in close collaboration with wind energy companies. Starting salaries for those technicians were about $47,000 a year, and experienced ones could earn up to $90,000.

Wind produced about 22% of the electricity generated in Texas in 2025, and much of it has to travel to reach the people who use it. About 3,500 miles of high-voltage lines, finished in 2013, were built to carry wind power from West Texas and the Panhandle to the rest of the state.

2. Iowa

Wind turbines in Iowa come with a lease check. MidAmerican Energy, which operates more than 3,500 turbines across the state, paid landowners about $45.7 million in 2025, and the Iowa Land Company put the average payment at about $9,000 per turbine per year in early 2025. MidAmerican paid roughly $60 million more in property taxes on those turbines in 2025, spread across 35 counties, and drivers on Interstate 80 pass one of the state's wind farms in Adair County, west of Des Moines. Counting every company's turbines, wind generated 58.5% of Iowa's electricity in 2025, the highest share of any state in the top ten, from 43.6 billion kilowatt-hours of output.

3. Oklahoma

Oklahoma has a wind farm that a federal court has ordered removed. Its 84 turbines stand on 8,400 acres of Osage County between Pawhuska and Fairfax, and in December 2023 a federal judge ruled that the developer, Enel, had dug into the Osage Nation's mineral estate, which the tribe owns under a 1906 federal law, without the required mining lease. The removal order was put on hold during Enel's appeal, and the turbines were still turning in early 2026.

In Weatherford, a western Oklahoma city on Interstate 40, turbines are visible from city hall, and north of town, in Blaine and Custer counties, the 356-turbine Traverse wind farm was the largest wind farm built in a single phase in North America when it opened in 2022. Oklahoma generated 37.3 billion kilowatt-hours from wind in 2025, about 41% of its electricity, and public radio station KGOU reported that year that landowners collect an estimated $98.8 million a year in wind payments, while local schools have received about $660.5 million.

4. Kansas

Kansas got its first large wind farm in 2001, when 170 turbines went up in Gray County near the small town of Montezuma. Wind farms are exempt from property tax in Kansas, so counties negotiate their own payments, and the Gray County project meant $5.3 million for the county. The nearby Cimarron school district received $3.6 million from wind farms over a decade and spent part of it on a new grandstand at the district's football stadium. Orville Williams, who had farmed around the towers for 20 years by 2021, signed up for another 20-year lease.

By 2024, Kansas had about 4,000 wind turbines, and roughly one in ten stood taller than the Statue of Liberty. In 2025, the state's wind farms generated 29.2 billion kilowatt-hours, or 47% of its electricity. New wind installations are barred in about one-fifth of Kansas counties.

5. Illinois

Illinois generated 25.1 billion kilowatt-hours from wind in 2025, but in a state that produced 191.8 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity overall, that came to only about 13%. Much of the state's wind is made in the farm counties of central and north-central Illinois. Twin Groves, just east of Bloomington along Illinois Route 9, puts 240 turbines on two moraines in eastern McLean County. Since it began operating in 2007, it has paid $36.9 million to landowners and $47 million toward public services, according to its owner, EDP Renewables.

McLean County had five wind farms on its tax rolls in 2021, paying a combined $9.4 million in property taxes, and the industry group American Clean Power counted that as about 24% of the county's revenue that year. In nearby Logan County, the same group found that wind companies made 73% of the tax payments from the county's ten largest property taxpayers in 2021.

6. Colorado

Colorado's largest wind farm was built mostly from parts made in Colorado. Rush Creek, owned by Xcel Energy, began operating in 2018 with 300 Vestas turbines on 262-foot towers, and most of its components came from Vestas factories in the state. The company's blade plant in Windsor and nacelle plant in Brighton were hiring in 2026. The turbines themselves stand on the Eastern Plains across Elbert, Lincoln, Kit Carson, and Cheyenne counties, around towns such as Limon, Hugo, and Simla. Rush Creek and the state's other wind farms produced 30% of Colorado's electricity in 2025, a total of 17.0 billion kilowatt-hours.

7. North Dakota

Every spring and fall, endangered whooping cranes migrate through central North Dakota along a corridor that crosses the Great Plains. A U.S. Geological Survey study published in 2021 found that the number of wind towers in that migration corridor tripled between 2010 and 2016 and quadrupled in its center. The cranes avoided towers when they picked places to stop and rest.

North Dakota climbed from 10th in 2024 to seventh in 2025 on 15.4 billion kilowatt-hours of wind generation, which supplied about 36% of the state's electricity. The state's largest wind farm, Aurora Wind, entered service in early 2021 near Tioga in Williams County, in northwestern North Dakota.

8. California

California's turbines cluster in windy passes and hills, and the most visible ones line both sides of Interstate 10 in the San Gorgonio Pass outside Palm Springs. Palm Springs Windmill Tours takes visitors behind the fence onto a private, working wind farm there. The state's largest project is farther north and west in the Tehachapi area of Kern County, where the Alta Wind Energy Center is the second-largest wind farm in the country.

East of the San Francisco Bay Area, the Altamont Pass wind area dates to 1980, and its older turbines have long been blamed for killing birds of prey, including golden eagles. Alameda County has pushed to replace them with newer machines to substantially reduce those deaths. Wind generated 7.4% of California's electricity in 2025, or 15.1 billion kilowatt-hours. In 2026, the federal government canceled one of two offshore wind leases off Humboldt County and one off Morro Bay, where a second lease is set for cancellation, and California has sued over the Morro Bay cancellations. No turbines stand in the ocean off the state's coast.

9. Minnesota

Lincoln County, in southwest Minnesota, collected about $3.91 million in wind production tax in fiscal year 2024, roughly $709 for every resident, according to state revenue figures compiled by the Center for Rural Affairs. More than 450 turbines stand along Buffalo Ridge in the county, where Minnesota's first utility-scale wind farm began commercial operation in 1994. The town of Lake Benton calls itself the "Windpower Capital of the Midwest" and runs the Heritage and Windpower Learning Center downtown. Statewide, Minnesota's turbines generated 15.0 billion kilowatt-hours in 2025, about a quarter of its electricity, and finished barely behind California.

10. New Mexico

For Dan Bell, a fifth-generation cattle rancher north of Corona in central New Mexico, wind lease income matters most during a drought, as he explained in 2022. The 377 turbines of the Western Spirit project stand on ranch country across Guadalupe, Lincoln, and Torrance counties in that part of the state. New Mexico's wind farms turned out 14.4 billion kilowatt-hours in 2025, and that came to about 36% of the state's electricity.

That total was set before the state's largest project switched on. SunZia Wind began commercial operation in June 2026 with 916 turbines in Lincoln, Torrance, and San Miguel counties and 3,650 megawatts of capacity, making it the largest wind farm in the country and more than three times the size of Alta in California. It nearly doubled New Mexico's wind capacity, from 3,997 megawatts to 7,647, and sends most of its power over a 550-mile transmission line to Arizona and California.

Most of America's wind power in 2025 came from farm and ranch country in the middle of the nation, and the people who live among the turbines collect their share close to home, in lease payments on Iowa farmland and in county tax money that, in Minnesota's Lincoln County, came to about $709 per resident. The electricity often goes much farther. Texas strung about 3,500 miles of high-voltage line to move West Texas and Panhandle wind power to the rest of the state, and SunZia's 550-mile line now carries power from central New Mexico's ranch land to Arizona and to California, the state with the smallest wind share in this top ten. SunZia played no part in the 2025 totals that placed New Mexico 10th, and its first full calendar year of output will come in 2027.

text:
An aerial view of the Venice Gas Plant, a methane gas processing facility operated by Targa Resources near the southern tip of Louisiana’s Mississippi River Delta. The plant emitted 194,855 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2023, according to the EPA. The “Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026” would make it easier for the Trump regime to help the powerful fossil fuel industry build facilities like this one by weakening environmental review. (Photo: Andrew Villeneuve/NPI)

Before going on its Thanksgiving break last week, the United States Senate passed a deeply flawed “permitting overhaul” bill that would give the Trump regime a green light to to make corrupt deals and greenlight harmful projects of all kinds.

Deceptively dubbed the “Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026,” this legislation would short-circuit federal environmental review laws that have helped protect public lands and shared common resources for decades.

Here’s a Cliff Notes summary from Earthjustice:

The bill would make it faster and easier for the president to hand out federal approvals and financial assistance without transparency or meaningful review, courtesy of provisions that would significantly limit or even dispense with requirements under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), and the Clean Water Act (CWA). Notably, the bill would exempt from NEPA and NHPA review all federal loans, loan guarantees, and other forms of federal financial assistance, giving the president the ability to provide federal backing that would speed the financing for major capital projects.

BAAJA would insulate Trump actions from the many successful lawsuits that are currently operating as a check on the abuse of power. The bill is designed to make it harder to (1) get into court, (2) win, and (3) get meaningful relief, and it expressly prohibits judges from issuing injunctions or vacating decisions in NEPA and NHPA cases. Even if a court found that the Trump administration was issuing permits in clear violation of NEPA and NHPA, the projects could still go forward. In other words, the Trump administration could violate the law without consequences.

BAAJA includes many provisions that would bar consideration of new information and science, while significantly increasing deference to federal agencies to define the scope of their reviews. Taken together, these provisions would legitimize the Trump administration’s efforts to suppress science and exclude consideration of the best available data.

Most sweepingly, the bill’s certainty provisions would render Trump permitting decisions irrevocable with very limited exceptions. The next administration would likely inherit a raft of destructive and unpopular projects, and BAAJA would make it wildly risky financially and even impossible for the next president to revisit them. To be clear, the damage would not be confined to energy-related projects. Think detention centers, petrochemical complexes, data centers on public lands — whatever kinds of projects appeal to this president.

Our own Senator Maria Cantwell has been helping lead the opposition to BAAJA. In a recent press briefing, she explained some of her concerns, remarking: “We certainly don’t want to go back on clean water writ large when there are pollutants that could affect consumption and impact humans. And yet, that is what we seem to be doing with this legislation. So I hope our House colleagues will ask for more time and attention.”

BAAJA wouldn’t have had a chance if Democrats had been uniformly opposed to it. But unfortunately, they weren’t. While our senators voted no — meaning, Cantwell, Patty Murray, Ron Wyden, and Jeff Merkley, who represent Washington and Oregon — fourteen other Democratic senators voted for this bad bill.

Those Democratic U.S. senators are:

Chris Coons (D-DE)

John Fetterman (D-PA)

Ruben Gallego (D-AZ)

Martin Heinrich (D-NM)

John Hickenlooper (D-CO)

Amy Klobuchar (D-MN)

Gary Peters (D-MI)

Jack Reed (D-RI)

Jacky Rosen (D-NV)

Brian Schatz (D-HI)

Chuck Schumer (D-NY)

Elissa Slotkin (D-MI)

Mark Warner (D-VA)

Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI)

Also voting yea was Angus King (I-ME), who is an independent caucusing with the Democrats. Two Republican senators voted nay: Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Josh Hawley of Missouri. Several Democrats voted for the substitute amendment from Shelley Moore Capito that loaded BAAJA into H.R. 2347 (a bill to amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to exclude from gross income any damages, other than punitive damages, received on account of any sexual acts or sexual contact) but then voted against the bill on final passage: Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock of Georgia, and Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire.

If you’re reading from beyond the Pacific Northwest and are represented by one of these senators, please send them a message letting them know how disappointed you are in their vote. With each month, week, and day that have elapsed since January 20th, 2025, we have been reminded that this regime cannot be trusted with any kind of power, especially delegated power. The tariff nonsense is a perfect example.

Yet, despite what has happened with tariffs, the above Democratic senators thought it was a good idea to give this regime the explicit power to bypass longstanding environmental review laws. They need to know that they made the wrong decision.

text:
GOOSE CREEK, S.C. (WCSC) — Neighbors will gather Monday to discuss a federal lawsuit against Century Aluminum over air quality in Goose Creek.

Resident Joan Spencer said, “I want them to follow the law.”

Lawsuit allegations

The Sierra Club, represented by Earthjustice and the South Carolina Environmental Law Project, filed the federal lawsuit against Century Aluminum in October.

The lawsuit claims the Mount Holly aluminum plant has violated the Clean Air Act since 2018. It also claims the plant has exceeded the air pollution limits in its permit.

The plant in the Goose Creek area is 40 years old. It is an aluminum smelter that uses high heat to turn alumina into aluminum.

Residents’ concerns

Spencer said she learned the plant has exceeded state standards for particulates.

“I found out that they’ve been exceeding the state standards for particulates in our air for a long time,” Spencer said.

The lawsuit says neighbors report breathing problems, irritated eyes and white dust on their property. The lawsuit says they blame pollutants for these effects.

Spencer said particles “that are small like 2.5 microns, 10 microns, those are the ones you can’t see at all and those are the ones that can travel deeply into your lungs.”

Plant emissions and equipment

Environmental Protection Agency records show the plant releases various chemicals each year, including sulfur dioxide, fluoride and particulate matter.

Mount Holly says it has equipment to capture these pollutants, including hoods, fans, scrubbers and baghouses.

The Sierra Club argues the installations do not capture all the particles. The group also says the scrubbers and baghouses themselves contain fluoride.

What plaintiffs and residents want

Residents say the lawsuit is not about money. They say they want to feel safe.

“I want them to partner with the community and treat us the way we should be treated and according to the laws that protect the citizens of Goose Creek,” Spencer said.

The plaintiffs want a federal judge to order Century to follow air pollution rules. They also want the company to address environmental damage and pay civil penalties.

Century Aluminum said in a statement:

“Environmental stewardship is a top priority for Century Aluminum. We are committed to responsible operations and environmental compliance, and we work continuously to meet our obligations to the communities where we operate, to regulators, and employees.

As members of the local community, Century Aluminum takes our environmental, health and safety responsibilities seriously and we care very much about the well-being of the residents in the communities surrounding our plant, many of whom are our employees and their families.

Many of the issues raised in the lawsuit have already been resolved by regulatory agencies. Any remaining issues that have not yet been resolved, Century is already in close coordination with the appropriate regulatory agencies to do so.

Century continues to make substantial investments in environmental and operational improvements at Mt. Holly reflecting our ongoing commitment to safe, responsible operations and environmental stewardship.

Operating at full capacity, Century Aluminum’s Mt. Holly plant supports hundreds of high-quality manufacturing jobs, strengthens the regional economy, and helps sustain a critical domestic aluminum supply chain. As one of the nation’s primary aluminum smelters, Mt. Holly also plays an important role in supporting U.S. economic competitiveness and national security.

text:
Ford confirmed its midsize electric pickup, the Fathom, will deliver more than 10 kW of alternating-current power to a home. Five utilities, including Pacific Gas & Electric Co., have aligned on scalable interconnection principles for AC-capable bidirectional electric vehicles.

Why it matters

Nearly all bidirectional EVs need external inverters to convert battery direct current into household alternating current, and that adds cost and installation complexity for owners. Ford's stated backup-package price, which is up to about 60% lower than its previous offering, would make home power backup from a vehicle more accessible if delivered.

Ford's pre-Fathom vehicle-to-home package retails above $5,000 excluding installation, while the Fathom package costs up to about 60% less. Automakers sell more than 20 bidirectional-capable light-duty EV models in the United States, though only California and Maryland have adopted vehicle-to-grid interconnection standards for AC-capable EVs.

The players

Ford Motor Company

Ford is a long-established American automaker known for its F-Series pickup line, and it is positioning the Fathom as an electric midsize pickup with home power capability.

Pacific Gas & Electric Co.

PG&E is a major investor-owned utility serving Northern California and operates vehicle-to-everything programs aimed at grid integration of bidirectional electric vehicles.

Tesla, Inc.

Tesla is an electric vehicle manufacturer that sells the Model 3 and Model Y and has begun taking orders for AC-capable versions of those cars.

The details

Ford invited Pacific Gas & Electric Co. and four other utilities to align on interconnection principles in July, and the working group published three principles in October. Tesla began accepting orders in October for AC-capable Model 3 and Y vehicles, while PG&E offers up to $3,000 in upfront incentives for residential bidirectional charging equipment.

Timeline

July 2026: PG&E and four other utilities teamed up at Ford's invitation.

October 2026: The working group published its blog post on three interconnection principles.

Late October 2026: Tesla began accepting orders for AC-capable Model 3 and Y vehicles.

Late October 2026: Ford confirmed the Fathom's 10 kW AC power capability.

Scheduled for 2027: Ford's Fathom is slated for release.

Related coverage

Electric Vehicles

Nov. 23

Ford Opens Battery Plant Doors Ahead of Fathom

Electric Vehicles

Nov. 18

Ford Starts U.S. Battery Cell Production With CATL Tech

Utilities

Nov. 24

Ann Arbor, Kitsap Reject Public Utility Measures

Roadmap

The Fathom's home-power capability extends a trend in which vehicles double as backup batteries, a role the Tesla Powerwall's roughly $12,000 installed cost has long defined as the stationary alternative. Automakers are now selling more than 20 bidirectional-capable light-duty EV models in the United States, signaling that vehicle-to-home power is moving from niche to mainstream.

A vehicle-to-home package costing up to about 60% less than Ford's prior offering could lower the entry cost for owners wanting home backup power. Buyers should still plan for inverter and installation costs, since nearly all bidirectional EVs require an external inverter.

The takeaway

Vehicle-to-home power is becoming a practical option, so buyers comparing EVs should check whether a model supports AC bidirectional charging and what installation will add to the total cost.

What happens next

Ford's Fathom is scheduled for release in 2027, and Connecticut regulators are set to expand energy storage compensation to commercial EV charging sites next month.

Further reading

For more on the broader shift, explore Electric Vehicles coverage on Wisevoter.
