The same rationale that keeps recurring when the president tries to justify his takeover of America's energy markets: "national security."
Trump's National Energy Emergency and the Defense Production Act When President Donald Trump was on the campaign trail in 2024, he promised to unleash America's energy dominance.
In May 2025, citing Trump's national energy emergency order, Energy Secretary Chris Wright ordered J.H.
under the second Trump administration: using seemingly justifiable, though mostly bogus, national security claims to bolster favored companies and industries.
text:
The sandy shores of Virginia Beach are idyllic, but what makes the place truly special lies about 27 miles off the coast, at the site of the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project, the largest offshore wind farm under construction in the country.

The project has been more than a decade in the making. In 2013, Dominion Energy secured a leasing agreement with the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management. In 2017, during the first Trump administration, the agency approved Dominion's site plan for the project, and in 2020 its two pilot turbines turned on. But it wasn't until October 2023 that federal regulators gave the final stamp of approval, allowing the rest of the farm to begin construction.

From the shore, it's hard to tell that construction has been underway. Except at certain times at night, the turbines are pretty much impossible to see with the human eye. (If you want to see them from the shore, you have to find the perfect spot and use binoculars.) But if you take a boat ride out to the Outer Continental Shelf, you'll begin to appreciate the scale of the project: 800-foot-tall turbines towering over the open seas like skyscrapers capable of withstanding Category 3 hurricane winds, anchored to the ocean floor with 1,500-ton metal tubes that are 31 feet in diameter.

Despite their industrial appearance, the turbines have been a net positive to the local environment. They serve as artificial reefs for fish and other wildlife, and they have allowed fishermen to continue catching flounder, cobia, and mahi in the Atlantic's deep waters.

When construction is completed—an event scheduled for late 2027—the wind farm will be the largest such project in the country. Its 176 turbines are expected to deliver 9.5 million megawatt-hours of clean energy to the Virginia grid every year. That will be enough to power 660,000 homes, according to Dominion. At this point, the company expects the farm to support 1,100 jobs and generate $200 million in annual economic output for the region.

And one needn't wait until 2027 to see that the project is proving beneficial to the area. Every year during its construction phase, Dominion estimates, the wind farm has supported 900 direct and indirect jobs and generated $143 million in economic output.

But in December 2025, the Interior Department issued a stop-work order for the Coastal Virginia project out of the blue.

What might compel the Trump administration to halt the construction of a project that supported countless jobs and was backed by the first Trump administration? The same rationale that keeps recurring when the president tries to justify his takeover of America's energy markets: "national security."

Trump's National Energy Emergency and the Defense Production Act

When President Donald Trump was on the campaign trail in 2024, he promised to unleash America's energy dominance. "We're going to be energy-dominant, we're going to make a fortune, we're going to supply it all over Europe, all over the world," he told Fox News' Maria Bartiromo that August. "We're going to be double and triple what they're doing. We're going to have tremendous energy, and we're going to lower our prices of energy."

Depending on the energy source, Trump's first 22 months back in office have been either "tremendous" or a toil. Fossil fuels are enjoying favorable policies, and their production has reached new heights. Renewable energy projects face government roadblock after government roadblock (in addition to the cancellation of wasteful subsidies).

On Day 1—the same day Trump "temporarily" halted all permitting for offshore wind projects in federal waters—Trump signed an executive order declaring a National Energy Emergency. "The policies of the previous administration have driven our Nation into a national emergency, where a precariously inadequate and intermittent energy supply, and an increasingly unreliable grid, require swift and decisive action," the order read.

The "swift and decisive action" needed to fix such a dire situation? Increasing the government's power and reach. Specifically, the order directed federal agencies to "exercise any lawful emergency authorities available to them" to increase the generation of almost all energy sources—all but wind and solar—through the Defense Production Act (DPA).

The DPA was passed in 1950, a few months after the start of the Korean War, when Congress determined it "needed a mechanism for the president to direct industrial production towards defense needs without full nationalization," says Gabe Arrington, a national security expert and nonresident fellow at the Baker Institute for Public Policy at Rice University.

Once invoked, the DPA gives the president immense power, with nearly no congressional oversight, to meddle with private businesses. He can force private entities to prioritize certain contracts, award loans and loan agreements, and even block corporate mergers with foreign companies.

"We were coming right out of World War II, where we had a full nationalization effort. This was an intermediate step," says Arrington.

Yet the DPA has had a long legacy, and has been invoked at least once by each president since it passed. President Jimmy Carter used the act to fund research into synthetic fuels and to establish the Synthetic Fuels Corporation, which financed research and development into these energy sources from 1980 until Congress shut it down in 1986. President Ronald Reagan used the act to stockpile rare earth minerals for military purposes and to direct steel production.

After 9/11, its "use expanded dramatically," says Arrington, including for "body armor, military vehicles, [and] other military surveillance equipment." During the COVID-19 pandemic, both Trump and President Joe Biden used the DPA to procure billions of dollars' worth of personal protective equipment and medical and testing supplies. Biden then used it to boost production in the clean energy sector.

In April 2025, Trump decided to promote a different set of energy producers. In an executive order, the president declared it "the policy of the United States that coal is essential to our national and economic security." The order also designated coal a "critical mineral," opening up the door for future DPA funding.

With these moves in place, the Trump administration was ready to use the full weight of the federal government to shape the energy sector as it saw fit.

'The American People Won and the Special Interests Lost'

During the first Trump administration, the president signed deregulatory reforms for nuclear energy, modernized federal environmental reviews, and scrapped expensive restrictions on power plants. The market responded to Trump's (mostly) anti-interventionist approach: Inflation-adjusted energy spending fell, renewable energy generation and investments reached new heights, and in 2017 the U.S. became a net exporter of liquefied natural gas—a remarkable feat considering the first export of the fuel from the lower 48 states occurred only a year earlier.

Trump's successor scrapped this hands-off approach.

On Day 1 of his presidency, Joe Biden axed the Keystone Pipeline and paused new oil and gas leasing on federal lands. Then, in 2022, Biden signed his legacy-defining (and ironically named) Inflation Reduction Act into law.

"With this law, the American people won and the special interests lost," Biden said at the bill signing in August 2022. A few months later, climate czar John Kerry predicted the bill would jumpstart "the biggest transformation, economically, since the Industrial Revolution."

That transformation never materialized. Instead, the government shelled out huge sums to the green energy industry.

The Inflation Reduction Act appropriated billions in new spending, $12 billion of which was funneled to the Energy Department's Loan Programs Office. This sum, and the office's $100 billion in new lending authority, was directed to support such projects as a Ford factory in Tennessee (which displaced the area's residents), grid upgrades for California's largest power utility, and a solar facility for a South Korean manufacturer owned by Stellantis (formerly Chrysler).

The law also offered expensive tax credits and subsidies for renewables and green tech. Wealthy homeowners and large corporations claimed the majority of tax credits. Renewable energy production, which reached then-historic highs in 2024, lagged significantly behind fossil fuels.

Meanwhile, grid operators were issuing dire warnings about the status of the power grid. In 2023, PJM Interconnection, the largest grid operator in the country, reported that grid demand—driven by electrification and data centers—was outpacing supply. A year later, the operator warned that "continuing generator retirements and increasing demand" were eroding its energy reserves, which could impact its response to the summer's extreme heat. Trump's Energy Department would later release a report finding that, if power plant retirements continued, blackouts would be 100 times more likely to occur in 2030.

This price crunch, coupled with record spending, prompted conservative policy wonks to demand drastic action. Diana Furchtgott-Roth, then of the conservative Heritage Foundation, wrote in the days leading up to Trump's second inauguration that "America faces a national energy emergency because the Biden administration has created a serious and dangerous energy situation so damaging to ordinary people and our country that it requires immediate action." By taking "immediate action" and declaring a national energy emergency, she wrote, "Trump can ensure that America does not walk down the same yellow brick road of Europe's energy and climate policies."

Trump's National Security Claims Are a Weak Justification To Block Wind and Prop Up Coal

Enough people agreed that the Biden green agenda was a disaster that Trump reentered office with significant leeway to recreate his first term's lighter-touch approach to energy markets. Instead, he doubled down on Biden's intrusiveness.

For example, in 2026 Trump adopted a novel strategy in his battle against wind projects: Pay them to stop operating. In March, the administration reached a deal with TotalEnergies to shutter two of the company's offshore wind projects in North Carolina and New York. Under the agreement, TotalEnergies was given $928 million—a "dollar-for-dollar" payback from what it spent on procuring its offshore leases—which it then invested in oil and natural gas projects. The company also pledged "not to develop any new offshore wind projects in the United States," according to a government press release.

The Interior Department cited national security concerns when spearheading the deal. It has since brokered four other agreements to pay developers to cancel permitted offshore wind projects and invest in fossil fuel generation. Meanwhile, the Defense Department has stalled approvals for onshore wind farms on private lands under the guise of "national security," the Financial Times reported in May.

Projects like these regularly require approval from the Defense Department to ensure they don't mess with radar systems. If they do, the fix is simple: The developer can negotiate with the Pentagon on a fee to update the radar system. If they don't, the project can move forward. As the Financial Times points out, 50 of the projects facing a shutdown would "probably have been declared risk-free." Meanwhile, 30 had "undergone negotiations, received verbal signoffs and were waiting for written confirmation," making Trump's national security justification all the more thin.

As Jason Grumet, CEO of the American Clean Power Association, told the Financial Times, "The fact the administration is telling private landowners they're not allowed to pursue economic activity and generate value from their property is hard to reconcile with conservative values."

Luckily for developers, a federal judge froze the Pentagon's wind order in August. In November, the Senate passed a sprawling bipartisan permitting reform bill that would, among other things, prohibit the executive branch from rescinding or altering an approved permit or impeding the construction of a previously approved project. Certain conditions—including new information on national security risks—would still allow a federal agency to interfere. But even then, the agency would have to provide advance written warning to justify its actions. At press time, the legislation is in the House of Representatives; the White House says it backs the bill.

The government has also intervened to prop up favored industries, especially coal. In May 2025, citing Trump's national energy emergency order, Energy Secretary Chris Wright ordered J.H. Campbell—a 1,560 megawatt coal-fired power plant in Michigan that was scheduled to shut down that month—to "temporarily" remain open for the summer. Over a year later, J.H. Campbell is still open. Consumers Energy, the plant's majority owner, is seeking $303 million in cost recovery from ratepayers in the region. In September, a federal court vacated the Energy Department's initial order to keep the power plant open. Despite this ruling, the agency issued a 90-day order in November to keep the plant open through mid-February.

"I think that the reliability and stability of the grid is both an economic concern and there can be national security concerns," such as brownouts and cybersecurity threats, says Nick Loris, president of C3 Solutions, a free market energy think tank. But "it doesn't seem like [J.H. Campbell is] generating that much electricity, so I don't know if it's actually solving a problem."

Loris warns that decisions like these can have "secondary and tertiary effects" on the market and prevent investments into cleaner, cheaper technologies. That's happening in Indiana, where an Energy Department order to keep a retiring coal plant open has made it impossible for one of the units to be replaced by cleaner-burning natural gas.

The Trump administration has kept pumping money into coal. Using its DPA authority, the Energy Department has given $425 million to modernize coal plants, while opening up other funding opportunities for the industry. Thanks to an April order, more DPA funding is incoming for the industry to support its supply chains and extend other coal power plants. Yet exports are down.

Nuclear energy, too, has enjoyed favored status under Trump 2.0, including using the DPA to enrich nuclear fuel. This move has been praised by the industry, which sees America's lack of uranium enrichment—nearly all of America's enriched uranium is imported—as a national security threat. Christo Liebenberg, president of LIS Technologies, a startup that uses laser technology to enrich uranium, argues that the Energy Department's use of the DPA to finance uranium enrichment is "needed because the demand is just so big, and the supply is so small." Liebenberg says that to meet the government's goal of quadrupling nuclear power by 2050, the U.S. will need a 12-fold increase in its domestic enrichment capabilities.

The administration used the same national security rationale to take an ownership stake in Westinghouse last year. In June, the Energy Department unveiled a $17.5 billion loan program to deploy 10 Westinghouse AP1000 reactors. Not coincidentally, per the terms of the ownership agreement, the government will "get a 20% share in any dividends paid out by Westinghouse above a $17.5 billion threshold," according to Bloomberg.

So even when a national security argument may have some truth to it, it can become a slippery slope. "Rather than making an investment that is targeted for a specific national security need," says Loris, "it ends up being more of a balloon payment to industries and companies writ large that really aren't addressing the legitimate national security questions."

This seems to have been the M.O. under the second Trump administration: using seemingly justifiable, though mostly bogus, national security claims to bolster favored companies and industries. Trump is certainly not the first president to do this. But he is doing it even as administration officials such as Wright have identified a better set of fixes to America's energy challenges—namely, deregulation.

Consumers may not immediately feel the negative impacts of Trump's energy socialism, but the continued distortion of energy markets will soon be seen in higher utility bills and steeper power-plant construction costs. They may also be felt politically when President Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez halts all oil and gas projects and supercharges solar development with the same "national security" tools that Trump is using now.

What Happened to the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind Project?

Despite being targeted by the Trump administration, the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project lives on. In January, a federal judge struck down the administration's work stoppage, and later that month a turbine generator was installed. In March, the farm delivered its first power to the grid.

But in August, Dominion reported that the project's cost had risen by nearly $300 million, thanks to Trump's tariffs and to updated turbine installation projections.

Trump came into office promising to reverse Biden's energy policies. But while he may have changed who directly benefits from those policies, he has used many of the same policy levers, which in turn have yielded similarly expensive and harmful outcomes. The U.S. needs more energy, but bogus national security claims are getting in the way.

text:
Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan emphasized the necessity of introducing a corporate tax credit for domestic electric vehicle (EV) production and sales on the 25th, stating, “We will not allow this to become a special favor for large corporations.” His remarks came amid industry requests led by Hyundai Motor to counter the influx of Chinese EVs.

During a press briefing at the Government Complex Sejong on the same day, Minister Kim explained, “While China can build a new EV ecosystem from scratch, South Korea must bear the high cost of overhauling its existing internal combustion engine ecosystem into one centered on EVs and autonomous driving.” He added, “The tax credit is intended to strengthen the competitiveness of cooperating companies, not Hyundai alone,” warning, “If large corporations insist on monopolizing it, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy will not remain passive.”

The minister also highlighted past semiconductor industry support during a downturn three years ago, which he credited for the sector’s current prosperity. “The ministry sees automotive support as essential,” he said. “Automotive components share strong similarities with robotics and could become a new growth engine depending on how we approach them.”

Stressing the technological gap with China, Minister Kim repeatedly urged the introduction of a special exception to the 52-hour workweek for R&D personnel, currently under discussion in the Super-Mega Special Zone Act, the Mega Special Zone Act. “Prices are already losing to China, and the final battleground is R&D,” he said. “Why prevent R&D professionals earning over 100 million Korean won annually from working if they wish to, provided their health rights and wages are guaranteed? We should start tomorrow.”

He criticized South Korea’s debate over the 52-hour workweek, stating, “China asks if we have the luxury to argue over this.” He added, “I fear we cannot envision a future if we fail to resolve this. For AI, robotics, and biotechnology, the workweek exception is the minimum we must achieve.”

The company launches a competitive bidding process for up to 150 megawatts of new Michigan solar energy.

Get Solar Panels

DTE Energy has announced plans to add up to 150 megawatts of new solar energy in Michigan, creating construction jobs, supporting local communities, and saving customers money on fuel costs.

Get Solar Panels

Because solar generation does not require fuel, the new projects will help reduce the company’s exposure to changing fuel prices over their operating lives. The projects will also support DTE’s work to provide customers with energy that is reliable, increasingly clean, and affordable.

“These projects are an investment in Michigan and the communities we’re proud to serve. By producing more Michigan-made energy that doesn’t require us to purchase fuel, we can help lower energy costs for our customers and reduce our reliance on fuel from outside our state. Project and bidding details

DTE is seeking competitive proposals for up to 150 megawatts of new Michigan-based solar generation. The procurement supports the requirements of the settlement agreement in Michigan Public Service Commission Case No. U-21662, approved May 15, 2025.

Get Solar Panels

Projects must achieve commercial operation by June 30, 2030, be located in Michigan and connect to either the MISO transmission system or DTE’s distribution system. Interested bidders can register and obtain additional information through PowerAdvocate. Proposals are due Jan. 19, 2027, and DTE expects to execute contracts in the second or third quarter of 2027.

text:
Washington, D.C. – Congressman Andrew R. Garbarino (R-NY) led a letter to Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin urging the agency to swiftly reinstate the Solar for All program following two federal court rulings rejecting the program’s termination. The effort seeks to restore $7 billion in congressionally approved funding intended to lower electricity bills and strengthen the nation’s energy grid.

The Solar for All program was established to help more than 900,000 households nationwide reduce their electricity bills by at least 20 percent. New York was awarded nearly $250 million through the program, funding that would help expand access to affordable energy for families across the state, including on Long Island.

“At a time when families on Long Island and across the country are struggling with rising electricity bills, we should be doing everything we can to bring costs down,” said Rep. Garbarino. “Solar for All is an opportunity to deliver real savings for American families while supporting domestic manufacturing, creating jobs, and strengthening our energy independence. Congress already approved this funding, and states are ready to put it to work. We should be focused on getting these projects moving, not standing in the way of affordable American energy.”

Congress appropriated $7 billion for Solar for All, and the EPA fully obligated those funds before terminating the program in August 2025. Two federal district courts have since ruled against the termination, reaffirming Congress’s intent for the program to move forward.

In their letter, Garbarino and his Republican colleagues emphasize that restoring the program is consistent with an all-of-the-above American energy strategy. Beyond lowering household electricity bills, Solar for All was designed to expand domestic manufacturing, strengthen American supply chains, create jobs, and improve grid reliability as electricity demand continues to rise.

Garbarino urged Administrator Zeldin to act quickly to allow states, territories, and tribes to resume implementation of their approved projects and deliver the benefits of the program to American families.

“This letter from Rep. Garbarino and House Republican colleagues makes clear what American families stand to gain from the Solar for All program: lower energy bills and new jobs. Now, it’s time for EPA to release the funding so that states, tribes, and territories nationwide can move forward with much-needed projects,” said Nick Torrey, Senior Attorney, Southern Environmental Law Center.

“Solar for All would deliver meaningfully lower energy costs for more than 900,000 households. It would also build a local clean energy workforce and strengthen grid resilience. We applaud Congressman Garbarino and his colleagues for urging the reinstatement of these critical funds. Their continued leadership shows that solar belongs in any all-of-the-above energy strategy,” said Erin Duncan, Vice President of Congressional Affairs at the Solar Energy Industries Association.

text:
Hyundai Glovis is partnering with the domestic automobile dismantling and recycling industry to create an automotive circular economy ecosystem.

Amid strengthening global environmental regulations, the company plans to build a supply chain that covers everything from recovering key resources such as used batteries and aluminum from end-of-life vehicles to utilizing recycled raw materials.

The company said Thursday that it signed a memorandum of understanding with the Korea Automobile Dismantling and Recycling Industry Association for "the promotion of the automotive circular economy industry and the creation of a sustainable ecosystem."

The signing ceremony, held on Nov. 24 at the Hyundai Glovis headquarters in Seongdong-gu, Seoul, was attended by Lee Kyu-bok, President (CEO) of Hyundai Glovis, Kim Jong-sik, Chairman of the Korea Automobile Dismantling and Recycling Industry Association, and others.

The two parties agreed to build an automotive circular economy network and expand the recycling of materials such as used batteries and aluminum generated during the safe dismantling of electric vehicles, hydrogen fuel cell vehicles, and internal combustion engine vehicles.

As the adoption of electric vehicles expands, the value of utilizing key resources recovered at the end-of-life stage, such as nickel, cobalt, lithium, and aluminum, is increasing. Global mandates for using recycled raw materials to reduce carbon emissions are also becoming stricter.

The European Union (EU) is pushing a plan to mandate the use of recycled plastics and recycled aluminum in the vehicle manufacturing stage through the End-of-Life Vehicles Regulation (ELVR).

Under the EU Battery Regulation (EUBR), standards requiring the use of at least 16% recycled cobalt, 6% lithium, and 6% nickel in battery manufacturing will apply from 2031.

In response to these environmental changes, the two parties will cooperate to share policies, systems, technologies, and market trends related to the automotive circular economy industry, as well as to improve the efficiency of dismantling operations.

They also plan to develop cooperation models for improving supply chain management (SCM) efficiency of recovered resources and securing recycled materials.

The initial area of cooperation is the recycling of used batteries from electric vehicles. Hyundai Glovis will provide technology necessary for safe battery removal, transportation, and storage, and will be responsible for the recycling process of the recovered batteries.

In the long term, the company plans to build a supply chain connecting the stage of resource recovery from end-of-life vehicles to the stage where recycled raw materials are reused in related industries, thereby supporting the growth of the domestic end-of-life vehicle industry.

Hyundai Glovis and the Association said, "This is to establish an automotive circular economy cooperation system in line with a market environment where carbon reduction has become a future corporate competitiveness and a new global standard," adding, "We will elevate the domestic automotive circular economy ecosystem to a global level."

text:
Highlights:

The Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) of 2026 (S.5653). Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) introduced the bill to streamline permitting for major federal energy infrastructure projects. BAAJA aims to increase transmission lines and grid capacity, strengthen regional and interregional transmission planning, ensure that data centers pay their fair share of energy costs (rather than pass those costs to consumers), and create jobs across the energy supply chain. To learn more about the interregional transmission issues in this bill, check out EESI’s briefing, Bridging the Transmission Gap.

The House passed the Earth MRI Reauthorization Act of 2026 (H.R.9640), led by Reps. Robert Wittman (R-Va.) and Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.). The bill would reauthorize the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative—a U.S. Geological Survey program that helps generate baseline data on geologic hazards, critical minerals, and geothermal resources across the United States—through 2031.

The Don Young Doug LaMalfa Indian Buffalo Management Act (H.R.7954) also passed the House. Reps. Jeff Hurd (R-Colo.), Teresa Leger Fernandez (D-N.M.), Julie Fedorchak (R-N.D.), and Dan Newhouse (R-Wash.) introduced the bill, which would require the Secretary of the Interior to work with tribal governments—through grantmaking, consultation, and collaborative agreements—to restore and manage American bison populations.

description: MIAMI, Nov. 25, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- NAED Energy Holding Inc. today announced the Helium series of continuous-Czochralski crystal-growth furnaces. Helium F2 and Helium F4 are designed, built and fabricated
text:
MIAMI, Nov. 25, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- NAED Energy Holding Inc. today announced the Helium series of continuous-Czochralski crystal-growth furnaces. Helium F2 and Helium F4 are designed, built and fabricated in the USA, with NAED fabricating its components in-house. Together with NAED’s PV-1 PECVD solar-cell line, they form a single American path from silicon feedstock to finished solar cells for terrestrial and space markets: Helium F2 & F4 Meet PV-1 — America’s Silicon-to-Cell Chain.
Twelve patent-pending applications cover both furnace lines, protecting the continuous-Czochralski architecture, the weir-crucible melt management and the gate-valve exchange sequence that lets NAED grow multiple ingots per hot-zone campaign. The full engineering package — master drawing set, Technical User Manual (TUM), Facility User Manual (FUM) and complete Bill of Materials (BOM) — is available to qualified customers for site planning, qualification and integration.
Helium F2
Helium F2 is NAED’s production furnace for photovoltaic-grade monocrystalline silicon ingots. It runs in two configurations: a standard 210–230 mm ingot platform and a 300 mm kit for G12 and G12R wafers. Its continuous-Czochralski design grows the crystal without interrupting the melt: granular polysilicon and dopant are fed to the melt as the ingot grows, while a water-cooled DN450 gate valve isolates the pull chamber so a grown ingot can be removed without cooling the melt.
Five 4,000 mm ingots come from a single 36 in quartz crucible with a Ø610 mm weir. The furnace holds a 250 kg melt-in charge, pulls at 1.4–2.0 mm/min body rate and runs under 80–150 slm argon at 10–25 Torr absolute, with 3 × 80 kW side heaters plus a 60 kW bottom heater. It stands 8,620 mm overall on a 1,200 mm raised base frame with an integrated equipment bay.
Helium F4
Helium F4 is NAED’s continuous-Czochralski (CCz) platform. Its F4-PV, F4-S and F4-SP lines grow up to five ingots per hot-zone campaign using continuous granular-silicon feed and, on the S and SP lines, magnetic-field control for the low-oxygen material that high-efficiency and space solar cells need. The 300S configuration grows 300 mm prime ingots (305–310 mm as grown) for logic, memory and power wafers, with a superconducting horizontal field of 0–0.40 T.
The Unseen Mountain
“We watch the known and predicted storms above. We count all the money in the world. We chase the identities; the names others make for themselves. We lavish our praise, our polish, our possessions, the things we hope will prove we matter, and call it living. But what sends the currents flowing north and south, east and west? The unseen mountain beneath the sea. Its power is not in thunder, but in the silence, it holds; its riches are not in gold, but in the silence it gives. Silent mountain, wealth of quiet, deep that moves the world without a word. ™”
— RCR
Who Helium and PV-1 serve
Domestic solar cell and module manufacturers seeking a resilient, made-in-USA supply of monocrystalline wafers sized and doped for their cell lines.
Space-power and satellite builders for whom the F4-S and F4-SP low-oxygen, radiation-tolerant silicon offers a lower-cost complement to III-V cells on suitable missions.
Semiconductor wafer producers served by the 300 mm F4-S configuration for logic, memory and power devices.
Feedstock and materials partners extending the domestic chain upstream into the Helium crucible.
Government, defense and utility-scale programs that need domestic-content supply for terrestrial and space solar.
Why the furnaces and PV-1 fit together
One supply chain under one roof. Ingot growth (Helium), wafering and cell fabrication (PV-1 PECVD) are planned as a matched set, so wafer size, doping and oxygen targets are set once, for the cell.
Domestic fabrication. Helium F2 and F4 are fabricated in the USA, with no imported pumps, magnets or power supplies, supporting buyers who need domestic-content documentation.
Continuous-growth economics. NAED’s internal cost model projects a lower cost per wafer for Helium F4 than for Helium F2.
Space-grade material. The F4-S and F4-SP lines are built for the low-oxygen, radiation-tolerant silicon that space solar cells require.
Closed-loop silicon. Qualified offcuts and process scrap are recycled as feedstock rather than discarded, closing the loop from crystal to wafer.
Protected architecture. Twelve patent-pending applications cover the furnace architecture and process.
NAED welcomes engineering discussions with solar manufacturers, semiconductor producers, space-power developers and satellite companies under NDA.
About NAED Energy Holding Inc.
NAED Energy Holding Inc. is an American energy-technology manufacturer headquartered in South Florida, with operations in New York and Nevada and an international presence in Indonesia. Through its NAED Nexus Core™ platform, the company designs and builds crystal-growth and solar-cell manufacturing equipment in-house, including the Helium F2 and Helium F4 continuous-Czochralski furnaces and the PV-1 vertical PECVD tandem-cell line, serving terrestrial solar, semiconductor and space-power markets. NAED controls its supply chain from its own high-purity silica sand resource in Indonesia through crystal growth, wafering and cell production. The NAED Energy Continuum™ spans atomic lattice, photon conversion, energy storage, grid infrastructure, mobility torque and aerospace propulsion. For more information, visit NAED.energy.

This photo provided by Edmunds shows the 2026 Mustang. The high-performance Dark Horse SC version is supercharged to make 795 horsepower.

This photo provided by Honda shows the 2027 Prelude. This agile sport coupe is a hybrid and gets more than an EPA-estimated 40 mpg combined.

This photo provided by Jeep shows the 2027 Wrangler 392. This version of Jeep's iconic SUV has a logic-defying 470-horsepower V8.

This photo provided by Mazda shows the 2026 MX-5 Miata. The Miata is the least expensive new convertible you can buy. It's also a blast to drive.

The car business isn’t sentimental, even if buyers are. Models that don’t sell, don’t meet the latest regulations, or simply don’t fit the latest corporate plan tend to disappear. So it’s surprising when a handful of vehicles that, by any reasonable measure, should be gone are still in showrooms. In the spirit of the season, here are five models Edmunds’ editors are thankful you can still buy. Some are fast, some are cheap, and at least one is a little ridiculous. All of them deserve a look before someone in the boardroom decides they’ve run their course. All of the following prices include destination charges.

It’s true that electric vehicles are more expensive than comparable gas-powered cars, and the end of the federal EV tax credit last year made it all the more obvious. That’s why we are glad that the Chevrolet Bolt is back. Chevy brought back its small electric car for 2027 with a starting price under $30,000.

It’s not a penalty box either. The Bolt has about 260 miles of range, offers plenty of room for adults, and now charges far quicker at public charging stations than the old version did, making road trips more practical. The catch is that this Bolt appears to be a one-year offering. If an inexpensive electric car sounds appealing, now is the time to look.

2027 Bolt starting price: $28,995

Not long ago, you had three choices if you wanted a traditional V8-powered muscle car. Well, Chevy stopped building the Camaro after 2024, and Dodge retired the Challenger in favor of a larger, very different Charger. That leaves the Mustang on its own, which isn’t an entirely new scenario for this American classic. Its rivals have come and gone over the decades, but the Mustang has been on sale without a break since 1964.

Ford, to its credit, keeps finding ways to make it more exciting. The newest version, the Mustang Dark Horse SC, adds a supercharger, bringing the total to 795 horsepower. At $108,085 to start, it’s a lot of money for a Mustang. But the Mustang GT is still available with a V8 and a six-speed manual, and it’s the one most fans are grateful for.

2026 Mustang starting price: $34,990

By most business measures, the Prelude shouldn’t exist. Sporty two-door coupes are a tiny slice of the market, and one that’s a hybrid and has a price north of $40,000 makes even less sense. But here we are with the 2027 Honda Prelude, and we’re pleased that Honda found a way to bring back the Prelude after a two-decade-plus hiatus.

The Prelude borrows hardware from the performance-focused Civic Type R to make it one of the best-handling front-wheel-drive cars Edmunds has ever driven. It offers an adaptive suspension, powerful brakes and precise steering. It’s not nearly as quick as a Mustang, but its hybrid powertrain lets it earn 44 mpg combined, according to the EPA.

2027 Prelude starting price: $43,695

In some ways, it’s hard to believe that the Wrangler is still around. It’s pretty bad at the things most SUV shoppers want, whether it be comfort, fuel economy or cutting-edge technology. It’s therefore even harder to believe that you can get a Wrangler with a massive V8 making 470 horsepower. Putting that much engine into a boxy SUV built to crawl over rocks makes very little sense. Jeep did it anyway.

Jeep actually spent two years telling everyone that the Wrangler 392 was going away. In a truly American parting prank, it sold final editions in both 2024 and 2025. Then the brand’s CEO announced in 2025 that the V8 would stay in production indefinitely. The 2027 V8-powered Wrangler will likely give you sticker shock, but trust us, there’s nothing else quite like it.

2027 Wrangler Willys 392 starting price: $72,990

Two seats, a folding roof and not much else. That’s been the Miata’s recipe since 1989, and it’s the reason the little Mazda has outlasted every convertible that came along after it. It’s light and simple, and it makes an ordinary back road feel like an event at speeds that won’t put you in jail. Like the Mustang, it’s also one of the few new cars you can buy with a stick shift.

The current Miata has been on sale for more than a decade, and it doesn’t appear that Mazda has a timeline for a replacement. Prices start a little over $30,000, which is about as low as it gets for a genuine sports car.

2026 Miata MX-5 starting price: $32,045

Our featured vehicles all sell in small numbers. But each exists because enough people still want a car that’s fun and not just sensible. That’s worth being grateful for. Here’s hoping they stick around.

title: The canceled Tesla Cybertruck is the fastest-selling used truck in America - TechCrunch
description:
Tesla Cybertruck sales never reached the lofty heights CEO Elon Musk predicted when it launched.
The upshot: The Tesla Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used truck, averaging just 39.1 days on the market compared with 65.5 days for trucks overall.
EVs are even edging out hybrids in terms of average days on market.
Keep in mind that these were October sales, the month before Musk announced Tesla would stop making the Cybertruck in 2027.
The impending cancellation will likely fuel used Cybertruck sales, although the pace may ebb and flow over the next year.
text:
Tesla Cybertruck sales never reached the lofty heights CEO Elon Musk predicted when it launched. But the futuristic, steel-clad EV is finding new life in the used car market, according to analysis of sales figures by iSeeCars.com.

The automotive search engine and research platform analyzed more than 1.1 million sales of one- to five-year-old used vehicles in October 2026 and measured the average days on market by drivetrain, vehicle type, and individual model. The upshot: The Tesla Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used truck, averaging just 39.1 days on the market compared with 65.5 days for trucks overall. Used Cybertrucks sold faster than any other truck, including the Ford Maverick Hybrid, which held the No. 2 spot, and the Rivian R1T, in third place.

According to , the Cybertruck’s sales performance lines up with a broader pattern in the used vehicle market: Used battery electric vehicles are hot sellers right now, with 16 of the 25 fastest-selling used cars fully electric. EVs are even edging out hybrids in terms of average days on market. EVs average 45.6 days on market compared to 54.5 days for hybrids and 61 days for gasoline-powered vehicles. Not every EV is selling well, however. For instance, found that the Cadillac Escalade IQ was the slowest-selling vehicle in the study, averaging 134.3 days on the market, more than twice the overall industry average.

Karl Brauer, executive analyst at , told TechCrunch that high gasoline prices have changed consumer-buying habits, prompting more people to opt for an EV or hybrid over an internal combustion engine vehicle. If high prices persist, as they have since March, that trend could continue.

Keep in mind that these were October sales, the month before Musk announced Tesla would stop making the Cybertruck in 2027. Fuel prices and the relative rarity of Cybertrucks in the used car market were driving demand even before the cancellation announcement, Brauer said.

“The Cybertruck has only been out for a few years, so you have a lot of used ones coming off lease and entering the used car market for the first time,” he said, adding that used Cybertrucks are cheap relative to their MSRP.

The impending cancellation will likely fuel used Cybertruck sales, although the pace may ebb and flow over the next year.

“The canceling of the new Cybertruck is making people kind of aware — it’s like, oh wow, these things aren’t going to be coming anymore,” Brauer said. “Whatever demand is for them, supply will not be continuing to grow.”

Brauer said that once production of the Cybertruck ends — which is expected in summer 2027 — sales of used versions may pop once again.

“When the last one is being produced, that’ll probably reignite things again, and for a few months after that,” he said.

text:
(AP) - King tides are the highest tides of the year, and they are increasingly flooding coastal communities as sea levels rise.

King tide is a non-scientific or colloquial term that people often use to describe these exceptionally high tides. The 2026 super El Niño — the natural and temporary warming of parts of the Pacific — has raised coastal water levels and intensified the effects of king tides.

“Tides are incredibly complicated. Really every location has different tidal cycles and that’s the basis for what a king tide is,” said Alec Bogdanoff, an oceanographer and meteorologist in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. “It’s a local term for the highest high tides of the year in a location. And when it impacts you, that’s when they call it a king tide.”

King tides are happening more often

King tides typically occur when the sun, moon and Earth are nearly aligned because their gravitational pull adds together. This raises water levels and produces the greatest tidal effects of the year. This can happen on both coasts around the same time because the tides are responding to the same alignment and proximity of the moon and sun. In 2026, El Niño caused higher baseline water levels on both coasts, Bogdanoff said.

The highest high tides happen during full moons and new moons and seasonal cycles that can raise or lower sea levels, he added.

Historically, many coastal areas saw king tides once or twice a year, but some places are experiencing them more often than that as sea levels rise.

King tides can cause floods in coastal communities

Because king tides bring unusually high water levels, they can cause local tidal flooding. Strong winds and storms can make that flooding worse.

Bogdanoff said the stormwater systems don’t function normally when ocean water is higher than the levels they were designed for.

Climate change is raising risks

Climate change is driving and accelerating sea level rise. Glaciers and ice sheets are melting and the sea’s waters are expanding as they warm. As this happens, flooding from king tides is becoming more frequent and it’s increasingly disrupting life along the coasts.

Four California locations recorded their all-time highest observed water levels in late October, and near-record king tides flooded some low-lying communities there as Thanksgiving travel ramped up.

“El Niño is natural, the sea level rise we’re seeing now isn’t,” Bogdanoff said. “The flooding we’re seeing with these king tides is a preview of what’s to come in the 2030s and beyond.”

In 2011, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said sea level rise will make current king tides become the future’s everyday tides.

Coastal areas prepare for king tides

Bogdanoff said coastal communities can do stormwater assessments and adaptation plans that take into account future projections for sea level rise, like his home state is doing with its Resilient Florida Program. Bogdanoff is principal scientist and co-founder of Brizaga, an engineering and consulting firm that helps communities plan for flooding and sea level rise.

Next steps could include raising roads, figuring out better ways to protect the coastlines, finding more green space that absorbs water and building bigger stormwater systems that rely more on pumps than gravity to drain the water quicker — projects that will take time, he added.

“In some communities it’s a much bigger conversation about what the future looks like,” he said. “We don’t have to fix everything at once. We just need to make sure the next decision is a little smarter than the last one.”

title: Ineos Moving Production to America, Sells French Factory to China's BYD
description:

However, this has required that the automaker sell off its main production facility in France.
It fills a similar niche as the Toyota Land Cruiser 70 Series, which has been in continuous production since roughly 1984.
The big difference is that the Ineos Grenadier is a wholly unique model that was inspired by the beloved British SUV and is actually available on our market.
Since Ineos does a significant amount of business inside North America, it makes sense to relocate to the United States to help avoid tariffs.
text:
Ineos has expressed its intention of building the Grenadier SUV and Quartermaster pickup variant within the United States as soon as possible. However, this has required that the automaker sell off its main production facility in France.

On the surface, this announcement seems like a good deal for the brand. Ineos has been building the Grenadier to effectively cater to the kind of people who want mechanically simple vehicles with serious off-road potential and traditional controls. The model is basically an homage to the classic Land Rover Defender that was built from 1990-2016, as well as the Land Rover 90 and 110 models that preceded it.

It fills a similar niche as the Toyota Land Cruiser 70 Series, which has been in continuous production since roughly 1984. The big difference is that the Ineos Grenadier is a wholly unique model that was inspired by the beloved British SUV and is actually available on our market.

Since Ineos does a significant amount of business inside North America, it makes sense to relocate to the United States to help avoid tariffs. Some of the reasons we don’t get the Land Cruiser 70 Series is because it’s based on an older model that would likely have trouble passing the modern U.S. safety and emissions regulations.

The Toyota would also be subject to the current tariffs, with pickup variants falling prey to the dreaded chicken tax that adds 25 percent. The classic Land Rover would likewise steal sales from other Toyota models. Plenty of Tacoma or 4Runner buyers would gladly pivot to the 70 Series were it ever made available here.

Ineos plans on getting around all of the above by simply building its vehicles stateside. It also doesn’t have to worry about the Grenadier or Quartermaster stealing sales from other models.

Despite promoting itself as a British company that only exists because of its affinity for iconic vehicles originating from the United Kingdom, Ineos does the brunt of its business on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean and has its main production facility based in Hambach, France.

That facility was a former Mercedes-Benz site, responsible for the Smart ForTwo, and will reportedly be sold to China’s BYD and is assumed to be repurposed to build all-electric vehicles sold on the European market.

The big question is what will happen in the interim period. Ineos needs a place to build its vehicles and is reportedly targeting U.S. production for 2028. That almost assuredly means that it will be buying a preexisting facility that it can retool, rather than building something from the ground up. We’re assuming Ineos won’t be handing over the keys to BYD until after it has things up and running in the United States, unless it’s fine with an extended period of not selling anything.

Details on the arrangement haven’t yet been finalized. We haven’t heard anything on where Ineos wants to set up shop in the United States, nor when the Chinese brand expects to move into France. But the deal with BYD sounds like it’s been solidified and the British company has certainly already been browsing American real estate.

This is a massive undertaking for what is effectively a very small automaker. Ineos has only sold about 35,000 vehicles since commencing production three years ago. But volumes have been increasing and the brand estimates that about 70 percent of those sales went to people living in North America.

That alone probably makes moving to the U.S. a foregone conclusion. Continuing to eat the cost of international shipping and regional tariffs makes little sense when you can just relocate to your core market. Ineos has suggested that the scheme will also help keep prices on the Grenadier and Quartermaster lower — which presently start around $73,000 and $84,000, respectively.

Assuming Ineos could bring those figures down by a few thousand dollars, it’s possible that the Grenadier could see more mass appeal. But they are likely to remain niche products. Due to boasting extremely traditional architecture, these models lack most modern convenience features and tend to drive like classic off-road vehicles.

That said, buyers' growing disdain for connectivity features and electronic gatekeeping could play into Ineos’ hands. Despite your author’s belief that modern pickups and SUVs have received some of the most useful tech features in recent years, that’s still accompanied by plenty of invasive boatware nobody really wants.

The Grenadier simply existing as an alternative to that, while still offering serious off-road performance reliant on mechanical hardware, could result in a sales boom for the brand. Ineos products don’t even come with an internal modem that can do more than send out an emergency signal, requiring customers to pair vehicles to their phone if they want to use the internet. There are no over-the-air updates, telemetry data, or in-car apps to speak of — which is something Ineos seems rather proud of.

Expect more information about the company’s relocation plans as they surface.

text:
NYLCV and a group of two dozen environmental, labor, clean energy, and community organizations are urging Governor Kathy Hochul to deploy previously committed Sustainable Future Program funds and invest another $3 billion dollars in the FY28 budget.

In a letter sent last week, the groups thanked the governor for championing the $1 billion SFP in the FY27 State Budget and applauded her Climate Week announcement to allocate that funding to key areas of the state’s climate plan to help make the energy cleaner and more affordable for all New Yorkers — from no-cost energy efficiency upgrades for low- to moderate-income households, to union job-creating thermal energy networks, to cleaner, healthier schools.

These investments are vital and come at a moment that calls for bold action on energy security and affordability, a healthier environment, and climate change mitigation. Advancing these projects and programs quickly is critical for delivering cleaner air, union jobs, improved public health, energy bill savings, stronger communities, and investments in disadvantaged communities for New Yorkers.

The Sustainable Future Program allocations in the FY 2026 and FY 2027 budgets are the largest climate investments in New York’s history. With this precedent set, the geopolitical energy landscape and the rapidly worsening climate crisis demand that we accelerate our commitment to clean energy and clean air investments that deliver immediate and long-term health, affordability, job, and economic benefits to New Yorkers.

“We urge you to deploy the past years’ funding commitments as quickly as possible and double down on these commitments by including a $3 billion allocation for the Sustainable Future Program in your FY 2028 Executive Budget as the state works towards sustained funding with labor standards for these projects,” the letter stated.

The groups also requested that the funding be directed through the Climate Action Fund, with all funding subject to the same public reporting requirements included in the Clean Water, Clean Air and Green Jobs Environmental Bond Act.

The Sustainable Future Program is a critical down payment for the kinds of investments that can be scaled and sustained through the Clean Air Initiative — New York’s emerging cap-and-invest program — once it is operational. The Clean Air Initiative could initially generate $3 billion each year from polluters, and this number should grow over time.

This program would provide urgently needed funding to directly support household energy affordability — for example, through electricity bill credits — and scale programs like those funded by the SFP that would help New Yorkers access energy efficiency, clean energy upgrades, and clean, affordable transportation, further driving down household energy costs across the state.

New York has laid the groundwork for a cleaner, healthier, and more affordable energy future. Now is the time to build on that progress by getting committed dollars out the door, scaling up investments in the coming budget, and establishing an ongoing source of funding that will deliver benefits to New Yorkers for generations to come.

text:
On November 19, 2026, the U.S. Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) as a substitute amendment to H.R. 2347. BAAJA would amend several federal statutes that govern the permitting of infrastructure, energy, and development projects, including the Clean Water Act (CWA), 33 U.S.C. § 1251 et seq.; the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), 42 U.S.C. § 4321 et seq.; the Endangered Species Act (ESA), 16 U.S.C. § 1531 et seq.; and the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), 54 U.S.C. § 300101 et seq. BAAJA would also impose new agency deadlines and limit how and when project approvals may be challenged in court. BAAJA is not yet law; the House must still act on the Senate’s version, which it could amend further, and the President must sign the final bill to become law.

BAAJA’s Key Elements

Section 401 water quality certification would be subject to a clear and convincing evidence standard and firm deadlines.

An applicant for a federal permit or license for an activity that would result in a discharge into “waters of the United States” (WOTUS), such as a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) dredge-and-fill permit under CWA § 404, 33 U.S.C. § 1344, must first obtain under CWA § 401, 33 U.S.C. § 1341, a certification that the discharge will comply with water quality requirements from the “certifying authority,” which BAAJA would define as the state or interstate agency to which the application is submitted (including a tribe treated as a state under 40 C.F.R. § 131.8) or, where none has authority, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). A denial generally prevents the federal permit from being issued. Under BAAJA, review would be limited to water quality requirements, and the certifying authority could deny certification only if it determines, by clear and convincing evidence, that no modification or reasonable condition would allow the project to comply, or that the application remains incomplete after the applicant has had a reasonable opportunity to supply missing materials. Each condition would have to meet the same standard and be the least burdensome necessary to ensure compliance with water quality requirements. If a denial or condition is litigated, the certifying authority, rather than the applicant, would bear that burden of proof. The federal licensing or permitting agency, in consultation with the certifying authority, would set a reasonable period for final action on the application (grant, grant with conditions, deny, or waive) of no more than one year from receipt (nine months for direct point source discharges from Natural Gas Act § 7 pipelines and bulk-power system transmission projects). If the certifying authority fails to act within that period, certification would be waived unless the applicant requests, and the certifying authority agrees in writing to, an extension.

CWA § 402 NPDES permits could last up to ten years, and WOTUS rules would be reviewed directly in the court of appeals with jurisdiction.

Pursuant to CWA § 301, a facility that discharges pollutants from a point source (such as a pipe or outfall) into WOTUS generally must obtain a CWA § 402 National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit. NPDES permits have a maximum five-year term; BAAJA would extend that maximum term to ten years. BAAJA would also require EPA to adopt water quality criteria through notice-and-comment rulemaking and would send challenges to those criteria, and to EPA rules defining WOTUS, directly to the federal court of appeals with jurisdiction. BAAJA would not itself change the WOTUS definition, which has been the subject of varying and confusing rulemakings and litigation for decades.

Section 404 permits would provide longer and more secure coverage.

CWA § 404 requires a USACE permit to discharge dredged or fill material into WOTUS, including many wetlands and streams. Smaller scale impacts often associated with certain designated development or infrastructure projects and activities may proceed under general permits, including nationwide permits (NWPs), rather than individual permits. BAAJA would extend Section 404 general permit terms from five to ten years, deem discharges into less than two acres as having only minimal effects, and require USACE to maintain NWPs 12, 14, 27, 43, 57, and 58 for discharges into less than two acres per project. For applications submitted after enactment, EPA could exercise its Section 404(c) “veto” authority to prohibit or restrict a dredge spoils disposal site only between submission of a complete application and permit issuance, foreclosing such veto after permit issuance.

Section 404 challenges would be subject to a 150-day deadline and limited remedies.

Challenges to Section 404 permits and general-permit verifications generally would have to be filed within 150 days. Where a draft permit is published in the Federal Register with a comment period of at least 30 days occurring after enactment, only parties that raised the issue in sufficiently detailed comments on the proposed permit could sue. That limitation would not apply to NWP coverage determinations that are not subject to such a public-comment period, but the 150-day deadline would still apply. A court could not vacate, enjoin, or otherwise limit a permit or verified activity unless the permitted activity would present an imminent and substantial danger to human health or the environment for which no other equitable remedy is available.

NEPA would be confirmed as procedural and subject to firm review deadlines

NEPA requires federal agencies to evaluate the environmental effects of major federal actions, including many permits, through an environmental assessment (EA) or a more detailed environmental impact statement (EIS). BAAJA would provide that NEPA establishes a procedure and does not mandate any particular outcome. At a project sponsor’s request, agencies would have to consider relying on existing federal, state, or tribal analyses, and no NEPA document would be required where the lead agency determines that a state or tribal review, or compliance with another federal law, serves a similar function. Lead agencies would have one year to complete an EA and two years to complete an EIS. After an EIS is published, the lead agency would have 45 days to issue a record of decision, and other agencies would have 90 to 120 days to act on remaining approvals.

NEPA challenges would be subject to a 150-day deadline, direct appellate review, and limited remedies.

NEPA claims generally would have to be filed within 150 days by parties that submitted sufficiently detailed comments on the issue (where the comment period occurs after enactment), and most would proceed directly in the federal court of appeals for the circuit where the project is located. If a court finds a violation, it generally could only remand the approval for correction within 180 days, and the project could proceed during remand. Preliminary injunctions would be available only in limited circumstances and only for violations of laws other than NEPA and the NHPA.

ESA Section 7 consultation would be shorter and aligned with NEPA.

A federal agency that permits, funds, or carries out an action that may affect a threatened or endangered species must consult with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service or the National Marine Fisheries Service, a process that concludes with a biological opinion. BAAJA would shorten formal consultation from 90 to 60 days and allow applicants to seek judicial relief if an extension would exceed 145 days without a written statement to the applicant or the applicant’s consent. Where an EA or EIS is required, BAAJA would generally require consultation to be completed by the NEPA completion deadline for that document—that is, by the date the EA is completed and made public or, for an EIS, the date the final EIS is published. It would also exempt certain transportation projects in operational rights-of-way, and challenges to biological opinions generally would have to be filed in the D.C. Circuit within 150 days after the opinion is made public.

NHPA Section 106 review would be narrower and tied to the NEPA schedule.

Section 106 requires federal agencies to consider the effects of their permits, funding, and actions on historic properties and resources. BAAJA would exclude several categories of activities from review, including certain financial-assistance-only projects and minor or routine repair and maintenance, and would limit review to historic properties within the area of potential effects identified by the permitting agency. For projects requiring an EA or EIS, consultation would have to begin when NEPA review begins and would generally have to be completed when the EA is completed and made public or the final EIS is published. As under NEPA, a court finding a violation generally could only remand the matter for correction within 180 days. Federal agencies would remain obligated under the Section 106 process to consult with tribes as to the potential impacts on historic resources.

Do Not Forget About State/Local Programs

Regulated parties should keep in mind that most states, and some regional and local jurisdictions, administer the CWA § 402 NPDES program under EPA authorization. These programs must be at least as stringent as the federal program, and the CWA and NPDES regulations allow them to be more stringent. In addition, certain states (like Virginia) have their own state-law permitting programs for impacts to surface waters, including wetlands, that overlap with or are more stringent than the USACE and EPA § 404 program, or that reach waters beyond WOTUS. So, while BAAJA may provide welcome relief at the federal level, state programs may not necessarily follow suit. Regulated parties should therefore track applicable state permitting and water quality standards programs regardless of BAAJA and, where needed, be prepared to pursue a parallel state permitting track for the same activity, with potentially different procedures and outcomes.

Looking Forward

If enacted as currently passed by the Senate, BAAJA would require each federal agency to revise its NEPA regulations and procedures within 180 days, and, beginning December 31, 2027, a certifying authority that has not adopted rules specifying additional Section 401 application materials would have to treat an application as complete if it contains the basic information BAAJA specifies. BAAJA could shorten permitting timelines and reduce litigation risk for many projects, but, because the final legislation may differ, developers, utilities, and other permittees should monitor its fate closely and consult legal counsel regarding how it may affect their pending or planned projects.

text:
By Alton Wallace | The Center Square

Federal energy regulators report the U.S. electric grid enters the 2026-27 winter season with more power generation than last year, and surging data center demand leaves a smaller margin for error increasing the risk of outages during periods of extreme cold.

In its annual winter assessment, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission reported that the addition of 75 gigawatts of net new power generation capacity in the last year along with the deferred retirements of 15 aging coal-fired plants should ensure enough energy is available to meet normal electricity demand.

Nationwide winter peak electricity demand is forecast to be 2.6% higher than last year, according to the assessment. A strong El Niño weather pattern, however, could cause sudden swings in temperatures and temporary regional fuel shortages.

The North American Electric Reliability Corp., authorized by the commission to enforce grid reliability standards, issued a companion report Nov. 18 warning that pipelines carrying natural gas to power plants could be strained during periods of intense cold. Natural gas deliveries to residential consumers receive priority on interstate pipelines ahead of power generation plants, the regulator noted in the report.

“Regionally constrained natural gas infrastructure limits available fuel for generators during cold snaps, risking outages when generators lack alternate fuels,” said Mark Olson, the grid watchdog group’s manager of reliability assessments. “For example, gas-fired generators in the Pacific Northwest are predominantly single-fuel, exposing them to more fuel risk during peak demand periods.”

While the commission anticipates potential pipeline constraints during hard freezes, record-high domestic natural gas production and above-average storage levels are forecast to keep prices lower than last winter across nearly every region.

Natural gas futures for the winter at Louisiana’s Henry Hub – the nation’s pricing benchmark – traded at $3.19 per million British thermal units on Nov. 10, down 42% from last winter’s settled price of $5.52, commission staff noted in the report.

Marc Brown, vice president of state affairs for the Consumer Energy Alliance, a Houston-based advocacy group, told The Center Square that low winter gas prices mask other problems.

“While lower natural gas prices will bring much-needed relief, cheaper fuel this winter due to milder weather doesn’t fix the underlying problems customers will continue to face,” Brown said. “Customers deserve an energy system that supports economic growth and the electricity demand that comes with it, not one that relies on mild weather and emergency band-aids to get through the winter.”

Of 16 coal-fired power plants scheduled for retirement this year, 15 will remain operating that have total generating capacity of about 6,400 megawatts, according to U.S. Energy Information Administration data verified by The Center Square. Seven of those coal-fired generation units remain operating under emergency orders issued by the U.S. Department of Energy, while regional utilities voluntarily postponed the retirement of seven others.

“New data centers draw power around the clock, including on the coldest mornings when millions of families turn up the heat,” Michelle Bloodworth, president and chief executive officer of America’s Power, a trade group representing the coal-fired power industry, wrote in an email to The Center Square. “That surge in heating demand can leave gas-fired power plants short of fuel just as electricity demand peaks. Coal plants store fuel on site and can keep generating through a prolonged cold snap.”

Regulators warned, however, that El Niño’s warmer average temperatures in the nation’s northern climates and more sudden, severe storms could quickly deplete regional supplies of natural gas and backup fuel oil. In New England, distillate fuel-oil inventories entered the winter heating season at 2.5 million barrels – 46% below the five-year average, according to U.S. Energy Information Administration data.

“El Niño shifts winter storm tracks and increases the likelihood of polar vortex outbreaks in the Central and Eastern United States, along with severe storms and flooding across the South,” Brady Tyra of the commission’s Office of Electric Reliability told commissioners during a presentation last Thursday.

The Southeast, New England, Midwest, and the Plains face increased risk of supply shortfalls during severe cold snaps this winter, while drought across the Intermountain West has reduced hydroelectric production at major dams along the Colorado River, according to the report.

description:

I would like to see things move faster just as you’re vividly suggesting that this bill is a bill that’s finely crafted for transmission, for pipelines that will predominantly serve data centers and LNG.
And, you know, like today you have Mike Levin, Representative Levin and Representative Kasten recommitting to getting the Energy Bill Relief Act move forward.
