text:
You can also add the show’s RSS feed to your podcast app to follow us directly.

Robinson Meyer:

Hello, it’s Wednesday, November 25, and the House of Representatives is due to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, also known as the Permitting Reform Bill. I think it’s fair to say it’s divided climate, clean energy folks, and the broader Democratic coalition more than any other policy or decision I can think of. A few weeks ago, we had on Lena Moffitt and Pete Wyckoff from Evergreen Action to discuss why that relatively new climate and clean energy focused organization was supporting the bill, why they were one of the few environmental groups that was not just, opposing it or sitting on the sidelines, but affirmatively saying, yes, it should pass. It was a great conversation. But of course, you can’t just talk to the supporters. You have to talk to the opponents as well. And so for this show, I wanted to get one of the most respected opponents of them all. My guest today is Abbie Dillen. She’s an environmental lawyer and the president of Earthjustice, the world’s largest nonprofit environmental law firm. She’s been at Earthjustice since 2000, where she was previously vice president of litigation for climate and energy and involved in that organization’s work to shut down coal plants. We had a great conversation. It is very long, as you can tell from the runtime. We talked about the part of the bill that Abby is most worried about, where she stands now on the National Environmental Policy Act, how we got here politically, and where the climate movement goes from here. I’m Robinson Meyer, the founding executive editor of Heatmap News, and all that more. It’s all coming up on this special episode of Shift Key.

Robinson Meyer:

Abbie Dillen, welcome to ShiftKey.

Abbie Dillen:

Thank you. I’m glad to be here.

Robinson Meyer:

It’s great to have you. I mean, we’ve talked in the past, but it’s so great to have you here, and I appreciate you coming on. I mean, first of all, what a few months it has been, and we have all been very busy working on or around this bill. And so we had evergreen action on ShiftKey a few weeks ago, and they are endorsing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which I’m interested to hear what your pronunciation for the initials are, because at this point, I feel like I’ve heard every variation. And so I started off that conversation by asking them, why are you supporting this bill?

Robinson Meyer:

So let me now start off this conversation with you by asking you, Abbie, why is Earthjustice opposing the bipartisan permitting bill that’s just passed the Senate and is now facing a vote in the House?

Abbie Dillen:

Well, I like how you got me to introduce my pronunciation of the acronym. It’s gone through some iterations, but I’ve landed at Baja. So as you know, Earthjustice has this gigantic clean energy program, and we have made our biggest bet on deploying clean energy. And so I can’t help but start with the real sentiment that this is the first time we’ve ever seen a true transmission package that’s well-designed to unleash clean energy, pass any House of Congress. So that’s a big deal. And I want to make clear that we don’t oppose everything about this bill. The red line for me and for Earthjustice is that it gives this president so much more power over the next two years to do his worst. And by that, I mean corrupt deals that he could monetize and projects that will be inordinately harmful. And while much of the debate about Baja is about what it does in the sphere of energy regulation, these provisions around project certainty, and I know we’ll get more into the details, are about every kind of thing that a developer could do that requires some kind of federal authorization. And as thrilled as I am, and we are about these election results and all the possibilities that they unleash, we also know that these are going to be two extraordinarily scary years. This president doesn’t obey the law, and his White House is making it clear that they want to find all the ways they can to stretch the law and to insulate themselves from court review. And for all of the kind of issues that we work on, this bill gives them that. And then in addition, does things to our bedrock environmental laws within the energy sphere, which is a big enough scope all by itself, but again, across the board. And so as much as I’ve spent my professional career working on climate, we know that there are other dials on the dashboard blinking red, whether it’s water or a crisis for species. And this bill takes away so many protections that we desperately need and that I think would be very difficult politically to ever win back in the foreseeable future.

Robinson Meyer:

I want to get one more philosophical kind of high-level view from you, which is one argument that supporters of the bill have made, and that I think I find to be true, is that, the status quo for energy permitting is very bad. And under the status quo, it is already much easier to build fossil fuels than it is to build clean. And we can get into the various ramifications of this. But I just want to get your sense at a high level. Do you think today’s permitting system helps or hurts clean energy more than it does fossil?

Abbie Dillen:

Here’s how I frame that for myself. We need transmission to get clean energy online at the scale that’s needed to decarbonize everything. So we have to have an expanded grid. We need more transmission and we need different rules about who has access to it. So that’s, I think, uncontroversial and non-negotiable. And then the question is, are we building enough transmission? Are we building that fast enough? Are we reforming our energy regulatory system fast enough? No, on all three. And so what Earthjustice has been focusing on for the last several years is creating more understanding of what transformative regulation of the transmission system could be. You just need to get over all of the vetoes that are currently in the system and have better planning,

Abbie Dillen:

Better siting, with a federal backstop, and also answer the question of who’s going to pay for all this expensive new infrastructure. That’s what this bill does. And I think it’s uncontroversial that, or at least I think it is, that it would help us unleash the transmission that we absolutely need. So in that regard, the status quo is failing and Baja would improve it very much. For permitting in general and building everything. I’d like to say maybe two points. One is just this basic point that we could make the status quo worse. And I think over the next two years, taking down the law’s eliminating effective remedies against this administration and creating new powers, we would live to regret that. And I think we would regret it very quickly. I think there’s a larger question. And I mean, you’re the one who gets to ask the questions, but I’ll throw this out there because I’m interested in how you think about this. I take the central and I think very important point of the book Abundance and the best way that that idea is being interpreted as government needs to deliver for people if we have laws in process that give too many vetoes from litigants and who have their own specific interests. And we hamstring government and the kind of building that we need, that’s a problem. And you know, I have some objections too where people take that argument, but just stipulate it.

Robinson Meyer:

And we’re going to talk about them. We’re going to talk about them too.

Abbie Dillen:

But just stipulating that that’s right. This bill overarchingly does something very profound, which is shift the power to developers to decide what they want to build, how they want to build it, on what enforceable timelines, so that the government is becoming more of a concierge for building everything. And I worry very much that that’s an overcorrection to put the most powerful industries in the country in charge of what we build, because they’re not driven by a balance between the private and public interest. They’re driven by a profit motive. And that’s a really big shift to make, dropping a bill, what was it, September 30th, that even... The colleagues of the four drafters in the Senate hadn’t seen. And so if we’re going to make that kind of tilt to big industry, and you don’t take that kind of thing back, not with the money and politics that we live with, we ought to have some more clear debate about what the consequences are.

Robinson Meyer:

So Baja, Baja, Beja, I’m increasingly using Beja because it sounds like the Steely Dan album. So let’s say that broadly it is a law with three sections that has the transmission title, which does a bunch of things, some of which we’ve talked about. It has the kind of environmental review title or the section, and it has the project certainty title. And the Project Certainty title, the way that it’s described or the Project Certainty policies, the way they’re described. Is that they would keep a president, any future president, from reversing decisions or, kind of making politicized decisions about energy permitting in a way that has characterized how the Trump administration has made political decisions about especially wind energy over the past two years. It is an attempt by the legislators, obviously I think it’s not a successful attempt, but it is an attempt by the legislators, to end what has kind of become a tit-for-tat in energy, where there are some projects that Democrats want to block. They are fossil fuels and Democrats have substantive, you know, scientific reasons to block these projects. We can debate whether it’s the best political strategy, but that has resulted in a situation now where Donald Trump comes in or a future Republican president comes in and says, actually, all these projects that you want to build, like block, block, block, block, block, we’re going to pull permits from them. We’re going to find new federal nexuses for permits so that we can deny, for instance, onshore wind permits. This has created a very congested kind of space where developers don’t feel like they have any certainty in the projects that they’ve gotten. That even were previously permitted. Certainly, I would say wind developers do not feel like this today. They came into the Trump administration, and then they had a lot of projects they thought they were going to get built, and they’re not getting built right now. This was kind of one of Senator Whitehouse’s big reasons for getting this bill done, is that he wanted to end this tit-for-tat war. He wanted developers of clean energy to feel secure in the permits they had gotten. Other than data centers, which I want to get to, it’s become one of the most controversial aspects of the bill, and certainly kind of the most high-level controversial aspect of the bill. Where did these noble intentions go awry in your mind? And what concerns you about these provisions? And is there some part of the summary I just gave that you think is incorrect?

Abbie Dillen:

Look, I think the intentions were noble, certainly coming from Senator Whitehouse. And he had a red line, which was, we can’t do this deal if we can’t get this president to relent and release these hostage wind projects. And that still hasn’t happened. I mean, there’s a straightforward way to do that, which is name the projects and require that they be released.

Robinson Meyer:

Yeah, there’s really two different things happening here and they get bundled together. One of them is this kind of, you know, tacit deal they seem to have with the president that the president may have already gone back on and which the bill sponsors have basically been like, well, we’d like to see this get done. But if it doesn’t get done, we think the bill’s worth it. And then there’s the policy, which is, and the situation that has happened to these wind projects can never happen to another project again.

Abbie Dillen:

So the intent is never again, never shall a president do this again. One quibble I had with your layout, which is, I just don’t think it’s a tit for tat. There’s... People cite Keystone, people cite an LNG pause, but what President Trump has done around a whole sector of projects, I don’t think we’ve seen anything like it before. And so I understand the desire to make sure that it never happens again, because the way that I think of market signals and the kind of certainty that will draw investors to big projects, it’s just making sure that these big projects can get done. So if you were living in a world without Trump and his arbitrary and lawless persecution of certain kinds of projects, it would be enough to have a reliable policy path to, for example, get transmission done. And I think this kind of is evidence why it’s so hard to get this done when we have the kind of president we do, because this policy won’t work in a backward facing way. It won’t relieve these projects that have gotten stuck. And in terms of a forward looking way, I don’t think it gives developers anything faster to get their wind projects back up and running than the lawsuits that are already underway.

And so the question is, what does it do? And it gives this president the ability to give any developer, you want to do the boundary waters, you want to do a whole big new petrochemical facility in Cancer Alley, you want to privatize water in the Mojave Desert, like the Cadiz project that we were able to defeat in the first Trump administration, go for it. And what’s different this time around is that every federal authorization that you need from us to do that project and the permit as a whole will be immune from change, improvements, conditions, much less revocation in the next administration. So we can move fast. We can move in ways that may well be unlawful. And, you know, even if there’s ongoing litigation, say we sue over permits for the boundary waters, those lawsuits take a long time.

And it may well be that the mining goes forward during the pendency of that litigation. The way it usually works is an incoming president who probably would make, particularly in the upper Midwest, boundary waters an important issue. I would never do this. I would fix it. I would fix it on day one. That can no longer happen. to freeze in time the policies of this president, so damaging. Why would we do that, particularly after this election, where I think we can say one through line is we reject this president? And for a next president, I’m not sure that what we want is for any president to be able to freeze things in time and become less accountable to voters.

Robinson Meyer:

Why wouldn’t a lawsuit under this law that you bring against, say, the Boundary Waters or another project like you just stated, stop work on the project now? In an ongoing way that would then make it unfixable in a future administration or why? What are the tools that work today that will not work under Baja, as you describe? Yeah.

Abbie Dillen:

And and so I may talk a little bit about how this these certainty provisions also interact with other provisions in the bill, which weaken laws and diminish access to effective legal remedies. So. Much of this bill is meant to give developers claims and access to the courts and extraordinary remedies and prevent anyone else from suing in the venue of choice, from bringing claims under the laws as they stand, or securing remedies. So I just want to note that overarchingly, the intent of this bill is to make public interest litigation more difficult, and it does that. So you’re already kind of climbing a different hill. And let me say, Earthjustice, we win a lot of our cases because we choose ones where we think we’re right on the law and where the equity is like that a generalist judge would agree that we should be entitled to a remedy. We do very well, but it is still, in those cases, very, very, very difficult to get any court to enjoin the president of the United States or a federal agency. So you are already climbing a significant hill.

And these litigations tend to play out over years, not months. And there’s an appellate process, and increasingly, developers or the federal government can go straight up to the Supreme Court. So you’re going up and down the courts in very complex litigations. Even assuming that you are correct on the merits, you cannot assume that you will get an injunction. Now, if one of your claims is under the National Environmental Policy Act or under the National Historic Preservation Act, you can no longer get an injunction no matter what kind of project it is. And you cannot, the only remedy available is remand, sorry, without vacatur, so that the order will stand, the project can go forward. And then if you have a Clean Water Act violation, a remedy under the Clean Water Act has gotten much, much more difficult to secure. So assume we’re in a situation where it’s six months into the Trump administration, We’re back at the Boundary Waters. The mine has been approved. And we run into court and the court says, we don’t think you’ve proven enough harm immediately. We’re just going to let this keep going, keep going, keep going. And by the time there’s a new president, I think a sane Republican, as much as a Democrat, might say, I’d prefer not to have this unbelievably important place mined. In the current situation, they’d be able to review the filings and change their position and say, you know what, we think this was hastily granted. We have problems with the underlying analysis. We think that the best science wasn’t considered. And we have some new information about the aquifer, for example. I mean, these are all hypotheticals. As the law stands today, there would be no question that the president and his administration or her administration could do that. Under Baja, the mining developer could sue and say, no, these are permits. We have investment-backed expectations, President of the United States. You cannot go back on these authorizations that we’ve received from Trump. And in fact, if you want to try us in litigation, you could be subject to paying us enormous amount of the whole value of this project. So then the government has to think, are we willing to take that risk? And how many times are we willing to take that risk? If we’re relying on earth justice or groups like ours to be holding the line, I mean, we’re already at about 200 percent of the amount of litigation that we’re capable of doing against the federal government. Like, that’s no way to craft policy. You want to unleash the elected officials to be able to do a reasonable and prudent thing.

There are so many poison pills in this bill as it stands that are correctly poisonous. They’re intolerable. We could do better than this. That’s my point. If your point is someone will always have a problem with it, I’m sure that’s the case. I’m sure that’s the case.

Robinson Meyer:

My point is it divides the Democratic coalition in a way that would make it, rapidly have it fall out of consideration next year. And it requires a lot of folks in Congress to suddenly take positions that they have opposed in the past.

Abbie Dillen:

What do you think are the provisions that would have to be part of this that would inherently make it impossible to keep Democrats together, at least in numbers that you couldn’t compensate for?

Robinson Meyer:

I think transmission is extremely divisive. I think transmissions would prove to be divisive again.

Abbie Dillen:

More so on the Republican side.

Robinson Meyer:

But I think it would be as soon as Democrats are in charge of it, this is a giveaway to the big tech. They need more energy. They’re going to eminent domain property through the back of your land, through the back of your house to feed data centers. And what we’ve seen on this bill is that even with the data with the ratepayer protection provisions, it’s like people see those as bad, too, because they help solve the problem. The data centers need electricity.

Abbie Dillen:

I’m not sure I’m following because I didn’t hear a single Democrat in the Senate base their opposition or concerns on the transmission provisions. Of course, there were Hawley and Co. Who had theirs on the Republican side, and that is a dynamic. And then there’s, of course, the Duke and Southern Company issue, which I think watered down this package. But on the Democratic side, I didn’t see that in the Senate. And I do think there’s a danger. I think there’s a danger of ramming through a bill that is so harmful in so many ways, because right now you and I both know this. You cover it exceptionally well on Heatmap. There is a well-funded, organized effort to try to brand clean energy as a problem.

Robinson Meyer:

Yes, totally. I agree.

Abbie Dillen:

And so we don’t want clean energy to have the taint of a bill that’s doing so many unpopular things. Why not position it in a bill that is not so unpopular with so many people?

Robinson Meyer:

But I think that that is going to be the issue of bringing it up in a next Congress.

Abbie Dillen:

So just jam it through now, notwithstanding all of the problems.

Robinson Meyer:

That it creates? No, but I think that that is what is driving some of the kind of bird in the hand thinking here. And I think that the... And perhaps you’re right on NEPA. Maybe NEPA is a solved problem, so to speak. I guess I would say, I think the six-year statute of limitations requires a statutory remedy. And I would say what I’ve seen. Well, what I’ve seen from the Democrats who are about to lead negotiations on this, including Representative Huffman, who would lead negotiations in a future Congress, are a sense that only understaffed agencies and inadequate reviews are the problems, that cause NEPA to hamstring major federal initiatives. I don’t agree with that. And I think people who believe that, for instance, there needs to be a statutory remedy on NEPA, who believe the next Democratic president should be, more empowered to build infrastructure of the type that I think we both think the country needs, look at kind of the set the lineup of principles and their what they’ve said historically and go.

Abbie Dillen:

So I disagree. I disagree. I mean, I’ve spent a lot of time with the players on the Democrat side. And I think there is a seriousness about this that the situation warrants. And I think part of what we’re dealing with is the sense that this is a gigantic overhaul. Can we please think about the unintended consequences of this? And so I understand that the political calculus is difficult. It’s difficult to do anything. That’s not through reconciliation with 51 people. Anything durable is difficult. I get it. But when we look at, I mean, you and I have both lived through the last two years. Everything I imagined when I read Project 2025, I was like, they can’t really do that. They’re doing it. They’re doing it. And so what I’m asking you to hear me on today. Can we not do something that hasn’t been thought through, I think that has predictable consequences, however unintended, of empowering someone who will abuse this extra power and I think leave all of us much worse off?

This conversation becomes so abstract. But what I’m hearing from clients, whether it’s, you know, in the Gulf South or Appalachia is, oh, my goodness, the wave of new development that’s coming. Or we work on deep seabed mining. How many leases could you give out? The president just sold two, even though a court had already found the ESA analysis was invalid. That’s what we’re going to have to be dealing with. And as someone who’s been dealing with it for the last two years, I want you to hear me that the next two will be worse. The next two will be worse because there’s no prospect of an election to restrain anyone. It makes a difference that someone like Stephen Miller is the chief of staff. I just think, you know, Mike Levin said this well in his remarks today, and I think it captured it. He says there’s real promise on costs and clean energy, but taking the current deal would mean giving up protections we may never win back in exchange for gains that are not guaranteed. And when you add that dimension to who is president now, that’s why I am where I am.

Robinson Meyer:

Isn’t the challenge here that we never know who will be president in the future and you could roll back? I mean, you do it in a year and oopsie daisy, you have empowered people. A president, you know, Tucker Carlson or someone else.

Abbie Dillen:

Even a president Vance.

Robinson Meyer:

Right. And so it just seems to me that as long as the fear, is of what a future president could do, we’re never going to allow what needs to happen on the Democratic side or on the decarbonization side because there will always be. And in fact, Democrats will continue to govern basically at a disadvantage because Republicans won’t care. Whoever the next Republican president after Trump is will have no problem doing all the things they’ve done the first two years of this. But the next Democrat comes in, well, first they have to staff the full Department of Energy, and they have to staff all the permitting agencies, and then they have to kind of cross their T’s and dot their I’s. And what it means is that the status quo, as long as we’re scared of what a future president or a current president could do, The status quo will create speed limits that only apply to Democrats.

Abbie Dillen:

We have to bet on ourselves, but I’m talking about the project certainty provisions that allow bad things to happen now. That’s not just fear. And then either it allows bad things to continue under a Vance administration or it prevents a better president of either party from repairing the damage. So I don’t think that sort of just take the risk that on the future applies in this context, because I think it’s like a lose lose whoever the next president is.

Robinson Meyer:

But then that president gets to lock in there.

Abbie Dillen:

I guess, but they’re already locked into the Trump world. That’s a carry forward problem. And then they can’t fix the problems that they probably ran and won on. If they’re a good president and if they’re a bad president, it’s just compounds. I think these provisions were well intended, but they’re really, really problematic.

Robinson Meyer:

And so it’s really just so if you were to pick this up next year, it’s you take out that. Yeah.

Abbie Dillen:

If you want to figure out how to make developers who’ve gotten skittish about expensive projects that have run into permitting barriers, let’s do that. And if there’s something in addition, let’s just really think it through. This is the problem with very closed door negotiations. And so I feel skeptical about it getting fixed. We will continue to try. We will leave no stone unturned. But if we’re starting over in a next Congress, I think it’s very hard to do this well.

Robinson Meyer:

So I asked the Evergreen folks, what keeps you up at night about the bill? I feel like we’ve been talking about this, so I’m not going to. Let me ask you, last question. What is the outcome for this bill that you would look at it and say, you know, this was actually worth it?

Abbie Dillen:

The whole project of our work at Earthjustice for all the clients that we represent, whether it’s the 80 tribes or the many community-based groups or big national groups, is to find a way. We’ll always work and find a way. Yeah. If this bill were to pass without significant improvements for tribal sovereignty, for the president’s unleashed power, for protection of water and endangered species, I know that our job would get so much harder. And I would just have to hope that we could summon the political will to get reforms for the future, and that we could do our very best to stop the worst and surprise ourselves. I went into this administration feeling that we would lose many more cases given the Supreme Court and the composition of the courts. And so far, we’ve been winning much more than I even would have expected. And so it’s possible that we surprise ourselves. This election surprised me. I would love, okay, I would love nothing more than you forgive me for being such a contentious guest. And you bring me back two years from now. And I say you were right. This is great.

Robinson Meyer:

My view on this bill is, let me put it this way. I think that the dynamic on this bill has been that there has a lot of folks who are very skeptical of changing any aspect of the status quo. I’m not putting earth justice in this bucket. Suddenly got religion on transmission really fast after the bill text came out, and suddenly kind of got religion on some aspects of, how the existing kind of permitting status quo benefits private developers on private land in a way that it discourages public development on public land, or the federal government actually building things. And I would say as someone who I have never, i mean obviously i think my work stands for itself but i haven’t said congress should do this on this bill i have been like we need permitting reform for a long time and as someone interested in that line i think, there’s a lot of groups that are opposed to anything that looks like this, and I think a lot of lawmakers basically feel that the contours of the issue are dominated by one fringe here or one kind of side here and.

Robinson Meyer:

Means that they’re just kind of more willing to take the plunge. And I think the politics of saying, hey, these laws don’t work has been very unpleasant for, and I realize it’s now unpleasant for everyone, but has been really unpleasant for a long time. And I think that has led to the moment that we’re in now. I’m just not convinced that after Jan 1, if this bill dies, we don’t immediately go back to having the same transmission fights we were in May or June. Maybe I’m wrong.

Abbie Dillen:

I see it differently.

Robinson Meyer:

Okay. Listen, if Baja now doesn’t pass in the House, there’s got to be a transmission bill next year. So I am doubtful the politics of it will be favorable, and I expect it to be dropped relatively quickly, but I would love to be wrong.

Abbie Dillen:

Okay. Well, let’s remember.

Robinson Meyer:

Let’s end it there.

Abbie Dillen:

11/23 next year. We’ll see where we are. Exactly.

Robinson Meyer:

Thank you. Abby, thank you so much for joining us.

Abbie Dillen:

Thanks for having me, Rob.

Robinson Meyer:

And thank you for being here.

title: Federal regulator warns electric grid at risk in winter cold | National | thecentersquare.com

text:
(The Center Square) – Federal energy regulators report the U.S. electric grid enters the 2026-27 winter season with more power generation than last year, and surging data center demand leaves a smaller margin for error increasing the risk of outages during periods of extreme cold.

In its annual winter assessment, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission reported that the addition of 75 gigawatts of net new power generation capacity in the last year along with the deferred retirements of 15 aging coal-fired plants should ensure enough energy is available to meet normal electricity demand.

Nationwide winter peak electricity demand is forecast to be 2.6% higher than last year, according to the assessment. A strong El Niño weather pattern, however, could cause sudden swings in temperatures and temporary regional fuel shortages.

The North American Electric Reliability Corp., authorized by the commission to enforce grid reliability standards, issued a companion report Nov. 18 warning that pipelines carrying natural gas to power plants could be strained during periods of intense cold. Natural gas deliveries to residential consumers receive priority on interstate pipelines ahead of power generation plants, the regulator noted in the report.

“Regionally constrained natural gas infrastructure limits available fuel for generators during cold snaps, risking outages when generators lack alternate fuels,” said Mark Olson, the grid watchdog group’s manager of reliability assessments. “For example, gas-fired generators in the Pacific Northwest are predominantly single-fuel, exposing them to more fuel risk during peak demand periods.”

While the commission anticipates potential pipeline constraints during hard freezes, record-high domestic natural gas production and above-average storage levels are forecast to keep prices lower than last winter across nearly every region.

Natural gas futures for the winter at Louisiana’s Henry Hub – the nation’s pricing benchmark – traded at $3.19 per million British thermal units on Nov. 10, down 42% from last winter’s settled price of $5.52, commission staff noted in the report.

Marc Brown, vice president of state affairs for the Consumer Energy Alliance, a Houston-based advocacy group, told The Center Square that low winter gas prices mask other problems.

“While lower natural gas prices will bring much-needed relief, cheaper fuel this winter due to milder weather doesn't fix the underlying problems customers will continue to face," Brown said. "Customers deserve an energy system that supports economic growth and the electricity demand that comes with it, not one that relies on mild weather and emergency band-aids to get through the winter."

Of 16 coal-fired power plants scheduled for retirement this year, 15 will remain operating that have total generating capacity of about 6,400 megawatts, according to U.S. Energy Information Administration data verified by The Center Square. Seven of those coal-fired generation units remain operating under emergency orders issued by the U.S. Department of Energy, while regional utilities voluntarily postponed the retirement of seven others.

"New data centers draw power around the clock, including on the coldest mornings when millions of families turn up the heat," Michelle Bloodworth, president and chief executive officer of America’s Power, a trade group representing the coal-fired power industry, wrote in an email to The Center Square. "That surge in heating demand can leave gas-fired power plants short of fuel just as electricity demand peaks. Coal plants store fuel on site and can keep generating through a prolonged cold snap."

Regulators warned, however, that El Niño’s warmer average temperatures in the nation’s northern climates and more sudden, severe storms could quickly deplete regional supplies of natural gas and backup fuel oil. In New England, distillate fuel-oil inventories entered the winter heating season at 2.5 million barrels – 46% below the five-year average, according to U.S. Energy Information Administration data.

"El Niño shifts winter storm tracks and increases the likelihood of polar vortex outbreaks in the Central and Eastern United States, along with severe storms and flooding across the South," Brady Tyra of the commission's Office of Electric Reliability told commissioners during a presentation last Thursday.

The Southeast, New England, Midwest, and the Plains face increased risk of supply shortfalls during severe cold snaps this winter, while drought across the Intermountain West has reduced hydroelectric production at major dams along the Colorado River, according to the report.

title: Small Modular Reactors Finally Have Real Momentum in the U.S. | OilPrice.com
description:

Wind and solar projects are facing increasing roadblocks to expansion in the United States thanks to competition over scarce land resources and tensions with local communities.
At the end of September, the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) became the very first U.S. power utility to receive authorization to build a commercial SMR.

text:
Years of hype have been followed by years of fizzling and delay for what was supposed to have been the small modular reactor revolution. These new small versions of nuclear reactors were supposed to usher in the new nuclear era with their cheaper, safer approach, but today just a very small handful are in use around the world, and only in Russia and China. But it looks like that could finally be set to change thanks to a series of milestones achieved in the United States in recent months.

Small modular reactors, commonly known as SMRs, are miniature nuclear reactors that can be built in a factory setting and then assembled on-site in varying numbers and configurations according to a particular plant's needs. This approach is vastly cheaper than traditional, large-scale nuclear reactors, which are bespoke projects by nature and require huge investments and long timelines to develop, and often face skilled labor shortages in the United States, where only one new nuclear plant has been added to the grid in the last decade.

In addition to being more cost-effective, SMRs are considered to be safer thanks to their built-in safeguards, and take up a whole lot less land. This latter benefit makes the models highly competitive not only with the standard nuclear power sector, but also with other low-emissions energy sources like wind and solar. Wind and solar projects are facing increasing roadblocks to expansion in the United States thanks to competition over scarce land resources and tensions with local communities. Plus, unlike those variable renewable energies, SMRs can produce clean energy around the clock.

But despite the benefits of SMRs and the considerable buzz they garnered in recent years, only two designs have been approved for use in the United States and many more have fizzled out worldwide. "While there has been widespread government support for SMR development, many hurdles have stood in the way of commercial deployment," Oilprice.com reported back in June. "Several companies have already presented compelling prototypes and positive laboratory results, but translating this into repeatable commercial deployment is a complex task. Over 120 distinct SMR designs have been recorded globally, compared to 83 in 2022. However, many have not achieved licensing, and most are still on the long road to commercial deployment."

But in the intervening months since that article was published, there has been considerable movement in the SMR sector in the United States. At the end of September, the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) became the very first U.S. power utility to receive authorization to build a commercial SMR. The project will use the GE Vernova Hitachi's BWRX-300 reactor, representing the second-ever reactor construction granted domestically. "Although TVA has not set a date to break ground, the decision represents a turning point for American civilian nuclear energy," Interesting Engineering reported.

And now, just this week, a new engineering alliance between Sargent & Lundy and ENTRA1 Energy announced that it would be banding together to bring scalable SMR plants to grids around the globe. The initiative will be using NuScale's certified reactors, the first and only proprietary SMR design to receive regulatory approval from the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

The collaboration will allow the SMRs to move beyond the hypothetical and regulatory pipeline and into the real world. While the deployment of SMRs sounds simple and streamlined in theory, bringing this new and complex technology into existing energy systems will be a complicated endeavor, as "converting new generation plans into dependable power demands rigorous engineering from the very start," according to Interesting Engineering. This is where this partnership between a well-established firm with 7 decades of experience in the nuclear sector and a startup with innovative momentum and agility can make a difference.

"This collaboration strengthens our ability to advance projects and meet growing demand for reliable power," stated a LinkedIn announcement from ENTRA1 Energy.

description:

text:
The bill would make it easier to build transmission lines that carry electricity from wind and solar farms to customers. Federal regulators could approve qualifying interstate lines when states reject them or fail to act. Neighboring grid regions would plan new connections together, and developers would connect their projects to the grid faster.

For Democrats, the changes to the Federal Power Act would make it easier to build transmission lines and connect wind and solar projects to the grid, while Republicans would get limits on environmental reviews and lawsuits that have delayed pipelines, wells, and other infrastructure.

The Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act by a seemingly strong 62-33 vote last Thursday night, but procedural maneuvering by the bill’s most determined opponents prevented a vote on a key amendment that could have secured more Democratic support.

The four bipartisan sponsors of the bill had come to an agreement on a manager’s amendment that would have narrowed exemptions to the National Historic Preservation Act, increased spending on the Historic Preservation Fund, and made it harder for states to use eminent domain for transmission projects.

But Sens. Jeff Merkley (D-OR) and Ron Wyden (D-OR) refused to consent to a time agreement that would have allowed votes on up to a dozen amendments, including the bipartisan manager’s amendment, thus blocking changes to the legislation on the floor. This meant that while 21 Democrats voted to end a filibuster and move on to the bill, just 14 voted for final passage. Those who switched from yes to no included two possible presidential candidates, Sens. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) and Raphael Warnock (D-GA).

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act now moves to the House, where the chamber’s lame-duck status will complicate efforts by Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) to get it across the finish line. In theory, Johnson should have the votes to move the bill to the floor and pass it as is, but he can’t force his members to show up, especially those who lost and have no reason to come back other than the quaint, old-fashioned idea of doing their jobs and serving their country. Republicans were missing an average of 30 members per vote last week.

While much of the language in the Senate bill is taken from the bipartisan work of Reps. Bruce Westerman (R-AR) and Jared Golden (D-ME), Democratic opposition to the latest Senate version of the bill has grown thanks in part to the Democratic Party’s overwhelming victory earlier this month.

“From what I’ve seen, Sens. Whitehouse and Heinrich have done some good work, but they’ve been negotiating from a position of weakness,” future House Natural Resources Committee Chairman Jared Huffman (D-CA) said of the bill. “Folding our hand now or in the lame duck makes no sense when we can keep working on this and, in a few more months, have a much better deal that works for everyone.”

EDITORIAL: TRUMP DIDN’T GET THE CORRUPTION MESSAGE

Huffman is not alone. He is joined by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY), an array of green activist organizations (such as Defenders of Wildlife, Earthjustice Action, Friends of the Earth, the Natural Resources Defense Council, and the Sierra Club), and Democratic attorneys general from 15 states, including California, New York, and Massachusetts. It is hard to see how House Democrats would be willing to give President Donald Trump such a policy victory after soundly beating him at the polls when they are set to take power in two months.

Democrats want to make it easier to build infrastructure, but only infrastructure they like. That is the problem with the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act from their perspective. It makes it easier to build transmission lines to solar projects, but it also makes it easier to build natural gas pipelines and data centers. Democratic states have an abysmal track record of building homes, pipelines, and high-speed rail projects. Now voters have handed that party control of Congress. If House Democrats run out the clock on permitting reform, Americans will start getting the anti-growth policies they voted for before the new majority is even sworn in.

name: Clean Energy
title: BAAJA would deliver affordable energy and cleaner air for California families
description:
OPINION — Year after year, California families face impossible choices.
BAAJA would institute real deadlines and rules for every stage of permitting and every type of project, including clean energy.
Clean energy, like wind and solar, offers a way to get cheaper energy onto the grid.
California families, particularly those from already marginalized and climate-impacted communities, would feel that most acutely.
They must do it once more and help pass BAAJA this year, so California can build the clean energy our neighborhoods were promised.
text:
Capitol Weekly welcomes Opinions on California public policy or politics. Please read our guidelines for opinion pieces before submitting an Op-Ed. Submissions that do not adhere to our guidelines will not be considered for publication.

OPINION — Year after year, California families face impossible choices. Utility bills keep rising, with rates up by almost 40% between 2019 and 2025. And in the summer, when demand peaks, the options shrink. This comes at a time where families can no longer withstand added pressure on household budgets.

As a pastor and civil rights advocate in Sacramento, I believe energy policy must be measured by its impact on working families. Households can run their air conditioner almost 24/7 and risk a bill they can’t cover. Or they can suffer as temperatures reach triple digits and hope there aren’t any health impacts. Families in Sacramento and across the state make these choices every week, and I’ve seen them firsthand.

Climate change has added another strain. It has meant a longer, smokier wildfire season, which brings its own challenges, including that families are forced to run air purifiers around the clock. To power those systems adds another expense to California’s already soaring cost of living.

Many Californians are struggling with rising costs and the dirty air they’ve breathed for generations. The families I work with in South Sacramento know this better than most, having lived for decades in the shadow of gas power plants, industrial sites that release fossil fuel emissions into the air, and recurring wildfire smoke as temperatures rise. While clean energy was supposed to help on these fronts, it hasn’t arrived quickly enough.

California has led the nation on climate law, including 100% clean electricity and carbon neutrality by 2045. But those are just targets, and without the corresponding clean energy infrastructure, they can’t be met. Right now, too many of the projects that make those goals a reality are stuck waiting on Washington.

That’s why Congress must pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) before this session ends, ensuring its final provisions protect public health and encourage community participation.

Federal permitting is the bottleneck that stops new clean energy projects from being built. BAAJA would change the process to fix that. California’s attorney general and other state leaders have raised concerns about provisions affecting environmental protections and state and tribal authority. Congress should address those concerns so that faster decisions also preserve meaningful safeguards for the communities most affected by new infrastructure.

Families in our state deserve a permitting process that is timely and responsive to their health and economic needs. BAAJA would institute real deadlines and rules for every stage of permitting and every type of project, including clean energy. That includes transmission lines, environmental reviews under NEPA, lawsuit filings, and consultations under the National Historic Preservation Act, the Clean Water Act, and the Endangered Species Act.

The bill would not remove these laws. Projects would still be required to meet their requirements. The difference is a deadline that would give project developers the certainty to invest and build.

California families already face sky-high rates. Couple that with rising demand, and it’s an untenable situation. If new supply doesn’t keep up, prices go up, as does the risk of rolling outages or other electricity issues. Clean energy, like wind and solar, offers a way to get cheaper energy onto the grid. That lowers costs for families.

And clean power means cleaner air. Clean energy projects that go unbuilt can’t cut carbon emissions. Meanwhile, the gas plants that would be replaced stay online, and those emissions continue. Passing BAAJA would fight back against this. The Solar Energy Industries Association estimates the bill would cut power sector carbon emissions by about 20% from 2028 to 2035, compared with current law.

That reduction in emissions is also projected to avoid $54 billion in public health damages. That means fewer trips to the hospital, less asthma and fewer lung issues, and better outcomes. California families, particularly those from already marginalized and climate-impacted communities, would feel that most acutely.

Working families can’t afford another decade of waiting. Neither can our climate or our health.

The California delegation has long stood with the communities I represent. They must do it once more and help pass BAAJA this year, so California can build the clean energy our neighborhoods were promised.

Dr. Tecoy M. Porter Sr. is President and Executive Director of the National Action Network Sacramento Chapter and Senior Pastor of Genesis Church Sacramento.

text:
Georgia communities have paid a steep price for decades of reliance on coal, and the bill keeps growing with no end in sight. Plant Bowen and Plant Scherer have polluted surrounding communities for decades, threatening Georgia families with higher electricity bills and deadly public health hazards.

On Wednesday, Nov. 18, the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy joined the Climate Action Campaign (CAC) and community leaders in Decatur, Ga., to speak out against the state’s continued reliance on coal. Speakers called on the Public Service Commission (PSC), state officials, and federal leaders to chart a path toward clean energy.

Data Center Demand

Plant Bowen, owned and operated by Georgia Power, spans more than 3,000 acres and has a capacity of roughly 3,499 megawatts across four coal-fired units.

“Coal power plants are inefficient and expensive to run,” said SACE Climate Advocacy Director Chris Carnevale. “That’s why, four years ago, Georgia Power themselves chose to close half of Plant Bowen’s units, stating at the time that continued operation is not economic or in the best interest of customers.”

Georgia Power had initially planned to end coal operations at the plant by 2035, but rising grid demand driven by data centers, along with federal regulatory changes, has pushed that timeline back several years; closure is now estimated for 2038 or 2039.

“Big tech is abandoning net zero goals to cash in on the AI boom. I hope and pray that our newly elected officials won’t let them get away with it. I hope they will adopt policies and regulations that put our people and our planet ahead of obscene company profits,” Lisa Coronado, co-founder of Decatur Cares About Climate, said.

DeKalb County was among the first counties in the state to enact a moratorium on new data center developments. In September, SACE announced a call for an 18-month moratorium on new large data centers across Tennessee, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, and Florida.

Sign on to SACE’s call for a data center moratorium in Georgia

The Cost to Ratepayers

According to the Southern Environmental Law Center, Georgia Power customers have seen six bill increases in the past three years and now pay nearly $500 more per year.

“For over three years it has been proven that continuing to operate existing coal plants costs more than building new, local renewable resources such as solar and battery backup,” DeKalb County Super District 6 Commissioner Ted Terry said. “Our residents spoke loud and clear this November; DeKalb residents want clean energy now. DeKalb residents want affordable solutions.”

Terry also described Georgia Power’s choice to keep operating coal units it had previously planned to retire as disappointing, citing its effect on both the environment and household costs. He urged stakeholders with decision-making power to “end the costly polluting coal plants” and expand clean energy resources across the state.

Coronado widened the cost discussion beyond the monthly bill. She cited health care costs, coal ash cleanup, the water use of coal and gas plants, and the billions of dollars spent importing coal into a state with no coal mining or drilling.

Meanwhile, she said, many Georgians are forced to choose between keeping the lights on and buying food or medicine. Some Georgians’ utility bills, she noted, are now as large as a mortgage payment.

“Georgia could have thriving rooftop solar and battery installation industries, creating thousands of jobs,” Coronado said. “Schools, churches, hospitals, and local governments could afford solar and storage, lowering utility bills and freeing up money for teachers and community services.”

Coronado also pointed out that solar and battery storage are more resilient and can keep homes and community buildings powered during outages.

“Georgia Power spent a billion dollars repairing Hurricane Helene’s damage, a storm made far more destructive by record warm ocean waters,” Coronado said. “[Georgia Power] passed nearly all of that cost onto us.”

The Health Toll

Dr. Anne Mellinger-Birdsong, a pediatrician and medical and health advisor for Mothers & Others For Clean Air, focused on how coal pollution affects human health, particularly for children.

Children, she said, are “more vulnerable because they are still growing and every organ in their body is still developing, and because they breathe more air for their size than adults.” They also spend more time outdoors. She cited damage to lung growth, asthma, effects on cognitive development, and mental health problems. In adults, she said, exposure can contribute to lung disease, heart attacks, heart failure, strokes, and dementia.

“Plant Bowen is one of the deadliest coal power plants in the country, and it is still causing deaths today,” Mellinger-Birdsong said.

Plant Bowen ranks second-deadliest among 480 plants nationwide, with Scherer also in the top 25. An estimated 7,500 deaths in the region between 1999 and 2019 can be attributed to climate pollution from Bowen alone. And the metro Atlanta area ranks 43rd worst in the nation for smog, according to the American Lung Association’s 2026 report.

“It baffles me why we continue to allow power plants that cause so much health and economic damage to operate when less expensive and healthier alternatives are available,” Dr. Mellinger-Birdsong said.

Federal Policy and Local Goals

At the local level, DeKalb County committed in 2021 to powering its needs with 100% clean energy and clean transportation by 2050. On Earth Day 2025, the county approved a transition plan laying out how to reach that goal.

“It’s very clear that since we’ve passed that plan, we cannot reach it simply by ourselves. We are part of the Georgia Power Utility Network, and so even if we choose as the government to electrify, have more electric vehicles, the utility and the regulatory sector ultimately determine what that greenhouse gas content will be for most of our community’s power bills,” Terry said.

Terry called on local, state, and federal leaders, including the PSC, to work with community partners and commit to clean energy. Carnevale also emphasized the state and federal government’s responsibility to listen to constituents.

In recent years, the Trump administration has made costly energy decisions with lasting repercussions for both the climate and utility bills. Rollbacks of environmental protections allowed coal and gas plants to pollute the climate without limits, while the administration illegally withheld grant money that would have given 16,000 Georgia households low-cost solar, cutting their electric bills by 20% or more.

“This isn’t just another debate about clean energy,” Carnevale said. “This is about whether the people who live near these plants and pay electricity bills actually have a seat at the table when it comes to the energy decisions that will impact them for years.”

Looking ahead, Terry recommended the PSC advocate for affordable, clean energy in the long-range planning process with Georgia Power, noting that the next two Integrated Resource Planning (IRP) processes will be crucial for getting the state back on track. Terry also pointed to residential and community solar programs as additional tools for speeding up Georgia’s clean energy transition.

“Georgia is one of the best states for solar. I would love to see solar on our rec centers, on our tennis courts, on our parking lots, and all throughout Georgia, spreading the wealth that comes with producing our own domestically sourced energy,” Terry said.
