title: Recycled power is the new Normal for Rivian - Automotive Manufacturing Solutions
description:
Battery reuse Rivian is now capable of providing 10MWh of energy to the Normal plant with the energy storage system of repurposed batteries provided by Redwood.
The batteries deemed suitable for energy storage are integrated into the Redwood Energy system and supported by Redwood Pack Manager technology (see box).
Recycling for independence Batteries recovered that are not useful for battery storage are being recycled by Redwood Materials for their critical minerals.
Redwood’s Battery Materials Campus in Nevada, is the only calcining facility for battery recycling in North America.
This expanded partnership with Redwood Materials reflects a broader shift underway in how American manufacturers source power.
text:
Rivian is advancing the circular economy of its plant in Normal, Illinois with its energy technology partner Redwood Materials by reusing end-of-life batteries for energy storage, as well as recycling batteries and production scrap. Redwood can recycle battery scrap generated at Rivian's manufacturing operations and recovering critical minerals such as lithium, nickel, cobalt and copper at rates exceeding 95%. It is helping Rivian to close the loop on the battery supply chain.

BASF takes a mass-balance approach to Toyota’s truck bed

Toyota’s Tacoma short-bed pickup is now fitted with a sustainable thermoplastic truck bed made from an innovative material from BASF

Rivian produced 19,751 vehicles at its Normal plant between January and the end of September this year. It currently makes the R1S, R1T and R2 crossover at the plant. The company ramped up production of the R2 in the third quarter and has raised its delivery guidance for 2026 to between 67,000-70,000 vehicles.

At the same time, it assembles the battery modules on site at Normal with battery cells supplied by Samsung SDI in South Korea for the R1S and R1T, and from LG Energy Solution in Queen Creek, Arizona for the R2.

Currently, Rivian is already using renewable energy sources to support energy demand at Normal, and thanks to the expanded collaboration with Redwood Materials, it is supporting this with energy from vehicle batteries recovered for storage.

Battery reuse

Rivian is now capable of providing 10MWh of energy to the Normal plant with the energy storage system of repurposed batteries provided by Redwood. The system comprises of 100 former R1 battery packs, mostly sourced from Rivian’s engineering test fleet. They are being used to reduce peak energy costs and relieve the strain on the local energy grid.

"Every Rivian battery pack that comes back to us is a potential source of domestic grid energy storage in addition to critical materials," according to JB Straubel, founder and CEO of Redwood Materials. In a statement last month, he said his company’s ability to integrate and redeploy Rivian batteries was an opportunity to enable fast, flexible and more cost-efficient energy storage. “As the demand and cost for energy keeps rising, working with companies like Rivian is how we help meet these challenges,” he said in October.

Redwood is collecting used Rivian EV battery packs that are no longer suitable for in-vehicle use. It evaluates each battery pack to determine best use case – whether to repurpose it for energy storage at the Normal plant or to recycle it. The company is collecting the batteries through three channels. The first is from what Rivian calls manufacturing fallout – batteries from the production process that cannot be used in vehicles yet remain ideal for second-life stationary energy storage. Secondly, it is recovering batteries directly from Rivian’s service network that are no longer suitable for EV remanufacturing. Finally, it is looking to end-of-life vehicle recovery, where packs are salvaged post-vehicle retirement that retain adequate state-of-health for repurposed stationary storage uses.

The batteries deemed suitable for energy storage are integrated into the Redwood Energy system and supported by Redwood Pack Manager technology (see box). The system is scalable and enables faster, more flexible deployment of energy capacity directly where demand is high, according to Redwood. Rivian’s CEO RJ Scaringe has previously stated that, as the company’s energy needs grow, it will need an energy grid that is flexible, secure and affordable.

“The project will help avoid an estimated 600+ metric tons CO2e each year by reducing load during peak events, times when the grid is typically run on fossil fuel peaking generators,” confirms a spokesperson for Rivian.

Charge down on production

The battery system is helping control high energy costs in manufacturing at the Normal plant by lowering operational expenditure. “By lowering Rivian's electricity demand during periods of high grid stress, the battery energy storage system assists in managing and minimising our demand charges,” adds Rivian’s spokesperson.

72% have Circularity targets. Only 20% have closed the loop

As assembly lines evolve into closed-loop ecosystems, vehicle manufacturers across Europe are redefining sustainability through advanced recycling, low-carbon steel adoption and radical factory overhauls.

During periods of low demand or when low-cost renewable energy is most productive, the packs can store electricity for easy dispatch during periods of higher demand. According to Redwood, when paired with Rivian EV battery packs, Redwood's proprietary technology architecture offers an integrated system that can respond intelligently to the needs of the facility it is serving.

Rivian says that saving a few dollars in cost of goods sold represents a significant achievement in automotive manufacturing.

“A key differentiator of Redwood's proprietary pack manager technology is its capability to blend diverse battery chemistries and makes into a single, cohesive stationary storage system,” says the spokesperson.

That stimulates the development of a circular, domestic supply chain for battery materials in the US, something of note given the anticipated energy demands over the next five years. Redwood Materials cites estimates that more than 600 GWh of energy storage will be needed to meet demand by 2030, as well as stabilise peaks and power technology innovation as time goes on.

Recycling for independence

Batteries recovered that are not useful for battery storage are being recycled by Redwood Materials for their critical minerals. “Once a battery has truly exhausted its useful life, it enters a third phase that further secures American energy independence,” says Rivian’s spokesperson. As mentioned, through advanced recycling, critical minerals such as lithium, nickel, cobalt and copper can be recovered at rates exceeding 95%.

The company’s proprietary hydrometallurgy process purifies the recovered materials into intermediates – partially processed materials – or converts them into chemicals to produce high-grade cathode-active materials to minimise environmental impact and bolster domestic supply.

Redwood Materials is also recycling battery scrap produced from Rivian's manufacturing operations. Using battery scrap for remanufacturing involves strict technical, economic, safety and regulatory requirements. Rivian says that working with Redwood it has developed visual and functional inspections, as well other technical criteria, including ISO standards, to ensure the packs can be used effectively.

Digital product passports move from compliance to production tool

The Digital Product Passport is intended to ensure transparency, sustainability and quality throughout the entire vehicle life cycle. Will the DPP become a gamechanger for quality, warranty and remanufacturing or a bureaucratic monster?

Redwood’s Battery Materials Campus in Nevada, is the only calcining facility for battery recycling in North America. Calcination is a controlled thermal process that heats battery materials (or black mass) below their melting point. The process drives off volatile components, burns or vaporises organic binders and electrolytes, and prepares metals or active materials for recovery. According to Redwood, it is used for processing all types of live battery feedstocks efficiently and enables it to handle live battery cells, consumer electronics, and electric vehicle modules. The Nevada campus can process over 40,000 metric tons (about 15-20 GWh) annually.

R2 recycled interior

Looking beyond the repurposing or recycling of batteries and the recycling of manufacturing scrap, Rivian is looking more extensively into what goes into its vehicles, as well as what comes out.

“R2 reached a milestone with 25% of its materials coming from recycled or bio-based sources,” says Rivian’s spokesperson. “This required developing supply chains for many different materials, including those for steel, aluminium and polymers.”

Rivian is sourcing over 550kg of recycled and bio-based materials in every vehicle. Among the recycled materials in the R2 are interior textiles using Nordic paper-industry waste and floor mats made from 99% ocean waste. The frunk and trim are 85% post-consumer recycled material, and the resin cell trays are 100% recycled.

This expanded partnership with Redwood Materials reflects a broader shift underway in how American manufacturers source power. Rivian says that as grid connections take years to secure and the supply of conventional infrastructure remains constrained, companies are increasingly looking for partners who can recover materials, manage recycling and rollout battery storage as a single system. Rivian says its work with Redwood is a model for that approach – a partnership spanning the full lifecycle of a battery.

text:
A new study from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) finds that the expansion of data centers for artificial intelligence (AI) has had substantial negative health and air quality impacts — not just in the areas where most of these centers are being built, but also in regions far away from them.

As a result, hundreds of people across the U.S. are dying annually, the study suggests, with researchers finding that pollution from electricity demands of data centers resulted in around 650 premature deaths in 2023 alone. Considering the rapid expansion of data centers since that time, the number could be even higher.

“States hosting the largest data center loads do not necessarily experience the highest attributable mortality rates, while some states with little data center demand bear substantial burdens,” a summary of the study states.

Researchers compared electricity that was generated from areas with data centers and those without them. They then modeled the electrical output increase due to data centers in both areas, monitoring air pollution rates in various areas of the country.

Because the U.S. grid is interconnected, data center electricity demand is more spread out than many people realize. Different types of power plants also emit different amounts of pollution. So, while more data centers are being constructed in states like Virginia and Texas, Midwestern states, including Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota, and Kansas, are seeing higher per capita rates of death as a result of pollution from data centers.

“When people think about the negative impacts of data centers, they usually focus on the neighbors,” said Noelle Selin, senior author of the study. “But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centers are very widespread across a large region.”

“Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” Selin added.

In their findings for 2023, researchers found that data centers likely accounted for 513 premature deaths from fine particulate matter, while 137 deaths were associated with increases in ozone or fog that the data centers helped to create.

A separate study published earlier this month also demonstrated the enormous output of electricity — and pollution — due to the explosive growth of data centers in the U.S.

In that Harvard-based study, it was determined that data centers across the country emitted a total of 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide per year. That number is equivalent to the output of some countries, including Bolivia and Denmark.

Much of the research amounted to “detective work,” the authors of the study said, due to lax federal requirements on public disclosure.

title: Inside Toyota's New Forklift Factory - Assembly Magazine

One of the companies leading the charge to electric forklifts is Toyota Material Handling North America (TMHNA).

text:
Electrification is transforming airplanes, boats, buses, cars, motorcycles, tractors, trucks and other forms of transportation. The material handling industry has also been adopting battery-powered vehicles. Electric forklifts, tuggers and other devices are in big demand in factories, warehouses and distribution centers.

Many companies are transitioning away from gas, diesel and propane-powered material handling equipment toward electric alternatives. In fact, some projections predict the market for environmentally friendly products will grow more than 12 percent annually between now and 2033.

The transition is fueled by stricter emissions standards, rising fossil fuel costs and an increasing commitment to sustainability. Forklifts equipped with lithium-ion batteries offer numerous advantages, including reduced maintenance and longer operational cycles.

Electric models also enhance safety and precision with features like smooth acceleration, optimized torque control, reduced exhaust emissions and quieter operation indoors.

One of the companies leading the charge to electric forklifts is Toyota Material Handling North America (TMHNA). It recently opened a state-of-the-art factory in Columbus, IN, devoted to battery-powered equipment.

The 295,000-square-foot facility is located just north of the company’s 36-year-old flagship factory along I-65, a busy thoroughfare that links Indianapolis and Louisville. The new plant expands TMHNA’s local footprint to 1.9 million square feet.

“Electric forklifts make up 65 percent of the North American market and this trend toward electrification in the material handling industry will continue to grow,” says Brett Wood, president and CEO of TMHNA and senior executive officer at parent company Toyota Industries Corp. (TICO).

He sees no end in sight for continued growth. In fact, within the next decade, electric models are expected to account for up to 80 percent of the forklift market.

“We hope this announcement shows our customers that we are a proactive company, not a reactive one,” explains Wood. “We do not just plan for next week or next year. We’re preparing for the next decade, and this new initiative perfectly represents our commitment to that strategy.”

“We are excited about this significant strategic expansion to our Columbus campus,” adds Tony Miller, senior vice president of engineering, operations and strategic planning at TMHNA. “At Toyota, we will always be driven by what is best for our customers.

“Electric products are more popular than ever, and we are committed to doing whatever it takes to keep up with increased demand,” claims Miller. “This new factory will allow us to deliver those electric units to customers faster than we can today.

“We made a decision to do some things differently than in the older facility,” Miller points out. “For instance, the flow in the new plant is very simple and easy to follow.

“The building is expandable to the north, south and east, because we don’t want to repeat the same kind of growth challenges that we have experienced in the older factory,” says Miller. “If we need to expand welding, for instance, we’ll build an addition on the south side.”

The new $100 million factory has several other unique design features. For instance, the roof can accommodate multiple solar panels. The electrical infrastructure is also designed to use battery packs for energy storage and can be easily tied into switchgear.

Hoosier Roots Run Deep

TICO has a long heritage and traces its roots back to 1926, when it was established to manufacture an automatic loom invented by Sakichi Toyoda. It branched into automobiles in the mid-1930s. Today, TICO is part of the Toyota Group, which includes the Toyota Motor Corp.

Toyota has been active in the material handling industry for 70 years. Its first lift truck was built in 1956, followed by a tow tractor in 1957. Ten years later, Toyota sold its first forklift in the United States.

The company opened a state-of-the-art assembly plant in Columbus in 1990. It was expanded 14 times over the next 20 years to keep up with growing demand.

Along the way, the company focused on just-in-time delivery and waste elimination as it implemented key principles of the Toyota Production System, such as heijunka, jidoka, kaizen, kanban and poka yoke. It’s one reason why TMHNA excels at quality and continues to rank No. 1 in a competitive industry.

Today, the facility, which is referred to as Plant 1, encompasses more than 1 million square feet and recently produced its 750,000th vehicle.

The high-mix, high-volume factory assembles a wide range of industrial equipment, including three- and four-wheel lift trucks with various capacities. Options include battery-, diesel-, gasoline- and compressed natural gas-powered drivetrains. The factory typically builds more than 160 vehicles a day and exports to 20 countries.

Just about every machine moving down the assembly line features a different configuration. Products vary by engine size, lifting capacity, maximum lift speed and turning radius. Lifting capacity determines the type of mast and counterweights that are used on each product. For instance, two-, three- and four-rail masts are available.

Other variables include various front and rear axles, fuel tanks, hydraulic cylinders and transmissions. More than 12 different varieties of seats that can be installed in any vehicle. And, depending on the application, forklifts are equipped with either solid rubber, cushion or pneumatic tires.

The vertically integrated plant builds a wide variety of subassemblies internally, such as front and rear axles, fuel tanks, hydraulic cylinders and overhead guards, which vary from vehicle to vehicle.

Toyota acquired the Raymond Corp. in 2001, but operated it as a separate subsidiary under the TICO umbrella for 24 years. Both operations were integrated in 2025 when TMHNA was formed. While the brands share flexible assembly plants in Columbus, IN, and Greene, NY, each maintains a separate identity and dealer network in the marketplace.

Electrified Products

Toyota unveiled its first electric forklift, the 7FBEU, in 2003. Since then, it has continued to innovate and develop new products. In fact, the company shocked the material handling world in 2021 by launching 22 electric models.

Today, it offers more than 80 products powered by either lithium-ion or thin-plate pure lead batteries, which also act as counterweights. The lineup includes both three- and four-wheel configurations, with payload capacities range from 3,000 to 17,500 pounds.

Beyond sit-down and stand-up rider forklifts, Toyota also offers electric reach trucks, order pickers, electric pallet jacks, walkie stackers, tow tractors and automated guided vehicles (AGVs).

According to Miller, battery-powered forklifts are less complex that traditional gas- or propane-powered machines. “That’s because there’s no transmission and there’s just an electric motor mounted to a relatively simple gearbox,” he explains. “There is no drivetrain connection between wheels, so that entire axle assemble is eliminated. It is a significantly simpler product to build.”

Advanced AC drive and lift motor systems deliver energy efficiency, while providing responsive acceleration and supporting precise load control. Energy efficiency is also a core outcome of regenerative plugging, which returns energy to the battery, increasing runtime.

Many of TMHNA’s electric models feature the company’s new 5/35 lithium-ion batteries. The devices are available in multiple configurations, including 24-, 36- and 48-volt power capacities, to fit various customer needs and enhance operational productivity. Batteries are made at the company’s two-year-old Energy Solutions Center of Excellence in Kirkwood, NY.

The new assembly plant in Columbus currently produces electric Class 1 stand-up counterbalanced forklifts, which until recently were only built at Raymond’s state-of-the-art factory in Greene.

“However, in the future, additional products will be added to the mix, such as three-wheel sit-down models,” says Miller. “The move will enable Raymond to focus on other material handling devices, such as order pickers and reach trucks.”

Unlike traditional sit-down forklifts, stand-up models typically use padded backrests and lean pads rather than seats. They offer several advantages, including better line-of-sight vision for drivers and enhanced maneuverability in tight indoor spaces. Their compact footprint, with three- and four-stage mast options and a lift height of 270 inches, navigates narrow aisles easily.

Lean Plant Layout

The new TMHNA plant will enable the company to leverage cutting-edge manufacturing processes to produce electric products much more quickly. The facility is laid out to maximize efficiency, while addressing ergonomics, flexibility, lean manufacturing, productivity and safety. For example, the entire facility is climate controlled.

All weld fumes in the fabrication department are confined to each weld gun source. There’s also a solid wall to contain any weld smoke that escapes and prevent it from reaching other parts of the factory.

Electric forklifts are built to order, based on unique customer needs. They are assembled on AGVs at workstations equipped with digital work instructions.

“The AGVs are height adjustable, because our goal is to not lift anything with cranes,” explains Miller. “We minimized the use of cranes and hoists in the factory through a variety of lift-assist devices.

“Unlike Plant 1, where we primarily use paper work-instructions, instructions are integrated digitally into each operator’s work process at the new facility,” says Miller. “When a lift truck is ready to enter a production area, the person at the first workstation selects the next unit from an electronic schedule fed by the plant’s manufacturing execution system (MES) and enterprise resource planning (ERP) system.

“Based on each product’s bill of materials, the systems provide configuration-specific instructions to the assembler,” explains Miller. “The MES also indexes critical process information down the line so that equipment parameters can be adjusted for each truck at each stage of production.

“It records data such as torque results, component serial numbers, equipment faults and problems identified during the assembly process,” Miller points out. “We use this data to support continuous improvement efforts and help prevent issues from recurring.

“Nearly all of our fastening tools are electric, with pneumatic tools used only for a small number of high-torque applications,” says Miller. “During the line-design process, we identified joints that are critical to the safety or functionality of the lift truck.

“For those joints, we incorporate torque monitoring and poka yoke error-proofing controls to help ensure that each fastening operation is completed to specification within the process,” explains Miller. “This monitoring is tied to the assembly line through our MES. The line will stop if the torque requirements are not met within the takt time.

“We have used Atlas Copco tools successfully for critical joints in Plant 1 for many years,” adds Miller. “However, for the new plant, we chose Desoutter transducerized battery tools because they have a lower reaction force and improved ergonomics. In addition, we continue to use battery-powered Makita tools for noncritical fastening applications.”

Most fastening tools are attached to balancers to improve ergonomics and counter the downside of performing repetitive tasks. “They’re mounted from the top down on movable rails so that as processes change or production volumes increase, we can easily move lift-assist devices from workstation to workstation,” notes Miller.

Sequential Parts Delivery

Many parts are delivered in sequence to the assembly line, which is balanced based on workload. Products that require a specific option or configurations requiring higher labor content are spaced in between to level the amount of work and not overburden operators.

Subassembly processes are grouped in a common area, which enables operators to support one or multiple processes depending on the amount of work required for each task.

“This layout allows us to adjust staffing more efficiently as capacity requirements change, while also minimizing the amount of walking between subassembly stations,” says Miller. “We eventually plan to use an autonomous mobile robot to deliver kits from the subassembly area to line-side workstations.”

The plant currently uses a CB18 automated guided forklift from Toyota Automated Logistics to move the overhead guards and frames from welding through paint and into assembly.

“Most of our other AGVs move loads either by pulling them or by carrying them on top of a load-handling frame,” explains Miller. “Because the CB18 can pick up, lift, transport and lower the load itself, it requires less auxiliary material-handling equipment.”

The mast assembly line uses two conveyor systems that work together. The first provides stationary work positions for the initial three processes, which supports the safe assembly and shimming of the mast sections. The remaining nine processes use continuous motion to maintain a consistent production flow.

“Designed and built by Toyota Automated Logistics, the system combines the safety benefits of stationary work with the efficiency of continuous movement,” says Miller. “It also includes multiple fail-safe features to ensure that the two conveyors operate in unison and maintain consistent flow.

“The mast and lift-truck assembly lines are coordinated through our MES and ERP systems,” Miller points out. “The mast line feeds three different truck assembly lines—one in the new factory and two in the older, main plant. The MES and ERP connection helps us maintain the planned level of work-in-process inventory between the lines.”

While various levels of automation are used throughout in the factory, only a handful of six-axis robots are currently in operation. For instance, the majority of each frame is robotically welded. There are two cells in the fabrication department, with three robots in each cell.

“In the near future, we plan to robotically weld the mast,” says Miller. “We also use robots in our paint shop to powder coat the frame.

“Welding is an excellent application for robotics,” notes Miller. “Over the next decade, demand for welders will continue to outpace supply and we are focused on overcoming this challenge with robotics.

“However, much of the type of assembly tasks we do in our factories is very difficult to automate,” explains Miller. “The conveyor is constantly indexing forward, so the location is not as repeatable as welding. Some smaller subassembly processes can be automated in fixed positions, and we focus our automation efforts on assembly elements that are ergonomically challenging for humans.

“We believe that humans are inherently very good at complex and detail-oriented work,” says Miller. “Assembly of a truck moving down an assembly line is complicated and detail-oriented work. The other challenge we are faced with is that 70 percent of our production includes a special design. This introduces a very high level of variability where automation is not effective.”

title: What is holding back bidirectional EV charging as a grid resource? - Utility Dive

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Late last month, Ford confirmed that its midsize electric pickup, Fathom, will be able to deliver more than 10 kW of alternating-current power to a home when it hits the market next year.

Though it’s the sort of technical detail that may be lost on drivers more concerned with sticker price, styling or battery range, experts say it’s potentially game-changing for utilities hoping to harness the vast quantities of energy stored in hundreds of thousands of bidirectional-capable EVs on U.S. roads.

Drivers of EVs that can discharge AC power don’t need to install pricey, code-sensitive inverter equipment to back up their homes or send power back into the grid, said David Almeida, director of clean energy transportation at Pacific Gas & Electric Co. A Ford spokesperson told Utility Dive that the automaker’s pre-Fathom vehicle-to-home backup package retails for more than $5,000, not including professional installation. The Fathom’s package will cost up to about 60% less, they said.

“You take that cost from the customer [and reduce the] complexity of installation, and you make it a lot easier for them to take this option and … for the utility to tap into that,” Almeida said.

More accessible equipment is not the only precondition for bidirectional-capable EVs to realize their full potential, however. Utilities, regulators and automakers will also need to coordinate on enabling regulation, utility program design, product development and customer education, experts tell Utility Dive.

High cost holds back bidirectional charging, for now

Automakers sell more than 20 bidirectional-capable light-duty EV models in the United States. Nearly all are “grid-parallel,” meaning they have the technical capability to both back up a home and export power to the grid, said Zach Woogen, executive director of the Vehicle-Grid Integration Council.

Some of these can be described as mass-market rides. The Chevrolet Equinox EV’s base trim retails for just over $35,000, about $16,000 less than the average cost of a new vehicle in 2026.

But nearly all require external inverters to convert their batteries’ direct-current power to AC flows that homes can use, Almeida said. Before this fall, the slow-selling Tesla Cybertruck — with a sticker price north of $80,000 — was the only AC-capable bidirectional EV on U.S. roads. Tesla began accepting orders in October for AC-capable versions of its more affordable Model 3 and Y vehicles, but drivers will still need a Powerwall home backup battery at an installed cost of around $12,000.

Low AC-capable vehicle stock is one reason why PG&E, which has more EVs than any other U.S. utility in its Northern California territory and aims to support 2 million bidirectional-capable vehicles by 2030, has seen limited uptake so far for its vehicle-to-everything program, Almeida said.

“We are still in the hundreds” of enrolled vehicles, including commercial vans, trucks and buses, he said.

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Utility Dive free daily newsletter

PG&E provides up to $3,000 in upfront incentives for eligible residential customers to install bidirectional charging equipment at home, thousands less than the full cost of a DC-to-AC conversion package with installation.

Another reason is that, cost aside, installing a home DC-to-AC inverter is not as simple as mounting and wiring a new light fixture.

Some inverter models “take up quite a bit of space on the wall” and, at least in PG&E’s territory, must meet building codes requiring minimum setbacks from a home’s gas meter, Almeida said. That gives a homeowner with a tight garage or carport the difficult choice of moving their gas meter — if that’s even possible — or forgoing vehicle-to-home capability, he said.

“It’s not just that it’s costly,” Almeida said. “Any time you add more complexity, it’s going to make it that much less likely that the customer is going to do it.”

While disclaiming inside knowledge of automakers’ plans, Almeida said Tesla’s and Ford’s recent moves suggest other automakers are working on designs for AC-capable vehicles. New car designs can take five years or longer to move from concept to showroom, he said.

Ford and Tesla offer “a good signal of what the market is going to be,” he said. “I’d imagine that … other major automakers have [onboard AC capabilities] in the plan and they’re just not ready to share with us.”

At Ford’s invitation, PG&E in July teamed up with American Electric Power, BC Hydro, Consumers Energy and Exelon to develop what Dave McCreadie, Ford’s director of energy and grid services, called “scalable interconnection processes” ahead of Fathom’s 2027 release.

Read More in Building & Transportation Electrification

In an October blog post, McCreadie said the five utilities aligned on three key principles: clarifying when interconnection regulations should apply to bidirectional EVs, and specifically to require interconnection only for customers operating a vehicle in parallel with the grid rather than for charging or “isolated backup power;” updating interconnection procedures and/or regulations to accommodate newer standards, such as AC-capable vehicles; and maintaining collaboration between utilities, regulators and equipment manufacturers to reduce barriers to interconnection.

The working group was “a head start” for electric utilities in places where it expects the Fathom to sell well, Almeida said. After the midsize truck arrives, “it’s totally possible that we will see thousands of vehicles that have this kind of capability” on PG&E’s system, he added.

“We’ve been kind of in the ‘crawl’ stage. In the next year or two we’re going to be in the ‘walk’ stage before we run,” he said.

Bidirectional EVs can be worth a lot — to utilities and consumers

Bidirectional charging is one component of a portfolio of distributed resources that PG&E, with encouragement from state regulators, can use to get more value from an increasingly constrained grid, Almeida said.

“How can we tap into this technology to mitigate the need for us to build infrastructure to help save all of our customers money,” he said, paraphrasing a question PG&E has kicked around internally and in regulatory filings for years.

Electric vehicles play into other PG&E flexibility initiatives. Most customers participating in Flex Connect, its flexible interconnection program for larger distribution-connected loads, are commercial EV-charging sites, a PG&E manager responsible for the program told Utility Dive earlier this year. PG&E also serves more than 70 bidirectional-capable electric school buses in Oakland, California, which has one of the country’s biggest fleets today. It plans to add infrastructure for more than 230 electric buses over the next two years across three sites in San Francisco, a particularly constrained load pocket.

Utilities, regulators and state energy offices elsewhere see value in private and commercial EVs.

Read More in Building & Transportation Electrification

In New England, residential and business customers with enrolled thermostats or stationary batteries have for years taken advantage of the region’s ConnectedSolutions virtual power plant program, which pays battery owners upwards of $200/kW-year to participate in both traditional peak-shaving and more targeted local events. This year, the Massachusetts Clean Energy Center deployed dozens of fully subsidized bidirectional chargers to bring electric vehicles into the fold. One Highland Electric Fleets bus earned nearly $12,000 per summer in a two-year pilot earlier this decade, though “more like $6,000 per year is the norm” moving forward, company CEO Duncan McIntyre told Utility Dive.

Still, even after accounting for equipment installation costs, “that is not hard to make pencil — it is a lot of money if you’re able to show up” for called events, Woogen said.

Regional regulators keep upping the ante. Next month, the Connecticut Public Utilities Regulatory Authority is set to expand the state’s energy storage compensation framework to include commercial EV charging sites. The program would pay $325/kW-year for the first five years of enrollment and $175/kW-year for the next five.

The proposed decision would also clarify bidirectional EV interconnection standards, including for residential customers. But residential EVs aren’t yet eligible for demand-response compensation in Connecticut, highlighting the challenge of bringing regulation in line with technical capability, Woogen said.

In fact, only California and Maryland have adopted vehicle-to-grid interconnection standards for AC-capable EVs, according to Woogen’s group.

“In some cases, technology and customer interest are ahead of the market and regulatory capability to support [them]. That is the long pole in the tent — it’s very fragmented, and that tends to slow things down,” said Greg Guthridge, global power and utilities customer experience transformation leader for EY.

Program design will be key to uptake

That said, utilities and their partners may also need to work on “consumer interest” through education, incentives and innovative program design, Guthridge said. Recent EY market research found that only 18% of U.S. customers have an “immediate interest” in energy-flexibility services, a broad category that includes bidirectional EV charging, he said.

“We have a bit of a challenge here. … We need to convince consumers that there’s value. Either they don’t understand that or they’re not buying into [it] just yet,” Guthridge said.

EY’s research suggests customers will be more receptive to “packaged” bidirectional charging programs that meet certain criteria, Guthridge said.

One is financial benefit: generous compensation for participation, ideally with an upfront component so customers feel they’re benefiting early. Control over or at least visibility into a program is another. Customers want to understand what’s happening in their home — and in this case, to their vehicle — and be looped into the process, Guthridge said. They also want participation that isn’t inconvenient or otherwise detrimental to their lifestyle or business activities, he said.

For inspiration, utilities and their automaker partners can look to companies like Rheem, which sells water heaters that play a significant role in some utilities’ distributed resource portfolios and has a reputation for “working with the utility closely to allow a seamless, effortless adoption process,” Guthridge said.

In that light, Ford seems to be making a shrewd move to get key utility partners onboard before Fathom hits the road.

name: Indiana Environment
title: Destroying our environment is costing us our health - The Record
description: Governments cannot be allowed to use our health and a healthy environment as acceptable collateral damage in pursuit of short-term economic interests, writes Susan Koswan.
text:
Wildfire smoke obscured the view from McLennan Park in Kitchener in July. The Air Quality Health Index indicated a “very high risk” to health that week due to pollution from wildfires.

Susan Koswan is a freelance contributing columnist for the Record, based in Waterloo Region. Reach her at greyandstillgreen@gmail.com .

Climate change and environmental damage are ruining our health and driving up health-care costs. A November 2026 World Health Organization report notes that in low- and middle-income countries, between 2026 and 2050, the economic costs of the health effects of climate change are estimated at $8.6 trillion (U.S.) to $15.4 trillion.

It’s the air pollution and ozone, as well as wildfire smoke that destroys our lungs, increases asthma attacks and chronic pulmonary disorders filling emergency rooms. It’s the hormone-disrupting, carcinogenic chemical and microplastics soup in our water that is not removed through water treatment. It’s the ticks that cause Lyme disease that have expanded their range because of our warming planet. It’s the heat we cannot escape, the flooding that leaves us traumatized and the anxiety that goes with it.

In a recently released collaborative report “ Microplastics in Me ,” the Canadian Association of Physicians for the Environment wrote, “research is mounting regarding possible links between plastic contamination of our bodies and negative health outcomes like heart disease, neurodegenerative disorders, and reproductive issues including infertility.”

Less easy to quantify are mental health issues like depression and anxiety, already costing billions of dollars in lost productivity, reports the Canadian Institute for Climate Choices .

Yet both our provincial and federal governments continue to play fast and loose with this reality. With sweeping omnibus bills, they have both gutted protective environmental legislation and our right to know and comment about projects and permit applications that impact us directly, increase greenhouse gas emissions and threaten our health.

The latest blows are Bill 140: Building Ontario Faster Act, 2026 and the federal Bill C-39: Building Canada Strong Act . My inbox is flooded with analysis and comments by all the major environmental NGOs and law firms in Canada calling for them not to be passed.

The Ontario Bill 140 scraps the 30-year-old Environmental Bill of Rights that has allowed us to comment on potential legislation, regulations and permits and provide local knowledge that may not have been considered or even thought of.

It also eliminates third-party appeals. The Canadian Environmental Law Association illustrates the importance of these appeals. Grassy Narrows First Nation challenged a water-taking permit for a gold mine. The Ontario Land Tribunal assessed the situation and, recognizing the potential for serious environmental impacts from methylmercury production and the release of contaminants, revoked the permit.

Environmental Defence comments on both the Ontario Bill 140 and the federal Bill C-39 , referring to the latter as the “Bulldoze Nature Bill” and the “single worst weakening of Canada’s environmental law safety net in Canadian history.” With the creation of regions of economic interest, projects could “proceed before biodiversity, ecological, climate, social, economic and cumulative risks are adequately understood, leaving Canadians in the dark about impacts.”

Full details are available on the respective websites of the organizations named.

Contact your MPP and MP. We cannot allow our governments to use our health and a healthy environment as acceptable collateral damage in pursuit of short-term economic interests.

Opinion articles are based on the author’s interpretations and judgments of facts, data and events. More details

Susan Koswan is a freelance contributing columnist for the
Record, based in Waterloo Region. Reach her at greyandstillgreen@gmail.com .

name: Detroit and Evs
title: Automakers raise concerns China will use Canada's EV policy to import gas vehicles
description:
Earlier in November, the Liberal government announced that a second Chinese EV manufacturer was cleared to start importing vehicles to Canada for sale.
The Chinese EV import quota would rise to 70,000 Chinese vehicles by 2030.
Lucas Malinowski of Global Automakers of Canada (GAC) says the government needs to be transparent about how it’s dividing up the quota among Chinese companies.
Under the guidelines, it’s possible that EV companies, already subsidized by China’s Communist government, could also be eligible for Canadian grants.
Kingston says Canada needs to learn from the experiences of European nations who let in Chinese EVs.
text:
OTTAWA -- As Canada prepares for the first batch of Chinese EVs to arrive under the new quota regime, concerns are mounting among some stakeholders that Prime Minister Mark Carney has let in a “Trojan horse” that will hollow out domestic manufacturing.

The concerns are compounded by loopholes in the Liberal government’s electric vehicle policies that could result in Beijing-supported companies benefitting from subsidies granted by Ottawa.

Brian Kingston, CEO of the Canadian Vehicle Manufacturers’ Association, told CTV News the deal Carney signed with President Xi Jinping will allow Chinese companies to import an unlimited amount of conventional gas-powered vehicles once it establishes an EV foothold in Canada.

How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Under the terms of the strategic partnership deal signed in January, 49,000 Chinese EVs would be allowed into Canada this fiscal year under the most-favoured-nation tariff rate of 6.1 per cent.

According to Kingston, the deal allows a carve-out for electrified vehicles, including hybrids from the previous 100 per cent tariff imposed on China but, “there’s no limit to the access gas-powered vehicles have into this market.”

Kingston says under the agreement Chinese companies would pay 6.1 per cent tariff on their petrol vehicles just like a manufacturer in Japan, Korea or Europe.

“EVs are a Trojan horse that give (Beijing) access to the market on the grounds that these vehicles will be affordable and will help countries meet their emissions reductions targets. What then happens, once they’ve established a dealership presence and a logistics network is that they start to sell other types of vehicles, gas vehicles in particular.”

Appearing before a parliamentary committee on Tuesday, Kingston called on the government to quash that risk by eliminating the Canada-China strategic partnership signed earlier this year.

The CVMA represents the three major North American automakers: Ford, GM and Stellantis.

Kingston said the 49,000 EV quota represents 30 per cent of the total EVs sold in 2025 and says the agreement “undermines Canada’s auto sector and puts the integrated North American supply chain at risk.”

Kingston told the Standing Committee on Environment and Sustainable Development that Canada should not turn to China even if it means cheaper EVs.

He said Chinese companies pay their workers the equivalent of $4 per hour compared to Canadian unionized wages of $45 per hour.

Earlier in November, the Liberal government announced that a second Chinese EV manufacturer was cleared to start importing vehicles to Canada for sale. The Chinese EV import quota would rise to 70,000 Chinese vehicles by 2030.

At least four Chinese motor companies: BYD, Chery, Geely and Dongfeng have expressed interest in the Canadian market.

Lucas Malinowski of Global Automakers of Canada (GAC) says the government needs to be transparent about how it’s dividing up the quota among Chinese companies.

GAC represents most automakers selling vehicles in Canada, including Asian and European manufacturers.

Malinowski, GAC’s president, says the federal government has a role to ensure a fair playing field for all automakers and that it should not be giving the Chinese auto industry a reduced tariff rate.

“China is on track to export more vehicles produced in all the car plants in the United States. In any other trade situation that would be viewed as dumping its excess capacity.”

In addition to the favorable tariff rates, Chinese companies could also benefit from the government’s greenhouse gas (GHG) credit system.

Under the program, manufacturers producing vehicles that emit tailpipe emissions above the targets set by the federal government can buy offset credits from companies that are under the limit.

The latest data from Environment Canada indicates the North American “Big Three” and Japan’s Toyota and Honda had to buy credits from either Tesla or Lucid, two companies that do not have a manufacturing presence in Canada.

So far Tesla, which has a manufacturing plant in Shanghai, has received the bulk of the EV quotas so far.

It is also the biggest beneficiary of the GHG policy. Kingston says Tesla has already earned hundreds of millions of dollars from selling greenhouse gas credits.

Kingston said it is “egregious” that the framework would also apply to the new Chinese manufacturers moving in.

“A Chinese (manufacturer) will be able to take a sale away from a domestic company that builds here and employs Canadians. Then they can turn around and say to the same company that they just took the sale from that they now have a credit to sell them for the pleasure of continuing to operate in Canada.”

International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu has said the Chinese companies are currently preparing for their entry into the Canadian market by investing in charging infrastructure and building dealerships.

In its 2026 federal budget, the Carney government also allocated nearly $600 million to add more than 55,000 public EV chargers under the Zero Emission Vehicle Infrastructure Program.

Under the guidelines, it’s possible that EV companies, already subsidized by China’s Communist government, could also be eligible for Canadian grants.

Kingston says Canada needs to learn from the experiences of European nations who let in Chinese EVs.

Europe lost 104,000 auto jobs over the past two years. Germany shed 44,000 jobs in the first six months of 2026.

Consumers got access to cheaper vehicles, but the trade-offs may have been too high.

name: American Energy
title: Don't Bet on It | American Enterprise Institute - AEI
description:
My views have not changed, nor has the real world: carbon dioxide removal is promising, but its economics are daunting.
The IPCC: “Anthropogenic activities removing carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere and durably storing it.” Air capture (direct air capture, DAC).
This post uses ‘air capture’ as in my 2009 paper: direct air capture with permanent storage, which fits under both CCUS and CDR, though much CCUS and CDR involves no air capture, but rather capture from power plants and other facilities.
When a budget is exhausted, air capture would be required to hold cumulative emissions to the level implied by the target.
The Larger Context The COP31 draft CCUS goals included carbon capture at power plants and factories as well as direct air capture.
text:
Is large-scale carbon dioxide removal from the atmosphere at scale “unavoidable” or “required”?

Many climate scientists and the IPCC believe that the answer to this question is “Yes.” Today’s post takes a close look at this question by updating a 2009 analysis where I first took it on.

My views have not changed, nor has the real world: carbon dioxide removal is promising, but its economics are daunting.

The stylized exercise I perform here seeks to help to clarify how we think about mitigation alternatives, and in particular technology costs and feasibility.

Let’s dive in . . .

At COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, carbon capture was at the center of the initially proposed cover decision intended to reflect the headline political commitments agreed upon at the conference. In a draft of that decision, the Presidency called for carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) at gigatonne scale — reaching 500 million tonnes annually by 2035 on its way to 2.5 billion. In the end, the talks crashed and burned, ending on 22 November with no agreement on key issues.

However, the central focus on CCUS at COP31 prompted me to replicate and revisit my 2009 stylized analysis of the economics of the air capture of carbon dioxide.

A quick note on terminology

Carbon capture. The European Commission: “Capture involves the extraction of CO2 emissions from various sources”. The sources include industrial processes, fossil fuel combustion, biomass and the air.

Carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS). The International Energy Agency (IEA): “the capture of CO2 from large point sources, including power generation or industrial facilities”. The captured CO2 then goes into products or into permanent storage underground.

Carbon dioxide removal (CDR). The IPCC: “Anthropogenic activities removing carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere and durably storing it.”

Air capture (direct air capture, DAC). The IEA: “technologies extract CO2 directly from the atmosphere at any location”, unlike capture at the point of emissions.

This post uses ‘air capture’ as in my 2009 paper: direct air capture with permanent storage, which fits under both CCUS and CDR, though much CCUS and CDR involves no air capture, but rather capture from power plants and other facilities.

In that paper I estimated what the world would pay — if it relied on the direct removal of CO2 from ambient air — to stay within a specified carbon budget. With carbon capture back on the agenda of climate diplomacy, I have updated that analysis to 2026.

Where I Wind Up in 2026

Before getting into the details, here are my top line conclusions — and remember, this is a stylized analysis with the numbers serving to illustrate rather than offer anything precise about the real world:

First, air capture remains a useful cost benchmark. Under current policies, holding warming to 2°C with air capture alone would cost 0.8% of cumulative world GDP from 2026 to 2100 at $100 per tonne of CO2 and 7.5% at $1,000 per tonne. At $100 to $250 per tonne, air capture would cost in the neighborhood of IPCC estimates of the costs of conventional mitigation to hit a 2°C target. Today’s estimates of the costs of direct air capture are about $1,000 per tonne, far from that neighborhood.

Second, we should be very skeptical of any cost projections for technologies that have yet to be deployed at scale. For instance, in 2017 Climeworks projected $100 per tonne by 2025 or 2030, about $130 in 2025 dollars. In 2024 the company reported costs near $1,000 per tonne. A significant role for any form of carbon dioxide removal in mitigation policy depends upon real world costs that have yet to be achieved.

Third, at $1,000 per tonne and the upper range of the COP31 draft proposal of 2.5 billion tonnes of carbon, removal would cost $2.5 trillion per year, or about 1.7% of world GDP in 2035. I find that to be utterly implausible — much too costly. If carbon removal at this price costs too much, then so too would be conventional mitigation with the same costs.

A Review of my 2009 Analysis

In 2009 I published “An idealized assessment of the economics of air capture of carbon dioxide in mitigation policy” in Environmental Science & Policy. The paper was a spin-off of my work on what would become The Climate Fix and completed while I was in residence at the James Martin Institute at Oxford University.

I used a simple bathtub model of the carbon cycle. Anthropogenic emissions fill the tub and natural sinks drain some of it — and to stabilize concentrations of atmospheric carbon dioxide the world must hold net inflow at or below the rate of drainage.

I used IPCC AR4 allocations of cumulative 21st-century emissions for stabilization below 440 ppm, at 480–570 ppm, and above 855 ppm, along with EIA and IPCC projections of emissions.

Then I asked: if the world emitted along the projected paths until it exhausted an allocation consistent with stabilization, and then used air capture to offset every additional tonne, what would that level of air capture cost?

I assumed air capture costs of $100, $360 and $500 per tonne of carbon, based on estimates from Klaus Lackner and David Keith. In 2025 dollars per tonne of CO2, those figures equal $41, $147 and $204.

I was surprised at what I found.

For stabilization at 450 ppm, air capture would cost 0.4% to 2.1% of global GDP through 2100 at 2.9% annual growth, and 0.5% to 2.7% at 2.5% growth. Those costs fell within the range of IPCC and Stern Review estimates for stabilization through conventional mitigation. These costs were lower than what I expected.

I drew three conclusions.

The greater the imperative to reduce emissions, the greater the importance of air capture.

Air capture deserved a much larger role in policy debates.

And discussions of air capture could help separate the climate goals of mitigation policy from its other aims.

I also described air capture as an unambiguous cost benchmark against which to compare other approaches to mitigation.

I have replicated the original analysis and extended it to 2026. The table below compares the inputs of the two analyses.

I made four main changes:

remaining carbon budgets from Forster et al. (2026), following IPCC AR6 methods, in place of AR4 allocations;

a simplistic current-policies baseline that holds fossil CO2 emissions flat at about 38 Gt per year;

no subtraction of a natural sink, because the new budgets already account for ocean and land uptake;

and a larger world economy.

In the Technical Appendix below, I describe each input in more detail and at the bottom of this post, paid subscribers can find a spreadsheet with sources, data, and methods as well as a PDF of Pielke (2009).

The table below shows the updated inputs to the analysis.

The biggest change since 2009 is in the cost of air capture, which are larger than those I used in 2009. In 2017 Climeworks, the most prominent air capture company, reported costs of $600 per tonne of CO2. In 2024 the company put its costs higher — near $1,000 per tonne. Independent analysts and buyers report current costs and prices of roughly $500 to $1,300 per tonne and project $200 to $580 per tonne by 2050.

The table below summarizes these estimates in 2025 dollars.

The updated 2026 analysis uses four costs in 2025 dollars per tonne of CO2:

$1,000, today’s first-of-a-kind cost

$500, the Climeworks 2030 target and the 2030 market forecast

$250, projections for 2050

$100, the goal of the U.S. Department of Energy’s Carbon Negative Shot

Under the assumption of current policies used in this exercise, the world exhausts carbon budgets implied by various temperature targets through the century. When a budget is exhausted, air capture would be required to hold cumulative emissions to the level implied by the target.

The amount of carbon dioxide to be removed combined with a cost per tonne of that removal gives an estimate of the cost, which can then be related to a projected GDP. The time value of money is not considered in this stylized exercise.

Example: At $1,000 per tonne, holding warming to 2°C with air capture would cost 7.5% of cumulative world GDP from 2026 to 2100, assuming 2.5% annual GDP growth. At $100 per tonne, the cost drops to 0.8% of cumulative world GDP.

The table below shows various combinations of costs and targets.

In this update I follow the original methods of the 2009 paper and add two new scenarios: gradual deployment and learning by doing.

Updating the original approach, annual costs reach their highest share of GDP in the first full year of capture, when the world would need to remove about 40 Gt CO2. For the 2°C case, I estimate 2052 costs of 17.7%, 8.9%, 4.4% and 1.8% of world GDP at $1,000, $500, $250 and $100 per tonne.

By comparison, the IPCC AR6 authors estimated that conventional mitigation consistent with 2°C would reduce 2050 global GDP by 1.3% to 2.7%.

That means that an air capture cost approaching $100 per tonne rivals the IPCC AR6 projected costs of conventional mitigation. More generous assumptions — such as declining emissions in the baseline — would make the comparison favorable at a higher cost per tonne.

At the same real price per tonne, the update has lower costs than my analysis in 2009, which is due to lower projected emissions, a larger economy, and a later start for air capture.

In the gradual deployment scenario, air capture starts earlier and offsets a rising share of emissions each year until net zero. A 2030 start requires about 1 Gt CO2 of new capacity each year and reaches net zero in 2073.

With an earlier start, the peak annual burden falls. For 2°C at $1,000 per tonne, the peak drops from 17.7% of world GDP with an all-at-once start in 2051 to 10.4% with a start in 2030.

However, the total stays fixed. Air capture through 2100 must equal cumulative emissions minus the budget, about 1,960 Gt CO2 for 2°C, whatever the start date, so undiscounted cumulative cost stays at 7.5% of GDP at $1,000 per tonne. The Technical Appendix expands this discussion.

Learning by Doing

In 2009 I noted that the costs of new technologies often decline with experience. In this variation of the exercise, the price per tonne falls with cumulative deployment of air capture, at learning rates of 5%, 10%, 15% and 20% per doubling, a range that spans the assumptions of the IEA and of Kanyako and Craig 2025.

The exercise starts with a price at $1,000 per tonne at 1 million tonnes of cumulative experience and reduces it by the learning rate with each doubling of cumulative capture — down to an imposed floor of $100 per tonne, the Department of Energy goal. The figure below shows these assumptions.

Total cost depends far more on the learning rate than on the start date. For 2°C with a 2030 start, cumulative cost through 2100 falls:

from 7.5% of GDP with no learning,

2.8% at 5% learning,

1.0% at 10%,

and 0.8% at 15% or 20%.

The table below summarizes these results.

This finding suggests that some public resources might be fruitfully devoted to trying to accelerate cost reductions for air capture — is it actually feasible? The notion of utilization is particularly tantalyzing, such as for liquid fuels or cement.

We cannot learn anything about learning rates with stylized exercises, targets set at conferences, or in integrated assessment models. Deployment in the real world provides the only true test.

The Larger Context

The COP31 draft CCUS goals included carbon capture at power plants and factories as well as direct air capture. The proposed 2.5 Gt CO2 per year equals about 6% of the ~40 Gt CO2 per year that air capture would need to remove if used to fully offset emissions. The Climeworks Mammoth facility in Iceland, which opened in 2024, has a nameplate capture capacity of 36,000 tonnes per year.

Removal of 2.5 Gt CO2 per year would require almost 70,000 such plants — a deployment rate of almost 10 per day starting tomorrow until 2050. removal of all 40 Gt CO2 per year would require more than a million plants.

At the $450 per tonne that market analysts forecast for 2030, 2.5 Gt of air capture would cost about $1.1 trillion per year, or 0.7% of 2035 world GDP.

To update an example I used in my 2009 paper: Air capture of the CO2 from U.S. motor gasoline would add $8.49 per gallon at $1,000 per tonne and $0.85 at $100.

In 2009. I wrote that air capture deserved a place among the options in international climate policy. Whether it proves useful at meaningful scale remains to be determined and will be a function of its costs.

In the 17 years since my original analysis has published, there has not been any improvement in these costs, leading me to conclude that air capture is a promising technology, and might always be just that.

name: Texas Environment
title: The Failed Climate Agreement Raises Larger Ethical Questions About How We Want to Live ...
description:
Texas Impact and our partners arrived home from Turkiye this week amid the news that the climate negotiations in Antalya had ended in tears and recriminations.
We must also recognise that this COP process has two tracks.
Texas Impact will be working with the GEST leadership at the Center for Earth Ethics to ensure US faith and community-based organizations have opportunities to participate.
After COP30, Texas Impact and our partners created a 5-part study curriculum on climate change and ethics called Changing by Choice.
Texas Impact is Texas’ oldest and largest interfaith advocacy network.
text:
Texas Impact was on the ground in Antalya, Türkiye, at the United Nations climate negotiations known as COP31, where each day Texas Impact staff and other U.S. faith delegates reported on the proceedings and shared conversations with global colleagues about the state of play and the urgency of the moment. Find more of Texas Impact’s coverage at austinchronicle.com/COP31.

Texas Impact and our partners arrived home from Turkiye this week amid the news that the climate negotiations in Antalya had ended in tears and recriminations. The only significant consensus at the conclusion of COP31 appears to be the universal acknowledgement that everyone better straighten up and fly right before COP32 – because, as UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on Sunday:

This setback does not change the facts.

There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.

Temperatures keep shattering records. Climate extremes keep intensifying. Emissions remain far too high. And every delay makes our task harder and more costly.

The world is now poised to exceed the globally-agreed limit of a 1.5 degree temperature rise. The window to keep that overshoot as short and shallow as possible is rapidly closing.

The take-home message from COP31 is clear: The world must do much more to confront the climate crisis – and it must do it now.

Meanwhile, as Guterres, other world leaders, and our civil society colleagues were calling the outcome of COP31, U.S. faith representatives were standing in the ruins of the Agora at the ancient city of Perga, considering parallels between the ancient world and the one we live in now. It was hard to miss the connections between the highly stratified society and conspicuous consumption of the Roman Empire.

During the 2nd century AD there was a construction boom in the city, fueled by the Pax Romana and excessive wealth. The city center was expanded to the South side of the city and new monuments were erected. Perga also had many philanthropists during the Roman Empire period who financed the construction of monumental structures. (Wikpedia)

There’s an especially harsh parallel between the dehumanizing practices of the Roman Empire and dehumanizing impacts of the fossil fuel industry. The language of COP has become the language of slavery and human sacrifice, as the most vulnerable nations and people – who have done the least to bring about climate change – face existential threats and beg for financial aid from the sheltered wealthy of the world.

Much of the coverage of COP31 – even before the negotiations collapsed – questioned the utility of the UN consensus model where every participating party in a negotiation must agree, meaning any nation can scuttle a decision the rest of the world has agreed to.

But it’s not fair to praise the process when you win and blame the process when you’re disappointed in the outcome. As UNFCCC Executive Secretary Simon Stiell stressed:

The world cannot afford a repeat of this moment. Our process – including the rulebook and precedents – are designed to bring almost 200 countries together.

As we have seen repeatedly over the past decade, that delivers results.

Agreeing on temperature targets,

New climate finance goals,

To transition away from fossil fuels, in a just, orderly, and equitable manner.

And a global goal on adaptation,

There are lessons that must be learned.

This process belongs to 194 Parties. Consensus works best from the ground up.

With full transparency, taking time to listen to all views, always building on what came before.

Clearly there is also scope to improve, modernise, and reform. But not only because of what happened here.

But also, because we must evolve, in this era of implementation.

We must also recognise that this COP process has two tracks. And across the Action Agenda, COP31 has delivered real progress and concrete results.

Landing solutions across its six axes:

From transforming agriculture and food systems to building resilience for cities and infrastructure.

Through individual country pledges and the Leaders’ Summit, COP31 has shown that around half the global economy is accelerating electrification.

The COP31 Electrification Delivery Package also made important real-economy progress.

Together, these advances should lead to more innovation and investment.

Helping the world to accelerate towards positive tipping points.

Antalya will reinforce our resolve for an ambitious outcome.

This process has suffered setbacks before and come back stronger. It must do so again.

As Stiell pointed out, nations and civil society have agency to reduce emissions now, and many are doing so. Moreover, the Fossil Fuel Treaty process begun earlier this year is gathering momentum.

What’s at stake in the UN process is more than technical solutions or supermajority rule: It’s ethical questions about how we are called to live together as part of creation. To quote our friend Lisa Sullivan:

“COP31 ended without a final agreement because nations refused to sign a climate deal that erased fossil fuels – which would be like a fire department showing up to a blaze and banning the word ‘fire.’ Even as the U.S. government walked away from the table, U.S. states, cities, and faith communities stayed in Antalya as memory keepers and justice makers, because our neighbors are trapped in a burning building and our faiths call us never to abandon them. Now, we are rallying a bucket brigade of the willing – rooted in the Pacific spirit of tuakoi, showing up when a neighbor’s house is on fire – through bold efforts like the upcoming Transition Away from Fossil Fuels conference led by Ireland and Tuvalu. We don’t need the arsonists’ permission to start putting out the flames.” – Lisa Sullivan, Maryknoll Office for Global Concerns

Which brings us to the Second Global Stocktake and the Global Ethical Stocktake.

Despite the failure to deliver a policy platform at COP31, the UNFCCC parties did succeed in launching the Second Global Stocktake (GST2), which is one of the central pillars of the Paris Agreement.

The GST process lasts two years, and results in a decision, which serves as a guidance document for countries to plan their next tranche of emissions reductions toward the global goal of net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.

The first GST concluded at COP28 in Dubai. The GST1 decision, under the leadership of the UAE, for the first time specifically called for ending the use of fossil fuels:

Outcome of the first global stocktake

The Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of the Parties to the Paris Agreement…

…Further recognizes the need for deep, rapid and sustained reductions in greenhouse gas emissions in line with 1.5 °C pathways and calls on Parties to contribute to the following global efforts, in a nationally determined manner, taking into account the Paris Agreement and their different national circumstances, pathways and approaches:

(a) Tripling renewable energy capacity globally and doubling the global average annual rate of energy efficiency improvements by 2030;

(b) Accelerating efforts towards the phase-down of unabated coal power;

(c) Accelerating efforts globally towards net zero emission energy systems, utilizing zero- and low-carbon fuels, well before or by around mid-century;

(d) Transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in a just, orderly and equitable manner, accelerating action in this critical decade, so as to achieve net zero by 2050 in keeping with the science;

(e) Accelerating zero- and low-emission technologies, including, inter alia, renewables, nuclear, abatement and removal technologies such as carbon capture and utilization and storage, particularly in hard-to-abate sectors, and low-carbon hydrogen production;

(f) Accelerating the substantial reduction of non-carbon-dioxide emissions globally, in particular methane emissions by 2030;

(g) Accelerating the reduction of emissions from road transport on a range of pathways, including through development of infrastructure and rapid deployment of zero- and low-emission vehicles;

(h) Phasing out inefficient fossil fuel subsidies that do not address energy poverty or just transitions, as soon as possible.

That’s what we all said in 2023. So GST2 is where we evaluate how we’re doing a few years on.

And YOU can participate!

2027 constitutes the “technical” phase of GST2, and the first step of that phase is the Information Collection and Preparation step. In other words, we are in the public comment submission period.

As Americans, we don’t currently have a seat in the negotiations – but everyone gets to submit comments into the GST portal. That includes businesses, local governments, special interest groups, Rotary clubs, Scout troops, NGOs, denominations, congregations, creation-care groups, and even individuals.

Texas Impact and other U.S. faith groups will be developing our own submissions, and we hope you and your climate friends will consider offering your own input to the process. We’ll provide additional guidance as soon as possible, but for now, here’s the skinny:

Submission Guidelines for the Second Global Stocktake

Guiding Questions (if you need help getting your thoughts centered)

Here’s the Actual Submission Portal (NOTE: You will need to register to make your submission–it’s not difficult)

Still unclear what a submission should look like? Here’s a great example of a pretty detailed submission from GST1 from the UN’s Children and Youth constituency, and here’s the very readable, enlightening, and poignant submission from Queers X Climate and OUT for Sustainability.

Still feeling daunted by the GST process? In that case, let us introduce you to the Global Ethical Stocktake. While the GEST is not part of the Paris Agreement, it’s now part of the GST process through the work of the Brazilian COP30 presidency.

Texas Impact will be working with the GEST leadership at the Center for Earth Ethics to ensure US faith and community-based organizations have opportunities to participate. Join our email list to stay updated and get involved.

After COP30, Texas Impact and our partners created a 5-part study curriculum on climate change and ethics called Changing by Choice. We’ll have a follow-up curriculum ready for Lent 2027, so stay tuned for that.

Meanwhile, we’ll be working to elevate climate change in the Texas Legislature. Over the years, various lawmakers have proposed that Texas establish a formal climate planning process like a number of other states have done. With Super-El Nino gathering steam, and a sea-change in the Texas Capitol, 2027 should be the year we get it done.

A final thought: COP31 is being billed as only the second COP to end in a full meltdown, the other “failed COP” being in Copenhagen in 2009. So it’s interesting that just one month before COP31 convened, the international energy information platform energynews.pro published a COP process retrospective titled COP15 Copenhagen 2009: the failure that led to Paris. Under the Paris Agreement, projected warming by 2100 has dropped from about 4°C to 2.6°C today (assuming countries honor their existing commitments.) It’s not enough, but it’s not nothing. And, as our friends in the UNFCCC Secretariat say, “After COP is before COP.”

COP32 is in 11 months – so let’s get busy.

Texas Impact is Texas’ oldest and largest interfaith advocacy network. Based in Austin with members in every corner of the state, Texas Impact equips and mobilizes Texans of faith and conscience to advocate for public policies that reflect widely shared, deeply held values of love and justice. Learn more and get involved at texasimpact.org.

text:
Chevron Corporation CVX entered the U.S. lithium sector in June 2025, when it announced two leasehold acquisitions in the Smackover Formation in Northeast Texas and Southwest Arkansas. The company initially put the combined position at about 125,000 net acres and later revised that figure to about 135,000 net acres. Chevron acquired the leases to find out whether it can produce lithium from salty water found deep underground. The company is pursuing lithium mainly for energy storage, including batteries used in electric vehicles and on the power grid.

Chevron is assessing the underground resource, testing direct lithium extraction and designing the facilities it would need. The process separates lithium from salty water pumped to the surface, then returns the remaining water to the underground reservoir. That work draws on skills Chevron already uses in its oil and gas business, from assessing reservoirs to drilling wells and handling fluids. The company is also refining its product specifications so it can discuss with potential customers what they need and what the project might eventually be able to supply.

Chevron plans to develop the acreage in phases and adjust the pace to market conditions. The company has yet to announce when commercial production might start or how much lithium it aims to produce. Oil and gas production still drives most of Chevron’s earnings, so the near-term question for investors is what the extraction tests reveal about the project’s economics. How much lithium Chevron can recover from the brine, and what it costs to recover it, will help determine whether the acreage can support a profitable business.

A U.S. lithium supply chain depends on producers being able to meet battery makers’ quality standards consistently. Producing battery-grade lithium in small batches is an early step. The next test is whether that quality holds as output increases.

Energy Biggies Test U.S. Lithium Projects

ExxonMobil Holdings XOM holds brine rights across more than 300,000 net acres in the Smackover Formation. ExxonMobil has produced battery-grade lithium carbonate at its Texas pilot facility using brine from southern Arkansas. ExxonMobil’s preliminary agreement with LG Chem for a potential lithium supply deal is nonbinding. The company aims to produce enough lithium for about one million electric vehicles a year by the first half of the 2030s.

Occidental Petroleum OXY is testing direct lithium extraction in California’s Imperial Valley through a joint venture with BHE Renewables. Occidental’s TerraLithium subsidiary and its partner produced battery-grade lithium carbonate from geothermal brine and converted lithium chloride into lithium hydroxide in separate tests. Occidental and its partner expect demonstration operations to continue through 2027 as they assess whether the process is economically viable at commercial scale.
