text:
The Forestry Research Institute of Sweden is evaluating the application of electric trucks in the Swedish forestry sector. The TREE (Transition to Efficient, Electrified Forestry Transport) pilot began in 2023 and concluded in November 2026. A performance evaluation will determine the next steps in scaling electrified transport for the forestry sector.

A fleet of 12 battery-electric Scania trucks is operating at various forestry sites throughout Sweden, transporting timber from seven Swedish forestry sites to sawmills and terminals, from Småland in the south to Norrland in the far north.

A variety of electric trucks are taking part in the project.

A 94-metric-ton, 33-meter Scania woodchip hauler is operating on behalf of Stora Enso, which claims it is the world’s largest electric truck. (We know some mining firms that would probably contest that claim.)

SCA and Rolf Lövgrens Åkeri have jointly commissioned a 74-metric-ton Scania electric timber truck with a loading crane.

In northern Sweden, where winter temperatures can be as low as minus 30 degrees Celsius, Eklunds Åkeri operates a 70-metric-ton Scania electric timber truck.

In the Småland area of southern Sweden, Södra has deployed a 64-metric-ton Scania 45R woodchip truck with 624 kWh of battery capacity.

The remaining 8 trucks are heavy-duty Scania battery-electric vehicles used in logistics networks by companies such as Dalafrakt and Alltransport.

“We must work together and develop business models, logistics and technology,” said Ulf Ceder, Senior Research Manager at Scania. “Scania contributes with our expertise, and of course our electric trucks.”

text:
Why It Matters

The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee advanced President Donald Trump's nominee to oversee federal air pollution regulations on Nov. 18, despite Democratic concerns that he would undermine the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) statutory responsibilities. ​

Justin Schwab's nomination to lead the EPA's Office of Air and Radiation advanced by a 10-9 vote at a business meeting, according to Bloomberg Law. The committee's ranking Democrat also opposed a proposal to relocate the Department of Energy's headquarters.

The Big Picture

Schwab's confirmation hearing was held Nov. 10, and ranking member Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) said at the business meeting that he had already addressed the nomination there.

According to the committee's release, the committee also approved eight General Services Administration resolutions. Chairwoman Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV) moved to approve a prospectus authorizing the relocation of the Department of Energy's headquarters and disposal of the James V. Forrestal Building. Whitehouse opposed the resolution, which passed 10-9.

Schwab previously served as general counsel of the Council on Environmental Quality and deputy general counsel of the EPA during Trump's first administration. Between Trump's two administrations, he represented regulated entities and advised clients on the Clean Air Act and other environmental matters. NPR reported that the Trump administration was repealing limits on greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel-fired power plants.

What They're Saying

Whitehouse acknowledged that Schwab "may be well qualified" but called him "ill-motivated," arguing that Schwab intended to undermine the EPA's statutory responsibilities. He urged colleagues to "vote no on Mr. Schwab."

Whitehouse tied his opposition to climate-related financial risks, citing rising insurance rates in Iowa and testimony from former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell that some regions could become uninsurable. He also said relocating the Energy Department's headquarters was part of the administration's broader efforts to dismantle federal agencies under Project 2025.

Capito defended Schwab's qualifications, highlighting his experience in environmental law and understanding of the Clean Air Act. She argued that Schwab would help the agency avoid regulations that threaten energy affordability and electric grid reliability. Capito also praised her work with Whitehouse on permitting reform. Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-WY) thanked both lawmakers and said she was disappointed that her bipartisan legislation failed in a partisan vote in early September.

Political Stakes

The votes divided the committee along party lines. Bloomberg Law reported that Democrats and independents opposed Schwab's nomination. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce wrote the committee on Nov. 16 that it strongly supported the nomination.

Despite their disagreements over Schwab, Capito and Whitehouse continued to cooperate on permitting reform. The Senate passed their bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act by a 62-33 vote on Nov. 19, according to Capito's statement. The legislation seeks to accelerate energy and infrastructure permitting while maintaining environmental and historic preservation safeguards.

The Bottom Line

Schwab's nomination, PN1366-5, advanced to the full Senate for consideration. Capito indicated that the committee could meet again in December. If confirmed, Schwab would oversee the EPA office that administers federal air quality and emissions regulations as the Trump administration pursues changes to environmental protections.

text:
BY NICK EVANS

Ohio Capital Journal

The Ohio Manufacturers’ Association is urging federal regulators to “break the mold and retool” energy markets.

A letter from the association sent earlier this month comes as regional grid operators like PJM Interconnection, state regulators, and lawmakers continue to wrestle with how to manage demand from data centers.

The association’s critiques aren’t new. The group contends regulators aren’t doing enough to scrutinize major transmission projects or data centers’ forecasts for their future demand. At the heart of the debate is the question of who pays for data centers’ development. In both cases, the association contends, ratepayers wind up covering the bill.

GET THE MORNING HEADLINES FROM OHIO CAPITAL JOURNAL

Industry groups like the Data Center Coalition have repeatedly insisted they’re ready to pay their own way. In a statement, the coalition’s Aaron Tinjum said coalition members “are committed to paying the full cost of infrastructure built to serve their facilities to ensure those costs aren’t shouldered by homes and other businesses.”

“When data centers pay their full cost of service, they share in existing fixed grid costs,” Tinjum went on. “Because those fixed costs would have otherwise been paid by existing customers, new data centers can help alleviate pressure on rates for other customers.”

The magnitude of the industry’s demand is vast — prompting utilities to invest in broader grid improvements and roiling the capacity marketplace PJM uses ensure reliability. Those indirect costs could eventually land on consumers’ bills if policymakers don’t step in to assign them differently.

State lawmakers drafted a data center bill this summer but failed to pass the measure before recess. Ohio House Speakers Matt Huffman told reporters that lawmakers are continuing to work on the bill.

The Ohio Manufacturers’ Association sees a more direct path. To make sure data centers cover their costs, the organization wants them to contract and pay for their infrastructure and power generation up front.

“Risky investment decisions of this magnitude should not be made by government or utility intermediaries who bear no risk,” Ohio Manufacturers’ Association President Ryan Augsburger wrote. “Competitive markets are the obvious solution.”

Augsburger is particularly critical of PJM’s capacity market, which uses an auction to ensure power is available to meet peak demand. Capacity prices have ballooned in recent years as a sharp increase in demand from data centers mixed with a logjam in PJM’s queue for new power plants.

[RELATED: Data centers go 0-for-21 in ballot initiatives around Ohio]

Augsburger thinks the grid operator should lose its control over the capacity market. Under PJM’s leadership, he said, the market is “more political than functional” and “produc(es) economy-crushing electric costs with little to show.”

“To have a true market,” Augsburger went on, “multiple sellers need to compete for multiple buyers. To get politics and stalemates out of the capacity market, PJM’s sole-buyer role for capacity needs to go.”

What comes next?

For months, PJM officials have acknowledged their approach to the capacity market may no longer work, and the organization is publicly mulling what might replace it.

Following a 2024 auction that saw capacity prices climb more than 833%, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro sued PJM. As part of a court order, PJM capped capacity prices for several years.

“The capacity market’s done great,” PJM’s Asim Haque told Ohio lawmakers last May. “(It) did great during the shale revolution. It’s done its job for a particular period, but what we’ve done by putting this cap on the marketplace is we bought ourselves some time to potentially re-imagine what that marketplace should look like.”

In a recent white paper, PJM floated three different possibilities.

One would move to a longer-term model to ensure reliability instead of updating capacity prices through annual auctions.

Another would abandon the longstanding idea that all energy users should have the same standard of reliability.

Instead, PJM and its stakeholders would have to figure out ahead of time how to prioritize customers when demand peaks.

Third, PJM could move away from a capacity market — commitments to provide power on demand in the future — and instead structure its efforts around buying energy itself.

PJM doesn’t take a position on which approach is best. In a statement, spokesman Jeff Shields said, “PJM and its stakeholders expect to take action on evolving this market in the very near term.”

[RELATED: Will Ohio lawmakers pass data center legislation during lame duck?]

Shields also noted two Ohio stakeholders have weighed in on how PJM should proceed.

The Ohio Energy Group, whose members include energy intensive companies like Cleveland Cliffs, Ford, and Intel, proposes drawing a line in the sand.

Data centers that haven’t come online by June of next year would be placed in a new category, responsible for the cost of building new power.

That new power should have no price caps, but OEG thinks with a few tweaks, legacy power plants could continue operating with the current capped capacity market.

The Public Utility Commission of Ohio said it “feels strongly” that PJM should continue running the capacity market and favors PJM’s first path which avoids volatility by moving to longer-term capacity purchases.

Unlike the Ohio Manufacturers’ Association’s call for a wide-open market, the commission sees efficiencies in PJM operating as the sole buyer.

“It is unclear why the benefits of centralized procurement should be discarded in favor of a less-efficient, balkanized model,” the commission stated.

From the Ohio Manufacturers’ Association’s perspective, however, PJM’s long-term approach just locks in risk.

“PJM’s auction design could commit regular customers to finance the riskiest bets made by the wealthiest of technology and energy companies,” Augsburger wrote. “This is the antithesis of customer protection.”

Shields dismissed the Ohio Manufacturers’ Association’s critiques, particularly when it comes to group’s skepticism about data center demand forecasts.

The organization’s “motivations for continuing to express that data center load growth is not real should be examined by its members and state government to ensure accountability for the organization,” Shields said.

Also from Ohio Capital Journal

Ohio OKs gas plant for data centers despite local voter backlash

Ohio regulators just greenlit construction of a big gas plant to power a data center complex, despite local residents’ overwhelming rejection of the projects in this month’s elections.

The permit approval itself is not unique: Around the U.S., energy-hungry data center developers are racing ahead with controversial plans to build natural gas–fired generation. But critics of the recent Ohio ruling say it highlights the state’s leniency toward fossil-fuel projects compared with its tight restrictions on solar and wind farms, which are often denied permits due to local opposition.

“There’s a huge double standard for fossil fuels and renewables in the state of Ohio,” said state Rep. Tristan Rader, a Democrat who serves as ranking minority member on the Ohio House Energy Committee and took part in the case as a nonvoting member of the Ohio Power Siting Board.

name: American Energy
title: 5 Things You Didn't Know About BAAJA and Data Centers
description:
For the data center industry, the appeal of permitting reform is readily apparent.
Here are five provisions that warrant particularly close attention from data center developers, operators, investors and technology suppliers.
Data centers could find themselves bidding against one another for electricity Perhaps the most striking language in Section 2107 concerns how states could allocate access to electricity among competing data center projects.
The provision is especially noteworthy in light of the increasingly organized opposition to data center development examined in DCF's recent feature, The Data Center Backlash Has a Playbook.
The end of business as usual for data center power procurement For much of its history, the data center industry operated within a relatively conventional framework of real estate development, utility service agreements and economic development incentives.
text:
For an industry increasingly accustomed to measuring its growth prospects in gigawatts, the most consequential development in American data center infrastructure this November may have come not from a hyperscaler, a semiconductor manufacturer or an electric utility, but from the floor of the U.S. Senate.

On Nov. 19, the Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, better known as BAAJA, by a vote of 62-33. The sweeping legislative package seeks to accelerate the development of American energy and transmission infrastructure through changes to federal permitting, environmental review, judicial proceedings and electricity regulation. The legislation now faces consideration in the House.

For the data center industry, the appeal of permitting reform is readily apparent. As DCF has reported, transmission infrastructure is emerging as a defining constraint on AI data center development, with the timelines required to construct new electrical infrastructure increasingly at odds with the deployment schedules envisioned by AI infrastructure investors and developers.

But a closer reading of the Senate-passed legislation reveals something more consequential than an attempt to accelerate the construction of power plants and transmission lines. BAAJA is also an attempt to establish the economic and regulatory terms under which America's rapidly expanding computational infrastructure will interact with the nation's electricity system and the communities that host it.

Here are five provisions that warrant particularly close attention from data center developers, operators, investors and technology suppliers.

1. BAAJA is no longer just about hyperscale data centers

One of the more significant changes between the legislation introduced on Sept. 30 and the version passed by the Senate concerns the size of the data centers subject to its ratepayer protection provisions.

The original legislation established a 20-megawatt threshold for its retail ratepayer protections, as outlined in an October analysis by attorneys at Foley Hoag. That threshold is absent from the Senate-passed version of Section 2107, which instead defines covered computational facilities primarily by their function. Computing equipment supporting an otherwise unrelated commercial or industrial operation is excluded.

The change potentially brings a much broader segment of the industry into the scope of these provisions, including regional colocation facilities, emerging AI infrastructure providers and smaller inference-oriented developments.

For new data center interconnections following enactment, the legislation would protect other utility customers against the incremental costs of serving those facilities. Utilities would require financial assurances or contributions ahead of necessary infrastructure investments, while service agreements would provide for continued cost recovery even if a data center customer ceases purchasing electricity before those investments have been recovered.

The implications extend beyond electricity pricing. A hyperscaler with an investment-grade balance sheet may be considerably better positioned to accommodate such requirements than an independent developer pursuing a speculative campus or an emerging neocloud seeking to finance its next phase of expansion.

As Metlen's Lillian Kasa discussed in a recent interview on the DCF Show, the distinction between announced infrastructure capacity and capacity that can actually be delivered is becoming increasingly important to the industry's investment calculus.

BAAJA could add another dimension to that distinction: the ability of a developer or its customers to financially stand behind the electrical infrastructure their projects require.

2. Data centers could find themselves bidding against one another for electricity

Perhaps the most striking language in Section 2107 concerns how states could allocate access to electricity among competing data center projects.

The legislation explicitly recognizes state authority to use competitive solicitations or open seasons to award electric service opportunities according to the financial benefits projects would provide to other ratepayers, measured on a net present value basis, rather than simply according to the order in which applications were received.

States could also establish distinct retail electricity customer classifications for data centers, offer them less favorable service terms or priorities than traditional industrial and manufacturing customers, and condition electric service on commitments to secure additional generation or accept restrictions on grid withdrawals.

These provisions would not establish a mandatory national bidding system for data center power. They instead affirm existing state authority and provide a framework that individual jurisdictions could elect to employ.

At the federal level, BAAJA would also direct the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to revise its transmission pricing policy so that eligible data center loads bear both a share of existing transmission costs and an assessment of the additional costs attributable to serving them.

A Nov. 2 analysis by power sector consultancy Grid Strategies estimated that transmission pricing reforms under the earlier version of BAAJA could generate $55 billion in payments from data centers over a decade, including $35 billion beyond what the industry might otherwise pay under existing policy. The estimate predates Senate passage and should be understood as a modeled outcome rather than a definitive assessment of the final legislation.

For developers competing for scarce electrical capacity in established and emerging data center markets, the implications could be substantial. Securing land and an early position in a utility's service queue may prove less advantageous in jurisdictions that elect to prioritize projects according to their broader economic contribution to the electricity system.

Competition for power could increasingly become competition over the quality of the financial proposition a developer brings to the grid.

3. BAAJA could turn data center power infrastructure into a revenue-generating asset

While much of the attention surrounding BAAJA has centered on what data centers might be required to pay for electricity, another provision addresses how certain distributed energy resources might earn revenue by participating in electricity markets.

Section 2108 seeks to remove barriers to wholesale market participation for aggregated behind-the-meter resources, including qualifying battery storage systems, fuel cells and generators. Individual resources would need to fall within a capacity range of 5 kW to 5 MW, respond to dispatch requests within 15 minutes and satisfy applicable metering and telemetry requirements. Aggregations would require a combined capacity of at least 100 kW.

The provision builds on the framework established by FERC Order 2222, which sought to enable distributed energy resource aggregations to participate in organized wholesale electricity markets.

It is important to distinguish this opportunity from a blanket authorization for hyperscale data center power plants to sell electricity into the grid. Eligibility would depend on the configuration of individual resources, market participation requirements and applicable interconnection, reliability and environmental restrictions.

Nevertheless, the provision arrives at an intriguing moment in the evolution of data center electrical architecture. The industry's embrace of onsite generation, battery storage and microgrids is coinciding with growing interest in the ability of AI computing infrastructure to respond dynamically to electricity system conditions.

Section 2107's separate provision for preferential transmission pricing for eligible customers accepting non-firm service reinforces that direction of travel.

As DCF examined in its recent feature on the evolving economics of AI infrastructure, power procurement decisions are becoming inseparable from decisions about facility architecture, operational flexibility and long-term capital efficiency.

Under the right circumstances, electrical assets traditionally designed around the singular objective of uptime could also acquire an economic value outside the walls of the data center. That possibility could influence how operators evaluate investments in storage, UPS systems, microgrid controls and workload orchestration, provided that participation in energy markets does not compromise mission-critical operations.

4. The federal government would start counting data center electricity consumption separately

For all the attention devoted to forecasts of AI electricity demand, the federal government's principal annual survey of electric utilities does not currently report data centers as a distinct end-use sector.

Section 2114 of BAAJA would change that by directing the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) to revise its Form EIA-861 annual electricity industry survey to separately capture information on computational facilities.

The significance of the provision becomes apparent when considering how electricity demand projections are currently constructed. Estimates of future data center consumption frequently draw on utility load forecasts, developer announcements, semiconductor deployment projections and assumptions concerning the utilization and efficiency of AI infrastructure. Differences in methodology can produce substantially different estimates of the industry's trajectory.

More consistent reporting could provide policymakers, utilities and infrastructure investors with a firmer empirical basis for evaluating that trajectory. It could also help distinguish data center electricity consumption from the broader commercial and industrial demand categories in which it has historically been reported.

The legislation does not establish a publicly accessible, facility-by-facility inventory of data center electricity consumption, nor does it directly impose a reporting obligation on every individual operator. The granularity and usefulness of the resulting information will depend on how EIA implements the provision.

But in an industry increasingly characterized by announced megawatts, contracted megawatts and energized megawatts, better federal reporting could help establish a more credible measure of how much electricity America's computational infrastructure is actually using.

5. Washington wants to teach local communities how data centers work

Perhaps the most unexpected provision in the Senate-passed legislation concerns neither electricity pricing nor energy infrastructure permitting.

Section 2117 would require the Department of Energy to establish a Data Center Community Assistance Program within 180 days of enactment, providing state, local and tribal governments with access to technical expertise as they evaluate proposed data center developments.

The scope of the program is remarkably broad. It encompasses electricity demand, required grid investments, water consumption, cooling alternatives, onsite generation, backup power, employment, tax revenues and the public incentives associated with individual projects.

DOE would also be required to publish a plain-English Data Center Community Toolkit explaining fundamental industry concepts, including the distinction between megawatts and megawatt-hours, power usage effectiveness (PUE), water usage effectiveness (WUE), cooling technologies and utility rate structures.

Local governments could request independent technical evaluations of developers' projections and underlying assumptions, although the provision of project information by developers would be voluntary. DOE would not be empowered under the program to approve or reject individual data center projects, or to recommend such decisions to local authorities.

The provision is especially noteworthy in light of the increasingly organized opposition to data center development examined in DCF's recent feature, The Data Center Backlash Has a Playbook.

Municipal officials and planning boards confronted with proposals for large-scale computational infrastructure are frequently being asked to evaluate complex engineering and economic questions that fall well outside their traditional areas of expertise. Meanwhile, developers accustomed to conducting sophisticated commercial negotiations are finding that the technical and financial assumptions underlying their projects are becoming matters of intense public scrutiny.

BAAJA's proposed community assistance program represents a federal acknowledgment of that information asymmetry.

For the industry, its emergence could raise the standard of technical disclosure expected during local development negotiations. It could also provide an opportunity for developers with credible resource-use projections, transparent infrastructure agreements and demonstrable economic benefits to differentiate their projects.

The end of business as usual for data center power procurement

For much of its history, the data center industry operated within a relatively conventional framework of real estate development, utility service agreements and economic development incentives. The unprecedented electricity requirements of AI infrastructure are forcing a reconsideration of that framework.

BAAJA's broader permitting provisions remain contentious. Supporters argue that lengthy approval processes impede the development of energy infrastructure necessary to meet rising demand and contain electricity costs. Environmental organizations and other critics have expressed concern that changes to federal environmental protections and judicial review could come at the expense of communities and natural resources.

The legislation must still clear the House, and further revisions remain possible. Even if enacted, BAAJA would not eliminate electricity supply constraints, guarantee faster data center deployments or resolve the increasingly difficult question of community acceptance.

But the five provisions examined here point toward a new bargain between the data center industry and the country hosting its expansion: greater opportunity to build energy infrastructure, accompanied by greater financial responsibility, incentives for operational flexibility and heightened public accountability.

For data center developers, the question increasingly may not simply be whether they can secure the power they need, but what they are prepared to contribute in return.

text:
U.S. data centers are driving greater power demand, and with it, more pollution from coal and gas power plants. Researchers estimate that worsening pollution is leading to hundreds of early deaths.

The new modeling study finds that, in 2023, the added power demand from data centers led to an estimated 650 early deaths across the U.S. Given the rapid buildout of data centers, their impact would likely be even greater today, authors say.

The study further suggests that pollution is often intensifying far from where data centers are located. For instance, data centers in Virginia — which are connected to a large regional power grid — might spur power plants in the Midwest to ramp up. As their power output grows, so does particulate pollution, a contaminant linked to heart attacks, strokes, and lung disease.

“Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” said coauthor Noelle Selin, head of the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy at MIT. The findings were published in Environmental Research Letters.

A separate study, published this month in Nature Sustainability, looks at the impact of more than 400 hyperscale data centers across the U.S. It found the facilities are using as much electricity as 8 million homes. In Oregon and Virginia, two data center hotspots, they are consuming more than 15 percent of the electricity sold in each state.

name: IRA Tax Credits
title: 'Ugly and mishmashy' U.S. solar manufacturing policy leaves important questions unanswered
description:
Spurred by the manufacturing production tax credits under Section 45X, domestic solar module nameplate capacity has increased from less than 10 GW four years ago to a reported 80.6 GW today, according to the latest numbers from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA).
“There’s really no denying that 45X was the most important policy driver,” said Elissa Pierce, a solar module supply chain analyst at Wood Mackenzie.
But Pierce went further, adding that tariffs have been “an important piece” to support domestic manufacturing.
Pierce explained that Wood Mackenzie anticipates about 30 GW of domestic solar cell manufacturing capacity by 2030, but said that current policy is not likely to result in a great deal more upstream production.
After so many years of lagging behind, the road to onshoring solar manufacturing in both the U.S. and India still runs through China.
text:
In the years since the passage of the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022, the United States solar manufacturing sector has seen growth in its capacity to produce finished modules using domestic components that might have seemed unimaginable prior to the law’s introduction.

Spurred by the manufacturing production tax credits under Section 45X, domestic solar module nameplate capacity has increased from less than 10 GW four years ago to a reported 80.6 GW today, according to the latest numbers from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA).

But module assembly represents only the final step of a long chain of raw material supply and manufacturing, and the ability of U.S.-based companies to produce upstream components like crystalline silicon ingots, wafers and cells has lagged severely behind that of China. With something like 10 GW each in operating ingot, wafer and cell manufacturing facilities, the U.S. now has a severe imbalance in the inputs to the module assembly process.

That imbalance is largely due to the lack of a clear roadmap for onshoring production of the upstream materials, according to a panel of three experts who participated in a recent session at RE+ 2026 called “Hot Takes, Hard Numbers: The Future of U.S. Solar Manufacturing According to Leading Analysts.”

One of those experts, Alex Barrows, head of PV analytics at CRU Group, described recent U.S. policy in his opening remarks as “a piecemeal mishmash of AD/CVD cases, 45X, 232, [and] various other tariffs.”

Barrows pointed specifically to the Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit under Section 45X of the U.S. tax code as the policy that has driven most domestic manufacturing expansion. The other panelists agreed.

“There’s really no denying that 45X was the most important policy driver,” said Elissa Pierce, a solar module supply chain analyst at Wood Mackenzie. But Pierce went further, adding that tariffs have been “an important piece” to support domestic manufacturing.

The third analyst, Intertek CEA research manager for policy Christian Roselund, pushed back on that idea, explaining that in his view, tariffs like those imposed following antidumping and countervailing duty (AD/CVD) investigations have done little more than raise prices for upstream components and cause manufacturing to move around the world to places not subject to the added duties.

“Those who have suggested that the AD/CVD cases are an effective way to onshore don’t really have any evidence to support that,” Roselund said. “I think there’s a lot of evidence in the opposite: that actually it just simply chased manufacturing around the globe.”

Later in his comments, Roselund doubled down on his distaste for tariffs, this time mentioning the tariffs imposed in 2018 under Section 201 of the 1974 Trade Act and the tariffs set to take effect in December under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.

“The challenge that we come to [with tariffs]… is when you live in a world of globally interconnected supply chains, if you tariff the upstream component that manufacturing is dependent on, you don’t support manufacturing,” Roselund said.

On the topic of the Section 232 proclamation establishing minimum import prices, Pierce pointed out that she looked forward to future guidance from the Commerce Department on certain parts of the plan that were not well defined in the initial document.

“If you’re actively building upstream manufacturing facilities in the U.S., you should get some kind of exemption or discount to those tariffs so that you can import the components you need in order to bring those factories online at scale and ramp them up,” she said. “This takes time, obviously, but I do think that there needs to be some future goal to implement these to spur manufacturers to bring those factories online.”

Barrows called Section 232 “a good example of where U.S. policy is sort of ugly and mishmashy,” adding, “we all spent a year waiting… and it came out and we all had a whole bunch of questions around how it’s going to work that still aren’t answered. We don’t quite know how onshoring is going to work and who’s going to get what deals. It is not a good way to set a nice roadmap for manufacturers to know what they can do, what they should do, when they can do it, and what they can rely on.”

India’s predictable roadmap

In pointing to an example of a more straightforward nationwide manufacturing onshoring policy, Barrows identified the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) framework put into place by India’s Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE).

“I really like the Indian approach of [having] a clear roadmap,” Barrows said. “It was very well signposted that 2024 was the year where you needed to go to domestic module, 2026 for cell, 2028 for wafer… I think it’s a pity that the U.S. did not take that approach.”

Under the ALMM framework, all solar projects that receive government backing in India must include modules assembled in the country that are made using India-manufactured cells from a list of approved suppliers. The framework has evolved over time, with an initial deadline for module assembly in the country by April 1, 2024 (ALMM List-I), a secondary deadline for cells on June 1, 2026 (ALMM List-II). A third deadline for the domestic production of ingots and wafers (ALMM List-III) is set for June 1, 2028.

Roselund expressed agreement with Barrows’s assessment of India’s strategy, contrasting it with what he called a “chaotic jumble of policies that are utterly unpredictable in the United States.”

“Let’s not forget that one of the things that manufacturers need more than anything is predictability in policy,” Roselund said. “I think India has managed that much more successfully in terms of having clear, predictable, relatively stable policies that now have resulted in giving India a larger module and cell manufacturing capacity than the United States.”

Still, he cautioned, India continues to struggle to bring ingot and wafer manufacturing online ahead of the coming 2028 deadline.

The “safe bet premium”

When asked by moderator and SEIA manufacturing and supply chain senior director Jade Jones how U.S. solar module buyers have evolved in their expectations in the past several years, Roselund was quick to reply.

“Well, they’ve had to get used to worse product,” he said, adding “their best sources of supply were progressively cut off.” He explained that product quality issues have become a major concern for buyers as suppliers both new and existing have worked to stand up new module assembly lines.

Roselund went on to point out that options available to domestic buyers include modules made with older PERC cell technology, imported products which now cost more than 40 cents per watt following the Section 232 proclamation or premium products made with a limited supply of domestic TOPCon cells.

Barrows agreed, noting that the “safe bet premium” is worth more in the U.S., where supply chain traceability and intellectual property risks are a bigger factor than in other countries. “Elsewhere, essentially people are competing mostly on price and technology. In the U.S., you can get away with being relatively low efficiency if you have a product that’s considered a safe bet and you have that product available,” he said, then reiterated, “In the U.S., you can run a PERC line. There’s kind of nowhere else in the world that you can get away with that.”

Responding to the concerns raised by the two other panelists about how non-market factors affect competition among module producers in the U.S., Pierce had this to say: “Sometimes it’s just the price you have to pay to compete with a country that’s been doing this at such [a] larger scale for decades. We’re really coming from behind here. Sacrifices have to be made in order to scale up our domestic manufacturing industry.”

Demand dynamics and future uncertainty

Asked to look into their proverbial crystal balls, the analysts expressed mixed opinions about the likely future of polysilicon-based solar materials manufacturing in the United States.

Pierce explained that Wood Mackenzie anticipates about 30 GW of domestic solar cell manufacturing capacity by 2030, but said that current policy is not likely to result in a great deal more upstream production. “I wouldn’t expect to see a lot of growth in polysilicon or wafer manufacturing,” she said. “The incentives are just not there right now.”

Barrows expressed his “bullish” belief that the 45X manufacturing tax credits will be extended and the Department of Commerce would issue sensible rules that allow companies to continue to import upstream materials as they onshore production. By 2030, he said, “we’ll be seeing mostly U.S. modules using a mix of imported cells, but those cell manufacturers are still mostly going to be using imported wafers, even if we’ve got some more ingot and wafer factories being built by then.”

Barrows ended his comments by saying “I’m optimistic that we’ll get some more incentives and we’ll at least be building more ingot and wafer factories,” but noted that no matter what transpires, manufacturers would still need to use a lot of Chinese supplies, such as silver paste.

Roselund added a final word, saying he also anticipates an extension to Section 45X tax credits, but not until 2029, a deadline he described as “too late to effectively incentivize anything in the near term, but maybe not so late that it causes a mass die-off in the industry when 45X expires.”

He went on to caution that building new factories takes a special interest from sources of “patient capital” willing to wait five years or more for return on their investment, as well as expertise, which mostly comes from China.

After so many years of lagging behind, the road to onshoring solar manufacturing in both the U.S. and India still runs through China.

text:
Friends of the Earth (Hong Kong) has backed the government’s proposed Battery Traceability Mechanism, saying it could help keep electric-vehicle batteries within regulated recycling channels.

The proposed system would require suppliers, scheme operators, vehicle maintenance workshops, scrapyards, recyclers and vehicle owners to submit declarations based on their roles at different stages of a battery’s lifecycle. Depending on the stage, information could include battery identification numbers and weights, quantities distributed, vehicle chassis numbers and battery movements.

The environmental group said EV batteries are valuable and require complex handling procedures. Without a traceability system, batteries could be illegally dismantled, moved across borders without oversight or stored improperly, it warned.

In addition to the proposed electronic declaration system, Friends of the Earth (HK) also called for a public channel to release aggregated statistics to improve transparency and accountability. It urged the government to publish how the recycling levy is calculated, annual review findings and a breakdown of recycling costs, and to adjust the levy when needed.

The group called for tighter safety requirements at vehicle scrapyards and maintenance workshops to reduce the risk of lithium-ion battery fires. It also urged the government to begin preparatory work promptly, including setting up a voluntary battery registration and tracking system by 2027 so major EV suppliers, repair workshops, scrapyards and recyclers can test the declaration process.

It said the government should also provide advance details of battery return-point locations, safety procedures and the levy calculation method so businesses and vehicle owners have time to prepare.

text:
Scout Motors, the new Volkswagen Group-owned brand aiming to launch an off-road pickup and SUV in the U.S. by 2028, confirmed its plans for Canada earlier this month, even as the tariff war continues and a new trade agreement remains up in the air.

As reported by Automotive News, seven dealerships—or "workshops," as the company calls them—will be established on this side of the border. When will they open exactly? That is still undecided.

Read also

All-New Scout Traveler, Terra Ready to Take on Rivian and More

Here’s Why VW Chose Scout for its New EV Truck Brand

There will be three in the Toronto area, two in Montreal, one in Ottawa and another one in Vancouver. All are expected to be open by 2033, handling both sales and service.

Validation and Pre-Production

The new Scout Motors plant in Blythewood, South Carolina, is nearing completion. Teams are currently welding, painting and assembling validation units of the Traveler SUV and Terra pickup.

As the company explains, these early prototypes will help validate vehicle engineering, buildability and parts maturity while confirming that newly installed equipment is set up and functioning as expected. That effort will continue and mature into 2027, with customer deliveries of new Scout vehicles expected to begin in 2028.

Premium Trucks With a Price to Match

The Scout Traveler and Terra EVs are aimed at off-road enthusiasts, more specifically those with a substantial budget, though pricing has yet to be announced. They will likely be a lot more expensive in Canada, unless an agreement is reached with Washington that would eliminate countertariffs on vehicles imported from the U.S. Basically, Scout Motors will occupy a market position similar to that of Rivian.

That being said, starting in 2029, Scout vehicles—with an optional, range-extending gas engine—will use batteries produced in Ontario by PowerCo, a subsidiary of the Volkswagen Group, which should help lower the cost. Remember, under current rules, the Canadian content of U.S.-made vehicles is not factored into the calculation of tariffs.

According to Scout Motors, approximately 85% of reservations to date are for a model equipped with a range extender. Canadians can reserve a unit with a refundable $150 deposit.

title: BAAJA threatens to disrupt environmental enforcement - Earthjustice
description:
One thing I have not seen adequately discussed is the ways the bill would profoundly chill federal enforcement of our pollution control laws.
For nearly 20 years, I served as an attorney in the Environmental Enforcement Section of the Department of Justice, enforcing those laws on behalf of the American people.
A great deal of government environmental enforcement consists of making sure companies comply with these conditions and imposing penalties to deter future violations.
This enforcement work is crucial to ensuring that the protections promised by environmental law are real.
In my two decades of experience at DOJ, environmental enforcement was approached with care and caution.
text:
I’ve seen many experts weigh in on how BAAJA will impact things like greenhouse gas emissions, electric transmission, and tribal rights. One thing I have not seen adequately discussed is the ways the bill would profoundly chill federal enforcement of our pollution control laws.

For nearly 20 years, I served as an attorney in the Environmental Enforcement Section of the Department of Justice, enforcing those laws on behalf of the American people. My concerns stem from the much-discussed Section 1401 of the bill, which prohibits any government action that “interferes” with the operation of a permitted facility. As others have observed, this provision may protect renewable energy companies from the Trump administration, but it also threatens to insulate other companies from government intervention to protect public health and the environment.

For context, virtually every major industrial facility operates under permits that govern the amounts of pollution they can emit, the pollution controls they must install, and how they must monitor their emissions. A great deal of government environmental enforcement consists of making sure companies comply with these conditions and imposing penalties to deter future violations. This enforcement work is crucial to ensuring that the protections promised by environmental law are real. If there are no consequences for violating the law, there’s little incentive to comply and lots of financial reasons not to.

Doing enforcement work inevitably “interferes” with a facility’s operation within the meaning of Section 1401. That’s the whole point of enforcement lawsuits: to force lawbreaking operators to do things differently so they comply with the law. But Section 1401 is written so broadly that even routine government inspections, which occupy staff time and can require pauses in operation, might fall within its scope.

The bill’s drafters presumably believe that they preserved enforcement authority by including two exceptions to Section 1401. First, the original bill allows the government to act if a permit holder has “materially breached” the terms of a permit or “materially violated applicable law.” And second, a manager’s amendment allows the government to act “pursuant to any applicable law or regulation.” Neither goes far enough.

Section 1401 flips the world of government enforcement on its head by presuming that government action to investigate or enforce the law is unlawful. Instead of exempting enforcement, the bill forces the government to prove that an exception applies. Yes, the government can technically still do its work. But now before taking action the government must demonstrate that a violation has occurred and is “material,” not to mention give the permit holder “a detailed explanation of the action” and “the evidence supporting the action.” It’s hard to inspect facilities or investigate potential wrongdoing, let alone prosecute it, under this approach.

The second exception, which allows the government to act “pursuant to” any laws, might seem to help. Federal law does specifically authorize EPA and the Justice Department to inspect and enforce the law, after all. The problem from my perspective is that this exception is so broad that judges are likely to find ways to narrow its scope. Specifically, judges will want to avoid reading the “pursuant to” exception in ways that swallow the much narrower exception for action against “material” violations. And that’s not just my perspective or that of Earthjustice; prominent scholars and experts agree.

On top of all that, the government faces real risk if it tries to invoke either of these exceptions. Section 1401 allows companies to sue to stop any interference, including enforcement interference. And they have a strong incentive to do so, because it will slow down any enforcement action, because it’s the government that bears the burden of proving that it acted properly, and because a company can recoup punitive damages of no less than 25% of the total of all development and construction costs. While a recent amendment limits these damages to actions taken in bad faith, the potential that an unreasonable and industry-friendly judge could impose damages that dwarf the budget of government enforcement divisions can’t help but exacerbate the chilling effect of the bill.

In my two decades of experience at DOJ, environmental enforcement was approached with care and caution. Every case was vetted through multiple layers of management at DOJ and EPA; litigation risks were considered carefully; substantive decisions made by delegated authorities. There is no doubt that adding additional hurdles, and additional layers of risk, will decrease the number of cases the government is willing to bring—putting the health of our communities at risk.

description:

text:
Top discussion points

• Fashion’s transition is closely tied to the global energy transition, requiring cleaner industrial energy and a move away from fossil-based production.

• Trade and geopolitics shape the cost and feasibility of fashion’s transition because energy disruptions, tariffs, and variable trade rules can raise costs across global fashion supply chains.

• Materials and circularity solutions require a systems approach that addresses emissions, water, pollution, durability, and waste while meeting industry requirements for quality, price, and scale.

• Financing and policy must bring brands, suppliers, and policymakers into alignment around incentives in cleaner production across the supply chain.

Introduction

On September 21, 2026, the Fashion, Energy, and Climate Network at the Columbia Climate School and the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University SIPA convened the inaugural Columbia Fashion, Energy, and Climate Summit, in partnership with the Global Fashion Agenda and with support from Apparel Impact Institute and the Bezos Earth Fund. Under the theme Fashion and the Climate Future, the summit brought together participants from fashion, energy, business, finance, academia, policy, and design to examine how energy systems, materials, markets, trade, finance, regulation, and culture are reshaping the industry.

In the opening keynote, Columbia Climate School Dean Alexis Abramson emphasized that fashion, the energy transition, and climate change are closely linked. Energy powers the full lifecycle of a garment, from fiber processing and dyeing to factories, logistics, laundering, repair, and recycling. As she put it, “The energy transition is not peripheral to the future of fashion. It is woven through it.” The sessions that followed examined how energy and material choices affect fashion production, and how trade, financing, regulation, and design can shape the industry’s transition. The following summarizes key insights that emerged from the discussion.

Fashion’s transition is also an energy and industrial transition

On fashion’s industrial transition, participants noted that much of fashion’s climate impact occurs upstream, before a garment reaches a store. Producing yarn, fabric, and finished clothing requires machinery, electricity, and heat. Dyeing, for example, uses large quantities of heat and water. Emissions from these processes depend partly on the fuels burned in factories and the sources of electricity available in manufacturing regions. Fossil fuels also supply material inputs: petrochemicals made from oil are used to produce synthetic fibers such as polyester. Cleaner factory electricity does not, by itself, change the fossil-based materials used in those fabrics.

The discussion also highlighted methane emissions linked to livestock-derived materials, such as leather, wool, and cashmere. This broadens the industry’s climate footprint beyond carbon dioxide from energy use. These considerations also brought the challenges of sustainable luxury into focus, with participants questioning the use of inexpensive polyester in high-priced products and weighing the trade-offs involved in using natural materials. Examples raised included incorporating deadstock textiles, reducing packaging waste, and designing for durability, illustrating how environmental choices intersect with profit margins and product strategy.

One participant cited China’s power transition as an example of how changing energy systems shape fashion’s emissions. As the participant explained, expanding non-fossil electricity requires investment in storage and long-distance transmission, as well as power-market reform. These changes help reduce emissions from textile manufacturing because factory electricity emissions depend on the power supply in the locations where production takes place.

Energy security, geopolitics, and trade affect supply-chain resilience

Fashion’s reliance on global energy and materials markets makes it vulnerable to disruptions, even when they occur far from where clothing is sold. Participants discussed how conflict in the Middle East disrupted energy supplies and petrochemical feedstock exports to China and raised oil prices and shipping costs. Because oil is key to producing synthetic fibers and fuel is essential to moving goods, these disruptions increased costs across the fashion value chain. One participant noted that earlier decisions to use recycled polyester or lower-carbon shipping could have reduced exposure to these price increases.

Trade is equally central to these supply-chain dynamics. Participants emphasized that textiles and apparel constitute a major globally traded sector, with production concentrated in parts of South and Southeast Asia. As in other internationally traded industries, the transition to more sustainable production raises questions about how to maintain competitiveness and share costs among governments, brands, suppliers, and consumers. Conditions in major manufacturing economies can therefore affect businesses far beyond their borders.

Climate change adds risks at the factory level. Participants described the health consequences of extreme heat for garment workers, especially where equipment and processes make indoor temperatures hotter than outdoors. As they pointed out, brand purchasing terms and delivery deadlines can constrain suppliers’ ability to reduce or pause production during dangerous heat, while unreliable electricity can lead factories to burn diesel to keep operating. Resilience thus depends on production conditions, not only sourcing locations.

Lower-impact materials must be practical as well as innovative

Participants cautioned that materials cannot be considered “low impact” based on carbon emissions alone. Water use, pollution, farming practices, human health, durability, and the ability to reuse or recycle also matter. Changing materials may reduce one impact while increasing another.

Participants discussed technologies that could help reduce environmental impacts earlier in production. Several researchers described using machine learning and cotton genetics to identify varieties suited to different growing conditions. Others described how biofabrication—the use of biological processes to create materials—can lead to alternatives to conventional textiles. Examples raised included silkworms engineered to produce colored silk and cotton that grows with color, both of which could reduce the need for dyeing. Participants also considered lessons from research on degradable medical materials, the potential for digital models to identify manufacturing waste, and whether textile and footwear waste could find new uses in construction materials.

Yet, as participants noted, technical promise does not guarantee adoption. New technologies must meet requirements for appearance, quality, price, performance, and large-scale production. Farmers and manufacturers also need an incentive and the capacity to make the change. Speakers stressed the value of involving farmers and manufacturers early in the development process, rather than developing an innovation first and looking for a supply chain afterward. While new technologies are still in development, using existing material stock, repairing products, and improving textile sorting can reduce waste.

Transition finance must account for who pays and who benefits

The financing discussion highlighted a structural challenge: the businesses expected to invest in decarbonization are not always those that receive its most visible benefits. A textile supplier may need to borrow money for efficient equipment or cleaner production processes, even though the factory serves many brands. As participants observed, the resulting emissions reductions help those brands meet their Scope 3 goals, which cover indirect emissions in their value chains. The supplier, meanwhile, remains responsible for the debt and for keeping production running during installation.

Participants discussed how this mismatch explains why capital alone is insufficient. Suppliers may need technical advice to select suitable equipment, reliable orders to justify repayment, and agreement among customers on how a new process will affect product specifications. For example, a factory may be reluctant to invest in waterless dyeing if its brand customers disagree about the technology or will not accept initial adjustments in product quality.

One collaborative approach discussed at the summit involved bringing together brands that share suppliers to agree on which decarbonization projects to support. Technical assistance can help define the investments, while commercial-bank loans backed by brand guarantees can reduce the suppliers’ financing costs. Participants also stressed that decisions should account for the cost of inaction, including exposure to future energy prices, regulation, and disrupted production. Financing mechanisms must align demand, risk, and benefits, not simply provide loans.

Regulations are changing the terms of global fashion trade

Global Fashion Agenda, the summit’s event partner, hosted its Policy Master Class during the summit, examining how sustainability rules are being integrated into everyday business operations. Emerging European requirements on product design, traceability, waste, and extended producer responsibility could compel companies selling into EU markets to change how they source materials and document products. Extended producer responsibility, for example, makes producers responsible for managing products after their useful life has ended, creating financial incentives to incorporate collection and recycling considerations into product design.

Because fashion supply chains span many countries, rules adopted in one major consumer market can affect manufacturers elsewhere. Participants compared the EU’s broad policy agenda with a more fragmented US approach, where state-level measures play a larger role. Different reporting definitions and product requirements can make compliance costly, particularly for suppliers selling to brands in several markets. Greater alignment among regulatory frameworks could reduce that burden while maintaining environmental objectives.

Participants also questioned whether new rules would create opportunities for manufacturing countries or mainly impose obligations on them. Building circular supply chains across borders will require investment in collection and sorting systems, recycling facilities, and workforce skills in producing economies, including in the Global South. Yet collecting and processing used textiles can cost more than making products from virgin materials. Participants suggested that investment and trade rules therefore must support demand for recovered fibers and markets where circular materials can be sold.

Design and culture can help make circularity viable

Designers help determine which materials are used, how garments are constructed, and whether they can be repaired, reused, or given another life. The final panel highlighted approaches such as zero-waste cutting and using deadstock textiles, which reduce waste during design and production rather than addressing it only afterward.

Independent designers may have limited budgets for researching new materials, but participants described creative experimentation and cooperation as valuable resources. For example, small brands can pool orders to meet a material supplier’s minimum purchase requirement. At the same time, a business need not follow a single growth model: smaller collections, longer-lasting products, and more direct customer relationships can support different approaches to making and selling clothes.

Participants also observed that culture influences whether these models succeed. Repair, craftsmanship, secondhand markets, and garments with personal or historical meaning can encourage people to keep using what they own. Keeping garments in use longer can reduce demand for new materials.

Looking Ahead

The summit demonstrated why fashion’s energy and climate transition cannot be addressed within fashion alone. Textile manufacturing depends on the energy systems of producing countries, and material choices connect the industry to oil, agriculture, and other industries. Trade and policy determine the conditions under which products enter markets, while financing arrangements influence whether factories can invest in cleaner production.

Participants concluded that turning ambition into action will require materials that can be produced at scale, financing and reliable orders that suppliers can count on, and buyers for reused products and recycled fibers. Progress will also depend on linking scientific research with decisions in design, manufacturing, finance, and policy. By bringing these communities together, the summit provided a forum to explore how choices across all these areas can reinforce one another.

text:
California’s clean air rules for cars and trucks have come under fire from the Trump administration. But a lesser-known rule targeting pollution from ships docked at the nation’s busiest ports is also at risk.

The ports of L.A. and Long Beach are the single largest fixed source of smog in Southern California. The biggest cause of that pollution is ships from all over the world traversing the ports and idling at their docks.

And some of the densest neighborhoods in the region are right nearby.

“Long Beach, Wilmington, San Pedro,” said Earthjustice attorney and longtime clean air advocate Adrian Martinez. “In those communities, you have people literally living right next to where these ships were belching out really toxic pollution.”

Those fumes, largely from burning diesel fuel, have been linked to higher rates of cancer.

“We cannot solve our air pollution crisis in a place like Los Angeles unless we meaningfully and significantly drive down pollution from ships,” Martinez said.

The effort to revoke California’s clean ship rule

That’s why, back in 2007, the state approved the first version of what’s called the ocean-going vessels at-berth regulation. In general, the law requires certain ships to either turn off diesel engines and plug in to electrical power at the port when they’re unloading or capture the pollution that comes out of their smokestacks.

Container ships, passenger ships and refrigerated-cargo ships have been phased into compliance since 2014, reducing smog-forming emissions from those sources by 80%, according to the California Air Resources Board. Since 2023, the rule has expanded to include more stringent emissions standards and more types of vessels.

“It's really one of the most important public health measures,” Martinez said.

Still, work remains to cut pollution. Southern California regularly exceeds federal air quality standards for fine particulate matter and ground-level ozone.

But one of the key tools to cut such pollution, the at-berth rule, has gotten caught in the crosshairs of the Trump administration’s attacks on California’s clean air regulations. In September, the Republican-controlled House voted to revoke California’s at-berth clean ship waiver.

Now the issue rests with the Senate. But there's a deadline for the Senate to vote, and it’s unclear whether the Republican-dominated chamber will take up the issue before time runs out this year.

Those fighting the at-berth regulation argue that it increases costs, which get passed on to consumers, and that the technology just isn’t ready.

Capturing at-berth pollution

The ability for ships to connect to power at dock, called shore power, is slowly growing. But most ships still don’t have the ability to connect to that power, and there’s still not enough renewable energy to support it.

Plugging into clean electric shore power is the ideal solution, Martinez said, but ”the public health crisis from shipping is so great that we need all sorts of solutions.”

That’s why a handful of companies, including Stax Engineering, have invested in pollution capture.

At the company’s berth at the Port of Long Beach one recent morning, two huge neon green barges were docked. Each had a massive, folded mechanical arm that can extend more than 250 feet to connect to the smokestacks of ships.

“It's like a big elephant nose at the end, and it connects to the stack,” said Mike Walker, Stax’s chief executive.

The arm directs soot and smog-forming nitrogen oxides, or NOx, into a processing unit inside three 20-foot containers. There, fine particulate matter is filtered, and a catalyst breaks apart the nitrogen oxides, releasing them back into the atmosphere as nitrogen and oxygen, the components of the air we breathe.

The process captures about 95% of smog-forming NOx and 99% of particulate matter, Walker said.

It has yet to help with planet-heating emissions like carbon dioxide, and small amounts of carbon dioxide are released as part of the process. In terms of pollution from the barges themselves, Walker said, the company also treats its own exhaust and uses lower-carbon fuels like biodiesel.

The company is also expanding into carbon capture. That’s more of a challenge to implement because captured carbon needs to be used or disposed of somewhere, Walker said.

“Longer term, what people are trying to do is reduce carbon across the entire shipping process,” Walker said.

Stax has partnered with the London-based company Seabound to demonstrate how to capture carbon and other pollutants while ships are at sea.

Mike Walker, CEO of Stax Engineering, stands on one of the company's pollution-capturing barges, next to the attachment that directs a ship's exhaust to the processing unit.

(

Erin Stone

/

LAist

)

Stax can customize the smokestack attachment to fit a variety of ships.

(

Erin Stone

/

LAist

)

A growing industry that doesn't drive up costs

Meanwhile, Stax Engineering continues to grow its efforts to capture NOx and particulate matter. The company has eight pollution-capturing barges, with three more coming online soon. The goal is to have 18 operating in the coming years.

Stax employs about 200 people, mostly union jobs. They’re expecting to nearly double that number as new requirements of the at-berth regulation are set to take effect in Northern California. With strong backers, including actor Edward Norton, the company’s chief strategy officer, Walker said the company is well-positioned to meet the state’s evolving at-berth regulations.

“The reality is we're not going to have [cleaner] alternative fuels for 30 years at scale,” Walker said. “So are we just going to pretend those emissions for the next 30 years don't need to be captured? When those alternative fuels come, we're going to have to find another line of business, which we're good with.”

Across the water from the company’s berth, far on the other side of the port, Walker pointed to another Stax barge attached to a massive auto-carrying cargo ship. Instead of dark diesel exhaust spewing from the smokestack, there’s just the green arm of the Stax barge.

“You'd be seeing black exhaust, diesel exhaust,” Walker said. “The numbers are somewhere between 20 [thousand] to 60,000 cars' worth of emissions a day coming out of those vessels.”

The federal government estimates this could add $7.66 to the price of the cars on that ship. For consumer goods, it adds fractions of pennies on the dollar.

That’s why Walker says the argument that the at-berth rule is a significant factor in high prices is "ludicrous.”

“It's kind of what the marching orders are to go against this regulation,” Walker said, “but the math just doesn't add up.”

After the blue wave in the midterm elections, and with other priorities on the minds of Congressional Republicans, Walker hopes the clock on revoking the at-berth regulation waiver just runs out.

The California immunology research institute that is likely to receive over $4 billion under Proposition 38 still has no chief executive.

The institute also had only three workers as of September even though it was supposed to employ more than 50 by the start of the year, CalMatters previously reported. The detail about the chief executive was disclosed last week at a University of California Board of Regents meeting.

Prop. 38, which voters passed this month 54% to 46%, will allocate up to $8.4 billion in bonds for immune system research, with an emphasis on finding treatments for Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The ballot measure stipulates that a single, unnamed research institute will receive half the money to conduct research and partner with other researchers if it meets highly specific criteria. Taxpayers will pay back the bond at about $500 million to $600 million for the next 20 years.

Previous reporting by CalMatters found only one institute in California currently meets those criteria: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, known as CIII. The institute’s principal funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign.

The institute’s board is made up of several wealthy members, including Michelson, as well as Napster co-founder and early Facebook executive Sean Parker, and Michael Milken, an investor sentenced to prison after pleading guilty to securities violations in 1990.

Agreement with UCLA

The university signed an affiliation agreement with the institute in 2024 and four top officials at UCLA also sit on the board. The institute will be one of the main tenants of a new research park owned by UCLA in West Los Angeles that’s under construction.

After obtaining internal records from UCLA about the institute, CalMatters reported last month that the institute’s 5-year business plan called for the nonprofit to hire 51 employees by 2025. They would include six executives, five “world-class” scientists who can lead research labs, and 40 other employees, such as data scientists, lab technicians, biologists and administrative personnel. The agreement stated that between 2025 and 2027, the institute planned to hire roughly 90 more workers, including 10 research lab leaders.

At the November meeting of the UC board of regents, Michael Cohen, a regent, told a member of the institute’s board, UCLA Health CEO John C. Mazziotta, that “there's been some reports” the institute is “well behind schedule from what the original business plan articulated.” Cohen then asked Mazziotta what UCLA Health is doing about it.

Mazziotta said the institute is “in the process of recruiting teams.” He also said it has yet to find a chief executive. He indicated the high salaries CEOs typically earn has slowed the search.

“These are very high-end people who have lots of other opportunities, and so it's taken a little longer than anticipated,” Mazziotta said.

He added that the money from the Prop. 38 bond "will be a huge boon” for hiring employees.

That reliance on the bond funding signals new confidence that the institute will receive the money. In July, Claudia Briggs, a spokesperson for the campaign to pass Prop. 38, said the measure wasn’t written to exclude all California nonprofits other than the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. By October, another spokesperson, Robin Swanson, said while the institute is “very likely” to qualify for the bond funds, it’s not a guarantee.

Where the institute is on its plan

CalMatters asked UCLA Health if the institute still only has three employees; a spokesperson, Phil Hampton, emailed back to say, “We have nothing to add.” A spokesperson for the institute, Becky Warren, emailed to say her remarks for last month’s story still stand. Her written statement didn’t answer CalMatters’ questions about the institute employing far fewer people than the 5-year plan laid out. Nor would she confirm the staffing levels or if a CEO has been hired in an email Tuesday.

While the institute is well behind its hiring goals, it’s moved closer to hitting its spending benchmarks on construction and renovations. It has committed $146 million to build out the research space, which will be owned by UCLA. That’s funded by $250 million Michelson and the other institute founders poured into the nonprofit.

Mazziotta told UC regents in September that the institute had by then spent a total of $20 million on “operating expenses, hires” and other costs.

An opponent of the ballot measure, David Panush, said the lack of a CEO shows Prop 38 was sold on false assurances.

“Prop. 38 proponents promised voters that their institute would be ‘ready-to-go, competitive, and world-class,’” said Panush, who co-led the No on Proposition 38 campaign. “But now we’re learning that CIII just has ‘initial thoughts’ and is still trying to find a CEO. When will we see a plan?”

The No campaign raised $12,000 compared to the Yes on 38’s nearly $72 million.

The next test for the institute begins when the secretary of state certifies the passage of Prop. 38 and it takes effect five days later, on or around Dec. 16.

At that point the California Department of Public Health will have up to 90 days to name the institute that will receive the billions allocated under the proposition. The ballot measure’s language is silent on what that selection process will look like and whether it will be open to public scrutiny.

For now, the department isn’t commenting. CalMatters sought details about the selection process, but Grant Boyken, a spokesperson for the department, said it doesn’t comment on ballot measures before they’re certified.
