The pipes that carried hundreds of thousands of cubic yards of sand and silt onto the Long Beach Peninsula went quiet on Monday, as crews finished a dredging project that city officials hope will protect coastal homes and keep the Peninsula’s historic boardwalk open to the public for decades.

Workers were seen Tuesday dismantling the steel pipeline that for weeks funneled sediment from a dredging barge in the Alamitos Bay entrance channel, over a stone jetty, and onto the thin strip of beach that fronts the Peninsula. A slurry of sand, water and dark clay poured out at the far end, where dozers shaped it into a new beachfront.

The project — the first for the bay in more than 20 years — pulled about 415,000 cubic yards of built-up sediment from the channel so boats could pass safely and retasked it as beachfront.

Planned and funded in 2023, it was slated to start in February, but the city sped up work after a series of storms sent powerful waves that battered the row of multimillion-dollar homes, city boardwalk and bulkhead.

The project finished weeks ahead of schedule and a hair under budget — at about $11.1 million against the $11.4 million projected cost,” said Josh Hickman, the city’s public works director.

Timing was dire, officials said, after waves from Hurricane Marie, which struck over Labor Day weekend, and Hurricane Rachel pounded the shoreline, ripping away most of the beach’s sand.

Without that protective barrier, about a dozen homes were damaged to the point that they became uninhabitable, at risk of collapse. Stretches of the nearly mile-long boardwalk were splintered, and video of the destruction circulated worldwide. The peninsula became an emblem of what rising seas — driven by El Niño’s warm waters — can do to a coastal city.

Todd Leland of the city’s Marine Bureau said that before the storms, the Peninsula had only 30 to 35 feet of beach. With the dredging and the city’s earlier sand work, he said, it will have upward of 200 feet.

“We haven’t seen a sand beach replenishment project to this scale in decades in our city,” Mayor Rex Richardson said.

Officials hope to keep building up the beach, as final approvals are expected to pass this week for a second dredging effort — also years in the making — pushed by the city seaport. This project will bring another 500,000 cubic yards of sediment starting in December and completed by April.

City Manager Tom Modica said the two — along with another 200,000 cubic yards restored through round-the-clock trucking — would put more than 1.1 million cubic yards of sand on the area, the second most in nearly 100 years. Over the longer term, the city hopes to reach a beach 350 feet wide, with 200 feet of flat sand and 150 feet of slope.

Meanwhile, crews should start replacing the decking of the city boardwalk this week, and then move to an excavated area to repair the bulkhead from 62nd Place heading east. Repairs between 66th and 68th Places are essentially complete, he said, and crews will move next to 62nd and 64th Places. The city is only about a third of the way through the bulkhead work overall. The city wants the boardwalk reopened by spring.

“This is going to extend the ability for public access on our boardwalk for decades,” said Councilmember Kristina Duggan, who represents the area.

Officials were careful to describe the new sand as a buffer, not a barrier. Waves can still carry it away, and a bad storm could scatter it west along the shoreline, a process known as littoral drift. That is why trucks work the beach each morning, hauling sand from West to the East. It’s a process known as backpassing.

The city has a fallback, a boulder wall known as a rock revetment, that would need City Council approval to build. “If all the sand that we’re putting out there goes away, do we need to put rock on there? So we have designed that,” Modica said. The city has obtained emergency permits, he said, and is holding the roughly $7 million project in reserve.

But, he said, “Rock isn’t the best way to manage this long term. It really is the sand.”

Whether the council would support such a plan — expected to cost up to $8 million — is unclear. Public Works has already put the total cost of the storm response and related projects at up to $24 million, with about $9.5 million already committed to emergency work, king tide preparations and immediate bulkhead repairs.

The city just exited a budget crisis earlier this summer, escaping a $51 million deficit with sharp cuts to city jobs and programs.

As for the ruined homes behind along the beach, Modica said the city had already issued its first demolition permit, but the timing of any teardown is up to owners and their contractors. Rebuilt homes must meet 2026 building codes, he said, a significant change for houses largely built in the 1940s, ’50s and ’60s.

When asked to describe the role the city should play in helping defend and rebuild homes along the shore or in the canal community of Naples, Richardsons said the city is doing its part but invited residents to help share the cost.

“The reality is, if they want to see more happen and more infrastructure, then they have to be a part of investing in that infrastructure as well, and expecting that the city, under a different financial situation, invest in higher seawalls at a faster pace, at a higher price point, without looking at the reality of the fiscal impact of that, is unreasonable,” he said.

text:
The car business isn’t sentimental, even if buyers are. Models that don’t sell, don’t meet the latest regulations, or simply don’t fit the latest corporate plan tend to disappear. So it’s surprising when a handful of vehicles that, by any reasonable measure, should be gone are still in showrooms. In the spirit of the season, here are five models Edmunds’ editors are thankful you can still buy. Some are fast, some are cheap, and at least one is a little ridiculous. All of them deserve a look before someone in the boardroom decides they’ve run their course. All of the following prices include destination charges.

0:08

It’s true that electric vehicles are more expensive than comparable gas-powered cars, and the end of the federal EV tax credit last year made it all the more obvious. That’s why we are glad that the Chevrolet Bolt is back. Chevy brought back its small electric car for 2027 with a starting price under $30,000.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

It’s not a penalty box either. The Bolt has about 260 miles of range, offers plenty of room for adults, and now charges far quicker at public charging stations than the old version did, making road trips more practical. The catch is that this Bolt appears to be a one-year offering. If an inexpensive electric car sounds appealing, now is the time to look.

2027 Bolt starting price: $28,995

Not long ago, you had three choices if you wanted a traditional V8-powered muscle car. Well, Chevy stopped building the Camaro after 2024, and Dodge retired the Challenger in favor of a larger, very different Charger. That leaves the Mustang on its own, which isn’t an entirely new scenario for this American classic. Its rivals have come and gone over the decades, but the Mustang has been on sale without a break since 1964.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Ford, to its credit, keeps finding ways to make it more exciting. The newest version, the Mustang Dark Horse SC, adds a supercharger, bringing the total to 795 horsepower. At $108,085 to start, it’s a lot of money for a Mustang. But the Mustang GT is still available with a V8 and a six-speed manual, and it’s the one most fans are grateful for.

2026 Mustang starting price: $34,990

By most business measures, the Prelude shouldn’t exist. Sporty two-door coupes are a tiny slice of the market, and one that’s a hybrid and has a price north of $40,000 makes even less sense. But here we are with the 2027 Honda Prelude, and we’re pleased that Honda found a way to bring back the Prelude after a two-decade-plus hiatus.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The Prelude borrows hardware from the performance-focused Civic Type R to make it one of the best-handling front-wheel-drive cars Edmunds has ever driven. It offers an adaptive suspension, powerful brakes and precise steering. It’s not nearly as quick as a Mustang, but its hybrid powertrain lets it earn 44 mpg combined, according to the EPA.

2027 Prelude starting price: $43,695

In some ways, it’s hard to believe that the Wrangler is still around. It’s pretty bad at the things most SUV shoppers want, whether it be comfort, fuel economy or cutting-edge technology. It’s therefore even harder to believe that you can get a Wrangler with a massive V8 making 470 horsepower. Putting that much engine into a boxy SUV built to crawl over rocks makes very little sense. Jeep did it anyway.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Jeep actually spent two years telling everyone that the Wrangler 392 was going away. In a truly American parting prank, it sold final editions in both 2024 and 2025. Then the brand’s CEO announced in 2025 that the V8 would stay in production indefinitely. The 2027 V8-powered Wrangler will likely give you sticker shock, but trust us, there’s nothing else quite like it.

2027 Wrangler Willys 392 starting price: $72,990

Two seats, a folding roof and not much else. That’s been the Miata’s recipe since 1989, and it’s the reason the little Mazda has outlasted every convertible that came along after it. It’s light and simple, and it makes an ordinary back road feel like an event at speeds that won’t put you in jail. Like the Mustang, it’s also one of the few new cars you can buy with a stick shift.

Article continues below this ad

The current Miata has been on sale for more than a decade, and it doesn’t appear that Mazda has a timeline for a replacement. Prices start a little over $30,000, which is about as low as it gets for a genuine sports car.

2026 Miata MX-5 starting price: $32,045

text:
U.S. electric vehicle sales fell off a cliff last year after Republicans deleted the federal EV tax credit. But sky-high gasoline prices are causing EV adoption to soar among one of the populations most exposed to fuel costs: Uber drivers.

The ride-hailing company tracks EV adoption on its platform to measure progress toward a corporate goal to reach 100% electric by 2030 in the U.S., Canada, and Europe. Uber is not on track to hit that ambitious timeline, but a striking trend has emerged from the latest data: Uber drivers in the U.S. and Canada made a smaller share of rides in EVs in the last quarter of 2025 and the first quarter of this year. But from April through September, U.S. Uber drivers set consecutive monthly records for miles driven electric, said Santosh Rao, the company’s global head of mobility electrification.

The U.S. and Israel launched their war with Iran at the end of February, prompting Iran to close the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation. The loss of this key energy supply line rippled through the global market. As the blockade continued, even the U.S.’s world-leading oil production couldn’t shield its drivers from price spikes in this globalized commodity. Domestic average gasoline prices broke $4 per gallon at the end of March, according to AAA, and have stayed above that for almost all the year since.

Uber can’t command its drivers to pick a certain vehicle — they are independent contractors, after all. Its EV data reflects the aggregated decisions of millions of individuals making economic choices about their livelihood. As gas prices ticked higher, the people who routinely fill up a tank once or more per day felt it the hardest, and for six months running, more of them chose electric driving than ever before.

U.S. Uber drivers chose electric cars for one in 10 miles driven as of September. In Europe, which bought more EVs in September than ever before, EVs traversed one in 5 miles driven on the platform.

Globally, the quarterly count of zero-emission Uber trips rose 34% since the first quarter, to 207 million trips. And Uber now hosts 434,000 EV drivers, up 28% since the Q1 report — compare that with the total 10.8 million active drivers and couriers Uber reported in the third quarter (though the electrification reporting tracks only ride-hail drivers, not couriers). A few cities lead the pack: EV miles driven on Uber are now over 50% in Amsterdam, over 40% in London, and over 35% in Vancouver.

In a recent survey of its drivers, Uber found that access to charging has now displaced the cost of EVs as the No. 1 obstacle to adoption. The company is looking for ways to help with that, like testing software in France that helps drivers find a low-priced charger, navigate to it, and pay for charging in the driver app.

More than one in four cars sold worldwide this year will be EVs, according to the International Energy Agency. The actual share of cars on the road that are electric is far smaller — Uber’s analysis pegged it at 2.3% of the vehicle stock in the U.S. and Canada last year, and 3.2% in Europe. Uber’s fleet is tracking ahead of that in those regions, though the company remains a long way from hitting 100%.

“We’re not going to get to those 2030 goals that we have in U.S., Canada, and Europe,” Rao admitted. ​“We need to see more coordinated industry and policy action for us to be able to get anywhere close to these goals, which we’re not seeing right now.”

The Uber data, then, offers a limited sign that people will make the switch when market conditions favor electric driving. But it also portends that even favorable market conditions won’t drive decarbonization fast enough for the leading climate commitments on that front.

text:
TEXAS — Changes are coming to the Texas state government, and some campaign promises from Democrats about data centers are leaving developers in a sort of state of limbo.

As the new year comes, Democrats will hold the state’s highest executive offices alongside a Democratic-controlled Texas House of Representatives. That’s got some data center developers unsure about what comes next.

“Everyone was kind of shocked,” said Balaji Tammabattula, the CEO of BarUpOn — the developer of the Liberty Advanced Manufacturing and Power (LAMP) campus just outside of Houston.

Tammabattula has been on a rollercoaster ride through the state’s changing attitudes and policies on data centers. First came Gov. Greg Abbott’s September directive halting permit approvals from the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) pending a review by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT).

“They put a pause,” Tammabattula said regarding the LAMP project.

Just a week after Election Day, there was news from the governor’s Office. A memo sent to TCEQ stated that “ERCOT has completed the community impact review … TCEQ should resume its normal permit review process.”

The agency tells Spectrum News that it has resumed reviewing data center permits. The LAMP project hasn’t yet gotten its approvals.

“Right now, what has happened is data centers have moved into mostly rural communities, and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans,” said Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa during a recent interview with CNN.

On the campaign trail, Hinojosa signaled a tougher stance, and that’s continuing to fuel Tammabattula’s uncertainty about the future of his campus.

“What’s gonna happen next year once the new governor’s in office?” Tammabattula said. “What actions is she going to take? Is she going to be friendly with businesses, or is it going to be a problem? We don’t know, right? It’s just wait and see.”

Already, more than a dozen bills have been pre-filed ahead of the next legislative session addressing data centers, many focusing on repealing sales tax exemptions for them.

“They don’t pay sales tax like you and I do when we go to the store and we buy things,” said state Rep. Vincent Perez, D-El Paso. “That was a big reason why they located here in Texas. I mean, that is a huge savings for many of these companies.”

Perez is among the many state legislators who pre-filed data center legislation, along with state Rep. Cody Vasut, R-Angleton.

“I think this perhaps is one of the most bipartisan issues that we have for this next session,” Vasut said. “I’m actually genuinely not aware of a single member of the House or Senate who wants to continue the sales tax exemption for data centers.”

As for Tammabattula, he says the LAMP project has taken no sales tax exemptions. However, uncertainty about the future of data centers in Texas has caused him to take certain measures.

“Nobody knows what’s going to happen, but until then, we want to put all our efforts on the data center build out in North Dakota and Wyoming and Texas purely manufacturing,” Tammabattula said.

For now, a data center won’t be included in the Texas campus.

The American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy (“ACEEE”) issued a report/toolkit titled:

Engaging Communities to Inform Electric Truck Infrastructure Decisions (“Report”).

The stated purpose of the Report is to:

… guide local, regional, and state government agencies, freight hubs, charging hub developers, and electric truck fleets in the important work of partnering with communities as they plan for and invest in electric truck charging infrastructure.

The authors of the Report include:

Christi Nakajima.

Maggie Kelley Riggins.

Jasmine Mah.

Research is stated to have been undertaken by interviewing members of six community-focused organizations and representatives from:

a state agency;

a port; and,

a charging hub developer.

The Report groups strategies into what are described as four key steps in the community engagement timeline:

Preparing for engagement.

Early contact and planning.

Communicating and making decisions with the community.

Post-project follow-through.

The authors conclude that the community engagement described in the Report is critical because:

… it helps maximize the benefits derived from electric truck deployment and supports the communities most impacted by diesel truck pollution.

ACEEE believes such engagement can:

Build support for projects.

Mitigate delays due to opposition.

Ensure the development of long-lasting solutions by incorporating transparency and investment from the outset.

ACEEE describes its organization as an independent nonprofit that works across buildings, transportation, and industry to bring together rigorous research, policy expertise, and technical assistance to deliver real savings for households and businesses.

Sierra Club and RISE St. James Louisiana (collectively, “Sierra Club”) filed a November 20th Petition for Judicial Review (“Petition”) in the Louisiana 19th Judicial District Court/Parish of East Baton Rouge challenging the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality’s (“LDEQ”) granting of an extension to the commencement of construction deadline for a Clean Air Act Prevention of Significant Deterioration (“PSD”) and Part 70 Operating Permit issued to Hyundai-POSCO Louisiana Steel LLC (“HPLS”).

The Petition states that the PSD and Title V Operating Permit address HPLS’s proposed construction and operation of an integrated iron and steel production facility in Ascension Parish, Louisiana.

The Petition initially argues in part:

The Permits would authorize the facility to emit substantial quantities of:

Greenhouse gases

Nitrogen oxides

Particulate matter

Carbon monoxide

Lead

Mercury

Ammonia

Area around the planned facility already bears a toxic air pollution burden greater than 96% of the rest of the country, and ranks high across a range of environmental and socioeconomic indicators.

Sierra Club further contends that the Permits must be vacated for the following reasons:

LDEQ did not conduct a proper environmental justice analysis.

LDEQ did not give full and careful consideration to mitigation measures like electrified components and green hydrogen.

LDEQ did not assess any environmental costs in the cost-benefit analysis, nor adequately evaluate feasible pollution-reducing alternatives and mitigation measures.

LDEQ’s Best Available Control Technology (“BACT”) analysis was issued without conducting and documenting the case-by-case analysis required for evaluating electrified technologies or incremental blending of green hydrogen.

LDEQ’s conclusion that the HPLS plant will not cause or contribute to exceedances of the ozone National Ambient Air Quality Standards by relying on the Dutchtown neighborhood-scale ozone monitor rather than the closer Carville regional-scale monitor is incorrect.

text:
TEXAS — Changes are coming to the Texas state government, and some campaign promises from Democrats about data centers are leaving developers in a sort of state of limbo.

As the new year comes, Democrats will hold the state’s highest executive offices alongside a Democratic-controlled Texas House of Representatives. That’s got some data center developers unsure about what comes next.

“Everyone was kind of shocked,” said Balaji Tammabattula, the CEO of BarUpOn — the developer of the Liberty Advanced Manufacturing and Power (LAMP) campus just outside of Houston.

Tammabattula has been on a rollercoaster ride through the state’s changing attitudes and policies on data centers. First came Gov. Greg Abbott’s September directive halting permit approvals from the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) pending a review by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT).

“They put a pause,” Tammabattula said regarding the LAMP project.

Just a week after Election Day, there was news from the governor’s Office. A memo sent to TCEQ stated that “ERCOT has completed the community impact review … TCEQ should resume its normal permit review process.”

The agency tells Spectrum News that it has resumed reviewing data center permits. The LAMP project hasn’t yet gotten its approvals.

“Right now, what has happened is data centers have moved into mostly rural communities, and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans,” said Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa during a recent interview with CNN.

On the campaign trail, Hinojosa signaled a tougher stance, and that’s continuing to fuel Tammabattula’s uncertainty about the future of his campus.

“What’s gonna happen next year once the new governor’s in office?” Tammabattula said. “What actions is she going to take? Is she going to be friendly with businesses, or is it going to be a problem? We don’t know, right? It’s just wait and see.”

Already, more than a dozen bills have been pre-filed ahead of the next legislative session addressing data centers, many focusing on repealing sales tax exemptions for them.

“They don’t pay sales tax like you and I do when we go to the store and we buy things,” said state Rep. Vincent Perez, D-El Paso. “That was a big reason why they located here in Texas. I mean, that is a huge savings for many of these companies.”

Perez is among the many state legislators who pre-filed data center legislation, along with state Rep. Cody Vasut, R-Angleton.

“I think this perhaps is one of the most bipartisan issues that we have for this next session,” Vasut said. “I’m actually genuinely not aware of a single member of the House or Senate who wants to continue the sales tax exemption for data centers.”

As for Tammabattula, he says the LAMP project has taken no sales tax exemptions. However, uncertainty about the future of data centers in Texas has caused him to take certain measures.

“Nobody knows what’s going to happen, but until then, we want to put all our efforts on the data center build out in North Dakota and Wyoming and Texas purely manufacturing,” Tammabattula said.

For now, a data center won’t be included in the Texas campus.

title: Wisconsin's new Democratic trifecta could be a boon for clean energy - Wisconsin Watch
authors: Kari Lydersen / Canary Media, Mark Rice, Kari Lydersen, Canary Media, Tom Kertscher, Wisconsin Watch
description:
​“The Democratic leadership has a very ambitious agenda, which includes clean energy and renewables.
A 100% clean energy target Last spring, Democratic state lawmakers introduced a bill mandating that Wisconsin electricity generation be 100% emissions-free by 2050.
The bill did not advance, but clean energy advocates are hoping a similar initiative will be a top priority for the new Democratic legislature.
“We think all Wisconsinites deserve the freedom to have cleaner air and cleaner water and the (lower) bills that come with clean energy,” she said.
Powering data centers with clean energy could be dependent on limiting the number and size of data centers in the state.
text:
Reading Time: 6 minutes

The Democratic sweep in this year’s midterm elections has opened up new opportunities for advancing the clean energy transition in states across the country. That’s particularly true in Wisconsin, where Democrats will have a trifecta for the first time in 16 years, and which has lagged behind its Midwestern neighbors on renewables.

Indeed, Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley and legislative leaders have pledged to promote clean energy as a way to address affordability and meet demand from planned data centers. Advocates say they have already been talking with legislators and drafting proposals that they hope will advance once new lawmakers take office on Jan. 4.

“It’s very exciting to see these changes,” said Beata Wierzba, government affairs director at RENEW Wisconsin, a nonprofit advocacy group that works to advance clean energy policies. ​“The Democratic leadership has a very ambitious agenda, which includes clean energy and renewables. We know we’re on their plate.”

Here are six key areas where advocates expect to see the most progress.

A 100% clean energy target

Last spring, Democratic state lawmakers introduced a bill mandating that Wisconsin electricity generation be 100% emissions-free by 2050. The bill did not advance, but clean energy advocates are hoping a similar initiative will be a top priority for the new Democratic legislature. The only such mandate on the books right now is woefully outdated, calling for 10% renewable energy by 2015. The state has long surpassed that, with a fifth of the electricity delivered to customers currently coming from renewables.

Shifting to net-zero emissions by 2050 — including 100% clean energy — would create over 68,000 jobs and avoid at least $2 billion in health care costs, according to a report by RENEW, the nonprofit Clean Wisconsin and other groups.

Abby Novinska-Lois, executive director of the nonprofit public health advocacy group Healthy Climate Wisconsin, noted that ​“Wisconsin is really behind” states like Illinois — which mandates fossil-fuel-free electricity generation by 2045 — when it comes to emissions that harm the climate and public health.

“We think all Wisconsinites deserve the freedom to have cleaner air and cleaner water and the (lower) bills that come with clean energy,” she said. ​“We are hearing interest from policymakers that they want to accelerate affordable energy for all Wisconsinites. We know clean energy is the most affordable.”

Community solar

Advocates have long pushed for state legislation to make it easier to build community solar, wherein residents subscribe to off-site medium-size solar arrays in order to lower their bills and access clean energy. The model is especially beneficial for those who are unable to install solar on their own property.

Right now in Wisconsin, only utilities can build solar arrays that provide energy to customers. Twenty-four states plus Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico allow companies other than utilities to build community solar, including Wisconsin’s neighbor Illinois, which provides robust incentives.

Wisconsin legislators have considered community solar bills multiple times in the past five years, most recently in the last session. That bill and a 2023 proposal were backed by Republicans, but Democratic legislators rejected both measures, reportedly in part because of opposition from labor unions. RENEW’s Wierzba noted that the new Democratic majority could draft a community solar bill that includes prevailing-wage provisions that unions want. However, lawmakers could still face intense opposition from the state’s powerful utilities, which opposed the 2025 bill, arguing that community solar subscribers wouldn’t be paying their fair share to utilities to help maintain the grid.

“Now with the Democratic majority, we might be able to work something out where both sides will see it’s good for the workers and good for the people,” Wierzba said.

Third-party solar

For almost a decade, Wisconsin has been a battleground over third-party-owned distributed solar. Under such arrangements, a solar developer owns the array that provides power to a home, business, organization, or government agency. The model eliminates up-front costs for the customer and helps nonprofits and government entities tap tax incentives that might not otherwise be available since they don’t pay taxes. But the state’s largest utility, We Energies, has long argued that this lets solar developers illegally act as utilities. Solar advocates and developers want a law to clarify that third-party-owned solar is legal so that projects can move forward.

In 2021, Republican legislators drafted a bill meant to address utilities’ concerns about third-party-owned solar and affirm the model’s legality, but it didn’t pass. Ensuing efforts through the state’s Public Service Commission and courts have also faltered. A state court overturned regulators’ 2022 decision allowing a Stevens Point family to have third-party-owned solar — a case that advocates hoped would set a pro-solar precedent — but a state appeals court dismissed the family’s plea for relief.

Wierzba is uncertain about the prospects for third-party solar in the next legislative session but said she hopes lawmakers will be up for tackling the issue.

“If there is the appetite for this, we will bring the ingredients,” she said.

Balcony solar

For people who can’t install solar on their homes, an even simpler, if lower-scale, solution is balcony solar — small solar panels that can be positioned on a balcony or in a yard, plugged into a regular household outlet and used to meet some of a home’s energy demand.

Legislation addressing safety concerns and setting uniform standards is considered crucial to facilitate the widespread deployment and marketing of balcony solar since most utilities prohibit people from plugging solar panels directly into their home electrical systems.

Balcony solar legislation hasn’t been introduced in Wisconsin, but at least a dozen states have passed such laws. Lawmakers in neighboring Illinois may consider a balcony solar bill in their fall veto session, after the measure failed to pass last spring. Wierzba said Democratic lawmakers have expressed interest in pushing balcony solar, seeing it as a ​“money-saving measure.”

Integrated resource planning

Advocates have for years pushed Wisconsin to adopt an integrated resource planning (IRP) process of the type used by at least 40 states, wherein regulators and utilities study and agree on plans to meet long-term energy demand, including through renewables, distributed generation, energy efficiency, and demand response.

This kind of planning is especially important given the expected spike in demand from data centers, advocates say. Wisconsin previously had an IRP process, but scrapped it in the late 1990s in favor of a much weaker program.

At a recent press conference on energy affordability hosted by advocacy groups, Democratic state Rep. Angela Stroud, who won reelection representing a district in the state’s far north, said she expects bipartisan legislation instituting an IRP to pass in the upcoming session.

Tom Content, executive director of the Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin, a consumer watchdog organization, also said he expected an IRP-related bill to pass ​“regardless of who won, because of this affordability moment.”

IRPs help regulators avoid the unnecessary and expensive buildout of fossil-fueled generation since the planning takes into account other options for alleviating strain on the grid, such as utility-scale renewables as well as battery storage, rooftop solar, energy efficiency, and reducing demand during peak times.

“Whatever is cost-effective is going to be favored” in an IRP, said Content, who gave examples of excess spending by utilities in a recent op-ed for WisPolitics. ​“Utilities race to build more infrastructure if they can profit from it. When you have an IRP, it just levels the playing field across all kinds of energy sources and, more importantly, between supply and demand.”

Lawmakers could also tell regulators to require utilities to prioritize clean energy in their planning.

“Under a Democratic majority, the Legislature could decide to make carbon emissions matter more in Public Service Commission decisions,” Content said. ​“That would be the shortest piece of legislation with the most impact.”

Running data centers on clean energy

At least three major AI data centers are under construction in Wisconsin, and a half dozen other major data centers have been proposed. These facilities are predicted to increase the state’s energy demand manyfold.

So the question of how data centers are powered is central to the state’s energy future. Crowley has said he wants to require data centers to get at least 70% of their energy from renewables in order to qualify for state and local tax incentives.

Prescott Balch, president of the village of Caledonia in southeast Wisconsin and leader of a successful fight against a data center planned there, said it could be extremely difficult for renewables to meet the needs of all the proposed data centers, given the sheer scale of the energy demand and the difficulty of finding enough sites for large renewable arrays.

Utilities are ​“hell-bent for leather on building out more fossil-fuel- driven energy” to meet data center demand, Balch said.

We Energies is building a massive 1,100-megawatt gas plant near the site of a coal plant on Lake Michigan’s coast and has proposed a 750-megawatt gas plant 100 miles farther north. In October, regulators approved the Chicago developer Invenergy’s plans for two additional large new gas plants to help meet data center demand in We Energies’ territory. The Citizens Utility Board noted that other new gas plants or conversions of coal plants to gas have also been floated.

The issue is complicated, as Balch sees it, by the fact that residents of Wisconsin’s ​“charming rolling hills and small towns and farming communities” often oppose not only data centers but also sprawling solar farms. ​“The scale of the (data center) buildout picks at so many of the normal wounds around here — the urban-rural divide, left-right, pro-labor or pro-business.”

Last year, a Republican-backed bill to prevent regular customers from subsidizing energy for data centers died in part because of a provision that any renewable energy to power data centers be built on-site. Wierzba said RENEW considered that unrealistic and did not support the bill.

Powering data centers with clean energy could be dependent on limiting the number and size of data centers in the state. Crowley has said he would sign a bill repealing the state’s sales tax exemption for data centers, which could reduce their total number — and hence power demand.

Stroud said at the press conference that she is ​“interested in expanding access to renewable energy” and noted that data centers will be a priority for the new Legislature.

“Finally, after 16 years, we will have a governing majority in the Legislature that is actually focused on solving problems that the people of this state have been begging us to fix,” Stroud said. ​“We will be ready to pass legislation that will bring down utility costs, protect Wisconsin ratepayers and make sure that the public interest will come before the interests of giant corporations.”

description:

text:
Voters just asked Congress to slow down. The permitting legislation would do the opposite.

Earlier this month, voters took to the polls and overwhelmingly voiced their desire to slow the build-out of data centers in their communities. Now, a debate is raging about what the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA)—the permit reform bill that has passed the Senate and now awaits consideration in the House—will mean for data centers.

After carefully considering all 500 pages of the bill, NRDC experts weigh in with our conclusion: BAAJA will make data centers pay for grid upgrades, but it will also make it easier to build infrastructure projects of all kinds, including pipelines and data centers, and harder to stop or improve them. Data centers are in a race to get online faster, and “speed to power” is often their biggest constraint. Unsurprisingly for a bill that includes many of the Data Center Coalition’s highest priority asks, BAAJA will ease that constraint in multiple ways.

Streamlined federal permits for data centers: Like other industrialized facilities, data centers frequently need a permit under the Clean Water Act. Currently, many data centers are subject to Nationwide Permit 39 (Commercial and Industrial Developments), but those that require permits and exceed the thresholds for general permitting must apply for individual permits. BAAJA section 1204 relaxes general permitting thresholds, allowing facilities to displace up to 2 acres of streams, wetlands, and other waters without needing an individual permit. This quadruples the prior limit and is consistent with the Data Center Coalition’s recommendations relating to how to speed development under the Clean Water Act.

Learn More

More gas pipelines: Data centers require huge amounts of energy, and they need it fast to keep up with the artificial intelligence boom. Multiple sections of BAAJA expedite permitting for gas pipelines, which will speed delivery of fuel to data centers building on-site power generation facilities.

Section 1202 constrains the ability of states and Tribes to review and place water quality conditions on federal permits, including Federal Energy Regulatory Commission permits for gas pipelines.

Section 1204 requires the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to maintain a fast-track permit for filling in waters associated with oil and gas pipelines, and it would quadruple the area of a waterway or wetland that can be harmed by a pipeline at each water crossing.

Section 2102b allows pipeline expansions in existing rights-of-way without any additional environmental review.

Combined, these provisions mean that pipelines can be built faster and with greater impact on the environment. And while BAAJA’s transmission provisions will also unlock more clean power in the long term, the Trump administration has made clear that it intends to continue to block clean energy. For the next two years, it is safe to take the president at his word that the bill will mean pipelines rather than clean alternatives. Data center developers also indicate that they expect to have permanent on-site gas resources, even once transmission bottlenecks improve.

Courts that are powerless to stop illegal projects on public lands: The Trump administration is currently considering upwards of 35 data centers on public lands. Presently, these proposals are required to go through a robust public National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) process to evaluate their environmental consequences. If the Trump administration skips that process today, judges can stop projects from being built until the process is followed—in fact, a judge did exactly that when the Trump administration tried to fast-track a data center on public lands in Nevada. Section 1110 of BAAJA would prohibit judges from stopping projects or suspending construction until the law is followed—even if the Trump administration skips the required process completely. Former D.C. Circuit Judge David Tatel warns that BAAJA would make NEPA cases “futile.”

“Forever permits” for data centers: The Trump administration has made clear that it wants to permit data centers as fast as possible. BAAJA section 1401 makes it harder for the government to revoke or amend any permits issued by the current administration, even when they have been issued illegally or when they authorize a project that is causing harm to human health or the environment. This means that if the Trump administration issues permits to data centers on public lands or exempts on-site gas power generation from site-specific permitting requirements and pollution controls, it will be hard for a future administration to modify those permits to better protect human health and the environment.

All of these changes significantly undermine the states’ abilities to protect their residents and natural resources and the communities’ abilities to meaningfully participate in decisions about where and how data centers are built. They also substantially curtail the role of Tribes in assessing projects that directly affect their sovereign interests.

What about BAAJA’s “ratepayer protection provisions”?

Many BAAJA supporters have described it as a bill that will make data centers pay their own way. Section 2107(b) of the bill does protect residential customers and businesses from paying for federally regulated grid upgrades triggered by data centers. However, BAAJA does not protect people from other data center–driven costs, like higher wholesale electricity prices, increased gas utility bills, or more expensive supply chain components.1

1 BAAJA also includes provisions about state authority to do things like implement large load tariffs to further protect ratepayers. These provisions are just guidance—they do not mandate that states do anything.

title: Reflections from COP31: The energy transition goes beyond the climate negotiations
description:
Open data is no longer just a tool for understanding the energy transition.
We are in what I often refer to as the messy middle of the energy transition.
What struck me most at COP31 was the extent to which the energy transition dialogue is shifting toward energy security, affordability, and economic competitiveness.
When climate objectives align with national economic interests and the everyday needs of citizens, the drivers of the energy transition become considerably more powerful.
The energy transition will not be determined by the climate negotiations alone.
text:
Open data is no longer just a tool for understanding the energy transition. It is becoming essential infrastructure for delivering it.

This was my biggest takeaway from spending the past week at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye.

For the first time since 2009, COP31 closed without an overarching agreement, with disagreements over fossil fuel language and climate finance for developing countries still unresolved. It’s hard not to be disappointed by the lack of meaningful progress. Nearly 11 years after the landmark Paris Agreement and three years after the historic commitment in Dubai to transition away from fossil fuels, the international community continues to struggle to translate collective ambition into concrete action.

Meanwhile, the International Energy Agency's newly released World Energy Outlook 2026, while recognizing the significant growth of renewables, raises questions about whether conventional energy modelling is failing to capture the full pace and scale of the solar revolution, particularly the rapid deployment of distributed solar across emerging economies.

As I shared during my keynote at the Asia Climate Solutions Pavilion at COP31, Global Energy Monitor's (GEM) is tracking more than 29,000 utility-scale solar, wind, and hydropower projects in development globally. Our data tell a different story about the remarkable progress of the transition already underway — specifically:

Proposed clean energy projects in the pipeline represent over 80% of the additional capacity needed to achieve the global renewables tripling target by 2030.

Global utility-scale solar capacity has reached nearly 1.3 TW, with a record 221 GW coming online in 2025 alone.

Distributed solar accounts for more than half of operating solar capacity in 17 of the 31 countries GEM tracks.

The challenge is increasingly not one of ambition or technological feasibility, but of implementation — overcoming the policy, financing, grid, and institutional barriers that stand between projects being announced, and those same projects becoming operational.

Navigating the messy middle

Despite the shortcomings of the climate negotiations, I came away from COP31 cautiously optimistic.

We are in what I often refer to as the messy middle of the energy transition. In 2025, global clean energy investment reached $2.2 trillion, twice the amount invested in fossil fuels, as detailed in Figure A below. The IEA predicts a similar trend in 2026. Yet significant investment in fossil fuel infrastructure continues, and the transition remains uneven across countries and sectors.

Figure A: World energy investments, 2025

Against this backdrop, the Strait of Hormuz crisis may ultimately prove to be one of the most meaningful geopolitical turning points in the global response to climate change.

While the immediate economic and human consequences are deeply concerning, the crisis has exposed the structural vulnerabilities associated with dependence on imported fossil fuels. It is forcing governments to fundamentally reassess how they meet their energy needs.

What struck me most at COP31 was the extent to which the energy transition dialogue is shifting toward energy security, affordability, and economic competitiveness.

Increasingly, the case for clean energy is being made not solely on environmental grounds, but on its ability to reduce exposure to volatile international commodity markets, strengthen national energy security, and provide affordable energy to households and businesses.

Pakistan's extraordinary bottom-up solar revolution is a compelling example. Households and businesses are adopting solar not primarily because of international climate commitments, but because of economics and the need for reliable, affordable electricity.

When climate objectives align with national economic interests and the everyday needs of citizens, the drivers of the energy transition become considerably more powerful.

The growing importance of open data

Three interconnected trends stood out to me at COP31:

1. From targets and pledges toward implementation, verification, and accountability. The global climate community is increasingly focused on what countries and companies are actually delivering. Independent, evidence-based assessments are essential to understanding whether commitments are translating into real-world outcomes.

2. Growing demand for granular, interoperable, asset-level data. As the international community prepares for the second Global Stocktake, there is increasing recognition of the need to connect national commitments with what is happening on the ground. Specifically, what energy infrastructure is being built, operated, financed, and retired.

This same data is critical to developing credible and independently verifiable national energy plans that meet countries' economic, energy security, affordability, and climate objectives.

3. Information and data integrity are becoming major governance priorities, particularly with the rise of AI. AI presents an extraordinary opportunity to democratize access to energy intelligence. But its effectiveness and credibility will ultimately depend on the quality and integrity of the underlying data.

In an increasingly fragmented information ecosystem, independent, openly accessible data grounded in transparent methodologies and verifiable sources has never been more important.

Holding the center on facts

At GEM, we see both an opportunity and a responsibility to help build the global energy data infrastructure required for this next phase of the transition.

Over the past year, more than 15,000 distinct organizations across 197 countries downloaded GEM's data. From governments and financial institutions to researchers, civil society, the media, and increasingly AI platforms, decision-makers across the world are relying on independent energy data to navigate a rapidly changing landscape.

Regardless of where one sits on the political spectrum, there is a shared interest in building energy systems that are secure, affordable, reliable, and sustainable. Achieving this requires a shared understanding of the facts.

The energy transition will not be determined by the climate negotiations alone. It will be shaped by millions of decisions made by governments, businesses, investors, communities, and households around the world. Ensuring that those decisions are grounded in credible, transparent, and accessible information is one of the most consequential contributions we can make.

description:
Under immense lobbying pressure from right-wing groups like the Heritage Foundation and the oil and gas industry, the BAAJA bill passed through the U.S. Senate 62-33 on November 19.
Though BAAJA is marketed as an “affordability” bill, it is an enormous shortcut for mining, oil and gas interests, and data centers.
The Revelator warned this would dismantle the bedrock of U.S. environmental law.
BAAJA could quickly lead to a “bonanza” of new pipelines and natural gas-fueled data centers on formerly pristine public land.
Bill supporters believe it will support decarbonization and enable bringing cleaner energy projects into the power grid.
text:
Washington, D.C. – The nearly 500-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) would cut a huge swath in the environmental laws passed since the Nixon Administration – including diminishing protections in the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, National Environmental Policy Act and National Historic Preservation Act. This bill would slash the consultative process and legal paths to prevent harms, including deadly pollution exposure, faced by Native tribes.

Under immense lobbying pressure from right-wing groups like the Heritage Foundation and the oil and gas industry, the BAAJA bill passed through the U.S. Senate 62-33 on November 19.

Though BAAJA is marketed as an “affordability” bill, it is an enormous shortcut for mining, oil and gas interests, and data centers. It would sweep aside decades-old roadblocks and speed bumps energy and tech companies face under U.S. law, enabling companies to accelerate projects that create pollution and health damage for humans and the environment. The Revelator warned this would dismantle the bedrock of U.S. environmental law.

Tribal governments and Native organizers are warning that the bill will severely damage the fates of their people, and obviously benefits gold and silver mining corporations. Unicorn Riot heard from one organizer that BAAJA would systematically remove a decade of activist tactics to block harmful industrial projects.

BAAJA could quickly lead to a “bonanza” of new pipelines and natural gas-fueled data centers on formerly pristine public land. Trillions of dollars are at stake. Hyperscaler companies like Oracle that are trying to build data centers that would include colocated natural gas turbines which need new pipelines — such as a pipeline blocked by New Mexico’s land commissioner in July for Oracle’s Jupiter project — stand to benefit from this legislation’s passage.

According to Politico, on November 19, U.S. Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-OR) tried to force a vote on an amendment that would ban data centers on public land, but was stifled.

Native Consultation Would be Slashed

One critical issue for the tribal nations is called Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), elected to become Minnesota’s next governor, voted for BAAJA. Retiring U.S. Sen. Tina Smith (D-MN) voted against it.

Robert Deschampe, Chairman of the Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa warned the November 7 version of the bill would “strip the Band of the authorities we rely on to protect our cultural and treaty-reserved resources throughout the 1854 ceded territory … by eliminating the Band’s existing authorities under Section 106, this bill would open the door to that pollution.” They warned “Section 106 enables the Band to seek judicial relief before irreparable damage occurs. BAAJA would eliminate each of these protections.”

Deschampe said additionally that “federal agencies, not tribal nations, would determine what is protected … agencies could disregard tribal concerns at their discretion” and that “Tribes would lose meaningful judicial remedies.”

One of the most critical elements involves Tribal Historic Preservation Offices. The earlier version of the bill let the Secretary of the Interior take over those powers directly. The latter version introduces a different yoke: those programs “could still be found deficient, and its funding suspended for failing to ‘regularly’ meet federal timelines or undefined ‘required metrics,'” cautioned Deschampe.

By dropping regulations around industrial projects, the controversial Twin Metals proposal could become unstoppable even if the corporation breaks laws around environmental reviews, and the Minnesota State Legislature would have far less leverage to curtail the project, Boundary Waters advocates warned.

Several tribes around Minnesota have called to stop BAAJA and warn of irreparable harm, amid Klobuchar’s support for this legislation, Sahan Journal found. The Coalition for Tribal Sovereignty lists dozens of similar letters from tribal governments to politicians in Washington, along with guides to Section 106 and the other laws.

Data Centers and Decarbonization

As a piece of pro-corporate legislation, BAAJA would make industrial projects nearly impossible to appeal, and it would prevent third-party organizations like Earthjustice from filing lawsuits to stop construction. Cleverly, local residents would be forbidden from suing over harms from projects unless that specific harm was addressed in the comment period, according to Indigenous organizer Dallas Goldtooth. The Bipartisan Policy Center, which supports the bill, agreed in their analysis that “BAAJA would limit standing to parties that raised their concerns during the comment period and can show direct harm.”

Across the country, dozens of data center projects, and new electrical transmission lines, have gotten stopped or slowed in permitting. Bill supporters believe it will support decarbonization and enable bringing cleaner energy projects into the power grid.

Citizens Climate Lobby, a 501(c)(4) advocacy group, endorsed BAAJA in early October, saying the bill included “measures that will speed the buildout of transmission lines and get new clean energy projects connected to the grid faster.”

Decarbonization of the U.S. economy has been a frustrating goal for the environmental advocacy world. Energy projects with lower emissions than fossil fuel-powered facilities, like solar and wind farms, as well as nuclear projects, require an enormous new supply of copper and placing new transmission lines and substations all over the country. According to Scientific American, BAAJA also would streamline nuclear development, an industry that historically has especially harmed Native communities.

Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) supports parts of the bill but acknowledges that dirtier industry interests are the main winners:

“Even as amended, however, it could still benefit fossil fuel, mining, data center, and other industrial projects more than clean energy. It also threatens to limit agencies’ ability to address newly discovered harms, constrain future pollution regulation, and create large taxpayer-funded corporate handouts.”

Natural Resources Defense Council

NRDC concedes “these rollbacks would represent the most significant weakening of federal environmental laws since they were established more than a half a century ago.”

Path in U.S. House is Narrow

The congressional elections this year swung towards the Democrats in part due to large-scale organizing against data centers. Across swaths of the public, from the usual environmental crowd to disengaged people, libertarians and the right wing, voters gave the next Congress, after the “lame duck” period, a strong anti-data center mandate.

The U.S. Senate passed the legislation through cloture to limit debate, with a large part of the Democratic caucus in support.

However, in the U.S. House, outgoing Republican speaker Mike Johnson is currently working to pass a major defense bill, and it’s unclear if they can get a vote on BAAJA before the next term starts on January 3, 2027.

Dozens of now-defeated Republicans are swiftly losing interest in staying in Washington before the next session. Johnson told Politico he would first “try to pass the bill under suspension, a fast-track procedure that requires a two-thirds majority and bars floor amendments” and then try to bring it up under the standard rules of procedure which require a simple majority.

Democrat Hakeem Jeffries has already been tapped to become Speaker of the House. He could rally the House Dems to cover for missing Republicans and drag BAAJA over the finish line, even though many of his colleagues were elected on promises to curtail precisely these kinds of noxious and aggressive industrial projects. Jeffries told Politico BAAJA “‘falls short’ and needs changes” to NEPA and tribal provisions. If it isn’t passed by the time Jeffries takes over, the bill is dead and the process would start over.

Friends of the Boundary Waters is strongly opposed to BAAJA and warn about devastating provisions “buried” in the bill including:

“Locking in mining leases — if the Trump administration hands mineral leases over to Twin Metals, future administrations could be barred from revoking or even amending them.

Limiting your day in court — people would have just 150 days to challenge a project. Even when a court finds an environmental review broke the law, the project could keep going.

Weakening the Clean Water Act — states and tribes would have a harder time stopping projects that threaten their water.”

Friends of the Boundary Waters

Video: Honor the Earth BAAJA Power Hour with Dallas Goldtooth.

Think Tanks and ‘Abundance Movement’ Line Up for BAAJA

The broad sweep of this bill helps illustrate that the climate movement could get caught between opposing forces, a piece by Grist detailed in October. It shows the hand of centrist and center-right think tanks, as well as their allies in the newly fashioned “abundance movement.” Here’s a quick snapshot to understand the players involved.

“Abundance” became a messaging vehicle for refocusing on neoliberal market deregulation, named after a book promoting this agenda released by Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson last year. Silicon Valley billionaires have lined up a whopping nine-figure commitment to move their “abundance” points of view forward in public discourse.

Not surprisingly, leaders in this crowd are brimming with enthusiasm for BAAJA, which would greatly simplify industrial projects for the ultrawealthy figures funding their scene. The director of the Breakthrough Institute boasted that BAAJA is “culminating years of energy abundance advocacy.”

A non-profit called Inclusive Abundance did message testing and backs the bill. Amid the dozens of organizations that signed onto an Abundance Institute letter, many are affiliated with key conservative umbrella groups, like the Council for National Policy and State Policy Network.

Centrist Blue Dog Coalition Democrats and New Democrat Coalition are on board. Third Way, the principal centrist think tank, supports the bill, as does the Searchlight Institute, another centrist think tank founded last year aimed at “curbing the influence of liberal groups,” according to the New York Times. The Heritage Foundation, a cornerstone of D.C.’s right-wing think tank scene, supports the bill. The Bipartisan Policy Center supports the bill and published a long analysis of its details.

The National Association of Counties strongly supports the bill for a variety of subtle reasons. The center-right American Action Forum and libertarian Cato Institute support the bill.

The Center for Climate and Energy Solutions supports the bill and provided a long analysis, as does the Center for Public Enterprise. The National Taxpayers Union supports the bill.

Liskow, a law firm involved with fossil fuels, touted the bill’s Senate passage as important, and a similar law firm called Hunton is monitoring it closely. The Environmental Defense Fund released an ambiguous statement saying it was “worth the hard work to fix.”

NAACP and Defenders of Wildlife are strongly opposed, along with hundreds of environmental groups. The political non-profit 5 Calls Civic Action pushed members to oppose the bill and the beltway insider website Punchbowl News leaked an internal Zoom chat transcript between BAAJA opponents.

It looks like BAAJA faces steep odds in the U.S. House before the end of the year. However, the situation is still worth looking at carefully. A huge bill like this brings countless interested players in Washington out into the open.

It clearly shows that even after an election that is going to move Congress to the left, cuts to the Clean Water Act and other bedrock legislation are considered acceptable sacrifices when carrots like transmission line construction got put on the table.

Alliances of convenience between conservatives, oil and gas lobbyists, abundance evangelists, and the cleaner end of the energy industry could keep turning up.

text:
Côte d’Ivoire has tied its transport and e-mobility strategy to its NDCs, targeting EVs to make up 10% of the public administration vehicle fleet by 2030, alongside a broader goal to have in excess of 5,400 EVs on the road by 2035.

To prevent the West African country from becoming a dumping ground for ageing vehicles, Côte d’Ivoire is enforcing technical rules alongside its tax breaks, such as a strict five-year age limit from the date of first registration for passenger vehicles entering the country.

A panel discussion at the trade fair and conference Salon International des Ressources Extractives et Énergétiques en Côte d’Ivoire (Sirexe 2026), attended by ESI Africa, began by asking what ultimately drives a country’s decision to electrify its transport vehicles and systems. Is it climate commitment, industrial ambition, energy security, or is it linked to the economics of users?

To understand the landscape, Kartik Gopal, global electric vehicle industry specialist for the International Finance Corporation (IFC), part of the World Bank Group, very quickly enumerated the reasons countries take that initial step.

Follow our WhatsApp channel for insights on how the power, energy and water sectors are evolving

Whatever the reason, every country has to make its own decision

Gopal prefaced his remarks by explaining that while the question of electric mobility is pertinent to every country, each must find its own rationale.

“Globally, in our work in emerging markets, what we see is there are six different reasons why countries have looked at promoting electric mobility. The first one, which is sort of self-evident, is on the environment, which is more related to CO2 emissions reduction and greenhouse gas reductions through transportation.

“But that reason is not generally a sufficient reason to drive action on the ground,” he said drily. “I mean, we all know that it’s the right thing to do, but it’s a hard thing to do. So, it becomes challenging to put money and effort behind that.”

Contact our sales team to position your smart solution to power Africa’s grids

For Gopal, the second reason is closely tied to the first aspect of the environment: unclean air. In 16 years in the EV industry, he has seen only two countries cite air pollution as the reason to green their transport systems through electrification.

He raised the example of Ho Chi Minh City in Viet Nam, which banned two-wheelers and other vehicles from its city centres, and Delhi, which instituted a multi-year initiative designed to reduce air pollution and strengthen air quality management in Delhi’s National Capital Territory.

A third reason is turning into a very important reason for many countries around the world – energy security.

“Many countries are import-dependent for their oil supplies, and we know what’s been happening with the oil markets this year, in particular. It’s not just about the price of oil; it’s about the availability of oil, and that is driving action towards electrification.”

Have you read? The end of fossil fuel safety and 5 lessons from the latest energy shock

In the end, cost of ownership is very important

Gopal finds the fourth reason particularly interesting and says it applies to countries which are exploring value chain participation, such as Indonesia, which is home to the world’s largest nickel reserves.

“So, they want to exploit those resources and build a battery manufacturing value chain around their sources of nickel. Similarly, South Africa has abundant sources of manganese. All of these are important critical minerals for the battery value chain.

“And that’s kind of what is driving action towards electric mobility in those countries.”

Of interest: Electric two-wheeler sales expose charging, finance and grid gaps

A fifth reason some countries turn to electrification of transport systems and vehicles is the lower total cost of ownership.

“In commercial fleets, and this is actually the biggest driver of electrification in many of our markets, they actually save money by driving electric vehicles in commercial fleets. We have Gocabs here in Côte d’Ivoire. They were hopefully attached to this fact.

“But in markets, especially, the important caveat here is fuel subsidies can alter that equation. But foundationally, that can be a huge driver of commercial fleet electrification and public transport electrification.”

Transport is going electric, whether you want it to or not

The World Bank, through the work of the IFC, hones in on that public transport electrification sector in particular through its focus on the electrification of two-wheelers, three-wheelers, trucks and buses.

“This aligns very well with the World Bank agenda of more and better jobs because, at the end of the day, the driver or the fleet owner, which is very often an individual or an MSME, they make more money using electric vehicles.

“And the last one, and I can say this with a little bit of certainty in the last year or so, it’s a very interesting one. For me, the most interesting one, because the last reason why countries are starting to promote electric mobility is a sense of inevitability.

“I think it is finally dawning that you can be in denial, you can delay it, but you cannot prevent it from happening eventually. So, you may as well get your act together,” said Gopal.

Did you know? How EV batteries could stabilise South Africa’s power grid

Specific to Côte d’Ivoire

“I think eventually it is for every country to find its reasons for promoting such a massive transformation of an entire sector, but what we see at a very practical and pragmatic level is that the point about commercial fleet electrification can be a great starting point for the overall transformation of the industry.

“It helps the drivers and the fleet owners to earn more. It creates the infrastructure that is required, which can then be reused for the charging infrastructure. [It] can then serve the needs of personal mobility as well.

But it builds the foundation for a commercially driven, rational fleet adoption models to be created. So, that’s something that we do encourage and we hope that we can support.”

title: The Permitting Bill Threatens Our Endangered Species - Earthjustice
description:
Last week, the Senate passed a permitting bill that would dramatically weaken the Endangered Species Act (ESA), edging imperiled wildlife closer to extinction in order to fast-track fossil fuel, mining, logging, and other environmentally harmful projects.
There’s no reason lawmakers cannot advance clean energy infrastructure without sacrificing protections for our endangered species.
The proposed changes in the Senate’s permitting bill would threaten that track record, significantly decreasing the law’s effectiveness in the future.
Here is what’s at stake for endangered species under the current version of the permitting bill: It shifts responsibilities for protecting endangered wildlife from federal agency experts to a patchwork of state agencies with little experience and fewer resources.
Far from making decisions more science-based, it could severely restrict what and how information can be used when considering species protections.
text:
Last week, the Senate passed a permitting bill that would dramatically weaken the Endangered Species Act (ESA), edging imperiled wildlife closer to extinction in order to fast-track fossil fuel, mining, logging, and other environmentally harmful projects.

The bill falsely presumes that protecting our wildlife and biodiversity somehow stands in the way of clean energy development. It doesn’t. There’s no reason lawmakers cannot advance clean energy infrastructure without sacrificing protections for our endangered species. But as written, the bill would cut the heart out of the ESA, stripping essential safeguards at a time when dwindling species are under increasing pressure from climate change, accelerating habitat loss, over-exploitation like overfishing, and a de-regulatory onslaught from the Trump administration that threatens to dissolve programs bolstering their survival.

Since its passage in 1973, the ESA has prevented 99% of the species from becoming extinct. The proposed changes in the Senate’s permitting bill would threaten that track record, significantly decreasing the law’s effectiveness in the future. The bill would undercut fundamental safeguards in the ESA that apply to all activities, including logging, industrial fishing, pesticide use, and dredging. And its provisions reach beyond project reviews to make it more difficult to protect a species or its habitat in the first place.

All told, the bill makes it far more likely that species like sea turtles, grizzly bears, and manatees — centerpieces of our nation’s culture, cornerstones of our outdoor economy, and the pride of communities from Alaska to Florida — could disappear into history books.

Here is what’s at stake for endangered species under the current version of the permitting bill:

It shifts responsibilities for protecting endangered wildlife from federal agency experts to a patchwork of state agencies with little experience and fewer resources. The ESA tasks two federal agencies, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service, with conserving threatened and endangered species. Congress crafted a federally run system for these agencies to evaluate actions to ensure that they do not jeopardize a species’ survival. There is good reason for that unified approach—it ensures that species protections are based on scientific expertise and applied across the species’ range, which in most cases does not match up with state lines. This bill proposes shifting the responsibility of consultation onto state agencies that generally lack the staffing, resources, and expertise to manage listed species. It would create a patchwork of enforcement handled by staff with less experience and fewer resources to work with, weakening and fragmenting species protections, with more imperiled wildlife slipping through the cracks of a more complex, multi-layered and confusing system.

It upends the idea that the government should take precautionary measures to prevent extinction before species are on the brink. The ESA embodies what courts have called “institutionalized caution”—that is, the recognition that extinction is irreversible but our understanding of rare and imperiled species is often imperfect. Often, the only way to ensure their continued survival and recovery is to take precautionary action in the face of some uncertainty based on the guidance of experts. The permitting bill includes new language redefining the phrase “best available science” that would essentially weaponize scientific uncertainty and turn it into a reason not to protect species at all. Far from making decisions more science-based, it could severely restrict what and how information can be used when considering species protections. For example, some species of fish, like the Arctic grayling found in Montana and salmon in the Pacific Northwest, can only survive in very cold water. Yet rising temperatures driven by climate change already pose a threat; one that is exacerbated by dams, streamside logging, and industrial discharges. There is often scientific uncertainty in projections about precisely how hot a river might get and when. Right now, the ESA’s command to use the “best available science” requires agencies to avoid or minimize the harms from things like proposed dam operations that worsen the outlook for a species even if the agency can’t precisely predict the future. But the bill would turn that uncertainty into a reason to reject that evidence, even when it’s abundantly clear that hotter rivers pose an existential threat to the fish. This change could affect thousands of species whose existence hangs in the balance due to habitat loss, changing climate conditions, or other threats on the horizon that scientists are actively warning about.

It makes it nearly impossible for agencies to compel a developer to protect a species when new information is discovered after a permit has been issued. The bill’s “project permitting certainty” provisions would make it nearly impossible for an agency to revisit necessary protections or correct any mistakes if new information arises showing that a species is at greater risk of extinction than previously thought – or even if a project proves far more harmful than anyone anticipated. And it would hand the power to grant these “forever” permits to the Trump administration, which has regularly sought to open coasts and public lands throughout the nation to oil and gas drilling and other harmful development.

It would allow new highway construction to cut right through critical habitat for endangered wildlife, without any accountability for following the law. A so-called “operational right-of-way exemption” would exempt a wide variety of federal highway projects from the Endangered Species Act, eliminating the need for any analysis whatsoever on how projects in these areas would impact imperiled wildlife’s continued survival. This is especially troubling because roads are notorious for creating habitat fragmentation – and habitat loss is the leading driver of biodiversity loss.

Imperiled wildlife are resilient and capable of coming back from near-extinction – but they need humans on their side to facilitate recovery. Congress should heed the overwhelming support from American voters for upholding the federal government’s responsibility to protect endangered wildlife and remove these destructive provisions.
