title: Lawmakers approve RGGI changes, warn of ratepayer costs - Inside Investigator
description:
The RGGI program auctions off carbon credits that fossil fuel electric energy producers must purchase, and the proceeds of that auction are then distributed to the eleven participating states.
According to Eversource, RGGI is costing Connecticut ratepayers upwards of $250 million in hidden costs per year but is only returning roughly $80 million per year to the state.
She questioned how the program benefits Connecticut residents and how the state could revise how RGGI proceeds are allocated.
However, recognizing that participating in RGGI would increase ratepayer costs, Virginia moved to send most of the proceeds money back to consumers as a credit on their bills.
“In fact, the energy savings programs supported by RGGI receive funding from multiple sources, including ratepayers through assessments in the public benefits charge,” DEEP wrote.
text:
Bipartisan lawmakers on the Regulation Review Committee on Tuesday voted to allow the Department of Energy and Environmental Protection (DEEP) to move forward with once again lowering the number of carbon credits available for electric energy producers to purchase through the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, potentially increasing future electric energy costs, but indicated they wanted to see some changes to how Connecticut utilizes the program.

The RGGI program auctions off carbon credits that fossil fuel electric energy producers must purchase, and the proceeds of that auction are then distributed to the eleven participating states.

However, since the program began in 2008, the price per credit has increased by at least 900 percent as the number of credits is continually lowered. According to Eversource, RGGI is costing Connecticut ratepayers upwards of $250 million in hidden costs per year but is only returning roughly $80 million per year to the state.

Because Connecticut participates in a regional wholesale energy market, leaving RGGI wouldn’t spare residents from having to pay the costs, but would simply exclude the state from receiving any of the proceeds, which are currently used to pay for the Connecticut Green Bank, electric vehicle rebates, and energy efficiency programs – all of which are also supported by the public benefits charge on ratepayer bills.

And while the bipartisan Regulation Review Committee approved the regulatory changes to allow DEEP to lower the credit cap further, lawmakers indicated they wanted to see the money do more to offset the cost of energy in Connecticut for ratepayers, who pay some of the highest electric costs in the country.

“I have real concerns with the way this program has been established. Honestly, I think it’s a bit upside down,” said committee chairwoman Rep. Christie Carpino, R-Cromwell. “Anyone who does not understand the crushing effect energy prices are having on our residents has their head in the sand. The way the credits are allocated under this program are backwards. Far too little of the credits are going to the people who actually deserve it and that is the ratepayers. That needs to change.”

“This is a problem we have to address,” said Sen. Sujata Gadkar-Wilcox, D-Trumbull, co-chair of the Regulation Review Committee. “Today the regs that we’re voting on is different than voting on policies in the long run and I do also look forward to working with my good co-chair and the commissioner and everyone else to figure out how we in fact get that direct savings to consumers.”

“The concern here is that energy is the real pain point in our economy, and our personal lives, business, residential, you name it,” said Sen. Joan Hartley, D-Waterbury. She questioned how the program benefits Connecticut residents and how the state could revise how RGGI proceeds are allocated.

Acting DEEP Commissioner Emma Cimino said – and DEEP has previously claimed – that RGGI is, on the whole, a net positive for the state by allegedly reducing the health costs of pollution, reducing electricity costs through better efficiency, and generating job growth in green energy sectors.

“There have been some economic studies that have been done on the program that show RGGI provides net economic benefits to states, including things like enhanced GDP growth and support for new jobs,” Cimino said, adding that RGGI proceeds are distributed according to state statute, something General Assembly lawmakers could take up next session if they wished to revise the program.

“It ought to be in statute that rate relief is the number one goal in returning these dollars to Connecticut,” Hartley said.

Virginia previously exited RGGI but later returned after a political change in leadership. However, recognizing that participating in RGGI would increase ratepayer costs, Virginia moved to send most of the proceeds money back to consumers as a credit on their bills.

Rep. Tracy Marra, R-Darien, ranking member of the General Assembly’s Energy and Technology Committee, issued a press release much to the same effect and calling for more transparency into RGGI’s cost to consumers.

“Affordability has to mean more than a talking point,” Marra said. “Before we make electricity more expensive, lawmakers owe residents an honest accounting of the costs.”

Gov. Ned Lamont praised passage of the regulations, stating that RGGI-funded programs save Connecticut ratepayers money by driving down carbon emissions while simultaneously supporting clean energy programs.

“These updates will maintain affordability protections for ratepayers and make sure Connecticut residents continue to benefit from rebates, energy efficiency and clean energy programs that lower bills, and clean vehicle rebates that help consumers avoid high gas prices at the pump,” Lamont said.

Connecticut has long had some of the highest electric rates in the country, but rates became a political hot potato in 2024 after the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (PURA) allowed pandemic-related public benefits charges to accumulate over multiple years and created a spike in ratepayer bills, leading to public outcry.

Unlike the public benefits charge, which is broken out on a ratepayer’s bill, the cost of RGGI is built into the supply price for electric generation. According to comments submitted to DEEP regarding its regulatory change proposal, Eversource estimated RGGI costs ratepayers $250 million per year in higher energy prices and commented that “RGGI is an inefficient revenue generation mechanism for unaffiliated clean energy programs.”

DEEP officials disputed Eversource’s claims in their response, arguing RGGI proceeds help keep the cost of the public benefits charges lower.

“In fact, the energy savings programs supported by RGGI receive funding from multiple sources, including ratepayers through assessments in the public benefits charge,” DEEP wrote. “RGGI funding supplements these programs, while also helping to lower the public benefits charge for ratepayers through RGGI’s ratepayer relief returns.”

In a 2026 letter to the Massachusetts Department of Energy Resources, Eversource estimated RGGI cost Massachusetts ratepayers roughly $500 million in 2025, but the program returned only $200 million to the state.

“Families in our districts are paying for these RGGI fees every month and they don’t even know it,” said Rep. Nicole Klarides-Ditra, R-Derby. “Our ratepayers pay about $250 million per year into this program, and what does Connecticut get back? I think it’s only a third. And now we’re asking our ratepayers to make it scarcer and more expensive.”

“People can’t afford to pay a penny more with anything in our economy today,” Klarides-Ditra said.

“However, as much as we would like to attend, we have been informed that to attend your event, we would be required to cross a union picket line,” they wrote to university president Alan Garber, Harvard Kennedy School director of programs and events Jacob Watts, and provost John Manning.

The Harvard Graduate Students Union-United Auto Workers (HGSU-UAW), which represents more than 4,000 graduate and undergraduate student workers, has been on strike since October 27.

After more than 20 months of contract negotiations, thousands of teaching fellows, research assistants, and other hourly student workers walked out for the second time this year because Harvard had failed to meet the union’s demands for higher wages and benefits, protections for noncitizen workers, and an independent process for handling harassment and discrimination complaints, according to The Harvard Crimson.

"As newly elected members of the 120th Congress, we were elected because of our commitments to helping working people, and we remain steadfast in our support for unions and collective bargaining," the lawmakers wrote. "So long as these workers are on strike, any trip we take to Harvard would be to stand in solidarity with our striking union siblings."

Support from union members was a critical factor in Democratic victories across the map in November. According to the AFL-CIO, the nation’s largest labor federation, a record 639 card-carrying union members were elected in federal, state, and local races around the country.

Three longtime union organizers and leaders elected to the House this month spearheaded the Harvard boycott: Montana smokejumper Sam Forstag, former vice president of National Federation of Federal Employees Local 60; New York UAW organizer Claire Valdez; and Bob Brooks, president of the Pennsylvania Professional Fire Fighters Association.

“I’ve never crossed a picket line, and I don’t intend to start,” Forstag said in a video posted Tuesday. "Harvard has an endowment of $68 billion. They can afford to pay people a living wage."

The union has asked for annual pay of at least $53,800 for salaried graduate workers, $45,000 for graduate teaching fellows, and for hourly workers to make at least $24 per hour. It also wants pay to increase by 4.5% each year.

According to the UAW, some graduate teaching fellows currently earn just $26,000 annually, low enough to qualify for food assistance in Massachusetts in some cases. The school’s endowment, meanwhile, increased by $11 billion this year.

“Elite universities are unimaginably wealthy, and they massively underpay their graduate students, substituting real compensation for the hope of eventually landing an elite faculty job,” said Rep.-elect Daniel Biss (D-Ill.), another incoming lawmaker who signed the letter. “They even often insist grad students aren’t workers, even though they give their labor (teaching and research) in exchange for money.”

In the letter, the lawmakers said they’d reconsider attending the orientation, scheduled for December 6-8, if the university agreed to a fair contract with the workers.

Forstag told the school's administrators, "If me and so many other members of Congress are going to be making a trip out there in December, it's going to be to join our brothers and sisters on the picket line until and unless you engage in good faith in contract negotiations and give those workers a fair deal."

Harvard receives hundreds of millions of dollars from the federal government each year to support scientific and medical research.

“The richest university in the world should be able to pay its workers a fair wage,” said Denish Jaswal, the president of HGSU-UAW. “It is not too much to ask for Harvard to protect noncitizen workers and to create a workplace free from harassment and discrimination. If Harvard is going to be asking newly elected members of Congress for funding, Harvard shouldn’t be surprised when those same members demand that Harvard treats its workers with dignity.”

Jaswal told The Boston Globe that the support from newly elected Democrats was “incredibly telling, and it really sets a strong tone that is positive for labor that they reached out to us, and that this is their first act to support us.”

Other Massachusetts Democrats have also expressed support for the picketers, including Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Ed Markey, incoming House Majority Leader Katherine Clark, and Rep. Ayanna Pressley.

"We stand with the Harvard Graduate Students Union and the Harvard Academic Workers as they strike and fight for good wages, workplaces free of harassment, and a university that works for all," they said in a joint statement last week.

Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.), who helped to organize faculty at the University of Pittsburgh with the United Steelworkers before being elected to Congress in 2022, praised his incoming colleagues' unapologetic stand with organized labor.

"Being pro-worker means knowing which side of a picket line to stand on," he said, adding that it was "great to see" Forstag, Brooks, and Valdez "leading so many new members in solidarity."

Rep.-elect Brad Lander (D-NY), who also signed the letter, congratulated his colleagues on their pro-union leadership. Democrats plan to prioritize passing the landmark Protecting the Right to Organize Act, or PRO Act, after retaking Congress in January.

Lander said, "Let’s make this the most pro-labor Democratic majority in generations."

After dropping her 5-year-old son off at school on the morning of October 10, 2025, Dayanne Figueroa—a single mother and US citizen by birth—suddenly had her car rammed on West Hubbard Street by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents.

Video shows that agents pointed guns at Figueroa, then 31, dragged her out by her legs, threw her onto the pavement, and pinned her face down using their knees. According to the complaint, one of the agents placed a knee near an incision from a recent kidney surgery, which she said “caused acute and severe pain.”

Despite repeatedly identifying herself as a US citizen, Figueroa was detained without a warrant. She said agents put her phone into airplane mode, preventing her friends and family from contacting her. They then spirited her away in an unmarked red van with other detainees.

While en route to Broadview Detention Center in suburban Chicago, Figueroa suffered a panic attack, according to the complaint.

As she shook, cried, and gasped for air, agents photographed her, and one told her: “You’re a criminal. No one will help you.” Figueroa had no prior criminal record and was never charged with a crime.

While at Broadview—an ICE processing facility that became notorious for overcrowding and conditions described as "dehumanizing" after it became a de facto detention center during Midway Blitz—Figueroa said she was subject to “invasive body searches and to sexualized and degrading comments, mockery, and coercive questioning.”

The complaint alleges that before being permitted to use a restroom, she was subject to another purported search involving an agent “touching her private parts.” She said she was eventually allowed to use the restroom under surveillance, without any privacy.

She said agents knew she was recovering from recent major kidney surgery but withheld water and medical assistance until she began urinating blood.

After several hours in custody and a transfer to another facility in Lombard, Figueroa was released and transferred to a hospital for emergency evaluation.

When Figueroa’s boyfriend, mother, and family lawyer arrived at the Lombard facility in search of her, an agent informed them that she was “fine.”

In fact, the complaint said the force used by the officers had broken one of her dental crowns and caused internal bleeding. Meanwhile, her surgical wounds were aggravated, and the denial of medical care exacerbated her underlying kidney condition and delayed her recovery.

The damage to Figueroa went beyond the physical. The lawsuit says the ordeal "destroyed her sense of safety, security, and peace," and that she "suffers from severe emotional and psychological trauma, which continues to affect her ability to live her life as she did prior to the incident."

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) blamed Figueroa for the collision, accused her of assaulting federal officers, and described her as an “agitator," who "violently resisted arrest," claims contradicted by video evidence.

An investigation by the Illinois Accountability Commission released this April found that there was "no credible evidence suggesting that Figueroa intentionally rammed her vehicle into the agents’ vehicle."

The report concluded that agents “may have falsified the narratives” in their report to justify forcefully detaining Figueroa. It cites multiple glaring inaccuracies—including the claim that Figueroa kicked officers using black high-heeled shoes, when in fact her shoes had fallen off as she was dragged out of her vehicle.

In December 2025, Figueroa was one of five US citizens who testified about their mistreatment by federal immigration agents at a congressional forum convened by Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.).

Figueroa, a first-generation Mexican American, described her experience as "violence, blatant racial profiling, and a shocking abuse of federal authority."

Last week, while confronting DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.), a Chicago native who is seeking to chair the House Homeland Security Committee’s oversight subcommittee next year, described Figueroa’s case as an example of how federal agents have abused their power under President Donald Trump.

"They don’t respect the civil rights of our neighbors or the rule of law; they terrorize our communities; they act with impunity," Ramirez said.

The assault of Figueroa fits into a much broader pattern of documented abuse during the Trump administration's mass deportation campaign, including the violent detention of US citizens, warrantless arrests, racial profiling, denial of medical care, and official accounts of confrontations that have been contradicted by video evidence.

During Operation Midway Blitz, federal agents shot US citizen Marimar Martinez five times and falsely accused her of ramming their vehicle, dragged US citizens from their homes and detained them for hours during a military-style apartment raid, and denied medical care to a man after an agent repeatedly punched him in the head.

As of October, ProPublica had identified at least 519 US citizens who had been detained by federal immigration agents since Trump returned to office, and said the real number was likely higher.

“What happened to me is what happens to people when our government is allowed to act with impunity and trample our Constitution,” Figueroa said in a statement on Tuesday. “A badge—or in my case, a police Velcro patch that looks like it was bought off Amazon—is not a free pass to intimidate, terrorize, or mistreat people.”

"These reckless federal agents are an insult to every legitimate law enforcement officer and a complete and utter embarrassment from the very top all the way down,” she added. “They have made a mockery of everything this country claims to stand for, and I hope this lawsuit helps hold those responsible for my attack accountable, and puts an end to this horrific abuse.”

The rise of lethal autonomous weapons systems, popularly called killer robots, has added an unprecedented level of risk—and urgency—to the equation.

authors: Superpower Daily Editorial Desk, superpowerdaily.com, editorial-standards

text:
AI data centers could gain access to more electricity under a Senate-passed package that would also make them cover their grid costs. The Senate approved the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, 62–33 on November 19, 2026. The permitting and transmission overhaul still needs House approval before it can become law.

The package targets both the approval of energy projects and the transmission infrastructure needed to carry their electricity. That combination matters for new wind and solar projects, which can be held back by insufficient transmission capacity. It also offers a potential benefit to the technology industry as electricity-hungry data centers seek more power.

The bargain includes a condition for the largest computing operators: they would have to pay for grid upgrades. Senator Jon Husted’s office says provisions he negotiated would protect consumers from data-center energy and infrastructure costs. His office also says the package would preserve Ohio’s authority over transmission-line siting and data-center electricity rates.

The possible supply gains are substantial, but far from certain in scale. Rhodium Group estimates the legislation could enable additional clean-energy construction by 2040, with a wide gap between its low and high estimates. Those figures describe projected construction, not electricity capacity already approved or built.

The bill would change both how federal agencies review projects and how opponents challenge them. According to Husted’s office, environmental assessments would have a one-year deadline, while fuller environmental impact statements would have a two-year deadline. These are federal review deadlines, not promises that projects would be built within those periods.

Senator Dan Sullivan’s summary describes further changes under the National Environmental Policy Act, the federal environmental-review law. They reach beyond setting a faster clock:

Court challenges would have to be filed within 150 days. Parties bringing them would need to have raised their specific concerns during public comment periods.

The legislation would narrow the scope of environmental reviews and clarify which projects trigger the law, codifying the Supreme Court’s Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County decision.

For violations of that law, the prescribed remedy would send the decision back for correction without automatically setting it aside.

The package would also limit when federal agencies could rescind or suspend issued permits. Separate provisions would streamline reviews under the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act and National Historic Preservation Act, while accelerating permitting for geothermal, critical-mineral and renewable-energy projects on federal lands.

Clean-energy and fossil-fuel groups both welcomed Senate passage. The American Clean Power Association argued that the measure would modernize energy systems and lower consumer prices. The American Petroleum Institute praised its potential to reduce delays and support infrastructure. As negotiated, the package would benefit both renewable and fossil energy projects.

Environmental opponents see a different bargain. The Natural Resources Defense Council urged the House to reject the bill, arguing it would give President Donald Trump excessive latitude to favor oil and gas companies and data-center developers. Tribes also objected to changes affecting their participation in permitting; senators amended the package before the vote to address those concerns.

That dispute split Senate Democrats: more voted against the package than for it, though more than a dozen supported passage. Senator Martin Heinrich, a Democratic author, emphasized affordability and the opportunity to connect more clean energy to the grid. Opponents warned that the environmental rollbacks would give data-center development too much freedom.

The division now follows the bill to the House. Representative Scott Peters urged passage before this Congress ends, while House Natural Resources ranking member Jared Huffman urged Democrats to reject it and pursue a better deal.

text:
The car business isn’t sentimental, even if buyers are. Models that don’t sell, don’t meet the latest regulations, or simply don’t fit the latest corporate plan tend to disappear. So it’s surprising when a handful of vehicles that, by any reasonable measure, should be gone are still in showrooms. In the spirit of the season, here are five models Edmunds’ editors are thankful you can still buy. Some are fast, some are cheap, and at least one is a little ridiculous. All of them deserve a look before someone in the boardroom decides they’ve run their course. All of the following prices include destination charges.

Chevrolet Bolt

It’s true that electric vehicles are more expensive than comparable gas-powered cars, and the end of the federal EV tax credit last year made it all the more obvious. That’s why we are glad that the Chevrolet Bolt is back. Chevy brought back its small electric car for 2027 with a starting price under $30,000.

It’s not a penalty box either. The Bolt has about 260 miles of range, offers plenty of room for adults, and now charges far quicker at public charging stations than the old version did, making road trips more practical. The catch is that this Bolt appears to be a one-year offering. If an inexpensive electric car sounds appealing, now is the time to look.

2027 Bolt starting price: $28,995

Ford Mustang

Not long ago, you had three choices if you wanted a traditional V8-powered muscle car. Well, Chevy stopped building the Camaro after 2024, and Dodge retired the Challenger in favor of a larger, very different Charger. That leaves the Mustang on its own, which isn’t an entirely new scenario for this American classic. Its rivals have come and gone over the decades, but the Mustang has been on sale without a break since 1964.

Ford, to its credit, keeps finding ways to make it more exciting. The newest version, the Mustang Dark Horse SC, adds a supercharger, bringing the total to 795 horsepower. At $108,085 to start, it’s a lot of money for a Mustang. But the Mustang GT is still available with a V8 and a six-speed manual, and it’s the one most fans are grateful for.

2026 Mustang starting price: $34,990

Honda Prelude

By most business measures, the Prelude shouldn’t exist. Sporty two-door coupes are a tiny slice of the market, and one that’s a hybrid and has a price north of $40,000 makes even less sense. But here we are with the 2027 Honda Prelude, and we’re pleased that Honda found a way to bring back the Prelude after a two-decade-plus hiatus.

The Prelude borrows hardware from the performance-focused Civic Type R to make it one of the best-handling front-wheel-drive cars Edmunds has ever driven. It offers an adaptive suspension, powerful brakes and precise steering. It’s not nearly as quick as a Mustang, but its hybrid powertrain lets it earn 44 mpg combined, according to the EPA.

2027 Prelude starting price: $43,695

Jeep Wrangler 392

In some ways, it’s hard to believe that the Wrangler is still around. It’s pretty bad at the things most SUV shoppers want, whether it be comfort, fuel economy or cutting-edge technology. It’s therefore even harder to believe that you can get a Wrangler with a massive V8 making 470 horsepower. Putting that much engine into a boxy SUV built to crawl over rocks makes very little sense. Jeep did it anyway.

Jeep actually spent two years telling everyone that the Wrangler 392 was going away. In a truly American parting prank, it sold final editions in both 2024 and 2025. Then the brand’s CEO announced in 2025 that the V8 would stay in production indefinitely. The 2027 V8-powered Wrangler will likely give you sticker shock, but trust us, there’s nothing else quite like it.

2027 Wrangler Willys 392 starting price: $72,990

Mazda MX-5 Miata

Two seats, a folding roof and not much else. That’s been the Miata’s recipe since 1989, and it’s the reason the little Mazda has outlasted every convertible that came along after it. It’s light and simple, and it makes an ordinary back road feel like an event at speeds that won’t put you in jail. Like the Mustang, it’s also one of the few new cars you can buy with a stick shift.

The current Miata has been on sale for more than a decade, and it doesn’t appear that Mazda has a timeline for a replacement. Prices start a little over $30,000, which is about as low as it gets for a genuine sports car.

2026 Miata MX-5 starting price: $32,045

Edmunds says

Our featured vehicles all sell in small numbers. But each exists because enough people still want a car that’s fun and not just sensible. That’s worth being grateful for. Here’s hoping they stick around.

text:
The sandy shores of Virginia Beach are idyllic, but what makes the place truly special lies about 27 miles off the coast, at the site of the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project, the largest offshore wind farm under construction in the country.

The project has been more than a decade in the making. In 2013, Dominion Energy secured a leasing agreement with the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management. In 2017, during the first Trump administration, the agency approved Dominion's site plan for the project, and in 2020 its two pilot turbines turned on. But it wasn't until October 2023 that federal regulators gave the final stamp of approval, allowing the rest of the farm to begin construction.

From the shore, it's hard to tell that construction has been underway. Except at certain times at night, the turbines are pretty much impossible to see with the human eye. (If you want to see them from the shore, you have to find the perfect spot and use binoculars.) But if you take a boat ride out to the Outer Continental Shelf, you'll begin to appreciate the scale of the project: 800-foot-tall turbines towering over the open seas like skyscrapers capable of withstanding Category 3 hurricane winds, anchored to the ocean floor with 1,500-ton metal tubes that are 31 feet in diameter.

Despite their industrial appearance, the turbines have been a net positive to the local environment. They serve as artificial reefs for fish and other wildlife, and they have allowed fishermen to continue catching flounder, cobia, and mahi in the Atlantic's deep waters.

When construction is completed—an event scheduled for late 2027—the wind farm will be the largest such project in the country. Its 176 turbines are expected to deliver 9.5 million megawatt-hours of clean energy to the Virginia grid every year. That will be enough to power 660,000 homes, according to Dominion. At this point, the company expects the farm to support 1,100 jobs and generate $200 million in annual economic output for the region.

And one needn't wait until 2027 to see that the project is proving beneficial to the area. Every year during its construction phase, Dominion estimates, the wind farm has supported 900 direct and indirect jobs and generated $143 million in economic output.

But in December 2025, the Interior Department issued a stop-work order for the Coastal Virginia project out of the blue.

What might compel the Trump administration to halt the construction of a project that supported countless jobs and was backed by the first Trump administration? The same rationale that keeps recurring when the president tries to justify his takeover of America's energy markets: "national security."

Trump's National Energy Emergency and the Defense Production Act

When President Donald Trump was on the campaign trail in 2024, he promised to unleash America's energy dominance. "We're going to be energy-dominant, we're going to make a fortune, we're going to supply it all over Europe, all over the world," he told Fox News' Maria Bartiromo that August. "We're going to be double and triple what they're doing. We're going to have tremendous energy, and we're going to lower our prices of energy."

Depending on the energy source, Trump's first 22 months back in office have been either "tremendous" or a toil. Fossil fuels are enjoying favorable policies, and their production has reached new heights. Renewable energy projects face government roadblock after government roadblock (in addition to the cancellation of wasteful subsidies).

On Day 1—the same day Trump "temporarily" halted all permitting for offshore wind projects in federal waters—Trump signed an executive order declaring a National Energy Emergency. "The policies of the previous administration have driven our Nation into a national emergency, where a precariously inadequate and intermittent energy supply, and an increasingly unreliable grid, require swift and decisive action," the order read.

The "swift and decisive action" needed to fix such a dire situation? Increasing the government's power and reach. Specifically, the order directed federal agencies to "exercise any lawful emergency authorities available to them" to increase the generation of almost all energy sources—all but wind and solar—through the Defense Production Act (DPA).

The DPA was passed in 1950, a few months after the start of the Korean War, when Congress determined it "needed a mechanism for the president to direct industrial production towards defense needs without full nationalization," says Gabe Arrington, a national security expert and nonresident fellow at the Baker Institute for Public Policy at Rice University.

Once invoked, the DPA gives the president immense power, with nearly no congressional oversight, to meddle with private businesses. He can force private entities to prioritize certain contracts, award loans and loan agreements, and even block corporate mergers with foreign companies.

"We were coming right out of World War II, where we had a full nationalization effort. This was an intermediate step," says Arrington.

Yet the DPA has had a long legacy, and has been invoked at least once by each president since it passed. President Jimmy Carter used the act to fund research into synthetic fuels and to establish the Synthetic Fuels Corporation, which financed research and development into these energy sources from 1980 until Congress shut it down in 1986. President Ronald Reagan used the act to stockpile rare earth minerals for military purposes and to direct steel production.

After 9/11, its "use expanded dramatically," says Arrington, including for "body armor, military vehicles, [and] other military surveillance equipment." During the COVID-19 pandemic, both Trump and President Joe Biden used the DPA to procure billions of dollars' worth of personal protective equipment and medical and testing supplies. Biden then used it to boost production in the clean energy sector.

In April 2025, Trump decided to promote a different set of energy producers. In an executive order, the president declared it "the policy of the United States that coal is essential to our national and economic security." The order also designated coal a "critical mineral," opening up the door for future DPA funding.

With these moves in place, the Trump administration was ready to use the full weight of the federal government to shape the energy sector as it saw fit.

'The American People Won and the Special Interests Lost'

During the first Trump administration, the president signed deregulatory reforms for nuclear energy, modernized federal environmental reviews, and scrapped expensive restrictions on power plants. The market responded to Trump's (mostly) anti-interventionist approach: Inflation-adjusted energy spending fell, renewable energy generation and investments reached new heights, and in 2017 the U.S. became a net exporter of liquefied natural gas—a remarkable feat considering the first export of the fuel from the lower 48 states occurred only a year earlier.

Trump's successor scrapped this hands-off approach.

On Day 1 of his presidency, Joe Biden axed the Keystone Pipeline and paused new oil and gas leasing on federal lands. Then, in 2022, Biden signed his legacy-defining (and ironically named) Inflation Reduction Act into law.

"With this law, the American people won and the special interests lost," Biden said at the bill signing in August 2022. A few months later, climate czar John Kerry predicted the bill would jumpstart "the biggest transformation, economically, since the Industrial Revolution."

That transformation never materialized. Instead, the government shelled out huge sums to the green energy industry.

The Inflation Reduction Act appropriated billions in new spending, $12 billion of which was funneled to the Energy Department's Loan Programs Office. This sum, and the office's $100 billion in new lending authority, was directed to support such projects as a Ford factory in Tennessee (which displaced the area's residents), grid upgrades for California's largest power utility, and a solar facility for a South Korean manufacturer owned by Stellantis (formerly Chrysler).

The law also offered expensive tax credits and subsidies for renewables and green tech. Wealthy homeowners and large corporations claimed the majority of tax credits. Renewable energy production, which reached then-historic highs in 2024, lagged significantly behind fossil fuels.

Meanwhile, grid operators were issuing dire warnings about the status of the power grid. In 2023, PJM Interconnection, the largest grid operator in the country, reported that grid demand—driven by electrification and data centers—was outpacing supply. A year later, the operator warned that "continuing generator retirements and increasing demand" were eroding its energy reserves, which could impact its response to the summer's extreme heat. Trump's Energy Department would later release a report finding that, if power plant retirements continued, blackouts would be 100 times more likely to occur in 2030.

This price crunch, coupled with record spending, prompted conservative policy wonks to demand drastic action. Diana Furchtgott-Roth, then of the conservative Heritage Foundation, wrote in the days leading up to Trump's second inauguration that "America faces a national energy emergency because the Biden administration has created a serious and dangerous energy situation so damaging to ordinary people and our country that it requires immediate action." By taking "immediate action" and declaring a national energy emergency, she wrote, "Trump can ensure that America does not walk down the same yellow brick road of Europe's energy and climate policies."

Trump's National Security Claims Are a Weak Justification To Block Wind and Prop Up Coal

Enough people agreed that the Biden green agenda was a disaster that Trump reentered office with significant leeway to recreate his first term's lighter-touch approach to energy markets. Instead, he doubled down on Biden's intrusiveness.

For example, in 2026 Trump adopted a novel strategy in his battle against wind projects: Pay them to stop operating. In March, the administration reached a deal with TotalEnergies to shutter two of the company's offshore wind projects in North Carolina and New York. Under the agreement, TotalEnergies was given $928 million—a "dollar-for-dollar" payback from what it spent on procuring its offshore leases—which it then invested in oil and natural gas projects. The company also pledged "not to develop any new offshore wind projects in the United States," according to a government press release.

The Interior Department cited national security concerns when spearheading the deal. It has since brokered four other agreements to pay developers to cancel permitted offshore wind projects and invest in fossil fuel generation. Meanwhile, the Defense Department has stalled approvals for onshore wind farms on private lands under the guise of "national security," the Financial Times reported in May.

Projects like these regularly require approval from the Defense Department to ensure they don't mess with radar systems. If they do, the fix is simple: The developer can negotiate with the Pentagon on a fee to update the radar system. If they don't, the project can move forward. As the Financial Times points out, 50 of the projects facing a shutdown would "probably have been declared risk-free." Meanwhile, 30 had "undergone negotiations, received verbal signoffs and were waiting for written confirmation," making Trump's national security justification all the more thin.

As Jason Grumet, CEO of the American Clean Power Association, told the Financial Times, "The fact the administration is telling private landowners they're not allowed to pursue economic activity and generate value from their property is hard to reconcile with conservative values."

Luckily for developers, a federal judge froze the Pentagon's wind order in August. In November, the Senate passed a sprawling bipartisan permitting reform bill that would, among other things, prohibit the executive branch from rescinding or altering an approved permit or impeding the construction of a previously approved project. Certain conditions—including new information on national security risks—would still allow a federal agency to interfere. But even then, the agency would have to provide advance written warning to justify its actions. At press time, the legislation is in the House of Representatives; the White House says it backs the bill.

The government has also intervened to prop up favored industries, especially coal. In May 2025, citing Trump's national energy emergency order, Energy Secretary Chris Wright ordered J.H. Campbell—a 1,560 megawatt coal-fired power plant in Michigan that was scheduled to shut down that month—to "temporarily" remain open for the summer. Over a year later, J.H. Campbell is still open. Consumers Energy, the plant's majority owner, is seeking $303 million in cost recovery from ratepayers in the region. In September, a federal court vacated the Energy Department's initial order to keep the power plant open. Despite this ruling, the agency issued a 90-day order in November to keep the plant open through mid-February.

"I think that the reliability and stability of the grid is both an economic concern and there can be national security concerns," such as brownouts and cybersecurity threats, says Nick Loris, president of C3 Solutions, a free market energy think tank. But "it doesn't seem like [J.H. Campbell is] generating that much electricity, so I don't know if it's actually solving a problem."

Loris warns that decisions like these can have "secondary and tertiary effects" on the market and prevent investments into cleaner, cheaper technologies. That's happening in Indiana, where an Energy Department order to keep a retiring coal plant open has made it impossible for one of the units to be replaced by cleaner-burning natural gas.

The Trump administration has kept pumping money into coal. Using its DPA authority, the Energy Department has given $425 million to modernize coal plants, while opening up other funding opportunities for the industry. Thanks to an April order, more DPA funding is incoming for the industry to support its supply chains and extend other coal power plants. Yet exports are down.

Nuclear energy, too, has enjoyed favored status under Trump 2.0, including using the DPA to enrich nuclear fuel. This move has been praised by the industry, which sees America's lack of uranium enrichment—nearly all of America's enriched uranium is imported—as a national security threat. Christo Liebenberg, president of LIS Technologies, a startup that uses laser technology to enrich uranium, argues that the Energy Department's use of the DPA to finance uranium enrichment is "needed because the demand is just so big, and the supply is so small." Liebenberg says that to meet the government's goal of quadrupling nuclear power by 2050, the U.S. will need a 12-fold increase in its domestic enrichment capabilities.

The administration used the same national security rationale to take an ownership stake in Westinghouse last year. In June, the Energy Department unveiled a $17.5 billion loan program to deploy 10 Westinghouse AP1000 reactors. Not coincidentally, per the terms of the ownership agreement, the government will "get a 20% share in any dividends paid out by Westinghouse above a $17.5 billion threshold," according to Bloomberg.

So even when a national security argument may have some truth to it, it can become a slippery slope. "Rather than making an investment that is targeted for a specific national security need," says Loris, "it ends up being more of a balloon payment to industries and companies writ large that really aren't addressing the legitimate national security questions."

This seems to have been the M.O. under the second Trump administration: using seemingly justifiable, though mostly bogus, national security claims to bolster favored companies and industries. Trump is certainly not the first president to do this. But he is doing it even as administration officials such as Wright have identified a better set of fixes to America's energy challenges—namely, deregulation.

Consumers may not immediately feel the negative impacts of Trump's energy socialism, but the continued distortion of energy markets will soon be seen in higher utility bills and steeper power-plant construction costs. They may also be felt politically when President Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez halts all oil and gas projects and supercharges solar development with the same "national security" tools that Trump is using now.

What Happened to the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind Project?

Despite being targeted by the Trump administration, the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project lives on. In January, a federal judge struck down the administration's work stoppage, and later that month a turbine generator was installed. In March, the farm delivered its first power to the grid.

But in August, Dominion reported that the project's cost had risen by nearly $300 million, thanks to Trump's tariffs and to updated turbine installation projections.

Trump came into office promising to reverse Biden's energy policies. But while he may have changed who directly benefits from those policies, he has used many of the same policy levers, which in turn have yielded similarly expensive and harmful outcomes. The U.S. needs more energy, but bogus national security claims are getting in the way.

text:
Government Capacity

Big Bets: Anchoring a Next-Era Climate Agenda

11.25.26 | 10 min read | Text by Hannah Safford & Loren DeJonge Schulman & Craig Segall

In the 2024 presidential election, voters pushed back against a growing sense of government ineffectiveness; in the 2026 midterms, they pushed back even more strongly against a reckless government unconcerned with the safety, stability, and economic security of its populace. Americans want neither sclerosis nor sabotage. They want a government that sees the world as it is, that understands the concerns of the governed, and that charts a bold, coherent strategy to respond.

For climate, the 2026 midterms mean that we don’t have to wait until 2029 to begin crucial reconstructive work. Through budgetary and oversight powers at the federal level, and far more expansive opportunities for climate progress at the state level, that work can start next year. But this also means that the next president will have no excuses. They will have to hit the ground running – sprinting, hurdling, careening. They must be ready to not simply undo past damage but to usher in a brighter future that’s both visible and sustainable. To not simply mourn the toll of extreme weather but to do something serious about it. To not simply make existing systems cleaner but to shift our economy off its fossil foundations entirely.

To deliver this next-era climate agenda – for us to help them deliver it – they, and we, must focus on two central developments that set the next era of climate decisively apart from the past.

Clean Technology is Now Finally Winning on Its Merits

Look around the world – clean technology is ascendant and disrupting fossil systems in earnest. In 2025, renewables overtook coal as the world’s largest source of electricity, while solar and wind met essentially all growth in global demand. Clean-energy investment is now nearly double fossil spending. One in four new cars sold worldwide is now electric; further game-changing innovations like solid-state batteries and multi-layer solar are on the horizon. Today’s corruption and backsliding can obscure but cannot change the fact that clean technology is increasingly dominant, while fossil fuels need to be propped up.

This is exciting! When clean technologies are commercial, leaders at all levels can spend less political capital on expensive subsidies and focus instead on the popular policies that will allow those technologies to spread like wildfire: ensuring open and competitive markets, fair prices, fast interconnection, and a power grid that keeps up. To date, we’ve relied heavily on the federal government and California to move first on climate. Now, leaders at all levels have more levers than ever to pull on their own.

Yet even when clean technologies are cheaper and better, it’s impossible to switch overnight. Fossil-based jobs, infrastructure, and revenue are woven into communities across the country. Pulling those planks out heedlessly risks inflicting real pain: on the workers who fix cars and run oil rigs; on the states and towns whose budgets depend on a particular kind of energy. Navigating the messy middle of the energy transition well – so that ordinary Americans gain real agency in the new economy, with high-road jobs, solid public services, and a good future for their kids – is as much a task of economic, labor, and infrastructure policy as it is of energy policy. This task depends on a capable, visionary government that can harness the energy transition as an engine of shared prosperity and renewed public trust.

Climate Overshoot Is Here, And The Threats It Brings Are Different Not Only in Level But In Kind

Rebuilding a government that can adeptly handle challenges is critical, because as the world careens past 1.5 degrees of warming, the danger isn’t just that the extreme weather we’re already familiar with – storms, heat, floods, fire – becomes more frequent and dangerous. Rather, fundamental Earth systems are destabilizing. The collapse of the massive Thwaites Glacier, which can no longer be stopped by cutting emissions alone, would have us measuring sea-level rise in feet instead of inches. The Atlantic circulation that regulates much of our planet’s climate is at real risk of breaking down, an outcome that would make the impacts we’re struggling with today seem minor by comparison.

Climate overshoot also means that worst-case climate scenarios are still on the table. Projections that the world is likely to avoid the highest levels of warming assume that momentum behind clean technology will continue to build. But countries in the throes of catastrophe can’t plan out the infrastructure that a clean economy depends on. A global order upended can’t maintain the supply chains needed to build it. Facing a very real threat of derailment, in which we fully lose our capacity to bring the world back to a safe operating space, we have to walk and chew gum at the same time – managing a complex energy transition even as we grapple with a step change in global risk.

In this new era, restoring emissions standards and federal climate funding remains necessary. It’s decidedly not sufficient. If the only thing we do between now and the next administration is prepare to run the same plays harder and faster, we will lose. This era demands that we evolve the strategies and laws that catalyzed the energy transition into strategies that can see it through.

It also demands that we anchor those strategies in the realities of daily life. “Climate” is an abstraction for most Americans, but its impacts are not. Families feel climate change in their spiking electricity bills and insurance premiums, in their disrupted flights and vacations, in the days where their kids can’t play outside because it’s too hot or smoky or both. They are rightly angry at a system that lets big corporations pollute for free while ordinary people pay the price. A next-era climate agenda has to lower costs, restore stability, deliver accountability, and give people the things they’re asking for, instead of trying to sell them on stuff they’re not.

Five Big Bets for Our Climate Future

At the Center for Regulatory Ingenuity, we’re laying out the “big bets” that make all of that possible. To move quickly and effectively in the next U.S. administration, we need to invest in the core capabilities that will underpin any technocratic policy agenda we stack on top of them, regardless of what issues dominate, which coalitions hold power, and what policy vehicles become available. Without these enablers, progress will be incremental; with them, we have an opportunity to shift our economic and political systems off their fossil foundations.

The five bets we’ve identified below are based on conversations we’ve had with policymakers, funders, and field leaders over the past year, as well as our own observations. They aren’t all that’s needed to deliver on climate goals. Continued legal defense against further backsliding remains crucial, as are ongoing efforts to communicate about climate in ways that resonate with everyday Americans and to ensure that climate is a priority for our elected leaders. Success also depends on broader reconstructive work, from judicial reform to fixing the national debt.

And yet we also need to invest in the goals that feel almost too audacious now, but that our future selves will wish we’d swung for. They are the capabilities that climate leaders at every level and branch of government will need to secure the health, safety, and prosperity of our nation.

We offer them in the spirit that animated past eras of American renewal: a belief that government can be made to do big things, and a refusal to be tethered only to the tools that got us this far. If you share these sentiments, and want to explore how we can collaborate more closely, please reach out. We have much to build, little time to build it, and a great deal worth protecting.

Bet 1. Radically reimagine federal government structure and function

From Reconstruction to the New Deal to the Great Society, our nation used to regularly reorganize its government in response to major needs and visions. It is deeply odd, then, that we largely still run on the agencies and processes we had in the 1970s, and on the workforce system we had in the 1940s. These outdated structures have struggled to keep up with new economic and environmental realities. For reasons of legacy far more than strategy, federal technical expertise on electric vehicles is concentrated at the Department of Energy yet scarce at the Department of Transportation; the EPA is charged with compelling a shift to clean technology but lacks authority over the economic policy needed to enable it; agencies built to suppress and respond to disasters struggle to also help communities prepare and recover.

The bet is that we can move beyond incremental process reform toward audacious, blue-sky visions of how government is structured and how it delivers. That means treating government capacity as a core tool of climate action. It means designing a “mission state” where agencies are oriented around north-star objectives like minimizing derailment risk and navigating the mid-transition. It means focusing less on method and more on outcomes, and being fearless about experimentation. Done well, this reimagination can spark a positive spiral in which climate progress restores public trust in government to do big things, and in which that strengthened trust accelerates progress still further.

Bet 2. Empower state and local governments as the engines of climate progress

States, counties, and cities are ultimately the core planners of the grid and of the transportation system, the architects of economic development, the drivers of housing construction. They have unique authorities and opportunities for creative climate leadership, ranging from divesting public banks and pension funds from volatile fossil holdings to expediting review of low-emission, resilient buildings. They are also, of course, key federal implementers.

The bet is that deep investment in state and local capacity will unleash a torrent of durable climate progress. This will involve long-term efforts to secure new and sustainable revenue sources for state and local governments, intentionally directing talent into subnational public service, far more efficient peer-to-peer learning networks, and providing the legal and technological expertise that governments need in order to reduce kludge and keep pace with society. It means experimenting with “horizontal federalism”, in which cities, counties, and states move together, ahead of and shaping federal action. Imagine, for instance, Western states banding together around regional models of clean economic development; joint procurements or bundled financing among municipalities that make it easier for small businesses to break into the clean energy economy; or climate “clubs” that develop shared governance for challenges like overshoot, via MOUs among science directors across states, international bodies, and federal agencies. Climate change is a polycentric crisis – the bet is on polycentric leadership.

Bet 3. Expand the ambit and vision of American environmental law

American environmental law is largely built around 20th-century environmental laws – the Clean Water Act, the Clean Air Act, NEPA – enacted to deal with industrial pollution. Those laws remain vital and worth defending for many purposes, but there is no remaining legal or political path to use them as the primary tools for driving an economy-wide transition to clean energy. The climate challenges we now face are as often problems of infrastructure, economic, trade, and social-safety-net law (frequently exacerbated by legacy state budget restrictions or the complexities of the tax code) as they are problems of pollution control. There is deep desire across the political spectrum for an updated and expanded legal regime purpose-built for climate progress.

The bet is that taking American environmental law out of its 20th-century box will powerfully underpin a new suite of climate tools and strategies. This means training American environmental lawyers to wade confidently into legal domains that have significant climate implications but that are often underindexed in climate legal strategy, while also bringing specialists in those domains up to speed on climate science and policy. It means conceptualizing new statutory frameworks that better integrate market-shaping, economic development, and pollution and carbon management, harmonized across levels of government. It means going on offense by exploring affirmative legal strategies that can hold corporate polluters accountable, shape new investments, and make the new economy fair, even against the significant headwinds of a hostile judiciary.

Bet 4. Reclaim American innovation leadership

The world has made huge strides on small, modular technologies like solar PV and batteries. But those alone won’t deliver net-zero emissions, nor will they manage impacts already locked in. We also need tremendous advances in low-emission fuels for ships and planes, far cheaper carbon removal, next-generation nuclear and geothermal, regenerative agriculture that pencils out, clean concrete and steel, and more. We need innovation in adaptation and resilience, from efficient cooling and water recycling to super-resistant building materials, to protect against climate-fueled extreme weather.

The bet is that we can rebuild the foundations of American innovation to reposition the United States as a leader in the climate technologies the world has not yet mastered. This means creating the systems, incentives, and career tracks that make it much easier for our nation’s researchers and entrepreneurs to work on these technologies. It means wielding the market-shaping powers of government at every level – e.g., advanced market commitments, bulk procurement, and price transparency – to de-risk exploratory research into frontier climate solutions and bridge the lab-to-market divide. It means tightly coupling our national science to our economic strategy and to mission-state goals like addressing overshoot. It means treating “innovation”, in the climate space, not as a buzzword but as a shared national project.

Bet 5. Extend the runway

The overshoot era demands more tools to protect people and planet. Fundamental Earth systems are teetering, and yet today it is effectively no one’s job to keep track of these systems and stop them from falling apart. That’s a dangerous gap.
