text:
Introduction

There is bipartisan support among both policymakers and the general public for expanding safe and reliable nuclear power to meet growing demand for electricity. On May 23, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14302, which set a bold goal: commence construction on 10 new large nuclear reactors in the United States by 2030. The most likely candidate for fulfilling this goal is the Westinghouse AP1000, the only fully licensed design that has been recently constructed in the United States. Two AP1000 reactors, Vogtle Units 3 and 4 in Georgia, entered service in 2023 and 2024, respectively, and are now generating large amounts of firm “always on” electricity. The Vogtle project — the first set of new nuclear reactors fully built in the United States in over a generation — was completed significantly behind schedule and over budget. Consequently, financiers and the electric utility industry have been reluctant to embark on the next set of AP1000 projects, and nuclear projects more broadly. New financial modeling from Employ America is set to reveal a credible path to allaying investors’ fears — new nuclear projects can “pencil” for equity investors if the Trump administration unleashes the full power of the financing supports each party backed when it controlled Congress. This credible path to investment viability for new nuclear hinges on administrative policy actions that unlock the full value of what Congress has enacted, specifically with respect to the §48E Investment Tax Credit.

The Fission Possible series from Employ America will detail how new nuclear construction projects can pencil — projects are financially viable and attractive under an attainable set of financial and policy assumptions. Key to establishing these conditions is a set of administrative actions that can maximize the potential of the §48E Investment Tax Credit, which plays a critical role in shaping financial returns for nuclear projects. The next piece in the series will break down the assumptions, calculations, and insights stemming from our financial modeling of a hypothetical AP1000 project. This will be followed by pieces that identify how administrative implementation of §48E can be improved, including Domestic Content Requirements, Direct Pay monetization, and the Energy Communities bonus.

Our Analysis Shows Vogtle Costs Are No Longer Fatal

Employ America’s financial modeling demonstrates that the next two AP1000 reactors can “pencil” for investors across several scenarios. By “pencil,” we mean that new AP1000 projects can achieve the requisite internal rates of return (IRRs) and returns on equity (ROEs) under relatively conservative construction cost assumptions. Project equity can earn mid-teens returns, comparable to other large renewable infrastructure projects, even in a scenario where the next pair of AP1000 reactors are built at the same high construction costs as the Vogtle project. This is a conservative assumption because the Vogtle project broke ground with an incomplete reactor design, had to stand up a workforce and supply chain from scratch, and overcame the bankruptcy of its lead construction contractor in the middle of the build phase. The project also faced additional construction delays stemming from the once-in-a-generation global pandemic. These unique factors resulted in significant cost escalation that the next reactor builds should be able to avoid. In fact, significantly greater upside exists for investors who facilitate stronger project execution than the Vogtle project experienced.

Employ America has dedicated significant resources to building a robust financial model of a two-reactor AP1000 project, the only project type with both a completed design and a recent construction track record in the United States. We conducted an extensive literature review of other AP1000 financial modeling efforts, and also pulled specific line item costs from the Vogtle project’s public filings to strengthen our estimates. We built our financial model in collaboration with Pooja Reddy, an investment banker with significant experience in capital-intensive and regulated industries, and with previous transaction experience in infrastructure project finance.

The financial viability of the next AP1000 projects, when using conservative assumptions of total capital expenditures, depends on the Trump administration both unlocking the full potential of the §48E Investment Tax Credit (ITC) and deploying the lending power of the Department of Energy’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing (DOE EDF). This memo goes through the range of implementation barriers that are currently stymieing the full potential of the ITC, and is the first in Employ America’s series exploring how a revitalized ITC, paired with DOE EDF lending, can catalyze the promised nuclear launch.

The Current ITC Implementation Falls Short of Its Promise

The ITC is one of the two principal tax credits authorized by Congress to incentivize new emissions-free electricity generation; the other is the §45Y Production Tax Credit (PTC). The ITC is calculated as a percentage of total eligible project costs and is traditionally claimed in the tax year when the project is placed in service, commonly called the Commercial Operations Date (COD). The PTC, on the other hand, is calculated based on the amount of electricity, measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh), that a project generates once operational during the 10-year credit window. Both credits are claimed by the project owner during tax season. The ITC should, at least in theory, be far more valuable than the PTC for new nuclear projects due to their high upfront capital costs, as shown in analysis within DOE’s Pathways to Commercial Liftoff: Advanced Nuclear report. Given this, our analysis focuses solely on strategies to unlock the ITC.

The One Big Beautiful Bill (OBBB), passed by a Republican Congress in 2025, maintained the full ITC for new nuclear projects that commence construction by 2033, even as OBBB made many other changes to energy policy relative to what was legislated under a Democratic Congress in the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) of 2022.

The base and bonus structure of the ITC is consistent across the IRA and OBBB, and breaks down as follows:

6% Base ITC when no bonus conditions are met: If a nuclear project meets none of the bonus conditions, the “base” credit only covers 6% of eligible project costs.

30% ITC with Wage & Apprenticeship: The ITC is quintupled to 30% of eligible project costs if Prevailing Wage & Apprenticeship (PW&A) requirements are satisfied. The additional bonuses described in the following bullets, Domestic Content Requirements and Energy Communities, are quintupled as well.

40% ITC with Wage & Apprenticeship + Domestic Content: If the project satisfies Domestic Content Requirements (DCR) by being constructed with specified amounts of domestic materials and manufactured inputs, the project receives a 2% bonus credit, but when coupled with the PW&A quintupling, it becomes a 10% bonus credit. Therefore, when the PW&A requirement is met and DCR is satisfied, the ITC will cover 40% of eligible project costs.

50% ITC with Wage & Apprenticeship + Domestic Content + Energy Communities: Finally, if project construction occurs in an “Energy Community” as defined in the ITC statute, an additional bonus credit is unlocked. As before, if PW&A requirements are not met, the Energy Communities bonus credit is 2%, but quintuples to 10% if PW&A requirements are met. If all three conditions are met — PW&A, DCR, and Energy Communities — then the federal government will pick up half of all eligible project costs.

The Current ITC Struggles to Catalyze New Nuclear Builds

At first glance, the current ITC seems incredibly valuable for new nuclear. Leaders at the Department of Energy have occasionally touted the ITC provisions as “buy one reactor, get one free” — a compelling proposition for utilities and project developers. Unfortunately, the guidance issued during the Biden administration established a much more challenging environment to fully monetize the ITC for new nuclear construction projects. There are at least five major roadblocks keeping the maximum ITC out of reach for developers of new nuclear:

Developers typically monetize the value of their tax credits by selling them to taxpayers with sufficient tax liability, but this type of transaction has never occurred at the scale required to build large nuclear reactors. There is a narrow set of taxpayers that would have both sufficient tax liability and interest in purchasing the tax credit. They would likely demand a steep haircut for making such a purchase.

The net present value of the ITC is significantly diluted when it is paid at project completion, which weighs on technologies and assets that require longer construction timelines.

Congressional and IRS “normalization” requirements — discussed further below — prevent regulated utilities from immediately passing ITC savings to ratepayers (consumers).

The IRS has yet to issue Domestic Content Safe Harbor Tables for new nuclear, which creates multiple limitations, including making it harder to capture the 10% DCR bonus.

IRS guidance on the Energy Communities bonus issued during the Biden administration did not account for key implementation and interpretation realities, including nuclear-specific considerations related to longer development timelines and higher pre-construction reliance interests.

Markets Have Never Monetized a Credit at This Scale

Assuming that a new nuclear project earns a 50% ITC, it is unclear whether the tax equity market is deep and liquid enough to monetize what would amount to a $10 to $17 billion tax credit for a single two-reactor build. The tax equity market refers to the group of buyers and sellers trading energy tax credits issued by the federal government. The IRA, passed by a Democratic Congress in 2022, enabled energy tax credits to be transferred and sold at scale for the first time, as described in 26 U.S.C. §6418. This provision of the law aimed to address the issue of energy project developers not having the requisite tax liability to monetize tax credits on their own books. The new transferability regime enabled project developers to legally sell and transfer the tax credits to any willing buyer with a large enough tax liability to monetize the credit. New markets formed: tax credits were traded privately between different parties, with banks acting as intermediaries, and traded on new online tax equity marketplaces like Crux. The OBBB accelerated the phaseout of tax credits for traditional renewables and prohibited tax credit transfers to specific foreign entities of concern, but otherwise left the transferability regime established by the IRA in place. The federal government collected a total of $452 billion of corporate income taxes in FY25. Setting aside the misalignment of corporate tax reporting years with federal budget years, the closest publicly reported proxy of a company’s federal tax liability is the ‘current federal income tax expense’ that companies report in their annual 10-K filings to the SEC. Individual companies also calculate this figure differently, but the general scale of the figures is what matters. The top five public companies with the largest federal income tax expense in their most recently reported fiscal year were:

NVIDIA — $19.0 billion

Reporting period January 2025 to January 2026.

Alphabet (Google) — $13.4 billion

Reporting period January 2025 to December 2025.

Berkshire Hathaway — $13.0 billion

Reporting period January 2025 to December 2025.

Apple — $11.3 billion

Reporting period September 2025 to September 2026.

Wells Fargo — $5.1 billion

Reporting period January 2025 to December 2025.

Corporate income taxes are noisy, full of one-time payments, deferrals, and a litany of additional intricacies that muddy these simplified figures. Even when read with error bars, these numbers do provide a ballpark for estimating the maximum possible ITC that could be monetized by an individual corporation in one tax year. DOE estimated in 2024 that the last two AP1000s were built at an overnight capital cost of ~$11,000/kW, which the report inflation adjusts to ~$15,000/kW in 2024 dollars. Most public cost modeling, including a separate estimate from the DOE, assumes that the next two AP1000s would come in below $15,000/kW. Employ America will publish the results of our own cost modeling in future pieces. Even so, the $15,000/kW figure provides a reasonable ceiling estimate on the total cost for the next two reactors, and therefore acts as a helpful high-water mark on the potential quantum of a 50% ITC. If the next two AP1000s were built at $15,000/kW, the total project cost would be $33.5 billion and the 50% ITC would be close to $17 billion, larger than all but one annual corporate tax bill.

There is some potential for a consortium of corporations to jointly monetize portions of such a gargantuan ITC. Offshore wind is the closest comparable: Vineyard Wind 1 closed on what was described as “the largest single asset tax equity financing” deal in United States history with JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo in 2023. But even the size of that tax equity package, $1.2 billion, is an order of magnitude smaller than what is required for two new AP1000s. The purpose of the transferability regime was to enable energy tax credits to be sold and transferred to entities that have the requisite tax liability to monetize the credits, but there is a very short list of entities capable of absorbing even a portion of the tax credits that a new large nuclear project would generate. The purchasers of these tax credits, upon realizing their significant market leverage, would be able to demand a steep haircut per dollar of credit, diluting the value of the tax credits for the nuclear developer. It is challenging to estimate what size haircut an ITC would take for a new nuclear build, given that a transaction of this scale has never occurred. The energy tax equity marketplace Crux reported in its 2026 Mid-Year Market Intelligence Report that ITCs transacted at an average of $0.91 on the dollar in the first half of 2026, representing a 9% haircut for project developers. However, the idea that a nearly $17 billion ITC could be successfully monetized at this same 9% haircut warrants significant skepticism given that Crux also estimates that the total size of the entire tax credit transferability market in 2025 was $42 billion. Based on this assessment of the market’s depth, a transaction for a pair of AP1000s could easily exhaust potential purchasers of the tax credits.

Utilities and state governments are only in the initial phases of grappling with how the ITC would be practically monetized. New York Governor Kathy Hochul called for a 5 gigawatt new nuclear backbone to be constructed in New York State. NYSERDA and NY DPS released an Advanced Nuclear Policy Options paper laying out in extensive detail a strategy for the state to procure additional nuclear power. The paper models a 40% ITC for new large light water reactor projects, but “does not include a quantification of the transaction costs” on the tax credits themselves. The scale of the transaction costs is indeed a black box, but simple supply-demand reasoning suggests that the haircuts on transacted tax credits would be unprecedentedly steep under current policy. Solutions must be brought to this tax equity monetization challenge because the ITC represents the linchpin tax incentive for building modern nuclear reactors, which would represent some of the most ambitious commercial power projects ever pursued.

The Net Present Value of the ITC Is Diluted When Paid at Project Completion

Even assuming that the ITC can be monetized without a steep haircut, the timeline for monetization is generally suboptimal for developers and ratepayers. Treasury regulations for the ITC state that tax credits are typically earned the year that the power plant is “placed in service,” what developers commonly refer to as the Commercial Operations Date (COD). Construction timelines between the pouring of first nuclear concrete and the project COD can span the better part of a decade. The “backloaded” nature of the ITC significantly dilutes its net present value for the nuclear developer. At a 7–10% cost of capital, a dollar of credit arriving eight years later is worth roughly half as much as it would be at Final Investment Decision (FID), when the developer first commits capital to construction. Banks could offer bridge financing to help developers capture the value of an ITC monetized in the future, but that path involves additional value dilution via transaction costs, bank fees, and interest rates.

Normalization Requirements Prevent Utilities from Passing ITC Savings to Ratepayers

Regulated investor-owned utilities (IOUs) are typically subject to ‘normalization’ requirements when claiming Investment Tax Credits for any new assets they develop and own. Normalization is an arcane feature of public utility accounting and tax law that requires any tax credits earned by IOUs to be “normalized” across the lifetime of the asset, as stated in §50(d)(2). Put simply, this requirement prevents an IOU that builds new nuclear from passing their ITC windfall along to ratepayers immediately — instead they can only pass the savings on to ratepayers extremely gradually, over the multi-decade lifespan of the new nuclear power plant. The perverse result: the public utility commission that oversees the IOU is less likely to approve the construction of new nuclear because the savings from the ITC cannot be passed on to ratepayers promptly, making the project look artificially expensive on ratepayer bills in the short run.

The 10% Domestic Content Bonus Requires Safe Harbor Tables

The high price tag of new nuclear will be easier to stomach for developers, public utility commissions, and ratepayers if there is a clear path to the projects earning the full 50% ITC. That path does not exist today for either of the 10% bonus credits. The first, the Domestic Content bonus, requires that new nuclear projects meet a two-part requirement:

The ‘Steel and Iron’ requirement: 100% of structural steel and iron products must be produced in the United States.

The ‘Manufactured Products’ requirement: 55% of the total value of all Manufactured Products must be made in the United States.

The test starts with a nuclear power plant being broken down into distinct systems, referred to as “Applicable Project Components” (APCs). These macro-level APCs are classified as either structural ‘Steel and Iron’ products or ‘Manufactured Products.’

The federal government has yet to release information on what the APCs of a nuclear power plant are, or how the APCs are categorized into either the ‘Steel and Iron’ category or the ‘Manufactured Products’ category. The Treasury Department issued Notice 2023-38, which states that the ‘Steel and Iron’ requirements only apply to “construction materials that are made primarily of steel or iron and are structural in function” — this is somewhat helpful, but more specifics are needed in order for nuclear developers to accurately classify all of the components of a nuclear power plant into the correct category. It would be especially helpful if the Treasury released Safe Harbor Tables that define APCs for nuclear projects and provide standardized cost percentages. Treasury has already issued tables for other energy technologies including hydro, solar, wind, and battery energy storage systems. Treasury should take a careful approach for nuclear that both incentivizes domestic manufacturing and recognizes the complexity of nuclear power plants and the supply chains for their subcomponents. Many of these subcomponents are unlikely to be manufactured domestically on a reasonable timeline. If classification is conducted with prudence, a pathway for new nuclear to earn the Domestic Content bonus can be preserved within the constraints of the global supply chain.

The Energy Communities Bonus Does Not Apply to the Most Promising Sites for New Nuclear

The second 10% bonus — the Energy Communities bonus — is earned when a new nuclear project is constructed in specific parts of the country, but the implementation was poorly calibrated to the sites best suited for the next wave of nuclear construction, namely at existing nuclear sites. The pathway for most existing nuclear sites to capture the Energy Communities bonus runs through a definition the Treasury Department suboptimally implemented, making it excessively unstable for investment planning.

To satisfy the Energy Communities bonus, the new nuclear project must meet at least one of the following definitions:

Be located in a brownfield site as defined in the US Code;

Be located in a Metropolitan or Non-Metropolitan Statistical Area that meets specific labor market criteria, including a meaningful share of direct employment related to hydrocarbon industries and an unemployment rate at or above the national average; or

Be located in a Census tract with either a coal mine closure after 1999 or a coal-fired power plant retirement after 2009, or an adjacent Census tract.

These definitions are complex enough that the Treasury Department had to clarify which sites do and do not qualify. Treasury published a 44-page document laying out their methodology to determine the full list across the second and third definitions. It updates this list every year because the qualifying locations change over time.

The first and third definitions are relatively stable and aligned with what is generally required to target investment, in contrast to the second definition. They tend to only expand their geographic scope over time, and do not remove any geographic location that has previously qualified. On the other hand, the second definition, as currently interpreted by the Treasury, is highly unstable because of how local area unemployment rates are estimated and compared to the national average. Sites that satisfy this Energy Communities definition in one year can easily fail to do so in a subsequent year, thereby making it difficult to plan investments into these sites.

The unfortunate fact for nuclear and other ITC-supported technologies is that the first and third definitions, despite their stability, are poorly suited to the other geographic factors relevant for siting development. The next wave of new nuclear projects is likely to be built at the sites of the existing nuclear fleet. Existing nuclear sites have benefits including established interconnection infrastructure and strong support from local communities who recognize the benefits of hosting nuclear power. The first definition disfavors sites that previously required permits related to the Clean Water Act, which disfavors existing nuclear sites. The third definition is useful for existing or previous coal sites, but offers little relevance to new nuclear projects planned at existing nuclear sites. Employ America will discuss these issues in greater detail in a forthcoming piece on the limitations of Energy Communities definitions.

If existing nuclear sites are to capture the Energy Communities bonus for the ITC, the second definition will need an implementation overhaul. There is no way for a nuclear developer to site a project — a decision made years in advance of when construction actually commences — to ensure that the second Energy Communities definition is satisfied based on the current IRS guidance. Employ America will be publishing a detailed whitepaper outlining our potential solutions for making the bonus substantially more effective through revised IRS guidance.

There was a flawed attempt in the OBBB to create a fourth Energy Communities definition to grandfather in existing reactor sites. This definition only applied to the PTC and was explicitly made inapplicable to the ITC. This attempt at grandfathering also comes with its own deficiencies, and has thus complicated the IRS’s ability to provide the requisite guidance to make this definition fully usable for nuclear developers interested in pursuing the nuclear PTC.

Taken together, this litany of challenges highlights the gulf between the “buy one, get one” claim and the tough policy reality on the ground. The good news is that these challenges can be addressed. In fact, a bold administration can address these issues credibly without additional congressional action.

Potential Congressional Fixes Face an Uphill Climb

The discussed problems could be solved by passing bills through Congress. Multiple pieces of legislation have been introduced that are targeted at some of these challenges, including bills introduced by Representatives Pat Harrigan and Dan Newhouse as well as Senator Tim Scott.

The Department of Energy has signaled that they are interested in pursuing legislative solutions to these ITC challenges. DOE EDF Director Greg Beard and Acting Chief Investment Officer Julie Kozeracki joined Thomas Hochman on the Right of Way Podcast to push Congress to pass legislation that would deliver a range of fixes to the ITC for new nuclear development. Employ America is supportive of these efforts, but legislation is always a challenging exercise. What may prove more promising: an alternative pathway to those same policy outcomes, but based solely on administrative actions and authority.

Unlocking Direct Pay and QPEs for Projects through Administrative Action

Congress has already legislated a solution that allows a certain class of project owners to bypass many of these ITC challenges: Direct Pay. This provision of the tax code, which is also referred to as Elective Pay, bypasses the need to sell the ITC through “transferability” and allows a project developer to monetize the value of the tax credit as a direct cash payment from the IRS. The steep haircut that a developer would face by selling the tax credit would be fully avoided. Direct Pay under current law also allows the project owner to monetize the ITC through Qualified Progress Expenditures (QPEs). QPEs allow a portion of the ITC to be paid out every year based on construction spending during that year, rather than in one lump sum at project COD. Current law bans the transfer (sale) of QPE tax credits into the tax equity market, but Direct Pay bypasses the need for transferability altogether. It is hard to overstate how transformative these payments during construction would be for improving project economics and lowering perceived project risk.

The success of Direct Pay and QPEs as an ITC monetization mechanism can be seen in a different industry with similar levels of capital intensity: semiconductors. The bipartisan CHIPS Act of 2022 provided direct funding and tax credits to encourage domestic semiconductor fabrication in the United States. $38.2 billion of direct funding was appropriated by Congress for FY2022 through FY2026 for manufacturing incentives, with awardees selected by the Commerce Department. Additionally, the law created the §48D ITC (unrelated to the §48E ITC that applies to nuclear). The §48D ITC provided a 25% tax credit for qualifying semiconductor advanced manufacturing facility investments that break ground by the end of 2026. Notably, the law allowed for-profit chip manufacturers to claim their tax credits using Direct Pay and QPEs. The CHIPS Act achieved its desired goal: billions of new investment dollars flowed into semiconductor production on domestic soil. In fact, estimates on uptake of the §48D ITC have been larger than what was initially anticipated by the Congressional Budget Office. At least some of this outsized uptake can be attributed to the frictionless mechanics of Direct Pay and QPEs.

There are two challenges to making Direct Pay and QPEs viable for the nuclear ITC. The first is that claiming Direct Pay requires that a nuclear project also satisfy virtually the same Domestic Content Requirements as those specified for the 10% Domestic Content bonus. This requirement magnifies the importance of the federal government issuing Domestic Content guidance that enables a path for new nuclear to earn the Domestic Content bonus within existing supply chains. The second challenge appears more daunting. The current statute states that Direct Pay can only be claimed by the following entities:

Tax-exempt organizations (non-profits, universities, religious organizations, etc.)

States or political subdivisions of states (e.g., the New York Power Authority)

The Tennessee Valley Authority

Any Indian tribal government or Alaska Native Corporation

Rural electric cooperatives

It is essential to appreciate that access to Direct Pay depends on how the IRS defines and determines the owner of a particular project. The IRS’s inquiry is highly qualitative, doctrinal, and substantive. In some important ways, this inquiry diverges from conventional understandings of ownership. Employ America has identified a potentially viable pathway for IOUs and Independent Power Producers (IPPs), by contracting with and for a tax-exempt entity, to access the benefits of Direct Pay and QPEs for §48E ITC projects. This pathway would also allow IOUs to potentially avoid normalization requirements. Employ America will offer more details about this potential pathway in a separate piece.

In an ideal world, the IRS would adopt additional guidance that provides a safe harbor framework for defining the ownership structures that are eligible for Direct Pay under the §48E ITC. This outcome is economically desirable, legally feasible, and politically aligned with the administration’s broader energy policy objectives. If guidance proves too time-consuming to promulgate, private developers and tax-exempt entities can pay for a Private Letter Ruling from the IRS to assess eligibility for Direct Pay in their specific circumstances.

How to Make a 50% ITC a Reality for New Nuclear

Direct Pay and QPEs are most valuable for new nuclear if they are paired with a full 50% ITC. The path to earning a 50% ITC is not clear today for new nuclear — but it can be. The clarification required to unlock the 50% ITC pathway can even be achieved without congressional action, and the simplicity and speed of this solution is worth pursuing.

First, the Treasury Department and the IRS can promulgate a Domestic Content Safe Harbor Table that is strategically structured to account for the complexity of new nuclear, its existing supply chains, and the reality that final manufacturing processes are occurring in the United States. This is critical to enable both the 10% Domestic Content bonus and the only Direct Pay pathway for the ITC that does not require new legislation.

Second, the validity of the existing Direct Pay pathway could be formalized through additional IRS guidance, or, more narrowly validated through individual Private Letter Rulings. Tax-exempt organizations can serve as project owners for the purposes of the IRS and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission by taking on certain requisite burdens, while still giving developers and utilities the upside and project risk profile that they seek. The incomplete V.C. Summer project in South Carolina is one example of an AP1000 project that could benefit from identifying a structure that maintains sufficient ownership burden on the tax-exempt entity, even as there are contractual arrangements involving a for-profit developer. Santee Cooper, a state-owned utility eligible for Direct Pay, remains the official owner at V.C. Summer, even as it has sought out Brookfield, a private for-profit entity, to lead the development efforts. If the ownership structure and contractual arrangements can satisfy all relevant tax laws and doctrines, the ITC for V.C. Summer’s development could be monetized through Direct Pay & QPEs. Employ America has identified the potential for such an ownership structure that could still satisfy the relevant tax and nuclear regulatory considerations for ownership.

Third, the Treasury Department can revise the Energy Communities guidance to align it with the realities of project development timelines for technologies that currently qualify for the ITC. The original Energy Communities guidance was implemented suboptimally and remains poorly aligned with any technology that involves substantial pre-FID reliance interests. Revised guidance could yield a more functional and stable definition compared to the one Treasury originally adopted, which ignored some basic realities of how the Bureau of Labor Statistics develops its estimates. Employ America has identified an alternative interpretation of the statute that is superior on legal, statistical, and economic grounds. As noted earlier, Employ America will lay out the full set of issues associated with the current Energy Communities guidance, which inadvertently puts a thumb on the scale against technologies that involve higher upfront costs prior to construction.

The US Treasury Department can demonstrate its commitment to following through on the 10 reactor goal articulated in President Trump’s 2025 Executive Order by using its administrative authority to unlock the full force of the ITC for new nuclear. Absent Treasury action, these fixes would require a rare bipartisan window to pass complex energy tax law revisions — an admirable but substantially more speculative proposition.

Conclusion

The United States invented and commercialized civilian nuclear reactors: a safe, clean, and reliable way to generate large amounts of electricity. The financial support Congress has passed, with Democratic and Republican endorsement, can open up a real chance to scale the relevant learning curves and bring down costs. The promise of delivering new large nuclear projects on time and on budget is simply too valuable — whether for economic security, technological leadership, or broader prosperity — to pass up.

Employ America’s forthcoming public financial model indicates that the future of nuclear deployment is quite bright, but it hinges on maximizing the tools that Congress has already passed on a bipartisan basis. The next AP1000 projects will struggle to pencil with DOE EDF debt alone, and will require that debt be paired with a revitalized ITC. ITC fixes can occur through new legislation, but there is a more straightforward path that relies solely on administrative action. Employ America will publish a series of pieces that show how this pathway can be realized across the dimensions of Domestic Content, Direct Pay with QPEs, and Energy Communities.

text:
Avore Electric, the electric mobility brand of Samarth E-Mobility, sources 90 per cent of its components from within India as it looks to reduce dependence on imports and strengthen domestic electric vehicle manufacturing. The company has also developed in-house capabilities to manufacture critical EV components, including motor controllers, digital displays, battery packs, motors and position lamps.

The company's localisation strategy involves working closely with micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) to develop a domestic supplier network that meets automotive manufacturing standards.

The company manufactures and integrates several critical systems, including its motor controllers, digital instrument displays, battery packs and rare-earth-free motors. It also produces its signature tank lights and position lamps in-house.

To strengthen supplier quality, Avore Electric has introduced Advanced Product Quality Planning (APQP) and Production Part Approval Process (PPAP), ensuring components undergo design, engineering and tolerance validation before entering mass production.

At its manufacturing facility, the company follows quality management practices aligned with IATF 16949 and ISO 9001 standards. These include Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), Statistical Process Control (SPC) and Poka-yoke systems to minimise manufacturing errors.

Testing And Manufacturing Capabilities

Avore Electric has also developed in-house testing capabilities across its battery and motor production lines. Its battery manufacturing process includes automated cell grading, sorting, laser marking, wire bonding and charge-discharge cycle testing.

The motor production line uses controlled thermal processes, precision bearing assembly and dedicated dynamometer testing before components are integrated into motorcycles.

Manufacturing Capacity Of 15,000 Units Per Month

Avore Electric operates a 150,000 sq. ft. manufacturing facility in Chhatral, Gujarat, with an installed production capacity of 15,000 electric two-wheelers per month.

The company said it had spent three years developing an indigenous technology stack at its research and development facility in Ahmedabad as part of its Make in India approach

title: Investors in 'cheaper, faster, better' energy solutions outrun backsliding policymakers - ImpactAlpha
description:
Institutional impact Long-term fiduciary investors like pension funds are also doubling down on climate and resilience investments.

text:
The COP was a flop.

But the dithering of politicians and bureaucrats at the global climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, seemed a world away for climate investors, who continue to follow the inexorable logic of the energy transition despite the mixed signals.

“In energy, at a time when the policies have, by and large, gotten worse around the world, our business has grown,” Tom Steyer of Galvanize said at last week’s Allocating for Impact event, hosted by ImpactAlpha at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

The energy transition toward renewables and away from fossil fuels is inevitable because of the low, and still-falling, prices of solar, wind, batteries and other technologies, said Steyer, author of “Cheaper, Faster, Better: How We’ll Win the Climate War.”

“This is a business-driven, capitalism-driven change in the world,” Steyer told the audience of more than 100 limited partners and other asset allocators.

Institutional impact

Long-term fiduciary investors like pension funds are also doubling down on climate and resilience investments.

Two powerhouse pension funds – the $310 billion New York State Common Retirement Fund and the New York City Comptroller’s office, which oversees the $330 billion in assets of the five New York City pension funds — are among the institutional climate leaders. These LPs are bound by strict fiduciary obligations and set high single-digit hurdle rates, yet they are setting net-zero goals and doubling down on climate investments.

Andrew Siwo, who leads Sustainable Investments and Climate Solutions at the New York State Common Retirement Fund, and Nina Chen, senior climate finance officer at the Office of New York City Comptroller, joined ImpactAlpha at the Allocating for Impact event.

When New York Common, the state fund, met its initial $20 billion climate investment goal in early 2024, it doubled the target to $40 billion by 2035. The retirement fund has made more than $26 billion in climate investments so far across public equity, private equity, private credit, fixed income and other asset classes.

The New York City pension’s net zero plan includes a commitment to invest $37.8 billion or about 14% of its total assets under management, in climate solutions across asset classes by 2035.

In September, New York Comptroller Mark Levine announced a “strategic expansion” of private market climate investments, proposing $5 billion in capital to new private market climate investment opportunities for the New York City Teachers’ Retirement System, Employees’ Retirement System, and Board of Education Retirement System. The city’s pension system has made its first private-market climate allocation under Levine, with a $116 million investment in Sandbrook Climate Infrastructure Fund II.

Another giant pension fund, California’s $630 billion CalPERS, has grown its climate investments to $71 billion, an increase of $11 billion since last year.

“Since the physical climate risk is likely to grow across our portfolio, our targets include investments that make assets, communities, and supply chains more resilient to a changing world,” CalPERS’ Peter Cashion said in announcing the increase this month.

Social challenges

Steyer, who returned to Galvanize earlier this year after an unsuccessful run for governor of California, said even hard-to-abate sectors like trucking and air travel were yielding to the falling costs of clean-energy technologies. In China, nearly two-thirds of new long-haul trucks are electric (in the US, the figure is less than 1%). Even air travel is electrifying, with electric planes already flying short-haul routes. As much as 95% of new generating capacity is from renewable sources. For two decades, solar deployments have consistently exceeded even the best-case scenarios of the International Energy Agency.

“Nearly every prediction about the cost of clean energy was wrong and underestimated how quickly costs would fall,” Steyer said. “I want a level playing field for clean energy and fossil fuel energy, because I believe clean energy will come out on top, and its advantage will only grow.”

“Every single prediction is wrong, and it’s wrong on the low side. And they continue to miss the point that cheaper, faster, better wins,” Steyer said. “I want a level playing field for clean energy and fossil fuel energy, because I know that if we have a level playing field, we are going to kick their ass. We are going to kick their ass today, and that advantage is only going to grow.”

Steyer said he favors the permitting reform currently being considered in Congress because of the time it takes to build infrastructure, such as interstate electric lines.

“If businesses pollute, they should pay for it. Taxpayers shouldn’t have to cover the costs of the pollution that makes them sick and drives damages their communities are already paying to prevent and repair. The companies who cause those costs should pay for them. That’s what I call a level playing field.”

Chronic social challenges like affordable housing and health care are a tougher case than energy, but “cheaper, faster, better” still applies, Steyer argued. In housing, for example, factory-built modular units are considerably cheaper than traditional building methods.

“Is there a technological way to do this differently? Yes. Can we drive down costs dramatically? Yes. Does that fly in the face of powerful interests? Absolutely,” he said. “In healthcare, we have to change our system to change inflation. But powerful organizations and institutions like it exactly the way it is.”

“Investment can help solve huge problems when it backs products that are undeniably great.”

He said such companies have even better growth prospects now than at the beginning of this year, with more attractive valuations and lower multiples.

“I can’t tell you how the market is going to value things, but I can look forward and say, ‘In the context of this very volatile and complicated world, we are betting on a transition that we believe is going to go on for decades,’” he said.

“I sleep well about where the world is going and, I promise you, it’s going to change more than people expect.”

description:
Chevy brought back its small electric car for 2027 with a starting price under $30,000.

text:
The car business isn’t sentimental, even if buyers are. Models that don’t sell, don’t meet the latest regulations, or simply don’t fit the latest corporate plan tend to disappear. So it’s surprising when a handful of vehicles that, by any reasonable measure, should be gone are still in showrooms. In the spirit of the season, here are five models Edmunds’ editors are thankful you can still buy. Some are fast, some are cheap, and at least one is a little ridiculous. All of them deserve a look before someone in the boardroom decides they’ve run their course. All of the following prices include destination charges.

Chevrolet Bolt

It’s true that electric vehicles are more expensive than comparable gas-powered cars, and the end of the federal EV tax credit last year made it all the more obvious. That’s why we are glad that the Chevrolet Bolt is back. Chevy brought back its small electric car for 2027 with a starting price under $30,000.

It’s not a penalty box either. The Bolt has about 260 miles of range, offers plenty of room for adults, and now charges far quicker at public charging stations than the old version did, making road trips more practical. The catch is that this Bolt appears to be a one-year offering. If an inexpensive electric car sounds appealing, now is the time to look.

2027 Bolt starting price: $28,995

Ford Mustang

Not long ago, you had three choices if you wanted a traditional V8-powered muscle car. Well, Chevy stopped building the Camaro after 2024, and Dodge retired the Challenger in favor of a larger, very different Charger. That leaves the Mustang on its own, which isn’t an entirely new scenario for this American classic. Its rivals have come and gone over the decades, but the Mustang has been on sale without a break since 1964.

Ford, to its credit, keeps finding ways to make it more exciting. The newest version, the Mustang Dark Horse SC, adds a supercharger, bringing the total to 795 horsepower. At $108,085 to start, it’s a lot of money for a Mustang. But the Mustang GT is still available with a V8 and a six-speed manual, and it’s the one most fans are grateful for.

2026 Mustang starting price: $34,990

Honda Prelude

By most business measures, the Prelude shouldn’t exist. Sporty two-door coupes are a tiny slice of the market, and one that’s a hybrid and has a price north of $40,000 makes even less sense. But here we are with the 2027 Honda Prelude, and we’re pleased that Honda found a way to bring back the Prelude after a two-decade-plus hiatus.

The Prelude borrows hardware from the performance-focused Civic Type R to make it one of the best-handling front-wheel-drive cars Edmunds has ever driven. It offers an adaptive suspension, powerful brakes and precise steering. It’s not nearly as quick as a Mustang, but its hybrid powertrain lets it earn 44 mpg combined, according to the EPA.

2027 Prelude starting price: $43,695

Jeep Wrangler 392

In some ways, it’s hard to believe that the Wrangler is still around. It’s pretty bad at the things most SUV shoppers want, whether it be comfort, fuel economy or cutting-edge technology. It’s therefore even harder to believe that you can get a Wrangler with a massive V8 making 470 horsepower. Putting that much engine into a boxy SUV built to crawl over rocks makes very little sense. Jeep did it anyway.

Jeep actually spent two years telling everyone that the Wrangler 392 was going away. In a truly American parting prank, it sold final editions in both 2024 and 2025. Then the brand’s CEO announced in 2025 that the V8 would stay in production indefinitely. The 2027 V8-powered Wrangler will likely give you sticker shock, but trust us, there’s nothing else quite like it.

2027 Wrangler Willys 392 starting price: $72,990

Mazda MX-5 Miata

Two seats, a folding roof and not much else. That’s been the Miata’s recipe since 1989, and it’s the reason the little Mazda has outlasted every convertible that came along after it. It’s light and simple, and it makes an ordinary back road feel like an event at speeds that won’t put you in jail. Like the Mustang, it’s also one of the few new cars you can buy with a stick shift.

The current Miata has been on sale for more than a decade, and it doesn’t appear that Mazda has a timeline for a replacement. Prices start a little over $30,000, which is about as low as it gets for a genuine sports car.

2026 Miata MX-5 starting price: $32,045

Edmunds says

Our featured vehicles all sell in small numbers. But each exists because enough people still want a car that’s fun and not just sensible. That’s worth being grateful for. Here’s hoping they stick around.

description:
Still, although no final decision was reached, countries made several deals and announcements on climate finance and the energy transition.

text:
Key points

Cop31 in Antalya ended without a final cover decision, after objections to a text that did not mention fossil fuels and unclear finance commitments.

More than 20 countries published or announced fossil fuel phase-out plans, and about 80 signed a global electrification pledge.

Development banks and governments announced new climate finance initiatives, but decisions on the just transition mechanism were deferred to 2027.

Cop32 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopa inherits the unfinished business, and campaigners see an opening for greater African leadership.

Countries failed to reach a major agreement at Cop31, the longest-ever UN climate summit on record.

The event, held in Antalya, Turkey, ran into Sunday as countries tried to agree on the final cover decision after the draft failed to mention fossil fuels. Several parties, including the EU, UK, Pacific island nations, Norway, and others, objected to a text about climate change that did not mention the biggest driver of global emissions.

Others objected to unclear financial commitments from rich countries to help developing countries pay for climate adaptation. Countries in the global majority are often the hardest hit by climate change despite having contributed very little to global emissions.

Country leaders expressed their disappointment over the outcome, with the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, attributing it to “difficult geopolitical times”. Climate finance commitments were shaky even before talks began, with public funding pledges falling by 70%, according to Carbon Brief.

Still, although no final decision was reached, countries made several deals and announcements on climate finance and the energy transition.

Countries extend support for the energy transition

Several countries affirmed their support for the energy transition away from fossil fuels. More than 20 countries across Europe, Latin America and Asia have published or announced fossil fuel phase-out plans.

In the EU, leaders described the plans as a path towards energy and economic independence.

Germany’s environment minister, Carsten Schneider, called his country’s roadmap a “declaration of independence”.

“It’s good for our economy, and it’s good for the world,” he said.

Electrification was also a key theme at Cop31, with about 80 nations signing a global pledge for electricity to account for reaching 35% of energy consumption by 2035. While praised as being a clear path towards a green transition, some cautioned that the pledge does not constitute a fossil fuel phase-out and does not require the electricity to come from renewable sources.

Several countries also signed deals on the energy transition.

Denmark and Australia announced a climate and energy partnership covering offshore wind and renewable energy, batteries, and renewable hydrogen, as well as a collaboration on global climate action and improving access to climate finance for developing countries.

Separately, Australia signed a deal with Indonesia to support its energy transition and develop its electricity sector, including technical cooperation, investment, and workforce development.

Central banks and finance ministers set out 2027 priorities

Meeting on the sidelines of Cop31, finance ministers, central bankers and supervisors agreed to continue a joint dialogue platform to bring together fiscal, monetary and financial experts on climate-related economic and financial risks.

The two groups – the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) and the Coalition of Finance Ministers for Climate Action (CFMCA) – first announced the initiative at Cop30 in Brazil.

The group of 150 central bankers and 106 finance ministers agreed to focus on financing the transition to a low-carbon economy and strengthening economic, fiscal, and financial resilience in 2027.

“While our mandates differ, we face interconnected economic and financial challenges arising from climate change and the transition,” said Olaf Sleijpen, chair of the NGFS and president of the De Nederlandsche Bank.

“Strengthening dialogue and mutual understanding across our institutions can help us better fulfil our respective responsibilities and support greater economic and financial resilience,” he said.

The two groups are planning more joint activities, dialogues, and analytical work in the coming year, with a joint report on transition finance and physical and nature risks expected in April 2027.

Development finance groups pledge climate finance support

Development finance institutions used Cop31 to announce several initiatives.

The World Bank Group announced several projects to mobilise $10.7bn in private capital and $6.9bn in investments to create jobs and strengthen resilience in various sectors, including renewable energy, agriculture and manufacturing.

The announcement builds on the World Bank’s climate investments so far in 2026, which is already 21% higher than the previous year. That’s despite pressure from the US and other members for the World Bank and other development banks to sideline climate and focus instead on creating jobs.

Meanwhile, the UK made an inaugural contribution of £400mn to the Climate Investment Funds new financing mechanism – Accelerating Mobilisation of Private Leverage (Amplifi) – aimed at mobilising investment in clean energy projects in developing countries. The hope is that the catalytic capital will encourage more investment by making risk-tolerant financing more attractive to private investors.

Separately, development finance institutions in the UK, Canada, and Norway launched a $10bn initiative to finance climate projects in emerging markets by 2030. The three state-backed lenders – British International Investment, FinDev Canada and Norfund – will coordinate on due diligence, investment pipelines and climate reporting. The group plans to support renewable energy projects, transmission grids, energy storage, and sustainable fuels and decarbonisation.

Just transition mechanism delayed

Setting up the just transition mechanism – first agreed on at Cop30 in Belém – proved one of the most contested issues in Antalya.

Talks opened constructively, with broad agreement on a two-tier structure: a political governance body and a technical operational arm. A key sticking point was whether the mechanism would simply be a vehicle for sharing knowledge or would also help mobilise finance.

The EU, Norway and the UK favoured dialogues and reports. The G77 and China pressed for a “constituted body” with the power and resources to drive implementation. The final decision took a “phased approach” with little substance, deferring key decisions about the mechanism’s functions to talks in Bonn in June, for adoption at Cop32.

Civil society groups said the move delayed action, and accused the EU of blocking the mechanism.

The European Commission said it had sought to “fully operationalise” the mechanism, “rooted in human and labour rights”.

Despite the delay, countries agreed to extend the wider just transition work programme for three years.

Early signs of progress on green industrialisation

Progress was also made on critical minerals and green industry.

The final document from the just transition work programme was the first UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) decision to mention critical minerals.

It called for “equitable value chains” that would help developing countries “build productive capacity” and move into “higher-value segments” alongside decarbonisation. Resource watchdogs welcomed these steps but condemned the removal of explicit human rights protections.

These advances sit alongside two voluntary green industrialisation initiatives. The UN Industrial Development Organisations (Unido)’s Global Green Industrialisation Agenda (GGIA), launched with the support of 57 countries, aims to move countries “from parallel national strategies to a shared multilateral agenda” for green industrialisation, with a particular focus on improving access to finance for developing economies.

The Antalya Green Industrialisation Compact, endorsed by the EU, recognises the GGIA as the international coordination framework. It also casts green industrialisation as “a strategic pillar of climate action and national development”, while noting stark financing gaps and the “high costs of capital” for developing nations. It points to the need for concessional and blended finance.

Wael Aboulmagd of Egypt, a co-chair of the GGIA’s oversight group, said green industrialisation requires “affordable finance, technology transfer and international cooperation that supports a just transition”.

Road to Addis Ababa

Cop32 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia next year will inherit Antalya’s unfinished business. With the US absent and Europe describing climate finance talks as “dead in the water”, civil society groups say this leaves an opening for greater African leadership.

That leadership was already emerging in Antalya. The African Group held firm alongside other global majority blocs on climate finance, even as Europe’s ambition faltered. African countries also reportedly sent more delegates than any other continent this year, with Nigeria’s delegation being the third-largest for a single country, behind only this year’s and last year’s hosts.

“We look to Ethiopia’s leadership to champion genuine justice for the global majority,” said Angela Asuncion of the Resource Justice Network, calling for “binding rights-based mineral governance” and a strong just transition mechanism.

To step into that role, however, African negotiators need their heads of state behind them, Fadhel Kaboub, a professor of economics at Denison University and a member of the UN’s High-Level Advisory Board on Economic and Social Affairs, told Green Central Banking.

African leaders, he said, must build real leverage through joint industrial policy, technology partnerships, and solutions capable of addressing the structural drivers of external debt.

China, Kaboub said, is the obvious place to start, as “the one economic bloc that’s willing to share technology”.

Written by

Moriah Costa is the Editor-in-Chief of Green Central Banking and has over a decade of experience writing about banking and finance. She is an award-winning American journalist based in Paris and has written for major international publications, including Reuters, The Guardian, and S&P Global. Having grown up in water-stressed Arizona, she has always had a strong interest in bringing awareness to climate and environmental issues.

text:
LAS VEGAS (KTNV) — Nevada's two Democratic senators came out on opposite sides of a major bill that would streamline environmental rules for projects built on federal lands.

Sens. Catherine Cortez Masto and Jacky Rosen differed on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, which passed the Senate 62-33 last week.

The bill now heads to the House of Representatives for consideration.

WATCH: Bipartisan permitting reform bill passes Senate

Nevada senators divided on permitting reform bill

In a statement, Cortez Masto said she cast a no vote on the bill because "...it contains harmful changes to the National Historic Preservation Act that undermine Tribal sovereignty and fail to protect government-to-government Tribal consultation."

"This county needs permitting reform. I support efforts to lower energy costs and have championed proposals to make it easier to build clean energy projects, upgrade our electrical grid, and grow our critical mineral supply chain in the U.S.," Cortez Masto's statement reads. "But there is no reason to threaten Tribal sovereignty to accomplish these goals."

But Rosen said the bill would be good for Nevada's clean energy projects and bring jobs to the Silver State.

"As the state with the most solar jobs per capita and tremendous geothermal potential, Nevada stands to greatly benefit from historic federal investments in renewable energy projects that create good-paying jobs and lower energy costs, all while reducing carbon emissions. Unfortunately, current government red tape has made it nearly impossible to bring these clean energy projects online, which is why sensible reform like this bipartisan bill is needed," Rosen said. "While we fought to strengthen this bill, Senate Republicans refused to accept any changes and I believed we couldn't squander this opportunity to lower energy costs for hardworking Nevada families."

Rosen said she tried to remove sections reforming the National Historic Preservation Act, but was unsuccessful.

Of the 62 yes votes, 14 were Democrats. Just two Republicans joined the 33 senators voting no.

Patrick Donnelly, Great Basin director for the Center for Biological Diversity, said the bill would erode rules that govern not just clean energy projects, but also mines, fossil fuel plants and even data centers.

"Permits are where our environmental protection laws come to bear," he said. "If you want to get clean air and clean water, you've got to make sure a project goes through permitting in such a way that it's not going to harm the environment. And so, permitting is seen as this bad word, but it's actually essential for us to have a livable planet."

Although most of the focus has been on clean energy — think solar, wind or geothermal projects — Donnelly said the reform bill will apply far more broadly.

"Everything the federal government permits, whether it's mining, whether it's data centers on public land, whether it's military operations and nuclear waste disposal, all of that is governed by these environmental laws, and these protections are being stripped away across the board," he said. "And so we're going to see more development on public lands, more data centers on public lands, more polluting industry, and the protections that are built in to protect our clear air and water and our wildlife are being stripped away by this bill."

In the House, lawmakers could pass the Senate version as is or could add amendments to the bill, in which case it would have to go back to the Senate for concurrence before moving on to President Donald Trump, who supports the measure.

Donnelly said there's still a chance the House may kill it, although it would require both Republicans and Democrats to vote no.

Reps. Susie Lee and Steven Horsford were not available on Monday. Rep. Dina Titus said she's still considering the measure before taking a position on it.

ANDERSON — As battery energy storage systems proliferate in the United States, officials have sought to dispel what they say are misconceptions about their safety.

Battery energy storage systems, or BESS, help stabilize electrical grids by “providing steady power flow despite fluctuations from inconsistent generation of renewable energy sources and other disruptions,” according to the United States Environmental Protection Agency.

The Clean Coalition, a nonprofit organization “whose mission is to accelerate the transition to renewable energy and a modern grid through technical, policy and project development expertise,” says BESS helps sources like solar panels and wind turbines reach their full potential by storing excess energy produced during times of high generation and dispersing it when those sources are unavailable.

The facilities operate by using lithium-ion batteries to receive and store electrical currents, according to the Indiana Office of Energy Development.

“Individual battery cells are grouped together to form battery packs,” according to a study commissioned by the IOED. “Each system has cooling and fire systems to manage safety risks. Each battery storage facility is required to provide emergency response plans as a condition of project approval through Indiana Department of Homeland Security. Operators are required to provide training to first responders, offering instruction on proper responses to battery storage system emergencies.”

The Clean Coalition goes on to point out several benefits of BESS, including job creation and the generation of tax revenue for local governments.

The Clean Coalition’s website also mentions that BESS is essential in reducing the “environmental footprint of energy generation,” and Rebecca TeKolste, the director of climate and energy at the Hoosier Environmental Council, said BESS is an important tool.

“You’re really able to leverage those renewable resources throughout all times of the day, regardless of whether or not the wind is blowing and the sun is shining,” TeKolste said. “Batteries can store any kind of energy. It could be they’re storing energy from gas plants, solar — it really just depends on what the utility has in excess.”

TeKolste acknowledged that some people hold safety concerns related to BESS, with several fires breaking out at facilities years ago. TeKolste said batteries are considerably safer now than they were in the past.

“There’s always going to be some challenges with safety considerations,” TeKolste said. “Largely, those have been mitigated with the improvements of technology over the last couple of decades. I think now what we are seeing is the primary challenges with batteries rather than safety. Now they’re much more in the supply chain.

“Batteries rely on rare Earth metals, and in some cases, there are some concerns about labor when it comes to where those metals are being mined.”

Currently, there are nine operating utility-scale battery energy storage systems in Indiana. TeKolste said regulating them is difficult because decisions are typically made through local zoning ordinances. With 92 counties in Indiana, that means up to 92 different potential sets of rules.

Sean Coffington, a clean energy organizer at Greenlight America, said that “battery energy storage systems, as part of the electrical grid, are a net environmental positive.”

When talking about the placement of BESS facilities, Coffington said their installations near population clusters are logical.

“You hear a lot about these systems being built near population centers,” Coffington said. “You can think of it like a water tower on top of an apartment building. We need electricity where the people are, and if we’re producing extra electricity, it makes sense to hold it in storage near where it will need to be used.”

TeKolste said when looking at other alternatives, BESS is a better option.

“If you look at an apples-to-apples comparison between mining, burning and storing coal ash, that is a known, certain risk to communities, whereas the battery technology has lower risk on almost every metric,” TeKolste said. “Everything has some level of risk, but the level of risk to a battery system is a lot lower than the level of risk of running a coal plant for the same amount of energy.

“It’s all part of a system where there are trade-offs,” she continued. “From our perspective, batteries are a solution to get some of these more polluting, more expensive and more carbon-intensive resources offline faster and used significantly less.”

text:
The event will bring together speakers from energy, manufacturing and technology sectors in Detroit.

Speakers from Black & Veatch, Boeing, Carrier, Eaton, Google, Siemens Energy, Schneider Electric and Westinghouse are among those scheduled to lead sessions at the first ASME CATALYZE Summit. The American Society of Mechanical Engineers will host the two-day event April 20-21, 2027 at The Department at Hudson’s in downtown Detroit. Registration is open.

The summit comes as energy demand continues to rise, manufacturing capacity is being rebuilt in multiple regions, artificial intelligence is changing business operations and climate-related risks are increasing. The Energy Institute’s Statistical Review of World Energy, published in June 2026, said renewables were the largest source of global energy supply growth in 2025 for the first time. Accenture’s Destination Net Zero 2025, published in November 2025, said decarbonization is increasingly linked to business value and that only a limited number of companies are on track.

CATALYZE is intended to address the gap between technologies that have been demonstrated and technologies that can be deployed at scale. The event will bring together engineering leaders, entrepreneurs, investors and regulators to discuss project financing, workforce development, supply chains, standards and production scale-up.

Industry speakers bring deployment into focus

Sessions will focus on sustainable energy systems, industrial efficiency and electrification, digital and next-generation design and production, and workforce development. Standards, finance, artificial intelligence, policy and resilience planning will also be part of the program.

The speaker lineup includes:

Alain Lefevre, sustainability strategy director at Schneider Electric and CATALYZE conference chair, opening remarks

Jigar Shah, co-managing partner at Multiplier and former director of loan programs at the U.S. Department of Energy, plenary remarks on “The Business Case to Build”

Maggie Nordall, director, fuel handling equipment and manufacturing facility at Westinghouse Electric Company, Track 1, “Powering Growth”

Deepa Poduval, chief sustainability officer at Black & Veatch, Track 2, “Industry Reimagined”

Ravi Annapragada, director of energy and sustainability strategy at Carrier, Track 3, “Next-Gen Manufacturing”

Eric Johnson, Ph.D., director of advanced materials and manufacturing R&D at Eaton, Track 3, “Next-Gen Manufacturing”

Prem Pandian, global head of strategic initiatives and partnerships for hardware at Google, Track 3, “Next-Gen Manufacturing”

Carla Reynolds, senior technical fellow at Boeing, Track 4, “Future Workforce”

Additional speakers will be announced.

A collaborative summit in Detroit

Rather than a traditional panel-based conference, CATALYZE will use structured discussions and collaborative problem-solving to address cost, risk, standards and time to market. ASME is organizing the event with a cross-sector group of organizations involved in energy and industrial technology. ASME says it has a 145-year history in standards development and 75,000 members.

Detroit has a long manufacturing history and has expanded into advanced manufacturing and clean technology. The Department at Hudson’s, located downtown, provides meeting space and technology-equipped facilities.

Oklo Inc. is a founding sponsor of CATALYZE. The company works in advanced nuclear energy, fuel recycling and infrastructure development. Its participation aligns with the summit’s focus on standards and cross-sector collaboration.

ASME is developing the CATALYZE community with input from advisors and collaborators across the energy, manufacturing, technology, investment and policy sectors.

More information about CATALYZE, including registration, programming and sponsorship opportunities, is available at catalyze.asme.org.

title: Power, Politics, and the Changing Geography of America's Data Centers
description:
America’s data center geography was changing well before the facilities became a political issue in the 2026 elections.
Since its earliest days, data center development has focused on access to resources and proximity to users.
Because of the grid congestion and delays in the Northeast and in California, data centers began looking elsewhere.
Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s halting of data center permits made the news, and Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated him in part based on her promise of a data center moratorium.
There were 47 ballot initiatives about data centers; for all but one, the forces against data centers won.
text:
America’s data center geography was changing well before the facilities became a political issue in the 2026 elections. Virginia has been “Data Center Alley” for decades, but now states in the South are rising in importance because they can credibly deliver large quantities of power quickly while balancing local interests. The elections will complicate this geographic shift and raise the cost of providing AI, but an examination of where data centers were likely to be built suggests the direct effects of the election may be less extensive than the headlines imply.

Since its earliest days, data center development has focused on access to resources and proximity to users. The pattern began in the 1960s when the military’s Arpanet made northern Virginia a technology hub. But the key event was the 1992 creation of MAE-East—a major internet hub placed in Vienna, Virginia. Within five years, it was handling about one-third of internet traffic.

Internet service providers, like pioneering companies AOL and Equinix, clustered around MAE-East, and Equinix became a data center pioneer, building its first major neural peering hub to serve AOL and other early dot-com enterprises. There was a snowball effect: Companies built fiber-optic infrastructure and carrier ecosystems, which attracted more internet pioneers, which built more infrastructure. Dominion Energy contributed as well, providing reliable power at relatively low prices.

Northern Virginia’s success eventually began to erode some of its advantages. Virginia is part of PJM, an energy market that is experiencing severe constraints—a situation that is exacerbated by data centers but would exist without data center growth.

The average wait time for a data center to be connected in PJM has grown from under two years in 2008 to more than eight years in 2025. These delays are costly. A 30-month increase in time to power for a 100-megawatt hyperscaler costs up to $1 billion, and these costs must be passed on to customers.

Because of the grid congestion and delays in the Northeast and in California, data centers began looking elsewhere. According to the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI), five other leading states—Arizona, Georgia, Indiana, Ohio, and Texas—will account for 30 percent of data center growth over the next four years.

While grid congestion and time to connect are major drivers of data center location decisions, other considerations matter. Third-party centers tend to cluster in dense urban markets to be close to priority customers, such as hospitals and financial centers for low latency and regulatory compliance. Cloud providers are more likely to emphasize operating costs and land availability.

The politics of the 2026 election campaigns affected data center development, but perhaps not as much as headlines could lead us to believe. Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s halting of data center permits made the news, and Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated him in part based on her promise of a data center moratorium. In Georgia, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the gubernatorial race on a platform that explicitly promised to impose a moratorium on data center development. There were 47 ballot initiatives about data centers; for all but one, the forces against data centers won.

The election results were striking, but their economic significance depends on where voters expressed their opposition. EPRI identifies 13 states that together are expected to account for more than 80 percent of the nation’s additional data center capacity through 2030. Only three of these states—Ohio, Illinois, and Nevada—had ballot measures in which voters opposed data centers. Together, these three account for about 11 percent of projected national growth, and the ballot measures affected only individual communities within those states.

Also, eight of the 12 states with data center ballot initiatives were unlikely to attract much new capacity under EPRI’s forecast. The election results demonstrate public unease with data centers, but the aggregate numbers exaggerate the likely direct impacts.

The 2026 elections will change the geography and timing of America’s AI investment. Some states will lose opportunities to other states. Americans will continue to demand AI, but providing it will become more expensive as developers move to less advantageous locations and wait longer for electricity. Policymakers should emphasize solutions that benefit both AI customers and local communities.
