text:
SENATE PASSES HISTORIC BILL TO CUT ENVIRONMENTAL RED TAPE ON ENERGY PROJECTS

With the bill having passed the Senate, one environmental group lobbyist involved in the discussions, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, described the next few days and possibly weeks as the “only chance” to delay the bill, or broader permitting reform, to the next Congress.

“It’s the last stop before it goes to Trump’s desk,” they said.

Better known as BAAJA, the bill passed the Senate last week in a 62-33 vote, with 14 Democrats and one independent who caucuses with Democrats voting in favor of the legislation.

The legislation would accelerate federal permits and approvals for projects such as pipelines, power lines, renewable energy projects, and more. Proponents of the bill — on both sides of the aisle — argue that these laws have created unnecessary red tape, making it difficult to build in the United States because of the threat of legal challenges and regulatory delays.

The bill has support from some climate hawks, such as co-sponsor Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), who argue that it would allow for more transmission infrastructure to be built, allowing more clean energy to be connected to the grid, accelerating the phase-out of fossil fuels, and slowing the rise of greenhouse gas emissions.

But it would speed up construction in large by overhauling some of the oldest environmental laws on the books, including the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act.

That is a step too far for a range of environmentalists and tribal groups, such as the Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council, and Earthjustice, who say that the harms caused by the changes to the environmental laws would outweigh the benefits of the bill.

HERE’S WHAT’S IN THE BIPARTISAN MEGABILL MEANT TO ALLOW THE US TO BUILD AGAIN

Bigger chamber, bigger challenges

The House has 435 voting members (setting aside vacancies), more than quadrupling the number of lawmakers lobbyists have to target compared to the Senate.

“With the Senate, there are just fewer members, so having one-off meetings with each office and going into each office was the play,” another lobbyist involved in discussions said, calling the House “a whole different animal in a lot of ways.”

While several Democrats have voiced their opposition to the legislation, hundreds of lawmakers have remained silent on it.

“Over 200 Democrats have said nothing yet,” the lobbyist said, calling it a “black box.”

“We’re trying to do the most high-impact things that we can to get as much paper in front of as many people as possible,” the lobbyist added.

Yet most members of the House have already left Washington, D.C., for Thanksgiving. This is forcing groups to rely on phone calls and emails to plead their case.

A lobbyist with a conservation nonprofit group, also granted anonymity to speak freely, told the Washington Examiner that phone calls are “not enough” to get the message across.

“I’m reaching out to offices where I have close staff-level relationships for those kinds of conversations,” the lobbyist said. “I’m sending our opposition statement to every House Dem office and Republican office, just so they have that basic level of information.”

Some organizations have moved to directly partner with vocal bill opponents in the House, such as Reps. Jared Huffman (D-CA) and Melanie Stansbury (D-NM). Both Democrats joined groups such as Earthjustice, the Natural Resources Defense Council, and the Wilderness Society on a press call this week to appeal to members to reject the bill.

Others are also highlighting modeling of the economic and environmental impacts of the legislation. But that isn’t always helpful for their message, since some analyses have found the measure would lower costs and cut emissions.

“A lot of folks in the Senate and beyond are talking about this bill as a way to address affordability, and I can understand the appeal of that,” Lisa Frank, executive director of Environment America, told the Washington Examiner. “It’s certainly something voters are concerned about.”

Frank said most of the modeling conducted, however, has focused on specific provisions, not the legislation as a whole. She pointed to research conducted by the Rhodium Group earlier this month, which estimated that BAAJA would lower electricity bills by $50-$78 annually in 2040.

For Frank, that still feels like a “terrible trade-off” for the changes to environmental laws.

Another tactic groups are using is pointing to the fact that the legislation has moved so quickly through Congress, as the text was only released at the end of September.

The conservation nonprofit lobbyist told the Washington Examiner that a bill of this size and importance should have more time for consideration, deliberation, and public engagement.

“The bill has definitely not had enough time for staff to wrap their heads around it,” the lobbyist said.

Ticking clock

Since BAAJA passed the Senate, several organizations said they were concerned that House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) would try and move the bill under suspension of the rules as soon as the Monday after Thanksgiving.

This fast-tracked procedure would allow Republicans to pass the bill quickly, limiting debate on the floor and blocking floor amendments. Under this process, they would need to secure a two-thirds majority vote to successfully pass the bill.

Not only would Republicans need a significant number of Democratic votes, they would also need to ensure each of their members returns to Washington after the holiday.

Johnson was forced to postpone a vote last week because there weren’t enough members in town. On Friday, the Republican leader issued a letter to the caucus asking everyone to return to Washington after the holiday.

Meanwhile, more liberals in the House Democratic Caucus have expressed their opposition to the bill as written, including Reps. Mike Levin (D-CA) and Sean Casten (D-IL).

House Republicans appeared to feel the pressure of absences and a lack of Democratic votes earlier this week, with Punchbowl News reporting Tuesday evening that leadership was planning to bring the bill forward under a rule, requiring a simple majority vote to pass.

The vote, now expected next week, could be complicated further, as Politico reported some Democrats are seeking an open amendment process on the bill. If successful, this would send the legislation back to the Senate for consideration with just three weeks left on the legislative calendar.

Passing BAAJA at that stage would grow even more difficult, as both chambers are still considering multiple must-pass measures. This includes government funding and the National Defense Authorization Act.

“There’s so many more important must-pass, expiring bills that should be part of the lame duck,” said the environmental group lobbyist, who also doubted that there is any pathway to amend the bill in a meaningful way.

“It is not credible to think that there is an opportunity to debate on amendments and fix the most harmful positions,” the lobbyist said.

Momentum from the Senate

When BAAJA passed in the Senate last week, more Democrats voted against the legislation than negotiators had hoped, in part because they were unable to put any Republican or Democratic amendments to a vote on the floor.

Negotiators attempted to put together a package of amendments to vote on, but they were stymied by Sens. Ron Wyden (D-OR) and Jeff Merkley (D-OR).

The two Democrats blocked amendment votes to demand provisions cracking down on data centers and retaining certain environmental protections. Some fellow Democrats accused Merkley of purposefully tanking the bill, as their colleagues in the House would be wary of supporting the bill without tweaks.

And while several green groups would have liked to see changes made to the legislation, they plan to use the existing text to their favor to block the bill entirely.

“There were some minor technical amendments … but none of the substantive changes that people were seeking,” the conservation nonprofit lobbyist said. “I think it’s a lot less likely that House Democrats would support it in the absence of an amended version.”

GREEN GROUPS SPLIT AS PERMITTING REFORM BILL CREATES FORK IN THE ROAD

Frank told the Washington Examiner that Environment America hopes House members will realize that “there aren’t going to be significant changes made.”

“They should reject this deal and start again to make a much better one,” she said.

text:
The House will take up a Senate-passed bill to overhaul the federal permitting system under a rule when it returns next week, a House aide said on Tuesday. The bill, which passed the Senate on Nov. 19 in a 62-33 vote, has the endorsement of President Donald Trump and a wide range of industry groups that are generally GOP allies. Adoption of the rule, typically a party-line affair, would almost certainly lead to final passage and Trump's signature.

But it may come down to GOP attendance, with many departing members not showing up to vote in the days following the midterms. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., in a Nov. 20 letter to colleagues, implored them to come back to work next month to finish out the lame-duck session, citing the permitting bill vote among other things. But it remains to be seen whether defeated lawmakers will take him up on that.

And several Republicans, led by House Freedom Caucus members, have used their leverage in rule votes to extract last-minute changes to legislation from leadership.

Last December, the House considered a bill to overhaul the National Environmental Policy Act from Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, and House Natural Resources Chairman Bruce Westerman, R-Ark. Ahead of the vote on that rule, Republicans including Freedom Caucus Chairman Andy Harris, R-Md., sought last-minute changes to portions of the bill they were concerned would allow offshore wind projects in the Atlantic Ocean to move forward. Westerman agreed, which in turn caused the American Clean Power Association to withdraw support for the bill.

Harris hasn’t commented yet on the Senate-passed permitting measure. Nor has Freedom Caucus Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, who has called for permitting generally to be a lame-duck priority but was another one of the holdouts on Westerman’s bill last year. Still, the Freedom Caucus is generally on board with permitting legislation and specifically cited it as a priority for the session's waning days.

Republicans are generally expected to support the bill, which enjoys backing from industry groups like the American Petroleum Institute, National Mining Association and Edison Electric Institute, which represents investor-owned utilities. The bill’s supporters go beyond the energy sector, including groups like the American Road and Transportation Builders Association and National Association of Home Builders.

And two Democrats — Golden and Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington, both members of the Blue Dog Coalition — have taken the rare step of crossing the aisle to support Republican rules this year in order to move legislation they support. Both have issued statements that speak favorably of the permitting bill.

Senate Environment and Public Works Chairman Shelley Moore Capito, one of the bill's lead authors, was enthusiastic about the bill's chances in the other chamber.

"I think there’s a real will there," the West Virginia Republican said Tuesday after presiding over a pro forma session. "We’ve got to get enough Republicans there to vote, and I think that’s what the speaker is hoping to do. I think he wants to do it under a rule, it sounds like, but I’m very excited about it because I think it’s very, very doable."

Divided Democrats

With the path through the House yet to be fully illuminated, a vote under suspension of the rules, which requires two-thirds of members present and voting to pass, remains an option. But that's a trickier path given the split among Democrats.

The Senate-passed bill emerged from that chamber in a weaker position than advocates anticipated earlier this month, when 73 senators backed advancing it on an initial procedural vote.

After opponents got through with the measure — including an amendments blockade by Oregon Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden that left backers unable to incorporate changes necessary to shore up support — there were just 62 "yes" votes, although there were four absent GOP supporters.

Just 15 out of 47 Democratic caucus members voted for it, including only one member of the Environment and Public Works panel — Rhode Island’s Sheldon Whitehouse, who wrote the bill with his GOP and Democratic counterparts on EPW and Energy and Natural Resources.

If there is full attendance on both sides, the threshold for passage on suspension would be about 290 votes. Permitting bill supporters would need about one-third of House Democrats to vote in favor — 71 with current vacancies — similar to their level of Senate Democratic support, assuming all Republicans were on board.

That doesn’t seem out of the question given that the leadership of the 112-member-strong New Democrat Coalition has expressed support led by the current chair, Brad Schneider of Illinois; the incoming chair, fellow Illinoisan Nikki Budzinski; and Scott Peters, D-Calif., chair of the coalition’s Environment, Climate and Clean Energy Working Group. So has the centrist Blue Dog Coalition.

Clean energy groups like the Solar Energy Industries Association and American Clean Power Association back the bill, as do key labor unions including the AFL-CIO, Laborers’ International Union of North America and International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers. The AFL-CIO sent a legislative alert on the bill, which indicates it may include the measure on its annual legislative scorecard.

But Rep. Jared Huffman, D-Calif., ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, is a firm “no” on the current bill. He offered a series of changes on Monday needed to win his support — which have negligible chance of acceptance by the bill’s authors or by Trump, who last week said the bill would put money “back in the pockets of hardworking Americans” and lead to “tremendous amounts of new building.”

Huffman wants to roll back proposed limits on Endangered Species Act reviews as well as the bill's 150-day limit on judicial challenges and “project certainty” protections intended to bar future administrations from revoking approved permits. Huffman said the certainty protection would legislate “a third term for Trump” by preventing future administrations from revoking permits for projects that could have detrimental environmental impacts, such as fossil fuel or mining projects.

Meanwhile, the official position of the nearly 100-member Congressional Progressive Caucus is opposed. And the House Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition said it couldn’t support the Senate bill without changes, arguing the measure “includes environmental rollbacks that are concerning to us.”

Two influential Democrats on energy and climate issues came out against the measure in its current form this week — Reps. Sean Casten of Illinois and Mike Levin of California, who are among the SEEC’s vice chairs. Casten and Levin have worked together on legislation intended to overhaul the transmission permitting system and address energy affordability.

In a statement Casten said the bill would make it “impossible” for a future administration “to undo the damage being done by the Trump Administration’s willful disregard of current environmental law and judicial precedent,” adding he would vote "no" on the Senate-passed bill “with confidence in our ability to craft a better version in the 120th Congress.”

Casten, who co-founded a clean energy startup before coming to Congress, is currently challenging House Financial Services ranking member Maxine Waters, D-Calif., for the gavel next year, in a bid resting in part on his environmental bona fides, including sustainable investment and climate-risk regulation.

Levin, an environmental lawyer by trade, praised the bill’s provisions making it easier to build interstate transmission lines, a key bottleneck barring the development of more wind and solar power generation.

“These grid reforms are real, and there’s no guarantee a better bill comes along that can actually become law soon,” Levin said in his statement. But he said it wasn’t worth the potential environmental costs, adding that “taking the current deal would mean giving up protections we may never win back in exchange for gains that aren’t guaranteed either.”

Major environmental advocacy groups like the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council have long been opposed to the measure, as have Native American tribes and representative organizations like the National Congress of American Indians.

Fate of manager’s package

Another factor affecting the debate in the House is how to handle a bipartisan package of Senate changes agreed to on both sides of the aisle, but blocked on the floor by Merkley, a staunch opponent of the bill.

That amendment included language making it more difficult to circumvent National Historic Preservation Act rules; giving landowners and state regulators more time to resolve disputes before eminent domain is invoked for transmission projects; and closing loopholes in the bill’s language aimed at making data center developers pay for their own electric-grid upgrades.

If that amendment had been included, the Senate vote count may have been higher. But attaching it in the House would send it back to the Senate for another round of votes, which may not be practical given the dwindling legislative session. An alternative would be to tuck the amendment into another must-pass bill, like government funding legislation or the National Defense Authorization Act.

The New Democrat Coalition’s statement, while overall supportive, said the group “will look for opportunities to negotiate changes that reflect environmental and Tribal concerns.”

Senate Indian Affairs Chairman Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, and ranking member Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, worked on changes in the amendment to address concerns tribes and Native American organizations raised about the NHPA section.

“I'm not going to abandon it just because the bill has been passed now. So working it on the House side, looking for other opportunities to advance it yet this Congress,” Murkowski said Nov. 20. “So we're not done.”

Capito told reporters Tuesday that the permitting bill's fate has been invading her dreams.

"My husband Charlie wakes me up, I’m like in sleep going ‘huh, huh, huh.’ He goes, ‘What’s wrong? What’s wrong?’ I said, ‘I’m just dreaming about permitting reform,'" Capito recalled. "That’s kind of a sad state of affairs. It was our 50th anniversary.”

Lauren Green, Jackie Wang and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

text:
Burlingame, Calif.-based Peak Energy, a developer of sodium-ion battery systems for grid-scale energy storage, has expanded its Series B financing to $157 million, adding $49 million to its previously announced $108 million round. The financing comprises $132 million in equity and a $25 million debt facility from HSBC. The original round was led by General Motors Ventures, with participation from Maverick Silicon, Florida’s Infinite Capital, Eclipse, Xora Innovation and LG Technology Ventures.

Founded in 2023, Peak Energy is led by co-founder and CEO Landon Mossburg. The company says its team includes professionals with previous experience at Tesla, Enovix, and Fluence, bringing backgrounds in battery technology, manufacturing, and energy storage deployment. Peak Energy is developing sodium-ion storage systems specifically for stationary grid applications rather than adapting battery technologies primarily designed for electric vehicles.

Built on the idea that electricity grids need something resembling a reservoir, which can store power when it is available and release it when demand rises, Peak Energy is developing sodium-ion battery systems designed to serve that role, using sodium rather than lithium to store and release electricity for large-scale applications.

Peak’s systems also use passive cooling, eliminating the need for conventional active cooling equipment. That design could make energy storage simpler to operate, much like an appliance that does not need a separate cooling system running constantly.

“Customers are telling us they need a lot more energy storage, and they need better options,” said Mossburg. Data centers are driving a new wave of electricity demand and Peak has been built not only to solve the economics of storage at scale, but also to build systems that are easier to live with, he added.

Mossburg is a battery industry executive whose career spans Tesla, Northvolt and Einride. At Tesla, Mossburg held leadership roles spanning vehicle connectivity, software engineering and supply chain automation. He subsequently spent five years at Northvolt, serving as chief automation officer and later president of North America, before becoming chief operating officer of autonomous and electric freight company Einride in 2022.

The financing comes as data centers consumed 192 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, representing 4.7% of national consumption, according to a report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The report projects usage could reach 649 TWh by 2030, or 11.8% of U.S. electricity consumption.

Separately, the North American Electric Reliability Corp. forecasts summer peak demand will increase by 224 gigawatts over the next decade, with AI data centers accounting for much of the projected growth.

Fleetzero and AET will unveil the AET Innovator, a plug-in hybrid-electric vessel, in New Orleans on December 1. The vessel is an existing diesel ship converted to hybrid-electric propulsion using Fleetzero technology.

Why it matters

The project brings new electric propulsion technology into one of AET's core businesses, which supports ship-to-ship lightering operations in the US Gulf. AET says the change is meant to improve performance, reduce emissions and strengthen customer value.

The vessel carries about 11MWh of lithium iron phosphate batteries in two former diesel fuel tanks, with an estimated 500 nautical mile all-electric range. Tank-to-wake emissions are forecast to fall about 82%, avoiding an estimated 1,220 tonnes annually, though these are projections not yet independently verified.

The players

AET

AET is a maritime operator that runs approximately 80 vessels globally and conducts ship-to-ship lightering operations in the US Gulf.

Fleetzero

Fleetzero is a company that supplies electric and hybrid propulsion systems for marine vessels, including the modular system used in the AET Innovator.

The details

Two former diesel fuel tanks were converted into battery rooms, and Fleetzero's modular propulsion system was factory-built and pre-commissioned to reduce installation time and vessel downtime. The vessel also incorporates autonomous-ready technology. AET operates approximately 80 vessels globally.

Timeline

December 1, 2026: AET Innovator unveiled in New Orleans.

The AET Innovator applies Fleetzero's factory-built modular propulsion system to a retrofitted diesel ship rather than a new build. It extends electrification from road vehicles into commercial marine operations that have historically relied on diesel.

description:

Frequently Asked Questions Who is suing Tesla over the Arlington test drive crash?
Ask for the gentlest acceleration mode, ask how regenerative braking is set, tell staff you are new to EVs, and start slowly in a quiet area.
text:
A 59-year-old Arlington woman wants Tesla to change how it hands over the keys. WTOP News reports calls for change after Alemzewd Lawgalet was seriously hurt test-driving a Tesla Model Y. She crashed it into a hair salon in Pentagon City/Crystal City on September 21, 2024. Her lawsuit says the car was set to Tesla’s “Insane” acceleration mode and that nobody explained what that meant.

The complaint seeks $10 million in compensatory damages plus $350,000 in punitive damages. Some outlets round the total to $10.3 million. It names Tesla and two representatives or agents. None of it has been tested in court, and several key facts remain unconfirmed, including which Tesla location handled the drive and who, if anyone, changed the vehicle’s settings.

The case lands in a news cycle already crowded with questions about how much drivers understand their Teslas. Our earlier look at Tesla’s senior FSD pitch and its 2,400 crashes with no age data raised a related problem: the gap between what the software can do and what a new user knows. This story sits in the hardware cluster because the heart of it is a control interface. A mode setting, a pedal map and a braking behavior decide what happens when a newcomer touches the accelerator for the first time.

·

Google · Preferred Sources

Don't miss new tech stories on Google

Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.

Add now

The Arlington Tesla Test Drive Crash: What Is Confirmed

The core facts are narrow but consistent across the outlets that covered the story. The vehicle was a Tesla Model Y. The location was Arlington, Virginia, and the crash ended at a salon in the Pentagon City/Crystal City area. The date was September 21, 2024. Lawgalet was 59, according to the lawsuit reporting, and she was seriously injured.

Local outlet ARLnow reported on September 23, 2024 that one person was seriously hurt after a car was driven into a salon in Pentagon City. That coverage came two days after the crash and predates the lawsuit by almost two years. It gives the incident a contemporaneous record that does not depend on the plaintiff’s version of events.

The injuries listed in the reporting are heavy. They include fractured vertebrae, a broken leg, a broken arm, a broken hand and a damaged section of bowel. Reports also say Arlington Fire and EMS took her to a hospital. Those details come from the complaint and the coverage of it, so they carry the weight of allegations in a legal filing rather than findings by a court.

Inside the Lawsuit: Claims, Damages and Defendants

Northern Virginia Magazine covered the suit on August 5, 2026, under a headline saying the car was left in “Insane Mode” during the test drive. Yahoo’s headline called it a $10 million lawsuit, and The Independent described the plaintiff as a federal employee. Taken together, the coverage paints a consistent picture of a single negligence-style claim with a large damages figure attached.

The money breaks into two parts. Lawgalet seeks $10 million in compensatory damages, which cover medical costs, lost income and pain. She also seeks $350,000 in punitive damages, which courts award to punish especially bad conduct. Add the two and you get $10.35 million, though several outlets describe the total as $10.3 million. We use the conservative rounded figure when quoting a total and the individual figures wherever possible.

The complaint reportedly characterizes the defendants’ conduct as reckless and willful, a framing that opens the door to punitive damages. That wording is the plaintiff’s characterization, not a ruling. Tesla had not issued a substantive public response in the reporting we reviewed, which is common at this stage of a civil case.

Who Is Actually Being Sued

The defendants are Tesla and two people described as representatives or agents. Their identities are not on the public record in the coverage we reviewed. The precise Tesla dealership or delivery location is also unconfirmed. That matters because liability in test-drive cases often turns on who employed the person in the passenger seat and what instructions they gave.

How Tesla’s Chill, Standard and Insane Modes Work

The lawsuit and the coverage name three acceleration settings: “Chill,” “Standard” and “Insane.” Per the reporting, Chill limits acceleration for a smoother, gentler drive. Standard delivers a normal level. Insane delivers the maximum acceleration the car makes immediately available. We have not published horsepower or 0-60 figures for the Model Y here because the reporting does not confirm any.

The point of the table is not the exact performance gap, which the sources do not give. It is that the same pedal travel can produce very different results depending on a setting buried in a touchscreen menu. A driver who has spent decades with a gasoline engine builds muscle memory around gradual power delivery. An electric motor delivers torque at once, and a performance setting sharpens that further.

The complaint’s central grievance is about disclosure. According to Jalopnik’s coverage of the filing, the suit alleges: “Defendants did not inform Plaintiff of the properties of varying acceleration modes prior to the test drive.” In other words, the claim is less about the car’s top performance and more about what the person handing over the car said, or failed to say.

Regenerative Braking: The Second Piece of the Complaint

The lawsuit says Lawgalet was also not adequately informed about regenerative braking. In an electric car, lifting off the accelerator makes the motor act as a generator, which slows the car and sends energy back to the battery. Many EVs let drivers choose how strong that effect feels. At the strongest setting, the car slows noticeably as soon as the foot eases up, which is why people call it one-pedal driving.

For an experienced EV owner this feels natural. For a newcomer it can feel like the car is fighting back. A driver who panics and lifts off may get an unexpected stop. A driver who tries to brake by pressing harder on the right pedal, a classic pedal misapplication, gets the opposite of what they want. The complaint’s two disclosure claims, acceleration mode and regeneration, point at the same underlying risk.

Reporting on the complaint says Lawgalet had never driven an electric vehicle before and that she told staff so. The same reporting says she was assured the car operated like a gasoline vehicle. We attribute that account to the complaint and the outlets that summarized it. It is her side of the story, and Tesla has not publicly answered it.

The question of what counts as an adequate briefing will matter. A short walkthrough that covers mode, regeneration and the touchscreen takes a few minutes. A longer one risks annoying a customer who wants to feel the car. The lawsuit effectively asks a court to decide where that line sits when the buyer is new to the technology.

What Remains Unconfirmed

Four points remain open, and we flag each one so readers do not mistake allegation for fact. First, the precise Tesla dealership or location is unconfirmed. Second, the names of the two representatives or agents are not public in the coverage we reviewed. Third, nobody has established whether dealership personnel changed the vehicle’s settings or whether the car was already in Insane mode when staff handed it over.

Fourth, and most important, no court has found Tesla legally liable. The headline reads like a verdict because the damages figure is large and the quotes are vivid, yet this is a filed complaint. Defendants in civil cases routinely dispute the facts, argue comparative fault, and move to dismiss. Readers should treat every causal statement in this story as the plaintiff’s allegation.

Nor has any report we reviewed shown that a regulator tied this specific crash to a vehicle defect. The research behind this article found no determination by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) on the Arlington crash. Absent that, the case rests on a disclosure theory rather than a defect theory, and the distinction shapes how it could play out.

Why Test Drives Are a Hardware Interface Problem

Hardware coverage usually starts with silicon and ends with benchmarks. This case starts at the other end of the chain, with the human interface to a very fast machine. A modern EV hides its most important performance and braking behavior behind software menus. Nothing about the pedal itself tells a driver whether the next press will produce a gentle push or a sharp lunge.

Defaults and Persistence

A setting that persists across drivers creates a hidden hazard. If a previous customer or employee selected a spirited mode, the next person in the seat inherits it. The lawsuit’s allegation that the car was set to Insane before Lawgalet started driving fits that pattern, though how the setting got there is exactly what remains unconfirmed. A safer design would reset to the mildest mode on every new driver profile or every new session.

The Briefing at the Curb

Tesla’s sales model leans on web booking and short handoffs. The research notes that Lawgalet arranged the drive through Tesla’s website. A web flow can ask a customer whether they have driven an EV before, then tell the staff to adjust the briefing. Whether Tesla’s process does that today is not something the sources confirm, so we frame it as a design question, not a finding.

Compare that with how performance EVs from established brands reach the road. In our report on the Porsche Boxster EV prototype drive and its sub-3-second claim, the pitch centers on performance numbers. Fast EVs are now ordinary, and the interface that governs them has not caught up with how new the typical driver is.

What the Plaintiff’s Attorney Says Should Change

The “calls for change” in the WTOP headline come from the plaintiff’s side, and they go beyond money. The attorney told reporters, in comments carried by WTOP News: “The big thing that we want out of Tesla, other than something that has to do with our client, is making sure that people understand.” The statement frames the case as a push for clearer customer education.

The attorney also pointed at the systems themselves. In another comment reported by WTOP, the attorney said: “We would love to see that change, see those systems change, especially for people who are newer to electric vehicles.” That second quote matters more for product design. It asks for changes to the software and the process, not only a settlement.

These quotes are advocacy by a party to the case, so readers should weigh them that way. They still show where the plaintiff wants the conversation to go. The goal is a sharper onboarding for new EV drivers, and it echoes broader worries we covered in Tesla’s 9x safer claim meeting seniors with unverified data.

Regulatory Context: NHTSA and Pedal Misapplication

Sudden-acceleration complaints are not new to Tesla or to the auto industry. NHTSA materials cited in our research say regenerative braking controlled through the accelerator pedal is common among electric vehicles and is not unique to Tesla. A separate NHTSA review of Tesla complaints found that available event data indicated pedal misapplication in the cases examined.

That history cuts both ways. Tesla can point to regulator findings that drivers pressed the wrong pedal in earlier complaints. The plaintiff can respond that pedal misapplication is exactly what happens when a new driver gets a car with unfamiliar behavior and no briefing. The lawsuit does not need to prove a defect. It needs to prove the defendants failed a duty of care when handing over the car.

Event data recorders could settle part of the factual dispute. Modern cars log pedal position, speed and braking in the seconds before a crash. Whether either side has released that data is not stated in the coverage we reviewed. If the logs show the pedal pinned to the floor, the debate shifts to why. If they show modest pedal input and a violent surge, the plaintiff’s account gains weight.

Competitive Comparison: First-Drive Handoffs Across Sellers

Every seller of fast cars faces the same problem, how to put a stranger behind the wheel safely. The table below is our analysis of the three common models, not a survey of specific brands, and it makes no claims about what any named company does today.

The lesson from the table is that safety does not depend on the model alone. It depends on whether the briefing happens and whether the car starts in a forgiving state. Tesla’s own vehicles sit across several of these categories, and its direction toward lean retail has been a theme in our coverage, including the report on a $11,800 Model 3 with 160,000 miles and a Supercharger lockout.

Historical Context: Fast EVs and First-Time Drivers

Performance modes have been part of Tesla’s identity for years. The names are the point. A mode called Insane signals to enthusiasts that the car will pin them to the seat, and the humor is part of the brand. That same humor looks different in a courtroom, where a plaintiff’s lawyer can argue the name itself shows the company knew the setting was extreme.

The industry’s shift to electric power changed the baseline. Gasoline cars build speed through revs and gear changes that give the driver cues. Electric cars deliver instant torque with almost no warning. NHTSA’s long-running look at Tesla sudden-acceleration complaints, which concluded that pedal misapplication showed up in the data examined, reflects how often confusion rather than a faulty part sits behind these events.

Tesla keeps pushing performance hardware to the edge, and the next product shows how far the envelope goes. Our report on the Tesla Roadster’s three trims and $50K to $250K deposits shows a company still selling acceleration as a headline feature. The more extreme the pitch, the more a briefing matters.

Market Impact: Dealers, Insurers and Brand Risk

One lawsuit will not move Tesla’s financials. The company has faced many complaints and the sources give no sign of a stock reaction, so we publish no price figures. The real impact is on process. A $10 million demand gives risk managers at every retailer a reason to review how they hand over fast EVs, and insurers who cover test-drive liability are likely to ask sharper questions.

The reputational angle is harder to quantify. Tesla’s marketing leans on speed and software, and a story that ties both to a seriously injured customer travels fast. WTOP, Yahoo, The Independent, Jalopnik and Northern Virginia Magazine all carried versions of it, which gives the case unusual reach for a single-plaintiff suit.

For the wider hardware market, the case adds weight to a design trend. Expect more attention to mode resets, startup defaults and on-screen prompts. Buyers comparing fast EVs on spec sheets may start asking a new question about how safely each one introduces a stranger to its power. You can follow related reporting in our hardware coverage hub.

The Legal Path: What Happens Next

Civil suits like this move slowly. Tesla and the two named representatives will answer the complaint, and they may file motions to dismiss or to narrow the claims. Discovery would follow if the case proceeds, forcing both sides to produce records of the booking, the vehicle’s settings, the vehicle data log and any internal guidance on test drives.

Defendants usually argue that the plaintiff bore some responsibility, that the car worked as designed, and that warnings were adequate. The plaintiff will counter with the briefing failure and the alleged assurance that the car behaved like a gasoline vehicle. A settlement before trial is common in cases with heavy injuries, but the sources give no hint either way and we will not guess.

Punitive damages carry a higher bar than compensatory damages. A court generally needs to see conduct that goes beyond ordinary negligence. The complaint’s language about recklessness and conscious disregard aims at that bar. Whether the evidence reaches it depends on records nobody outside the case has seen.

Five Predictions for the Case and the Industry

These are our analysis, not reporting, and each could prove wrong.

Tesla contests the facts. Expect a response that disputes who set the mode and what staff said, since both points are unconfirmed.

Discovery decides it. Vehicle data logs and booking records will carry more weight than any public statement.

Copycat claims follow. Plaintiffs in other test-drive injury cases will likely cite the same disclosure theory.

Retailers tighten briefings. Checklists that cover acceleration modes and regeneration become standard practice across the industry.

Software defaults get scrutiny. Automakers face pressure to reset performance settings between drivers.

What Drivers Can Do Before Any EV Test Drive

You do not need a lawsuit to take the lesson. Before you pull away in any electric car, spend two minutes on the basics. Ask the person with you to show the current acceleration setting and switch to the gentlest one. Ask how regenerative braking is set and how the car slows when you lift off.

Say plainly that you are new to EVs, and ask for a walkthrough.

Confirm the acceleration mode before you shift out of park.

Check the regenerative braking level and what it feels like.

Start in an empty lot or quiet street and press the pedal gently.

Keep your foot over the brake until you understand the car.

Those steps will not settle the Arlington case, and they put no blame on Lawgalet. They simply reflect the disclosure gap the lawsuit describes. If a seller cannot answer these questions, that tells you something too.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is suing Tesla over the Arlington test drive crash?

Alemzewd Lawgalet, 59, filed the suit against Tesla and two representatives or agents. She was seriously injured when the Tesla Model Y she was test-driving crashed into a salon in Pentagon City/Crystal City on September 21, 2024.

How much money does the lawsuit seek?

The complaint seeks $10 million in compensatory damages plus $350,000 in punitive damages. Some reports describe the total as $10.3 million.

What is Tesla’s Insane mode?

It is the highest of the three acceleration settings named in the complaint, alongside Chill and Standard. Reporting describes it as delivering the maximum acceleration immediately available.

Has a court found Tesla responsible?

No. The case is a filed complaint, and the allegations have not been tested. Whether Tesla bears legal liability is unconfirmed.

Did dealership staff change the car’s settings?

That is unconfirmed. The lawsuit says the car was in Insane mode and that she was not told about the modes, but the coverage does not establish who set it or when.

What injuries did Lawgalet suffer?

Reports list fractured vertebrae, a broken leg, arm and hand, and a damaged section of bowel.

What changes does the plaintiff’s attorney want?

The attorney told WTOP the aim is to make sure people understand how these systems work, and said they would like to see the systems change, especially for newer EV drivers.

How can I stay safe on my first EV test drive?

Ask for the gentlest acceleration mode, ask how regenerative braking is set, tell staff you are new to EVs, and start slowly in a quiet area.

title: High-Renewable Grids Can Produce More Power Than Demand Immediately Uses
description:

text:
As the U.S. expands its reliance on renewable energy, a considerable amount of excess electricity will be generated by solar and wind power plants. A new study explores how this energy could potentially be harnessed by certain technologies or production processes, reducing costs and increasing energy efficiency.

Researchers from MIT and Georgia Tech studied future situations in which the build-out of solar and wind farms has scaled up enough that 80 percent of the electricity supplied to customers in the U.S. is generated from renewable sources. They modeled systems with different mixtures of wind and solar power capacities.

They found that solar and wind farms could produce as much as 10 percent more power than the grid could immediately use or store in electricity systems that cost-effectively meet demand with 80 percent renewable energy. If not utilized, this excess electricity would go to waste.

This finding holds true even when the cost of energy-storage devices like batteries is low, and it remains largely consistent across the U.S. in many future scenarios.

The researchers' model reveals when excess electricity will likely be available. It shows that periods of excess will generally occur in the spring and fall and usually persist for several hours at a time.

This predictability presents an opportunity for some industrial processes that, with the right scheduling and capacity scaling strategy, could use this otherwise excess energy. Examples include raw materials grinding and even electrified steel production. The excess could also be tapped to help meet the growing electricity demands of data centers.

While it can be more challenging to run industrial processes intermittently than continuously, the predictability of potential excesses helps, the authors say. Additionally, strategies like designing less-capital-intensive machinery, or even sharing equipment across manufacturing sites, could also be useful.

"In this era where there is a need for additional electricity, where demands are growing to support data centers and other end users, we wanted to understand what this excess electricity will potentially look like so we can design processes to benefit from these excesses. Our work can help technology developers and other stakeholders plan for future infrastructure needs and start innovating toward these technologies now," says Jessika Trancik, a professor in the MIT Institute of Data Systems and Society (IDSS) and a senior author of this study.

She is joined on the paper by lead author Micah S. Ziegler, a former IDSS postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Georgia Tech; Aliza Khurram, a former IDSS postdoc now at the Toyota Research Institute; and Shannon Y.S. Hwang a PhD student in IDSS. The research appears today in Joule.

Examining Excess

Wind and solar energy are variable resources because they are dependent on weather. During periods when supply exceeds demand, operators often take measures to either store the excess or reduce energy production altogether.

But "another way to think about that curtailed energy is as an opportunity to use this excess electricity for some other processes," Trancik says.

"Excesses could instead be used productively in a range of processes including making materials and training AI models," Ziegler adds.

To help engineers design processes to utilize this resource, the MIT researchers modeled the dynamics, durations, and frequencies of excess energy events.

They used an energy systems model to study systems that combine wind, solar, and energy storage to meet different percentages of electricity demand in many future scenarios. The model can also simulate how these systems might operate hourly over decades.

They fed this model 40 years of data that captured weather extremes and fluctuations in wind and solar resources across the United States. They also incorporated technology-related factors, such as the cost of building different types of batteries or other kinds of energy storage, as well as electricity demand profiles for specific regions.

"All these costs are changing, so we wanted to study many different combinations of technologies to help people plan amid all this uncertainty about what the future power system is going to look like," Trancik says.

They designed the model to handle this enormous amount of data, while balancing the level of detail so the problem was computationally tractable.

In the end, the researchers found that significant amounts of excess energy would be generated in electricity systems that meet a significant portion of demand with renewable energy. Even when systems are designed to minimize the costs of delivering renewable energy, the amount of potentially excess power available would regularly double the amount used to meet demand.

"We found that considerable excess energy could be available even in systems with very low-cost storage, including at costs an order of magnitude lower than what battery storage costs today," Ziegler explains.

"There is a huge amount of renewable energy that might be wasted in these cost-optimal systems, and there is not as much sensitivity to location as one might have thought. This energy is broadly available across the U.S." Trancik says.

The model shows that the greatest potential periods of excess energy would occur in the spring, with smaller amounts of excess available in the mid- to late fall. These excess periods typically continue for seven to 12 hours, usually occur midday through the afternoon, and sometimes last for multiple days.

Leveraging Surplus Energy

Because these excess energy patterns are somewhat predictable, scientists and engineers could design processes to capitalize on this resource, Trancik says.

"In many of the scenarios, excess energy was often available for seven to 12 hours continuously, which suggests this duration could be a good target for technology developers and system planners when they design and schedule processes," Ziegler explains. "When the same characteristic is found consistently across a wide range of possible energy systems, it can be considered more robust to our uncertainty about the future."

For example, some industrial machinery, like electric arc furnaces in steel production or mills for grinding raw materials, could be switched on and operated during these times.

This electricity could also power equipment to manufacture products used seasonally, like fertilizer or concrete, which tend to be used more during spring, summer, and fall, and less during the winter. This coincides with several periods where more excess electricity is available. The energy could also power flexible computing, such as AI training processes that can be scheduled for times of day, or even months, when excesses are more likely available.

The researchers hope these results inform the development of technologies designed to utilize excess renewable energy, like periodic manufacturing processes that efficiently operate for a few hours at a time.

In the future, they plan to study the costs of developing infrastructure, equipment, and technologies that can benefit from these excesses.

"In many places today, we enjoy inexpensive electricity, but there could be more constraints on the system going forward. This excess renewable energy could be a resource that we might utilize to meet increasing demands," says Trancik.

"If we can develop cost-effective ways to use this excess energy, we could potentially reduce some costs of transitioning to low-carbon energy resources," Ziegler adds.

This research was funded by the MIT Climate Grand Challenges as part of the Weather and Climate Extremes project, and by the MIT Portugal Partnership Research Seed Fund Program, the MIT Technology and Policy Program, Georgia Tech, the MIT Energy Initiative, and the National Science Foundation (NSF).

text:
Waga Energy plans to build a renewable natural gas facility at Randolph Farms Landfill in Modoc that is expected to begin operating in early 2028.

Waga Energy signed an agreement with Randolph Farms Landfill and Best Way Disposal for the project, according to a community announcement. Randolph Farms and Best Way Disposal are part of The Balkema Companies, a family-owned group of businesses.

The Modoc facility will be the second project involving Waga Energy and The Balkema Companies. Their first, the Decatur Hills RNG Facility in Greensburg, was commissioned in August.

Under the agreement, Waga Energy will finance, build, own and operate the Randolph Farms facility for at least 20 years. Randolph Farms will manage the landfill gas collection system and assist with civil work. Waga Energy and Randolph Farms will share revenue from sales of renewable natural gas.

Facility could produce 407,000 MMBtu annually

The facility will use Waga Energy's patented WAGABOX technology to process up to 2,000 standard cubic feet per minute, or 3,200 cubic meters per hour, of raw biogas.

At full capacity, the facility is expected to produce up to 407,000 MMBtu, or 120 gigawatt-hours, of renewable natural gas annually, according to the announcement.

The WAGABOX unit will replace existing landfill gas upgrading technology at Randolph Farms, where renewable natural gas is already produced for Best Way Disposal's on-site fueling facility.

Renewable natural gas from the new facility will be delivered to a nearby interstate pipeline and distributed to natural gas markets, including transportation fueling.

Waga Energy estimates the facility will avoid about 31,700 tons of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions annually by replacing fossil natural gas, an amount the company says is equivalent to emissions from burning 2.8 million gallons of diesel. The estimate is based on a U.S. Environmental Protection Agency calculation methodology, according to the announcement.

Randolph Farms has many years of remaining disposal capacity, providing a long-term source of landfill gas for the project, according to the announcement.

Companies build on Greensburg partnership

Waga Energy's technology uses cryogenics to recover landfill gas and produce renewable natural gas that can be injected directly into gas grids regardless of the biogas composition, according to the announcement. The company said the technology is the result of 15 years of development.

“At Randolph Farms and Best Way, we're always looking for practical ways to improve our operations and manage costs,” said Jessica Routley, CEO of The Balkema Companies. “Landfill gas is a natural byproduct of our operations, and this project allows us to turn that resource into something valuable rather than letting it go to waste. We've had a successful partnership with Waga Energy at Decatur Hills, and we're pleased to build on that relationship at Randolph Farms.”

"This second facility strengthens our footprint in Indiana, where we are creating a true renewable energy hub," Waga CEO Guénaël Prince said.

text:
Chinese companies are accelerating global expansion through overseas manufacturing, strategic investments and international partnerships, reshaping industrial competition while adapting to geopolitical uncertainties and evolving market opportunities.

Chinese companies are entering a new phase of international expansion, increasingly establishing overseas manufacturing facilities, acquiring foreign businesses, developing regional supply chains and strengthening global brands. Across electric vehicles, battery technology, renewable energy, consumer electronics, chemicals and e-commerce, these businesses are reshaping international competition. Although overseas investment remains substantial, companies are adopting more selective strategies to navigate geopolitical tensions, trade restrictions and changing market conditions.

China's overseas investment has become an important component of its international economic strategy. Businesses are gradually moving beyond traditional export-based models towards overseas manufacturing, acquisitions, technology partnerships and local distribution operations. This transformation is particularly evident in electric vehicles, lithium-ion batteries, solar equipment, consumer electronics and industrial machinery, where manufacturers are seeking closer access to international customers, resources and regional supply chains.

China's outward direct investment reached US$174.38 billion in 2025, increasing 7.1% year-on-year. By the end of the year, Chinese investors had established more than 50,000 overseas enterprises across 190 countries and regions. These operations have expanded China's international commercial presence while supporting employment, infrastructure development and business partnerships in host economies.

However, developments during 2026 indicate a changing investment environment. China's outward direct investment reached US$128.6 billion during the first nine months of 2026, declining 0.2% year-on-year. Within this, non-financial outward investment decreased 8.8%, while financial investment increased 52%. This divergence suggests that Chinese companies are continuing their international expansion, but investment priorities, sectoral allocation and overseas strategies are evolving.

Major Macroeconomic Statistics Related to China's Global Expansion

GDP: Approximately US$19,600 billion in 2025, registering 5.0% economic growth.

Merchandise Exports: Approximately US$3,770 billion in 2025, reflecting China's strong manufacturing and export capabilities.

High-Tech Exports: Approximately US$731 billion in 2025, increasing 13.2% year-on-year, reflecting growing international demand for China's advanced technology products.

Belt and Road Trade: Approximately US$3,290 billion in 2025, demonstrating expanding commercial relationships with participating economies.

Why Chinese Companies Are Expanding Internationally

Several commercial and strategic factors are encouraging Chinese businesses to expand beyond their domestic market.

Access to new customers and revenue markets: Overseas expansion allows companies to reach customers in economies with growing demand for electric vehicles, consumer electronics, renewable energy systems, industrial equipment and affordable lifestyle products. International sales also help companies diversify revenue beyond domestic demand.

Local manufacturing and supply-chain development: Establishing factories closer to overseas customers can reduce logistics costs, improve delivery times and strengthen relationships with regional suppliers. It can also help companies meet local-content requirements and respond to import duties.

Technology and brand internationalisation: Chinese companies are increasingly competing through battery technology, electric mobility, solar equipment, digital platforms and consumer brands rather than relying only on low-cost manufacturing.

Strategic acquisitions and partnerships: Acquisitions, joint ventures and licensing agreements provide access to established distribution networks, technology, intellectual property and local market expertise. EY recorded US$43.6 billion in announced Chinese overseas M&A during 2025, nearly 40% higher than in 2024.

Geographic diversification: Companies are spreading their operations across Southeast Asia, Europe, Latin America, the Middle East and Africa. This enables them to access different consumer markets, industrial ecosystems and trade routes.

Top 15 Chinese Companies Expanding Internationally

BYD: BYD is strengthening its international automotive and battery business through overseas manufacturing facilities and regional partnerships. Its Thailand passenger-vehicle factory has an annual production capacity of 150,000 vehicles, while its Uzbekistan, Brazil and Hungary projects support its strategy of serving international markets through local production.

CATL: CATL is expanding its international footprint through battery manufacturing and energy-storage investments. Its German and Hungarian operations strengthen its European presence, while its proposed Spanish joint venture with Stellantis involves investment of up to €4.1 billion (US$4.50 billion). CATL reported 661 GWh of lithium-ion battery sales in 2025, reflecting its global manufacturing scale.

Geely: Geely is expanding through international automotive brands, technology partnerships and distribution networks. Its involvement in brands such as Volvo Cars and Lotus provides access to established international markets and premium customer segments. In 2025, Geely exported approximately 420,000 vehicles to 88 countries, supported by a network of more than 1,200 outlets.

Chery Automobile: Chery is strengthening its international position through vehicle exports, overseas dealerships and local manufacturing partnerships. Its expansion across the Middle East, Latin America, Southeast Asia and Europe demonstrates its focus on emerging automotive markets. In 2025, overseas markets generated RMB157.4 billion (US$23.61 billion), approximately 52.4% of its total revenue, highlighting the importance of international customers.

Great Wall Motor: Great Wall Motor is developing overseas manufacturing and distribution capabilities, particularly in Thailand and Brazil. Its international operations support regional production of SUVs, pickups and electric vehicles. Overseas sales reached 506,800 vehicles in 2025, increasing 11.6% year-on-year, while its sales network covered more than 170 countries and regions.

Sungrow: Sungrow is expanding its international renewable-energy business through solar inverter supplies, battery energy-storage systems and overseas project partnerships. Its international activities benefit from growing demand for utility-scale solar installations and grid-connected storage. Overseas markets contributed 60.54% of its total operating revenue in 2025, demonstrating the importance of international demand to its business.

Xiaomi: Xiaomi is strengthening its global presence through smartphones, consumer electronics, connected devices and electric vehicles. Its established international smartphone distribution network provides a platform for expanding its broader technology ecosystem. Overseas markets generated RMB151.1 billion (US$22.67 billion), or 33% of Xiaomi's total revenue in 2025, with Europe and India among its important markets.

Haier: Haier has developed a substantial international presence in home appliances through acquisitions, regional manufacturing facilities and established consumer brands. Its portfolio includes GE Appliances and Candy, allowing it to serve customers across North America, Europe and Asia. Overseas markets accounted for approximately RMB 155.8 billion, or approximately US$23.38 billion of its 2025 revenue, based on its reported geographical segments.

MINISO: MINISO is expanding its international lifestyle-retail business through shopping-centre stores, franchise partnerships and locally adapted product ranges. Its strategy focuses on affordable lifestyle products and high-volume retail operations. The company operated 8,151 MINISO stores worldwide as of December 2025, including 3,583 overseas stores, highlighting its extensive international retail network.

Pop Mart: Pop Mart is developing an international collectibles and entertainment business through overseas retail stores, intellectual property licensing and product collaborations. Its character-based collectibles have helped it build consumer demand beyond China. Overseas revenue reached RMB 16.27 billion in 2025, representing approximately 43.8% of total revenue, demonstrating the growing contribution of international markets.

ByteDance: ByteDance has established a major international digital-platform business through TikTok and related technology services. Its global operations generate opportunities in digital advertising, content distribution, e-commerce and creator-based marketing. Its 2025 overseas revenue was reported at approximately US$59.5 billion, reflecting the commercial scale of its international digital operations.

SHEIN: SHEIN is expanding its international fashion and e-commerce business through global logistics, digital retail platforms and supplier networks. Its demand-driven production model supports rapid product development and international distribution. Its 2025 revenue was estimated at approximately US$41.8 billion, illustrating its substantial international e-commerce presence.

PDD Holdings: PDD Holdings is expanding internationally through Temu, which connects overseas consumers with manufacturers and merchants through a cross-border e-commerce platform. Its model focuses on competitive pricing, digital marketing and international logistics. PDD Holdings reported total revenue of RMB431.8 billion (approximately US$61.8 billion) in 2025, reflecting the scale of its overall e-commerce operations.

SANY: SANY is strengthening its international industrial-equipment business through overseas sales offices, manufacturing facilities and after-sales service networks. Its construction machinery, mining equipment and industrial solutions serve infrastructure and industrial customers. International revenue reached approximately US$7.83 billion in 2025, accounting for 64% of total revenue, with products sold in more than 180 countries and regions.

Wanhua Chemical: Wanhua Chemical is expanding its international operations through production facilities, research capabilities and global distribution networks. Its polyurethane, petrochemical and advanced-materials businesses serve automotive, construction, electronics and industrial manufacturing customers. Overseas revenue reached approximately RMB 96.3 billion in 2025, representing nearly 47.6% of its reported regional business revenue and demonstrating its significant international market exposure.

Regional Expansion

Chinese companies are developing different expansion strategies according to local demand, manufacturing capabilities, trade conditions and regulatory environments.

Europe: The region remains a major destination for electric vehicles, batteries, renewable energy and advanced manufacturing. Chinese investment in Europe reached €16.8 billion in 2025, increasing 67% year-on-year. Hungary, Germany, Spain and France are attracting projects across automotive and battery supply chains. CATL's battery investments in Hungary and Spain demonstrate the importance of establishing production facilities closer to European customers.

Southeast Asia: Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam and Malaysia are emerging as important manufacturing bases for electric vehicles, electronics and batteries. In 2025, Southeast Asia accounted for more than half of Chinese automakers' overseas manufacturing footprint. BYD's Thai facility and manufacturing investments in Indonesia illustrate how companies are building regional production capacity to serve local and neighbouring markets.

Latin America: Brazil and Mexico offer opportunities in automotive manufacturing, renewable energy, mining, infrastructure and consumer products. BYD and Great Wall Motor are expanding vehicle production in Brazil, while Mexico provides access to regional manufacturing and distribution networks.

Middle East: Saudi Arabia and the UAE are attracting interest in electric mobility, solar energy, construction equipment, logistics and digital infrastructure. Industrial diversification programmes and infrastructure development create opportunities for long-term partnerships.

Africa: Chinese companies are expanding across mining, manufacturing, renewable energy and infrastructure. China-Africa trade reached a record US$348.05 billion in 2025, while solar panel imports from China increased 60%. Growing demand for mineral processing, agricultural machinery and local manufacturing offers significant long-term opportunities.

Overall, regional expansion enables Chinese businesses to reduce dependence on exports, improve market access and strengthen supply-chain resilience. However, local-content requirements, regulatory compliance and competition will determine the commercial success of these investments.

Competitive Implications for Global Industries

The international expansion of Chinese companies is reshaping global competition through large-scale manufacturing, competitive pricing, technological innovation and overseas production. In the automotive industry, BYD, Geely, Chery and Great Wall Motor are challenging established manufacturers through affordable electric vehicles, hybrid technology and expanding distribution networks. Chinese electric-car exports exceeded 2.5 million units in 2025, increasing competitive pressure across international markets. In batteries and renewable energy, CATL and other manufacturers are strengthening their global positions through production scale and supply-chain integration. China accounted for over 80% of global battery manufacturing capacity in 2025 and approximately 92% of global solar-cell manufacturing capacity.

Meanwhile, consumer brands such as MINISO and Pop Mart, alongside digital businesses such as SHEIN and PDD Holdings, are intensifying competition in retail and cross-border e-commerce. These developments are encouraging established international companies to accelerate automation, invest in research, diversify suppliers and strengthen local manufacturing. Overall, competitive advantage increasingly depends on cost efficiency, technological capabilities, supply-chain resilience and the ability to adapt products and operations to regional markets.

Challenges Affecting Chinese Companies' Global Expansion

Chinese multinational corporations face several challenges while expanding internationally. Trade restrictions and tariffs can increase costs and reduce product competitiveness, particularly in electric vehicles, batteries and solar equipment. Geopolitical and regulatory uncertainty may delay investments and restrict access to strategic industries. Supply-chain risks, including labour shortages, infrastructure limitations and logistics costs, can affect overseas operations. Additionally, brand perception and political scrutiny may create barriers in sensitive sectors such as telecommunications and digital technology. Addressing these challenges requires local partnerships, regulatory compliance, transparent operations and effective risk management.

Future Market Outlook

Chinese multinational corporations are expected to strengthen their international presence across manufacturing, technology, retail and infrastructure. Overseas expansion will increasingly focus on markets offering strong consumer demand, manufacturing advantages and reliable supply chains. text:
Reports related to this article:

Written by Paul Wiseman for, IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas)

Summary

Project Obsidian in Oregon will be the world's first commercial deployment of superhot (300°-500° C) enhanced geothermal systems (EGS), hoping to provide power by 2030

Power From the Ground Up

It's not often power contracts are signed for geothermal energy. Geothermal provider Quaise Energy has signed a power purchase agreement with Google for Quaise's 50 MW Obsidian Geothermal project in central Oregon. The plant is expected to begin providing power by late 2030.

Quaise says it will supply power to "Google's existing data center operations in The Dalles, Ore. and the region's communities." Starting with a 50 MW nameplate capacity, Quaise's plans for Obsidian include Phase Two reaching 250 MW, and Phase Three reaching 1GW. A company spokesperson said the latter two would come online "after 2030."

Plans are for excess generation capacity to be available to central Oregon's power grid, Quaise says.

At Least 30 Geothermal Projects Active the U.S.

Industrial Info Resources is tracking 30 U.S. geothermal projects including this one with a TIV of $5.88 billion. Of that, 21 involve power generation and 9 are for ground-source heat systems. With a total investment value (TIV) among Obsidian's three phases of $1.5 billion, it accounts for a significant amount of all tracked geothermal projects. But it is not the largest on the docket.

Four states account for 14 projects and $4.8 billion in TIV. They are, in order from high to low, Utah, Oregon, Idaho, and Nevada.

Regarding generation, 17 of the 21 are new builds, totaling about 1,395 MW of nameplate capacity.

Drilling Deeper

Phase one will use conventional drilling technology to reach one level of superhot rock (300°-500° C, or about 570°-930° F). Phase two is expected to be the first use of millimeter wave drilling. This is significant because traditional drill bits and machinery can't withstand the temperatures involved in superhot rock. Millimeter wave drilling uses surface-generated high-frequency electromagnetic waves instead.

Deeper drilling opens up more geographical options for geothermal, which currently is concentrated in the western U.S. Other companies are also perfecting their versions, and Quaise hopes to use this project as a springboard for the technology to expand.

Google's Power Funding

Over the last 15 years, Google has promoted the fact that it has signed more than 240 purchase agreements totaling almost 35GW of clean energy. Most of that (29GW) is in the U.S. The company also notes that it pays for 100% of power its data centers use, also covering the costs for the associated infrastructure.

Other Geothermal Growth

Another significant project--in fact, TIV-wise, slightly bigger than Obsidian--is the Cape Station Geothermal plant in Beaver County, Utah. TIV for its two phases is $1.6 billion, and its total power capacity is expected to be about 580 MW.

Third is Hell's Kitchen, California, with a total of $550M.

Nationwide Geothermal Status

According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), the U.S. had geothermal power plants in seven states, producing less than half of one percent (0.4% to be exact) of total utility-scale power generation. To be classified as a utility-scale power plant, a location must have at least 1,000 kilowatts (1 megawatt) of electricity generation capacity.

Other commercial geothermal uses include the aforementioned heating for buildings and greenhouses/agriculture, along with heat pumps. Geothermal heat pumps differ from more common versions in that instead of having an above-ground outdoor compressor and heat-exchanger coils, those coils are buried underground.

Because underground temperatures are steady, avoiding the seasonal hot-and-cold extremes of the air above them, they are considered more efficient year-round.

Significant Step

Quaise is not alone in developing EGS technology. Proponents hope that it will help geothermal generation as a sector become economically viable in a wider range of the U.S., beyond the Mountain West where hot rocks are closer to the surface.

Industrial Info's Assistant VP of Power Research Brock Ramey notes the sector's growth.

"Geothermal development has historically been limited by geographic availability, high investment costs, and lengthy development timelines. However, with growing electrical demand, advancements in drilling technology, continued federal tax incentives, and potential additional DOE funding, I expect investment to increase over the next five to six years."

He continued, "Efforts to streamline federal permitting could further support development. Geothermal's ability to provide reliable, around-the-clock generation also makes it a renewable resource with the potential to attract bipartisan support from Congress and the current administration. While development challenges remain, I believe geothermal will play a growing role in meeting the nation's future power generation needs."

Key Takeaways

Quaise's PPA with Google for geothermal power presents a new front in clean energy, the first commercial deployment of enhanced geothermal (EGS) technology.

As it becomes more economical, EGS could be a breakthrough for the sector.

Millimeter wave drilling uses surface-generated high-frequency electromagnetic waves to allow for deeper drilling, which opens up more geographical options for geothermal

Since 1983, IIR has provided comprehensive research, news and analysis on the industrial process, manufacturing and energy related industries. IIR's Global Market Intelligence (GMI) helps companies identify and pursue trends across multiple markets with access to real, qualified and validated plant and project opportunities. Across the world, IIR is tracking over 250,000 current and future projects worth $30.2 Trillion (USD).
