title: EVs More Common in Democrat-Governed States, by Daily Editorials | Creators Syndicate
description:
The freedom of movement has always been a central element of American freedom.
Not surprisingly, California beat all other states by a large margin for the percentage of its households that had at least one EV.
There also was a definite political pattern to the prevalence of possessing an EV: Households in Republican-governed states were less likely to have an EV; households in Democrat-governed states were more likely to have one.
Conversely, only four Republican-governed states ranked among the top 20 states (and the District of Columbia) for the percentage of households having an EV.
Limiting the movement of Americans is not consistent with the spirit of American freedom.
text:
The freedom of movement has always been a central element of American freedom.

It started with ships sailing across the Atlantic, bringing people to this open continent. Then, it blossomed as Americans moved westward on foot and horseback to settle in wilderness areas where they needed to depend on themselves for food and shelter.

Eventually, it continued in the private ownership of homes and automobiles, which are at the center of the modern American lifestyle, providing a place to live and a way to move freely.

But, unsurprisingly, there are politicians who would like to limit this freedom.

One of them is the current governor of California.

The Census Bureau last month published a table showing the percentage of households in each state in 2025 that had at least one electric vehicle.

Not surprisingly, California beat all other states by a large margin for the percentage of its households that had at least one EV. In this state, 13.8% of households had an EV. The second-ranking state was Washington, where 8.9% of households had an EV. The third-ranking state was Hawaii, where 8.5% of households had an EV.

There also was a definite political pattern to the prevalence of possessing an EV: Households in Republican-governed states were less likely to have an EV; households in Democrat-governed states were more likely to have one.

The nine states that had the lowest percentage of households with an EV all had Republican governors as of this November: North Dakota, where only 1.3% of households had an EV, Wyoming (1.6%), Louisiana (1.6%), Mississippi (1.8%), South Dakota (1.8%), West Virginia (2.0%), Arkansas (2.2%), Iowa (2.3%) and Alabama (2.3%).

The Democrat-governed state with the lowest percentage of households that had an EV was Kentucky (2.5%).

But 18 of the 20 states with the lowest percentage of households having an EV had Republican governors as of this November. Kansas, with 2.9% of households having an EV, was the only Democrat-governed state other than Kentucky that ranked in the bottom 20.

Conversely, only four Republican-governed states ranked among the top 20 states (and the District of Columbia) for the percentage of households having an EV. These four states were Nevada, which ranked fourth (8.2%); Vermont, which ranked fifth (7.7%); Utah, which ranked eighth (6.8%); and Florida, which ranked 13th (5.8%).

Why does California have such a large percentage of households with an EV when compared to other states?

In 2020, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, signed an executive order. "I, Gavin Newsom ... do hereby issue the following Order to pursue actions necessary to combat the climate crisis," it said. "It shall be a goal of the State that 100 percent of in-state sales of new passenger cars and trucks will be zero-emission by 2035."

Newsom's order went on to declare that state transportation agencies needed to focus on moving people into government-run mass transit and onto bicycles and walkways.

They should, he declared, "identify near term actions, and investment strategies, to improve clean transportation, sustainable freight and transit options" by "(b)uilding towards an integrated, statewide rail and transit network, consistent with the California State Rail Plan, to provide seamless, affordable multimodal travel options for all."

The order said agencies should also be "(s)upporting bicycle, pedestrian, and micro-mobility options, particularly in low-income and disadvantaged communities in the State, by incorporating safe and accessible infrastructure into projects where appropriate."

In June 2025, Newsom issued another executive order to advance his "zero-emission" vehicle agenda.

"I, Gavin Newsom ... do hereby issue the following Order to become effective immediately," it said. "The State of California reaffirms its commitment to accelerate the deployment of zero-emission technologies, including passenger, medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, consistent with the deployment targets and other actions directed in Executive Order N-79-20, to the extent consistent with State law and other legal requirements."

The effort to force Americans onto mass transit systems or sidewalks, or into EVs — which, according to the Department of Energy, "generally have a shorter range (per charge) than comparable conventional vehicles have (per tank of gas)" — is not consistent with the American way of life.

Limiting the movement of Americans is not consistent with the spirit of American freedom.

In the "The Significance of the Frontier in American History," as this writer has noted before, Frederick Jackson Turner argued that America's understanding of freedom was rooted in the freedom of movement that Americans had historically enjoyed.

"He would be a rash prophet who should assert that the expansive character of American life has now entirely ceased," Turner wrote in 1893. "Movement has been its dominant fact, and, unless this training has no effect upon people, the American energy will continue to demand a wider field for its exercise."

"This democratic society was not a disciplined army, where all must keep step and where the collective interests destroyed individual will and work," Turner wrote. "Rather it was a mobile mass of freely circulating atoms, each seeking its own place and finding play for its own powers and for its own original initiative. We cannot lay too much stress upon this point, for it was at the very heart of the whole American movement. The world was to be made a better world by the example of democracy in which there was freedom of the individual, in which there was the vitality and mobility productive of originality and variety."

Americans should not be forced into EVs and mass transit systems. They should be able to go where they want, when they want, how they want.

Input

2026-11-25 18:17:38

Updated

2026-11-25 18:17:38

China's automotive industry threatens South Korea with more than just electric vehicles. Hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles are another threat. China plans to increase its cumulative number of hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles, currently about 40,000, to 100,000 by 2030. Last year, China sold 7,797 hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles, surpassing South Korea's 6,802.

Hydrogen vehicles are a future automotive sector that South Korea is developing alongside electric vehicles. In September this year, South Korea became the first country in the world to surpass 50,000 hydrogen vehicles deployed. But China, which entered the field later than South Korea, is growing quickly. In September, Dongfeng Motor Corporation unveiled a 400-kW-class fuel-cell system for heavy-duty hydrogen trucks at the Hanover Motor Show in Germany. The system offers a range of up to 1,700 km on a single charge. Foton, a commercial vehicle maker under BAIC Group (BAIC), also unveiled a heavy-truck platform with a range of more than 1,000 km.

China's rapid growth in hydrogen vehicles is backed by full support from the Chinese government. Unlike South Korea, China focuses on commercial vehicles, and its government provided about 1.5 trillion won in support for the first pilot program, which ran from 2021 to 2025. With that funding, it deployed at least 25,000 hydrogen vehicles and built at least 250 refueling stations. It is reportedly planning incentives on a similar scale going forward.

With this support, China is expected to soon overtake South Korea in the number of hydrogen vehicles deployed and be the first to reach 100,000. Market research firm SNE Research forecast that China's annual hydrogen vehicle sales would surge to 933,000 in 2030.

Unlike China, our government's support is going in reverse. The Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment's budget for next year's hydrogen fuel-cell vehicle deployment program is 445.7 billion won, down 22.6% from this year. Local governments' worsening finances are also a problem. This year's national budget for hydrogen fuel-cell buses covers 1,800 vehicles, but 117 billion won remains unspent. The national subsidy for each hydrogen fuel-cell bus exceeds 200 million won, placing a heavy burden on local governments.

As the Ministry of Finance and Economy has effectively opposed a proposal to grant tax credits to electric vehicles produced and sold domestically, concerns are growing that the means of countering Chinese electric vehicles' offensive in the domestic market will be weakened.

At a tax subcommittee meeting of the National Assembly's Finance, Economy and Planning Committee held on the 24th, the government effectively opposed including electric vehicles among those eligible for the domestic production tax credit. The stated reason was that “determining the scope of eligible items and production costs could lead to substantial administrative inefficiencies, and there is a risk that the pool of eligible recipients could expand excessively.” The government also believes that domestically made electric vehicles are not significantly behind Chinese-made ones in price competitiveness. It therefore says there is no need for additional tax support for electric vehicles.

The industry sees it differently. It argues that the intensifying Chinese offensive makes this a critical moment for the competitiveness of South Korea's hydrogen industry. Industry players say the central government should secure stable funding and consistently pursue medium- and long-term deployment targets, rather than relying on local government budgets.

In trying to weigh institutional and legal issues and efficiency and ensure policies are free of flaws, the government invariably becomes cautious. This is the government's habitual attitude of trying to avoid taking any responsibility. The government should abandon this approach and show more initiative in pushing policies forward. Companies working on the ground understand market conditions better than the government does.

The government should listen to businesses and industry and make an effort to resolve the difficulties they face. If it ignores their concerns and fails to act, it will miss the critical window and soon see Chinese-made electric and hydrogen vehicles taking over our roads, as in Europe.

text:
One of the more frustrating bits of owning an electric vehicle is the downtime when it comes to charging. Unlike a traditional fuel-powered car, electric vehicles take a lot longer to “fuel up”. But scientists are working on a new battery technology, which might fully charge your EV by the time you go for a quick coffee run.

Researchers at Rice University have developed a new material that could bring four-minute EV charging a step closer to reality. The study figured out how to manufacture synthetic graphite, a critical component of lithium-ion batteries, in just 0.2 seconds. This method could also greatly reduce the energy consumption, emissions, and costs associated with producing the material.

According to Rice University’s announcement, the findings were published in the scientific journal Advanced Materials. This isn’t the first time we’ve seen such a claim, but the progress in battery tech/materials could soon make cleaner vehicles more viable.

A 0.2-second process that’s faster, cheaper, and somehow greener

Graphite is commonly used in the anodes of lithium-ion batteries, where lithium ions are stored during charging. The problem is that these ions can only move through the material so quickly, creating a bottleneck when manufacturers try to push charging speeds higher.

Conventionally, producing synthetic graphite also requires prolonged heating at extremely high temperatures, making manufacturing an expensive and energy-intensive process. The Rice University researchers found a new workaround to this. They mixed petroleum coke, a relatively inexpensive byproduct of oil refining, with a small amount of a nickel compound. Then they subjected the mixture to an intense electrical pulse, briefly heating it to approximately 2,500 degrees Celsius (4,532 degrees Fahrenheit).

Within two-tenths of a second, the carbon reorganized into highly ordered graphite. The nickel acted as a temporary scaffold, helping form a layered structure with slightly wider gaps between the carbon sheets. Those extra gaps allow lithium ions to move more easily during charging. Notably, the graphite retained its advantages even after researchers removed more than 99% of the residual nickel.

Four-minute charging, without sacrificing battery longevity?

When tested as a lithium-ion battery anode, the new graphite tolerated a charging rate equivalent to completing a charge in just four minutes. The researchers also reported that the material retained 80% of its capacity after 1,000 charge-and-discharge cycles, suggesting that its improved charging performance doesn’t necessarily come at the expense of durability.

This isn’t the only advantage, as the team estimates that its production method could reduce energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions by more than 80% compared with conventional graphite manufacturing. Its economic analysis also projects an approximately 80% reduction in production costs for premium fast-charging synthetic graphite.

It is also worth noting that the four-minute figure reflects laboratory charging-rate performance, rather than a full-sized EV battery undergoing a real-world charging session. Actual charging speeds depend on several additional factors, including battery design, temperature management, and the charging equipment as well.

The team will also need to demonstrate that its manufacturing process can be scaled commercially while maintaining the same material properties. But the results are promising, and there’s a lot of application even outside of EVs. For now, the research seems to offer solutions to the two major challenges that electric vehicles face.

text:
A group of over 160 climate scientists is urging the House to block the major bipartisan permitting reform bill from passage, warning that its entrenchment of fossil fuel infrastructure could likely prevent the U.S. from ever reaching net zero emissions, which would be disastrous for the climate.

In a letter published Tuesday, the scientists express “deep concern” that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), which passed the Senate on Friday, would drastically weaken key environmental laws like the National Environmental Protection Act (NEPA), while granting fossil fuel companies powerful tools to ensure its influence never wanes.

“BAAJA’s extensive changes to existing laws would make it almost impossible for a court to enjoin an action based on a violation of NEPA or of the National Historic Preservation Act, in effect pulling the teeth from these very important laws,” the letter says.

“Furthermore, we are concerned that BAAJA’s creation of the new ‘Disparate Treatment’ standard for energy permitting will prevent the rapid and nearly total phase out of coal, oil, and fossil gas from the U.S. and global energy systems. Without this phase out, and the subsequent reduction of emissions to (net) zero, the world will be unable to halt global heating,” the scientists wrote.

The letter effort was led by top climate scientists, including Michael Mann, of the University of Pennsylvania; Michael Oppenheimer, at Princeton University; and Robert Brulle and J. Timmons Roberts of Brown University, who have done critical research on the fossil fuel industry’s work to block action on the climate crisis.

The letter effort was necessary because “of the speed with which this deeply problematic bill seems headed toward passage without the due diligence and scrutiny any such far-reaching bill demands,” Mann told Truthout, “pushed through in the proverbial dark of night of the Thanksgiving holiday lull of a lame duck congressional session, and backed by a veritable who’s who of bad fossil fuel and dark money actors.”

The “disparate treatment” standard in the bill, the letter explains, empowers fossil fuel companies to file lawsuits to defang or overturn climate legislation. Under the standard, companies would be able to sue if they are being granted permits at a lower standard than in previous years, with the potential to reclaim up to 100 percent of projected construction costs plus damages and legal fees — footed by the American taxpayer.

At the same time, the bill would majorly hamstring federal agencies in their ability to revise or revoke rules and permits in the interest of public health or the climate, barring “immediate” harm.

Taken together, these provisions would prevent the U.S. from ever taking steps to meaningfully reduce its greenhouse gas emissions, they warn.

“As environmental law scholar David Bookbinder notes, this effectively insulates not only the construction but the operation at normal capacity of all existing fossil fuel infrastructure. Such a lock-in of extant fossil-fuel infrastructure would effectively prevent the U.S. from ever reaching (net) zero emissions,” the letter says.

The scientists also cite research finding that BAAJA would cause emissions to rise and contribute to air pollution-related mortality.

“[A]s written the bill would prevent the rapid and nearly total phase out of coal, oil, and fossil gas from the U.S. and global energy systems, which science says we must do if we’re going to halt global heating,” said Genevieve Guenther, founding director of End Climate Silence and organizer of the letter. The disparate treatment standard, Guenther said, “means that it effectively makes the current balance of energy sources permanent.”

“BAAJA is not progress. It is a step in the wrong direction, away from a (net) zero economy,” Guenther warned.

The climate concerns are the latest to be brought up against BAAJA, which opponents have warned would also help fast track data center construction and majorly sideline Tribal sovereignty. Critics have also noted several corruption concerns in relation to the bill, including former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema’s role in lobbying for the bill, and reports that a natural gas pipeline executive may have been involved in drafting the bill as the chief of staff for one of its key Senate backers.

Despite these concerns, 15 Democrats joined Republicans in voting for the bill’s passage in the Senate. This includes Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island), one of the top backers of the bill despite typically being known as one of the Senate’s top climate champions.

“It’s the very sort of thing he’s spent his whole career fighting, and it just doesn’t compute,” letter leader Mann said.

Mann said that Democrats should instead take advantage of their majority in the new Congress to pass climate legislation, including legislation to regulate data centers that they could force President Donald Trump and Republicans to oppose, exposing an unpopular view to the public.

“I hope that there are enough Democratic House members out there still listening to facts and reason that the bill — at least in its current form — can be blocked,” he said.

description:
Ensuring we meet that need is Colorado’s new Green Workforce Hubs.
Participants in these Green Workforce Hubs will receive career navigation, training support, employment connections and wraparound services to succeed in fields that are essential to our transition.
The Green Workforce Hubs will ensure we have people who are not only trained to fill those positions but excel in them.
More than 500 people have already been served by the Green Workforce Hubs.
These Green Workforce Hubs play an important role in that effort.
text:
Innovation, good jobs and a highly trained workforce have always been critical to Colorado’s success. In the coming years, our state will be at the forefront of the clean-energy transition and the unprecedented opportunities it presents. To fully capitalize on this generational moment, we need to educate, train and equip thousands of skilled workers with the tools they need to thrive in our future economy.

An analysis from the Colorado Energy Office projects a need for more than 13,000 additional full-time jobs by 2035. That includes an estimated 2,950 electricians, 2,140 automotive technicians and mechanics and 1,560 construction workers. To meet state and regional economic and environmental goals, we need a labor market that blends traditional trade skills with climate-focused innovation.

Ensuring we meet that need is Colorado’s new Green Workforce Hubs.

Recommended Stories

▶

Five new workforce centers specializing in green jobs launched recently to connect people to high-quality careers in the building decarbonization trades. These jobs help make homes and commercial buildings more energy-efficient, reduce their reliance on fossil fuels and lower greenhouse gas emissions.

Over the next three years, the Green Workforce Hubs — located in Aurora, Denver, Golden, Longmont and Westminster — will connect 3,800 job seekers in the metro region with training programs and employers. Blending traditional trade skills with climate-focused innovation, decarbonization trades offer career paths in construction, heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC), energy efficiency and weatherization.

Participants in these Green Workforce Hubs will receive career navigation, training support, employment connections and wraparound services to succeed in fields that are essential to our transition.

We will experience tremendous growth in the next few years for electricians, mechanics, plumbers, pipefitters, sheet metal workers, technicians and building inspectors. The Green Workforce Hubs will ensure we have people who are not only trained to fill those positions but excel in them. Job seekers can pursue training and certifications in HVAC, heat pump installation and service, electrical work, plumbing and pipefitting, sheet metal, building controls, weatherization, energy efficiency and building inspection.

A major priority in this effort is ensuring this transformation in our economy is a just transition. This program is designed to expand equitable access to good-paying jobs. Four out of the five hubs are located in federally-designated low-income communities so everyone — including our most vulnerable — can access training and careers that offer a path to stability and financial freedom.

Critical to this initiative are the Green Career Navigators who are there to support anyone interested in pursuing training or a job in the trades. These individuals are there for job seekers every step of the way, helping job seekers identify their goals, explore different career paths and connect with training providers and employers.

More than 500 people have already been served by the Green Workforce Hubs. Their personal stories are impactful. How these programs are helping give people a fresh start, find stability for themselves and their families and find a purpose that excites them for their future truly supports the economic incentive with real human impact.

To meet our ambitious climate goals, it will take more than investments in clean-energy technology and infrastructure. We need a skilled workforce that can turn those investments into action. Those are workers who are installing heat pumps, upgrading electrical systems and constructing and retrofitting buildings to be more energy efficient.

What is truly exciting about the acceleration of clean energy is the vast number of good-paying jobs it is creating. We are well on our way to meeting the demand for the jobs of tomorrow and ensuring Colorado’s economy is positioned to be a regional, national and global leader.

Gov.-elect Phil Weiser and I support a clean-energy transition that creates good-paying jobs, strengthens our skilled workforce and ensures that everyone in our state — regardless of their background or circumstances — has an opportunity to share in the economic benefits. These Green Workforce Hubs play an important role in that effort.

text:
▷ Minister Kim Sung-whan signs a decarbonization cooperation MOU and issues a joint statement with Australian Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen, while submitting a joint proposal to the UNFCCC Secretariat.

▷ (MOU) Strengthening cooperation on electrification, clean energy, and industrial decarbonization to support the implementation of the 2035 Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and achieve carbon neutrality by 2050.

▷ (Joint Statement) Outlining directions for Korea-Australia cooperation, including green industry collaboration and a Track 1.5 Dialogue.

▷ (Joint Submission) Sharing a model of bilateral cooperation with the international community to accelerate the implementation of the Paris Agreement.

The Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment (Minister Kim Sung-whan) will sign a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on Korea-Australia Joint Decarbonization Pathways with Australia's Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (Minister Chris Bowen), the COP31 Presidency, in Antalya, Türkiye, on the afternoon of November 17, where the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) is being held. The two countries will also issue a Joint Statement on Korea-Australia Bilateral Decarbonization Pathways.

In addition, the two countries will submit a joint submission to the UNFCCC Secretariat on the same day to share with the international community a model for bilateral cooperation in implementing the Paris Agreement.

The Korea-Australia decarbonization partnership, announced on the occasion of COP31, aims to strengthen cooperation in electrification, the transition to clean energy, and industrial decarbonization, thereby supporting both countries in achieving their 2035 Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and reaching carbon neutrality by 2050.

Through this partnership, the two countries seek to present an exemplary model of bilateral decarbonization cooperation that can accelerate the implementation of the Paris Agreement.

Korea and Australia have maintained close ties in the energy and resources sectors for many years and are key partners in these fields. Building on the Green Economy Partnership Agreement (GEPACE), signed in 2024, the two countries have continued to expand cooperation in clean energy industries and supply chains.

This partnership is particularly significant as it aligns with the direction of COP31, which seeks to translate declarations and commitments into concrete action, marking the 10th anniversary of the Paris Agreement's entry into force. Through cooperation with Australia, the COP31 Presidency, Korea aims to translate the two countries' climate targets into concrete industrial and energy policies, as well as technological and investment cooperation. By announcing the partnership during COP31, Korea also seeks to promote tangible climate action across the international community.

With its manufacturing-based industrial structure and strong capabilities in clean energy technologies, Korea complements Australia's abundant energy and natural resources and significant renewable energy potential. Building on these complementary strengths, the two countries will work together to identify practical solutions for industrial decarbonization while advancing the clean energy transition, strengthening energy security, and supporting economic growth.

The partnership will proceed along three main tracks: establishing a foundation for cooperation through the signing of an MOU on decarbonization pathways; setting out concrete directions for cooperation through a joint ministerial statement; and sharing a model for bilateral cooperation in implementing the Paris Agreement with the international community through a joint submission to the UNFCCC.

First, the two countries will sign the MOU on Joint Decarbonization Pathways to establish a concrete framework for cooperation on climate, energy, and industrial decarbonization.

Cooperation will cover six key areas: electrification and power grid development; technological cooperation and capacity-building; creating favorable conditions for investment in clean energy and industrial decarbonization; strengthening climate adaptation and resilience; supporting the implementation of national greenhouse gas reduction targets; and expanding the participation of civil society and young people.

The two countries plan to make use of existing ministerial-level consultation mechanisms and broaden participation by businesses and research institutions to strengthen both energy security and industrial competitiveness.

Second, the ministers of both countries will issue the Joint Statement on Korea-Australia Bilateral Decarbonization Pathways on the same day, outlining specific areas of cooperation and follow-up tasks based on the MOU.

The joint statement identifies key initiatives, including the development of green industry initiatives, research on clean energy supply chains and hydrogen certification to support the energy transition, and the establishment of a 1.5-track dialogue involving government and private-sector experts. Through these initiatives, the two countries will expand policy and technological cooperation to advance industrial decarbonization and the clean energy transition.

Third, the two countries will officially submit a Joint Submission on Bilateral Cooperation to Accelerate the Implementation of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) to the UNFCCC Secretariat. The submission aims to share an exemplary model of bilateral decarbonization cooperation with the international community and extend such cooperation to the multilateral negotiation process.

The joint submission outlines key areas of cooperation to support the implementation of both countries' 2035 NDCs, including electrification and power grid expansion, decarbonization technologies, and investment in clean energy and industrial decarbonization.

In particular, it presents bilateral cooperation as a practical way to translate national climate targets into concrete policy, technology, and investment partnerships. The two countries also plan to share their experiences in implementing NDCs and enhancing transparency, thereby contributing to the second Global Stocktake (GST2).

Meanwhile, a side event on Korea-Australia clean energy cooperation was held at the Australian Pavilion on November 16, where participants discussed opportunities for industrial collaboration in areas such as clean fuels.

In addition, in conjunction with the MOU signing ceremony, the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment will host two joint Korea-Australia side events at the Korean Pavilion in Antalya.

At the Global Climate Citizens Forum, to be held on November 17, the two countries will share with the international community the importance of inclusive climate action through the participation of diverse stakeholders, including young people, civil society, and climate-vulnerable countries.

Furthermore, a side event on industrial decarbonization, scheduled for November 18, will explore opportunities for decarbonizing industrial sectors, including low-carbon steel, as well as potential cooperation in technology and investment.

Minister Kim Sung-whan of the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment emphasized, "As we mark the 10th anniversary of the Paris Agreement's entry into force, the response to the climate crisis must go beyond declarations and lead to tangible changes across industries and the energy sector.“

He added, "This partnership will serve as an important opportunity for Korea and Australia to combine their respective strengths to advance industrial decarbonization, energy security, and economic growth together.“

"Building on this partnership, the Republic of Korea will expand its Korean Green Transformation (K-GX) initiative into a global green transformation in collaboration with the international community, and take a leading role in international cooperation with Australia to advance the effective implementation of the Paris Agreement," he said.

title: "Tax credits are a given, but 'subsidy regulations' should be learned from France"… What is ...
description:
In fact, analysis shows that among major countries worldwide, those where the penetration of Chinese-made electric vehicles has been limited have commonly had strong government-level regulations.
China's finished vehicle production system has a lower utilization rate of eco-friendly energy compared to Europe, Japan, and others.
First, unlike France, Germany and Spain did not implement separate policies that effectively excluded Chinese-made electric vehicles from subsidy eligibility.
The United States and India are also preventing the spread of Chinese-made electric vehicles through strengthened protectionist measures.
The U.S. imposes tariffs of up to 127.5% on Chinese-made electric vehicles, effectively blocking their entry into the local market.
text:
As an unprecedented crisis is expected to hit the domestic auto industry next year, voices demanding "strengthened policy responses" are rising within the industry. There are calls not only for the introduction of a domestic production tax credit that reduces taxes in proportion to domestic electric vehicle production, but also for considering various regulations to prevent the indiscriminate spread of Chinese-made electric vehicles. In fact, analysis shows that among major countries worldwide, those where the penetration of Chinese-made electric vehicles has been limited have commonly had strong government-level regulations.

France is a representative example. According to global market research firm Benchmark Mineral Intelligence (BMI), the new car market share of Chinese-made electric vehicles in France gradually decreased from 31.4% in 2023 and 16.4% in 2024 to 13.4% last year. Notably, while French electric vehicle new car sales increased by 9.6%, from 298,522 units in 2023 to 327,234 units in 2025, the share of Chinese-made vehicles dropped significantly.

The reasons for the decline in the market share of Chinese-made electric vehicles in France are cited as the French government's reform of its subsidy system and the imposition of tariffs by the European Union (EU). The French government strengthened the payment requirements for the electric vehicle purchase subsidy, "Bonus Ecologique," in December 2023. Specifically, it added "carbon emissions" at pre-operation stages such as electric vehicle production and transportation as a new criterion, in addition to existing evaluation factors for EV subsidies such as vehicle price and weight.

China's finished vehicle production system has a lower utilization rate of eco-friendly energy compared to Europe, Japan, and others. Additionally, electric vehicles produced in China must undergo long-distance transportation via ships, etc., to be sold in France, so they appear to have been significantly affected by these criteria.

The EU's imposition of tariffs of up to 45.3% on Chinese-made electric vehicles based on an anti-subsidy investigation also impacted the decline in market share. The EU applied countervailing duties in addition to the existing 10% basic tariff, depending on the scale of benefits from Chinese government subsidies: 45.3% for companies that did not cooperate with the investigation, such as SAIC Motor; 27.0% for BYD; and 28.8% for Geely Automobile.

However, even when EU tariffs were imposed similarly to France, changes in the market share of Chinese-made electric vehicles showed significant differences depending on detailed policy responses such as subsidies. First, unlike France, Germany and Spain did not implement separate policies that effectively excluded Chinese-made electric vehicles from subsidy eligibility. As a result, Germany's new car market share for Chinese-made electric vehicles decreased by only 2.2 percentage points (p), from 18.0% in 2023 to 15.8% in 2025. Spain's new car market share for Chinese-made electric vehicles rose by 6.3%p over the same period, from 29.6% to 35.9%.

The United States and India are also preventing the spread of Chinese-made electric vehicles through strengthened protectionist measures. The U.S. imposes tariffs of up to 127.5% on Chinese-made electric vehicles, effectively blocking their entry into the local market. India imposes a minimum basic tariff of 70% on imported automobiles and exceptionally applies a 15% tariff only if local investment conditions are met. As of 2025, the share of Chinese-made electric vehicles in the new car markets of the U.S. and India was merely 0.3% and 0.9%, respectively.

title: Korea EV Support Plan: Chinese Cars Hit 43.5% Share - shattered.io
description:
One idea is on the table: a tax credit for electric vehicles produced and sold in South Korea.
The Tax Credit Proposal: Produced and Sold in South Korea The proposal under discussion has two conditions packed into one phrase.
A vehicle would have to be produced in South Korea and sold in South Korea.
FAQ: South Korea’s EV Support Measures When will South Korea announce its EV support measures?
Tesla vehicles made at the company’s Shanghai plant were identified as contributing to Chinese-made EV sales in Korea.
text:
South Korea’s government will announce measures on November 26, 2026, to support the competitiveness of its electric-vehicle industry, according to the Finance Ministry, which told Reuters about the plan from Seoul. One idea is on the table: a tax credit for electric vehicles produced and sold in South Korea. The ministry added that no decision has been made on it, so the credit remains a proposal and not policy.

The pressure behind the plan is easy to measure. Chinese-made EVs took 43.5% of new passenger EV registrations in South Korea during the first nine months of 2026, according to the Korea Automobile & Mobility Association. Tesla cars built at the company’s Shanghai plant sit inside that Chinese-made total, a detail that complicates the usual picture of a simple domestic-versus-foreign contest. Our earlier report on Korea’s record car trade deficit with China covered the same Shanghai link from the trade-data side.

This analysis separates what Seoul has actually said from what commentators will inevitably add. The fact base is thin by design. We know the announcement date, the stated goal, one proposal under discussion and one market-share figure. We do not know the credit’s size, who qualifies, which models count, when it starts or what it costs. Everything past that point is analysis, and we label it that way.

·

Don't miss new tech stories on Google

Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.

Add now

What South Korea’s Finance Ministry Has Confirmed

Start with the narrow list of confirmed facts. The Finance Ministry told Reuters that the government will announce EV industry support measures on November 26, 2026. The stated purpose is to support the competitiveness of the country’s electric-vehicle industry. The ministry also named one proposal under discussion, a tax credit for EVs that are produced and sold in South Korea, and it said no decision had been made on that proposal.

That is the whole official record so far. No minister has been quoted by name in the reporting we can verify, and the ministry’s statements as summarized by Reuters do not describe a budget, a timeline for the credit or a list of eligible vehicles. Any headline that gives a won amount, a start date or a model list for the credit is running ahead of the facts.

The word support also carries a lot of weight. Governments use it for purchase subsidies, production tax breaks, research funding, charging-network spending and loan guarantees, and a single package can mix several of them. The ministry has confirmed that a package is coming and that a production-linked tax credit is one candidate. It has not confirmed that the credit will be in the final package, or that the package will contain only tax measures.

Why announce a day after the briefing? Governments often preview a policy date so that markets, automakers and suppliers can prepare. That is a normal pattern, not evidence about content. For readers tracking the story, the practical takeaway is simple: the real information arrives on November 26, and today’s coverage is a preview.

The Tax Credit Proposal: Produced and Sold in South Korea

The proposal under discussion has two conditions packed into one phrase. A vehicle would have to be produced in South Korea and sold in South Korea. Each condition does different work. The production condition rewards factories on Korean soil, while the sales condition keeps the benefit tied to the domestic market and stops it from turning into an export subsidy.

Under that wording, a car assembled abroad and shipped to Korean buyers would fall outside the credit, whatever the brand on the hood. That is the point of the design. It targets where a vehicle is built, not who owns the badge. A Chinese-built car and a Shanghai-built Tesla would sit on the same side of the line, and a Korean-built car from any maker would sit on the other.

Questions the ministry has not answered

The Finance Ministry’s summary leaves the practical details open. These are the gaps that will decide whether the credit changes buyer behavior:

The size of the credit, whether a flat amount or a percentage.

The eligibility threshold, including how much of a car must be made in Korea to count as produced there.

The vehicle list and any price cap.

The start date and the length of the program.

The budget and whether the credit replaces or stacks on top of existing incentives.

None of these items has been confirmed. We will not guess at them, because a guess dressed up as a number is the fastest way to mislead readers who plan a car purchase around the news.

Chinese-Made EVs Hold 43.5% of New Registrations

The anchor statistic comes from the Korea Automobile & Mobility Association. Chinese-made electric vehicles accounted for 43.5% of new passenger EV registrations in South Korea during the first nine months of 2026. Read the wording carefully. The figure covers passenger EVs, not all cars. It covers new registrations, not the cars already on the road. And it covers January through September, so it is a nine-month snapshot rather than a full-year result.

Still, 43.5% is large. More than four in every ten new passenger EVs registered in the country over those nine months were built in China. A share that size stops being a niche import story and becomes an industrial-policy problem. A government watching that number has to ask whether domestic plants, battery lines and parts suppliers can hold their ground.

The published data gives us no prior-year comparison, so we cannot say how fast the share rose or whether it is still climbing. That is a real limit on the analysis. A share that jumped from a low base in one year would imply a different policy urgency than one that crept up slowly. Seoul’s announcement may supply that context. Until it does, the honest framing is that the current level, by itself, is enough to explain why the Finance Ministry is acting.

One more caution. The statistic measures where cars are made, not what Korean consumers prefer or what they paid. It says nothing about prices, trims or battery sizes. Those details matter to buyers, and none of them are in the confirmed data.

Tesla’s Shanghai Plant Sits Inside the Chinese-Made Total

The reporting identifies Tesla vehicles made at the company’s Shanghai plant as contributing to Chinese-made EV sales in South Korea. That single detail changes how the debate reads. Chinese-made does not mean Chinese-owned. It means the car left a factory in China, and a US brand’s Shanghai output counts in the same bucket as a Chinese brand‘s cars.

For policy design, that matters a great deal. A tax credit keyed to Korean production would not discriminate by nationality of the automaker. It would discriminate by factory location. A Tesla built in Shanghai would lose out in the same way a Chinese-brand car would, and any automaker that chose to build in Korea could, in principle, qualify.

What the sources do not tell us is how much of the 43.5% comes from Tesla’s Shanghai cars and how much comes from Chinese brands. No split has been confirmed, and we will not estimate one. The only safe statement is that Tesla’s Shanghai output is part of the total and that the Korean government’s proposal, as described, would treat it by origin, not by badge.

That framing also explains why the story draws attention outside Korea. A production-linked credit puts pressure on any global automaker that serves Korea from a Chinese factory. Those companies face a choice between absorbing a price disadvantage, shifting production, or accepting a smaller share of Korean sales. The announcement will not settle that choice, but it will start the calculation.

Confirmed Versus Unconfirmed: A Fact Table

To keep the record clean, here is every claim in this story sorted by status and source. Treat the right-hand column as the test for anything you read elsewhere.

Three of the unconfirmed rows deserve a second look. The credit size, the eligibility threshold and the budget will determine whether this package is a symbolic gesture or a serious attempt to redirect the market. Each can swing the outcome far more than the headline proposal itself.

Why This Is a Hardware Story: Batteries, Packs and Chargers

An EV is a bundle of hardware. The battery pack, the motor, the inverter, the onboard charger and the thermal system make up most of the bill of materials, and each of those parts has its own supply chain. A tax credit that rewards production in Korea reaches past the final assembly line. It also puts a premium on suppliers that can deliver those parts close to the factory.

That is why the details of an eligibility threshold matter. If the rule asks only that a vehicle be assembled in Korea, then final assembly is enough. If the rule asks for a share of local content, the credit starts pulling battery cells, packs and power electronics toward Korean production as well. The published details confirm neither design, so both stay open.

Charging hardware belongs in the same conversation, though nothing confirms that the package includes it. Our earlier coverage of Hyundai’s slow charger due in Korea in 2027, with 7 kW and 11 kW versions and a Type 1 connector, shows that domestic charging products are already in the pipeline. Whether Seoul’s support measures extend to chargers is unknown, and we flag it as an open question and not as a prediction.

For readers who follow the hardware side of the car industry, our hardware coverage hub tracks the chips, batteries and devices that sit underneath stories like this one. The Korean announcement is a policy event, but its consequences land on component makers first.

How Other Markets Treat EV Origin and Incentives

South Korea is not the first government to tie EV support to where a car is made or sold. Our own reporting shows several markets using origin, content rules or import limits as policy levers right now. The table below pulls the headline figures from those reports, with sources named, so readers can compare the approaches side by side.

Two rows carry direct lessons for Seoul. First, the American example shows how sensitive demand can be to incentive design. When the federal credit expired, EV sales share halved from 12% to 6%, according to Cox Automotive. A credit can move a market in both directions, and removing or restructuring one can hurt volumes quickly.

Second, the European example shows how a content rule can reshape who benefits. We reported that EU EV incentives exclude Japan-made cars, with a 70% content rule cited. That case illustrates that eligibility thresholds do more than set a bar. They decide which automakers and which supply chains get access to the money, and they can create friction with trading partners.

Historical Context: From Buyer Incentives to Production Policy

Car manufacturing has long been a pillar of South Korea’s export economy, and EV policy there has traditionally focused on helping buyers switch to electric. A production-linked credit would point the policy in a different direction. Instead of asking how to make an EV cheaper for a household, it asks where the EV should be built.

That shift mirrors a wider pattern. As imported EVs gained share in several markets, governments moved from demand-side support toward measures that protect or attract local production. Europe’s hybrid import cap and its content-linked incentives, shown in the table above, belong to the same family. The US experience adds a warning about volatility when credits change.

We should be careful with the history. The published data for this story does not include earlier Korean incentive amounts, earlier registration shares or the timeline of when Chinese-made EVs first reached current volumes. So we cannot chart the trend with numbers. What we can say is that the 43.5% figure marks the point at which the Finance Ministry has put a production-linked credit on the discussion list.

The policy also arrives during a stretch of broader trade tension around vehicles and components. The EU’s move to cap Chinese hybrid imports from December 1 shows that Seoul is not acting in a vacuum. When one large market tightens, others watch for the diverted volume.

Who Gains and Who Loses if the Credit Passes

This section is analysis, not reporting. It applies the proposal as described by the Finance Ministry, a credit for EVs produced and sold in South Korea, to the groups most exposed. Every outcome below depends on details the ministry has not released.

Likely beneficiaries

Automakers that build EVs in Korea would gain the most, because their cars would qualify for a buyer-facing price advantage that imports could not match. Korean battery, motor and electronics suppliers would gain indirectly if the credit drives volume to local plants. Charging-hardware makers could benefit if the package widens, but that is unconfirmed.

Likely losers

Importers of China-built EVs face the clearest downside. That group includes Chinese brands and, because the reporting counts it inside the Chinese-made total, Tesla’s Shanghai-built cars. Buyers who prefer those models could see a relative price gap open against domestic cars. Importers could respond by cutting prices, trimming margins or shifting some production, and each response has a cost.

Consumers sit in the middle. A credit on domestic cars lowers prices for those models, but a narrower field of attractively priced imports can reduce choice. The net effect on a given household depends on the credit size and on how prices move, and the ministry has confirmed neither.

Trade and Legal Risk of a Production-Linked Credit

A credit tied to domestic production tends to attract trade scrutiny. Measures that favor locally made goods can conflict with commitments governments make to treat imports and domestic products alike. Nothing in the confirmed facts says Seoul has reached that stage, and the ministry has not said how it would structure the credit. Still, the proposal’s wording makes the question unavoidable.

The design details will decide the exposure. A credit open to any automaker that builds in Korea looks different from one that carves out specific origins. The first treats production location as the test. The second would target countries, and that invites a stronger reaction. The Finance Ministry’s description fits the first model, but the final text may differ.

Other governments are testing similar tools, and the reactions offer a preview. Our report on the EU’s cap on Chinese hybrid imports at 350,000 vehicles from December 1 shows a quantitative limit used as a safeguard. Korea’s proposal works through the tax code instead of a quota, which is gentler in form but aimed at a similar problem.

Market Impact for Buyers, Automakers and Suppliers

Because the credit is unfinalized, market impact so far is about expectations. Buyers who are close to purchasing an EV now face a timing question. If a credit for domestic cars is coming, waiting could pay off for those models, while buyers of imports might want to act before any gap opens. Dealers will watch the November 26 details closely for exactly this reason.

For automakers, the announcement sets planning assumptions. Companies that build in Korea gain visibility. Companies that import from China have to model a scenario where their price position weakens. The decision to localize production, to add a Korean assembly line or to source more parts locally, is a multiyear commitment, so a one-day announcement will not trigger immediate factory moves. It will, however, shape the next round of investment discussions.

Suppliers read the signal differently. A production-linked credit raises the value of nearby battery, motor and power-electronics capacity. Component makers that already sell into Korean assembly plants would see a stronger case for expansion, while those that depend on Chinese-built vehicle exports would see the opposite. For a broader view of how chips and components feed vehicle markets, see the reporting collected in our hardware section.

Public finances are the last piece. Any credit costs revenue, and the budget is unconfirmed. The scale of that cost will decide how long the program can run and whether lawmakers push back. Expect the budget line to draw as much scrutiny as the credit itself.

Competitive Comparison: Three Groups of Cars Under the Proposal

The proposal splits the Korean EV market into groups by where a car is built. The table below applies the Finance Ministry’s described condition, produced and sold in South Korea, to each group. It is an analytical reading of the proposal as stated, not a published eligibility list.

The table shows why Chinese-made price competition is the real target. Chinese-brand cars usually compete on price. Our comparison of the BYD Seal 06 and the Tesla Model 3 in China, at 109,900 versus 235,500 yuan, shows how wide that gap can be in the home market. Those are Chinese prices, not Korean ones, and Korean pricing is not confirmed. The comparison still shows the kind of advantage a domestic credit would aim to offset.

The last row in the table is the one to watch. A foreign brand that opens or expands production in Korea could move from the losing side to the winning side. That is the incentive structure the government may want, and it is a standard feature of production-linked policy.

Five Predictions for Korea’s EV Policy

These predictions are our analysis, not statements from any official or company. Each is conditional on facts the ministry has not yet released.

The package will go beyond a single tax credit. The ministry called its plan measures, plural, and a competitiveness package of this kind usually blends several tools. We expect at least one measure outside the credit.

The credit will key on production location, not brand. The described wording, produced and sold in Korea, points that way. A brand-based or country-based rule would be a larger departure and a larger trade risk.

The eligibility threshold will be the most debated detail. Whether it requires final assembly only or local content for batteries and parts will decide who benefits among suppliers.

Importers will respond with pricing or localization signals within weeks. Expect statements from brands that serve Korea from Chinese plants, though we cannot say which brands or what they will say.

The budget line will draw more scrutiny than the policy idea. Tax credits cost revenue, and lawmakers tend to press on cost once amounts appear.

If the announcement on November 26 contradicts any of these, the correction belongs to the facts, not to the forecast. We will update our coverage as the confirmed details arrive.

What to Watch on November 26

When the government speaks, check these points first. They separate a substantive package from a statement of intent:

Whether the tax credit is in the final package or was dropped.

The credit’s size and whether it is flat or percentage-based.

The local-production test and any content threshold.

Any language about specific countries of origin.

Reuters and the Finance Ministry are the primary channels for the announcement, and the Korea Automobile & Mobility Association is the reference for registration data. Treat figures from any other source with caution until they match those channels. The 43.5% share is the benchmark against which later data, including full-year registrations, will be judged.

FAQ: South Korea’s EV Support Measures

When will South Korea announce its EV support measures? The Finance Ministry told Reuters the government will announce them on November 26, 2026. The purpose is to support the competitiveness of the country’s EV industry.

What is the tax credit being discussed? It is a proposed tax credit for electric vehicles produced and sold in South Korea. The Finance Ministry said no decision has been made, so the credit is not final.

How large is the credit and who qualifies? Neither is confirmed. The amount, the eligibility threshold, the vehicle list, the start date and the budget have not been published, and any figure you see before the announcement is unverified.

How much of Korea’s EV market is Chinese-made? Chinese-made EVs accounted for 43.5% of new passenger EV registrations in South Korea during the first nine months of 2026, according to the Korea Automobile & Mobility Association.

Does Tesla count as a Chinese-made EV in Korea? Tesla vehicles made at the company’s Shanghai plant were identified as contributing to Chinese-made EV sales in Korea. The split between Tesla and Chinese brands inside the 43.5% share has not been confirmed.

Would the credit hurt Chinese-built cars? As described, a credit limited to cars produced in Korea would not apply to cars built in China, so those models would lose ground against eligible domestic cars. The final rules could change that, and prices are not confirmed.

text:
US biodiesel producers are bringing idle plants back into operation even as governors of Alabama and Louisiana have asked the federal government to ease biofuel blending requirements for 2027, raising uncertainty over future demand for renewable fuels, ResourceWise reported.

Alabama Governor Kay Ivey and Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry have asked the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to grant a partial waiver from the 2027 Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) volume requirements. They argue that the cost of complying with the mandates could increase fuel prices and cause serious economic harm in their states and across the southeastern United States.

If the EPA approves the request and reduces the 2027 requirements, refiners and fuel importers would need fewer compliance credits. This could weaken demand for biodiesel and renewable diesel at a time when producers are deciding whether to restart operations, increase output and purchase feedstock.

The RFS is a federal programme that sets annual targets for the use of renewable fuels in the US transport sector. The EPA converts these targets into percentage-based standards, which refiners and fuel importers use to calculate their individual Renewable Volume Obligations (RVOs) based on the volume of petrol and diesel they produce or import.

Companies meet these obligations by purchasing and retiring Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs), which are tradable credits generated by qualifying renewable fuels. Higher blending requirements generally increase demand for these credits and the fuels that generate them.

The EPA’s decision to increase the biomass-based diesel requirement for 2027 had provided a positive signal to biodiesel and renewable diesel producers by indicating that the market could absorb higher volumes.

However, the agency is also considering how to compensate for volumes removed from the programme through small refinery exemptions. In August, the EPA granted exemptions to small refineries for 2025, removing more renewable fuel obligations than initially projected.

In October, the agency proposed two options to make up for the shortfall: distributing the additional volume equally between 2026 and 2027, or assigning the entire volume to 2027. The decision will determine when refiners and importers will have to meet the additional credit requirements.

The governors’ petition seeks a waiver for fuel produced or consumed in Alabama and Louisiana, along with corresponding changes to the 2027 percentage standards. If the EPA reduces the national requirement, the move could offset some of the additional demand that the agency is considering restoring through the small refinery exemption reallocation.

To approve an economic hardship waiver, the EPA would have to determine that implementing the requirements would cause severe economic harm. The agency must also provide an opportunity for public comment before making its decision.

The impact of the biofuel requirements on retail fuel prices remains disputed. The governors argue that higher RIN compliance costs are passed on to consumers. The Renewable Fuels Association, however, has cited wholesale ethanol prices being lower than wholesale gasoline prices in opposing the state waiver requests.

The EPA’s decision on the waiver petition and its approach to reallocating exempted volumes will be important for the 2027 compliance market and demand prospects for US biodiesel and renewable diesel producers.

text:
The rapid expansion of electric vehicle (EV) adoption worldwide is creating a significant opportunity for the battery recycling industry. As automakers increase electric vehicle production and battery manufacturers expand manufacturing capacity, the need for sustainable battery disposal, material recovery, and circular supply chains is becoming increasingly important.

According to Cervicorn Consulting, the global EV battery recycling market was valued at USD 5.73 billion in 2025 and is projected to grow from USD 7.56 billion in 2026 to approximately USD 92.16 billion by 2035, registering a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 32% during 2026–2035.

The market’s expansion is being supported by rising demand for lithium, nickel, cobalt, and manganese, increasing volumes of end-of-life electric vehicle batteries, and stricter government regulations concerning battery waste management. Technological advancements in hydrometallurgical processing, direct recycling, and battery material recovery are further strengthening the industry’s growth prospects.

Battery Recycling Becomes Critical to the Global EV Supply Chain

Electric vehicle batteries contain valuable materials that can be recovered and reused in the production of new battery cells. Recycling helps reduce dependence on virgin mineral extraction, improves resource efficiency, and supports the development of a circular battery economy.

As the global EV fleet expands, battery manufacturers and recyclers are increasingly focusing on recovering high-value materials from manufacturing scrap, damaged batteries, and retired EV battery packs.

Lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese, and graphite are among the major materials targeted through recycling processes. Their recovery can help strengthen supply chain security while reducing the environmental impact associated with conventional mining and mineral processing.

Automotive OEMs, battery manufacturers, and recycling companies are also developing strategic partnerships to establish closed-loop recycling systems. These arrangements enable recovered materials to re-enter battery manufacturing, creating a more integrated and sustainable supply chain.

Advanced Recycling Technologies Transform Battery Material Recovery

Technological innovation is playing a major role in improving the efficiency, economics, and sustainability of EV battery recycling.

1. Hydrometallurgical Recycling

Hydrometallurgical recycling uses chemical solutions to extract valuable metals from used batteries. The process can achieve high recovery rates and produce materials with the purity required for battery manufacturing. Its relatively lower energy requirements compared with conventional high-temperature processing make it an important technology for the recycling industry.

2. Direct Battery Recycling

Direct recycling is gaining attention because it aims to preserve and restore the structure of battery cathode materials instead of completely breaking them down into individual metals. This approach can reduce material losses, energy consumption, and processing requirements.

The technology is particularly relevant for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, where recovering and restoring cathode functionality can improve recycling economics.

3. Pyrometallurgical Recycling

Pyrometallurgical recycling uses high-temperature processes to recover valuable metals from battery waste. It is an established recycling method, although energy consumption and the recovery of certain materials remain important considerations.

4. Mechanical Recycling

Mechanical recycling involves the physical dismantling, separation, crushing, and sorting of battery components. It is frequently used as an initial processing stage before advanced material recovery technologies are applied.

The development of automated dismantling, artificial intelligence based sorting, and digital battery tracking is expected to improve operational efficiency and worker safety.

Asia Pacific Dominates the EV Battery Recycling Market

Asia Pacific accounted for approximately 50% of global EV battery recycling market revenue in 2025, supported by its strong electric vehicle manufacturing ecosystem, battery production capacity, and growing investments in recycling infrastructure.

The regional market was valued at USD 2.87 billion in 2025 and is projected to exceed USD 46.08 billion by 2035.

China remains a major contributor due to its extensive EV production base, battery manufacturing capabilities, and regulatory focus on battery lifecycle management. The country’s battery recycling ecosystem is increasingly emphasizing traceability, material recovery, and integration between battery manufacturers and recyclers.

India is also emerging as an important market as electric mobility adoption increases and the country seeks to strengthen domestic access to critical battery materials.

India’s dependence on imported lithium, cobalt, nickel, and other battery minerals is creating opportunities for domestic recycling companies to recover valuable materials from manufacturing scrap and end-of-life batteries. Investments in hydrometallurgical processing, direct recycling, and battery-grade material refining can support the development of a stronger domestic battery supply chain.

North America Emerging as a High-Growth Recycling Market

North America is expected to experience significant growth during the forecast period, with the regional EV battery recycling market projected to increase from USD 1.09 billion in 2025 to approximately USD 17.51 billion by 2035.

The expansion of EV manufacturing, investments in battery gigafactories, government incentives, and increasing focus on domestic critical mineral supply chains are supporting regional growth.

The United States is witnessing growing collaboration between automotive manufacturers and battery recycling companies to establish closed-loop material recovery systems. Companies such as Redwood Materials, Li-Cycle, Cirba Solutions, and Ascend Elements are contributing to the development of the domestic battery recycling ecosystem.

These initiatives are intended to improve access to recovered lithium, nickel, cobalt, and other materials while reducing dependence on international mineral supply chains.

NMC and LFP Battery Chemistries Create Different Recycling Opportunities

By battery chemistry, lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC) accounted for approximately 40% of the EV battery recycling market in 2025.

NMC batteries contain valuable nickel and cobalt, making material recovery economically attractive. Their use in electric vehicles requiring higher energy density and longer driving ranges is supporting demand for specialized recycling processes.

Meanwhile, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries are expected to witness rapid growth in recycling demand. Their increasing adoption in electric passenger vehicles, commercial vehicles, and energy storage applications is creating a future stream of recyclable battery materials.

Although LFP batteries do not contain the same quantities of high-value nickel and cobalt as NMC batteries, improvements in direct recycling and material recovery technologies are expected to strengthen their recycling economics.

Manufacturing Scrap Creates Immediate Recycling Opportunities

Battery manufacturing scrap represented approximately 60% of the EV battery recycling market by battery source in 2025.

The rapid expansion of battery manufacturing facilities is generating substantial quantities of production waste, including defective cells, electrode materials, and other manufacturing residues.

Unlike end-of-life EV batteries, manufacturing scrap can often be collected and processed through more predictable supply chains. Its relatively consistent composition and availability make it an attractive source of recyclable materials.

However, end-of-life EV batteries are expected to become an increasingly important growth segment as the number of electric vehicles reaching retirement increases over the coming years.

Second-Life Batteries Open New Business Opportunities

Battery recycling is not limited to recovering raw materials. Retired EV batteries can also create value through second-life applications.

Many EV batteries retain approximately 70%–80% of their original capacity when removed from vehicles, depending on their age, usage patterns, chemistry, and operating conditions.

After appropriate testing, grading, and safety assessment, these batteries may be repurposed for stationary energy storage applications, including renewable energy integration, commercial backup power, and grid-support systems.

Second-life battery applications can extend battery utilization before final material recovery, improving resource efficiency and creating additional business opportunities for battery manufacturers, energy storage developers, and recycling companies.

Regulatory Developments Strengthen the Battery Circular Economy

Government regulations are becoming an important driver of the global EV battery recycling market.

The European Union’s Battery Regulation establishes requirements relating to battery sustainability, collection, recycling efficiency, material recovery, and recycled content.

In India, the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, provide an extended producer responsibility framework for battery manufacturers and producers, supporting organized collection, recycling, and environmentally responsible battery disposal.

China is also strengthening battery lifecycle management and traceability requirements to improve the collection and recovery of used EV batteries.

These regulatory developments are encouraging automotive OEMs, battery manufacturers, and recycling companies to invest in compliant recycling infrastructure and sustainable material recovery technologies.

Leading Companies Strengthen Their Competitive Positions

The global EV battery recycling industry includes battery manufacturers, material technology companies, specialist recyclers, and resource recovery businesses.

Some of the prominent companies operating in the market include:

CATL

GEM Co., Ltd.

Umicore

Li-Cycle Corp.

Glencore

Attero Recycling

Redwood Materials

Cirba Solutions

Ecobat

LOHUM

These companies are focusing on recycling capacity expansion, advanced material recovery technologies, strategic partnerships, and closed-loop battery supply chains.

Competition is increasingly shaped by recovery efficiency, processing costs, access to battery feedstock, recovered material quality, and long-term agreements with automotive and battery manufacturers.

Challenges That Could Influence Market Expansion

Despite strong growth prospects, the EV battery recycling industry faces several operational and economic challenges.

The high capital investment required to establish advanced recycling facilities can limit market entry for smaller companies. Recycling economics are also influenced by fluctuations in lithium, nickel, and cobalt prices, which affect the commercial value of recovered materials.

Battery pack designs, cell formats, and chemistries vary across manufacturers, making automated dismantling and standardized recycling processes difficult.

Additionally, damaged or improperly handled lithium-ion batteries can create thermal runaway and fire risks during transportation, storage, and processing. Companies must therefore invest in specialized safety systems, battery discharge technologies, and trained personnel.

Outlook: Building a Circular and Sustainable EV Battery Ecosystem

The EV battery recycling market is expected to become an increasingly important part of the global electric mobility value chain. Rising EV adoption, expanding battery manufacturing capacity, growing demand for critical minerals, and stricter environmental regulations will create long-term opportunities for recycling technology developers and material recovery companies.

Advancements in direct recycling, hydrometallurgical processing, automated battery dismantling, and second-life battery applications are expected to reshape the competitive landscape.

For automotive OEMs, battery manufacturers, investors, and recycling companies, developing reliable access to recyclable battery materials and establishing closed-loop supply chains will become essential to long-term competitiveness.
